6e50061af268.t: What changed in A.A. between 1939 and 1950? | Recovery Starts

af01ddfa04c5.t: A.A. grew from about 100 members in 1939 to about 8,000 by the end of 1941, and Dr. Bob put it at about 70,000 in late 1948.

484f58784f5a.t: What changed in A.A. between 1939 and 1950?

9d03de504c29.t: <0>Home</0> › <1>A.A. questions, from the books</1> › How A.A. began

b35564483a17.t: The message started travelling by book, mail and travelling members instead of only face to face, and a small New York office grew up to answer letters and help new groups.

da3a22b9dbbe.t: Fast growth brought quarrels over membership, money, leadership and publicity. Out of that experience came the Twelve Traditions, first published in 1946 and confirmed by the fellowship at Cleveland in 1950.

b47b40d5edfc.t: Leadership began to pass from the founders to the fellowship itself, and in 1950 the trustees authorized Bill and Dr. Bob to plan a General Service Conference, which first met in 1951. Dr. Bob died in November 1950.

6f1ce0be5fbe.t: The main account: Foreword to the Second Edition (1955)

1d1476560214.t: The 1955 foreword gives the story of these years in about two pages (pp. xvii–xix):

e38604c0f96e.t: <0>The book and the name.</0> The book came out in the spring of 1939, and the nameless fellowship "now began to be called Alcoholics Anonymous, from the title of its own book" (p. xvii).

88fc12c73f01.t: <0>Publicity and the mail.</0> A <1>Liberty</1> magazine article in the fall of 1939 brought 800 inquiries to the small New York office; each was answered, members travelling on business were sent to the prospects, and new groups started (p. xviii). Everyone was surprised to find that "A.A.'s message could be transmitted in the mail as well as by word of mouth" (p. xviii). John D. Rockefeller, Jr.'s dinner for A.A. in 1940 brought more inquiries, and membership reached 2,000 by March 1941 (p. xviii). Then Jack Alexander's <2>Saturday Evening Post</2> article, and "By the close of 1941, A.A. numbered 8,000 members." (p. xviii). "A.A. had become a national institution." (p. xviii).

90815e817a78.t: <0>Growing pains.</0> The foreword calls what followed an adolescent period. Could so many erratic alcoholics work together? "Would there be quarrels over membership, leadership, and money?" (p. xviii). Those problems came, in every group (p. xix). The conviction grew that "A.A.'s had to hang together or die separately" (p. xix).

00d45211b246.t: <0>The Traditions.</0> Just as members had found principles to live by, they had to find principles by which groups and A.A. as a whole could survive (p. xix). The foreword lists them in plain words: no alcoholic excluded, leaders who "might serve but never govern" (p. xix), autonomous groups, no professional class, no fees or dues, the least possible organization, attraction rather than promotion, anonymity in the media, and no endorsements, alliances or public controversy (p. xix). It adds that "none of these principles had the force of rules or laws" (p. xix), but by 1950 they were so widely accepted that the first International Conference at Cleveland confirmed them (p. xix).

7dfe7a23461a.t: Details from Bill W.'s later accounts

b4af40786983.t: <0>P-44, <1>A.A.'s Legacy of Service</1></0> (text through 1955; pamphlet © 2018): - The Rockefeller dinner was held early in February 1940. His son, speaking for him, said A.A. would need little or no money, and Rockefeller gave $1,000; Bill later saw that this saved A.A. from property management and professionalism (P-44). - A two-room office opened on Vesey Street in New York; book sales paid for it through 1940, and every letter got a personal reply (P-44). Lists of prospects went to travelling members, who started more groups (P-44). - The <2>Post</2> article ran March 1, 1941; six thousand appeals followed, and the groups were asked for the first time to help pay for the office (P-44). The year began with 2,000 members and ended with 8,000 (P-44). - From the office's mail and public-relations problems came the basic ideas of the Traditions. "The Traditions of Alcoholics Anonymous that resulted were first published in the so-called long form in the Grapevine of April 1946." (P-44). At first "Only groups in dire trouble took them seriously." (P-44). Five years later, at Cleveland in 1950, several thousand members declared them A.A.'s platform (P-44). - The founders and a few trustees ran A.A.'s overall services until 1950, and "Since we oldtimers couldn't live on forever" (P-44), a conference representing the members was needed. With Dr. Bob mortally ill, the trustees in 1950 authorized Bill and Dr. Bob to draw up the plan; the first Conference met in April 1951 (P-44).

dab911ac593c.t: <0><1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957):</0> - The New York members had parted from the Oxford Groups in 1937, and the Akron members withdrew later, after the book came out (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). - The Grapevine began in 1944 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); Bill's 1969 talk in P-53 gives the same year (P-53). - The long-form Traditions of 1946 were cut down to the short form starting around 1947, at the suggestion of Earl T. of Chicago, and the Grapevine printed them in every issue (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). P-43 (1971) also says the 1946 long form had been condensed by 1950 (P-43).

d3992b36de85.t: <0>Bill W., 1969</0> (talk printed in P-53): the oldtimers had run things, but as the troubles grew they began to be taught by the movement: "So, instead of being a teacher for A.A. any more, I, in particular, became a pupil of the Fellowship." (P-53).

9fc6122ffc46.t: <0>Dr. Bob, December 1948</0> (talk printed in P-53): membership was "conservatively estimated at 70,000" (P-53), and he named what would keep it growing: no entangling alliances, no controversial issues, unity, simplicity, and the job of getting sober and helping others (P-53).

c04816e9ccab.t: <0>When A.A. reached 2,000.</0> The 1955 foreword says by March 1941 (p. xviii). P-44 says about 2,000 at the end of 1940 (P-44), and Bill's 1969 talk says "By 1940" (P-53). These are close but not the same.

b687682359b8.t: <0>The Rockefeller dinner.</0> The foreword says the spring of 1940 (p. xviii); P-44 says early February 1940 (P-44).

1b0bd3055607.t: Is A.A. for people addicted to drugs or other things? | Recovery Starts

4e5f33ef37ca.t: A.A.'s own literature describes A.A. as a fellowship of alcoholics. The 1946 Long Form says A.A.'s membership "ought to include all who suffer from…

2db17962bbd3.t: Is A.A. for people addicted to drugs or other things?

e070e237b6b2.t: <0>Home</0> › <1>A.A. questions, from the books</1> › Who A.A. is for, and what it is not

e61d05cbfd6f.t: A.A.'s own literature describes A.A. as a fellowship of alcoholics. The 1946 Long Form says A.A.'s membership "ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism" (p. 563). The 1939 Foreword and the later short form of Tradition Three give one requirement, a desire to stop drinking (pp. xiv, 562).

cec3ed634047.t: An alcoholic with other problems is not shut out. In 1946 Bill W. wrote that if alcohol is an uncontrollable problem to a newcomer and he wants to do something about it, A.A. doesn't care "whether he has other complications or not" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). P-43 (© 1971; this printing updated 2023) names drugs directly: Tradition Three makes no demand that members have no history of drug abuse.

a02fa9beac39.t: What A.A.'s literature does not claim is to know how to treat drug addiction. In 1957 Bill listed carrying A.A. into "dope addiction" among the early dreams that taught A.A. it could not be all things to all men, and today's group pamphlet calls it "misleading" to suggest that A.A. "knows what to do about drug addiction" (P-16, 2018).

9c0b56fd640d.t: The 1939 text never speaks to someone whose problem is drugs and not alcohol. The A.A. pamphlet on that subject ("Problems Other Than Alcohol") is not in our sources, so this page doesn't report what it says.

313097ba3eaf.t: The book is about alcohol. The Foreword to the First Edition gives one requirement for membership, "an honest desire to stop drinking" (p. xiv), and the program chapters are addressed to the alcoholic throughout.

1bfc5f1aaf13.t: Other drugs come up as part of the drinker's decline. The "real alcoholic" of Chapter 2 starts using "a combination of high-powered sedative and liquor" to get to work, and a doctor may give him "morphine or some sedative with which to taper off" (p. 22). Bill describes drinking "both gin and sedative" (p. 7).

a418f832b08c.t: Two hospitals in the book treated both. Dr. Silkworth, who wrote "The Doctor's Opinion," directed a hospital "treating alcoholic and drug addiction" (p. xxvii), and Chapter 11 thanks an eastern hospital "for the treatment of alcoholic and drug addiction" (p. 162), whose doctor suggested A.A. to some of his patients. Those passages describe the hospitals. What the doctor writes about, and what Chapter 11 says members went there to do, concerns alcoholics.

7846f4afa678.t: Nothing in pages 1–164 says what a person addicted only to some other drug should do.

aa0e5248c12d.t: The 1946 Long Form and Bill's essay

d291040b1108.t: Tradition Three: "Our membership ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism." (p. 563). A.A. "may refuse none who wish to recover" (p. 563).

550a847af5c8.t: Tradition Five: each group's one primary purpose is carrying its message "to the alcoholic who still suffers" (p. 564).

d7d9ed9920f1.t: Bill's 1946 essay, which Tradition Three grew out of, is wide open about what else a member may be dealing with. Most early members, he wrote, would have been thrown out under the old membership rules, some "because they had mental as well as alcoholic difficulties" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). His conclusion: if alcohol is an uncontrollable problem to a newcomer and he wants to do something about it, "that is enough for us" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946), whatever other complications he has.

9fb0a7163ec3.t: <0>1957.</0> In <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> Bill recalls the early fear of the newcomer with "Complications, you know; alcohol mixed with other things" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957), and how A.A. got over it. In the same book, explaining Traditions Five and Six, he lists the dreams of the early years: hospitals, public education, law reform, and "We would carry A.A. into the dark regions of dope addiction and criminality." (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957). Experience ended those plans: "We of Alcoholics Anonymous could not be all things to all men, and we should not try to be." (<4>A.A. Comes of Age</4>, 1957). He then notes that groups dealing with gambling, delinquency, dope addiction and other problems borrowed from A.A., "but they made their own adaptations" (<5>A.A. Comes of Age</5>, 1957).

0282802563fa.t: <0>1971 (this printing updated 2023).</0> <1>The Twelve Traditions Illustrated</1> (P-43) says Tradition Three makes no demand that prospective members have no history of drug abuse: "All alcoholics are welcome." (P-43).

f9e42bb2cc7b.t: <0>2018.</0> <1>The A.A. Group</1> (P-16) says the General Service Conference has recommended that "alcohol and pill" meetings not be listed in A.A. directories. Its reason: "Experience with alcohol is one thing all A.A. members have in common." (P-16, 2018). And: "It is misleading to hint or give the impression that A.A. solves other problems or knows what to do about drug addiction." (P-16, 2018). The same pamphlet says open meetings are available "to anyone interested in Alcoholics Anonymous' program of recovery from alcoholism" (P-16, 2018), with nonalcoholics attending as observers.

7be5279aefc2.t: Read together, the texts say that A.A. is for alcoholics, that an alcoholic's other problems don't bar him, and that A.A. doesn't claim any special knowledge of drug addiction. They don't directly answer whether a person addicted to some other drug, with no drinking problem, can be an A.A. member. The 1946 essay says a member is a member "as long as he says he is" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946), and that he may join "on the mere suspicion" that he may be an alcoholic (same essay); the Long Form ties membership to alcoholism. The pamphlet that addresses the question head-on, "Problems Other Than Alcohol," is listed in P-16 and P-17 but isn't in our sources.

c49745c329ea.t: These texts describe what A.A. says about itself. They don't govern other fellowships, which, as Bill wrote in 1957, work their own fields.

08013b94f743.t: Why is A.A.'s birthday June 10, 1935? | Recovery Starts

bacac7b80a27.t: June 10, 1935 is the day Dr. Bob had his last drink. In his own story, written in 1939, he says: "That was June 10, 1935, and that was my last drink." (p.…

a7d1451cc9a9.t: <0>Home</0> › <1>A.A. questions, from the books</1> › The early program and how A.A. began

b1c47790499b.t: June 10, 1935 is the day Dr. Bob had his last drink. In his own story, written in 1939, he says: "That was June 10, 1935, and that was my last drink." (p. 180).

0642778170ae.t: Today's Big Book gives that as the fellowship's starting point: "The birth of our Society dates from his first day of permanent sobriety, June 10, 1935." (p. 171). That line is in the introduction to his story, written after his death in 1950, not in the 1939 text.

012e5aff6f35.t: The reason, as the 1955 foreword puts it, is that his recovery seemed to prove that one alcoholic could reach another as no one else could. Bill W. had been sober about six months, but he had not yet helped anyone else stay sober.

e9fbeea44f87.t: Other dates could have been chosen, and the sources say so: the meeting of Bill and Dr. Bob on Mother's Day, May 1935, and the first group, which no one realized had formed until later.

3fec60469e75.t: Dr. Bob's story, "Doctor Bob's Nightmare," was written "nearly four years" after he stopped (p. 180). After he met Bill, he stayed dry about three weeks, drank heavily at a medical meeting in Atlantic City, and was brought home by his new friend, who gave him a few drinks that night and a bottle of beer the next morning (pp. 179–180). "That was June 10, 1935, and that was my last drink." (p. 180).

1dfb9e74d1ac.t: Chapter 11, "A Vision for You," written the same year, tells the beginning without dates for Dr. Bob, and dates the third man's recovery: "That was in June, 1935." (p. 158). A footnote added in a later edition says the visit to that man resulted in "A.A.'s first group, at Akron, Ohio, in 1935" (p. 156).

b0f7ced8b6ca.t: <0>The 1955 Foreword to the Second Edition.</0> "The spark that was to flare into the first A.A. group was struck at Akron, Ohio, in June 1935" (p. xv). When the physician sobered for good, "This seemed to prove that one alcoholic could affect another as no nonalcoholic could." (pp. xvi–xvii). It adds that by the time the broker went home that fall the first group had formed, "though no one realized it at the time" (p. xvii).

0f23ff00105f.t: <0>The introduction to Dr. Bob's story</0> (today's edition; it mentions his death in 1950, so it was written after then): "The birth of our Society dates from his first day of permanent sobriety, June 10, 1935." (p. 171).

29ccdf8c9c39.t: <0>Dr. Bob, 1948</0> (his last major talk, in P-53) gave the same date for his last drink, "and that was on the 10th of June, 1935" (P-53).

bdefbc587722.t: <0>A.A. Comes of Age (1957).</0> The book opens with the 1955 St. Louis convention, held to commemorate "the twentieth anniversary of its founding" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill tells of the operation Dr. Bob performed that morning, and that "To the time of his death fifteen years later, Dr. Bob never took another drink of alcohol." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The timeline in our later printing lists the date as: "Dr. Bob has his last drink. Alcoholics Anonymous founded" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The 1951 memorial scroll says he "recovered from alcoholism on June 10, 1935" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

c82fe51b827f.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (1980):</0> "Although arguments have been and will be made for other significant occasions in A.A. history, it is generally agreed that Alcoholics Anonymous began there, in Akron, on that date: June 10, 1935." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

4a9a480d410c.t: <0>Pass It On (1984)</0> calls it the date "now honored as the date when A.A. really began" (Pass It On, 1984).

e66ea97bd50f.t: <0>The meeting.</0> Bill and Dr. Bob met on a Sunday in May 1935, Mother's Day (p. 179; A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill's biographical sketch in P-53 (pamphlet © 2017) ties the birth to that meeting: Dr. Bob "became the second successful recovery — and Alcoholics Anonymous was born." (P-53). Akron members held a party each Mother's Day to celebrate the meeting (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). See <1>How did Bill W. and Dr. Bob meet?</1>

f35e129b6863.t: <0>Bill's own sobriety.</0> Bill writes that at the hospital he "was separated from alcohol for the last time" (p. 13); his 1957 account dates that hospital stay to December 1934 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The sources don't date A.A. from it; the 1955 foreword notes that before Akron he "had succeeded only in keeping sober himself" (p. xvi). See <1>What happened to Bill W. at Towns Hospital?</1>

0ed76ef4b0c8.t: <0>The month of the meeting.</0> The 1955 foreword says the spark was struck in June 1935 during a talk between the two men (p. xv); Dr. Bob's 1939 story puts that first talk on Mother's Day, in May, weeks before June 10 (pp. 179–180). Our sources don't explain the foreword's month.

af82c23b3f9e.t: <0>The Atlantic City drinking.</0> If June 10 is the founding date, <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> notes, his Atlantic City drinking was before it and doesn't count as a slip, though "He, however, referred to it as a slip." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

05d0b15740be.t: <0>Our sources don't record</0> when or by whom June 10 was first called A.A.'s birthday; the earliest statement of it in our sources are the introduction to Dr. Bob's story, written after 1950 (p. 171).

0688ad71d76d.t: What happens at an A.A. meeting? | Recovery Starts

51a60e974c48.t: The 1939 text doesn't prescribe a meeting format. It describes the early gatherings in the "western city" of Chapter 11, Akron: informal evenings in…

6d132693593c.t: What happens at an A.A. meeting?

18bd540c512c.t: <0>Home</0> › <1>A.A. questions, from the books</1> › For the newcomer and the family

9bae811a29ce.t: The 1939 text doesn't prescribe a meeting format. It describes the early gatherings in the "western city" of Chapter 11, Akron: informal evenings in members' homes, and one night a week set apart as "a time and place where new people might bring their problems" (p. 160), where a newcomer heard the story of someone "whose experience closely tallied with his own" (p. 160).

f99f1f3ffa11.t: Today's group pamphlet describes the common kinds of meeting (discussion, speaker, beginners, Step, Tradition or Big Book) and says "No one type or format is the best for an A.A. meeting" (P-16, 2018). Each group decides its own format.

54a33e690ba0.t: Customs differ from place to place. P-43 says the local group "is free to work out its own customs" (P-43).

ebd656cddfc7.t: What every description shares is alcoholics talking with alcoholics about their own experience.

c06b3aee93e9.t: Chapter 11, "A Vision for You," gives the only account of meetings in the first 164 pages (pp. 159–162): - <0>Most evenings, informally.</0> "Scarce an evening passed that someone's home did not shelter a little gathering of men and women, happy in their release, and constantly thinking how they might present their discovery to some newcomer." (p. 159). - <1>One night a week.</1> It became customary to "set apart one night a week for a meeting" (p. 159) for "anyone or everyone interested in a spiritual way of life" (p. 160). Aside from fellowship and sociability, "the prime object was to provide a time and place where new people might bring their problems" (p. 160). - <2>What a newcomer found.</2> A man still dazed from the hospital heard, "in an upper room of this house," the story of a man whose experience matched his own (p. 160). The book names what reached him: "The very practical approach to his problems, the absence of intolerance of any kind, the informality, the genuine democracy, the uncanny understanding which these people had were irresistible." (p. 160). - <3>Size.</3> By 1939 the house could hardly hold its weekly visitors, "sixty or eighty as a rule" (p. 161). - <4>More than meetings.</4> "But life among Alcoholics Anonymous is more than attending gatherings and visiting hospitals." (p. 161). Members cleaned up old scrapes, settled family differences, and lent money and found jobs for each other "when justified" (p. 161). - <5>In the East</5>, there were "informal meetings such as we have described to you" (p. 162).

0eeaa0c29b14.t: Elsewhere the program chapters say nothing about how a meeting runs: no readings, no order of business, no way of introducing yourself. The nearest it comes is its description of its own stories, which disclose "what we used to be like, what happened, and what we are like now" (p. 58).

8d0be09ec54e.t: "When A.A. was very young we met in homes." (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947). People came miles for the meeting and stayed for hours afterward "at coffee, cake, and eager, intimate talk" (same essay). When homes became too small, New York moved to a tailor's workshop, a rented room at Steinway Hall, and then a club.

9de635ea90f8.t: Members dropped money in "the hat" to pay the rent (P-17, "Money", 1946).

d5f2edf9a6d5.t: In 1946 groups ran from near-secret meetings for alcoholics only to public meetings with speakers on the platform (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946). See <0>What's the difference between open and closed meetings? Can family or friends come?</0>

4e5696574216.t: <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16) describes what is common, not what is required: - <1>Kinds of meeting:</1> discussion (a chair picks a topic), speaker (members tell "what they were like, what happened and what they are like now," as the pamphlet puts it, after the Big Book), beginners (often questions and answers, or Steps One to Three), and Step, Tradition or Big Book study; also business, group inventory and service meetings. - <2>Usual procedure:</2> the chair "usually opens the meeting with the A.A. Preamble and a few remarks" (P-16, 2018). Some groups have a moment of silence or the Serenity Prayer, or a reading from the Big Book, often from Chapter 5 or Chapter 3. Many close with a moment of silence and a prayer, or the Responsibility Declaration. A basket may be passed for contributions. - <3>Who decides:</3> meetings, open or closed, are "conducted by A.A. members who determine the format of their meetings" (P-16, 2018). - <4>Before and after:</4> coffee and conversation, and members helping set up and clean up.

ac163d3d287c.t: The Foreword to the Fourth Edition (2001) adds that members with computers "can participate in meetings online" (p. xxiv).

30f675b90d7a.t: There is no single A.A. meeting. The 1939 text shows the purpose (a place where newcomers bring their problems and hear from people who have recovered), and the later pamphlets show that groups have built many formats around it, each group choosing its own. The opening Preamble, readings, prayers and introductions are customs described in later literature, not part of the 1939 program. See <0>Is the A.A. Preamble in the Big Book? Where did it come from?</0> and <1>Do I have to say "I'm an alcoholic"?</1>

144d3a05271d.t: How did Alcoholics Anonymous get its name? Was "The Way Out" the title? | Recovery Starts

a36b1901be1f.t: Until 1939 the fellowship had no name. The name came from the title of its book, Alcoholics Anonymous, and the fellowship "began to be called Alcoholics…

af1d98514cc8.t: How did Alcoholics Anonymous get its name? Was "The Way Out" the title?

cc57a549aac8.t: Until 1939 the fellowship had no name. The name came from the title of its book, <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, and the fellowship "began to be called Alcoholics Anonymous, from the title of its own book" (p. xvii).

8948bcb73e6d.t: "The Way Out" was the other leading choice. In Bill W.'s accounts the Akron and New York groups voted, and "The Way Out" won by a narrow majority. Then Fitz M. checked the Library of Congress and found many books already called "The Way Out" and none called "Alcoholics Anonymous," and the members didn't want to be one more "way out." So "The Way Out" was never the book's published title.

b5e5ad7b8455.t: Bill says nobody knows who first used the words "Alcoholics Anonymous"; he thought the phrase grew out of the New Yorkers calling themselves a "nameless bunch of alcoholics." Later books trace written uses back to mid-1938, and one says as early as 1937.

54c15e0b2713.t: The sources disagree on the details: how many titles were considered, and how many books Fitz found.

ba76dbbd465d.t: The Foreword to the First Edition already uses the name for the people as well as the book: "We, of Alcoholics Anonymous, are more than one hundred men and women" (p. xiii). It asks each member writing or speaking publicly to omit his name, "designating himself instead as 'a member of Alcoholics Anonymous.'" (p. xiii), and it is signed "Alcoholics Anonymous." (p. xiv). The book itself doesn't tell how the name was chosen. See <0>What does the Foreword to the First Edition say A.A. is for?</0>

9ac6fbc9c7ad.t: The 1955 Foreword to the Second Edition: "The fledgling society, which had been nameless, now began to be called Alcoholics Anonymous, from the title of its own book." (p. xvii).

fcd92a62fefb.t: In his 1946 Grapevine article on anonymity, reprinted in P-17, Bill writes that before the book "we had no name" (P-17, 1946). "We must have considered at least two hundred titles." (P-17, 1946). The choice narrowed to "The Way Out" or "Alcoholics Anonymous," and a last-minute vote of the Akron and New York groups went to "The Way Out" by a narrow majority (P-17, 1946). Then Fitz M., "who then lived in Washington," went to the Library of Congress: "He found exactly twelve books already titled 'The Way Out.'" (P-17, 1946). "When this information was passed around, we shivered at the possibility of being the 'Thirteenth Way Out.'" (P-17, 1946). "That's how we got a name for our book of experience, a name for our movement" (P-17, 1946), and, Bill adds, a tradition of anonymity.

a78083d8fa9b.t: Bill's longer account (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)

1e2e87ac434c.t: Bill had labelled the duplicated loan copies "Alcoholics Anonymous," but many still didn't like the title (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). It had appeared "probably in October, 1938." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "We do not know who first used these words." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). After leaving the Oxford Groups in 1937, the New Yorkers often called themselves a "nameless bunch of alcoholics" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and he says the name came from that phrase.

dc37070d7af1.t: He confesses a temptation: with "The Way Out" he could sign the book himself, and he even thought of calling it "The B. W. Movement" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957) before friends slapped him down. "We considered more than a hundred titles all told." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). New York, encouraged by a writer named Joe W., came to favor "Alcoholics Anonymous"; Akron favored "The Way Out," which had a bare majority overall (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill wired Fitz on his farm in Maryland to check the Library of Congress: twelve books were titled "The Way Out," none "Alcoholics Anonymous" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "We sure aren't going to make this book the thirteenth 'Way Out.'" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "That is how we got the title for our book, and that is how our society got its name." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

74a1463cda64.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (1980)</0> says that in Akron, because the Book of James was such a favorite, "'The James Club' was favored by some as a name for the Fellowship." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). It quotes a June 1938 letter in which Bill asked Dr. Bob: "What would you think about the formation of a charitable organization called, say, Alcoholics Anonymous?" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). It lists other proposed titles, among them "A Way Out" and "Comes the Dawn," and says the name was already in limited use, "references to it may be found as early as 1937" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). One Akron wife remembered thinking, "That's the awfulest name I ever heard." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

eed0b8e49ffd.t: <0>Pass It On (1984)</0> says most people thought Joe W. coined the name (Pass It On, 1984), but that "The first documented use of the name in the A.A. archives is in a letter from Frank Amos to Albert Scott dated June 24, 1938." (Pass It On, 1984), where the book was to be by "Alcoholics Anonymous" rather than a named author (Pass It On, 1984). It lists other titles, including "One Hundred Men," "The Empty Glass" and "Dry Frontiers," and says "One Hundred Men" was dropped after the only woman member objected (Pass It On, 1984). It also says the book's editor, Tom Uzzell, was firm that "Alcoholics Anonymous" was the right title (Pass It On, 1984).

86c29187d897.t: <0>How many titles.</0> "at least two hundred" (P-17, 1946); "more than a hundred" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; Pass It On, 1984).

3a125dc5b478.t: <0>What Fitz found.</0> Twelve books called "The Way Out" (P-17, 1946; A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1> says Fitz "is supposed to have replied by telegram" that the Library of Congress had "25 books entitled 'The Way Out,' 12 entitled 'The Way,' and none called 'Alcoholics Anonymous.'" (Pass It On, 1984). Our sources don't have the telegram.

16f1b9055e2a.t: <0>Where Fitz was.</0> "then lived in Washington" (P-17, 1946); "on his farm in Maryland" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); "near Washington, D.C." (Pass It On, 1984).

c6d13f6a928f.t: <0>When the name first appears.</0> Bill (1957): probably October 1938 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1>: documented June 24, 1938 (Pass It On, 1984). <2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2>: references as early as 1937 (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), though it doesn't quote one.

393432f0c9e1.t: <0>Who coined it.</0> Bill says no one knows (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); <1>Pass It On</1> reports that most credited Joe W. (Pass It On, 1984). Our sources don't settle it.

b80b75c0afc2.t: For which group first called itself by the name, see <0>How did the Cleveland group become the first to call itself Alcoholics Anonymous?</0>

7e40ab77eb80.t: Who was the third member of A.A., and how was he found? | Recovery Starts

2271c0f81093.t: A.A.'s third member was Bill D., an Akron lawyer and former city councilman, strapped to a bed in Akron City Hospital in June 1935 after his eighth…

1f93c3ee5212.t: Who was the third member of A.A., and how was he found?

d19d130f0150.t: A.A.'s third member was Bill D., an Akron lawyer and former city councilman, strapped to a bed in Akron City Hospital in June 1935 after his eighth hospital stay in six months.

707d6e4d4343.t: Bill W. and Dr. Bob found him on purpose: they phoned the hospital and asked the nurse for an alcoholic to work on, because they had seen they must help others to stay sober themselves.

c21f446ec03c.t: They told him their own drinking stories, told him what alcoholism was, and left him free to say no. He walked out of the hospital a few days later and never drank again.

6f98ed2f1e2a.t: The Big Book dates A.A.'s first group, at Akron, from that visit.

dfeb97c09e05.t: The Big Book's 1939 telling comes right after Bill and Dr. Bob meet. Both men "saw that they must keep spiritually active" (p. 156). So they called the head nurse of a local hospital and asked if she had "a first class alcoholic prospect" (p. 156). She had: a once well-known lawyer who had just beaten up a couple of nurses, had been in eight times in six months, and was strapped down (p. 156). One of them answered, "Put him in a private room." (p. 157).

6b43da8053fd.t: That is Chapter 7's method in action: ask the hospitals for a drinker who wants help, and go to him (see <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0>).

4584fbb1fe63.t: For an hour they told him about their own drinking, and he kept saying "That's me." (p. 157). They told him about alcoholism, then about their spiritual experience and the course of action they followed (p. 157). He doubted it: he had prayed on hangover mornings and been drunk again by nine (p. 158). On the third day he gave his life to the care and direction of his Creator, and that afternoon he walked out "a free man" (p. 158). "That was in June, 1935. He never drank again." (p. 158). A footnote in today's edition says this visit "resulted in A.A.'s first group, at Akron, Ohio, in 1935" (p. 156).

693d2dac405a.t: His side of it (his story, "Alcoholic Anonymous Number Three")

5495be164b92.t: Bill D.'s own story is in Part I of the personal stories. He had finished law school in Akron and served five years as a city councilman before drinking took everything (p. 182). In the first six months of 1935 he was hospitalized eight times, and on June 26, 1935, he came to in the hospital once more (p. 184).

0d74c10b9378.t: His wife told him two men had a plan to stop drinking, and part of the plan was to tell it to another drunk (p. 185). He agreed to listen because he felt he would be "a real stinker" (p. 185) if he refused to hear out two men it might help stay sober; his wife also told him he could not pay them even if he wanted to (p. 185). They told him plainly: if he didn't want it, "we'll be going and looking for someone else" (p. 186). They asked whether he could quit on his own, whether he believed in a Higher Power, and whether he would ask that Power for help (p. 186). They told him he had a disease (p. 187), gave him the idea of "twenty-four hours at a time" (p. 188), went over his faults with him like an inventory, and told him to take the program "to somebody else who needs it and wants it" (p. 190).

1ec482564adb.t: The editors insert Bill W.'s account in the middle of the story. It says Dr. Bob had told him two days before, "If you and I are going to stay sober, we had better get busy." (p. 188). Dr. Bob phoned the receiving nurse at Akron's City Hospital (p. 188). When Bill D. told his wife to fetch his clothes and walked out, "A.A.'s Number One Group dates from that very day." (p. 189).

4e007623a9c9.t: The 1955 Foreword to the Second Edition says the same in brief: their first case, a desperate one, "recovered immediately and became A.A. number three" (p. xvii).

3c8fa99cf38c.t: <0>Dr. Bob, 1948</0> (talk printed in P-53): they started looking for prospects at once, and before long one appeared, Bill D., a Sunday-school superintendent who Dr. Bob thought knew the Bible far better than he did (P-53).

5e5e2aad6d75.t: <0>Bill W., 1957</0>: <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> tells the same visit, calling Bill D. the first "man on the bed" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), though Bill also says he and Dr. Bob had tackled another man, Eddie, "just before our first visit with Bill D." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). It also names A.A. number four, Ernie, a young man who caught on quickly (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); Chapter 11 describes him without a name as a "devil-may-care young fellow" (p. 158).

78af26c88fc4.t: <0>The date.</0> Bill D.'s story says he came to in the hospital on June 26, 1935, before he heard of the two men (p. 184). <1>Comes of Age</1> (1957) has Dr. Bob phone the hospital the day after his last drink on June 10, and the two men see Bill D. two days later (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Those two timelines don't fit together, and our sources don't reconcile them. Chapter 11 says only "June, 1935" (p. 158).

07ed9ea18f79.t: <0>His hospital record.</0> The nurse in Chapter 11 says eight times in six months (p. 156), and Bill D.'s story agrees (p. 184). In <1>Comes of Age</1> he tells them six times in four months (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

19d029173c8d.t: <0>How long he stayed.</0> Chapter 11 says he left on the third day (p. 158); Bill W.'s insert has him leave during their second visit (p. 189); <1>Comes of Age</1> says two days after that visit (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). All agree he never drank again.

e2ae64a4ec1b.t: Is A.A. a religious organization? | Recovery Starts

8c34b6ac14bf.t: By its own description, no. The 1939 Foreword says A.A. is "not allied with any particular faith, sect or denomination" (p. xiv). Chapter 7 says we…

f3d828125827.t: <0>Home</0> › <1>A.A. questions, from the books</1> › The Steps

eda693d41d95.t: By its own description, no. The 1939 Foreword says A.A. is "not allied with any particular faith, sect or denomination" (p. xiv). Chapter 7 says we represent no particular faith or denomination (pp. 93–94). The 1955 Foreword states it outright: "Alcoholics Anonymous is not a religious organization" (p. xx).

19c63f14c0e3.t: Membership has no religious requirement. In 1939 the only requirement was "an honest desire to stop drinking" (p. xiv).

0daaa0152bc9.t: But the program is openly about God, and the book doesn't hide it: "we are going to talk about God" (p. 45). What it insists on is that the conception of God is the reader's own (pp. 46–47, 93).

3d27932e6724.t: Religion itself is left to each member: which church, if any, is "an entirely personal affair" (p. 28), and A.A. groups take no position on "sectarian religion" (p. 565).

db55f1bce485.t: The earliest statement is the Foreword to the First Edition (1939): "We are not allied with any particular faith, sect or denomination, nor do we oppose anyone" (p. xiv). In the same paragraph: no fees or dues, and "The only requirement for membership is an honest desire to stop drinking" (p. xiv).

4683fe2112ea.t: Chapter 2 adds: "We think it no concern of ours what religious bodies our members identify themselves with as individuals" (p. 28). It's "an entirely personal affair" (p. 28). Not all members join a church, though "most of us favor such memberships" (p. 28). Those with religious ties "will find here nothing disturbing to their beliefs or ceremonies" (p. 28).

426f8f19da52.t: Chapter 7 tells the helper the same: we represent no particular faith or denomination, and "We are dealing only with general principles common to most denominations" (p. 94).

49024fc958c7.t: Later statements keep this line. The Long Form of the Traditions (1946) says no group or member should express an opinion that implicates A.A. on outside controversies, "particularly those of politics, alcohol reform, or sectarian religion" (p. 565). The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) says it in so many words: "Alcoholics Anonymous is not a religious organization" (p. xx), and lists members who are Catholics, Protestants, Jews, Hindus, Moslems and Buddhists (p. xx). The A.A. Preamble, first printed in the Grapevine in June 1947 and based on the 1939 Foreword (<0>Service Manual</0>, the Grapevine section), says A.A. "is not allied with any sect, denomination, politics, organization or institution" (P-17, front matter).

bdc49b803f43.t: But the program talks about God

455009a8667a.t: It would be dishonest to stop there. The Big Book is plain that its program depends on a Power greater than ourselves and calls that Power God: - "Its main object is to enable you to find a Power greater than yourself which will solve your problem" (p. 45). "And it means, of course, that we are going to talk about God" (p. 45). - Five of the Twelve Steps name God or Him (Steps 3, 5, 6, 7 and 11), and Step 2 speaks of a Power greater than ourselves (p. 59), and the chapters that explain them are full of prayer (pp. 63, 76, 85–88). - "We Agnostics" (Chapter 4) doesn't leave the agnostic where he is. It argues for faith: "either God is everything or else He is nothing" (p. 53), and "deep down in every man, woman, and child, is the fundamental idea of God" (p. 55). - In the early Akron meetings described in the stories, meetings closed with the Lord's Prayer (p. 262), and Dr. Bob "always emphasized the religious angle very strongly" (p. 263).

7958624338e9.t: What the book refuses to do is tell anyone what God is. "Much to our relief, we discovered we did not need to consider another's conception of God" (p. 46). "When, therefore, we speak to you of God, we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47). Starting is simple: "Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe, that there is a Power greater than myself?" (p. 47). About half the original fellowship had thought they were atheists or agnostics (p. 44).

25bae08634b4.t: Chapter 7 makes this a rule for anyone carrying the message: - An agnostic or atheist "does not have to agree with your conception of God. He can choose any conception he likes, provided it makes sense to him" (p. 93). - Use everyday language. Don't raise theological issues, "no matter what your own convictions are" (p. 93). - "Let him see that you are not there to instruct him in religion" (p. 93). - If he prefers some other spiritual approach, encourage him: "We have no monopoly on God" (p. 95).

68ef39256b97.t: Appendix II says the same: "Willingness, honesty and open mindedness are the essentials of recovery" (p. 568), and an alcoholic can recover "provided he does not close his mind to all spiritual concepts" (p. 568).

1ffc56179525.t: Friendly to religion, not part of one

9de711730471.t: The book asks members to drop their prejudice "even against organized religion" (p. 49), says members who belong to a church keep its devotions (p. 87), and advises: "Be quick to see where religious people are right" (p. 87). For the Fifth Step it suggests a clergyman as one choice, or a close-mouthed friend, a doctor, or family (p. 74). Appendix V collects approving words from clergy of several churches (p. 572).

71a1b7146faa.t: A.A. as a fellowship belongs to no religion, allies with none, takes no side in religious questions, and asks no one to believe anything to join. Its program is spiritual and speaks of God throughout, but leaves each person to understand God in his own way. The Big Book doesn't use the slogan "spiritual, not religious." It says the things above, which is what that slogan tries to sum up.

29b5f18756c7.t: Is A.A. run from the top down? | Recovery Starts

2f6ad1f08bf5.t: Not over its groups and members. In Bill W.'s 1947 words, "Nowhere in A.A. is there to be seen any constituted human authority that can compel an A.A.…

08b68888a355.t: Is A.A. run from the top down?

c7a491e82640.t: <0>Home</0> › <1>A.A. questions, from the books</1> › The Concepts and service

b1d48eae8974.t: Not over its groups and members. In Bill W.'s 1947 words, "Nowhere in A.A. is there to be seen any constituted human authority that can compel an A.A. group to do anything" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947). The Long Form of the Traditions (1946) says A.A.'s servants "do not govern" (p. 565).

a93f5cf29ce0.t: For A.A.'s shared world services, authority runs from the groups. Concept I (1962) puts final authority in the groups; Concept II says they delegate the active work to the General Service Conference. Later literature calls this the "upside-down" structure.

ffd9a26f5788.t: Inside the service offices, though, the 1962 Concepts describe ordinary delegated management on purpose: the Conference over the trustees, the trustees over the service corporations, directors over executives, executives over staff. Bill chose the corporate form deliberately.

9a5229cc7d18.t: None of that reaches down into a group. The Conference is bound never to "perform any acts of government" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).

f1f033256315.t: <0>Long Form Nine (1946).</0> "Each A.A. group needs the least possible organization" (p. 565). Groups elect a secretary or a rotating committee; the trustees act as A.A.'s General Service Committee. All such representatives "derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern" (p. 565).

ecf21628a982.t: <0>Bill's 1946 essay on money.</0> Of clubs, local offices and the New York office: "These are places of service; they cannot really control or govern A.A." (P-17, Money, 1946). If one became overbearing, members could simply stop paying for it: "These services must always serve us well or go out of business" (P-17, Money, 1946).

83316f34916f.t: <0>Bill's 1947 essay on government.</0> It lists what A.A. lacks: "no fees, no dues, no rules and regulations, no demand that alcoholics conform to A.A. principles, no one set in personal authority over anyone else" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947). Group committees "have only the authorization to serve, never to command" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947). Even at A.A.'s headquarters, he says, "there can only exist a center of service" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947), with no authority to govern.

67dda0544545.t: World services: from the groups (Concepts I and II, 1962)

f556739bc757.t: Bill's Concepts put the final authority over world services at the base. "The A.A. groups today hold ultimate responsibility and final authority for our world services" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). In Concept II: "The operation is really theirs; they really own it" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept II).

998ef7e333f9.t: The groups can't run a world service office themselves, so they delegate. Each group chooses a general service representative; the representatives choose area committee members and a delegate; the delegates sit in the Conference with the trustees and staff. Bill calls the GSRs, committee members and delegates "the direct agents of the A.A. groups" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX).

6443317c5bd2.t: The "upside-down" image is not in Bill's 1962 essays. It comes from later pamphlets: P-8 (first printed 1986) says A.A. "has been called an upside-down organization" (P-8) because final authority rests with the groups, and the current Service Manual (2024–2026) draws it as the "upside-down triangle," with the groups on top (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Welcome to General Service).

e9a129282e14.t: Inside the service offices: a chain, by design

f8a808710b3e.t: Bill's own picture in 1962 is a business corporation, and he uses the words top and bottom for it: "From top to bottom, our whole service structure indeed resembles that of a large corporation" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VI). "The A.A. groups are the stockholders" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VI), the delegates their proxies, the trustees the directors of a holding company that owns the service corporations.

4d7c158320a5.t: Concept X spells out a line of ultimate authority: the delegates over the trustees, the trustees over A.A. World Services and the Grapevine, their directors over their officers, the officers over their staffs. "The principle of ultimate authority runs clear through our structure" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X). Concept XI adds that day-to-day executive direction "must always head up in one person" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI).

ab156a02c77f.t: So the honest answer has two parts. Inside the service corporations there is an ordinary chain of management, and Bill wanted it that way. Above them, the chain points back to the groups. And the Concepts limit how anyone uses authority:

e971ec645e77.t: Ultimate authority "should practically never be used in full, except in an emergency" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X).

dd15729e1b5c.t: Every level gets a "Right of Decision" (Concept III), a vote in proportion to its responsibility (Concept IV), and minorities get a right of appeal (Concept V).

bfe2ad4c6f8f.t: No Conference member may be placed "in a position of unqualified authority over any of the others" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).

50eaa870a31e.t: What the structure can't do to a group

ede5c948468f.t: Concept XII is the Conference's own bond with A.A. It "shall never perform any acts of government" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). Bill lists the liberties it must not touch: no penalties for nonconformity, no fees or dues, no expulsion, each group running its internal affairs as it wishes. When Tradition questions come up, "A.A.’s World Headquarters is not a police operation" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII); the most it can usually do is offer information or mediation.

34af5927031d.t: P-16, <0>The A.A. Group</0> (© 2018), says the same in plain words: "A.A. has no central authority, minimal organization, and a handful of Traditions instead of laws" (P-16).

17621df03022.t: Is A.A. a treatment program? Does it provide detox, housing or counselling? | Recovery Starts

1db0564bd2d0.t: No. A.A.'s literature describes a fellowship of alcoholics helping each other, not a treatment service. The 1946 Long Form says hospitals and "other…

4f2e61e8e55e.t: Is A.A. a treatment program? Does it provide detox, housing or counselling?

90434f9aaff2.t: No. A.A.'s literature describes a fellowship of alcoholics helping each other, not a treatment service. The 1946 Long Form says hospitals and "other places of recuperation" ought to be "well outside A.A.—and medically supervised" (p. 564), and defines professionalism as "the occupation of counseling alcoholics for fees or hire" (p. 564), which A.A. is never to become.

2a4f43a485dd.t: In the 1939 text, individual members did a great deal for newcomers: got them into hospital and visited them there, helped find jobs, lent money, took men into their homes (pp. 91, 96–97, 159, 161). The book also warns that putting this work "on a service plane" makes the newcomer rely on the helper instead of God (p. 98).

5bffa815bd60.t: Bill W. in 1946: "Hospitalization is most definitely the job of the doctor" (P-17, "Money", 1946), and there can never be an "A.A. therapist."

a695941f310e.t: Today's group pamphlet lists what A.A. does not do: no hospitalization, drugs or treatment; no housing, food, clothing, jobs or money; no domestic or vocational counseling (P-16, 2018).

b864f24fdc86.t: The Big Book's members weren't against medical help, and they did practical things for each other. But the help came from individual members, and the recovery itself came from somewhere else. - <0>Hospital care, through a doctor.</0> "If your man needs hospitalization, he should have it, but not forcibly unless he is violent." (p. 91). An approach through a doctor or an institution "is a better bet" than through his family (p. 91). For an employee still drinking, physical treatment "should, of course, be referred to your own doctor" (p. 143). - <1>Practical help, given with care.</1> If a newcomer is broke and homeless, "you might try to help him about getting a job, or give him a little financial assistance" (p. 96), without depriving your own family. You might take him into your home for a few days, with discretion (p. 96). Chapter 11 lists "lending money and securing jobs for each other, when justified" among everyday events (p. 161). - <2>The limit.</2> The man who expects you "to act only as a banker for his financial difficulties or a nurse for his sprees" may have to be dropped until he changes his mind (p. 95). "The minute we put our work on a service plane, the alcoholic commences to rely upon our assistance rather than upon God." (p. 98). Physical treatment "is but a small part of the picture" (p. 143).

00e51c7d5adb.t: See <0>Should I give a newcomer money or a place to stay?</0> for Chapter 7's full advice.

46fab309fc43.t: <0>Tradition Six.</0> Clubs and hospitals that need much property or administration should be incorporated separately and kept apart, so the groups can discard them if necessary; such facilities "ought not to use the A.A. name" (p. 564). "But hospitals, as well as other places of recuperation, ought to be well outside A.A.—and medically supervised." (p. 564).

bcf24913ff5d.t: <0>Tradition Eight.</0> "Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional." (p. 564). "We define professionalism as the occupation of counseling alcoholics for fees or hire." (p. 564). A.A.'s Twelfth Step work "is never to be paid for" (pp. 564–565).

d04d44b98119.t: "Years ago we used to think A.A. should have its own hospitals, rest homes and farms." By 1946: "Nowadays we are equally convinced we should have nothing of the sort." (P-17, "Money", 1946).

b0bd01927af1.t: "Hospitalization is most definitely the job of the doctor, backed, of course, by private or community aid." (P-17, "Money", 1946). It is not a function of A.A. in the sense of management or ownership; everywhere, A.A. cooperates with hospitals.

02e7f4bee2de.t: On counseling: an A.A. member may go into alcohol therapy as a trained social worker, psychologist or psychiatrist, but there is not, "and can never be, any such thing as an 'A.A. therapist.'" (P-17, "Money", 1946).

bd40e0b6a35b.t: Groups that set up their own drying-out places, Bill wrote in 1947, nearly always found it "backfired" (P-17, "Hospitals and A.A.", 1947), because it put the group into business.

4cd24c78be5e.t: <0>1971 (this printing updated 2023).</0> <1>The Twelve Traditions Illustrated</1> (P-43), on Tradition Five: a member may, with discretion, lend a few dollars or put up a broke alcoholic for a while, but the A.A. group as a whole "is not a friendly finance company, nor a welfare department, nor a housing bureau" (P-43).

e72f07171f24.t: <0>Undated statement in P-17 (2019 printing).</0> "A.A. and Alcoholism," a policy statement the General Service Conference has affirmed, says members recognize "that some may require professional counseling or treatment" (P-17, "A.A. and Alcoholism") and that the movement does not engage in medical or psychiatric treatment.

a9c7cf023616.t: <0>2018.</0> <1>The A.A. Group</1> (P-16), "What A.A. Does Not Do," includes: - Make medical or psychological diagnoses or prognoses. - "Provide hospitalization, drugs, or medical or psychiatric treatment." (P-16, 2018). - "Provide housing, food, clothing, jobs, money or other such services." (P-16, 2018). - "Provide domestic or vocational counseling." (P-16, 2018).

61d3914588e4.t: The same pamphlet: "There is no such thing as an 'A.A. hospital' or an 'A.A. halfway house'" (P-16, 2018), though A.A. meetings are held in many such places and many members work in them. Intergroup offices "sometimes provide information on treatment facilities, hospitals and halfway houses" (P-16, 2018).

f482c633865a.t: Read together, the texts draw the same line from 1939 on. Doctors and hospitals provide medical care; individual A.A. members may help a newcomer in practical ways, carefully; A.A. itself, as a fellowship and as groups, runs no treatment, housing or counseling service and has no professional class. The Traditions keep facilities outside A.A.; they don't say treatment is bad, and they don't govern the facilities themselves (see <0>Tradition Six: can an A.A. group partner with a treatment centre?</0>).

7481fafa45a6.t: P-16, <0>The A.A. Group</0> ("What A.A. Does Not Do," p. 39): <1>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/literature/p-16_0723.pdf</1>

89786fe9b622.t: What are the a, b, c of p. 60 ("probably no human power… God could and would if He were sought")? | Recovery Starts

c9ad3d8a076d.t: They're three "pertinent ideas" on page 60 of Chapter 5, right after the Twelve Steps: (a) "That we were alcoholic and could not manage our own lives."…

4ac0aab74d3a.t: What are the a, b, c of p. 60 ("probably no human power… God could and would if He were sought")?

0305b81600a2.t: <0>Home</0> › <1>A.A. questions, from the books</1> › Big Book passages often quoted alone

5129f2f912f6.t: They're three "pertinent ideas" on page 60 of Chapter 5, right after the Twelve Steps: (a) "That we were alcoholic and could not manage our own lives." (b) "That probably no human power could have relieved our alcoholism." (c) "That God could and would if He were sought." (p. 60)

dd428acb0e09.t: They're a summary of what the book has already said. "Our description of the alcoholic, the chapter to the agnostic, and our personal adventures before and after make clear three pertinent ideas" (p. 60).

2a4d744dda72.t: The next sentence moves the reader on: "Being convinced, we were at Step Three" (p. 60).

a332300dc480.t: Two small words carry weight: "probably" in (b) and "if He were sought" in (c). The book hedges and states a condition, and both match what it said in the earlier chapters.

f25c546b66a1.t: Page 60 finishes the list of Steps and then reassures the reader. "What an order! I can't go through with it." (p. 60) is answered with "Do not be discouraged." (p. 60) and "We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection." (p. 60)

0faa208b4936.t: Then come the a, b, c, introduced as ideas the book has already made clear, not as new rules. Being convinced of them, "we were at Step Three" (p. 60). The book goes straight into what Step Three means, starting with "The first requirement is that we be convinced that any life run on self-will can hardly be a success." (p. 60)

d4cba8c664ef.t: The three ideas cover the ground of Steps One and Two: (a) is close to Step One's wording, "our lives had become unmanageable" (p. 59), and (b) and (c) to Step Two's "a Power greater than ourselves could restore us to sanity" (p. 59). The book doesn't label them that way. What it says is that being convinced of them puts the reader at Step Three.

349a06429bb0.t: The book names its sources for them: the description of the alcoholic (Chapters 2–3), the chapter to the agnostic (Chapter 4), and the members' stories.

f1deb9e3436f.t: <0>(a) We were alcoholic and couldn't manage our own lives.</0> Chapter 3: "We alcoholics are men and women who have lost the ability to control our drinking." (p. 30) Chapter 2: "We are without defense against the first drink." (p. 24)

e66bc5178bf8.t: <0>(b) Probably no human power could have relieved our alcoholism.</0> The word "probably" fits the earlier chapters, which keep leaving a little room: - Chapter 3 says the alcoholic has no effective defense against the first drink, and "Except in a few rare cases, neither he nor any other human being can provide such a defense." (p. 43) - Whether a person can quit "upon a nonspiritual basis," it says, depends on how far he has already lost the power to choose (p. 34). - If anyone showing loss of control can turn around and "drink like a gentleman, our hats are off to him" (p. 31). - A doctor quoted on p. 43 says that two of the members "were 100% hopeless, apart from divine help" (p. 43).

9ce695d0bb0d.t: <0>(c) God could and would if He were sought.</0> Chapter 4 sets the condition low. The reader needs only to ask "Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe, that there is a Power greater than myself?" (p. 47) "We found that God does not make too hard terms with those who seek Him." (p. 46) And the God sought is the reader's own conception: "When, therefore, we speak to you of God, we mean your own conception of God." (p. 47)

5b6c7ad39665.t: Does context change the common reading?

1fe6a07c3d59.t: Mostly it confirms it. The a, b, c are what they look like: a short summary of the book's case so far, leading to Step Three. What context adds is a warning not to drop the small words. "Probably" is the book's own hedge, and it matches a book that says "except in a few rare cases" (p. 43). "If He were sought" is a condition, and Chapter 4 says how little the seeking has to begin with.

fcafc988fcca.t: Is "Acceptance is the answer" part of the main text? | Recovery Starts

3b4b3b99a598.t: No. The famous line, "And acceptance is the answer to all my problems today," is in a personal story, not in the Big Book's program text (p. 417).

8030c6270965.t: Is "Acceptance is the answer" part of the main text?

eef032de8ec4.t: No. The famous line, "And acceptance is the answer to all my problems today," is in a personal story, not in the Big Book's program text (p. 417).

5eae09712b27.t: The story is "Acceptance Was the Answer," number 16 in Part II, "They Stopped in Time," pages 407–420 of the fourth edition.

8c66eec630f1.t: It's one member's account of his own recovery. The first 164 pages never say it. In the main text the word "acceptance" appears once, in another sense (p. 48).

ffdc57bde653.t: "Acceptance Was the Answer" is the story of a physician who drank and took pills for years, each pill "medically indicated" in his own mind (pp. 407–411), until two locked wards and a psychiatrist got him to A.A. meetings (pp. 412–415). For seven months he went to meetings while still tapering off alcohol and pills (p. 416). Then: "At last, acceptance proved to be the key to my drinking problem" (p. 416). He accepted that he really was an alcoholic, "And it's all right with me. Now, what am I going to do about it?" (p. 417). From that moment, he says, he had no compulsion to drink.

5af577d24369.t: The famous passage follows on page 417: "And acceptance is the answer to all my problems today." He goes on to apply acceptance to his marriage, to meetings, and to God, and he means action, not passivity: "I never just sit and do nothing while waiting for Him to tell me what to do" (p. 420).

49d468b486d2.t: The story also mentions working the Steps. He and his wife took the Third Step aloud "just as it says in the Big Book" (p. 414), and he later redid all twelve with his marriage in mind (p. 420).

c6011ce38951.t: The Big Book itself draws the line. Its program is in the first 164 pages. The personal stories that follow are each writer's account "in his own language and from his own point of view" (p. 29). A search of the main text, the forewords and the appendices finds no "acceptance is the answer." The word "acceptance" appears in the main text only once, in Chapter 4, about why people readily accept scientific theories (p. 48).

bace3b20b202.t: <0>Which part:</0> It's sometimes placed in Part III. The fourth-edition text puts it in Part II as story 16 (p. 407), the part titled "They Stopped in Time."

68ded836595d.t: <0>Which edition:</0> Only the fourth edition was checked here, so the edition the story first appeared in can't be confirmed from these sources. The Preface says the personal stories were revised in the 1955, 1976 and 2001 editions (pp. xi–xii), so the story isn't part of the 1939 book.

037d67cfad65.t: The passage is often read aloud as if it were Big Book program text. It's a good passage, but it's one man's experience, written decades after the program was set down. Readers who want what the book itself says about the alcoholic's way out will find it in Chapters 5 to 7 (pp. 58–103).

1f74a327091c.t: How were Akron and New York different in the early years? | Recovery Starts

27163dc016d1.t: Akron was A.A.'s first group, formed in 1935 around Dr. Bob, and for its first years it was the larger and more successful of the two. New York, around…

3a47de41aa4b.t: How were Akron and New York different in the early years?

c53d2140ae14.t: Akron was A.A.'s first group, formed in 1935 around Dr. Bob, and for its first years it was the larger and more successful of the two. New York, around Bill W., took shape more slowly; for a long time the people he took into his Brooklyn home stayed drunk.

051b9d98ef15.t: New York's alcoholics left the Oxford Group in 1937. Akron's stayed inside it, meeting at the home of T. Henry and Clarace Williams, until late 1939. It had its own ways, hospitalizing prospects and having them make a formal "surrender" on their knees, and it kept the Oxford Group's morning quiet time, Bible reading and "absolutes."

7e66ca3efadf.t: When the Big Book was written, Bill said Akron gave him "the warmest support" while New York gave the drafts "a real mauling," and the two groups favored different titles. A later history adds that Akron had its own quarrels over the book.

a7b1aa047607.t: The 1939 Big Book itself says the same thing was happening in the East "under only slightly different conditions." The sources treat it as one fellowship with two centers.

9b69c1ccea17.t: Chapter 11, "A Vision for You," describes the "western city" (Akron) without naming it. After the first three, "A year and six months later these three had succeeded with seven more." (p. 159). A weekly meeting began, open to anyone interested in a spiritual way of life (pp. 159–160), and a couple "placed their large home at the disposal of this strangely assorted crowd" (p. 160). By 1939 that house drew sixty or eighty a week, and a community thirty miles away had fifteen members (p. 161).

607f9718609e.t: Then: "Under only slightly different conditions, the same thing is taking place in many eastern cities." (p. 161). In one of them was a hospital where a doctor sent them patients, and there were informal meetings "where you may now see scores of members" (p. 162). "There is a good bit of travel between East and West and we foresee a great increase in this helpful interchange." (p. 162).

6994e30c56a3.t: The 1955 Foreword to the Second Edition gives the order: the first group formed at Akron in the summer of 1935, "though no one realized it at the time" (p. xvii); "A second small group promptly took shape at New York" (p. xvii), followed by Cleveland.

374c0b8ddc24.t: New York's slow start (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)

830bed71133a.t: Bill had no success in New York until he came home from Akron in September 1935 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He and Lois filled their Clinton Street house with alcoholics and, he says, did not sober up a single one, though "we did pick up a lot of knowledge" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The first to recover were Henry P. and Fitz M. (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Meanwhile, "Out in Akron, in the houses of Dr. Bob and Wally, the home-sobering treatment fared better." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <0>How did A.A. grow from two people?</0>

b2fc537f1924.t: The New Yorkers parted from the Oxford Groups in the latter part of 1937 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In Akron the alcoholics went on meeting with Oxford Groupers at the Williamses' house until "well after the A.A. book was published" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Writing of the fall of 1938, Bill says that "In important matters there was still considerable disagreement" between the Eastern and Midwestern viewpoints (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957): Akron still talked of the four absolutes, which New York had dropped (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <0>What did early A.A. take from the Oxford Group, and why did it separate?</0>

19ac5d7741a9.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) describes the Akron practice. Prospects were hospitalized for five to eight days (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980) and had to make a "surrender," kneeling and praying in front of other members; one member recalled that "You couldn't go to a meeting until you did it." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Morning quiet time and spiritual reading were emphasized (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Akron members also told less of their drinking histories at meetings; one recalled that "Bill was in favor of having an A.A. member qualify or tell how he became an alcoholic" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

7deaf5ace7b4.t: <0>The 1937 plan.</0> When Bill and Dr. Bob put the idea of a book, hospitals and paid missionaries to eighteen Akron members, the members "really did work us over," and it passed by the barest majority (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Back home, "Our little New York group gave me more encouragement than had the Akronites." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

bb68513b5b0f.t: <0>The chapters.</0> Drafts went to Dr. Bob in Akron, "where we had nothing but the warmest support," while in New York the chapters "got a real mauling" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Akronites liked the new Steps; in New York the debate "was doubled and redoubled" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

32534babfafa.t: <0>The stories.</0> Akron, the larger group with more case histories, produced eighteen stories with the help of a former newspaperman, Jim S.; New York produced ten, written by the members themselves (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

0656be03602c.t: <0>The title.</0> New York leaned to "Alcoholics Anonymous"; in Akron a considerable majority favored "The Way Out" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <1>How did Alcoholics Anonymous get its name? Was "The Way Out" the title?</1>

b59767f9af4e.t: <0>Akron and the book.</0> Bill (1957) recalls only warm support from Akron (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) says some Akron members "wanted no part of the book" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), quotes Dorothy S. M.: "For a time, we thought the whole Akron group might break up over the book." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), and comments that Bill "might have been assuming that his part of the stove was warmer." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

209360692eb8.t: <0>Why New York argued more.</0> <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) suggests Akron members may have been more attuned to Bill's spiritual ideas and Dr. Bob's influence carried them, while New York had more agnostics and skeptics (Pass It On, 1984). That is the 1984 authors' guess; the earlier texts don't give a reason.

f3ecb42fb608.t: <0>The meditation.</0> Bill later wondered why Wally and Annabelle G. sobered up so many in their Akron home while he and Lois sobered none in theirs. He wasn't sure: "Maybe they just hit the right cases." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). But he also said, "I sort of always felt that something was lost from A.A. when we stopped emphasizing the morning meditation." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). The same book adds that "it was all one Fellowship" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

5c139be7a2bc.t: No. A.A.'s own literature calls Al-Anon a separate fellowship. The Big Book's later-edition note says Al-Anon Family Groups, "Though it is entirely…

8957e8287a1f.t: No. A.A.'s own literature calls Al-Anon a separate fellowship. The Big Book's later-edition note says Al-Anon Family Groups, "Though it is entirely separate from Alcoholics Anonymous," uses the general principles of the A.A. program as a guide for those close to alcoholics (p. 121).

2a8bceba481d.t: Al-Anon didn't exist when the Big Book was written. The same note says it was formed "about thirteen years after this chapter was written" (p. 121); a later history gives 1951 as the year it took its present form (<0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0>, 1980).

1d576760b784.t: It grew out of A.A.'s own families. <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) credits Anne Smith, Lois W. and others with urging the Twelve Steps on nonalcoholic husbands and wives, and family groups formed in many places before 1951.

09fc3036d2ea.t: The 1939 text's own word to families is in Chapters 8 and 9; Chapter 8 is written in the voice of members' wives.

f5a51d6cfe54.t: Before there was any Al-Anon, the Big Book spoke to the people around the drinker: - Chapter 8, "To Wives," speaks in the voice of members' wives to the wives of men who drink (later histories say Bill W. wrote it: <0>Pass It On</0>, 1984; <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1>, 1980), and "What they say will apply to nearly everyone bound by ties of blood or affection to an alcoholic." (p. 104). It urges the wife to try the program herself (pp. 116–117). See <2>My husband (or wife) drinks. What does the Big Book say to do?</2> - Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward," is about the whole family once the drinking stops (pp. 122–135). See <3>What happens to the family after the drinking stops?</3> - Chapter 7 tells the member to keep helping a drinker's family even if the drinker doesn't respond: "The family should be offered your way of life." (p. 97). See <4>What does the Big Book say about helping the drinker's family?</4> - The house where Chapter 11's weekly meeting was held welcomed wives, who found "loving and understanding companionship among women who knew her problem" (p. 160).

9cefbba9ab29.t: <0>1947.</0> Writing about clubs, Bill W. suggested a club corporation be named something other than A.A., "Alanon," for example. A later note in P-17 says that name is no longer appropriate because of possible confusion with Al-Anon Family Groups, "formed about five years after this was written" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, note).

dee3267c72be.t: <0>1957.</0> <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>: Anne (Dr. Bob's wife) and Lois (Bill's), in their homes and travels, had "urged A.A.'s Twelve Steps upon nonalcoholic wives and husbands as a way of restoring family life to normal" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957), and Katie, the wife of a Chicago member, carried on that precedent. No one knows exactly when the first family group started; early ones in Toronto, Long Beach and Richmond were well established by 1950. At the 1955 convention Lois reported that family groups had grown from fewer than 100 in 1950 to nearly 700. In her words, the family groups "follow the lead of you in A.A." (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957), applying the same Steps to themselves.

d3ce2074547f.t: <0>1980.</0> <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1>: "Al-Anon Family Groups took its present form in 1951" (<2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2>, 1980), and Alateen formed in 1957 as part of Al-Anon. Both use the A.A. program with slight adaptation "but are entirely separate from A.A." (<3>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</3>, 1980).

edbb76dbbbc6.t: The Big Book's Appendix VI, "How to Get in Touch With A.A.," suggests that a relative or friend of an alcoholic "who shows no immediate interest in A.A." (Appendix VI, p. 573) write to Al-Anon Family Groups, and gives its world service office.

ae157b2e227c.t: <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16, 2018) calls Al-Anon "a fellowship entirely separate from A.A." (P-16, 2018). It reports a General Service Conference recommendation that "family" meetings not be listed in A.A. directories, partly because the word "family" might be confused with Al-Anon. It lists an A.A. Guideline, "Relationship Between A.A. and Al-Anon," which is not in our sources.
