ea7fa55230ed.t: What was the Alcoholic Foundation? | Recovery Starts

7fc69004566d.t: The Alcoholic Foundation was A.A.'s first board of trustees, set up in New York in 1938 as a small tax-free trust. It had both alcoholic and nonalcoholic…

22caf647671a.t: The Alcoholic Foundation was A.A.'s first board of trustees, set up in New York in 1938 as a small tax-free trust. It had both alcoholic and nonalcoholic trustees, with the nonalcoholics in the majority by one, and an alcoholic trustee who got drunk had to resign at once.

81d5864443ec.t: It was formed to receive money from wealthy donors for hospitals, missionaries and a book. That money never came, and for its first years the treasury was nearly empty. In time it became the custodian of A.A.'s funds, its central office, its book and its Traditions.

74ef369fbf3f.t: The name was chosen to sound important, and its charter allowed it to do almost anything about alcohol except lobby for Prohibition. Later the members felt "Foundation" suggested charity, paternalism and big money.

38c7d72e3673.t: After the General Service Conference began in 1951, the Foundation became accountable to it, and in 1954 it was renamed the General Service Board of Alcoholics Anonymous.

9c6eed1f1a2b.t: The 1939 Big Book doesn't name the Foundation. In 1946 the Traditions' Long Form described its trustees' role: "The trustees of The Alcoholic Foundation are, in effect, our A.A. General Service Committee." (P-17, 1946). They were "the custodians of our A.A. tradition" and received the voluntary contributions that kept up the office in New York (P-17, 1946). In today's Big Book the same sentence reads: "The trustees of the General Service Board are, in effect, our A.A. General Service Committee." (p. 565), and P-17 notes the change of name in a footnote (P-17).

6b0d37382358.t: Bill's 1946 essay on money says the gifts of "devoted friends" had "made possible The Alcoholic Foundation, the book Alcoholics Anonymous and our General Office" (P-17, 1946), and reports a new resolution of the trustees to decline gifts carrying any obligation (P-17, 1946).

4b5d06a49183.t: How it was formed (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)

03240f58ae08.t: After John D. Rockefeller, Jr. refused large sums in early 1938, his associates Willard Richardson, Frank Amos and A. LeRoy Chipman, with Bill's brother-in-law Dr. Leonard Strong, still hoped to find other donors (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). By the spring of 1938 they agreed on a tax-free charitable trust, so that contributors could deduct their gifts (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). It was given a resounding name and a wide charter, to research, educate and do almost anything in the field of alcohol "except lobby for Prohibition" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "Thus the Alcoholic Foundation got its name and its charter." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

15ce533ddb5d.t: A young lawyer, John Wood, couldn't write a legal definition of an alcoholic and a nonalcoholic, so they used a simple trust agreement instead of a formal charter (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The first board had five trustees: Richardson, Amos and Strong as nonalcoholics, and Dr. Bob and a New York member as alcoholics (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The New Yorker soon got drunk; that had been foreseen: "Drunkenness on the part of an alcoholic Trustee meant immediate resignation." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "It was May, 1938." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

12e07942f02b.t: The fund-raising failed and the treasury stayed empty (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The first money it handled was a small fund to help Bill and Lois after they lost their home in 1939, then the gifts after Rockefeller's 1940 dinner (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In 1940 it took over the book company, and later owned the Big Book in trust for the fellowship (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <0>How was the Big Book paid for and published (Works Publishing)?</0> After 1941 the groups' contributions went to it "for A.A. office expenses only" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

ee7217e3ca0a.t: From trusteeship to General Service Board

eec9247c51ff.t: Bill says that by the late 1940s "The Trustees had authority over our services; A.A. itself had no authority." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). After years of argument, the trustees agreed to an elected General Service Conference, which first met in April 1951 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). At its first session the Conference suggested renaming the Foundation, and after two more years of consideration the change was made (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). P-44 (Bill, describing events through 1955) gives the reason: "The word 'Foundation' stood for charity, paternalism and maybe big money." (P-44).

e76beb23f8e1.t: In 1969 Bill recalled that "the original Foundation, now our General Service Board, was chartered to do everything in the world with respect to alcohol except lobby for prohibition" (P-53). In the Twelve Concepts (1962) he wrote that "At first the Trustees of our new Foundation took jurisdiction over money matters only." (Service Manual, Concepts, 1962), and that "in 1954 it was renamed The General Service Board of Alcoholics Anonymous" (Service Manual, Concepts, 1962). See <0>Concept VI: what do the trustees of the General Service Board do?</0>

0042d3ea7dad.t: <0>When it began.</0> Bill (1957) says May 1938 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and the timeline in our later printing of his book agrees (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) says the trust was "formally implemented on August 11, 1938" (Pass It On, 1984).

995822609ab5.t: <0>Who sat on the first board.</0> Bill's nonalcoholic trustees are Richardson, Amos and Strong (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1> lists Richardson, Amos and the lawyer John Wood, with Dr. Bob and Bill R. as the alcoholics, and says Bill served on a separate advisory committee (Pass It On, 1984).

5264dc83c961.t: <0>When it was renamed.</0> P-17's footnote and the Concepts say 1954 (P-17; Service Manual, Concepts, 1962). Bill's 1957 narrative says two years after the first Conference's suggestion (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), without naming a year; the timeline in our later printing of his book puts it in October 1954 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). P-44 tells it as if the renaming came quickly after the first Conference (P-44).

66d68231de88.t: What does the Big Book mean by alcoholism as an illness? | Recovery Starts

6a848a237c75.t: The Big Book calls alcoholism an "illness" and a "malady": "we have come to believe it an illness" (p. 18). It is an illness of body and mind together, it…

bd34e2495ba7.t: What does the Big Book mean by alcoholism as an illness?

1b78b6dc429f.t: The Big Book calls alcoholism an "illness" and a "malady": "we have come to believe it an illness" (p. 18). It is an illness of body and mind together, it gets worse over time, and it is never cured (pp. xxvi, 22–24, 30, 85).

bf54c1666c85.t: The book places the heart of the problem in the mind, the alcoholic's lack of defense against the first drink (pp. 23–24), and beneath that in the spirit. Its answer is a spiritual one: "an illness which only a spiritual experience will conquer" (p. 44).

942c148ebc5d.t: The main text uses "illness," not "disease." In the first 164 pages "disease" appears once, as "spiritual disease," about resentment (p. 64). Calling alcoholism "a disease" comes in the personal stories (pp. 187, 416).

1a200e9cd6b8.t: Calling it an illness doesn't excuse anything in the book. The same pages say our troubles are "of our own making" (pp. 62, 103), and the illness is the reason to act, not a reason not to.

c0b58b8c319c.t: Across the forewords, Chapters 1–11 and the appendices, the book's word is <0>illness</0> (Chapters 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 10) or <1>malady</1> (Chapters 2, 5, 7, 10), and it often calls the alcoholic a <2>sick</2> man. The word <3>disease</3> appears once in those pages: "From it stem all forms of spiritual disease, for we have been not only mentally and physically ill, we have been spiritually sick" (p. 64). "It" there is resentment, not alcoholism.

f4ae69c69258.t: "Disease" for alcoholism does appear in the personal stories. In "Alcoholic Anonymous Number Three" (Part I), Bill W. and Dr. Bob tell the man in the bed, "No, you have a disease" (p. 187), and Bill speaks of being cured "of this terrible disease" (p. 191). That story dates itself to about 1954 ("Nineteen years ago last summer," p. 188). In "Acceptance Was the Answer" (Part II), a member writes that it helped him to see "alcoholism was a disease, not a moral issue" (p. 416). These are members' own words in the stories, not the program text.

035920877655.t: The first voice in the book is a doctor's. Dr. Silkworth's theory is that alcohol works on these drinkers like an allergy, setting off a craving that "never occurs in the average temperate drinker" (p. xxviii). The A.A. members who introduce him agree that "the body of the alcoholic is quite as abnormal as his mind" and add that "our bodies were sickened as well" (p. xxvi). They're careful about the theory itself: "As laymen, our opinion as to its soundness may, of course, mean little" (p. xxvi).

f6b39c6d67c9.t: Chapter 2 says the same from experience. Once the alcoholic takes any alcohol at all, "something happens, both in the bodily and mental sense" that makes it almost impossible to stop (pp. 22–23). Chapter 7 tells the helper to talk about "the conditions of body and mind which accompany it" (p. 92).

f091af09aad3.t: But the book is clear about where the real trouble lies. Since the illness can't start unless the alcoholic takes the first drink, "the main problem of the alcoholic centers in his mind, rather than in his body" (p. 23). Most alcoholics "have lost the power of choice in drink" (p. 24). "We are without defense against the first drink" (p. 24). There is "the obsession that somehow, someday, they will beat the game" (p. 23). Chapter 3 shows that mental blank spot at length, in Jim, the jay-walker and Fred (pp. 35–43).

3504619f3088.t: It's also an illness that gets worse and doesn't go away. Chapter 3 calls it a progressive illness in which we get worse, never better, and compares alcoholics to men who have lost their legs and never grow new ones (p. 30). "Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic" (p. 33). Even after recovery, "We are not cured of alcoholism" (p. 85).

84c29af193dd.t: The book goes one level deeper. Resentment is the chief offender, and "When the spiritual malady is overcome, we straighten out mentally and physically" (p. 64). Drinking itself "was but a symptom" (p. 64). The root, the book says, is "Selfishness—self-centeredness!" (p. 62). That's why the illness can only be met by a spiritual experience (p. 44) and why Dr. Silkworth says recovery requires "an entire psychic change" (p. xxix).

c81a2279572f.t: How the book uses the idea

fd7d547d4e8c.t: The illness idea runs through the book's practical advice: - <0>To the newcomer:</0> the helper should tell him how "you finally learned that you were sick" and "Continue to speak of alcoholism as an illness, a fatal malady" (p. 92). You can be frank about how hopeless the illness is because you have a solution to offer, and the more hopeless he feels, the more likely he is to take your suggestions (pp. 92, 94). - <1>To families:</1> wives are reminded that "alcoholism is an illness over which we could not possibly have had any power" (p. 118). They're told to treat the man as a sick person (p. 100) and to tell friends "the nature of his illness" (p. 115). - <2>To employers:</2> "explain alcoholism, the illness" (p. 142), and treat the man as gravely ill. - <3>In resentment:</3> the people who wronged us were "perhaps spiritually sick" too (p. 66), to be treated as a sick friend (p. 67).

dd25c905e7ca.t: The illness doesn't take away responsibility. The book that calls alcoholism an illness also says our troubles "are basically of our own making" (p. 62), and Chapter 7 ends: "After all, our problems were of our own making" (p. 103). The illness explains why willpower failed. It's the reason the program asks for so much action (pp. 58–103), not a reason to wait.

86f26f15f443.t: And the book doesn't claim to settle the medical question. On why the alcoholic reacts as he does, "Perhaps there never will be a full answer to these questions" (p. 22).

0147051eeb13.t: Chapter 5, "How It Works," on resentment as "spiritual disease": <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt5.pdf</0>

5d3c824bf01f.t: How do I know if I'm an alcoholic? | Recovery Starts

cbfc41ad1fc3.t: The Big Book leaves the answer to you. "We do not like to pronounce any individual as alcoholic, but you can quickly diagnose yourself." (p. 31).

32c096663eee.t: How do I know if I'm an alcoholic?

aca3a33bc436.t: The Big Book leaves the answer to you. "We do not like to pronounce any individual as alcoholic, but you can quickly diagnose yourself." (p. 31).

3b8c880f5e10.t: Its plainest test is in Chapter 4: "If, when you honestly want to, you find you cannot quit entirely, or if when drinking, you have little control over the amount you take, you are probably alcoholic." (p. 44).

2c037b1baa41.t: It describes three kinds of drinker, the moderate drinker, the hard drinker and the "real alcoholic," and the mark of the last is losing control once he starts (pp. 20–21). It also suggests two experiments: try some controlled drinking (pp. 31–32), or try leaving liquor alone for a year (p. 34).

20576155789b.t: A.A. itself doesn't diagnose anyone. Today's group pamphlet says A.A. does not "Make medical or psychological diagnoses or prognoses" (P-16, 2018).

b8162412a3c8.t: Chapter 2 sorts drinkers this way (pp. 20–22): - <0>The moderate drinker</0> has "little trouble in giving up liquor entirely if they have good reason for it" (p. 20); he can take it or leave it alone. - <1>The hard drinker</1> may harm his health, but given a strong enough reason, such as ill health, falling in love or a doctor's warning, he "can also stop or moderate, although he may find it difficult and troublesome and may even need medical attention" (p. 21). - <2>The real alcoholic</2> "may start off as a moderate drinker" but "at some stage of his drinking career he begins to lose all control of his liquor consumption, once he starts to drink" (p. 21). The chapter describes him for a page and a half, then adds that this "is by no means a comprehensive picture of the true alcoholic" (p. 22).

cd2236ac2f95.t: The chapter's center is the first drink. Once the alcoholic takes any alcohol, something happens "both in the bodily and mental sense" that makes it virtually impossible for him to stop (pp. 22–23); and at certain times "We are without defense against the first drink." (p. 24).

f6eef843876e.t: Chapter 3 is about who is and isn't "one of us": - <0>The first admission is inside.</0> "We learned that we had to fully concede to our innermost selves that we were alcoholics." (p. 30). - <1>The methods that didn't work</1> are listed at length: beer only, limiting the number of drinks, never drinking alone, never in the morning, switching drinks, swearing off, and more (p. 31). - <2>The barroom test.</2> "Step over to the nearest barroom and try some controlled drinking." (p. 31). Try to drink and stop abruptly, more than once. "It will not take long for you to decide, if you are honest with yourself about it." (p. 32). - <3>The year test.</3> "If anyone questions whether he has entered this dangerous area, let him try leaving liquor alone for one year." (p. 34). If he is a real alcoholic and far advanced, there is "scant chance of success" (p. 34). But passing the test doesn't settle it either: "Though you may be able to stop for a considerable period, you may yet be a potential alcoholic." (p. 34). - <4>Length and amount aren't the measure.</4> "To be gravely affected, one does not necessarily have to drink a long time nor take the quantities some of us have." (p. 33). Several early members of thirty or less had been drinking only a few years and found themselves "as helpless as those who had been drinking twenty years" (p. 33). - <5>Why it's hard to see.</5> Most members had been unwilling to admit they were real alcoholics: "No person likes to think he is bodily and mentally different from his fellows." (p. 30). The obsession that "somehow, someday he will control and enjoy his drinking" (p. 30) is the great obsession of every abnormal drinker.

2c5aca9545da.t: The chapter states its own aim: to help readers "determine, to their own satisfaction, whether they are one of us" (p. 34).

aac5e97302f2.t: In "The Doctor's Opinion," Dr. Silkworth names one thing all his types of alcoholic have in common: "they cannot start drinking without developing the phenomenon of craving" (p. xxx). He also describes the restlessness, irritability and discontent of the alcoholic who can't feel at ease without a drink (pp. xxviii–xxix).

808398c8c675.t: The book is careful that this is your conclusion, not someone else's. A member talking with a prospect should "be careful not to brand him as an alcoholic" (p. 92), and let him draw his own conclusion. Bill W.'s 1946 essay on membership says a newcomer can join A.A. "on the mere suspicion that he may be one" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). And A.A. today does not diagnose (P-16, 2018). A doctor may tell a patient he is alcoholic; the book welcomes that (p. 92).

0d733d033664.t: For the spouse's side, Chapter 8 sorts husbands into four kinds, from the heavy drinker to the one his family despairs of, and says the second kind, who can't stay on the wagon even when he wants to, shows "the earmarks of a real alcoholic" (p. 109). See <0>My husband (or wife) drinks. What does the Big Book say to do?</0>

16eaa54cc3a3.t: What does "willing to go to any length" refer to?

3d47426a0bbc.t: The phrase appears three times in the Big Book's main text, each time tied to the Steps. It's on p. 58, just before the Steps are listed, and twice in the pages on amends: p. 76, opening Steps Eight and Nine, and p. 79.

eb12a07796ac.t: On p. 58 it's something the reader decides for himself: "If you have decided you want what we have and are willing to go to any length to get it—then you are ready to take certain steps." (p. 58)

7ba292ad2e70.t: In the amends pages it means accepting what it costs <0>us</0>: "We may lose our position or reputation or face jail, but we are willing." (p. 79)

4714b236cff7.t: The very next paragraph limits it where other people would pay: we "are not to be the hasty and foolish martyr who would needlessly sacrifice others to save himself" (p. 79). Read in place, "any length" is about what we'll bear ourselves, not about what we may do to others.

4e72af2c9f2d.t: <0>1. Before the Steps (p. 58).</0> The sentence opens with a decision the reader makes: "If you have decided you want what we have" (p. 58). Being willing to go to any length is what makes him "ready to take certain steps" (p. 58). The next paragraph says how the writers met that willingness: "At some of these we balked." (p. 58) They looked for an easier, softer way and "could not" find one (p. 58).

d55119a37403.t: <0>2. Starting the amends (p. 76).</0> After Steps Six and Seven, the book turns to Steps Eight and Nine: "Now we go out to our fellows and repair the damage done in the past." (p. 76) If we lack the will to do it, "we ask until it comes" (p. 76). Then it looks back to p. 58: "Remember it was agreed at the beginning we would go to any lengths for victory over alcohol." (p. 76)

32c55640a5ec.t: <0>3. The hard amends (p. 79).</0> For amends that could cost a job or bring legal trouble, the book reminds the reader "that we have decided to go to any lengths to find a spiritual experience" (p. 79). We ask for strength to do the right thing "no matter what the personal consequences may be" (p. 79). "We must not shrink at anything." (p. 79)

e1b93f5da2c6.t: Notice the goal is named two ways: "victory over alcohol" (p. 76) and "a spiritual experience" (p. 79). The book uses both.

e9c2bdf43db5.t: The sentence after "We must not shrink at anything" begins: "Usually, however, other people are involved." (p. 79) So we are not to be the "foolish martyr" who sacrifices others to save himself (p. 79).

ec9483f9e013.t: The book gives an example. A member had remarried and hadn't paid alimony to his first wife, and she got a court order for his arrest. He was just getting back on his feet. Walking up to the judge would have been "impressive heroics" (p. 79). The members thought he should be willing to do that if necessary, "but if he were in jail he could provide nothing for either family" (p. 79). So he wrote to his first wife, admitted his faults, sent a little money, and told her he was "perfectly willing to go to jail if she insisted" (p. 79). She didn't.

296035642e73.t: The next page adds a rule of thumb: "Before taking drastic action which might implicate other people we secure their consent." (p. 80) In its second example, the man who had ruined a business rival talked it over with his wife and partner before he made it right in public (p. 80).

9c31b92afd43.t: The same limit runs through the chapter. Step Nine makes amends "except when to do so would injure them or others" (p. 59). On the Fifth Step, the book says "We have no right to save our own skin at another person's expense." (p. 74) It puts it in one line: "The rule is we must be hard on ourself, but always considerate of others." (p. 74)

b5bf362a4495.t: It complicates it. Quoted alone, "any length" sounds unlimited. In the book it is real: losing a job, a reputation or even freedom is named, and the reader is told not to shrink. But it's a willingness about the cost to ourselves, limited wherever someone else would be hurt. And willingness isn't the same as doing the drastic thing: the man in the alimony story was ready to go to jail, and the members suggested a letter instead.

f8ba6fa839b8.t: Chapter 6, "Into Action" (pp. 72–88), with the amends on pp. 76–83: <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt6.pdf</0>

c27dada4e880.t: Can we approach someone who is still drinking? | Recovery Starts

74339dfccaa0.t: Yes. Chapter 7 of the Big Book, "Working With Others," is written about approaching alcoholics who are still drinking. It tells you how to find them and…

0652f1173c6c.t: Can we approach someone who is still drinking?

c9b24043cc25.t: <0>Home</0> › <1>A.A. questions, from the books</1> › Step Twelve and carrying the message

d80a3a9c579c.t: Yes. Chapter 7 of the Big Book, "Working With Others," is written about approaching alcoholics who are still drinking. It tells you how to find them and when to go and see them (pp. 89–91).

1f1d7af08885.t: It sets conditions. There should be some sign the man wants to stop; if he doesn't, "don't waste time trying to persuade him" (p. 90). Don't deal with him while he's very drunk, and never force yourself on him (p. 90).

89592073ea73.t: That is how A.A. began. Bill W. reached Dr. Bob while Dr. Bob was still drinking, and the two of them found their third man strapped to a hospital bed (pp. 155–157).

96ec3fe143f5.t: <0>Go and find them.</0> "Perhaps you are not acquainted with any drinkers who want to recover" (p. 89). Ask doctors, ministers, priests or hospitals (p. 89). "Remember they are very ill" (p. 89).

f7167cf146a5.t: <0>Look for a man who wants to stop.</0> "If he does not want to stop drinking, don't waste time trying to persuade him" (p. 90). If there's any sign he wants to stop, talk first with the person closest to him (p. 90).

4f75223d6a9a.t: <0>Pick the moment.</0> Sometimes it's wise to wait until he goes on a binge (p. 90). "Don't deal with him when he is very drunk, unless he is ugly and the family needs your help" (p. 90). Wait for the end of the spree, or at least a lucid interval (p. 90).

02a157562ab1.t: <0>Don't push.</0> "If he does not want to see you, never force yourself upon him" (p. 90).

d3364ff03624.t: <0>Go while he's still shaky.</0> "Call on him while he is still jittery. He may be more receptive when depressed" (p. 91). If he needs a hospital, he should have one (p. 91).

a16988ec5a1a.t: The rest of the chapter assumes the work happens in hard places: "innumerable trips to police courts, sanitariums, hospitals, jails and asylums" (p. 97), a drunk who may "smash the furniture in your home" (p. 97). "You should not hesitate to visit the most sordid spot on earth on such an errand" (p. 102).

d1e19688622d.t: How the first members did it

8376d8a33e1d.t: Chapter 11 tells the story without names (footnotes added in later editions name the people). A man sober only a few months, alone in a strange city, phoned a clergyman to find an alcoholic to talk to (pp. 154–155). The man he found was "nearing the nadir of alcoholic despair" (p. 155) and went on "a roaring bender" after their first talk (p. 155). A footnote identifies this as Bill's first visit with Dr. Bob (p. 155).

eb55ef4c73e4.t: Then the two of them called a hospital and asked the head nurse for "a first class alcoholic prospect" (p. 156). She described a man who had just beaten up two nurses and was "strapped down tight" (p. 156). One of them answered, "Put him in a private room. We'll be down" (p. 157). That man became A.A. number three (p. 156 footnote; p. 158).

7b9406bf2ed8.t: The book ends by telling the reader to ask, each morning, "what you can do each day for the man who is still sick" (Ch. 11, p. 164).

4fd7c0b22c49.t: The book doesn't tell you to chase everyone who drinks. It says the opposite about a man who doesn't want to stop (p. 90), and that it's "a waste of time to keep chasing a man who cannot or will not work with you" (p. 96). Its reason isn't to give up on him: leaving him alone may convince him he can't recover by himself (p. 96), and the time is better spent on "some other alcoholic" who is ready (p. 96). See: <0>What if the person I'm helping doesn't want it?</0>

4b9aac9e58f6.t: Nor does the book say "wait until he hits bottom" in so many words. Waiting for the end of a binge is about timing the visit (p. 90), not a reason to stay away.

93aed758ee80.t: Chapter 7, "Working With Others" (pp. 89–103), free from A.A.: <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt7.pdf</0>

8c85cd5d3d58.t: Page numbers are from the fourth edition (2001). The Preface says the program chapters have been "left largely untouched" since 1939 (p. xi), but our sources have no first edition to compare page numbers against.

28ccd0f901b5.t: Does the Big Book say to avoid bars and drinkers? | Recovery Starts

4e2897ee8b8d.t: No. It says nearly the opposite: "our rule is not to avoid a place where there is drinking, if we have a legitimate reason for being there" (p. 101). That…

e325b8b4fe97.t: Does the Big Book say to avoid bars and drinkers?

4751b1a5eeb6.t: <0>Home</0> › <1>A.A. questions, from the books</1> › Sayings: is it in the books?

7047b77913fa.t: No. It says nearly the opposite: "our rule is not to avoid a place where there is drinking, if we have a legitimate reason for being there" (p. 101). That includes bars, nightclubs, weddings and parties (p. 101).

c1413f3b11f5.t: It attaches two conditions: that you're spiritually fit (p. 100), and that your reason for going is a good one, not "to steal a little vicarious pleasure" (pp. 101–102).

9c184463f95e.t: If you're shaky, don't go: "you had better work with another alcoholic instead!" (p. 102).

398a23faa818.t: It says shielding an alcoholic from temptation doesn't work (p. 101), and it warns against withdrawing from friends who drink (p. 102).

b3c2cbcc6fa5.t: The passage comes at the end of "Working With Others." Read in order:

f4daa9fe6045.t: <0>The qualifier first.</0> "Assuming we are spiritually fit, we can do all sorts of things alcoholics are not supposed to do" (p. 100).

628e0493092b.t: <0>The usual advice, listed and rejected.</0> People had said we must not go where liquor is served, must shun friends who drink, must avoid films with drinking scenes, must not go into bars (pp. 100–101). "Our experience shows that this is not necessarily so" (p. 101). An alcoholic who can't meet these conditions "still has an alcoholic mind" (p. 101), and the book jokes that even the Greenland Ice Cap wouldn't be safe (p. 101).

035bfe96d1d1.t: <0>Why shielding fails.</0> "In our belief any scheme of combating alcoholism which proposes to shield the sick man from temptation is doomed to failure" (p. 101). A man who shields himself may manage for a while, but "usually winds up with a bigger explosion than ever" (p. 101).

d32a844d2fd5.t: <0>The rule, with its condition.</0> Don't avoid a place where there is drinking "if we have a legitimate reason for being there" (p. 101). Ask yourself each time whether you have "any good social, business, or personal reason for going," or are hoping for vicarious pleasure (pp. 101–102).

6fcb670e00c6.t: <0>The motive.</0> "Be sure you are on solid spiritual ground before you start and that your motive in going is thoroughly good" (p. 102). "Do not think of what you will get out of the occasion. Think of what you can bring to it" (p. 102).

44f379662f4b.t: <0>If you're shaky.</0> "But if you are shaky, you had better work with another alcoholic instead!" (p. 102).

e110339cad75.t: <0>Friends who drink.</0> Go along with a friend who wants to eat in a bar, and don't ask your friends to change their habits for you (p. 102). "Don't start to withdraw again just because your friends drink liquor" (p. 102).

f73a735dcb68.t: <0>The purpose behind all of it.</0> "Your job now is to be at the place where you may be of maximum helpfulness to others" (p. 102).

22e55918df3d.t: <0>Liquor at home, and attitude.</0> Some members keep liquor at home, some don't; each family decides (pp. 102–103). "We are careful never to show intolerance or hatred of drinking as an institution" (p. 103).

ff93ae33bcc3.t: Chapter 8, written to wives: "We never, never try to arrange a man's life so as to shield him from temptation" (p. 120). "Make him feel absolutely free to come and go as he likes" (p. 120).

c5c70a04a42e.t: Chapter 11 shows what "if you are shaky" looks like. A man sober a few months, alone in a hotel with a lively bar down the lobby, felt the old pull toward "that first drink" (p. 154). He turned away from the bar, went to a church directory and phoned a clergyman to find an alcoholic to help (pp. 154–155). That call led him to Dr. Bob (p. 155 footnote). He didn't test himself in the bar. He went to find a drunk.

2f2b8f361fba.t: It doesn't say a newcomer should start going to bars, or that anyone should go somewhere drinking is happening without a reason. Every permission in the passage rests on being spiritually fit and having a good reason, and the advice for anyone unsure is to work with another alcoholic instead (p. 102).

de2a21db4bbe.t: 1939 (the footnote naming Dr. Bob was added in later editions)

38d4876f26d0.t: "Bedevilments" is on page 52 of the Big Book, in Chapter 4, "We Agnostics." It's the book's word for a list of eight troubles the writers had with living…

a6c85de895a0.t: "Bedevilments" is on page 52 of the Big Book, in Chapter 4, "We Agnostics." It's the book's word for a list of eight troubles the writers had with living (p. 52).

903d1b8155a5.t: The list, in the book's order: trouble with personal relationships; couldn't control our emotional natures; a prey to misery and depression; couldn't make a living; a feeling of uselessness; full of fear; unhappy; couldn't seem to be of real help to other people (p. 52).

b9a6c6e503d0.t: Drinking isn't on the list. A page earlier the book says the members' stories, "Leaving aside the drink question," tell why living was so unsatisfactory (p. 51).

e698c29fb5d3.t: In its place the list is part of an argument to the agnostic reader: the modern age drops ideas that don't work for ones that do, so why not do the same with these problems? The answer follows: "Our ideas did not work. But the God idea did." (p. 52) The context confirms what the list says and shows what it's there for.

2307f968697f.t: Pages 51–53 make one argument, in steps: 1. <0>The world changes its mind when the evidence is in.</0> Material progress in the last century came from the spirit of scientific inquiry (p. 51). People once thought a round earth preposterous; newspapers were afraid to print the Wright brothers' flight; thirty years later air travel was ordinary (pp. 51–52). 2. <1>Are we doing the opposite about the spirit?</1> "Are not some of us just as biased and unreasonable about the realm of the spirit as were the ancients about the realm of the material?" (p. 51) The age is marked by the readiness to "throw away the theory or gadget which does not work for something new which does" (p. 52). 3. <2>Then apply that to our own lives.</2> "We had to ask ourselves why we shouldn't apply to our human problems this same readiness to change our point of view." (p. 52) 4. <3>The list.</3> The eight troubles above, ending with a question: wasn't "a basic solution of these bedevilments more important than whether we should see newsreels of lunar flight? Of course it was." (p. 52) 5. <4>What they saw work.</4> "When we saw others solve their problems by a simple reliance upon the Spirit of the Universe, we had to stop doubting the power of God." (p. 52) They had been relying on self-sufficiency; when others showed them that "God-sufficiency" worked, they felt like the people who had said the Wrights would never fly (pp. 52–53).

7a7a215fddeb.t: A few things the text shows: - <0>It's "we."</0> The list is the writers describing themselves: "We were having trouble with personal relationships" (p. 52). The book doesn't present it here as a test for the reader or name it a symptom of anything. - <1>It's about living, not drinking.</1> The book sets drink aside on purpose in this stretch (p. 51). The list is what was wrong with life itself. - <2>It ends with other people.</2> The last item is that "we couldn't seem to be of real help to other people" (p. 52). The book's chapter on Step Twelve later says "To be helpful is our only aim" (p. 89). - <3>It's offered as a reason, not a verdict.</3> The chapter is trying to persuade agnostic readers, as the writers once were, to give the spiritual side of life the fair hearing the writers admit they never gave it (p. 50). It says plainly it is arguing: "we are at pains to tell why we think our present faith is reasonable" (p. 53).

061bfa59285a.t: Does the context change the reading?

fb9ee318187d.t: It confirms it. The bedevilments are what the list says: troubles with people, feelings, work, fear and usefulness. Read in its place, the list is one step in an argument that ends with the writers dropping self-sufficiency for reliance on God, the step they say they had resisted out of prejudice.

f5ca46fb6872.t: Is "your best thinking got you here" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

908bd9f83aeb.t: No. The saying isn't in the Big Book or anywhere else in our sources.

5f43c1792ca1.t: Is "your best thinking got you here" in the Big Book?

0c9ef2964912.t: No. The saying isn't in the Big Book or anywhere else in our sources.

86f264054a11.t: Part of its idea is in the program text: the alcoholic's sound reasoning "failed to hold us in check" (p. 37), self-knowledge didn't keep Bill or Fred sober (pp. 7, 42), and "Our ideas did not work. But the God idea did." (p. 52).

a60acf3a8769.t: But the text doesn't tell anyone to stop thinking. It says "Logic is great stuff" (p. 53), reasons with the doubter for pages, and in Step Eleven says "God gave us brains to use" (p. 86). What it distrusts is the alcoholic's thinking about drink, thinking driven by self-will, and reason treated as the last word (pp. 49, 54).

3630268aa7fb.t: All our sources were searched for "best thinking," "thinking got," "thinking brought," "stinking thinking" and "your thinking," with page breaks joined. None of them turns up the saying, in the program text, the stories of any edition, the pamphlets or the history books.

cf201f30f984.t: Where the text agrees with the saying

2a88d56283b8.t: The Big Book does say, more than once, that the alcoholic's own mind couldn't get him sober:

60a344730109.t: <0>Reason lost to the first drink.</0> "Our sound reasoning failed to hold us in check. The insane idea won out." (p. 37).

bacc8a4f5444.t: <0>Self-knowledge failed.</0> After treatment Bill thought "Surely this was the answer—self-knowledge." (p. 7), and then drank again (p. 7). Fred, after his relapse, "saw that will power and self-knowledge would not help in those strange mental blank spots" (p. 42). The chapter says the real alcoholic "will be absolutely unable to stop drinking on the basis of self-knowledge" (p. 39).

2b234e43382e.t: <0>Their own ideas.</0> "Our ideas did not work. But the God idea did." (p. 52). Earlier the same chapter admits that "we agnostics and atheists chose to believe that our human intelligence was the last word" (p. 49).

c486df2e7111.t: <0>Self-will.</0> The alcoholic is "an extreme example of self-will run riot" (p. 62), and "our troubles, we think, are basically of our own making" (p. 62).

728261346ff0.t: <0>Reason has limits.</0> "Hence, we saw that reason isn't everything." (p. 54). Reason as most of us use it isn't entirely dependable, "though it emanate from our best minds" (pp. 54–55). The "best minds" there are the experts who once proved men could never fly (p. 55), not the alcoholic in particular.

d8b5dedd64c8.t: Where the text disagrees with how the saying is often used

a93cc8da5ec6.t: When the saying is used to mean "don't trust your mind, don't think, just do what you're told," the program text says otherwise:

f29b7725300e.t: <0>Reason is a gift.</0> "Logic is great stuff. We liked it. We still like it." (p. 53). "It is not by chance we were given the power to reason" (p. 53). The writers say they wouldn't be satisfied with a proposal that didn't lend itself to reasonable approach (p. 53), and they spend Chapter 4 giving reasons (pp. 48–55).

90b48717e7b0.t: <0>Thinking, cleaned up, is used every day.</0> Step Eleven's morning: ask God to direct our thinking, "especially asking that it be divorced from self-pity, dishonest or self-seeking motives" (p. 86). "Under these conditions we can employ our mental faculties with assurance, for after all God gave us brains to use." (p. 86). "Our thought-life will be placed on a much higher plane when our thinking is cleared of wrong motives." (p. 86).

0cd2a04003ec.t: <0>Bill's way of checking his thinking.</0> "I was to test my thinking by the new God-consciousness within." (p. 13).

c6f32154fe54.t: <0>Where the thinking goes wrong.</0> Apart from self-will (above), the book locates the trouble in drink: the alcoholic "is often perfectly sensible and well balanced concerning everything except liquor" (p. 21). "However intelligent we may have been in other respects, where alcohol has been involved, we have been strangely insane." (p. 38). Chapter 10 calls him "a victim of crooked thinking, directly caused by the action of alcohol on his brain" (p. 140).

85d7e9bae966.t: The saying holds a real point from the book: the alcoholic's own reasoning, will power and self-knowledge didn't stop him drinking, and self-will got him into trouble. The book doesn't conclude that thinking is the enemy. It says the mind fails on the subject of the first drink and when it is run by selfish motives, and that the answer is a Power greater than ourselves, after which the reader is told to use his brains with assurance (p. 86). See: <0>Is "it's not a drinking problem, it's a thinking problem" in the Big Book?</0>

d3a8cff2310f.t: Yes. Bill W. wrote the chapters through 1938, reading them to the New York group and sending them to Dr. Bob in Akron for comment. The first two chapters…

1355d2e2c961.t: Was there a draft of the Big Book before 1939?

7f5ec4a31f9b.t: Yes. Bill W. wrote the chapters through 1938, reading them to the New York group and sending them to Dr. Bob in Akron for comment. The first two chapters were copied in mid-1938 to use in a fund-raising prospectus.

2c831131c492.t: When text and stories were done, about the end of January 1939, 400 copies of the whole book were duplicated and sent out for comment, each stamped "Loan Copy." Bill calls them mimeographs; later books call them Multilith copies.

1c0f37ab52fa.t: The comments changed the book. A psychiatrist persuaded Bill to turn "you must" into "we ought," a Catholic committee suggested that "Heaven" at the end of Bill's story become "Utopia," and Bill's printer's copy was a marked-up loan copy with many small corrections. A 1984 biography adds that a professional editor cut the manuscript by at least a third.

91a4f2960f91.t: No copy of any draft is in our sources, so it can't show what the earlier versions said beyond these reported changes.

f01e380638d4.t: What the Big Book itself shows

71b5932ab369.t: The book points to its own revisions only after publication. Appendix II says "our first printing gave many readers the impression" that a spiritual experience had to be sudden and spectacular (p. 567), and was added to correct that. The Foreword to the First Edition in today's book is printed "as it appeared in the first printing of the first edition in 1939" (p. xiii). Bill's story ends: "Most of us feel we need look no further for Utopia." (p. 16), the word the Catholic reviewers suggested (see below). See <0>What changed between the four editions of the Big Book?</0>

ad8be04fe08a.t: Bill began the book in the spring of 1938 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). By the time the fund-raising campaign was under way he had written his own story and roughed out the second chapter; "Mimeographed copies of these two chapters were part of the paraphernalia for the money-raising operation" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). P-44 (Bill, describing events through 1955) says the same: copies of the two chapters "were used as part of the prospectus" (P-44). A Harper editor read those two chapters and offered to publish (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <0>How was the Big Book paid for and published (Works Publishing)?</0>

f73d76f5c060.t: Bill dictated rough drafts to the secretary, Ruth Hock, read each chapter at the weekly New York meeting, and sent copies to Dr. Bob in Akron (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In New York the chapters "got a real mauling," and he redictated them again and again (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In Akron, <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) says, one member remembered going over drafts with Dr. Bob among a "chosen few," while another remembered them being read at the Akron meeting (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

1851ad1560aa.t: With the text and stories finished in late January 1939, someone asked: "How do we know for sure that this book will be widely acceptable to everybody?" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). So "Four hundred mimeograph copies of the book were made and sent to everyone we could think of who might be concerned with the problem of alcoholism." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "Each mimeograph was stamped 'Loan Copy' in order to protect our coming copyright." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). While they waited, the arguments over the title and the Twelve Steps went on (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

38ae4e1285f9.t: What came back (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957): - A Montclair psychiatrist, Dr. Howard, "pointed out that the text of our book was too full of the words 'you' and 'must.'" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The aim was "to put our fellowship on a 'we ought' basis instead of a 'you must' basis." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill gave in, and Dr. Silkworth and Dr. Tiebout gave similar advice (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). - Dr. Harry Emerson Fosdick saw a prepublication copy early in 1939 and promised a review (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). - The Catholic Committee on Publications in New York suggested improvements to the section on meditation and prayer, and one real change, at the end of Bill's story: "Don't you think that Bill W. could change that word 'Heaven' to 'Utopia'?" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

710ae6c5f34a.t: The printer's copy was one of the mimeographs with all the corrections written in by Henry P. (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). There were "few large changes but the small ones were very numerous" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

6611b809fac6.t: Some loan copies went on doing their work. Dr. Tiebout gave one to his patient Marty, who after a second reading came to a meeting (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill handed one to a lawyer in Cleveland, whose client read it and went to Akron (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> says a member's sister "went to Chicago with a Multilith copy of the Big Book" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), which led to a woman member there.

1628a5c15f27.t: <0>Pass It On</0> says the first two chapters "were Multilithed immediately" for the 1938 money-raising (Pass It On, 1984), and that "By the end of January 1939, the manuscript was ready for preliminary distribution; 400 copies were Multilithed" (Pass It On, 1984). It adds details not in Bill's 1957 account: - "The Doctor's Opinion" was added after Dr. Esther Richards of Johns Hopkins suggested an introduction by a leading physician (Pass It On, 1984). See <1>What is "The Doctor's Opinion," and who wrote it?</1> - "Final editing of the book was done by Tom Uzzell" of New York University, who "cut the book by at least a third" (Pass It On, 1984), "some say half," from 800 pages to 400 (Pass It On, 1984). - A line in Chapter 5 now reading "followed our path" had read "directions" in the earlier manuscript (Pass It On, 1984).

beadeca8e7d9.t: <0>Mimeograph or Multilith.</0> Bill (1957) and P-44 say mimeographed (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; P-44); <1>Pass It On</1> and <2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2> say Multilith (Pass It On, 1984; Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Both are duplicating processes; the number, 400, agrees.

10c0ae18483c.t: <0>How much was cut.</0> Bill (1957) mentions only many small corrections (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); <1>Pass It On</1> reports a cut of a third or more by an outside editor (Pass It On, 1984). Our sources have no draft to check either.

c695503ed5d0.t: <0>Earlier wording.</0> The only earlier wordings our sources reports are "Heaven" for "Utopia" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), "you must" for "we ought" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), "directions" for "path" (Pass It On, 1984), and the reconstructed first draft of the Steps (see <1>How were the Twelve Steps written?</1>). Claims about other passages in a pre-publication manuscript can't be confirmed from our sources.

c1e1111fdaf1.t: There have been four editions: 1939, 1955, 1976 and 2001 (p. xi). In all of them the first part of the book, "describing the A.A. recovery program, has…

ebc7189600bd.t: What changed between the four editions of the Big Book?

e1a245ac7a86.t: <0>Home</0> › <1>A.A. questions, from the books</1> › About the sources themselves

3fb8f5ae7e5c.t: There have been four editions: 1939, 1955, 1976 and 2001 (p. xi). In all of them the first part of the book, "describing the A.A. recovery program, has been left largely untouched" (p. xi), and "The Doctor's Opinion" has been kept intact (p. xi).

8278ffaf57ca.t: The chief change each time was in the personal stories: stories were added, edited and dropped so the book would "represent the current membership" (p. xii) and reach more alcoholics.

aea4423fb4e0.t: The 1955 edition also added the appendices, the Twelve Traditions and directions for contacting A.A. (p. xi). The 2001 edition added the Twelve Concepts (p. xii). Each edition added its own foreword.

cedfe0755296.t: "Largely" is the honest word. Footnotes have been added to the 1939 chapters, and small details in the text follow the edition, such as the number of stories on p. 29. Our sources have only the fourth edition, so it can't show a line-by-line comparison with 1939.

f057ccd9cdcc.t: The Preface to the fourth edition explains why: because the book has become "the basic text for our Society" and helped so many recover, "there exists strong sentiment against any radical changes being made in it" (p. xi). So the program chapters were left largely untouched in the 1955, 1976 and 2001 revisions, and "The Doctor's Opinion" was "kept intact, just as it was originally written in 1939" (p. xi). The Foreword to the First Edition is reprinted "as it appeared in the first printing of the first edition in 1939" (p. xiii).

f198f28f3eec.t: Later accounts put it more strongly. Bill W., announcing the second edition at the 1955 convention, said "the old familiar text of the book stands unchanged" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) says the original text of the first 11 chapters was unchanged in 1955 (Pass It On, 1984). <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1> (2003) says the first 164 pages "have remained largely unchanged" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). The Preface's "largely" is the more careful word, and the text bears it out (see below).

e1df651658fd.t: <0>First edition, April 1939</0> (p. xi). Sixteen printings, 1939 to 1955 (p. iv). More than 300,000 copies circulated (p. xi). It even changed between printings: - The title page first described "More Than One Hundred Men," changed by the second printing to "Thousands of Men and Women" (Pass It On, 1984). - One story, "Lone Endeavor," "appeared only in first printing of first edition" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). - Bill (1969) recalled that an early printing "expressed great concern lest we be flooded with more people than we could take care of" (P-53), out of fear that "so-called undesirable people" (P-53) might come, and said "that part of the book was eliminated after the first printing" (P-53). P-53's footnote points to the first-edition foreword's worry about "the overwhelming number of personal appeals" (P-53), a line today's reprint of that foreword still carries (p. xiii); our sources can't show which passage Bill had in mind. - Appendix II, "Spiritual Experience," says "our first printing gave many readers the impression" (p. 567) that the personality change had to be sudden and spectacular, and corrects it, so it was written after the first printing; the Preface says the appendices entered the book with the second edition (p. xi). Our sources don't say exactly when Appendix II was written.

dbe733226784.t: <0>Second edition, 1955</0> (p. xi). More than 1,150,500 copies (p. xi). It added "the appendices, the Twelve Traditions, and the directions for getting in touch with A.A." (p. xi), and a new foreword describing the fellowship "as it was in 1955" (p. xv). The story section was rebuilt and divided into three parts, "Pioneers of A.A.," "They Stopped in Time" and "They Lost Nearly All" (pp. xi–xii). Bill's story, Dr. Bob's and one other were kept intact; three were edited (one retitled); two were rewritten under new titles; thirty new stories were added (pp. xi–xii). <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) adds that Bill made a point of including the story of A.A. number three, Bill D., who hadn't written one for 1939 (Pass It On, 1984). <2>Experience, Strength and Hope</2> (2003) quotes Bill's 1954 guidance: the audience "is people who are coming to Alcoholics Anonymous now" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003).

f4866667ef1d.t: <0>Third edition, 1976</0> (p. xi). About 19,550,000 copies in all formats (p. xi). Part I was left unchanged; Part II kept nine stories and added eight; Part III kept eight and added five (p. xii). A new foreword reported more than a million members in over 90 countries (p. xxii).

2ea3d9604639.t: <0>Fourth edition, 2001.</0> It added the Twelve Concepts for World Service (p. xii), now Appendix VII (p. 574), and a new foreword (p. xxiii). In the stories, Part I gained one new story and two moved from Part III, and lost six; Part II kept six, added eleven and dropped eleven; Part III added twelve and dropped eight, besides the two moved (p. xii). The book now has forty-two stories (p. xii). <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1> (2003) says the 1997 General Service Conference asked for the edition, that more than 1,200 manuscripts came in, and that the changes "were the most extensive yet" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). The new stories, the fourth-edition foreword says, represent a membership whose "characteristics—of age, gender, race, and culture—have widened and have deepened" (p. xxiii).

f3951c2ecc0a.t: The fourth edition shows its own seams: - <0>Footnotes.</0> Several notes carry later dates: membership figures for 2006 and 2007 (pp. 16, 162) and a 2003 survey of members' ages (p. 34). Others were plainly written later: a note on Al-Anon, formed "about thirteen years after this chapter was written" (p. 121), and one identifying Bill and Dr. Bob, who "later became co-founders of A.A." (p. 155). Chapter 8 now carries a note that it was "Written in 1939, when there were few women in A.A." (p. 104). Our copy is the thirty-second printing, December 2013 (p. iv), and the fourth-edition foreword has a note dated 2013 (p. xxiii), so notes are updated between printings, not only between editions. - <1>The story count.</1> Chapter 2 says the directions "are followed by forty-two personal experiences" (p. 29), the fourth edition's number. <2>Experience, Strength and Hope</2> (2003) says the first edition had 29 stories (Dr. Bob's and 28 others), so that sentence can't have read "forty-two" in 1939. Our sources have no first edition to show what it said.

7b26fc78e60b.t: <0>"Unchanged" or "largely untouched."</0> Bill (1955, printed 1957) and <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) say the main text was unchanged; the Preface (2001) and <2>Experience, Strength and Hope</2> (2003) say "largely" (p. xi). The examples above favour "largely."

dd0f0344df1f.t: <0>Second-edition stories.</0> The Preface counts three first-edition stories kept intact, including "Bill's Story," which is Chapter 1 (p. xi); <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1> says "Only two stories from the first edition were retained intact" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003), perhaps counting only the story section. Its own figures (two intact, three edited, two rewritten, 30 new) add up to 37, as the Preface's do without Bill's story, yet it gives the total as 38 stories (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). <2>Pass It On</2> (1984) counts six carried over besides Bill's and Dr. Bob's, and 30 new (Pass It On, 1984).

06208f838022.t: <0>Fourth-edition stories.</0> The Preface's figures add up to 24 new stories (p. xii); <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1> says 25 new stories and 17 kept from the third edition (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). Both arrive at forty-two. Our sources don't explain either difference of one.

439d9d22bd37.t: <0>When the fourth edition appeared.</0> The copyright page says first printing October 2001 (p. iv); the fourth-edition foreword says it "came off press in November 2001" (p. xxiii).

6fd4e4d3eb86.t: Because the program text has hardly changed, a reader of any edition is reading essentially the same 1939 words in Chapters 1 to 11. Whether the page numbers match from edition to edition, our sources can't check; it holds only the fourth edition. The stories are another matter: a story quoted from one edition may not exist in another. That's one reason the stories are read as members' experience rather than program text; see <0>Are the personal stories part of the A.A. program?</0> The stories dropped from the first three editions are collected in <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1> (2003).

40e20c32f521.t: On copyright, the <0>A.A. Service Manual</0> (2024–2026 edition) says the first and second editions are in the public domain in the United States only, while the third and fourth remain under copyright (A.A. Service Manual).

f97d49f3104b.t: What is a group business meeting for? | Recovery Starts

4eb5ac22dbe5.t: A business meeting is where a group looks after its own affairs: choosing its trusted servants, handling its money, planning its meetings, and hearing…

e0e16ad42a5f.t: What is a group business meeting for?

ab88a0041367.t: <0>Home</0> › <1>A.A. questions, from the books</1> › The Traditions

7ede665b7981.t: A business meeting is where a group looks after its own affairs: choosing its trusted servants, handling its money, planning its meetings, and hearing from the people who serve it. P-16 (2018) lists these jobs.

5635b9019cdb.t: The Long Form doesn't use the phrase "business meeting," but it covers everything such a meeting decides. A group answers only to "its own conscience" in its own affairs (p. 563), its leaders "do not govern" (p. 565), it pays its own way and avoids piling up money (p. 564), and its one purpose is carrying the message to the alcoholic who still suffers (p. 563).

c9a3a6e60f6d.t: So the Traditions are the guide for a business meeting. P-16 says the same: the spiritual nature of the Fellowship, "embodied in our Traditions and Concepts," gives ample guidance (P-16, 2018, p. 30).

d9b01e048cf2.t: What the Long Form gives a business meeting to work with (1946)

004daa68c6d0.t: <0>Whose decision it is.</0> For its group purpose there is but one ultimate authority, "a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience" (p. 563). In its own affairs each group "should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience" (p. 563).

269ddee305f0.t: <0>When to look beyond the group.</0> If its plans affect neighbouring groups, they should be consulted; and nobody should take action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole without conferring with the trustees (p. 563). "On such issues our common welfare is paramount" (p. 563).

4c482a4a2017.t: <0>The money.</0> The group is supported by its own members' voluntary contributions (p. 564). Large gifts and contributions with strings are unwise, and treasuries that keep growing "beyond prudent reserves" for no stated A.A. purpose are a concern (p. 564).

b31f2f6f1260.t: <0>The officers.</0> A group needs "the least possible organization," rotating leadership is best, and a small group may elect a secretary, a large one a rotating committee (p. 565). They are servants: "They derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern" (p. 565).

7dded1441a08.t: <0>What's off the table.</0> Going into business, affiliating with or endorsing anything outside A.A. (p. 564), and taking positions on outside controversial issues (p. 565).

a31d237d17f0.t: <0>What everything serves.</0> "But one primary purpose — that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers" (p. 563).

d1eba9f6df9d.t: Most groups, Bill wrote, didn't even choose leaders; they used rotating committees for their simple affairs, which "have only the authorization to serve, never to command" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38). Each committee "carries out what it believes to be the wishes of its group" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38). Committees that tried to discipline members, write detailed rules or judge people's morals achieved nothing lasting (P-17, p. 38).

930e44975623.t: A small historical note: in 1947 Bill used the phrase "business meetings" for the meetings of a <0>club corporation</0> electing its directors, while "strictly A.A. matters" stayed with the groups (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, p. 21; "Money", 1946, p. 29). See <1>What did Bill W. say about clubs and A.A.?</1>

4e719ae45e08.t: What P-16 says a business meeting does (2018, dated)

d9717f1297a2.t: <0>When.</0> Usually monthly or quarterly, called by the chairperson or another officer, before or after a regular meeting (P-16, 2018, p. 30).

f8830b53f655.t: <0>Who votes.</0> A group may ask that "only home group members participate or vote" (P-16, 2018, p. 30).

e8f08a7cdb0a.t: <0>What it covers.</0> Electing new officers; scheduling meetings; the treasurer's financial reports; reports from the general service representative and other servants; and "apportioning excess funds" among the local intergroup, GSO, and the area and district (P-16, 2018, p. 30). P-16 also describes business sessions as a place for officers' reports "to discuss group affairs and obtain group guidance" (P-16, 2018, p. 14).

1d04756bc6dd.t: <0>How.</0> Members get all the relevant facts before a vote; reaching an informed group conscience takes time; and "minority, or dissenting, views" must be heard, since they may even turn the tide (P-16, 2018, p. 30). P-16 describes group conscience as aiming at "substantial unanimity" (P-16, 2018, p. 28), and says its result "rests on more than a 'yes' or 'no' count" (P-16, 2018, p. 29).

392654bb23b5.t: <0>What it isn't.</0> Some groups tried Robert's Rules of Order and found members too intimidated to speak; the Traditions and Concepts give "ample guidance" (P-16, 2018, p. 30).

d655607e9636.t: P-16 isn't entirely consistent on how decisions are made. Its introduction says groups "function as a democracy, with all plans for group action approved by the majority voice" (P-16, 2018, p. 10), while its group-conscience section asks for substantial unanimity. See <0>Is group conscience a majority vote?</0>

effb353fe6a0.t: The Long Form doesn't prescribe a format or an agenda. It settles who decides (the group's own conscience, under God as expressed there), who doesn't (any officer, committee or outside body), what the money is for, and what the group exists to do. A business meeting run on those lines is the Traditions at work in one group.

050160088a67.t: What part did Carl Jung play in A.A.'s beginning? | Recovery Starts

da0eba887bb7.t: The Swiss psychiatrist Carl Jung treated an American alcoholic, later identified as Rowland H., in the early 1930s. When the man relapsed, Jung told him…

8371cdc9b28f.t: What part did Carl Jung play in A.A.'s beginning?

0fa64a53cd9c.t: The Swiss psychiatrist Carl Jung treated an American alcoholic, later identified as Rowland H., in the early 1930s. When the man relapsed, Jung told him that medicine could do no more for him, and that his only hope was a genuine spiritual experience, which in alcoholics like him was rare.

eb328d5035e9.t: The man joined the Oxford Group and got sober. He helped Ebby T. get sober in 1934, and Ebby brought the message to Bill W. That is the chain Bill later traced back to Jung.

42c3288058e9.t: The Big Book tells the story in Chapter 2 without naming the patient. Today's text names the doctor as "Dr. Jung"; our sources don't show whether the 1939 printing did.

ab7775288ce1.t: Our sources show no other part Jung played: no meetings, no membership. In 1961 Bill wrote to thank him, and Jung replied. Jung's reply is the source of the Latin phrase <0>spiritus contra spiritum</0>.

b0912724f527.t: Chapter 2, <0>There Is a Solution</0>, tells of an American businessman of ability and high character who went to Europe for treatment by "a celebrated physician (the psychiatrist, Dr. Jung)" (p. 26). He left with great confidence and was soon drunk (p. 26). When he went back and asked why, "In the doctor's judgment he was utterly hopeless" (p. 26). Asked whether there was any exception, the doctor said: "Here and there, once in a while, alcoholics have had what are called vital spiritual experiences." (p. 27). He described them as "huge emotional displacements and rearrangements" (p. 27). The man's religious convictions, the doctor told him, did not amount to that experience (p. 27).

9a9d7ad23bdc.t: The chapter goes on to say the man later had the experience and is free (pp. 26, 28), and that the other members "sought the same escape with all the desperation of drowning men" (p. 28). A footnote, added when the appendices were, points to Appendix II on spiritual experience (p. 27). See <0>What is the "spiritual awakening" in Step 12?</0>

d1dc61b4bda2.t: The Big Book names neither the patient nor Ebby's connection to him. Today's text names Jung in parentheses; our sources have only the fourth edition, so it can't say whether that parenthesis was in the first printing.

701889dd6a33.t: How Jung's words reached Bill (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)

fa8a00f21185.t: In Bill's 1957 account, after his own experience at Towns Hospital he read William James and saw the pattern of deflation at depth: "Dr. Carl Jung had told an Oxford group friend of Ebby's how hopeless his alcoholism was" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), Dr. Silkworth had told Bill the same, and then Ebby, another alcoholic, had brought the message (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Before Bill went to Akron, Silkworth reminded him that the doctor in Zurich had told this alcoholic "his only hope of salvation was a spiritual experience" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

c6f7abc52b5c.t: At the 1955 convention, the Rev. Sam Shoemaker listed "Dr. Jung's simple declaration that science had no answer" among the strands that went into A.A., along with Dr. Silkworth's help and William James (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

712384e7626a.t: The name, and the letters (Pass It On, 1984)

606d13b078db.t: <0>Pass It On</0> names the patient as Rowland H., of a prominent Rhode Island family (Pass It On, 1984). It says he was treated by Jung for about a year, got drunk soon after, and went back, to be told more treatment would be useless; in Jung's opinion only a spiritual awakening could help, and when Rowland said he already believed in God, Jung replied that "belief was not enough" and suggested he join a religious movement (Pass It On, 1984). Rowland joined the Oxford Group, got sober, and in 1934 helped Ebby (Pass It On, 1984). See <1>Who was the old school friend in "Bill's Story" (Ebby)?</1>

27ae28d059fe.t: In January 1961 Bill wrote to Jung to tell him that this conversation was "the first link in the chain of events that led to the founding of Alcoholics Anonymous" (Pass It On, 1984). Jung answered on January 30, 1961 (Pass It On, 1984). He said he had had to be very careful in what he told Rowland, and explained what he had really thought: "His craving for alcohol was the equivalent on a low level of the spiritual thirst of our being for wholeness" (Pass It On, 1984). He ended with a play on the Latin word for both alcohol and spirit: "Alcohol in Latin is spiritus" (Pass It On, 1984), and so the helpful formula was spirit against spirit (Pass It On, 1984). Bill wrote back in March; Jung died that June (Pass It On, 1984).

c03a5fd5f004.t: <0>The year of the treatment.</0> The timeline in our later printing of <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> says Jung's help to the alcoholic came in 1930 and was "later seen as" the first step toward A.A. (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill's 1961 letter, as <2>Pass It On</2> quotes it, says the man became Jung's patient about 1931 (Pass It On, 1984). The Big Book gives no year.

8bd28fd8722d.t: <0>What Jung advised.</0> The Big Book has the doctor say only that vital spiritual experiences sometimes happen and that the man's religious convictions weren't enough (p. 27). <1>Pass It On</1> adds that Jung told him to join a religious movement (Pass It On, 1984), and Bill's 1961 letter says Jung recommended that he "place himself in a religious atmosphere and hope for the best" (Pass It On, 1984).

c9522223b964.t: <0>"Founder" sayings.</0> Our sources don't support calling Jung a founder or member of A.A. The sources describe one conversation with one patient, which Bill came to see as the first link in a chain (Pass It On, 1984).

a9ec94c8c5df.t: What happened at the 1950 Cleveland convention? | Recovery Starts

d683750b0df3.t: In July 1950 A.A. held its first International Convention, in Cleveland, Ohio. Bill W.'s 1957 account puts attendance at about 3,000.

a8d07fa7fd23.t: What happened at the 1950 Cleveland convention?

0b6e511d04b7.t: In July 1950 A.A. held its first International Convention, in Cleveland, Ohio. Bill W.'s 1957 account puts attendance at about 3,000.

b328035b2dd4.t: The convention confirmed the Twelve Traditions, by then in their short form, as the principles A.A. groups and A.A. as a whole would stand on. Bill says the vote was unanimous.

66a7dbd377cd.t: It was Dr. Bob's last appearance. Already very ill, he gave a short talk: keep the program simple, it comes down to love and service, guard your tongue, and never be too comfortable to help the next alcoholic.

d05d069dcf87.t: The sources present it as a turning point: from then on A.A.'s unity would rest on the Traditions rather than on its founders.

2412dda7e3c5.t: The Foreword to the Second Edition, written five years later, describes the Traditions and then says: "Though none of these principles had the force of rules or laws, they had become so widely accepted by 1950 that they were confirmed by our first International Conference held at Cleveland." (p. xix). The foreword calls it a "Conference"; the other sources call it a convention.

da7743ca91ce.t: <0>P-44, <1>A.A.'s Legacy of Service</1></0> (Bill W., text through 1955). When the Traditions were first published in 1946 many groups ignored or resented them (P-44). Five years later, several thousand members meeting at Cleveland declared that the Traditions "constituted the platform upon which our Fellowship could best function and hold together in unity for all time to come" (P-44).

1b4d59606ce8.t: <0><1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957).</0> "About 3,000 were in attendance." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill names two highlights: Dr. Bob's last appearance, and the confirmation of the Traditions as the permanent platform of the fellowship (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The long form of 1946 had already been condensed into the short form that matches the Steps in length, and the Grapevine had printed it in every issue, so most members knew it by the time the convention met (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

c8df389fb54d.t: Bill says those present sensed that Dr. Bob and other early members would soon be gone: "In the future we could no longer depend upon the authority and influence of our pioneering people for A.A. unity." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "Henceforth we would have to rely upon spiritual principles, as set forth in the Twelve Traditions." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Several speakers presented the Traditions, Bill summed them up and asked for approval, and the convention consented with one voice: "It was a fine hour in that month of July, 1950." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

8a194e0bd5f3.t: <0>P-43, <1>Twelve Traditions Illustrated</1> (1971)</0> gives the same outline: the Traditions came out of A.A.'s first ten years, were published in the long form in 1946, and "By 1950, they had been condensed to their present form and were adopted by A.A.'s First International Convention." (P-43).

df0796cd2c92.t: P-53 says that in 1950, ill with the cancer that killed him that November, Dr. Bob found the strength for a brief appearance at Cleveland, where he pleaded: "Let's not louse it all up with Freudian complexes and things that are interesting to the scientific mind" (P-53), which have little to do with A.A. work (P-53).

9b043785bd9a.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) prints the whole short talk and notes that people usually remember only the line about simplicity, "But Dr. Bob said a good deal more than that" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). In it he says he had been in bed five of the last seven months (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), and makes three points: - Keep it simple, because the Steps "resolve themselves into the words 'love' and 'service.'" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - Guard the tongue, and use it with kindness, consideration and tolerance (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - None of us would be here if someone hadn't taken time to help us, so never become so complacent that we won't extend that help to others (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

5e8d3bc07b96.t: The same book says the effort left him so weak that he had to leave the stage at once (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). The talk is about carrying the message, the same work Chapter 7 asks for.

8e54dfe13da3.t: <0>Attendance.</0> <1>Comes of Age</1> says about 3,000 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); P-44 says "several thousand" (P-44). Our sources have no other count.

72d873a35e0d.t: <0>Exact days.</0> Our sources give only "July, 1950" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957) and "the summer of 1950" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
