2746ddd61e7c.t: How did the Cleveland group become the first to call itself Alcoholics Anonymous? | Recovery Starts

9bcd79ff83aa.t: In May or June 1939, Cleveland members who had been driving to the Akron meeting, held in an Oxford Group home, started their own meeting in Cleveland,…

34077d17ac0e.t: How did the Cleveland group become the first to call itself Alcoholics Anonymous?

967374757b63.t: In May or June 1939, Cleveland members who had been driving to the Akron meeting, held in an Oxford Group home, started their own meeting in Cleveland, open only to alcoholics and their families. Clarence S., one of its founders, said that they took the name "Alcoholics Anonymous" from the new book.

28518a1ab9b5.t: That Cleveland was the <0>first</0> group to use the name is Clarence's claim, as <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) reports it, right after saying the debate "continues." Our sources don't settle it.

32fce74023e8.t: The name itself is older than the Cleveland meeting: the Big Book, out in April 1939, already speaks for "Alcoholics Anonymous" (p. xiii). Bill W. dated the title to about October 1938; <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) finds it in letters from June and July 1938.

1ec72b081e49.t: The sources disagree on dates: May or June 1939 for the first Cleveland meeting, and the 1955 foreword even speaks of a group at Cleveland starting in 1937.

d4cb4da80b11.t: Background: Clevelanders at the Akron meeting

2bd14ac12930.t: Bill (1957) says Cleveland alcoholics had been going to the Akron meetings at the home of T. Henry and Clarace Williams, who were Oxford Group members, meeting Dr. Bob and Anne and going with Dr. Bob to the hospital (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Clarence S. and his wife Dorothy were among the earliest to come, and "By the early summer of 1939 a group had commenced to form around them in Cleveland" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

acb6f0e200a2.t: The break, in the members' words (1980)

e834f42c58d2.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) gives several members' memories, and says frankly that "There are several versions of how the split occurred" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

ea18884281be.t: <0>Why.</0> Clarence said many of the men he brought from Cleveland were Catholic and were uneasy with the Oxford Group's public confession and "guidance" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Dorothy added that the Cleveland contingent had simply grown too big to keep driving to Akron, and was putting a heavy load on Dr. Bob (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Clarence remembered telling Dr. Bob they could start "a group without all this rigmarole that's offensive to other people" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Dr. Bob answered, "We can't abandon these people," and "We owe our lives to them." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

546aea38f6ba.t: <0>Where.</0> Al G. (also called Abby), a patent lawyer with a big house in Cleveland, had just been through the hospital in Akron. Clarence asked Al's wife whether they could meet there, and when Al came out he offered his home for the Cleveland meetings (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

93f7cb121bc1.t: <0>The name.</0> Clarence said he announced at the Oxford Group meeting that the Cleveland members were starting a group "that would only be open to alcoholics and their families. Also that we were taking the name from the book 'Alcoholics Anonymous.'" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). He dated the first meeting to the following week, May 11, 1939, and said Oxford Groupers came and tried to break it up (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

fa799eee6c8b.t: The others remembered it a little differently: - Dorothy: "We didn't have any name," (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980) only that everyone knew it was not an Oxford Group meeting. - Al G.: the first meeting was "Toward the middle of May 1939" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), and there was debate over a name; "No others seemed to be fitting, so we began to refer to ourselves as Alcoholics Anonymous." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

c0bff8b3a876.t: The book adds that Dr. Bob supported the Cleveland group from the start and went to its early meetings (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Another member, Warren C., remembered that the meetings at Al G.'s were still a mix of Oxford Groupers and newcomers, and that the first group with no Oxford Group people in it was the Borton Group, formed in November 1939 (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

8ea46a23cc48.t: <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) reports the claim alongside the doubts. The book's title quickly became the fellowship's name, "although debate continues about where and how the name was first used by a group" (Pass It On, 1984). "Oldtimer Clarence S. stated that the Cleveland group he founded in May 1939 was actually the first group to use the name" (Pass It On, 1984). Whatever individual groups called themselves, it says, the name was used earlier for the fellowship as a whole, and it points to the Big Book's own foreword (Pass It On, 1984).

ac5ccaa0d065.t: The earlier uses are in our sources: - The Foreword to the First Edition (April 1939) opens: "We, of Alcoholics Anonymous, are more than one hundred men and women" (p. xiii). - Bill (1957) says the title "had appeared very early in the discussion, probably in October, 1938" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). - <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) says "The first documented use of the name in the A.A. archives is in a letter from Frank Amos to Albert Scott dated June 24, 1938." (Pass It On, 1984), and cites a letter from Dr. Richards of Johns Hopkins, July 18, 1938, showing Bill already using "Alcoholics Anonymous" as the book's working title and the fellowship's name (Pass It On, 1984). - <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) says the name was "already in some limited use as a name for the Fellowship; references to it may be found as early as 1937" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). It doesn't say what those references are.

fae3040865ae.t: So: the Cleveland members may well have been the first <0>group</0> to call its meeting by the book's name, as Clarence said; our sources have his word for it and no one else's. The name for the fellowship was in use before that. See <1>How did Alcoholics Anonymous get its name? Was "The Way Out" the title?</1>

a330d230a9b4.t: In the fall of 1939 the Cleveland Plain Dealer ran a series of articles on A.A., backed by editorials (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Calls flooded in, and about twenty members suddenly faced hundreds of newcomers (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). To cope, each prospect was assigned an older member who visited him and took him to his first meeting, and new members "sober only a month or even a week, had to sponsor alcoholics still drying up in the hospitals" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Abby's meeting outgrew his house and split into the Borton, Orchard Grove and Lee Road groups (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). A year later Cleveland had about thirty groups and several hundred members, and Bill (1957) wrote that the results were so good "that many a Clevelander really thought A.A. had started there in the first place" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; quoted in Pass It On, 1984).

a8a22a657a3e.t: <0>The first Cleveland meeting.</0> May 11, 1939 (Clarence, in the 1980 book); "Toward the middle of May 1939" (Al G., same book); June 1939 at Abby G.'s home (Bill, 1957: A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

c20bbe2de955.t: <0>1937?</0> The Big Book's 1955 foreword says a second group took shape in New York, "to be followed in 1937 with the start of a third at Cleveland" (p. xvii). That doesn't fit the 1957, 1980 and 1984 accounts, which have Clevelanders going to Akron until 1939. Our sources don't explain it.

0d80c71d0150.t: <0>When the name first appeared.</0> Bill (1957) says "probably in October, 1938" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) cites letters of June 24 and July 18, 1938 (Pass It On, 1984); the 1980 book says references go back to 1937 (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

f62dd850fa60.t: <0>The name.</0> Clarence says they took it from the book at once; Dorothy says they had no name; Al G. says they settled on it after debate (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

765ffd209b0e.t: <0>The first all-A.A. group.</0> Warren C. names the Borton Group, November 1939 (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), not the May meeting.

980a166a23ad.t: What did Bill W. say about clubs and A.A.? | Recovery Starts

ec345ca55fea.t: Bill W. was for clubs, for the members who want them. In 1947 he wrote that A.A.s who need and want clubs ought to have them, and that the real question…

25578a6e43c5.t: What did Bill W. say about clubs and A.A.?

e006f4a59e70.t: Bill W. was for clubs, for the members who want them. In 1947 he wrote that A.A.s who need and want clubs ought to have them, and that the real question was how to keep their troubles smaller than their benefits.

077f0a47ed93.t: But a club is not A.A. Experience in New York taught that a club should be separately incorporated under another name, run and paid for by the people who want it, and kept out of the A.A. groups' hands.

98d5889fbbee.t: The Long Form of Tradition Six says the same: clubs are "secondary aids" that should be set apart so the groups can drop them if they need to, and they shouldn't use the A.A. name.

712cdcc9d136.t: Bill warned against treating club life as a substitute for the program, a "Thirteenth Step."

932d6adb71bb.t: <0>Clubs were popular, and so was the opposition.</0> Bill opens by saying clubs had become part of A.A. life, and that a vote would bring a large "yes" (P-17, p. 17). He then names the danger on that side: some members acted as if a club were a sort of "Thirteenth Step" without which the other Steps wouldn't work, and they "are apt to depend upon clubs rather than upon the A.A. program" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, p. 17). A strong minority wanted no clubs at all, pointing to clubs that turned into hangouts, fights over money and authority, and bad publicity (P-17, p. 17).

ac51ab8659ae.t: <0>His middle ground.</0> "A.A.s who need and want clubs ought to have them" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, p. 18). The question was how to make them assets and keep their liabilities down (P-17, p. 18).

eeb9dcbd7fb0.t: <0>What New York learned the hard way.</0> Bill tells the story of the first club, at West 24th Street, as an average example, not a model (P-17, p. 18). Meetings had outgrown homes, a restaurant lacked the home atmosphere, and the members took over a former artists' club (P-17, p. 18). Then came the growing pains: dictators, drunks disrupting meetings, rent trouble, and a corporation whose directors seemed to compete with the A.A. rotating committee (P-17, pp. 18–19). The lease-holding corporation was named "Alcoholics Anonymous of New York, Inc.," and Bill admits they had effectively incorporated the whole state (P-17, p. 19). When the suburban groups grew, Manhattan expected them to pay for the club and its secretary; they never did, and the club, the area's common needs and the A.A. work stayed knotted together for a long time (P-17, pp. 19–20).

d6042ece8cdd.t: <0>The lesson.</0> The tangle came apart when they saw that clubs "ought to be strictly the business of those individuals who specially want clubs, and who are willing to pay for them" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, p. 20). A club should be separately incorporated under another name; its directors should look after club business only; and an A.A. group should never get into running a business (P-17, p. 20). If the A.A. committee tries to boss the club, or the club tries to run the groups, there is trouble at once; the only cure found was "to separate the material from the spiritual" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, p. 20). A group meeting in a club pays rent or splits the collection (P-17, p. 20).

f3072dd97acb.t: <0>Who belongs, who pays.</0> Bill says plainly they didn't yet know all the answers (P-17, p. 21). His suggestion: any A.A. member should be free to enjoy a club whether he contributes or not, and regular contributors should vote for the club's directors (P-17, p. 21). Large gifts to buy or build clubs lead to headaches, and public solicitation is "extremely dangerous" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, p. 21).

8ff23d7d8518.t: <0>Where clubs end up.</0> Outside small towns, A.A. outgrows any clubhouse, and the shared work of an area (hospital arrangements, a central office, local public relations) passes to a central or intergroup committee that every A.A. has an interest in, club member or not (P-17, pp. 21–22). The club is left outside, "where, in the opinion of many, it should be" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, p. 22).

668bdee77341.t: The Long Form of Tradition Six (1946)

6e7692d83b9d.t: The Long Form puts the same experience into one paragraph. Any considerable property of real use to A.A. should be separately incorporated and managed, "thus dividing the material from the spiritual" (p. 564). An A.A. group shouldn't go into business. Secondary aids "such as clubs or hospitals" should be incorporated and set apart so that, if necessary, "they can be freely discarded by the groups" (p. 564). They shouldn't use the A.A. name, and they should be managed by those who pay for them. "For clubs, A.A. managers are usually preferred" (p. 564), while hospitals belong well outside A.A.

6702c8db12c8.t: A year earlier Bill had already said club support should be an individual matter, not a group matter (P-17, p. 29). Groups in an area could fairly pay for a central-office secretary who serves them all, but it isn't a group or central-committee job to fund clubs, and "the majority ought not to try to coerce" the minority into paying for clubs they don't want (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 29).

c6a1d32e1d6e.t: The 2018 pamphlet <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16) carries this forward: owning and managing real estate isn't a group function, so "technically, there is no such thing as an" A.A. club (P-16, 2018, p. 40). Clubs are run by members acting as private individuals through separate nonprofit corporations, and the General Service Office doesn't take contributions from clubs (P-16, pp. 40–41).

621671333ba8.t: Concept I says: "Final responsibility and ultimate authority for A.A. world services should always reside in the collective conscience of our whole…

bc1ed38863fc.t: Concept I: who has the final say in A.A.?

0aa9b9eb2e9b.t: Concept I says: "Final responsibility and ultimate authority for A.A. world services should always reside in the collective conscience of our whole Fellowship" (p. 574). In plain terms, the A.A. groups, together, have the last word over A.A.'s shared services, not the trustees or the General Service Office.

f24ae4800e2b.t: Bill W. wrote it in 1962. The groups had taken that authority over from the co-founders at the St. Louis convention in 1955. What made it urgent, Bill says, was the news in 1948 that Dr. Bob was fatally ill; he died in 1950.

0660ec81a82d.t: Bill grounds it in Tradition Two, first printed in 1946: one ultimate authority, "a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience" (p. 563).

a6683c078529.t: Concept I is about world services. It doesn't give anyone authority over a group's own affairs.

8b1782f057cd.t: The earlier text first: Tradition Two (1946)

644239f0d5cc.t: The Long Form of Tradition Two: "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience" (p. 563). Long Form Nine adds that the trustees are, "in effect, our A.A. General Service Committee" (p. 565), and that A.A.'s servants "derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern" (p. 565).

5ff14432c855.t: In 1947 Bill described the trustees of the Alcoholic Foundation as "simple custodians" of the office, the Grapevine, A.A.'s funds and Traditions: "caretakers only" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947).

f6ae800f80a5.t: So in 1946–47 the principle was already stated. What hadn't been settled was how the groups, scattered across the world, could actually hold authority over the New York office and its board. Concept I tells how that was done.

6a2c7b886821.t: What Bill's Concept I essay says (1962)

0f32f4807908.t: <0>The claim.</0> "The A.A. groups today hold ultimate responsibility and final authority for our world services" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). World services are the things no single group or area can do: uniform literature, public relations, answering pleas for help, helping new groups form, a magazine, translations.

b655dd787b57.t: <0>The history.</0> In 1938 Bill and Dr. Bob, with nonalcoholic friends, formed a trusteeship, the Alcoholic Foundation, renamed the General Service Board in 1954. By 1950 membership had grown from about 50 to 100,000 and the Traditions had been written and adopted. Yet few members knew the trustees existed: "Not one member in a thousand could tell who our Trustees were" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). The trustees controlled money, but on policy they turned to the two founders.

0f12bb7694ca.t: <0>The turning point.</0> In 1948 it became known that Dr. Bob was fatally ill. "The fact had to be faced that A.A.’s founders were perishable" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). Many trustees and members opposed calling a representative conference, fearing politics, expense and strife; Bill says those arguments "were not without merit." But "For the first time it was seen that only a representative conference could take the place of Dr. Bob and me" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). The first Conference met experimentally in 1951; "The groups assumed that responsibility at the St. Louis International Convention of 1955" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I), where Bill made the transfer on behalf of Dr. Bob, the trustees and the old-timers.

d4e65c669f1e.t: <0>The reason in principle.</0> Bill quotes Tradition Two in full and says its principles are "crystal clear: the A.A. groups are to be the final authority; their leaders are to be entrusted with delegated responsibilities only" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). He notes "Tradition Two had been written in 1945" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I), but it took until 1955 for everyone to be convinced it applied to the trustees and founders as well: "It took five years more for all of us to be convinced that Tradition Two was for everybody" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I).

3b01069cd246.t: <0>Group conscience.</0> Bill admits the phrase is vague to many members, and contrasts A.A. with democracies where ignorance, apathy and power-seeking erode self-government. A.A.'s safeguard, he says, is that each life and group is built on the Steps and Traditions, and "the penalty for extensive disobedience to these principles is death for the individual and dissolution for the group" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I), together with the love members have for one another.

b4e952090905.t: <0>Not God's job alone.</0> One detail cuts against an easy faith: in the boom years of 1945–50, many members thought nothing could happen to A.A. "because God was protecting A.A." (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). Bill calls that attitude a strange contrast with how carefully members guarded their own sobriety, and says planning ahead was needed.

a3c5788becb9.t: How the authority is actually used

1533026f1e3b.t: Concept I gives the groups ultimate authority, and the next Concepts explain why they don't use it directly: they delegate the active work to the Conference (Concept II), give servants a Right of Decision (Concept III), and so on. See <0>Who has the final say in A.A.?</0> for how the pieces fit.

950536b3eafc.t: P-8 (first printed 1986; © 2017) opens Concept I with the line that A.A. "has been called an upside-down organization" (P-8). P-8 doesn't say who called it that; the phrase isn't in Bill's 1962 essay.

507fe3e5450f.t: The current Service Manual (2024–2026) quotes Concept I to explain the GSR's role: the GSR helps the groups carry out that final responsibility.

2bacfc468771.t: The short form of Concept I names "collective conscience"; Tradition Two names "a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." Bill's essay treats them as one principle and doesn't say what would happen if they were thought to differ.

2856cccc2c4b.t: Concept II: what is the General Service Conference, and what can it decide? | Recovery Starts

abd48916b17d.t: Concept II says the groups, when they confirmed the Conference's permanent charter in 1955, delegated to it "complete authority for the active maintenance…

7a17d16d4b66.t: Concept II: what is the General Service Conference, and what can it decide?

cae4df70b0c9.t: Concept II says the groups, when they confirmed the Conference's permanent charter in 1955, delegated to it "complete authority for the active maintenance of our world services" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept II). The short form: the Conference "has become, for nearly every practical purpose, the active voice and the effective conscience of our whole Society in its world affairs" (p. 574).

356ed821a2fe.t: Two things are excepted: any change in the Twelve Traditions, and any change in Article 12 of the Conference Charter (the Warranties of Concept XII). Those stay with the groups themselves.

9032838a632b.t: Bill W.'s reason, written in 1962: the groups hold all the final authority, but thousands of scattered groups can't run world services themselves, so authority has to be delegated.

5d0f239502e8.t: The Conference serves A.A.; it doesn't govern it. "The Conference represents us, but cannot rule us," as Bill put it in the first edition of the service manual (quoted in the current manual, which doesn't give that edition's date).

08ae59304673.t: Long Form Four (1946) already treated the trustees as the body to consult on matters affecting all of A.A.: no group, regional committee or individual should take action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole "without conferring with the trustees of the General Service Board" (p. 563); in 1946 that was the Alcoholic Foundation, renamed in 1954. Long Form Nine says the trustees "are authorized by the groups to handle our over-all public relations" (p. 565).

9a3c9fdfb01e.t: In 1946 Bill called the Foundation's trustees "our over-all service committee" (P-17, Money, 1946). So delegation from the groups to a service body was there from the start. What changed with the Conference was who stood between the groups and the trustees: no longer the two founders, but delegates the groups elected.

a3a39d2f3244.t: What Bill's Concept II essay says (1962)

be6b8af13abd.t: <0>The groups own it.</0> "The operation is really theirs; they really own it" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept II). Their power to change the structure and criticize it is "virtually supreme."

a585ffefb369.t: <0>But owning isn't running.</0> "In order to get effective action, the groups must delegate the actual operational authority to chosen service representatives who are fully empowered to speak and to act for them" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept II). Bill calls this the clear implication of Tradition Two's "trusted servants."

87b5af3210f1.t: <0>Delegation was always the rule.</0> Bill retraces it: - In 1937 the Akron and New York groups authorized him and Dr. Bob to create services to spread the message. - Dr. Bob handed most of that work to Bill, since New York had more friends and funds; in 1938 the Alcoholic Foundation was formed. - In 1940 the stock of Works Publishing, the company that published the Big Book, was turned over to the trustees, who then took over managing the office, since the book's income paid for it. Bill became "an adviser only" on money. - In 1941 groups began sending contributions to the Foundation; later the trustees took over public relations, then the Grapevine.

f80c06580392.t: <0>Ultimate versus immediate authority.</0> "In the course of these developments the great difference between ultimate and immediate service authority became apparent" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept II). The trustees could be given the immediate authority, but not the ultimate responsibility that Bill and Dr. Bob still carried: that couldn't go to "a self-appointing Board which was relatively unknown among AA’s as a whole" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept II). "At St. Louis it went from Dr. Bob and me to the A.A. groups themselves" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept II), and the groups in turn delegated the active work to the Conference.

123d1ea24ea4.t: <0>Why it mattered to Bill.</0> He closes hoping the old-timers had avoided the pitfalls "into which societies have so often fallen because their originators have failed, during their lifetimes, to properly delegate and distribute their own authority, responsibility and leadership" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept II).

0d5fa226117d.t: The 1955 St. Louis resolution made the Conference "the voice of the group conscience of our entire Fellowship, and the sole successors of its co-founders" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix L). It also said neither the Twelve Traditions nor the Warranties of Article 12 may be changed by the Conference without first asking the registered groups of the world, allowing at least six months, and receiving the written consent of three-quarters of those who respond.

725063aadd41.t: The current Service Manual (2024–2026) quotes Bill in "the first edition of this manual" (undated in our copy; the manual grew out of his Third Legacy Manual, first drafted in 1951): the Conference can direct the General Service Office, "it can never mandate or govern the Society of Alcoholics Anonymous which it serves" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Chapter 6), followed by "The Conference represents us, but cannot rule us" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Chapter 6).

5d0860f89d90.t: P-8 (© 2017) describes the current pattern: GSRs meet in area assemblies and every two years elect a delegate; each April the delegates from 93 areas in the U.S. and Canada meet for six days with the trustees and staff.

6579ed7733c4.t: The current Conference Charter opens: "The Conference shall be a service body only, never a government for Alcoholics Anonymous" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Current Conference Charter). The original 1955 Charter has the same sentence.

3ec6091d3a3e.t: Concept III: what is the Right of Decision, and must a delegate vote the way the group says? | Recovery Starts

85cca5f035d5.t: Concept III gives every element of A.A.'s world service (the Conference, the trustees, the service corporations, staffs, committees and executives) a…

1feb3913b8f0.t: Concept III: what is the Right of Decision, and must a delegate vote the way the group says?

f701c51d2be4.t: Concept III gives every element of A.A.'s world service (the Conference, the trustees, the service corporations, staffs, committees and executives) a traditional "Right of Decision": within their defined duties, they decide which problems to handle themselves and which to report on, consult about, or refer up.

855d7b8c637f.t: On the delegate question, Bill W.'s 1962 answer has two sides. The groups do have the right to instruct their delegates: "If they insist, they can give directives to their Delegates on any and all A.A. matters" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III). But he thought it unwise, and says delegates should cast final votes by their own judgment and conscience.

0988d03dbe57.t: The 1955 Conference Charter, written before the Concepts, already said: "Delegates should be free to vote as their conscience dictates" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955).

b097906ec914.t: The right comes with duties: report all significant actions, don't exceed a clearly defined authority, and consult those who should be consulted.

18cf3b7d1f17.t: Tradition Two's short form ends: "Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not govern" (p. 562). The Long Form of Nine calls true leaders "trusted and experienced servants of the whole" (p. 565).

256bea438b10.t: Bill's 1947 essay describes how group committees saw themselves then: "they have only the authorization to serve, never to command" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947), and "Each committee carries out what it believes to be the wishes of its group" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947). That leans toward the servant following the group, though "what it believes" already leaves the committee some judgment. Concept III, fifteen years later, gives servants more discretion explicitly.

5b12988b6ed3.t: The original Conference Charter (1955) gives delegates two freedoms: to vote as their conscience dictates, and "to decide what questions should be taken to the group level, whether for information, discussion or their own direct instruction" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955).

e633ec9844d9.t: What Bill's Concept III essay says (1962)

5ea500816d23.t: <0>The principle.</0> Within their general responsibilities, all world service boards, committees and executives should decide "which problems they will dispose of themselves and upon which matters they will report, consult, or ask specific directions" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III). Without that trust, no effective leadership is possible.

bd3148e6a498.t: <0>Why charters aren't enough.</0> The Conference Charter is broad and "can be variously construed." Under one reading the groups can instruct delegates all they like; under another the delegates and trustees can ignore instructions when they think best. Bill's examples of the problem: - Groups instructing delegates. Bill says this right exists, but "good management seldom means the full exercise of a stated set of ultimate rights" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III). A Conference with all the facts and the debate in front of it will nearly always decide better than delegates bound beforehand. "Nevertheless the ‘instructed’ Delegate who cannot act on his own conscience in a final Conference vote is not a ‘trusted servant’ at all; he is just a messenger" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III). - Delegates issuing hasty, flat directives to trustees who know the subject better. - Trustees managing the service corporations in detail, so that staff "would be turned into buck-passers and rubber stamps; their choice would be to rebel and resign, or to submit and rot" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III).

91ff9057edc0.t: <0>Three possible answers.</0> Throw away all charters and job descriptions (anarchy); add rules for every contingency ("altogether too much red tape"); or trust leaders, within their framework, to decide how to apply their authority to each situation as it comes up. Bill chooses the third, from "the latter part of Tradition Two, which provides for ‘trusted servants’" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III).

a673e0786b48.t: <0>The safety net.</0> "There will always be plenty of ultimate authority to correct inefficiency, ineffectiveness, or abuse" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III): groups can send better delegates; the Conference can censure or reorganize the trustees; the trustees can replace directors.

865d1c7686ca.t: <0>Applied:</0> - A. The Conference decides which matters it settles itself and which it refers to the groups. - B. "our Conference Delegates are primarily the world servants of A.A. as a whole, that only in a secondary sense do they represent their respective areas" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III); on final decisions they vote their own judgment and conscience. - C. The trustees decide when to act on their own and when to ask the Conference. - D. Headquarters corporations, committees, staff and executives decide when to act and when to refer up.

68d05ee0aaef.t: <0>The limits.</0> The Right of Decision is never an excuse for failing to report significant actions, for constantly exceeding a defined authority, or for failing to consult those entitled to be consulted.

e78ddd3a1d29.t: <0>The spirit.</0> "Our entire A.A. program rests squarely upon the principle of mutual trust" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III). "We trust God, we trust A.A., and we trust each other" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III).

00ac055ea6f4.t: P-8 (© 2017) applies the same idea one level down: if groups instruct their GSRs rather than giving them a Right of Decision, the area is hamstrung, and if GSRs instruct delegates, the Conference is. Bill's essay speaks of groups and delegates, and of area committee members and GSRs as people the Conference may consult; it doesn't discuss instructing GSRs as such.

aa5d7129b133.t: Concept IV: what is the Right of Participation, and who votes at the Conference? | Recovery Starts

9f7203390769.t: Concept IV says each kind of world servant should have a vote in proportion to its responsibility: "At all responsible levels, we ought to maintain a…

735130a57367.t: Concept IV: what is the Right of Participation, and who votes at the Conference?

081748f2850e.t: Concept IV says each kind of world servant should have a vote in proportion to its responsibility: "At all responsible levels, we ought to maintain a traditional ‘Right of Participation,’ allowing a voting representation in reasonable proportion to the responsibility that each must discharge" (p. 574).

b4d77141d6cb.t: So the General Service Conference isn't only delegates. Under its Charter the trustees, the directors of the service corporations and their staff also vote; and the service corporations' boards include trustees, outside volunteer experts and paid staff, all voting.

f0a9dc2b7144.t: Bill W.'s reason, written in 1962, is hard experience: when the early trustees held all the authority and the office staff all the work, the result was "grievous trouble." His deeper reason is that there should be no "second-class" servants.

6dba8bc6ef26.t: There are limits: paid staff can't become trustees, and trustees and staff shouldn't vote on reports of their own past work.

9b73703d494c.t: Long Form Eight (1946) already allowed A.A. to employ alcoholics for special services: "Such special services may be well recompensed" (p. 564). Bill's 1946 essay explains the principle: a secretary can run an office, an editor get out a paper, without professionalizing A.A.; "Clearly the principle seems to be that we may pay well for special services — but never for straight Twelfth Step work" (P-17, Money, 1946).

e68dd68e07aa.t: His 1947 essay names, among A.A.'s freedoms, "no one set in personal authority over anyone else" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947).

0a961d0ca371.t: Concept IV puts these together: paid workers are legitimate, and no class of servant should be set over another without a voice.

eca91515f716.t: What Bill's Concept IV essay says (1962)

e3fd20ffffac.t: <0>Where it's built in.</0> The Conference Charter makes the trustees, the directors of A.A. World Services and the Grapevine, and their executive staffs voting members of the Conference. The General Service Board could elect only trustees as directors of the service corporations, "But a powerful tradition has grown up to the effect that this never ought to be done" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IV). In 1962 A.A. World Services had seven directors, only two of them trustees; the rest were volunteer experts and the paid general manager and his assistant. (A footnote updates this: nine directors now, four of them trustees.)

9f0a466a6543.t: <0>No superiors at the ballot.</0> On the board's committees too, trustees, outside experts and staff sit together and vote. "When the time comes to ballot, there are no ‘superiors,’ no ‘inferiors,’ and no ‘advisers’" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IV).

dec28b0c4591.t: <0>The one exception.</0> "Members holding paid staff positions cannot become Trustees" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IV). It would interfere with the trustees' four-year rotation, and paid trustees could become a vested interest the Conference couldn't dislodge if the board ever had to be reorganized. Staff are still invited to the board's quarterly meetings, where they can speak but not vote.

e64f17b8716f.t: <0>How it was learned.</0> In the early years the trustees held all the authority and the money, while Bill, his assistant and her staff did the work with "practically no authority." Two trustee committees issued orders, sometimes conflicting ones; Bill's assistant, who carried most of the office load, couldn't get into a trustees' meeting. Then the publishing company's treasurer, an old friend of Bill's, tore up the staff's paychecks because they'd been issued two days early so the office workers could buy Easter bonnets. "Right then and there we began to wonder how much absolute authority over money and people any one of us drunks could handle" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IV). Bill's conclusion is that no one objects to final authority as such: "We are only against its misapplication or misuse" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IV).

2ad52d013d46.t: <0>Arguments he expected, and his answers.</0> - <1>Delegates will try to take away the trustees' and staff's Conference vote.</1> Bill agrees they should refrain from voting on reports of their own past performance, but says most Conference business is about the future, and their knowledge is needed. A footnote adds that delegates meet only a few days a year and can't know every problem firsthand. - <2>Trustees and staff might swing a close vote.</2> "But why not?" He notes they had never voted as a bloc. - <3>Groups might send delegates irrevocably instructed.</3> Then the delegates "would feel like agents and order-takers" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IV), not participants.

98e7a275d1a3.t: <0>The spiritual reason.</0> "All of us deeply desire to belong" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IV). "Just as there are no second-class AA’s, neither should there be any second-class world service workers, either" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IV). Participation, Bill says, softens the harshness of ultimate authority and helps servants accept the discipline their jobs need.

21078db83ad4.t: The current Service Manual (2024–2026) lists about 135 voting Conference members: 93 area delegates, who "make up at least two-thirds of the Conference body" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Chapter 6), 21 or 22 trustees, 6 nontrustee directors and 15 staff, each with one vote.

d59324d39064.t: P-8 (© 2017) adds that the Right of Participation "reinforces Tradition Two, that no member is placed in ‘ultimate authority’ over another" (P-8). Tradition Two itself doesn't say that; the idea is closer to Bill's 1947 essay and to Concept XII's Third Warranty.

53279b494719.t: Concept V: what are the Rights of Appeal and Petition?

adac8998d843.t: Concept V says: "Throughout our structure, a traditional ‘Right of Appeal’ ought to prevail, so that minority opinion will be heard and personal grievances receive careful consideration" (p. 574).

c4a2f5f0ed90.t: The <0>Right of Appeal</0> lets a minority on any staff, committee, board or among the trustees file a minority report, and on a grave issue obliges it to bring the report to the General Service Conference.

a93b10535974.t: The <0>Right of Petition</0> lets anyone working in A.A.'s service structure, paid or unpaid, take a personal grievance directly to the General Service Board "without prejudice or fear of reprisal" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).

8b80d90f0166.t: Bill W. wrote it in 1962, but said these practices were already in use: he was writing them down only as a way of "helping to confirm and enlarge their future applications" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).

3e089b8246e5.t: Long Form Three (1946): A.A. "may refuse none who wish to recover," and membership should never depend "upon money or conformity" (p. 563).

b222c9af8bf6.t: Bill's essay on money (1946), on clubs some members didn't want: "But the majority ought not to try to coerce the minority into supporting clubs they do not want or need" (P-17, Money, 1946).

5210acb56b53.t: Bill's essay on government (1947): A.A. has "no one set in personal authority over anyone else" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947).

ee7450d93e4d.t: The Conference Charter (1955): delegates elected "by a two-thirds written ballot or by lot" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955), so a narrow majority can't simply sweep the field.

f4ae84663400.t: What Bill's Concept V essay says (1962)

bcc1db213370.t: <0>Why minorities.</0> Minorities "frequently can be right" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V), and even when wrong they force a thorough debate. "The well-heard minority, therefore, is our chief protection against an uninformed, misinformed, hasty or angry majority" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).

78107e644507.t: <0>Petition.</0> Bill expected it to be seldom used, but "its very existence will always tend to restrain those in authority from unjust uses of their power" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). Workers should accept the direction their jobs need, but needn't "silently endure unnecessary and unfair personal domination."

b26c0c16f820.t: <0>A.A.'s charter of liberties.</0> "In Alcoholics Anonymous individual freedom is of enormous importance" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). A member belongs the moment he says so, and "Neither can we force our members to believe anything or pay anything" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).

e9e0409d0658.t: <0>Trusting a qualified minority.</0> The group conscience can't act directly in most world service matters because it can't be fully informed, and in a time of great disturbance it may not act wisely. So A.A. trusts "a small but truly qualified minority" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V), the hundred-odd members of the Conference, to act for it, keeping the power to recall and replace them.

24cfe9b23610.t: <0>Examples in 1962.</0> - Electing delegates: without two-thirds, the majority's candidate goes into a hat with the minority's choices, and lots are drawn. Bill admits this sometimes sets aside "democracy’s cherished principle of final decision by a simple majority vote" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V), and says it has strengthened the spirit of democracy. - The Conference: it often keeps debating even when two-thirds is easily available, and has usually refused to take important decisions on less. - The trustees: a Conference vote binds them only at two-thirds of a quorum, which gives them a veto over narrow majorities that they seldom use.

8eb94762aa37.t: <0>De Tocqueville.</0> Bill closes with the French writer's warning against the "tyranny" of apathetic, self-seeking, uninformed or angry majorities, and adds the other danger: "the even worse tyranny of very small minorities invested with absolute power" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). A.A., he says, needs no government that enforces conformity by punishment, only a service structure that holds up the Traditions and carries the message.

22a4daed3037.t: <0>A hope.</0> He hoped A.A. would "one day inscribe these traditional Rights" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V) in the Conference Charter.

fe6eb46b3e00.t: The current Conference Charter (in the 2024–2026 Service Manual) says the Conference recognizes "the Rights of Petition and Appeal reflected in Concepts IV and V" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Current Conference Charter), and may hear Concept V appeals from members below the Conference level. Our copy doesn't say when this was added.

6fd2ca59c71c.t: P-8 (© 2017) describes current practice: after a vote, those opposed are polled individually to see if they want to speak further, and the Conference has sometimes reversed itself. It adds that in A.A. a simple majority "is seldom sufficient basis for a decision" (P-8), so two-thirds is usually required.

04100e5338db.t: The 2024–2026 Service Manual: policy matters need substantial unanimity, defined as two-thirds, and after each vote the side that lost may speak.

6484d4e61896.t: Concept XII's Fourth Warranty (same 1962 text) says a minority may not use substantial unanimity to block urgently needed action; then "it would be the plain duty of the majority to override such a misuse of the principle of substantial unanimity" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). The right is to be heard, not to veto.

774bb09995dd.t: Concept VI: what do the trustees of the General Service Board do?

cbc7b4e68ca4.t: Concept VI says the General Service Conference has the principal responsibility for A.A.'s world services and the final decision on large matters of policy and finance, but "the chief initiative and active responsibility in most world service matters should be exercised by the trustee members of the Conference acting as the General Service Board" (p. 574).

08853b719b98.t: In Bill W.'s 1962 list, the trustees are responsible for A.A. World Services (with its publishing) and the Grapevine (Concept VIII explains that they oversee these rather than manage them day to day), lead on public relations and policy, act as "the active guardians of our Twelve Traditions," and are "A.A.’s bankers," responsible for the reserve fund.

721487023db9.t: Bill's picture is a business corporation: the groups as stockholders, the delegates as their proxies at an annual meeting, the trustees as directors of a holding company.

d7df605b8916.t: The earlier text (1946) already called the trustees A.A.'s General Service Committee, custodians of the Tradition and receivers of contributions.

072d6d2a9dcf.t: The earlier text first: Long Form Nine (1946)

0cdd8912df9b.t: "The trustees of the General Service Board are, in effect, our A.A. General Service Committee" (p. 565). The same paragraph says they are "the custodians of our A.A. Tradition and the receivers of voluntary A.A. contributions by which we maintain our A.A. General Service Office at New York" (p. 565), that the groups authorize them to handle public relations, and that they guarantee the integrity of the Grapevine. And of all such servants: "they do not govern" (p. 565). (In 1946 the board was the Alcoholic Foundation; it was renamed the General Service Board in 1954, and the Big Book prints the new name.)

ebf6d669f2ff.t: Long Form Six (1946) states the principle the Concepts later apply to the service corporations: any considerable property of genuine use to A.A. "should be separately incorporated and managed, thus dividing the material from the spiritual" (p. 564).

62178fd72720.t: What Bill's Concept VI essay says (1962)

f190a1971b45.t: <0>Delegation again.</0> Just as the groups can't act on world services without delegating to the Conference, the Conference must delegate "a liberal administrative authority" to the trustees so they can act when the Conference isn't sitting, which is most of the year.

21fc9474aa5c.t: <0>Next to the Conference, the most influential servants.</0> Bill says the trustees' authority, choosing and skills all need careful thought, and that the Charter can be amended if the arrangements prove flawed. But he wants the experience behind them written down so they aren't changed hastily: "These articles can then be relied upon as a point of safe return" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VI).

553616cf452e.t: <0>What they're responsible for (as of 1960).</0> The two service corporations, then with combined receipts approaching half a million dollars a year; A.A.'s worldwide public relations; leading on policy and seeing it carried out. "They are the active guardians of our Twelve Traditions" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VI). "The Trustees are A.A.’s bankers" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VI), responsible for investing and using the reserve fund.

1095309da4f5.t: <0>Business, for a spiritual end.</0> "Of course our objective is always a spiritual one" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VI), Bill writes, but the service aim can be reached only through an effective business operation, so the trustees must work almost exactly like the directors of a large corporation.

7ee8d7e8203d.t: <0>The corporate model, on purpose.</0> "We have deliberately chosen the corporate form rather than the institutional or governmental model" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VI). "The A.A. groups are the stockholders" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VI); the delegates are their proxies; the trustees are the directors of a holding company that owns the corporations doing the active work.

a152c2eab59b.t: Later changes (footnotes in the 2024–2026 Service Manual)

f76c8830a209.t: The 2024 operating revenue of the General Service Board, A.A. World Services and the Grapevine was $22,015,258 (Concept VI, footnote 1), against Bill's half million in 1960.

128f64f97cc4.t: There are now eleven standing committees, not five (footnote 2).

2d47a711693a.t: A.A. World Services and the Grapevine are described as "affiliates and not ‘subsidiaries’" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VI, footnote 3) of the General Service Board: separate not-for-profit corporations whose own boards run their routine affairs, though the trustees, as the corporations' members, elect their directors. Bill's 1962 word was subsidiaries.

b415c1e3b845.t: Concept VII: who really holds power, the Conference or the trustees? | Recovery Starts

fe0b3d2ee610.t: Concept VII says the trustees' Charter and Bylaws are legal instruments that fully empower them to manage A.A.'s world services, while "The Conference…

4903badb76f6.t: Concept VII: who really holds power, the Conference or the trustees?

04f2f8e4d1c5.t: Concept VII says the trustees' Charter and Bylaws are legal instruments that fully empower them to manage A.A.'s world services, while "The Conference Charter is not a legal document; it relies upon tradition and the A.A. purse for final effectiveness" (p. 575).

a4423b95d445.t: Bill W.'s answer, written in 1962, is both. The trustees hold the legal power; the Conference holds the practical power, and that practical power "will nearly always be superior" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VII), because most of its members are group-chosen delegates who could, in the last resort, cut off the groups' money.

c3f29bcbb75f.t: The trustees keep a legal veto. Bill expected it to be used seldom, and names three situations where using it would be their duty.

0bf0232a00b2.t: The idea that services are kept in line by members' money is already in Bill's 1946 essay: "These services must always serve us well or go out of business" (P-17, Money, 1946).

74008a5ff41a.t: Bill's 1946 essay on money explains why A.A.'s offices can't take over: "These are places of service; they cannot really control or govern A.A." (P-17, Money, 1946). If one grew inefficient or overbearing, "The average A.A. would stop his financial support until conditions were changed" (P-17, Money, 1946). That is the "power of the A.A. purse" sixteen years before Concept VII named it.

c665e37f0a0d.t: Long Form Four (1946) asks that no one take action greatly affecting A.A. as a whole "without conferring with the trustees of the General Service Board" (p. 563), and Long Form Nine makes the trustees the receivers of the groups' contributions (p. 565). So from the start the trustees held the money and the groups supplied it.

53743ddb11f8.t: What Bill's Concept VII essay says (1962)

197e0e157372.t: <0>The apparent contradiction.</0> "This concept may appear to be contradictory; it may look like the collision of an irresistible force with an immovable object" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VII). The board has complete legal power over A.A.'s funds and services; the Conference has enough traditional influence and financial power to overcome it.

93194ac3bb95.t: <0>Why the Conference wins in practice.</0> Its power comes from the Charter's traditional influence, from the large majority of group-chosen delegates, and in any great extremity from the delegates' ability to deny the board the groups' contributions. "Theoretically, the Conference is an advisory body only, but practically speaking it has all of the ultimate rights and powers that it may ever need" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VII). Since trustees have no salaried interest in their posts, Bill is "quite sure" they would never legally contest the clear, sustained will of the delegates.

dee2a0c7f324.t: <0>How it was settled (1950).</0> When the Charter was drawn in 1950, the question of the last word was open. Bill and the others agreed that final authority should not stay with "an isolated Board of Trustees who had an unqualified right to appoint their own successors" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VII). They considered and dropped three ideas: - incorporating the Conference, which would have meant giving all its members legal status, in effect incorporating the whole Fellowship; - nationwide elections for trustees, "a political shambles"; - having the Conference nominate and elect trustees, which delegates meeting briefly couldn't do well.

9fde4c26e008.t: So "the Conference was given the right to reject, but not to elect, new Trustee candidates" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VII). A footnote updates this: regional and at-large trustees are now elected during Conference week.

ee2eb6b3336c.t: <0>Both sides should hold back.</0> New trustees sometimes ask whether accepting a Conference directive violates their legal Charter. Bill says nothing compels them to use all their authority all the time; they can "simply refrain from using their absolute legal right to say ‘no’ when it would be much wiser, all things considered, to say ‘yes’" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VII). He compares it to a U.S. president's veto, legal but rarely used.

5d089cb078f3.t: <0>When the trustees should veto.</0> "Clearly, then, our Board of Trustees does reserve a veto power over any Conference action" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VII), "even though the veto will seldom be used" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VII). Bill's three examples: 1. A Conference action in clear violation of its own Charter or the board's, or so reckless it would seriously injure A.A.: the trustees should ask for reconsideration, then veto if refused, and could appeal directly to the groups. 2. The trustees may cut a Conference-approved budget during the year, though they shouldn't much exceed it without consulting the Conference. 3. A plan that becomes unworkable during the year may be cancelled.

793124db279b.t: <0>The balance.</0> "We believe this balance can be maintained indefinitely, because the one is protected by tradition and the other by law" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VII).

578af359a577.t: P-8 (© 2017) says the board's legal veto exists "but in actual practice, it never has done so" (P-8). That is P-8's statement about practice up to its own date; Bill's 1962 essay says only that the veto would seldom be used, and treats it as sometimes a duty.

1c20b026a33e.t: The current Charter (2024–2026 Service Manual) keeps the 1955 rule, as reworded by the 1986 Conference: a two-thirds vote of Conference members voting, with a quorum, is "considered binding upon the General Service Board" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Current Conference Charter), without impairing the board's legal right to conduct routine business.

e27c3ba46467.t: Concept VIII: do the trustees run the General Service Office and the Grapevine? | Recovery Starts

3e105d2f7897.t: Not day to day. Concept VIII says the trustees act in two ways: on large matters of overall policy and finance they plan and manage directly, but over the…

83901be30e68.t: Concept VIII: do the trustees run the General Service Office and the Grapevine?

028dbc3ceae1.t: Not day to day. Concept VIII says the trustees act in two ways: on large matters of overall policy and finance they plan and manage directly, but over the separately incorporated active services they have "custodial oversight," exercised "through their ability to elect all the directors of these entities" (p. 575).

35ac06a1d49d.t: So A.A. World Services (which runs the General Service Office and publishing) and the Grapevine each have their own board, executive, staff, money and offices. The trustees choose those boards and keep watch; they don't manage.

71858abe0e0f.t: Bill W.'s reasons, written in 1962: early attempts to run the office through trustee committees failed, and "There is always a powerful connection between money and authority" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VIII).

353319bb7340.t: The earlier text (1946) already wanted anything requiring much money or management separately incorporated, "thus dividing the material from the spiritual" (p. 564).

ce18a5630c58.t: Long Form Six (1946): considerable property "should be separately incorporated and managed, thus dividing the material from the spiritual" (p. 564).

4b62544eeb1f.t: Bill's 1946 essay on money notes "an encouraging tendency to incorporate all such special functions separately if they involve any great amount of money, property or management" (P-17, Money, 1946), because an A.A. group "is a spiritual entity, not a business concern."

0ffadaad4f29.t: His 1947 essay describes the Foundation's trustees as custodians "who guarantee the effectiveness of the A.A. General Office and The AA Grapevine" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947). Concept VIII keeps that word and spells out what it means.

e952a9de9599.t: What Bill's Concept VIII essay says (1962)

93df3306b2a8.t: <0>The board's real job.</0> Experience showed that the board as a whole must give itself "almost exclusively to the larger and more serious questions of policy, finance, group relations, public relations and leadership" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VIII). It can't be buried in the daily questions of running an office and a publishing business.

1fc3ea847178.t: <0>Custodians, not executives.</0> "Here the Board’s attitude has to be that of custodial oversight; it cannot be the executive" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VIII). The trustees guarantee good management by electing the corporations' directors, some of whom must always be trustees. Each corporation "should possess its own charter, its own working capital, its own executive, its own employees, its own offices and equipment" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VIII).

03c5b468eb9f.t: <0>Learned the hard way.</0> When the office and publishing company were run through several trustee committees, as departments of the old Foundation, responsibility and authority were rarely in balance; point-blank orders were the rule; and "those who handled money and signed checks assumed the greater authority" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VIII). Once the office became a single corporation with defined officers, its own capital and voting directors, things improved greatly.

3c8544184d40.t: <0>Why not one big operation?</0> Bill considers and rejects: - Turning the board into the operating company. It would need a full-time chief executive, and the board chairman, usually a nonalcoholic and unpaid as a trustee, can't be that. A hired manager couldn't be a trustee and would have no real standing. - One large corporation running everything, Grapevine included. It would over-concentrate executive authority, and such an executive would be hard to find and replace.

649df50d00cb.t: <0>Money and power.</0> "There is always a powerful connection between money and authority" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VIII). The reserve fund is held by the trustees and working capital is split between the two corporations, each with its own executive. "Therefore we should strenuously avoid placing too much money or too much authority in any one service entity" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VIII). Bill expected later workers to be tempted to consolidate for simplicity, tax savings or efficiency, and warned of an "administrative shambles." He adds that this is not meant to bar needed change.

7d00ac023607.t: A.A. World Services was incorporated as a not-for-profit corporation in 1962, the Grapevine in 1971; both are now membership corporations whose members are the trustees (Concept VIII, footnote 1).

bd5bbdf8d5c4.t: The two corporations are described as "affiliates and not ‘subsidiaries’" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VIII, footnote 3) of the General Service Board. Bill's 1962 text and P-8 call them subsidiaries.

6fa027c7d921.t: In 2020, 90% of the trustees lived "out of town" (footnote 2); in 1962 it was about half.

8bbd520a94ad.t: Concept IX: what makes a good leader in A.A. service? | Recovery Starts

22206669345e.t: Concept IX says: "Good service leadership at all levels is indispensable for our future functioning and safety" (p. 575), and that the world service…

b61b010d5f49.t: Concept IX: what makes a good leader in A.A. service?

50287c687724.t: Concept IX says: "Good service leadership at all levels is indispensable for our future functioning and safety" (p. 575), and that the world service leadership once given by the founders must now be taken on by the trustees.

43d8fcaf3910.t: Bill W.'s answer to the question, mostly from a 1959 Grapevine article he includes in the 1962 essay: a leader is neither a faceless order-taker nor a boss. Good leadership makes plans but consults widely, gives credit, never passes the buck, gives reasons, compromises when it can and stands firm when it must, takes criticism, and thinks ahead.

0c540e7de70e.t: The earlier texts already said the core of it. Long Form Nine (1946): "Rotating leadership is the best" (p. 565). Bill in 1947: a leader "can always guide by example or persuasion" but "can never boss" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947).

770127c69f3a.t: Bill also says the leadership question can never be solved for good: good leaders "can be here today and gone tomorrow."

882dccf612fb.t: Long Form Nine (1946) asks for the least possible organization in each group, and says: "Rotating leadership is the best" (p. 565). All representatives "are to be guided in the spirit of service, for true leaders in A.A. are but trusted and experienced servants of the whole" (p. 565). "Universal respect is the key to their usefulness" (p. 565).

a251b46036da.t: Bill's 1947 essay: some groups elect leaders, but "even with such a mandate each leader soon discovers that while he can always guide by example or persuasion he can never boss" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947), or he'll be passed over at the next election.

adf68ba1039f.t: What Bill's Concept IX essay says (1962)

00b5e8330527.t: <0>Structure isn't enough.</0> "Good leadership cannot function well in a poorly designed structure" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX), but weak leadership can hardly function even in the best one. Once a sound structure exists, that job is mostly done; leadership has to be found again and again.

4cf09ac853bf.t: <0>The base is the GSR.</0> The structure rests on thousands of general service representatives, hundreds of area committee members and nearly a hundred delegates: "These are the direct agents of the A.A. groups" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). Groups should choose GSRs with care; assemblies choosing delegates should set aside ambition and feuds and ask who is best qualified.

6961d4e4bd2e.t: <0>Choosing by lot.</0> Some members doubted the Third Legacy method (two-thirds or the hat). Bill says each time it was abandoned, the losing side felt defeated, and "Indeed the second-best man can often be as good a Delegate as the Assembly’s first choice; he may even be a better Delegate" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX).

5b40674ac78f.t: <0>The main theme: the trustees replacing the founders.</0> Bill says he is still advising and finishing leftover chores from 1955, these Concepts among them, but will soon have to withdraw from nearly all world service work. The board ran from 1938 to 1951 without a Conference; that change was resisted but proved right. Now he believes the board's leadership strength must be "considerably increased." "Students of history recognize that the transference of the original leadership of a society to its successors in leadership is always a critical turning point" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX).

b90f73e5cea5.t: <0>The 1959 article, "Leadership in A.A.: Ever a Vital Need."</0> Bill offers it for future servants. Its points: - A.A. sometimes twists "principles before personalities" so far that leaders become faceless automatons; at other times it demands they be practically infallible. Real leaders are in between. - "In effect, we are saying to them," Bill writes, "Act for us, but don’t boss us" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). - If a leader power-drives, members rebel; if he only takes orders, "he really isn’t a leader at all." - Good leadership originates plans, but consults widely on new and important matters, and "will often discard its own cherished plans for others that are better, and it will give credit to the source" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). - "Good leadership never passes the buck" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). - A statesman, unlike a "politico," knows that even large majorities can sometimes be dead wrong, and will stand against them when something vital is at stake. But opposition for its own sake is fatal: "When called upon, leadership must always give its reasons, and good ones" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). - Give and take: progress comes through "a series of improving compromises," yet sometimes one must "stick flat-footed" to a conviction. - Criticism: listen carefully to constructive critics, and even to destructive ones, because they may be telling the whole truth or a little of it. - Vision: the ability to make good estimates of the future. Bill says "One day at a time" refers to our emotional lives, not to refusing to plan. "As a matter of fact, all of A.A.’s Twelve Traditions were at first questions of estimate and vision for the future" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX), and he gives self-support and anonymity as examples. - Talents differ; choosing the best talent isn't creating a privileged class.

4d7fcfc7644e.t: <0>Twelfth Step work.</0> Bill ends by applying this to the work nearly every member does: "Every sponsor is necessarily a leader" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). The sponsor in his example is working with "his prospects," a person's life and family in the balance, and must estimate reactions, time his approach and lead "by personal spiritual example." This is the same situation as Chapter 7 of the Big Book, going to a man who is still drinking, though the Big Book's first 164 pages don't use the word sponsor (it appears only in the personal stories).

dd4b8f87224e.t: Concept IX says the board's leadership needs strengthening and that the change of leadership "must now be faced." The essay as printed in our copy then offers the 1959 article on personal qualities; it doesn't set out a specific plan for the board's composition.

460bd8a4ec4c.t: P-8 (© 2017) reprints most of the leadership points and adds that GSRs, together in their areas, elect the area's candidates for trustee. P-8 describes the GSR as the indispensable link between the group and A.A. as a whole; Bill calls GSRs, committee members and delegates together the indispensable linkage between the Fellowship and its world service.

6c4406388db7.t: Concept X: why must service authority equal service responsibility? | Recovery Starts

ac9b249e96d4.t: Concept X says: "Every service responsibility should be matched by an equal service authority, with the scope of such authority well defined" (p. 575).…

60a52af39dfb.t: Concept X: why must service authority equal service responsibility?

e3674205763c.t: Concept X says: "Every service responsibility should be matched by an equal service authority, with the scope of such authority well defined" (p. 575). The long form adds that the scope can be defined "by tradition, by resolution, by specific job description or by appropriate charters and bylaws."

26c91e81fa14.t: Bill W.'s reason, written in 1962: if people are given a job without the authority to do it, or authority without a defined limit, "personal clashes, confusion, and ineffectiveness will be inevitable" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X).

0e85de5286ba.t: Final authority must sit somewhere at each level, but should "practically never be used in full, except in an emergency" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X). And no job should have two equal bosses: "Authority can never be divided into equal halves" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X).

0584e0fd2749.t: Bill calls it all implied in Tradition Two: the group conscience as the ultimate authority, the trusted servant as the delegated one. "One cannot function without the other" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X).

0019a9a49cd1.t: Tradition Two (1946) holds both halves already: one ultimate authority expressed in group conscience (p. 563), and leaders who are "but trusted servants" (p. 562). Long Form Nine (1946) gives servants their role and its limit in one line: they "derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern" (p. 565).

612deb66fdcd.t: Bill's 1947 essay describes group committees that "have only the authorization to serve, never to command" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947). Concept X is about the service bodies, not groups, and adds what 1947 didn't spell out: a servant needs enough authority to actually do the job.

f5b3133d681d.t: What Bill's Concept X essay says (1962)

fab4f06b8123.t: <0>The principle.</0> Most societies and governments of the day, Bill says, break the rule that each responsibility needs a matching authority. The earlier Concepts were written to define the authority and responsibility of the groups, the Conference, the trustees and the service corporations so that they match at every level.

d404e79df252.t: <0>Four conditions.</0> Things go wrong unless authority and responsibility are well defined; those with final authority are able and willing to delegate; those with delegated authority feel free to use it as trusted servants; and there is some definite way to settle doubtful cases.

d27d53eaf35d.t: <0>A line of final authority.</0> "The principle of ultimate authority runs clear through our structure" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X): groups over the Conference, delegates over the trustees, trustees over the service corporations, directors over officers, officers over staff. Everything has to "head up somewhere" so each worker knows who the final boss is.

a07a3d332bca.t: <0>But not used in full.</0> Without delegated authority, Bill pictures groups directing delegates on every vote, delegates turning trustees into "a timid committee," trustees running the corporations by directive, and executives becoming "small czars." The proper uses of final authority are emergencies: groups can elect better delegates or withhold funds; delegates can censure or reorganize the trustees; trustees can do the same with the corporations; corporations can fire executives.

43d7fd49d244.t: <0>How authority is defined.</0> By legal means (corporate charters), by traditional means, and by principles for settling doubtful cases. The Conference Charter "is not a legal instrument, but practically speaking it is the substance of a contract between the A.A. groups and their Conference" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X). Delegates vote their conscience and the Conference decides what to refer back to the groups; the trustees insist on their legal right to administer, with a veto in rare cases; the corporations' charters and non-trustee directors protect their operating authority.

20167e7b87f2.t: <0>Conflicts.</0> Interlocking memberships between committees and corporations settle most routine conflicts. For the rest, there must be a senior jurisdiction, the junior one must be heard, and there must always be a known point of final decision.

888779ad9bc4.t: <0>No double-headed management.</0> "A condition to be avoided at all costs is double-headed business or policy management" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X). Bill takes this up again under Concept XI.

8557668f05c2.t: <0>Two more safeguards.</0> The Rights of Appeal and Petition, because "a bare majority is apt to constitute itself as a pseudo-ultimate authority" and executives "are apt to over-boss their assistants."

3570a92e2de6.t: <0>Summed up.</0> Be sure there is plenty of final authority to correct or reorganize, and equally sure every trusted servant has a clearly defined and adequate authority to do the daily work.

47184aacef01.t: The General Policy Committee Bill describes is now the General Sharing Session, meeting three times a year for about two hours; its functions "have changed markedly" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X, footnote 1).
