067732ed9e88.t: Concept XI: who helps the trustees, and how should paid A.A. workers be treated? | Recovery Starts

9656cd28fd14.t: Concept XI says: "The trustees should always have the best possible committees, corporate service directors, executives, staffs, and consultants" (p.…

d552b244cca8.t: Concept XI: who helps the trustees, and how should paid A.A. workers be treated?

cefba088251a.t: Concept XI says: "The trustees should always have the best possible committees, corporate service directors, executives, staffs, and consultants" (p. 575), and that how these people are chosen, rotated, related to each other and paid "will always be matters of serious concern" (p. 575).

339896c2d5fa.t: In his 1962 essay Bill W. describes the trustees' five standing committees then (Nominating, Finance, Public Information, Literature, General Policy), the two service corporations, and four principles for their paid staff: one executive in charge, fair pay, rotation, and full participation.

e09d5a612865.t: On pay he is direct: paid workers should be paid in reasonable relation to what similar work earns in the commercial world. The 1946 text already allowed that special services "may be well recompensed" (p. 564).

4ad6d1c4f928.t: Two dating cautions. P-8 calls much of Concept XI a picture of things "as they existed in 1962" (P-8). And a footnote says two paragraphs were removed from the published Concept XI by a later Conference action.

7e1760c24ef0.t: Long Form Eight (1946): A.A. should remain forever nonprofessional, "But we may employ alcoholics where they are going to perform those services for which we might otherwise have to engage nonalcoholics" (p. 564). "Such special services may be well recompensed" (p. 564).

2bfd351bb71e.t: Bill's 1946 essay on money argues the point. A janitor, a cook, a secretary or an editor can do their jobs without professionalizing A.A. "Why should these A.A.s work for nothing at jobs which the rest of us could not or would not attempt ourselves?" (P-17, Money, 1946). The line he draws: pay well for special services, never for Twelfth Step work.

c6167e2590b7.t: What Bill's Concept XI essay says (1962)

9d21b67ca462.t: <0>Why these people matter.</0> The non-trustee committee members, directors, executives and staff do most of the work, travel, meet visitors, and are what members see of world service. "Their quality and dedication, or their lack of these characteristics, will make or break our structure of service" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). They don't just support the trustees' leadership; they share it.

0194f34554ed.t: <0>The committees (as of 1962).</0> - <1>Nominating</1> fills vacancies with the best people available. Bill warns of a quiet decline: "Instinctively we look for associates rather like ourselves, only a little less experienced and able" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). - <2>Finance and Budgetary</2> keeps A.A. solvent. "This is the place where money and spirituality do have to mix, and in just the right proportion" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). Bill also tells how an earlier drive to build the reserve let the office run down, and group contributions fell by tens of thousands a year: prudence isn't hoarding. - <3>Public Information</3> needs professionals who can adapt to "Attraction rather than promotion"; "the techniques used to sell a big time personality or a new hair lotion would not be for A.A." (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). One public blunder could turn new prospects away. - <4>Literature</4> revises and creates books and pamphlets. Bill says the policy is "to aim at only the best," that a key figure "will necessarily be a paid writer and consultant" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI), and that getting the "A.A. feel" into the writing is vital. - <5>General Policy</5> filters business for the board, with minority reports, in long Sunday sessions.

64b6172ed9df.t: None of these committees is executive; they recommend.

3e1fa4a8ccfa.t: <0>The two corporations.</0> A.A. World Services (with its publishing division) and the Grapevine each have their own board of directors, made up of trustees, outside experts and paid executives. Bill explains why they shouldn't be merged with each other or with the board, and why publishing needn't be a separate company: "Most of our A.A. books are already written, and it is probable that not many more will be published" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI).

967b5374eafe.t: <0>Four principles for paid workers.</0> 1. <1>One executive.</1> "A board or a committee can never actively manage anything, in the continuous executive sense" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). Executive direction heads up in one person, who should be left alone while the work is done well, and who must learn when to act alone and when to consult. 2. <2>Fair pay.</2> Each paid worker "should be recompensed in reasonable relation to the value of his or her similar services or abilities in the commercial world" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). Bill rejects the idea that A.A. workers should accept charity-level pay, which would ask of them a sacrifice asked of no other member. Cheap help, he says, is insecure and costly: "This is neither good spirituality nor good business" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). 3. <3>Rotation.</3> Staff rotate assignments and are paid on the same basis, after an early collapse showed the danger of one highly paid person holding everything. On terms of service: "a Delegate has to serve two years, and a Trustee must serve four" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI), but staff shouldn't have a fixed term. 4. <4>Full participation.</4> Paid workers get votes on boards and committees, and more: they should be treated as friends and co-workers, and the fact that they depend on their pay should never be used as a lever against them.

d8fb7e104738.t: <0>A line to read in its context.</0> Explaining why members shouldn't see world service as charity they pay for, Bill writes that the services benefit members as much as newcomers: "We are helping others in order to help ourselves" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). That is his 1962 wording about service funding. Chapter 7 of the Big Book (1939) is the earlier text on why we help others: it too says plainly that helping others protects the helper's sobriety (pp. 89, 97), and it keeps turning the helper toward the other man's welfare (p. 94) (see <1>Is helping others selfish if it keeps me sober?</1>).

1d02a49f2bb4.t: Six more trustees' committees have been added since 1962 (footnote 1); the General Policy Committee became the General Sharing Session (footnote 2).

d6a7d0fbd0ae.t: GSO has had a full-time general manager since 1960; the Grapevine now has a full-time paid editorial staff; most GSO staff now rotate every two years (footnotes 6–8).

b90cd96883f5.t: "Due to an Advisory Action of the 66th A.A. General Service Conference, two paragraphs have been removed from the published version of Concept XI" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI, footnote 10). They are available on request from GSO's Archives. Our copy doesn't say what they said. (Counting from the first Conference in 1951, the 66th met in 2016.)

14a2f24b823b.t: Concept XII: what are the General Warranties of the Conference? | Recovery Starts

e6ba84377fe2.t: Concept XII is Article 12 of the Conference Charter (1955): six promises binding the General Service Conference to "observe the spirit of the A.A.…

c8f3cafd3e35.t: Concept XII: what are the General Warranties of the Conference?

248f3c761b1e.t: Concept XII is Article 12 of the Conference Charter (1955): six promises binding the General Service Conference to "observe the spirit of the A.A. Tradition" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). In order: never the seat of perilous wealth or power; enough operating funds plus an ample reserve; no member in unqualified authority over another; important decisions by discussion, vote and, whenever possible, substantial unanimity; no punitive action and no public controversy; never any acts of government, and always democratic.

0dbba7352a18.t: It is the hardest Concept to change. The Conference can amend the rest of its Charter, but changing a Warranty needs the written consent of three-quarters of the groups that respond, with six months to consider.

79f1d5d2e26e.t: Bill W.'s 1962 essay calls them "counsels of prudence" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII), protection against "our very natural human temptations to wealth, prestige, power, and the like."

8f51e4a183a1.t: Several of the Warranties echo what the 1946 Long Form already said to the groups: prudent reserves, no large gifts, no controversy, "they do not govern" (p. 565).

e2f9cfadfc47.t: <0>Wealth and reserves.</0> Long Form Seven (1946): accepting large gifts or gifts with obligations "is unwise," and "we view with much concern those A.A. treasuries which continue, beyond prudent reserves, to accumulate funds for no stated A.A. purpose" (p. 564).

f16a6c3204c8.t: <0>Authority.</0> Long Form Nine: A.A.'s servants "do not govern" (p. 565). Bill in 1947: "So long as we avoid any menacing accumulation of wealth or the growth of personal government at these centers, we cannot go astray" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947).

a33c8e78041c.t: <0>Controversy.</0> Long Form Ten: "The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one" (p. 565).

8acfa1fc9ba1.t: <0>Freedom.</0> Long Form Three: membership never to depend "upon money or conformity" (p. 563).

e93b980c868a.t: Concept XII turns these into promises made by the Conference itself.

b7786fed26c8.t: The Warranties and how they're protected

6342407bb4a5.t: The Concept "consists of Article 12 of the Conference Charter" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII), the 1955 agreement between the groups and their trustees. The first eleven Articles "can be readily amended by the Conference itself." Article 12 needs the written consent of three-quarters of the directory-listed groups who vote, with six months to deliberate. "Although changes in the Warranties of Article 12 thus have been made difficult, they have not been made impossible" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). Bill ranks them with the Traditions for world service.

b890af4ae8db.t: What Bill's essay says about each (1962)

3b0a2db6dd35.t: <0>One: never the seat of perilous wealth or power.</0> Not "no money, no authority," which would be "dangerous and absurd." The protection against wealth is the Tradition itself: decline outside contributions and keep individual gifts modest, and "we need only to avoid the temptation of taking money from the outside world" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). On a would-be dictator: "Our setup being what it is, such an aspirant couldn’t last a year" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII), since the delegates control the money. The one power the Conference can't do without is the spiritual kind, from humble and dedicated servants: "They do not drive us by mandate; they lead us by example" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).

f500d084f4b5.t: <0>Two: sufficient funds plus an ample reserve.</0> Members give time freely but are slower with money. The reserve then was about one year's office expenses, saved over twenty years mostly from book income, and it had covered the years when contributions fell short. Bill answers critics who wanted the Big Book sold at cost: charity to newcomers is the sponsor's, not the group's or A.A.'s: "But such charities are the responsibility of the sponsor and not of the A.A. group itself" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). Book income, he argues, isn't really profit but the sum of buyers' contributions: "This fund is not the property of private investors; it is wholly owned by A.A. itself" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). He also addresses his own royalties: "This royalty income from the book buyers has enabled me to do all the rest of my A.A. work on a full-time volunteer basis" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII), and hopes the arrangement will continue to be considered fair.

7c4e466dd0db.t: <0>Three: no unqualified authority.</0> This makes the Right of Participation (Concept IV) something the Conference alone can't take away. More broadly, "It really means that we of A.A. will not tolerate absolute human authority in any form" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). Some members already called Article 12 "The A.A. Service Bill of Rights."

e6ca9a53019d.t: <0>Four: substantial unanimity.</0> Debate should continue, time permitting, until a heavy majority can support each critical decision; then even a bad decision brings no recriminations. But there are limits: in an emergency, or when "a small minority obstinately tries to use the principle of substantial unanimity to block a clearly needed action," then "it would be the plain duty of the majority to override such a misuse of the principle of substantial unanimity" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).

ba18c21c827f.t: <0>Five: no punishment, no public controversy.</0> "When we of A.A. fail to follow sound spiritual principles, alcohol cuts us down" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII), so no human system of penalties is needed. Under public attack that has little or no justification, the best defense is almost always none, "complete silence at the public level"; justified criticism may be acknowledged privately, with thanks. On Tradition violators: the Conference is "guardian" of the Traditions, but suing or publicly punishing them "would place the Conference in the position of having violated one A.A. Tradition in order to defend another" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). Privately it can tell them they're out of order and use persuasion; in the long run it relies on A.A. and public opinion. Bill notes that "A.A.’s World Headquarters is not a police operation" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII), and that many local Tradition questions are gray areas best left to the people concerned.

b4c825688cec.t: On a split in A.A., Bill's answer is near-complete nonresistance: "We have no doctrine that has to be maintained" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). Members who want their own groups, retreats or Communion breakfasts are welcome to them: "Only we hope you won’t designate your efforts as an A.A. group or enterprise" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). A.A. will give away its knowledge and experience, "all excepting the A.A. name itself" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).

d86b7b3dfa41.t: On protecting the name: A.A. once considered incorporating it everywhere and asking Congress for a charter, but the early Conferences decided against it, since a public lawsuit is a public controversy. Bill refers readers to <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) for the story, which prints the committee's finding that a Congressional incorporation "would create by law a power to govern" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957) contrary to the Traditions.

ca2c976e33ed.t: <0>Six: no acts of government; always democratic.</0> Bill lists the freedoms the Traditions give: no penalties for nonconformity, no fees or dues, no expulsion, each group running its own affairs, and any group of alcoholics gathered for sobriety may call itself an A.A. group "provided that, as a group, they have no other purpose or affiliation" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). The Conference must "abstain completely from any and all acts of authoritative government which could in any wise curtail A.A.’s freedom under God" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).

85e7097a6b77.t: <0>"No other purpose or affiliation."</0> Long Form Three (1946) says a group may call itself an A.A. group "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation" (p. 563). Bill's 1962 list adds "purpose."

77b9addb0251.t: <0>The original wording.</0> The 1955 Charter's Article 12 read "an incitement to serious public controversy" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955). The current Charter and the Concept say "public controversy," without "serious." Our copy doesn't say when it changed.

48d4a10a35a2.t: <0>Two-thirds, then three-quarters.</0> The 1955 Charter as first printed required the written consent of two-thirds of all groups to change the Tradition; the St. Louis resolution the same year asked for three-quarters of the registered groups who respond. The 1957 Conference amended the Charter to three-quarters, covering Article 12, the Traditions and the Steps (Appendix K, footnote 4); a 1976 resolution confirmed the Steps (Appendix L, footnote 3).

56c1183c0b16.t: <0>The name.</0> Bill's 1962 text says the Conference decided against legal protection of the name. A 2024–2026 footnote adds: "However, the name Alcoholics Anonymous and the abbreviation A.A. were all legally registered in 1972" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII, footnote 3).

800be3b08539.t: <0>The reserve.</0> Bill's 1960 reserve was about one year's office expenses. P-8 (© 2017) says the reserve "should be one full year’s operating expenses" (P-8). The 2024–2026 footnote reports 6.47 months at the end of 2024.

8cc92b1ece61.t: Are the Twelve Concepts the same as the Twelve Traditions? | Recovery Starts

597fa70c67a8.t: No. They are two different sets of twelve, written sixteen years apart. The Traditions were first printed in 1946 and guide A.A. groups and A.A. as a…

86744a4fca0c.t: Are the Twelve Concepts the same as the Twelve Traditions?

318b42d9df40.t: No. They are two different sets of twelve, written sixteen years apart. The Traditions were first printed in 1946 and guide A.A. groups and A.A. as a whole. The Concepts were written by Bill W. in 1962 and describe how A.A.'s world service bodies (the General Service Conference, the trustees, the service corporations and their staffs) relate to each other and to the groups.

d7712c0b545a.t: The Big Book's Appendix VII says it in two lines: "A.A.’s Twelve Steps are principles for personal recovery" and "The Twelve Traditions ensure the unity of the Fellowship" (p. 574). The Concepts are there to keep the service structure "responsive and responsible to those they serve" (p. 574).

f6bdbdebedc6.t: They are connected. Bill builds the Concepts on the Traditions, Tradition Two above all, and the Twelfth Concept binds the Conference to "observe the spirit of the A.A. Tradition" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).

ae2c911af7aa.t: They are changed differently. Changing a Tradition needs the written consent of three-quarters of the groups that respond. Of the Concepts, only Concept XII (Article 12 of the Conference Charter) is protected that way.

28960c439de9.t: <0>The Traditions</0> were first printed in 1946 as twelve points in the Grapevine, the "long form"; the Big Book reprints them in Appendix I, saying the short form is "a condensed version of the original ‘long form’ A.A. Traditions as first printed in 1946" (p. 561). They were written while both co-founders were alive.

087796d84215.t: <0>The Concepts</0> were "Written by co-founder Bill W. in 1962" (p. 574), twelve years after Dr. Bob died, and adopted by the General Service Conference that April. Their one-sentence short form was approved in 1971 and added to the Big Book in the fourth edition, 2001 (p. xii).

d5fc3efd8def.t: The Long Form of the Traditions talks to groups and members: who may belong (any alcoholic who wants to recover), what makes a group (two or three alcoholics with no other affiliation), group autonomy, the one primary purpose, money, property, outside issues, anonymity (pp. 563–566).

c1d44b47f10c.t: The Concepts talk to the service bodies. Concept I is about where final authority over "world services" sits; the rest cover the Conference, the trustees, their committees, the two service corporations, executives and paid staff. Bill's introduction says the Concepts set out "the ‘why’ of our service structure" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction).

2e841e61581f.t: They are also written differently. Bill says that "Since each Concept is really a group of related principles" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction), they could not be made as short as the Steps and Traditions. Each Concept comes with a long essay; the Traditions' Long Form is a paragraph each.

109f2eb1f6eb.t: Bill doesn't present the Concepts as a second set of Traditions. He presents them as the Traditions applied to A.A.'s service center:

672012c81968.t: <0>Tradition Two.</0> The Long Form says: "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience" (p. 563). Concept I quotes Tradition Two and says its principles are "crystal clear: the A.A. groups are to be the final authority; their leaders are to be entrusted with delegated responsibilities only" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). Concepts II, III, IV, V and X all lean on its "trusted servants" line. Tradition Two is the one Bill names throughout. The links below are ours: the essays don't cite these Long Form passages, except that Concept XII grounds its first Warranty in declining outside money and its fifth in the Tradition against public controversy.

743765d72295.t: <0>Long Form Nine.</0> "The trustees of the General Service Board are, in effect, our A.A. General Service Committee" (p. 565); in 1946 the board was still the Alcoholic Foundation, renamed in 1954. Concepts VI to VIII spell out what those trustees do and don't do.

745645164fa3.t: <0>Long Form Six and Seven.</0> Property "separately incorporated and managed, thus dividing the material from the spiritual" (p. 564), and treasuries that pile up money "beyond prudent reserves" (p. 564). Concept VIII keeps the service corporations separate; Concept XII's first two Warranties are about wealth and a prudent reserve.

9d6fa7097e26.t: <0>Long Form Eight.</0> Special workers "may be well recompensed" (p. 564). Concept XI says how paid A.A. staff should be treated and paid.

736ce381de55.t: <0>Long Form Ten.</0> "The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one" (p. 565). Concept XII's Fifth Warranty: no public controversy, no punishment.

130e6c1318b4.t: The Traditions govern A.A. groups and A.A. as a whole. The Concepts were written for the world service structure. Bill does say their principles "can of course be used to good effect throughout our entire structure" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction), and P-8 (1986) says the Warranties express principles that "apply to all other A.A. entities as well" (P-8). But nothing in the Concepts gives anyone authority over a group. Concept XII forbids the Conference "any acts of government" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII), and the Long Form says a group "should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience" in its own affairs (p. 563).

ff441eeda63a.t: The Concepts say most of the service structure can be changed easily. Bill notes "that the Conference Charter itself can be easily amended" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction), with an exception or two.

fafa77fe206a.t: The exceptions are the Traditions and Article 12. The 1955 St. Louis resolution says neither the Traditions nor the Warranties of Article 12 may be changed without asking the registered groups of the world, giving them at least six months, and receiving in writing "the consent of at least three-quarters of all those registered groups who respond to such proposal" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix L). Concept XII is Article 12, which is why Bill writes "We have ranked them therefore with A.A.’s Twelve Traditions" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).

97149be2efe9.t: One dating detail: the 1955 Charter as first printed asked only for "the written consent of two-thirds of all the A.A. groups" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955) to change the Tradition. The 1957 Conference amended it to three-quarters, matching the St. Louis resolution, and added the Twelve Steps (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, footnote 4). Concepts I to XI have no such protection.

37eec805abbb.t: The Twelve Concepts for World Service are twelve statements, each with a long essay, written by Bill W. in 1962 about how A.A.'s world services are run:…

5aaf40c55f4f.t: What are the Twelve Concepts, and why were they written?

b91cf61d2492.t: The Twelve Concepts for World Service are twelve statements, each with a long essay, written by Bill W. in 1962 about how A.A.'s world services are run: the groups, the General Service Conference, the trustees of the General Service Board, and the service corporations and their staffs. The 12th General Service Conference adopted them on April 26, 1962.

263ed55c90d0.t: They are not about personal recovery or about how a group runs itself. The Big Book's Appendix VII puts it in one line each: the Steps are for personal recovery, the Traditions for unity, and the Concepts help keep the service structure "responsive and responsible to those they serve" (p. 574).

093e26f41668.t: Bill says he wrote them to record the "why" of the service structure so its lessons would not be lost once the founders were gone. Dr. Bob had died in 1950; Bill was preparing to step back.

372195bd5047.t: They are later than the Traditions (1946) and Dr. Bob's death. Where the 1946–47 texts already state a principle, the Concepts build on it, and these pages show the earlier text first.

4626d7d21253.t: The Concepts' own title page says they were written "by Bill W." and adopted "by the 12th Annual General Service Conference of Alcoholics Anonymous on April 26, 1962" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, title page).

2e8675e226f5.t: A 1985 preface from the General Service Office says they "were written by Bill W. in 1962" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Preface, 1985). Details went out of date, so the 1985 Conference asked that they be printed "in the original 1962 version, with required factual changes provided as numbered footnotes at the end of each chapter" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Preface, 1985). That is how our copy reads: Bill's 1962 text, with footnotes added as late as the 2024–2026 edition.

ecd69d451ed5.t: A one-sentence "short form" of each Concept came later. It was approved by the 1971 Conference and put in the Service Manual in 1974 (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Preface, 1985). The Big Book has printed that short form since the fourth edition (p. xii), as Appendix VII on pages 574–575, which says the Concepts were "Written by co-founder Bill W. in 1962" (p. 574).

c809c487af34.t: <0>To keep the experience.</0> His introduction says: "These Concepts therefore aim to record the ‘why’ of our service structure" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction). He expected later workers to change things, and warned that "change does not necessarily spell progress" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction). If a change went wrong, the Concepts would be a way back to what had worked.

812879f05e27.t: <0>Not to freeze it.</0> In the same introduction he rejects the idea that the Concepts should harden into gospel: "Nothing could stray further from the intent of these Concepts" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction). A good enough case, convincing to both the trustees and the Conference, is all a change needs.

44b247e6ca05.t: <0>Because of power.</0> He built them on "checks and balances" because alcoholics in charge tend to enlarge their own authority, and resist anyone else's. Of those traits he writes: "I’m the more sure of this because I possess these traits myself" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction).

6ad195bd4257.t: <0>Because the founders would not last.</0> Concept I tells the story. When Dr. Bob's fatal illness became known in 1948, it was clear that he and Bill were almost the only link between the little-known trustees and the groups. "The fact had to be faced that A.A.’s founders were perishable" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). The answer was a representative Conference, tried from 1951 and made permanent at St. Louis in 1955. Concept IX says the Concepts themselves were one of the chores left over from St. Louis, written as Bill prepared to withdraw from nearly all world service work (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX).

778b360a678c.t: Bill says each Concept is hard to state briefly: "Since each Concept is really a group of related principles" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction), they could not be as short as the Steps and Traditions.

372d28f9d47e.t: The earlier texts they rest on

f0c276714dd8.t: The service structure didn't start in 1962. The Long Form of the Traditions (1946) already says "The trustees of the General Service Board are, in effect, our A.A. General Service Committee" (p. 565), that they look after the General Service Office and public relations, and that all such servants "derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern" (p. 565). (The 1946 original named the trustees of the Alcoholic Foundation; the board was renamed the General Service Board in 1954, and the Big Book prints the new name.)

2d23a10e6027.t: Bill's 1947 Grapevine essay on government says the same of the New York office: "we can merely supply certain indispensable services" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947). The trustees, he wrote then, are custodians, "caretakers only" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947).

f76a0ef3bf1a.t: The Concepts keep coming back to Tradition Two. Concept I quotes it in full, and Concept X ends by saying its whole account of ultimate and delegated authority is "fully implied" in Tradition Two (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X). So the earlier text is the root; the Concepts explain how Bill applied it to a Conference, a board and two corporations.

d4368fcdfb3d.t: Each has its own page: - <0>I.</0> The groups hold the final authority over world services. <1>Concept I: who has the final say in A.A.?</1> - <2>II.</2> The groups delegated the active work to the Conference in 1955. <3>Concept II</3> - <4>III.</4> Trusted servants have a "Right of Decision". <5>Concept III</5> - <6>IV.</6> Each kind of servant gets a vote in proportion to responsibility. <7>Concept IV</7> - <8>V.</8> Minorities can appeal, and anyone can petition over a grievance. <9>Concept V</9> - <10>VI.</10> The trustees take the active lead, under the Conference. <11>Concept VI</11> - <12>VII.</12> The trustees hold legal power; the Conference holds practical power. <13>Concept VII</13> - <14>VIII.</14> The trustees oversee the service corporations rather than run them. <15>Concept VIII</15> - <16>IX.</16> Good leaders, chosen well, are indispensable. <17>Concept IX</17> - <18>X.</18> Authority must equal responsibility. <19>Concept X</19> - <20>XI.</20> The committees, directors and paid staff who work with the trustees. <21>Concept XI</21> - <22>XII.</22> The General Warranties of the Conference. <23>Concept XII</23>

afba1fc22656.t: The pamphlet P-8 (first printed 1986) sorts them this way: Concepts III through V, IX and XII deal with spiritual principles, and the rest mainly with how the service bodies relate (P-8). It also says plainly that "it is NOT the Concepts themselves" (P-8): for the real text, read the essays.

7c015173209b.t: The Concepts are Bill's work from 1962, twelve years after Dr. Bob died, about a structure begun in 1938 but reshaped after 1950, when the Conference was added (1951–55). That doesn't make them wrong, but they are later than the Big Book's text and the 1946–47 Traditions, and they describe a specific office in a specific year. Many details (the number of directors, the money, the committees) have changed, and the footnotes say so.

1197382a5074.t: One change is worth knowing: a footnote to Concept XI says that, by an Advisory Action of the 66th General Service Conference, two paragraphs were removed from the published version of Concept XI, and are available on request from GSO's Archives (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI, footnote 10). Our copy doesn't say what they contained. (Counting from the first Conference in 1951, the 66th met in 2016.)

6690f2b7f235.t: "Conference-approved" means a book, pamphlet or video has been reviewed by A.A.'s General Service Conference (the yearly meeting of delegates from the U.S. and Canada with A.A.'s trustees) and approved by a two-thirds vote. It may then carry the line "This is A.A. General Service Conference-approved literature."

f9c141edae8e.t: The label tells you the Conference accepted the text as expressing A.A.'s view. It doesn't tell you when the text was written.

aadc35559b54.t: The Conference first met in 1951, after the Big Book (1939), the Long Form of the Traditions (1946) and Dr. Bob's death (1950). Books and pamphlets written decades later carry the same line.

072c8fbde5ae.t: The Grapevine is not Conference-approved issue by issue; the Conference recognizes it as A.A.'s international journal instead.

f228a55499a8.t: <0>The A.A. Service Manual</0> (2024–2026 edition) describes the process (Service Manual, 2024–2026): - A need for a new piece is studied by Conference and trustees' committees; if it isn't urgent or broad enough, the project is dropped or put off. - Committee and staff members criticize and suggest from first draft to last, which can take months or years. - The finished manuscript goes to the right Conference committee, and if that committee recommends it, to the whole Conference. - "If two-thirds of Conference members agree to the manuscript as presented or with specific edits approved by the body, the new piece of literature is entitled to bear the designation" (Service Manual, 2024–2026).

478ed0345a23.t: Its glossary puts it in one line: literature produced under Conference and trustees' committees, reviewed and recommended by Conference committees, "and that have been approved by the Conference" (Service Manual, 2024–2026).

8eea31696401.t: P-43, <0>Twelve Traditions Illustrated</0> (1971), describes the same care in its own day: each new project "must first be approved by the Conference" (P-43), a trustees' committee watches it at every stage, and the finished piece must be okayed again by the Conference Literature Committee (P-43). The aim, it says, is that each piece expresses "the view of the group conscience of A.A. as a whole" (P-43).

e88c7d28b4b6.t: P-16, <0>The A.A. Group</0> (© 2018), separates Conference-approved books and pamphlets, which come from Conference actions, from the General Service Office's "service material," which is written to answer members' practical questions (P-16).

1cb808b87e51.t: What the label doesn't tell you

2c52041f00a1.t: <0>When a text was written.</0> The General Service Conference held its first meeting in April 1951 (P-44). The Big Book's text was written in 1938 and published in 1939; today's copy carries the Conference-approved line on its copyright page (p. iv), but our sources don't say when the designation was first applied to it. P-43 (1971), <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) and P-53 (© 2017) carry the same line (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

318fff5df5c2.t: So the label puts a 1939 text and a 1980 text on the same footing. It doesn't help with the question of which is earlier and closer to the events. For that, check each source's date. See: <0>Which A.A. books are oldest, and why does the date matter?</0>

6f3284b81632.t: <0>Who wrote the material inside.</0> Conference-approved items can contain material from other publishers. P-53 says Dr. Bob's 1948 talk is reprinted with the permission of AA Grapevine, Inc. (P-53), and the Big Book's copyright page says five of its personal stories are copyrighted by the Grapevine (p. iv).

c4246f1609e8.t: The Service Manual answers this directly: in 1986 the Conference said that since each issue of the Grapevine can't go through the approval process, "the Conference recognizes AA Grapevine as the international journal of Alcoholics Anonymous" (Service Manual, 2024–2026). The same recognition covers La Viña (Service Manual, 2024–2026).

c36d1c942aed.t: Where is "contempt prior to investigation," and who does the Big Book say said it? | Recovery Starts

dba8c970acc2.t: It's the last line of the Big Book's Appendix II, "Spiritual Experience" (p. 568). The book credits the quotation to Herbert Spencer.

acb1559c9c4f.t: Where is "contempt prior to investigation," and who does the Big Book say said it?

ba74072d1c97.t: It's the last line of the Big Book's Appendix II, "Spiritual Experience" (p. 568). The book credits the quotation to Herbert Spencer.

8a21622e6daf.t: Our sources have none of Spencer's writings, so it can't check whether he said or wrote it. This page reports only what the A.A. books print.

3f12fa91c5dc.t: In place, it follows the appendix's warning about the alcoholic who shuts his mind: any alcoholic who can honestly face his problems "can recover, provided he does not close his mind to all spiritual concepts" (p. 568), and "He can only be defeated by an attitude of intolerance or belligerent denial." (p. 568)

012a8b084941.t: The quotation was in the Big Book before Appendix II. It heads a first-edition personal story, "An Artist's Concept" (1939), which was dropped in 1955 and reprinted in <0>Experience, Strength and Hope</0> (2003).

a13f38cc5ef2.t: The Big Book prints it as a principle "which is a bar against all information, which is proof against all arguments and which cannot fail to keep a man in everlasting ignorance" (p. 568), and names it: "that principle is contempt prior to investigation" (p. 568). Below it: "—Herbert Spencer" (p. 568).

302d1bd982e7.t: Appendix II is short (pp. 567–568). In order: 1. The book uses "spiritual experience" and "spiritual awakening" for the personality change that brings recovery, which shows up "in many different forms" (p. 567). 2. The first printing gave many readers the impression these changes had to be sudden and spectacular; "Happily for everyone, this conclusion is erroneous." (p. 567) 3. Most experiences are what William James called the "educational variety" (p. 567), developing slowly. Members find they have tapped an inner resource they come to identify with their own conception of a Power greater than themselves (pp. 567–568). 4. "Most emphatically we wish to say that any alcoholic capable of honestly facing his problems in the light of our experience can recover" (p. 568), unless he closes his mind to all spiritual concepts. "He can only be defeated by an attitude of intolerance or belligerent denial." (p. 568) 5. "We find that no one need have difficulty with the spirituality of the program." (p. 568) "Willingness, honesty and open mindedness are the essentials of recovery. But these are indispensable." (p. 568) 6. The Spencer quotation.

a44926c4b94c.t: So the quotation closes an appendix whose last warning is against a closed mind: the only thing it says can defeat an alcoholic is intolerance or belligerent denial (p. 568).

e31c1202e287.t: Its first appearance in the book

d3e623463e82.t: "An Artist's Concept" was one of the personal stories in the first edition. <0>Experience, Strength and Hope</0> (2003) reprints the stories from Part One that were "deleted when the second edition of Alcoholics Anonymous was published" (<1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1>, 2003). The story opens with the same Spencer quotation, and its writer comments that it is "descriptive of the mental attitudes of many alcoholics when the subject of religion, as a cure, is first brought to their attention" (<2>Experience, Strength and Hope</2>, 2003). So the line was used by a member in 1939, about the same resistance Appendix II later speaks to.

ea1d6e82778f.t: Appendix II says it was written after the first printing, which had left readers with the wrong impression (p. 567). The Preface says "The second edition added the appendices" (p. xi), and the second edition was published in 1955 (p. xi). By the book's own account, then, the appendix and its use of the quotation are from after 1950, while the quotation itself was already in the 1939 story.

4ad81c4ab9fd.t: It confirms it. The line is usually used to mean: don't dismiss something before you've looked into it, especially the spiritual side of the program. That's how the appendix uses it, and how the 1939 story used it. As printed, the principle itself is general ("a bar against all information," p. 568); the book applies it to closing one's mind to all spiritual concepts. Who first said it is a separate question our sources can't settle.

d554082e1425.t: Where does "cooperation but not affiliation" come from?

c25bcb1a5273.t: The phrase isn't in the Big Book, in the 1946 Long Form or in Bill W.'s 1946–47 essays. In our sources it appears in later pamphlets: <0>The Twelve Traditions Illustrated</0> (P-43, © 1971, this printing updated 2023), <1>The A.A. Group</1> (P-16, 2018), and a Conference policy statement printed in P-17, which words it "cooperation but nonafiliation" (so spelled in P-17, "A.A. and Alcoholism").

47a0c1117786.t: The idea is in the Long Form of Tradition Six (1946): "While an A.A. group may cooperate with anyone, such cooperation ought never go so far as affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied." (p. 564).

75ceda5ed6d2.t: The cooperation half goes back to 1939. Chapter 7 tells members finding drinkers through doctors and ministers: "So cooperate; never criticize." (p. 89).

885f59b17602.t: It describes how A.A. and its groups relate to others. It doesn't bind the organizations A.A. cooperates with.

6acc2d4c89b5.t: All our sources were searched for the words <0>cooperation but</0> and <1>cooperate but</1>, with line breaks joined. Every hit is in P-43, P-16 or P-17's undated policy statement. None is in the Big Book, in the Long Form or in Bill's Grapevine essays of 1946–47.

49c4d27bb9c7.t: The idea, in the earliest texts

2a1192d87714.t: <0>1939.</0> The Big Book's members cooperated with doctors, ministers and hospitals from the start. To find drinkers who want to recover, ask "a few doctors, ministers, priests or hospitals" (p. 89); "Ministers and doctors are competent and you can learn much from them if you wish" (p. 89); "So cooperate; never criticize." (p. 89). "To be helpful is our only aim." (p. 89). An approach through a doctor or an institution "is a better bet" than through the family (p. 91). The book thanks a hospital that suggested A.A. to its patients (p. 162). The 1939 Foreword: "We are not allied with any particular faith, sect or denomination, nor do we oppose anyone." (p. xiv).

b07c91218306.t: <0>1946, the Long Form.</0> Tradition Six draws the line the later phrase names: an A.A. group "may cooperate with anyone," but never as far as "affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564). "An A.A. group can bind itself to no one." (p. 564). Tradition Three adds that two or three alcoholics may call themselves an A.A. group "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation" (p. 563).

e2ea73b96d5f.t: <0>1946–47, Bill W.'s essays.</0> - "Everywhere we cooperate with hospitals." Many give A.A. special privileges and working arrangements, "But none of these institutions are known as 'A.A. hospitals.'" (P-17, "Money", 1946). - "As groups, we cannot endorse, finance or form an alliance with any other cause, however good" (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947). Members may work in other fields as individuals, careful of the A.A. name.

17b01a48da6b.t: <0>1955 and 1957.</0> - "We will cooperate with practically everybody, yet we decline to marry our Society to anyone." (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955). - The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955): A.A. doesn't take any particular medical point of view, "though we cooperate widely with the men of medicine as well as with the men of religion" (p. xx). - <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957): no A.A. group should ally itself "with any particular brand of medical or psychiatric treatment" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957). In the next breath: "We can cooperate with anyone." (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957).

90c6d2ebc9e1.t: The phrase itself, in later pamphlets

4810374e3d7b.t: <0>P-43</0> (<1>The Twelve Traditions Illustrated</1>, © 1971; our copy is a 2023 update, so the passage can't be dated to 1971 for certain): "Toward outside agencies dealing with alcoholism, the A.A. policy is 'cooperation but not affiliation.'" (P-43). Its examples of cooperating: welcoming referrals from clinics, sponsoring A.A. groups in institutions. Its examples of crossing the line: soliciting money for a rehab at an A.A. meeting, and A.A. being listed as a beneficiary of a fund drive.

f02e99efab68.t: <0>P-17's policy statement, "A.A. and Alcoholism."</0> Undated, affirmed by the General Service Conference, printed in the 2019 pamphlet: the movement has adopted a policy of "cooperation but nonafiliation" (P-17, "A.A. and Alcoholism"; so spelled) with other organizations concerned with the problem of alcoholism.

87e57d6b5532.t: <0>P-16</0> (<1>The A.A. Group</1>, 2018) uses the phrase several times: service committees serve the community "through our Sixth Tradition of cooperation but not affiliation" (P-16, 2018); "A.A. has adopted a policy of cooperation but not affiliation with other organizations concerned with the treatment of alcoholism." (P-16, 2018); "Our Traditions encourage cooperation but not affiliation." (P-16, 2018).

6795fe4a9cdb.t: What it covers and what it doesn't

279c63802975.t: In all these texts the phrase describes what A.A. and A.A. groups do: work alongside doctors, hospitals, treatment facilities, courts and others, while never becoming part of them, financing them, endorsing them or lending them the A.A. name. It doesn't tell those organizations how to run, and A.A. members working in them do so as individuals. See <0>What does "no outside affiliation" mean in practice?</0> and <1>Tradition Six: can an A.A. group partner with a treatment centre?</1>

b8fde9c11ff7.t: Does A.A. sign court slips or write letters for courts and probation? | Recovery Starts

19be1773bcef.t: The Big Book says nothing about court slips, probation or letters to courts. Courts come up only in passing in the 1939 text: Bill's old school friend was…

03f1441a9e6a.t: Does A.A. sign court slips or write letters for courts and probation?

d4b46cca14f4.t: The Big Book says nothing about court slips, probation or letters to courts. Courts come up only in passing in the 1939 text: Bill's old school friend was spared commitment when two men "appeared in court, persuading the judge to suspend his commitment" (p. 9); a member making amends faced an arrest order over unpaid alimony (p. 79); and Chapter 7 expects members to make trips to "police courts" to help other alcoholics (p. 97).

134cd9bc763b.t: Today's group pamphlet lists, among the things A.A. does not do, "Provide letters of reference to parole boards, attorneys, court officials, schools, businesses, social agencies, or any other organization or institution." (P-16, 2018). A.A. also doesn't keep membership records or "Follow up or try to control its members" (P-16, 2018).

f869c44097eb.t: Whether a group or a member may sign an attendance slip is not settled by any text in our sources. P-16 refers to an A.A. Guideline, "Cooperating with Court, D.W.I., and Similar Programs," which isn't in our sources.

d9183d84a4d6.t: These texts describe what A.A. and its groups do. Courts and probation offices set their own requirements.

eabcd1f83d84.t: The Big Book doesn't address court-ordered attendance. Courts appear in three places. In "Bill's Story," the old school friend who brought Bill the message had been headed for commitment until "two men had appeared in court, persuading the judge to suspend his commitment" (p. 9). And in Chapter 7, helping others may mean "innumerable trips to police courts, sanitariums, hospitals, jails and asylums" (p. 97). In both, people go to court on a drinker's behalf. The third is in Chapter 6, on amends: a man whose first wife "went to court and got an order for his arrest" (p. 79) over unpaid alimony wrote to her instead of walking up to the judge, and the matter was settled (p. 79). None of the three involves reporting on anyone's attendance.

3e0c76fb8b40.t: What the book does say about pressure is mixed, and worth reading whole: - On the newcomer and the program, it is firm that no one should be pushed. "He should not be pushed or prodded by you, his wife, or his friends." (p. 95). When a man is given the book, "it is best that no one tell him he must abide by its suggestions" (p. 144). - On the drinking itself, it approves of outside firmness. Chapter 10 advises an employer to tell an alcoholic employee that his drinking "must stop" (p. 141), and says "A firm attitude at this point has helped many of us." (p. 142). If the man won't stop, he may as well be discharged (pp. 141–142).

743a9beefa3a.t: So the book separates pressure to stop drinking, which it doesn't object to from an employer, from pressure to follow its suggestions, which it advises against ("the more you hurry him the longer his recovery may be delayed," p. 113). It says nothing about anyone verifying attendance.

9f4a2435d823.t: Tradition Three's Long Form: membership never depends "upon money or conformity" (p. 563).

fa85ce472f37.t: Bill W. on the member, 1946: "He signs nothing, agrees to nothing, promises nothing." (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). "We demand nothing." (same essay).

648ce62980ee.t: On authority, 1947: A.A. has "no demand that alcoholics conform to A.A. principles, no one set in personal authority over anyone else" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947).

d598291b2ef3.t: Tradition Six: an A.A. group "may cooperate with anyone," but not as far as "affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564).

bae7e8c28ad0.t: None of these speaks to court slips. They describe a fellowship that keeps no hold over its members and is answerable to no outside body.

a648fa90c6aa.t: In 1955 Bill named one court-related practice that he counted among the harmful anonymity breaks of A.A.'s early years: members who "sat on benches with police court judges, advising which drunks in the lineup should go to A.A. and which to jail" (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955). His objection, in context, was to members publicly using the A.A. name in public affairs.

442ecd1f92e1.t: <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16), "What A.A. Does Not Do," includes: - Keep membership records or case histories. - Follow up or try to control its members. - "Provide letters of reference to parole boards, attorneys, court officials, schools, businesses, social agencies, or any other organization or institution." (P-16, 2018).

f42c3b217fe6.t: The same pamphlet describes cooperation with the courts at the level of service work: Cooperation with the Professional Community committees work with educators, physicians, clergy, court officials and others who meet active alcoholics, on the basis of "cooperation but not affiliation" (P-16, 2018), and corrections committees take A.A. meetings into prisons and jails where allowed. Among the A.A. Guidelines it lists is "Cooperating with Court, D.W.I., and Similar Programs." That guideline is not in our sources, so this page doesn't say what it contains.

d51bf99c0758.t: The texts in our sources say A.A. doesn't write letters of reference and doesn't track or follow up its members. They don't say whether a meeting secretary or a member may sign a slip showing that someone attended, and this page doesn't answer that. Ask the group, the local intergroup or central office, or see A.A.'s guideline on court programs.

b0cce336aec6.t: Where is "cunning, baffling, powerful," and what comes right after it? | Recovery Starts

fca1e2388caa.t: It's in Chapter 5, "How It Works," a few lines before the Twelve Steps are listed. The sentence runs across a page break: "Remember that we deal with…

93510352442f.t: Where is "cunning, baffling, powerful," and what comes right after it?

1eeeef91c034.t: It's in Chapter 5, "How It Works," a few lines before the Twelve Steps are listed. The sentence runs across a page break: "Remember that we deal with alcohol—cunning, baf-" (p. 58) / "fling, powerful!" (p. 59).

c8df6692db43.t: The very next sentence is "Without help it is too much for us." (p. 59) The one after that answers it: "But there is One who has all power—that One is God." (p. 59) Then: "May you find Him now!" (p. 59)

6422c59eefd4.t: Quoted alone, the three words describe alcohol as a crafty enemy. In place, they're the first half of a turn: alcohol is powerful and too much for us alone, and God has "all power." Context doesn't reverse the line. It completes it.

4b3ec514baf7.t: Read in order, the passage goes (pp. 58–59):

b70e2ab3538b.t: <0>Before:</0> some members held on to old ideas, "and the result was nil until we let go absolutely" (p. 58).

5e419a7283ed.t: <0>The line:</0> "Remember that we deal with alcohol—cunning, baf-" (p. 58) / "fling, powerful!" (p. 59).

a28bcd5eea7c.t: <0>Right after:</0> "Without help it is too much for us." (p. 59) "But there is One who has all power—that One is God." (p. 59) "May you find Him now!" (p. 59)

e45cf866a7de.t: <0>Then:</0> "Half measures availed us nothing." (p. 59) "We stood at the turning point." (p. 59) The members asked God's protection and care "with complete abandon" (p. 59).

49930357a305.t: <0>Then the Steps,</0> "suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59), beginning with "We admitted we were powerless over alcohol" (p. 59).

7069290867dc.t: The words answer each other: alcohol is "powerful," we are "powerless" over it, and God is the One "who has all power."

6703817ba10f.t: The same picture elsewhere in the main text

a00484849a40.t: "Cunning" appears only here in the first 164 pages. It comes up again in some fourth-edition personal stories (pp. 328, 350 and 352), which are members' accounts and change from edition to edition, not the 1939 text. The other two ideas run all through the book:

5ada2a2bda74.t: <0>Baffling.</0> Chapter 2 says that once the illness has a real hold, drinkers "are a baffled lot" (p. 23). Chapter 3 calls the "baffling feature of alcoholism" the "utter inability to leave it alone, no matter how great the necessity or the wish" (p. 34). Chapter 7 tells the helper to tell the newcomer "how baffled you were" (p. 92).

b1bc5fb1a833.t: <0>Powerful, and too much for us.</0> Chapter 4 names the problem as "Lack of power, that was our dilemma." (p. 45) The answer is a Power greater than ourselves (p. 45). Chapter 3 ends the same way: the alcoholic "at certain times has no effective mental defense against the first drink" (p. 43), and "His defense must come from a Higher Power." (p. 43)

3836f4feee60.t: <0>Subtle.</0> In Chapter 6, even after the problem has been removed, the book warns against resting on our laurels, "for alcohol is a subtle foe" (p. 85).

cf2d10717e7f.t: No, it confirms the description. The book does treat alcohol as something that outwits the alcoholic. What quoting the line alone leaves out is what the line is for. It sets up the next two sentences: without help this is too much for us, and there is One who has all power. In the book, the warning and the hope come in the same breath.

948008041569.t: Related: <0>What does "half measures availed us nothing" mean in context?</0> · <1>What does Step 1 say? Powerless over what?</1> · <2>What does the Big Book mean by alcoholism as an illness?</2>

6e3ce7f1ddad.t: What is the "daily reprieve," and what is it "contingent on"? | Recovery Starts

d3c8a8127e2c.t: It's on page 85 of Chapter 6, "Into Action," in the pages on Step Ten. "We are not cured of alcoholism." (p. 85) "What we really have is a daily reprieve…

421db51224b9.t: What is the "daily reprieve," and what is it "contingent on"?

1e4381d3454a.t: It's on page 85 of Chapter 6, "Into Action," in the pages on Step Ten. "We are not cured of alcoholism." (p. 85) "What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition." (p. 85)

aeecf389089b.t: So the book's answer is in the sentence itself: the reprieve depends on keeping up our spiritual condition. The pages around it say how that's done: Step Ten's daily watch (p. 84), carrying "the vision of God's will into all of our activities" every day (p. 85), the prayer and meditation of Step Eleven (pp. 85–88), and "action and more action" (p. 88), which leads into Step Twelve.

cb42e9e4f019.t: The reprieve isn't won by fighting drink each day. The paragraph before says "we have ceased fighting anything or anyone—even alcohol" (p. 84), and "We are not fighting it, neither are we avoiding temptation." (p. 85)

c64c56ff8efd.t: Context sharpens the common reading. "Daily" is in the text, but what has to be renewed each day is the spiritual condition, not a daily struggle against drink.

8cca5a05caed.t: <0>Step Ten.</0> Keep taking personal inventory. Watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment and fear, ask God to remove them, talk them over, and make amends quickly (p. 84). "Then we resolutely turn our thoughts to someone we can help." (p. 84) "Love and tolerance of others is our code." (p. 84)

566411c98568.t: <0>The problem removed.</0> "And we have ceased fighting anything or anyone—even alcohol." (p. 84) Sanity will have returned, and if tempted we recoil "as from a hot flame" (p. 84). "We are not fighting it, neither are we avoiding temptation." (p. 85) "Instead, the problem has been removed." (p. 85)

b04094fe66a9.t: <0>The condition.</0> "That is how we react so long as we keep in fit spiritual condition." (p. 85)

b12641376440.t: <0>The warning.</0> "It is easy to let up on the spiritual program of action and rest on our laurels." (p. 85) "We are headed for trouble if we do, for alcohol is a subtle foe." (p. 85)

1d6acee89ac8.t: <0>The line.</0> "We are not cured of alcoholism." (p. 85) "What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition." (p. 85)

2233d61f3472.t: <0>What each day asks.</0> "Every day is a day when we must carry the vision of God's will into all of our activities." (p. 85) The thought to carry: "How can I best serve Thee—Thy will (not mine) be done." (p. 85) "It is the proper use of the will." (p. 85)

6f00708ef77f.t: <0>More action.</0> "But we must go further and that means more action." (p. 85) Step Eleven follows: a review each night, and each morning thinking "about the twenty-four hours ahead" (p. 86).

184450c64b39.t: <0>End of the chapter.</0> "There is action and more action." (p. 88) "The next chapter is entirely devoted to Step Twelve." (p. 88)

1935b28da3e4.t: What "maintenance of our spiritual condition" involves

c220f8e8a9ec.t: The book doesn't define the phrase in one place, but the run of pages around it gives the content: the daily inventory and amends of Step Ten, turning to someone we can help, love and tolerance, the vision of God's will in every activity, and prayer and meditation. The chapter then hands off to Step Twelve.

a7f470a4f33d.t: Bill's story says the same about work for others. An alcoholic who failed "to perfect and enlarge his spiritual life through work and self-sacrifice for others" could not survive the trials ahead (pp. 14–15). Chapter 7 opens by saying "nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (p. 89), and later it uses the same picture of fitness: "Assuming we are spiritually fit, we can do all sorts of things alcoholics are not supposed to do." (p. 100)

93d0bd946456.t: "Reprieve" is set against "cured." The book has said the same since Chapter 3: "We know that no real alcoholic ever recovers control." (p. 30) "Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic" (p. 33). The reprieve doesn't change that. The problem is "removed" (p. 85), but only so long as the condition is kept.

508338f8815a.t: It sharpens it. Read alone, "daily reprieve" can sound like getting through today without a drink. In the book it's a reprieve from an illness that isn't cured, and it isn't kept by fighting alcohol. It depends on a spiritual condition kept up by action every day: the inventory, prayer, God's will in all our activities, and helping others.

d047a840228b.t: Is the definition of insanity in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

eb0fcb71792b.t: No. "Insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results" appears nowhere in the Big Book: not in the main text, the forewords,…

8b338cf19261.t: Is the definition of insanity in the Big Book?

2d9710da0faf.t: No. "Insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results" appears nowhere in the Big Book: not in the main text, the forewords, the appendices, or any of the personal stories.

e7e62053ab51.t: The Big Book doesn't define insanity at all. It says so: "Whatever the precise definition of the word may be, we call this plain insanity" (p. 37).

3f410890178c.t: What the book calls insane is narrower and stranger than the saying. It's the moment before the first drink, when an alcoholic who knows exactly what will happen drinks anyway, on some trivial excuse that beats all his sound reasoning (pp. 37–43).

2f9fc91572de.t: The whole fourth-edition text was searched for "same thing," "different result(s)," "over and over," "expect" near "different," and "definition." None of them turns up the saying. The nearest wording is in "The Doctor's Opinion," where Dr. Silkworth describes the drinker's cycle of craving, spree, remorse and resolution: "This is repeated over and over" (p. xxix). That describes a cycle; it isn't a definition of insanity.

63bd877f632e.t: One Part III personal story quotes a different saying, a dictionary definition of rationalization that calls socially unacceptable behavior "a form of insanity" (p. 550). That's one member's experience, and a different idea.

f3540c8b14e5.t: Where the saying came from is outside our sources. It didn't come from the Big Book.

5cfb660706e3.t: What the Big Book calls insanity

f88595559f0d.t: The word belongs mostly to Chapter 3 (pp. 30–43), "More About Alcoholism," which is about the thinking that comes before a relapse.

5571a623f316.t: <0>Jim and the whiskey in the milk</0> (pp. 35–37). Jim knows he's an alcoholic, knows another drunk means the asylum and losing his family, and still decides that whiskey mixed with milk on a full stomach can't hurt. The book says: "Whatever the precise definition of the word may be, we call this plain insanity" (p. 37). What makes it insane isn't repetition. It's that "parallel with our sound reasoning there inevitably ran some insanely trivial excuse for taking the first drink" (p. 37), and the excuse won.

17927004b853.t: <0>The jay-walker</0> (pp. 37–38). This illustration does involve repetition. A man keeps running in front of traffic, injury after injury, despite his own promises, until "Such a man would be crazy, wouldn't he?" (p. 38). Put alcoholism in place of jay-walking, the book says, and "where alcohol has been involved, we have been strangely insane" (p. 38). Even here the point is that the man can't stop despite knowing better. Nobody in the story expects a different result.

56605605619b.t: <0>Fred the accountant</0> (pp. 39–43). Fred had heard all about "the subtle insanity which precedes the first drink" (p. 40) and was sure his self-knowledge would protect him. It didn't. On a good day, with no trouble at all, he ordered a cocktail without thinking of the consequences (p. 41). The book's conclusion: the alcoholic at certain times has no mental defense against the first drink, and "His defense must come from a Higher Power" (p. 43).

60c0a8c6f7db.t: The same idea appears elsewhere: "We are without defense against the first drink" (p. 24); Bill's "insidious insanity of that first drink" (p. 8); resentment cuts us off from the Spirit, and "The insanity of alcohol returns and we drink again" (p. 66).

28cccc088988.t: The saying suggests a fix: stop repeating the same method and try something different. The Big Book says self-knowledge and new methods don't work for the real alcoholic (p. 39). Chapter 3 lists the methods they had tried, from beer only to swearing off (p. 31). Its answer is a Power greater than ourselves. Step Two speaks of being restored "to sanity" (p. 59), and Chapter 6 describes the result: "For by this time sanity will have returned" (p. 84), meaning the problem of drink has been removed rather than outsmarted.

addd81490db2.t: Chapter 5, "How It Works," Step Two on p. 59: <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt5.pdf</0>

da9cd171615b.t: Personal story in Part III (rationalization quote)

61c1864513a1.t: fourth edition or earlier; personal experience, not program text

4bd80d346317.t: What is "a design for living that really works"? | Recovery Starts

48d8858f970f.t: The phrase is on page 28 of the Big Book, near the end of Chapter 2, "There Is a Solution": "A new life has been given us or, if you prefer, 'a design for…

17897866eba5.t: What is "a design for living that really works"?

15d19cbaf53f.t: The phrase is on page 28 of the Big Book, near the end of Chapter 2, "There Is a Solution": "A new life has been given us or, if you prefer, 'a design for living' that really works." (p. 28)

92bda96aceab.t: In its place it's another name for the new life the writers say they were given. It comes in the sentence right after they describe what they found as "the loving and powerful hand of God" (p. 28). The book offers the phrase "if you prefer" and puts it in quotation marks; it doesn't say why.

96a1d5c026b8.t: The book uses the phrase twice more. In "Bill's Story," right after saying that work with another alcoholic saved the day when nothing else did, Bill writes: "It is a design for living that works in rough going." (p. 15) In the amends chapter, "Our design for living is not a one-way street" (p. 81): it holds for the wife as much as for the husband.

8b8a91f13e3c.t: Context confirms the usual reading, a whole way of life rather than a single rule, and shows where the book roots it: in a spiritual experience, in work with other alcoholics, and in the home.

f95aa4cb51d5.t: The last pages of Chapter 2 (pp. 25–29) build to the phrase: - "There is a solution." (p. 25) The writers didn't like the self-searching and confession it took, but they saw it working in others, and they picked up "the simple kit of spiritual tools laid at our feet" (p. 25). - Their central claim: they have had "deep and effective spiritual experiences" (p. 25) that changed their whole attitude to life, to other people and to God's universe. For an alcoholic as serious as they were, "we believe there is no middle-of-the-road solution" (p. 25). - The story of an American businessman whom a celebrated psychiatrist called hopeless (pp. 26–27). The only exception the doctor knew was the alcoholic who had "vital spiritual experiences" (p. 27); the man's religious convictions, the doctor said, weren't that (p. 27). - "Here was the terrible dilemma in which our friend found himself" (p. 28) before the experience that made him free. "We, in our turn, sought the same escape with all the desperation of drowning men." (p. 28) What seemed a flimsy reed proved to be the hand of God (p. 28). - Then the line: a new life, or "a design for living," that really works (p. 28).

f9b07acb658a.t: The paragraphs right after it widen the door. William James describes many ways men have found God, and "We have no desire to convince anyone that there is only one way by which faith can be acquired." (p. 28) Which religious body a member joins, if any, is "an entirely personal affair" (p. 28). The chapter then lists what the book will give: an explanation of alcoholism, a chapter for the agnostic, "clear-cut directions" for how they recovered, and the personal stories (pp. 28–29).

27fad72b97a8.t: Notice the verb. The sentence says the new life, or design, "has been given us" (p. 28). In this first use, the sentence presents the design as something received, not something the writers drew up.

0834ce282032.t: <0>Page 15, "Bill's Story."</0> In his first year and a half sober Bill found little work, wasn't well, and was troubled by waves of self-pity and resentment (p. 15). What saved him: "when all other measures failed, work with another alcoholic would save the day" (p. 15). Going to his old hospital and talking with a man there lifted him up. "It is a design for living that works in rough going." (p. 15)

b19579f093b3.t: <0>Page 81, "Into Action."</0> The amends section turns to infidelity at home. After advice on what to tell a wife, the book says: "Our design for living is not a one-way street. It is as good for the wife as for the husband." (p. 81)

eab2a0d95f5a.t: It confirms it. "Design for living" does mean a whole way of life in the Big Book. What the context adds is detail the phrase loses when it travels alone: the first time the book uses it, it comes as another name for a new life given through a spiritual experience, with "if you prefer" left open to readers who'd rather put it that way; Bill uses it right after describing how work with other alcoholics kept him going; and Chapter 6 uses it about the home.

f7401cf34369.t: Does the Big Book say to stay away from doctors, medicine or psychiatry? | Recovery Starts

38276da1e387.t: No. The 1939 text says the opposite: "God has abundantly supplied this world with fine doctors, psychologists, and practitioners of various kinds." (p.…

f73a8a927227.t: Does the Big Book say to stay away from doctors, medicine or psychiatry?

0ce5ecdea64b.t: No. The 1939 text says the opposite: "God has abundantly supplied this world with fine doctors, psychologists, and practitioners of various kinds." (p. 133). It tells readers not to hesitate to take their health problems to them, and that "we should never belittle a good doctor or psychiatrist" (p. 133).

b945f77c8370.t: The book was introduced by a doctor (pp. xxv–xxxii), favors hospital care for a drinker who is very shaky (p. xxvi), and has members call a doctor and give sedatives "under his direction" when needed (p. 97).

966bd818c224.t: It is just as plain about what doctors couldn't do for its members: no treatment had made an alcoholic able to drink normally (pp. 30–31), and recovery came through a spiritual change (pp. xxix, 143).

1615d8100b6d.t: Our sources have nothing on today's medications. The A.A. pamphlet on that subject ("The A.A. Member—Medications and Other Drugs") isn't in it.

cb1138467975.t: What the 1939 text says about doctors

4ffed446b487.t: <0>Health problems go to professionals.</0> Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward," after saying a spiritual way of living is a powerful health restorative: "But this does not mean that we disregard human health measures." (p. 133). Doctors' and psychiatrists' services "are often indispensable in treating a newcomer and in following his case afterward" (p. 133). A sexual problem after stopping drinking? "There should be no hesitancy in consulting a doctor or psychologist if the condition persists." (p. 134).

9fd404fe8898.t: <0>Mental illness.</0> The opening of "How It Works" says some people "suffer from grave emotional and mental disorders, but many of them do recover if they have the capacity to be honest" (p. 58). Chapter 8 tells a wife that when alcoholism "is complicated by other disorders," a "good doctor or psychiatrist can tell you whether these complications are serious" (p. 114), and that a doctor should always be consulted about a husband who may be dangerous (p. 114).

d6cae4073ba5.t: <0>Hospital care.</0> "Though we work out our solution on the spiritual as well as an altruistic plane, we favor hospitalization for the alcoholic who is very jittery or befogged." (p. xxvi). "If your man needs hospitalization, he should have it" (p. 91). Physical treatment for an employee coming off a spree is "desirable, even imperative" and should be referred to a doctor (p. 143).

76be31a381f0.t: <0>Medicine in a crisis.</0> Among the things carrying the message may require: "Sometimes you will have to call a doctor and administer sedatives under his direction." (p. 97).

60f7cddd4639.t: <0>Working with doctors.</0> Members find drinkers by asking doctors, ministers and hospitals (p. 89). "Ministers and doctors are competent and you can learn much from them if you wish" (p. 89). Even the Fifth Step can be taken with "our doctor or psychologist" (p. 74).

30b3b618f1ac.t: <0>Being honest with doctors.</0> Looking back, the members admit "We have seldom told them the whole truth nor have we followed their advice." (p. 73).

031d9e48b01c.t: What it says doctors couldn't do

a73bea65f062.t: The book doesn't pretend medicine had solved alcoholism. Dr. Silkworth himself writes that "we physicians must admit we have made little impression upon the problem as a whole" (p. xxix), that recovery takes "an entire psychic change" (p. xxix), and that the craving has never been permanently eradicated "by any treatment with which we are familiar" (p. xxx). Chapter 3: "Physicians who are familiar with alcoholism agree there is no such thing as making a normal drinker out of an alcoholic." (p. 31). Chapter 10: physical treatment "is but a small part of the picture" (p. 143). The businessman of Chapter 2 got the best psychiatric care available, including from Dr. Jung, and still drank (pp. 26–27).

1a06bf7bf174.t: So the book puts medicine in its place as help with the body and mind, alongside a spiritual solution for the drinking. It never tells a reader to stop seeing a doctor or to refuse treatment.

5a12c89e7352.t: <0>1946.</0> Bill W. saw no reason A.A. members couldn't work as doctors, nurses or psychiatrists in the alcohol field; they need only avoid presenting themselves as an "A.A. therapist" (P-17, "Money", 1946), since there can be no such thing.

a219abd96a80.t: <0>1955.</0> The Foreword to the Second Edition: "Neither does A.A. take any particular medical point of view, though we cooperate widely with the men of medicine as well as with the men of religion." (p. xx).

685282d92169.t: <0>1957.</0> "We know that theology is for clergymen and that the practice of medicine and psychiatry is for doctors." (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957).

9d3262a4234f.t: <0>1971 (this printing updated 2023).</0> Members "certainly shouldn't award themselves honorary medical degrees and hand out diagnoses and prescriptions" (P-43).

073a57b6c6d2.t: <0>Undated statement in P-17 (2019 printing).</0> Members recognize "that some may require professional counseling or treatment" (P-17, "A.A. and Alcoholism").

010212965c1d.t: <0>2018.</0> A.A. does not "Make medical or psychological diagnoses or prognoses" or "Provide hospitalization, drugs, or medical or psychiatric treatment" (P-16, 2018). That is about what A.A. provides, not about what members may receive from doctors.

9f611f847bb8.t: None of these texts addresses particular medications people take today, whether for alcoholism, depression or anything else. The A.A. pamphlet "The A.A. Member—Medications and Other Drugs" is listed in P-16 and P-17 but is not in our sources, so this page doesn't say what it contains. The 1939 text's own advice for health questions is the one above: take them to a good doctor.
