39e474a0781a.t: What is "The Doctor's Opinion," and who wrote it? | Recovery Starts

e641b1e557c0.t: "The Doctor's Opinion" is the section at the front of the Big Book, before Chapter 1 (pp. xxv–xxxii). It gives a physician's view of the alcoholic and of…

4d7775c60aab.t: What is "The Doctor's Opinion," and who wrote it?

c000331d2524.t: "The Doctor's Opinion" is the section at the front of the Big Book, before Chapter 1 (pp. xxv–xxxii). It gives a physician's view of the alcoholic and of A.A.'s way of recovery.

e644e5c4ea70.t: It was written by Dr. William D. Silkworth, who signs both his letter and his longer statement (pp. xxvi, xxxii). Short connecting paragraphs between them are written by A.A. members themselves (pp. xxv–xxvii).

5fe31920e0be.t: Silkworth was a New York specialist in alcoholism who had greatly helped Bill W. (p. xvi). The Preface says the section has been kept just as he wrote it in 1939 (p. xi).

3c32f04813c2.t: His main points: the alcoholic's body reacts abnormally to alcohol (his "allergy" theory), the result is a craving the normal drinker never has, the only relief he knows is not drinking at all, and real recovery takes "an entire psychic change" (p. xxix).

419d7a577e3b.t: The section has three voices: 1. <0>A.A. members</0> open it, introducing "the medical estimate of the plan of recovery described in this book" from a doctor "chief physician at a nationally prominent hospital specializing in alcoholic and drug addiction" (p. xxv). The text doesn't name the hospital. 2. <1>Dr. Silkworth's letter</1> "To Whom It May Concern" (pp. xxv–xxvi) is signed William D. Silkworth, M.D. 3. <2>A.A. members</2> then comment on his views (pp. xxvi–xxvii), and <3>his longer statement</3> follows (pp. xxvii–xxxii), signed again at the end (p. xxxii).

777e5a51d144.t: Who he was, from the book itself: the Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) calls him "a New York specialist in alcoholism" who had greatly helped Bill W. and from whom Bill "had learned the grave nature of alcoholism" (p. xvi). The Preface calls him "our Society's great medical benefactor" and says his section "has been kept intact, just as it was originally written in 1939" (p. xi). <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) adds that he was "then Physician-in-Chief of the Charles B. Towns Hospital in New York," and that he was with Bill in that hospital in December 1934 (<1>Comes of Age</1>, p. 13).

312103be8f89.t: The letter's patient of "late 1934" (p. xxv) and the "leading contributors to this book" who came under his care (p. xxvii) are not named in the section. <0>Comes of Age</0> identifies Silkworth as the doctor who treated Bill (<1>Comes of Age</1>, p. 13).

0f7f17cf48ee.t: <0>In his letter</0> (pp. xxv–xxvi): a hopeless patient picked up ideas about recovery and began passing them on to other alcoholics, telling them to do the same, and "This man and over one hundred others appear to have recovered" (p. xxv). The results seemed to him of "extreme medical importance" (p. xxv).

8d9a573e55a5.t: <0>In his longer statement</0> (pp. xxvii–xxxii): - <1>The body.</1> He suggests that alcohol acts on these drinkers as "a manifestation of an allergy" and that "the phenomenon of craving is limited to this class and never occurs in the average temperate drinker" (p. xxviii). He offers this as a theory, one he says he had "suggested a few years ago" (p. xxviii). - <2>The mind.</2> "Men and women drink essentially because they like the effect produced by alcohol" (p. xxviii). Without a drink they are "restless, irritable and discontented" (p. xxviii). After each spree comes remorse and a firm resolution, and "This is repeated over and over" (p. xxix). - <3>The way out.</3> "The only relief we have to suggest is entire abstinence" (p. xxx). But not drinking takes more than knowledge or willpower: "unless this person can experience an entire psychic change there is very little hope of his recovery" (p. xxix). - <4>What medicine can't do.</4> Doctors, he admits, "have made little impression upon the problem as a whole" (p. xxix). "One feels that something more than human power is needed to produce the essential psychic change" (p. xxix). - <5>Why he backs A.A.</5> He praises the members' unselfishness and "the entire absence of profit motive" (p. xxvii) and says he has found nothing that has done more for these men "than the altruistic movement now growing up among them" (p. xxviii). He closes with two case histories (pp. xxxi–xxxii) and a line every reader of the Big Book knows: the alcoholic who reads it, "though perhaps he came to scoff, he may remain to pray" (p. xxxii).

89daec145f5b.t: The members agree with the doctor that "the body of the alcoholic is quite as abnormal as his mind" (p. xxvi), and they take care over what they claim: "As laymen, our opinion as to its soundness may, of course, mean little" (p. xxvi). They also say they "favor hospitalization for the alcoholic who is very jittery or befogged," so that his mind is clear before he is approached (p. xxvi).

b0f31ea37bf8.t: Does A.A. cost anything? | Recovery Starts

290fdd5df08f.t: No. Membership costs nothing. The 1939 Foreword says: "There are no fees or dues whatsoever." (p. xiv). The 1946 Long Form says membership should never…

82af39648b8e.t: No. Membership costs nothing. The 1939 Foreword says: "There are no fees or dues whatsoever." (p. xiv). The 1946 Long Form says membership should never depend "upon money or conformity" (p. 563).

710ffc4f7cd8.t: Groups do have expenses, such as rent, coffee and literature, and they pay them from members' voluntary contributions, often by passing a basket. Giving is not a condition of membership: Bill W. wrote in 1946 that contributions are "in no wise a condition of our A.A. membership" (P-17, "Money", 1946).

b3cb5e6ea53b.t: A.A. groups pay their own way and decline outside contributions (Tradition Seven, short form, p. 562; the Long Form on p. 564 says the same).

ef6357bbb13d.t: The Big Book itself is sold by A.A., and A.A. also publishes it free on aa.org.

c5807d911bb0.t: <0>No fees or dues.</0> "There are no fees or dues whatsoever." (p. xiv).

6c22abf523a9.t: <0>Nothing to pay the person who helps you.</0> Among the conditions the early members found most effective when approaching a drinker: "there are no fees to pay, no axes to grind, no people to please, no lectures to be endured" (p. 18).

da382381508a.t: <0>The work is unpaid.</0> "None of us makes a sole vocation of this work" (p. 19). The Foreword calls it "an avocation" (p. xiii).

12a7ba102b6b.t: What the 1939 text describes members spending is their own: time, sleep, and sometimes "sharing your money and your home" with a newcomer (p. 97).

f7306172ba33.t: <0>Tradition Three:</0> "Nor ought A.A. membership ever depend upon money or conformity." (p. 563).

904e81637439.t: <0>Tradition Seven:</0> "The A.A. groups themselves ought to be fully supported by the voluntary contributions of their own members." (p. 564). Public solicitation using A.A.'s name is "highly dangerous" (p. 564), and large gifts, or contributions carrying any obligation, are unwise (p. 564).

f9eb70ca7344.t: <0>Tradition Eight:</0> A.A.'s Twelfth Step work "is never to be paid for" (pp. 564–565).

2a1bbfb4f604.t: In the first years there were no money problems at all. Members met in homes, and there were no group funds (P-17, "Money", 1946).

97edb3ecdf29.t: Once there were meeting places, clubs and offices, members dropped money in "the hat" to pay for them, "with the full understanding, of course, that such contributions are in no wise a condition of our A.A. membership" (P-17, "Money", 1946).

c1221c7facf1.t: "As our A.A. membership does not depend on fees or dues, we can always 'take our special facilities or leave them alone.'" (P-17, "Money", 1946). That, he argued, is what keeps A.A.'s offices from ever governing it.

eaa6b3c974f7.t: "In A.A. we have no fees or compulsory dues." (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947). Even a club, he suggested, should let any A.A. member enjoy its ordinary privileges "whether he makes a regular voluntary contribution or not" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947).

2e0d6c38d615.t: On a nonalcoholic friend at a meeting: it is hardly an exception to self-support "if a nonalcoholic friend comes to a meeting and drops a dollar in the hat" (P-17, "Money", 1946).

718772109803.t: The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) sums up the principle as it had settled: "There were to be no fees or dues; our expenses were to be met by our own voluntary contributions." (p. xix).

3f71d9340245.t: <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16): "There are no dues or fees for membership in A.A., but we do have expenses such as rent, refreshments, A.A. Conference-approved literature, meeting lists and contributions to services" (P-16, 2018). A group may "pass the basket" and members are encouraged to take part. The pamphlet also sets limits on what any one member may give the General Service Office in a year, and says GSO accepts bequests only from A.A. members. The A.A. Preamble, printed in P-16 and P-17, says: "There are no dues or fees for A.A. membership; we are self-supporting through our own contributions."

9959eb252924.t: <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0> is sold by A.A. World Services through its bookstore (https://onlineliterature.aa.org), and the whole fourth edition is also free on aa.org (see <1>Where can I read the Big Book free, from A.A. itself?</1>). In 1939 the book itself told members, on a first visit, to lend a prospect their own copy if he showed interest (p. 94).

2a1e656c34c2.t: What if the person I'm helping doesn't want it? | Recovery Starts

c8f1ca83d7d0.t: Don't try to talk him into it. "If he does not want to stop drinking, don't waste time trying to persuade him" (p. 90). "If he does not want to see you,…

bbdf9783e804.t: What if the person I'm helping doesn't want it?

4fcaa89a833f.t: Don't try to talk him into it. "If he does not want to stop drinking, don't waste time trying to persuade him" (p. 90). "If he does not want to see you, never force yourself upon him" (p. 90).

67f645416d9f.t: Leave him free. Tell him he's under no obligation and needn't see you again, and don't be offended if he calls it off (p. 94). If he prefers another way, encourage him to follow his own conscience and stay friendly (p. 95).

12da44575bb4.t: Then find someone who does want it. "Search out another alcoholic and try again" (p. 96). Keep being friendly to his family (p. 97).

fb171d5f8f11.t: The book doesn't treat this as giving up on him. Left alone, he may become convinced he can't recover by himself (p. 96), or change his mind "after he gets hurt some more" (p. 95).

f6f714842f51.t: <0>Before you meet.</0> If he doesn't want to stop, don't try to persuade him: "You may spoil a later opportunity" (p. 90). The same goes for his family, who should be patient with a sick man (p. 90). If he won't see you, don't force it; the family shouldn't plead with him, and should wait for the end of his next drinking bout (p. 90). "You might place this book where he can see it in the interval" (p. 90).

63501f01b3f7.t: <0>During the visit.</0> If he rebels against parts of the program, "Do not contradict such views" (p. 94). Tell him you once felt the same (p. 94). Make it clear "that he is not under pressure, that he needn't see you again if he doesn't want to" (p. 94). "You should not be offended if he wants to call it off, for he has helped you more than you have helped him" (p. 94). Don't wear out your welcome, and let him steer the talk (p. 95).

27fe8cf560ab.t: <0>If he isn't interested.</0> If he wants only a banker or a nurse for his sprees, "you may have to drop him until he changes his mind" (p. 95). If he's interested, he must still decide for himself, and "should not be pushed or prodded by you, his wife, or his friends" (p. 95). If he wants another spiritual approach: "encourage him to follow his own conscience" (p. 95), say you'd like to be friendly in any case, and "Let it go at that" (p. 95).

54c80ee34658.t: <0>Then move on.</0> "Do not be discouraged if your prospect does not respond at once" (p. 96). "We find it a waste of time to keep chasing a man who cannot or will not work with you" (p. 96). The reason is the next man: "To spend too much time on any one situation is to deny some other alcoholic an opportunity to live and be happy" (p. 96). One member failed with his first half dozen prospects, and says that if he'd kept at them he might have cost many others their chance (p. 96).

251654cb1d79.t: <0>Don't drop the family.</0> "Though an alcoholic does not respond, there is no reason why you should neglect his family" (p. 97).

05faba184755.t: Chapter 8 tells a wife whose husband is lukewarm or thinks he isn't an alcoholic to leave him alone and not urge the program on him: "The seed has been planted in his mind" (p. 113). "The more you hurry him the longer his recovery may be delayed" (p. 113).

d4b35193b83a.t: The first members met this too

03221c50a74a.t: Chapter 11: after the third man recovered, "After several failures to find others, a fourth turned up" (p. 158). Dr. Bob, in his 1948 talk, said that before Akron, Bill "had not created a single convert, not one" (P-53), though he had worked tirelessly. They kept looking for the next one.

7b6dd168d71b.t: It doesn't say to write him off. Every instruction here keeps the door open: don't spoil a later chance (p. 90), drop him "until he changes his mind" (p. 95), stay friendly (p. 95), keep helping his family (p. 97). What it rules out is pressure.

fae25088d9f9.t: When did Dr. Bob die, and what were his last words to A.A.? | Recovery Starts

e85604b3c932.t: Dr. Bob died of cancer at City Hospital in Akron, Ohio, on November 16, 1950. He had been sober since June 10, 1935.

26624c5b4055.t: When did Dr. Bob die, and what were his last words to A.A.?

88526a151c0a.t: His last public words to A.A. were a short talk at the Cleveland convention in July 1950: keep the program simple, it comes down to love and service, guard your tongue, and keep helping the alcoholics who come after you.

d1f2493721de.t: The last words Bill W. heard from him, a few weeks later, were "Remember, Bill, let's not louse this thing up. Let's keep it simple!" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

a6579d20fa20.t: The two books that report his words at the very end agree he knew death had come but give different wording, and our books warn that many sayings credited to Dr. Bob can't be confirmed.

43ad3a805ae7.t: The Big Book gives the year twice: the introduction to his story says he carried the message to more than 5,000 alcoholics "To 1950, the year of his death" (p. 171), and the 1955 foreword says he never drank again "up to the moment of his death in 1950" (p. xvi).

dedfb50ca0f2.t: P-53 gives the date and cause: "He died of cancer at City Hospital, Akron, November 16, 1950." (P-53). It says he had been stricken in the summer of 1948 (P-53). <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) and <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) give the same date (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill's 1969 talk, also in P-53, says an operation around 1947 missed the cancer (P-53).

b58323091094.t: He was buried in Akron, "buried just like other folks" with a simple headstone and no monument, after the funeral was conducted by Dr. Walter Tunks, the minister Bill had phoned from the Mayflower Hotel in 1935 (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). In Bill's 1969 talk, Dr. Bob had turned down a proposed mausoleum, saying he had a hunch "that we ought to be buried just like other people" (P-53).

21b6231a18db.t: His last words to A.A. as a whole: Cleveland, July 1950

0f3b0498d6d8.t: P-53 says he gathered his strength for a brief appearance at the first International Convention in Cleveland, where he stressed simplicity: "Let's not louse it all up with Freudian complexes and things that are interesting to the scientific mind" (P-53).

5605cdf52137.t: The full talk is printed in <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980). Besides simplicity, he said the Steps come down to "love" and "service"; asked members to guard the tongue and use it with kindness; and said none of us would be here if somebody hadn't taken the time to help us, so we should never become so complacent that we won't help "our less fortunate brothers" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). That book says most people remember only the line about simplicity, "But Dr. Bob said a good deal more than that" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). See: <1>What happened at the 1950 Cleveland convention?</1>

3191e610c351.t: His last words to Bill W.

15f8ad2e9009.t: In <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957), Bill tells of visiting Dr. Bob at his Akron home a few weeks after Cleveland, to ask his consent to a General Service Conference that would hand A.A.'s affairs to its members (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Dr. Bob thought it over and said, "Bill, it has to be A.A.'s decision, not ours." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Then, at the door, knowing he faced a serious operation the next week: "Remember, Bill, let's not louse this thing up. Let's keep it simple!" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill writes, "That was the last time I ever saw him." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

bd8d7a81effc.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) quotes Bill's same account and places the visit on the Sunday before Dr. Bob went into the hospital for the last time (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). P-43 (1971) says "Let's keep it simple" were "the last Bill W. heard from his fellow founder" (P-43).

e91c143d5728.t: So "keep it simple" was Dr. Bob's parting word to his partner, spoken at his door, about how A.A. should be run. It was not spoken on his deathbed, and it came together with a decision to hand A.A. over to its members.

1fd428049386.t: The two accounts in our sources agree that he knew the end had come, but not on his words: - <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) prints a tribute saying he remarked to his attendant, "I think this is it" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and died at noon on November 16. - <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) gives the account of Emma K., who with her husband cared for Dr. Bob in his last years. She says she did not reach the hospital in time; in her telling he looked at his blue fingernails and said, "Call the family." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), adding that this was it.

84f2e8cd6ba0.t: Neither account is from someone our sources show was in the room, and our sources don't settle the exact words.

8a8c346c1fa3.t: A caution the sources give themselves

c486ac79d09d.t: <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> also calls "Let's not louse this thing up; let's keep it simple" Dr. Bob's "famous final admonition" to A.A. (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> adds a warning: people often say "Dr. Bob said…" to give weight to their own point, and "Apart from 'Let's keep it simple,'" it is hard to tell which sayings are really his (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). If a quotation credited to Dr. Bob isn't in his story, his talks in P-53, or these books, treat it with care.

d838deb35181.t: Can an alcoholic ever drink normally again? | Recovery Starts

0f0332cd9d72.t: The Big Book says no, from its members' experience: "We know that no real alcoholic ever recovers control." (p. 30). "We are like men who have lost their…

6cd0be4aa9ab.t: Can an alcoholic ever drink normally again?

e38a2c73b8eb.t: The Big Book says no, from its members' experience: "We know that no real alcoholic ever recovers control." (p. 30). "We are like men who have lost their legs; they never grow new ones." (p. 30).

472eaf35c679.t: It rests this on experience and on the doctors of its day, and it leaves one door open: "Science may one day accomplish this, but it hasn't done so yet." (p. 31).

a0e7c20dd9b4.t: It also says the line falls at the real alcoholic. Heavy drinkers who aren't alcoholic can often stop or moderate (pp. 21, 39), and the book doesn't claim everyone who drinks too much is an alcoholic.

47385785c69f.t: Long sobriety doesn't change it. The book's example is a man who stayed dry for twenty-five years, drank again at fifty-five, and was dead within four years (pp. 32–33).

cac9345eca0d.t: <0>Chapter 3, "More About Alcoholism" (pp. 30–34)</0>, is the book's answer: - "The idea that somehow, someday he will control and enjoy his drinking is the great obsession of every abnormal drinker." (p. 30). Many pursue it "into the gates of insanity or death" (p. 30). - "We know that no real alcoholic ever recovers control." (p. 30). Periods when members thought they were regaining control were "inevitably followed by still less control" (p. 30). - "We are like men who have lost their legs; they never grow new ones." (p. 30). There doesn't appear to be any treatment that will make alcoholics of their kind "like other men" (pp. 30–31). - "Physicians who are familiar with alcoholism agree there is no such thing as making a normal drinker out of an alcoholic." (p. 31). Then: "Science may one day accomplish this, but it hasn't done so yet." (p. 31). - If anyone showing inability to control his drinking can turn around and "drink like a gentleman, our hats are off to him" (p. 31). The book isn't forbidding anyone to try; it is reporting that its members tried "hard enough and long enough" (p. 31) and couldn't. - The man of thirty who stayed bone dry until he retired at fifty-five, then believed his long sobriety had qualified him "to drink as other men": in two months he was in hospital, and he was dead within four years (pp. 32–33). "Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic." (p. 33). "Commencing to drink after a period of sobriety, we are in a short time as bad as ever." (p. 33). So there must be "no reservation of any kind, nor any lurking notion that someday we will be immune to alcohol" (p. 33).

dfd7743d0822.t: <0>The Doctor's Opinion</0> says the same from the medical side as it stood in 1939. "These allergic types can never safely use alcohol in any form at all" (p. xxviii). The craving "has never been, by any treatment with which we are familiar, permanently eradicated." (p. xxx). "The only relief we have to suggest is entire abstinence." (p. xxx). One of his types of alcoholic is the man "who always believes that after being entirely free from alcohol for a period of time he can take a drink without danger" (p. xxx).

c7fae8bf2909.t: <0>Chapter 6</0> describes what recovery gives instead of control: when tempted, "we recoil from it as from a hot flame" (p. 84), and the problem is removed so long as members keep in fit spiritual condition. "We are not cured of alcoholism." (p. 85). What members have is "a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition" (p. 85).

36910b3b6e9e.t: The book draws its "no" around the real alcoholic, not around everyone who drinks hard: - The hard drinker, given a strong enough reason, "can also stop or moderate" (p. 21). - "That may be true of certain nonalcoholic people who, though drinking foolishly and heavily at the present time, are able to stop or moderate" (p. 39). - With a prospect who insists he can still control his drinking, the member should "tell him that possibly he can—if he is not too alcoholic" (p. 92). - Of the heavy-drinking husband in Chapter 8, "Some will moderate or stop altogether, and some will not." (p. 109).

74733f262359.t: Who is a real alcoholic is the reader's own call; see <0>How do I know if I'm an alcoholic?</0>

234017c38a78.t: The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) describes the membership's results as getting sober and staying that way, some "after some relapses" (p. xx); it says nothing of anyone returning to normal drinking. A search of our later texts (the histories, pamphlets and Service Manual) for normal or controlled drinking found nothing that revisits the question. The Big Book's own sentence that "Science may one day" (p. 31) change the picture is still printed in the fourth edition (2001); our sources have nothing on later science.

b15c05f4f2a0.t: Related: <0>Does the Big Book say "once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic"?</0> · <1>How do I know if I'm an alcoholic?</1> · <2>What does the Big Book mean by alcoholism as an illness?</2>

779655e22cef.t: Big Book page numbers are from the fourth edition (2001). The Preface says the program chapters have been "left largely untouched" since 1939 (p. xi).

64cced6c3e72.t: What is a "dry drunk"? Is it in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

a5d527aacdaa.t: The phrase "dry drunk" is not in the Big Book: not in the 1939 program text, pages 1 to 164, nor in the forewords, the appendices, or any of the personal…

169a42bb49b3.t: What is a "dry drunk"? Is it in the Big Book?

3f2c9dc519e2.t: The phrase "dry drunk" is not in the Big Book: not in the 1939 program text, pages 1 to 164, nor in the forewords, the appendices, or any of the personal stories in the fourth edition.

62d6dd3e901c.t: In all our sources the phrase appears once, in <0>Pass It On</0> (1984). Describing Bill W. in late 1940, it says some people called him "on a dry drunk," which it explains as having "all the symptoms of being drunk except the alcohol."

f472f5425781.t: An older, similar phrase, "dry bender," is in <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957). Bill uses it for a sober member in 1940 who was angry and unreasonable, and for himself in the late 1940s.

4ab410194354.t: The Big Book doesn't use either phrase, but it does say that staying sober isn't the whole job (p. 82), and that what a member has is "a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition" (p. 85).

8dfaa1d69099.t: All our sources were searched for "dry drunk," "dry drunks," "dry bender," "white-knuckle" and other wordings.

45f6f24e9c41.t: <0>"Dry drunk"</0> appears only in <1>Pass It On</1> (1984), Bill W.'s biography. Late in 1940, Bill had no job, the Big Book wasn't selling, and A.A. wasn't getting the publicity it needed. He was "frustrated, impatient, restless, dissatisfied, and depressed" (<2>Pass It On</2>, 1984). Then: "Some even described him as being on a dry drunk" (<3>Pass It On</3>, 1984). The book defines the phrase in the same sentence: he had "all the symptoms of being drunk except the alcohol" (<4>Pass It On</4>, 1984). That is the only definition in our sources, and this page doesn't add to it. The book doesn't say who used the phrase.

f7aee41c784d.t: <0>"Dry bender"</0> is in Bill's own writing: - In spring 1940, a member who had been sober four years "was on what we nowadays call a 'dry bender'" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). He grew more and more "adamant and violent," then broke down and went back to drinking. - Writing about a furious memo he sent the Foundation's trustees before 1948, Bill says of himself: "Obviously I was on a dry bender of the worst possible sort" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957). - Recalling the 1940s, when psychiatrists warned that the fellowship was "emotional dynamite," Bill asks: "Now that we were sober, would dry benders and emotional jags blow us up?" (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957). - In his 1955 article "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous," he uses it about the whole world's hunger for power, fame and money: "On this appalling dry bender, society seems to be staggering down a dead-end road" (P-17, 1955).

95be35eabb23.t: So by 1957 Bill could call "dry bender" something "we nowadays" say. In both of his uses about people, the man is sober and behaving badly: "adamant and violent" in one case (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957), sending "blistering memorandums" in the other (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). Bill doesn't define the phrase further.

a566095c4ed9.t: <0>"White-knuckling"</0> turns up once, in a fourth-edition story, "On the Move" (Part III): "After white-knuckling it for almost two years in A.A., I finally broke down and saw that I could not stay sober all by myself" (p. 491). That is one member's word for staying dry on one's own strength; the story doesn't call it a dry drunk.

639ab1a6f413.t: What the Big Book says on the same subject

8c14825fe2d1.t: The program text doesn't use either phrase. These are the passages that speak to an alcoholic who is sober but still in trouble. They are given here for comparison, not as a definition of "dry drunk." - <0>Sobriety alone isn't enough.</0> Some alcoholics say all they need to do is keep sober. "Certainly he must keep sober," the book answers, but he's "yet a long way from making good" to his family (p. 82). A man who says sobriety is enough is like the farmer who came up from his cyclone cellar to a wrecked home and said, "Ain't it grand the wind stopped blowin'?" (p. 82). - <1>Not cured.</1> "We are not cured of alcoholism. What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition" (p. 85). It's easy "to let up on the spiritual program of action and rest on our laurels," and that leads to trouble (p. 85). - <2>Restless before the drink.</2> In "The Doctor's Opinion" (1939), Dr. Silkworth describes drinkers who, without alcohol, are "restless, irritable and discontented" unless they can again feel the ease a few drinks bring (pp. xxviii–xxix). He is describing the state that leads back to drinking, not a sober member of A.A. - <3>Resentment.</3> "If we were to live, we had to be free of anger" (p. 66). Harbored resentment shuts a man off from "the sunlight of the Spirit," and the insanity of alcohol returns (p. 66). - <4>Crankiness after the drinking stops.</4> Chapter 9 tells the family that the man, "though marvelously improved, is still convalescing," and that his "periods of crankiness, depression, or apathy" will pass with tolerance, love and spiritual understanding (p. 127).

3bc547382e96.t: Are "Easy Does It," "First Things First" and "Live and Let Live" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

0c45eb0efeac.t: Yes, all three are in the 1939 program text. They close Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward," set out on their own lines: "We have three little mottoes which…

6b71f785822f.t: Are "Easy Does It," "First Things First" and "Live and Let Live" in the Big Book?

69ec8ec0a7a9.t: Yes, all three are in the 1939 program text. They close Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward," set out on their own lines: "We have three little mottoes which are apropos." (p. 135). "Live and let live" also appears in Chapter 8: "Live and let live is the rule." (p. 118).

352a286a5254.t: The book doesn't explain them. It places them straight after a story about a wife who nagged her newly sober husband over his coffee and cigarettes until he got drunk in a fit of anger (p. 135). In that place they read as advice to a family about not making burning issues of small things.

b2a76c819143.t: Early members used them. Dr. Bob, in a 1948 letter, wrote that "Easy Does It" might be the best course in a dispute over A.A.'s services, and Bill's 1947 Grapevine essay says old-timers who once tried to run A.A. had come to find "Easy Does It" and "Live and Let Live" deeply meaningful.

af5ac6d6e9e9.t: Searching the whole fourth-edition text, the three mottoes appear together only at the end of Chapter 9 (p. 135). "Live and let live" is also in Chapter 8, "To Wives" (p. 118). Our sources have only the fourth edition; the Preface says the program chapters have been "left largely untouched" since 1939 (p. xi), and <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) says the slogans "appear in the first edition of the Big Book (at the end of the chapter on 'The Family Afterward')" (Pass It On, 1984).

5162a8ce32f0.t: The last pages of Chapter 9 are about the family's life together after drinking stops. They say: "We are sure God wants us to be happy, joyous, and free." (p. 133); don't belittle a good doctor (p. 133); be patient with health, sex relations and the children (pp. 133–134). Then the chapter's final point: "Whether the family goes on a spiritual basis or not, the alcoholic member has to if he would recover." (p. 135).

cc58bb978937.t: Then the story. A recovering man smoked and drank too much coffee. His wife, meaning to help, nagged him about it, "and her intolerance finally threw him into a fit of anger. He got drunk." (p. 135). The book doesn't excuse him: "Of course our friend was wrong—dead wrong." (p. 135). Today he is an effective member who still smokes and drinks coffee, "but neither his wife nor anyone else stands in judgment" (p. 135). "She sees she was wrong to make a burning issue out of such a matter when his more serious ailments were being rapidly cured." (p. 135).

e90ed6414beb.t: Then: "We have three little mottoes which are apropos." (p. 135), and the three lines. The book adds nothing more, so what each means is left to the reader. Read where they stand, they fit the story: the drinking comes first; others' lesser habits can be let be; and pressure, even well meant, can do harm.

200b59a69fde.t: "To Wives" asks the wife not to expect too much too soon: the husband's ways of thinking and doing "are the habits of years" (p. 118). "Patience, tolerance, understanding and love are the watchwords." (p. 118). "Live and let live is the rule." (p. 118). And: "If you both show a willingness to remedy your own defects, there will be little need to criticize each other." (p. 118). Here too the motto is about not criticising each other in the home.

f88276bba496.t: <0>Dr. Bob, 1948.</0> When Bill was pressing for a conference of delegates from the groups and the trustees resisted, Dr. Bob wrote to him in May 1948 that "for the moment, perhaps," Easy Does It "is the best course to follow" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). The letter is quoted in a 1980 book; it was written before 1950.

21d88f716617.t: <0>Bill W., 1947.</0> In "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", Bill says that old-timers who once felt called to "save the A.A. movement" from something had stopped playing Pharisee, "So those little maxims 'Easy Does It' and 'Live and Let Live' have come to be deeply meaningful and significant to them and to me." (P-17). There the mottoes are about members giving up trying to govern A.A.

013458368276.t: <0>Dr. Bob in Akron.</0> <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) has an Akron member remember Dr. Bob's hospital talks: "He always emphasized 'Easy Does It' and 'First Things First.'" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Dr. Bob told him that "Easy Does It" doesn't mean staying home from meetings and letting others work the program for you, but taking it a day at a time (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Asked about "First Things First," Dr. Bob is remembered answering with a Bible verse, "Seek ye first the kingdom of God" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). These are recollections printed thirty years after his death.

15863d0a7798.t: <0>The stories.</0> "The Vicious Cycle" (Part I) ends, years after the writer's 1938 start, with "Our pet slogan is 'Easy Does It.'" (p. 231). Several fourth-edition stories quote the mottoes among other sayings (pp. 293, 300, 345, 357, 401).

e99c3b8092cd.t: <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) thinks it "probable" that the slogans began with Bill, who "brought them with him from Vermont" (Pass It On, 1984). Our sources have nothing earlier to confirm or contradict that.

481711ad0d79.t: Who was the old school friend in "Bill's Story" (Ebby)? | Recovery Starts

27c3e1c00168.t: The friend who phoned Bill W. in November 1934 and came to his kitchen sober was Ebby T., a boyhood friend and old drinking companion from Vermont. The…

4340c0c09fd7.t: Who was the old school friend in "Bill's Story" (Ebby)?

b643083c1700.t: The friend who phoned Bill W. in November 1934 and came to his kitchen sober was Ebby T., a boyhood friend and old drinking companion from Vermont. The 1939 Big Book doesn't name him; later accounts do.

c0bcf00daef9.t: Ebby had sobered up a few months earlier through the Oxford Group, after friends from that group, among them Rowland H., came to him when he was in trouble with the law. He passed on to Bill what he had been given: admit you are licked, take stock of yourself, confess your defects to another person, make restitution, give of yourself, and pray to whatever God you think there is.

5b79eee20888.t: He is the friend who told Bill to choose his own conception of God (p. 12). In his 1957 book Bill calls him "my sponsor."

6115ceaea848.t: Ebby later drank again, for years. Our 1984 biography of Bill says he died sober in 1966.

49034cec3b52.t: Near the end of a bleak November in 1934, as Bill drank at his kitchen table, "an old school friend" phoned and asked to come over (p. 8). "He was sober." (p. 9). Rumor had it he had been committed for alcoholic insanity; instead "two men had appeared in court, persuading the judge to suspend his commitment" (p. 9). They had told him of a simple religious idea and a practical program of action. "That was two months ago and the result was self-evident." (p. 9).

055088bd73dd.t: When Bill offered him a drink, he refused, and said simply: "I've got religion." (p. 9). He told Bill that God had done for him what he could not do for himself (p. 11). When Bill balked at a God personal to him, his friend suggested: "Why don't you choose your own conception of God?" (p. 12). That, Bill writes, "hit me hard" (p. 12).

8b5ed21426b0.t: The friend kept coming. In the hospital he heard Bill's problems and deficiencies, and they made a list of people Bill had hurt (p. 13). He promised a new relationship with the Creator once these things were done (p. 13), and he stressed working with others: "Faith without works was dead, he said." (p. 14). The story ends with "my friend's simple talk in our kitchen" multiplying itself in a widening circle (p. 16).

685c4111c365.t: The 1955 Foreword to the Second Edition calls him "an alcoholic friend who had been in contact with the Oxford Groups of that day" (pp. xv–xvi). Bill's biographical sketch in P-53 (pamphlet © 2017) names him: in November 1934 Bill "learned from an old friend, Ebby, how the Oxford Group was able sometimes to help alcoholics; Ebby himself was a recent example." (P-53).

c8218f57a1ac.t: Bill calls Ebby "my old boarding-school friend and drinking companion" and says he had long marked him as a hopeless case (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Asked what brand of religion he had, Ebby said: "I just fell in with a group of people, the Oxford Groups." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He had learned to admit he was licked, take stock of himself and confess his defects to another person, make restitution, give of himself, and pray to whatever God he thought there was, even as an experiment (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "Ebby didn't try to pressure or evangelize me" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). A few days later Bill went looking for the Calvary Mission, where Ebby's Oxford Group friends had lodged him, and Ebby turned up there; he visited Bill again in Towns Hospital to give the same formula (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He then came to live with Bill and Lois in Brooklyn (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

2d8b44b03873.t: At the 1955 convention Bill wrote: "And there sat my sponsor Ebby, who had first brought the word that lifted me out of the alcoholic pit" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In his talk on service he said Ebby's phone call and subway ride, ten cents in all, were the first time "spirituality and money began to mix" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

d8393ea64312.t: He is also candid about what came after. By late 1937 "Ebby had slipped" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and in 1940 "My own sponsor, Ebby, also continued his drinking" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

9fbf8770042d.t: <0>Pass It On</0> says Ebby came from a family prominent in Albany for three generations; he and Bill met in 1911 and were classmates for a season at Burr and Burton (Pass It On, 1984). In 1934, drinking alone in Manchester, Vermont, and in trouble with the police, he was visited by two old drinking friends who had found the Oxford Group, and by Rowland H. (Pass It On, 1984). Rowland had been treated by Carl Jung (Pass It On, 1984); see <1>What part did Carl Jung play in A.A.'s beginning?</1> When Ebby was arrested for shooting at pigeons on his newly painted house, Rowland told the judge in Bennington he would be responsible for him (Pass It On, 1984). Ebby then went to New York and lived at the Calvary Mission, where he heard of Bill's condition (Pass It On, 1984).

0520c82b69da.t: Ebby's sobriety lasted until April 1937: "That was after two years and approximately seven months of sobriety" (Pass It On, 1984). Bill supported him for the rest of his life, "until Ebby died — sober — in 1966" (Pass It On, 1984). Lois is quoted in <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) as saying that with Ebby "it was more gratitude — and nostalgia" than close friendship (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

2adaf3b43a6f.t: <0>The court.</0> The 1939 story says two men persuaded the judge to suspend Ebby's commitment (p. 9). <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) has one man, Rowland H., telling the judge he would be responsible for Ebby after an arrest (Pass It On, 1984).

27ba37f3bfa5.t: <0>How long Ebby had been sober.</0> The 1939 story says two months (p. 9). In Bill's 1957 account Ebby says he hasn't had a drink "for months" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); a mission worker quoted in <1>Pass It On</1> heard him testify to "a number of months" (Pass It On, 1984).

e3cb127d2d4e.t: <0>"School friend."</0> The 1939 text says "an old school friend" (p. 8); Bill in 1957 says boarding-school friend (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); <1>Pass It On</1> says they were classmates for one season (Pass It On, 1984).

93a595cc9151.t: <0>When the slip began.</0> Bill's 1957 account mentions it as of November 1937 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); Ebby, in <1>Pass It On</1>, dates it to April 1937 (Pass It On, 1984). These agree.

c6c3e80dbbc8.t: Our sources give his surname only as "T." and doesn't say more about his last years than <0>Pass It On</0>'s one line.

9d3090658985.t: Is "faith without works is dead" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

83819cf64164.t: Yes. It appears three times in the Big Book's program text, not once: in "Bill's Story" (p. 14) and twice in Chapter 6, "Into Action" (pp. 76 and 88).

63e94b6cf9e1.t: Is "faith without works is dead" in the Big Book?

3d013e1e777e.t: Yes. It appears three times in the Big Book's program text, not once: in "Bill's Story" (p. 14) and twice in Chapter 6, "Into Action" (pp. 76 and 88).

e8d2a21d6ed1.t: Each time it points to action that follows: working with other alcoholics (p. 14), making amends (p. 76), and the Twelfth Step (p. 88).

48737c465ef9.t: The saying is usually traced to the New Testament's Letter of James. The Big Book never names a source. It uses the line as A.A.'s own.

e4b5c356e039.t: None of the personal stories use the phrase.

52d120598a3c.t: A search of the whole fourth-edition text finds the phrase in three places, all in the first 164 pages:

981d4a8f8f68.t: <0>"Bill's Story," p. 14.</0> Bill's friend, who brought him the message, stressed working with others as he had worked with Bill. "Faith without works was dead, he said" (p. 14). Bill adds that this was "appallingly true for the alcoholic" and explains why: an alcoholic who doesn't work for others won't survive the hard times, and "If he did not work, he would surely drink again, and if he drank, he would surely die" (p. 15).

a9547dbec50a.t: <0>Chapter 6, p. 76.</0> Right after the Seventh Step prayer: "Now we need more action, without which we find that 'Faith without works is dead'" (p. 76). The next lines start Steps Eight and Nine, making amends.

75e942dda041.t: <0>Chapter 6, p. 88.</0> The chapter's last lines: "There is action and more action. 'Faith without works is dead.' The next chapter is entirely devoted to Step Twelve" (p. 88).

bd20cd6eb4f8.t: It's often cited only to page 88. The text shows the phrase on pages 14 and 76 as well.

a5e38c2c31df.t: Each time, the "works" are definite actions and mostly toward other people: - In Bill's story, the works are "work and self-sacrifice for others" (p. 15), and especially carrying the message to other alcoholics (p. 14). - On p. 76 they are the amends of Steps Eight and Nine. - On p. 88 they are the work of Chapter 7, finding and helping an alcoholic who is still drinking.

3e210a554c1a.t: Chapter 7 says the same thing in other words when it describes a newcomer who already has religious faith. He may show "that faith alone is insufficient. To be vital, faith must be accompanied by self sacrifice and unselfish, constructive action" (p. 93). Bill's story closes on the same note: faith has to work in and through us all day, every day, or we perish (p. 16).

497116264c89.t: The words are usually traced to a verse in the New Testament's Letter of James . The Big Book doesn't name a source: the only James mentioned in the main text or the appendices is the psychologist William James (pp. 28, 567). So the honest answer to "is it just a Bible verse?" is that it's both. The Big Book took the line over and tied it to its own program of action.

d46cfa6fc399.t: Does the Big Book say "fake it till you make it"? | Recovery Starts

ba2bc2a930af.t: No. "Fake it till you make it" is nowhere in the Big Book, and the word "fake" isn't in it at all. It isn't in any other book in our sources either, in…

8ad4cfc16032.t: Does the Big Book say "fake it till you make it"?

86ca88608b6d.t: No. "Fake it till you make it" is nowhere in the Big Book, and the word "fake" isn't in it at all. It isn't in any other book in our sources either, in that form.

30f8b0e77b31.t: The nearest wording, "act as if," is in one personal story in today's edition (p. 366) and in a talk by a clergyman at the 1955 convention, printed in <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957). Both are about acting on faith before being sure of it, as an honest trial; neither is about pretending to be well.

524f0730d34f.t: The program text asks a doubter for willingness, honesty and an open mind (pp. 46–47, 568). It treats the alcoholic's pretending, his "stage character," as part of the trouble (p. 73). What it does ask is action on the strength of willingness, before full belief arrives (pp. 12, 47).

f9219c8ed86e.t: All our sources were searched for "fake," "fake it," "act as if," "acting as if" and "as if," with page breaks joined.

73e10f2619ea.t: <0>Big Book program text, forewords, appendices:</0> no "fake" and no "act as if."

21da3b4f0cd8.t: <0>Personal stories (fourth edition, 2001):</0> in "Tightrope" (Part II), an agnostic writer's sponsor told him A.A. was not a religious program, that it was all right to doubt God, and "that I might try occasionally to act as if I believed" (p. 366). The writer connects it with an idea he'd heard, that it is easier to act your way into a new way of thinking (p. 366). In "Empty on the Inside" (Part III), "acting as if" means the opposite: the pretending she had done all her life, acting as if she knew or didn't care (p. 512).

bfcbed416f09.t: <0>Stories printed in 1939 and later dropped</0> (<1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1>, 2003): neither phrase. One later-edition story there says "I didn't want to be a fake" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003).

0ffd0460114b.t: <0><1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957):</0> at the 1955 St. Louis convention, Dr. Samuel Shoemaker, an Episcopal clergyman and not an alcoholic, described finding faith as being more like science than philosophy: "We choose a hypothesis. We act as if it were true and see whether it works." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). If it doesn't work, he said, you discard it.

e9a1b79771fa.t: So where "act as if" appears with approval, it means acting on faith before being sure of it, to see whether it works. Nobody in these sources is told to fake being well.

d4d3de7d76e4.t: What the program text asks of a doubter

0ac322cbd588.t: Chapter 4, "We Agnostics," was written for the reader who can't believe. It asks for much less than belief, and it never asks him to pretend:

4856cb9050fb.t: "We found that as soon as we were able to lay aside prejudice and express even a willingness to believe in a Power greater than ourselves, we commenced to get results" (p. 46).

79834caf6c38.t: He is to use his own conception of God, "however inadequate" (p. 46), and ask himself one question: "Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe, that there is a Power greater than myself?" (p. 47).

53008b980023.t: "Do not let any prejudice you may have against spiritual terms deter you from honestly asking yourself what they mean to you." (p. 47).

43c3270ff8da.t: Bill W. tells the same thing of himself: "It was only a matter of being willing to believe in a Power greater than myself." (p. 12). Appendix II, added later, sums it up: "Willingness, honesty and open mindedness are the essentials of recovery." (p. 568).

11943a8d391a.t: The program does ask the reader to act before he is sure. Bill says growth could start from willingness alone (p. 12); Chapter 4 says that starting from their own conception of God, "however limited it was," was "all we needed to commence spiritual growth" (p. 47); and after the Third Step decision the book launches "on a course of vigorous action" (p. 63). Faith, Chapter 7 says, "must be accompanied by self sacrifice and unselfish, constructive action" (p. 93). That is close to the sense of the story in "Tightrope": act on willingness and let belief follow.

5f7cab33f9b8.t: What the book does not ask for is a show. It says the alcoholic already lives a double life: "He is very much the actor." (p. 73), presenting a "stage character" to the world (p. 73), and that this fear and tension "makes for more drinking" (p. 73). Its answer is the opposite of acting: the Fifth Step, telling someone the whole truth (pp. 72–75), and a way of life that "demands rigorous honesty" (p. 58).

ae5fea75cd34.t: So the text leaves room for "act on your willingness before you feel it," and none for "pretend you are what you aren't."

cbb7d797368b.t: added with the second edition, 1955 (p. xi); post-1950

43c27d8b1c8a.t: "Tightrope," Part II; "Empty on the Inside," Part III

82aa27cc86b6.t: fourth edition (2001); first edition of each not shown in our sources

16b07a7a81ba.t: <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, Dr. Samuel Shoemaker's 1955 talk

271c345cdf47.t: stories from the first three editions; collected 2003

0ef043c599a4.t: What happens to the family after the drinking stops? | Recovery Starts

7e08482687b2.t: Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward" (pp. 122–135), says stopping drinking is only a beginning: "Cessation of drinking is but the first step away from a…

442de025c3f8.t: What happens to the family after the drinking stops?

bf7e553f4d67.t: Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward" (pp. 122–135), says stopping drinking is only a beginning: "Cessation of drinking is but the first step away from a highly strained, abnormal condition." (p. 122). A doctor told the members that years of living with an alcoholic make the whole family, to some extent, ill (p. 122).

d70bcac90ef8.t: Its answer is that every member of the family, the alcoholic included, should "meet upon the common ground of tolerance, understanding and love" (p. 122), which means each one giving up the demand to have things his or her way.

feed8c6cf0a6.t: It names the usual troubles: expecting the good old days back at once, digging up the past, the man who rushes to rebuild his finances or who becomes a religious enthusiast, the shift of authority at home, jealousy of his new activities, and children slow to forgive.

3fa3e5d1e86b.t: It closes on health and happiness: see good doctors, don't belittle them (p. 133), and enjoy life: "We absolutely insist on enjoying life." (p. 132).

80285c45fa24.t: The chapter begins by correcting an impression Chapter 8 might give, that the recovering husband is to be wrapped in cotton wool and put on a pedestal: "Successful readjustment means the opposite." (p. 122). Each person in the family has fixed ideas about how the others should treat him or her, and "the more one member of the family demands that the others concede to him, the more resentful they become" (p. 122). The question it asks of everyone: "Is he not unconsciously trying to see what he can take from the family life rather than give?" (p. 122).

00e43055b1a8.t: <0>Wanting it all back now.</0> The family remembers father as he once was and expects the good old days back at once. But the wreckage of years "will take time to clear away" (p. 123); the new structures "will take years to complete" (p. 123). "The wise family will admire him for what he is trying to be, rather than for what he is trying to get." (p. 123).

7842e1b80a0f.t: <0>The past.</0> The first impulse is to lock the skeletons in a closet. The chapter calls that self-centered: the alcoholic's past "thus becomes the principal asset of the family" (p. 124), because it can help other families still struggling. But dragging up old misdeeds in anger, such as a past affair, can become "a veritable plague" (p. 124); unless some good purpose is served, "past occurrences should not be discussed" (p. 125). And "we do not relate intimate experiences of another person unless we are sure he would approve" (p. 125).

2dc0c8fb07e5.t: <0>The man who rushes at money.</0> If he throws himself into rebuilding his finances, the family feels neglected and resentful; he feels unappreciated (pp. 125–126). Both are partly right. The family should remember "dad, though marvelously improved, is still convalescing" (p. 127). He should remember he is "mainly to blame for what befell his home" (p. 127). "For us, material well-being always followed spiritual progress; it never preceded." (p. 127).

c23979d338fd.t: <0>The man who becomes a religious enthusiast.</0> If instead he has a stirring spiritual experience and talks of nothing else, the family may resent "a God who has stolen dad's affections" (p. 128). The chapter's advice: let him have his head, even let him go as far as he likes in helping other alcoholics in the first days; it will do more for his sobriety than anything else (p. 129), and he'll come down to earth sooner in an understanding family (p. 129). "We have found nothing incompatible between a powerful spiritual experience and a life of sane and happy usefulness." (p. 130).

d8b36f520ea2.t: <0>Who runs the house.</0> Drinking made mother the head of the house; when father comes back to life and asserts himself, there will be trouble unless the family "comes to a friendly agreement" (p. 131).

ca174276febf.t: <0>Outside interests.</0> The family may feel they hold "a mortgage on dad" (p. 131) and resent his time with other alcoholics, clubs or community work. Each must yield here and there, and his work with alcoholics "should be balanced" (p. 131). The family might join a religious body if it wishes; "there is nothing obligatory about it" (p. 132).

0d21b4c418a3.t: <0>The children.</0> They may "cordially hate him" (p. 134) for what he did to them and their mother, and stay hard long after their mother has accepted his new life. In time they'll see he is a new man and let him know it in their own way (p. 134).

932ac784bba8.t: <0>Seeing is believing.</0> "Whether the family goes on a spiritual basis or not, the alcoholic member has to if he would recover." (p. 135). In the story of the heavy smoker and coffee drinker, his wife nagged until he flew into a rage and got drunk. The book says he was "wrong—dead wrong" (p. 135) and had to mend his spiritual fences; she came to see she was wrong to make a burning issue of it while his more serious ailments were being cured (p. 135).

d525fcd34166.t: <0>Laugh.</0> "We absolutely insist on enjoying life." (p. 132). "We are sure God wants us to be happy, joyous, and free." (p. 133).

3c9fa65eaabc.t: <0>Health.</0> A body badly burned by alcohol doesn't recover overnight. A spiritual way of living is a powerful restorative, but "this does not mean that we disregard human health measures" (p. 133). Doctors and psychiatrists are "often indispensable" (p. 133). If a man is impotent after stopping, consult a doctor or psychologist if it persists (p. 134). See <1>Does the Big Book say to stay away from doctors, medicine or psychiatry?</1>

fb6816fa8982.t: The chapter ends with three mottoes: "First Things First," "Live and Let Live," "Easy Does It" (p. 135).

5f5ef9902de0.t: Related: <0>My husband (or wife) drinks. What does the Big Book say to do?</0> · <1>What does the Big Book say about helping the drinker's family?</1> · <2>Is Al-Anon part of A.A.?</2>

c950326648c5.t: Is "it's the first drink that gets you drunk" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

24284395f1f5.t: Not in those words. The saying isn't anywhere in our sources. Two members' stories come close: "I never knew it was the first drink that did it" (p. 292,…

428f75dbbb16.t: Is "it's the first drink that gets you drunk" in the Big Book?

32787f08c36f.t: Not in those words. The saying isn't anywhere in our sources. Two members' stories come close: "I never knew it was the first drink that did it" (p. 292, fourth edition), and, in a story dropped from the Big Book in 2001, "No one had ever told me it was the first drink that did the damage" (<0>Experience, Strength and Hope</0>, 2003, story from an earlier edition). A 1980 history says Dr. Bob kept repeating, "The first one will get you."

358d8fb20334.t: The idea is all through the 1939 program text. Once a real alcoholic takes any alcohol, "something happens, both in the bodily and mental sense," that makes it nearly impossible to stop (pp. 22–23). And "We are without defense against the first drink" (p. 24).

2d2df13d3298.t: The book puts its weight on the moment before the first drink: "the main problem of the alcoholic centers in his mind, rather than in his body" (p. 23). The saying points at what the drink does. The book points at why he takes it, and says the defense "must come from a Higher Power" (p. 43).

4028085ee693.t: All our sources were searched for "first drink," "first one," "one drink," "one is too many" and the saying itself.

9638a1b0375e.t: <0>A personal story,</0> "Fear of Fear" (Part II), about a woman whose husband also drank: "I never knew it was the first drink that did it" (p. 292).

db39675c4c98.t: <0>A dropped story,</0> "Desperation Drinking," printed in earlier editions and taken out in 2001, now in <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1> (2003). After nine sober months the writer took a drink at a party: "No one had ever told me it was the first drink that did the damage" (<2>Experience, Strength and Hope</2>, 2003, story from an earlier edition).

62fe77fc370c.t: <0><1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980):</0> "Another thing Dr. Bob put quite simply: 'The first one will get you'" (<2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2>, 1980). One member, John R., says Dr. Bob kept repeating it. A few lines earlier on the same page, a member who came in in 1942 says others are always repeating things Dr. Bob said "that I know he didn't" (<3>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</3>, 1980), and the book adds that apart from "Let's keep it simple," it's hard to tell which sayings are really his. The line comes up again later, in a member's own words: Jud O., who drank in 1969 one week before his thirtieth anniversary, says that however long you don't drink, the next one is close, "It never lets you go," and that Dr. Bob was right (<4>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</4>, 1980).

20d6f0fdde7a.t: <0>"First drink" in the program text</0> appears on pp. 8, 23–24, 35, 37, 40–41, 43, 92, 154 and 157. Every one is about the moment before drinking or the cycle the first drink starts.

98e44b9384b6.t: <0>What happens after the first drink.</0> "Once he takes any alcohol whatever into his system, something happens, both in the bodily and mental sense, which makes it virtually impossible for him to stop" (pp. 22–23). Dr. Silkworth's statement says the same in medical terms: these drinkers "cannot start drinking without developing the phenomenon of craving" (p. xxx). This part matches the saying.

4649cec2a2a5.t: <0>Why the first drink is the real problem.</0> The very next lines turn the point around. All that would be beside the point if he never took the first drink, which sets "the terrible cycle in motion" (p. 23). "Therefore, the main problem of the alcoholic centers in his mind, rather than in his body" (p. 23). Asked why he started his last bender, he'll give "any one of a hundred alibis," and usually "he has no more idea why he took that first drink than you have" (p. 23).

fabbed7a19c4.t: <0>No defense.</0> "We are without defense against the first drink" (p. 24). The memory of past suffering doesn't come to mind with enough force, and the "old threadbare idea that this time we shall handle ourselves like other people" wins (p. 24).

564e13748d2f.t: <0>Chapter 3's examples</0> are about the thinking before the first drink, not the drinking after. Jim decides an ounce of whiskey in his milk can't hurt on a full stomach (pp. 35–37). Fred, sure his self-knowledge will protect him, orders a cocktail on a perfect day without a thought (pp. 40–41). "Parallel with our sound reasoning there inevitably ran some insanely trivial excuse for taking the first drink" (p. 37).

dad1ac2ca9e4.t: <0>Where the defense comes from.</0> "Once more: The alcoholic at certain times has no effective mental defense against the first drink" (p. 43). Except in a few rare cases, neither he nor anyone else can provide one. "His defense must come from a Higher Power" (p. 43).

30b851d005db.t: <0>In helping others.</0> Chapter 7 tells the helper to show a newcomer "the mental twist which leads to the first drink of a spree" (p. 92), and how "the queer mental condition surrounding that first drink" stops the will power from working (p. 92).

b31ed2aca11e.t: What the saying gets right and what it leaves out

bd1286f8c672.t: The saying is right that for the alcoholic the first drink starts everything, and the book adds that a long dry spell doesn't change that. Chapter 3's man who stayed bone dry for twenty-five years was soon as bad as ever when he drank again (pp. 32–33).

436ac2b560b2.t: The saying can suggest the answer is simply not to take the first drink. The book says that's exactly what the alcoholic can't count on doing on his own. The "alcoholic of the hopeless variety" (p. 44) has no defense at certain times, and self-knowledge doesn't help (p. 39). The book's answer is the spiritual change the rest of it describes, after which, it says, "We will seldom be interested in liquor" (p. 84).

ba1c1d54a3af.t: What does the Foreword to the First Edition say A.A. is for? | Recovery Starts

753efcebdd99.t: The 1939 foreword says the book's main purpose is to show other alcoholics exactly how the first hundred members recovered.

093a52ca5573.t: What does the Foreword to the First Edition say A.A. is for?

b0fd428c36bc.t: The 1939 foreword says the book's main purpose is to show other alcoholics exactly how the first hundred members recovered.

1d7f44f2a546.t: It says A.A. is not an organization in the usual sense: no fees or dues, no tie to any religion, and one requirement for membership, an honest desire to stop drinking.

2437cd83e30a.t: Its one sentence of purpose for the fellowship is: "We simply wish to be helpful to those who are afflicted." (p. xiv).

a780f899641e.t: It asks especially to hear from readers who have started working with other alcoholics.

e8ecc3da607b.t: The Foreword to the First Edition is under two pages long (pp. xiii–xiv). The fourth edition prints it "as it appeared in the first printing of the first edition in 1939" (p. xiii). Read straight through, it says six things.

0c0161530eb2.t: <0>Who "we" are.</0> More than a hundred men and women who have recovered from "a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body" (p. xiii).

b2e3b2acfc9c.t: <0>What the book is for.</0> "To show other alcoholics precisely how we have recovered is the main purpose of this book." (p. xiii). The hope is that the account will convince them without further proof, help everyone understand that the alcoholic "is a very sick person" (p. xiii), and show that this way of living has advantages for all (p. xiii).

3df6a92c5403.t: <0>Why the members are anonymous.</0> The reason it gives is practical: there were too few of them to handle all the personal appeals the book might bring, and most had jobs to keep: "We would like it understood that our alcoholic work is an avocation." (p. xiii). Members writing or speaking in public are asked to call themselves "a member of Alcoholics Anonymous" (p. xiii), and the press is asked to respect that (p. xiii).

6cdb68c59d56.t: <0>What A.A. is not.</0> It is not an organization in the conventional sense of the word (pp. xiii–xiv). "There are no fees or dues whatsoever." (p. xiv).

a134f4807fd9.t: <0>Who can belong.</0> "The only requirement for membership is an honest desire to stop drinking." (p. xiv). A.A. is not allied with any faith, sect or denomination, and opposes no one (p. xiv).

6c103920deea.t: <0>What it wants.</0> "We simply wish to be helpful to those who are afflicted." (p. xiv). It asks to hear from readers who are getting results, "particularly from those who have commenced work with other alcoholics" (p. xiv), and offers to help them. It welcomes inquiry from scientific, medical and religious societies (p. xiv).

b0e8502051ac.t: In 1939 the fellowship's stated purpose was to help alcoholics recover, and the book was the way to reach the ones the members couldn't reach in person. The foreword's one request of its readers is about carrying the message: it wants to hear most from those who have started working with other alcoholics, the work Chapter 7 describes (see <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0>).

246de6c9fef9.t: Nothing in the foreword sets up rules for members, a program of meetings, or any kind of authority. It describes a loose fellowship of people helping drinkers.

e702641c0f55.t: <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) quotes the foreword's sentences about fees, membership and faith and says that, "With a few changes and additions," that statement of purpose came to be read as a preamble at meetings (Pass It On, 1984). Bill W.'s 1969 talk, printed in P-53, says the first printing of the book had expressed fear of being flooded with "undesirable" people, and that part was taken out after the first printing because A.A. was found to work for all sorts of people (P-53). P-53's footnote points to the foreword's phrase about "the overwhelming number of personal appeals" (P-53). The foreword as the fourth edition prints it still contains that phrase (p. xiii), so our text doesn't show exactly what was removed.

f9a43eaf220c.t: What were the "Four Absolutes"? Are they in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

2981f3038be8.t: The Four Absolutes were the Oxford Group's moral standards: absolute honesty, absolute purity, absolute unselfishness and absolute love. Early members in…

7ebffebfd584.t: What were the "Four Absolutes"? Are they in the Big Book?

3747c2f499a1.t: The Four Absolutes were the Oxford Group's moral standards: absolute honesty, absolute purity, absolute unselfishness and absolute love. Early members in both Akron and New York heard them in the Oxford Group before A.A. separated from it.

b83c3f4c5b08.t: They are not in the Big Book. A search of the whole fourth-edition text finds no "Four Absolutes" and no "absolute honesty," in the program chapters, the forewords, the appendices or the personal stories.

38da3aed9f28.t: The co-founders saw them differently. Dr. Bob, in 1948, called them "the only yardsticks we had in the early days, before the Steps," and still used them. Bill W. said the New Yorkers dropped the expressions because the dose was too strong for most drinkers, and that putting the word "absolute" in front of these ideals turned people away.

9fcc358f0482.t: A 1980 history says the absolutes were still being quoted at meetings in the Akron and Cleveland area.

eec04235c73f.t: What the Big Book says (and doesn't)

4e08b88d6502.t: The phrase "Four Absolutes" and the set "absolute honesty, absolute purity, absolute unselfishness, absolute love" don't appear anywhere in the fourth edition. The book does use some of the same words separately, as ordinary goals rather than absolutes; for example, a recovering man is unlikely to get far "if he fails to show unselfishness and love under his own roof" (p. 127), and members "have begun to learn tolerance, patience and good will toward all men" (p. 70). The program it does set out is the Twelve Steps, which, it says, are "guides to progress" (p. 60), with "spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection" as the aim (p. 60). See <0>Is "progress, not perfection" in the Big Book?</0>

718980c4273f.t: In his last major talk, printed in P-53, Dr. Bob said the Four Absolutes "were the only yardsticks we had in the early days, before the Steps" (P-53). "I think the Absolutes still hold good and can be extremely helpful." (P-53). When the right course wasn't obvious, he measured a decision against absolute honesty, unselfishness, purity and love; if it checked out against all four, his answer "can't be very far out of the way" (P-53). He linked trouble with Step One to a lack of purity of motive, and said absolute unselfishness meant giving of yourself, not a dime to a beggar (P-53). He also said no one ever fully reaches absolute love, "but that doesn't mean we can't try to get it" (P-53).

8df8d3d8f820.t: Bill W.: too strong a dose (1957, 1940)

287a62c9bae7.t: <0>A.A. Comes of Age (1957).</0> Before Bill went to Akron in 1935, Dr. Silkworth told him he was failing partly because he preached the Oxford Group precepts of being absolutely honest, pure, unselfish and loving: "This is a very big order." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill writes that alcoholics found the absolutes "frequently too much" when first contacted: "These ideas had to be fed with teaspoons rather than by buckets." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The terms were also the Oxford Group's own, and using them would have kept A.A. tied to that group in the public mind (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). By the fall of 1938, he says, Akron members still talked about the absolutes, but "This dose was found to be too rich for New Yorkers, and we had abandoned the expressions." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

fd63025ab2ff.t: <0>Bill's letter of October 30, 1940</0> (quoted in <1>Pass It On</1>, 1984). Honesty, purity, unselfishness and love remained goals for A.A. members, he wrote, but when "absolute" was put in front of them, "they either turned people away by the hundreds or gave a temporary spiritual inflation resulting in collapse" (Pass It On, 1984).

002bc464bc9a.t: How they reached Bill and Akron (later accounts)

b6b0c03fb7b6.t: <0>Ebby.</0> <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) says Rowland H., the Oxford Grouper who helped Ebby get sober in 1934, impressed on him the four principles of the Oxford Group, and that Ebby said Rowland was "particularly strong in advocating absolute honesty" (Pass It On, 1984). At the Oxford Group meetings Bill attended after his hospital stay, Bill recalled hearing little theology but "plenty of absolute honesty, absolute purity, absolute unselfishness, and absolute love" (Pass It On, 1984).

ef629aa367b5.t: <0>Akron.</0> <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) calls the four absolutes the core of the Oxford Group program (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). T. Henry Williams recalled that a newcomer at his house in 1938–39 was asked to surrender his life to God and "start in to really live up to the four absolutes" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Oxford Groupers were disappointed that the Big Book left them out, because "the Twelve Steps had replaced the four absolutes, which were not mentioned, either" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). The book adds that the absolutes "are still published and widely quoted at A.A. meetings" in the Akron–Cleveland area (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

6062062515b3.t: <0>Their value.</0> Dr. Bob, in 1948, said they "still hold good" (P-53). Bill, in 1940 and 1957, said the word "absolute" did more harm than good with most alcoholics and the New Yorkers dropped it (Pass It On, 1984; A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Both remain on the record; the Big Book itself uses neither the term nor the list.

99f19451201b.t: <0>The order.</0> Bill lists honesty, purity, unselfishness, love (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); Dr. Bob lists honesty, unselfishness, purity, love (P-53). The order doesn't change the meaning.
