417343196a04.t: What does "deep down in every man, woman, and child is the fundamental idea of God" say? | Recovery Starts

f1c025b84c24.t: The line is on page 55 of the Big Book, in Chapter 4, "We Agnostics": "deep down in every man, woman, and child, is the fundamental idea of God" (p. 55).…

73db821838d0.t: What does "deep down in every man, woman, and child is the fundamental idea of God" say?

e2fcb8490aa1.t: The line is on page 55 of the Big Book, in Chapter 4, "We Agnostics": "deep down in every man, woman, and child, is the fundamental idea of God" (p. 55). It goes on: the idea may be hidden "by calamity, by pomp, by worship of other things, but in some form or other it is there" (p. 55).

68d8ce7781d8.t: It is a claim about everyone, and the context doesn't soften the wording. What the context adds is how it's offered: as former agnostics admitting something about themselves ("Actually we were fooling ourselves," p. 55), with "in some form or other," and closing on "It was so with us." (p. 55)

0cf815180852.t: The next lines say where they found God: "We found the Great Reality deep down within us." (p. 55) "In the last analysis it is only there that He may be found." (p. 55) Then they limit their own part: "We can only clear the ground a bit." (p. 55)

62cc26e88683.t: So context complicates any use of the line, quoted alone, as a ruling on what other people secretly believe. In its place it's testimony, and it sends the reader to search within himself rather than to take the writers' word for it.

a46996a7e703.t: The chapter has been arguing that reason isn't everything (p. 54). The people who proved man could never fly were reasoning too (p. 55). Then the writers turn the flying image around: they had been seeing "another kind of flight, a spiritual liberation from this world, people who rose above their problems" (p. 55). "They said God made these things possible, and we only smiled." (p. 55) "We had seen spiritual release, but liked to tell ourselves it wasn't true." (p. 55)

e0677165e896.t: That's the setup. The line itself opens with a confession: "Actually we were fooling ourselves, for deep down..." (p. 55). The writers are telling the reader what they found out about themselves.

d956402e9f38.t: In order (p. 55): 1. The fundamental idea of God is deep down in everyone, though calamity, pomp or the worship of other things may hide it. 2. Faith in a Power greater than ourselves, and its "miraculous demonstrations" in human lives, "are facts as old as man himself" (p. 55). 3. "We finally saw that faith in some kind of God was a part of our make-up, just as much as the feeling we have for a friend." (p. 55) 4. "Sometimes we had to search fearlessly, but He was there." (p. 55) 5. "We found the Great Reality deep down within us." (p. 55) "In the last analysis it is only there that He may be found." (p. 55) "It was so with us." (p. 55) 6. "We can only clear the ground a bit." (p. 55) If their testimony helps the reader drop prejudice and think honestly, and "encourages you to search diligently within yourself" (p. 55), then "if you wish" (p. 55), the reader can join them on the Broad Highway.

ddedab6f869c.t: Notice the wording that keeps it open: "in some form or other," "some kind of God," "if you wish." And notice where the passage points: inward. It doesn't send the reader to a church, a creed or the writers' own beliefs, but "deep down within us" (p. 55).

a619f31c25ca.t: The chapter closes with the man who thought he was an atheist. Alone in a hospital room, he asked himself whether all the religious people he'd known could be wrong, and then the thought came: "Who are you to say there is no God?" (p. 56) His change was sudden. The book adds that it isn't so for everyone: "Some of us grow into it more slowly." (p. 57) Appendix II, added after the first printing (p. 567), says most members' experiences are slow, and that they find they have "tapped an unsuspected inner resource" (pp. 567–568), which they come to identify with their own conception of a Power greater than themselves (p. 568).

e2a19f2a87ae.t: It complicates it. The book does claim that the idea of God is deep down in everyone, and a fair page has to say so. But in its place the claim is the writers' testimony about what they found when they stopped fooling themselves. It's held open ("in some form or other"), it points the reader to look within, and the writers say all they can do is clear the ground. The chapter's own starting requirement, a few pages earlier, is only willingness to believe (p. 47).

3a059c2471e7.t: Related: <0>What does "either God is everything or else He is nothing" mean in its place?</0> · <1>Do I have to be religious to work the Steps?</1> · <2>What is the "spiritual awakening" in Step 12?</2>

23311f9bbd2b.t: written after the first printing (p. 567); the Preface says the appendices came into the book with the second edition, 1955 (p. xi). After 1950.

020b2b173233.t: Does the Big Book say "you have to give it away to keep it"? | Recovery Starts

370d360aac04.t: Not in those words. The saying isn't in the Big Book's 1939 program text, pages 1 to 164. It appears in one fourth-edition personal story: "I was told…

c8bd52529e2c.t: Does the Big Book say "you have to give it away to keep it"?

ccf211e18d82.t: Not in those words. The saying isn't in the Big Book's 1939 program text, pages 1 to 164. It appears in one fourth-edition personal story: "I was told that to keep it we have to give it away" (p. 345). Bill W. came close in a 1955 essay (after 1950): "We couldn't keep what we had unless we gave it away" (P-17).

b19e4e01ded5.t: The idea is in the program text, in its own words. Bill writes that an alcoholic who didn't work and sacrifice for others "would surely drink again" (p. 15). The first Akron members "felt they had to give to others what they had found, or be sunk" (p. 158). And Chapter 7 calls helping others "the foundation stone of your recovery" (p. 97).

cfa5d87dd66f.t: The book doesn't leave it as a bargain to keep yourself sober. Of those first members it says that motive "became secondary" (p. 159), and Chapter 7 asks the helper to think of "what you can bring" (p. 102).

b8b62134d478.t: All our sources were searched for "give it away," "to keep it," "giving away," "keep what you have," "keep what we had" and "freely given."

cfb1b247e780.t: <0>The saying:</0> one personal story, "Because I'm an Alcoholic" (Part II): "Commitment and service were part of recovery. I was told that to keep it we have to give it away" (p. 345).

90650314f2e1.t: <0>An older version:</0> "The Professor and the Paradox," a story printed in the second edition (1955) and dropped in 1976, now in <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1> (2003). Its writer lists four A.A. paradoxes, the second being "We give away to keep" (<2>Experience, Strength and Hope</2>, 2003, story from the 1955 edition).

b4664641fd76.t: <0>The nearest wording outside the stories, from Bill W. in 1955:</0> "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous" (printed in P-17, and as an appendix to <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957) looks back on the early days of carrying the message: "We couldn't keep what we had unless we gave it away" (P-17). The point there is sacrifice. Members gave time, energy and their own money, asked nothing of the prospect, and found that their Twelfth Step work "went flat" (P-17) when they demanded anything. It comes from after 1950, and the same essay quotes <2>Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions</2>, which is not a source here; the sentence is cited as Bill's own 1955 words only.

d5aa35d795f5.t: <0>"Give it away" in <1>Pass It On</1> (1984)</0> is about the unsold Big Book in 1939: they weren't sure they "could even give it away" (<2>Pass It On</2>, 1984). It isn't the saying.

2aee8bff92a4.t: <0>Bill's story (1939).</0> In the hospital Bill thought of the many hopeless alcoholics "who might be glad to have what had been so freely given me" (p. 14). His friend, the schoolmate who had brought him the message, insisted it was "imperative to work with others as he had worked with me" (p. 14). "Faith without works was dead, he said" (p. 14). Bill's own comment follows: an alcoholic who failed to enlarge his spiritual life "through work and self-sacrifice for others" (p. 15) could not survive the hard times ahead. "If he did not work, he would surely drink again, and if he drank, he would surely die" (p. 15). When all else failed, "work with another alcoholic would save the day" (p. 15).

8fbfd544a5ab.t: <0>Chapter 2.</0> The writers ask, "How then shall we present that which has been so freely given us?" (p. 19), and their answer is the book.

8596a7b0d796.t: <0>Chapter 7.</0> It opens: "nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (p. 89). The newcomer is told that "your attempt to pass this on to him plays a vital part in your own recovery" (p. 94). "Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery" (p. 97).

f37851aa7ab9.t: <0>Chapter 9.</0> A father who has just found a spiritual life may try "to hug the new treasure to himself" (p. 129). He hasn't yet seen that it is a lode which will pay dividends only if he mines it all his life "and insists on giving away the entire product" (p. 129). The same passage tells the family to let him help other alcoholics as much as he likes in those first days, because "this will do more to insure his sobriety than anything else" (p. 129).

ddc8eb58d738.t: <0>Chapter 11.</0> The first three Akron members "felt they had to give to others what they had found, or be sunk" (p. 158). This is the closest the program text comes to the saying.

e77467af172a.t: What the book adds to the saying

6a0c45a1df74.t: Taken alone, "give it away to keep it" can sound like a trade: help others so you stay sober. The program text says that motive is real and doesn't hide it (pp. 89, 94, 97). But it doesn't stop there: - Of the first Akron members: "Though they knew they must help other alcoholics if they would remain sober, that motive became secondary" (p. 159). "It was transcended by the happiness they found in giving themselves for others" (p. 159). - The helper tells the newcomer he is "under no obligation to you" (p. 94), and that the helper hopes only that he will try to help other alcoholics in turn (p. 94). - "Do not think of what you will get out of the occasion. Think of what you can bring to it" (p. 102). - "To be helpful is our only aim" (p. 89).

8f08eef002dd.t: So the book agrees with the saying's core, that a sober alcoholic who stops giving to others is in danger. It also expects the motive of keeping your own sobriety to become secondary to the other person and to the happiness of giving.

34faf6889866.t: See also: <0>Is helping others selfish if it keeps me sober?</0> and <1>What does Step 12 really say?</1>

0eb07b984453.t: Is "God doesn't make junk" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

f3c3aea9297a.t: Is "God doesn't make junk" in the Big Book?

8b87836b31ac.t: The program text doesn't take up self-worth in those terms. A few passages touch the subject: we are "the children of a living Creator" (p. 28), and "As God's people we stand on our feet; we don't crawl before anyone." (p. 83).

ca34f864039d.t: The same text is just as plain about what's wrong with us. Bill: "of myself I was nothing; that without Him I was lost" (p. 13), and the root of our troubles is "Selfishness—self-centeredness!" (p. 62). The book holds both, and the saying keeps only one.

2f6bc0d11e86.t: All our sources were searched for "junk," "doesn't make junk," "worthless," "uselessness" and related words, with page breaks joined. The saying isn't there. "Junk" appears only in its ordinary sense, in a story and the history books (stolen junk on a floor, p. 507; a "junker" of a car, p. 510).

f5c6a5082267.t: Passages that speak to a person's worth

eafd9f5f9211.t: <0>Children of God.</0> "all of us, whatever our race, creed, or color are the children of a living Creator" (p. 28). In Step Three's picture, "He is the Father, and we are His children." (p. 62).

ecbee2a37e1f.t: <0>Standing up.</0> Making amends, we are to be humble "without being servile or scraping" (p. 83). "As God's people we stand on our feet; we don't crawl before anyone." (p. 83).

d9ed5799df33.t: <0>Uselessness lifted.</0> "No matter how far down the scale we have gone, we will see how our experience can benefit others." (p. 84). "That feeling of uselessness and self-pity will disappear." (p. 84). The family's painful past, "in God's hands," becomes "the greatest possession you have" (p. 124).

9f298223b3a4.t: <0>What God made is good.</0> On sex: "our sex powers were God-given and therefore good" (p. 69).

868a58cb86ae.t: Passages that speak to what is wrong with us

53f01a2778f6.t: Bill, in the hospital: "I admitted for the first time that of myself I was nothing; that without Him I was lost." (p. 13).

5d73730c1faf.t: "Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles." (p. 62). "Above everything, we alcoholics must be rid of this selfishness." (p. 62).

0e0f54c7448c.t: In inventory, "When we saw our faults we listed them. We placed them before us in black and white." (p. 67).

294b46bc2896.t: The Big Book doesn't say anyone is junk, and it doesn't say the opposite in so many words. It calls people God's children who need not crawl before anyone, and also asks them to face their selfishness and defects honestly. Read alone, either set of passages would give a lopsided picture.

7c25f0e1d568.t: Where is "God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves," and what is it about? | Recovery Starts

9677e1b055a3.t: It's the last of the Promises, on page 84 of Chapter 6, "Into Action": "We will suddenly realize that God is doing for us what we could not do for…

c21c8678fb3d.t: Where is "God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves," and what is it about?

d63c7f12c047.t: It's the last of the Promises, on page 84 of Chapter 6, "Into Action": "We will suddenly realize that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves." (p. 84)

79e224a2b82e.t: The Promises are tied to the amends work of Steps Eight and Nine. They open with "If we are painstaking about this phase of our development" (p. 83), and after the list the book says: "They will always materialize if we work for them." (p. 84)

cdc3541ba2dd.t: The idea isn't only here. The book says it early on (p. 25), again at the end of the inventory, "faith did for us what we could not do for ourselves" (pp. 70–71), and on the next page, about drink (p. 85).

dfa9d30a4081.t: Context confirms the plain meaning: God does what we couldn't. It adds where the line sits, which is after work we do. The book holds both. The work is ours, and the change, in its words about liquor, comes "without any thought or effort on our part" (p. 85).

22d31ffd838b.t: Chapter 6 has taken the reader through Steps Eight and Nine: creditors, enemies, legal trouble, the family, and wrongs that can never be fully righted (pp. 76–83). Then comes the promise: if we are painstaking "about this phase of our development, we will be amazed before we are half way through" (p. 83). A list follows: a new freedom and happiness, peace, self-seeking slipping away, fear of people and of economic insecurity leaving us. The second-to-last item is "We will intuitively know how to handle situations which used to baffle us." (p. 84) The last is the line.

9a7155fdb57e.t: Then: "Are these extravagant promises? We think not." (p. 84) "They will always materialize if we work for them." (p. 84) And on to Step Ten (p. 84). The whole passage is laid out in <0>Where are "the Promises," and what do they promise?</0>

eeef3253ee62.t: So in place, "suddenly realize" belongs to the amends work: the book says we "will be amazed before we are half way through" (p. 83). It doesn't fix a time for each promise, though. They are being fulfilled "sometimes quickly, sometimes slowly" (p. 84).

69a9e9991dd4.t: The same idea across the book

16edf18fd712.t: <0>Chapter 2:</0> the members' Creator "has commenced to accomplish those things for us which we could never do by ourselves" (p. 25).

7f5e3fee2217.t: <0>Chapter 5, on self:</0> "Neither could we reduce our self-centeredness much by wishing or trying on our own power." (p. 62) "We had to have God's help." (p. 62)

0605297e2226.t: <0>Chapter 5, end of the inventory:</0> "In this book you read again and again that faith did for us what we could not do for ourselves." (pp. 70–71) The next sentence: "We hope you are convinced now that God can remove whatever self-will has blocked you off from Him." (p. 71)

1812a1927089.t: <0>Chapter 6, the next page:</0> after Step Ten, the book says our new attitude toward liquor "has been given us without any thought or effort on our part" (p. 85). "It just comes! That is the miracle of it." (p. 85) It adds a condition: "That is how we react so long as we keep in fit spiritual condition." (p. 85)

9847297509d4.t: It confirms the line's meaning and adds its setting. Quoted alone, the sentence can sound like a general comfort, or as if God does it all and nothing is asked of us. The book does say God does what we couldn't. It says so again and again, and it says some of the change comes without effort. But in each place, the book ties it to something the reader has done: the decision and the inventory (pp. 70–71), the amends (pp. 83–84), the daily Step Ten (pp. 84–85). On p. 84 the promise is plainly conditional: "if we work for them."

601c12efaa15.t: What does "either God is everything or else He is nothing" mean in its place? | Recovery Starts

097fadb98c95.t: The line is on page 53 of the Big Book, in Chapter 4, "We Agnostics," a chapter written in the voice of members who had thought they were atheists or…

9bb6ad7ebee9.t: What does "either God is everything or else He is nothing" mean in its place?

a7a0fa845d4a.t: The line is on page 53 of the Big Book, in Chapter 4, "We Agnostics," a chapter written in the voice of members who had thought they were atheists or agnostics, for readers who still are (pp. 44, 53).

7fb5710e07b7.t: In place, it describes the choice the writers say they faced once alcoholism had crushed them: "God either is, or He isn't. What was our choice to be?" (p. 53) The book does present it as a question that couldn't be dodged, and it argues that believing is more reasonable than leaving it at "We don't know" (p. 53).

a4ebde408e14.t: The same chapter says how small the start can be. Willingness to believe in a Power greater than yourself is enough to begin (pp. 46–47), and "we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47). The either-or is about whether God is, not about which idea of God to accept.

c65a724b4a67.t: So context complicates the reading of the line as an ultimatum. The choice is real and stark in the book. But it's the writers' account of their own turning point, argued for at length, inside a chapter that asks only for willingness at the start.

0f9ce43fe00f.t: Page 53 begins by praising reason: "Logic is great stuff. We liked it. We still like it." (p. 53) The power to reason is "one of man's magnificent attributes" (p. 53). The writers, being "agnostically inclined," wouldn't be satisfied with a proposal that couldn't be reasonably approached, so they set out to explain "why we think it more sane and logical to believe than not to believe" (p. 53). They call their old habit of throwing up their hands and saying they didn't know "soft and mushy" (p. 53).

9bae245070de.t: Then the line. When they became alcoholics, crushed by a crisis they couldn't postpone or evade, they had to face "the proposition that either God is everything or else He is nothing" (p. 53). "Arrived at this point, we were squarely confronted with the question of faith." (p. 53)

0dc85bfec6a7.t: The next paragraphs describe how that felt: - <0>The bridge.</0> Some of them had "walked far over the Bridge of Reason toward the desired shore of faith" (p. 53), and were grateful reason had brought them so far, but "somehow, we couldn't quite step ashore" (p. 53). - <1>Faith all along.</1> They saw they had already been living by a kind of faith: faith in their own reasoning (pp. 53–54), and worship of people, money, themselves, or a sunset (p. 54). "Hence, we saw that reason isn't everything." (p. 54) - <2>Where they looked.</2> They came to see that faith in some kind of God was part of their make-up, and that "We found the Great Reality deep down within us." (p. 55) - <3>Stepping ashore.</3> The chapter ends with the story of a minister's son who thought he was an atheist; after the thought "Who are you to say there is no God?" (p. 56), "He had stepped from bridge to shore." (p. 56)

eb4f8e861846.t: What the chapter asks for at the start

5f1767cbe434.t: Earlier, the chapter sets the entry point low: - They began to get results as soon as they could lay aside prejudice and express "even a willingness to believe in a Power greater than ourselves" (p. 46), even though none of them could fully define that Power (p. 46). - "Our own conception, however inadequate, was sufficient to make the approach and to effect a contact with Him." (p. 46) - "When, therefore, we speak to you of God, we mean your own conception of God." (p. 47) - The one question to ask yourself: "Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe, that there is a Power greater than myself?" (p. 47) - Different conceptions in the personal stories "are questions for each individual to settle for himself" (p. 50).

2213e954cd80.t: Both things are in the text, and a fair reading keeps both. The passage is not soft: it says the issue had to be faced, it treats "We don't know" as a place the writers left, and the chapter argues for belief over the next three pages. It is also not a demand to accept anyone's doctrine. It's set out as "we" (the writers' own experience), it comes with reasons rather than as an order, and it sits in a chapter whose starting requirement is willingness and whose God is the reader's own conception.

56128c5148b2.t: It complicates it. Quoted alone, the line can sound like a test of total belief that a newcomer must pass on the spot. In place, it's former agnostics describing the turning point they reached, after saying a newcomer can begin with willingness alone.

7f3c13733a34.t: Is group conscience a majority vote? | Recovery Starts

38915192dec9.t: The Long Form doesn't say. Tradition Two names the group conscience as the way "a loving God" expresses Himself for the group's purpose (p. 563), and it…

3649b381476a.t: Is group conscience a majority vote?

ea82189a2b49.t: The Long Form doesn't say. Tradition Two names the group conscience as the way "a loving God" expresses Himself for the group's purpose (p. 563), and it says nothing about votes, majorities or procedure.

47564a2826f8.t: Groups did vote from the start: the Long Form has them electing secretaries and committees (p. 565). But Bill W.'s 1946 essay on money says the majority "ought not to try to coerce" the minority (there, into paying for clubs it doesn't want), and his 1947 essays say the group's leaders only carry out what they believe the group wants.

c7a46e239916.t: The idea that a group conscience means "substantial unanimity," reached after everyone has been heard, is spelled out in later literature (the 1962 Concepts; the 2018 group pamphlet). Even there, the group still votes in the end.

f5bf9534c7db.t: So: not simply a show of hands, and not a rule against voting either. The early texts protect the minority more than they prescribe a method.

3d1b82d748a2.t: What the Long Form says, and doesn't

13a11f73512b.t: Tradition Two: "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." (p. 563). That's the whole of it. The group conscience is where the Tradition locates the authority, but the text doesn't describe how a group arrives at it.

b33e72a0ee98.t: Other Traditions show that groups made decisions in ordinary ways. "The small group may elect its secretary, the large group its rotating committee" (p. 565). Those elected are "trusted and experienced servants of the whole" who "do not govern" (p. 565). Elections were normal; government by the winners was not.

b34bf5b8eca8.t: What the 1946–47 essays say about majorities

2c9c0b65d472.t: The earliest texts on the question come from money and clubs, the subjects that divided groups most.

8f1bbf681750.t: <0>The majority can't make the minority pay.</0> In "Money" (1946) Bill notes that most members like clubs, but "the majority ought not to try to coerce" (P-17, "Money", 1946) the minority into supporting clubs they don't want or need. Clubs should be paid for by the people who want them.

95f538a7b339.t: <0>A majority view doesn't make policy by itself.</0> In "Clubs in A.A." (1947) he writes that "Were a vote taken tomorrow on the desirability of clubs a sizable majority of A.A.s would record a resounding 'yes'" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947). He takes the "strong minority" who wanted no part of clubs just as seriously, and the answer A.A. settled on served both: "A.A.s who need and want clubs ought to have them" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947), kept separate from the groups.

35d8b4eeb5df.t: <0>Committees serve the group's wishes.</0> In "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?" (1947): "Each committee carries out what it believes to be the wishes of its group." (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). Leaders can guide by example or persuasion but "can never boss" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). The New York office could "usually tell how the majority of A.A.s feel about our current problems" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947), but that made it a source of information, not a ruler.

782de2976370.t: None of this says how many hands make a decision. It does say a majority isn't entitled to coerce, and that knowing what most members think is useful, not binding on everyone.

5c2af20a4007.t: In <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> Bill describes learning that the conscience of the group, "when properly informed of the facts and issues and principles involved" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957), was often wiser than any leader. The stress is on being informed: facts, issues and principles, not just a count.

da3485dba17d.t: The word "unanimity" comes into the literature later. Concept XII (Bill W., 1962) asks that the Conference reach all important decisions "by discussion, vote, and, whenever possible, by substantial unanimity" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). P-16 (2018) quotes the same line as "wherever possible."

3d4076bc05b3.t: The A.A. group pamphlet (P-16, 2018) applies that to groups. It describes group conscience as representing "substantial unanimity on an issue before definitive action is taken" (P-16, 2018), with a "willingness to listen to minority opinions with an open mind" (P-16, 2018). On sensitive issues the group goes slowly, and the result "rests on more than a 'yes' or 'no' count" (P-16, 2018). But it also says all views are heard "before the group votes" (P-16, 2018), and that at business meetings "minority, or dissenting, views be heard along with those of the majority" (P-16, 2018). In this account the vote still happens. It comes last, after the listening.

b6e47a5e9aca.t: The text of Tradition Two doesn't settle the mechanics, and we shouldn't pretend it does. What the early writing does settle is the spirit: no one rules, the minority isn't steamrolled, and those who serve carry out the group's wishes rather than their own. A group that votes after a full hearing is consistent with all of it. A narrow majority pushing through something a large minority opposes runs against the spirit of what Bill wrote in 1946 and 1947, though his only direct words on it are about making the minority pay for clubs.

fc048d124d79.t: Can an A.A. group be named after a treatment centre or a person? | Recovery Starts

447aa5311d87.t: The 1946 Long Form doesn't mention group names. What it says is that a group may cooperate with anyone but must never go so far as "affiliation or…

0b29e7b8a09e.t: Can an A.A. group be named after a treatment centre or a person?

382201366148.t: The 1946 Long Form doesn't mention group names. What it says is that a group may cooperate with anyone but must never go so far as "affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564), and that a group counts as an A.A. group only if, as a group, it has "no other affiliation" (p. 563).

ad09df536443.t: The specific naming advice comes later, from P-16 (2018): a group meeting in a treatment facility, a church or a prison should not use the institution's name, so it's clear the group only rents space there.

cd7cbc6e4e6e.t: P-16 also reports a General Service Conference recommendation that no group be named after any actual person, living or dead, as a way to place "principles before personalities."

b9c3ee18f365.t: These are recommendations from group experience. The Long Form leaves each group's own affairs to its own conscience (p. 563).

d394f205c56f.t: <0>A group has no other affiliation.</0> Tradition Three: any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation" (p. 563).

57b175d83d9f.t: <0>Not even an implied link.</0> Tradition Six: "While an A.A. group may cooperate with anyone, such cooperation ought never go so far as affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564). "An A.A. group can bind itself to no one" (p. 564). The same paragraph says outside facilities such as clubs and hospitals "ought not to use the A.A. name" (p. 564), and that hospitals and other places of recuperation belong "well outside A.A." (p. 564).

78445cbca871.t: <0>Principles before personalities.</0> Tradition Twelve: anonymity reminds A.A. "to place principles before personalities" (p. 566).

d033f121201c.t: <0>The group decides its own affairs.</0> Tradition Four: in its own affairs each group "should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience" (p. 563), but should consult neighbouring groups when its plans affect them, and should confer with the trustees before any action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole (p. 563).

af6f77b71597.t: None of this mentions what a group calls itself. A name, though, is the most public thing a group has. A group named after the treatment centre it meets in looks like part of that centre, which is the "implied" affiliation the Sixth Tradition warns against.

29db4f926568.t: What later group experience recommends (P-16, 2018, dated)

b79a582eaf2c.t: The pamphlet <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16) has a section on naming (P-16, pp. 17–18):

5c070b33b458.t: Groups have learned to avoid any affiliation with or endorsement of any outside enterprise, "No matter how noble the activity or institution" (P-16, 2018, p. 17).

29dc230f5f22.t: "Even the appearance of being linked to any organization, club, or political or religious institution needs to be avoided" (P-16, 2018, p. 17).

55d3b4b48e6e.t: So a group meeting in a correctional or treatment facility or a church should not use the institution's name "but to call itself something quite different" (P-16, 2018, p. 18). That shows the group isn't affiliated with the place but "simply rents space there for meetings" (P-16, 2018, p. 18).

29f66a01027f.t: The General Service Conference has recommended that no group be named after "any actual person, living or dead, A.A. or non-A.A." (P-16, 2018, p. 18).

b64098f12675.t: P-16 also covers the reverse case. A treatment facility or halfway house should not carry the A.A. name, or a name like "Twelfth Step House" that wrongly implies A.A. endorsement (P-16, 2018, p. 41).

5f2180832d9d.t: What the text settles, and what it doesn't

79d573313bcd.t: The 1946 Long Form settles the principle: no affiliation, not even an implied one, and principles before personalities. It doesn't contain a naming rule. The naming guidance is later (P-16 is © 2018), and it's worded as experience and as a Conference recommendation, not a rule a group can be made to follow. No one in A.A. can force a group to change its name (see <0>Tradition Nine: is A.A. organized? Who runs it?</0>). A group choosing a name is weighing its own conscience against the Long Form's warning about implied affiliation.

550477584fb1.t: What is a GSR, a district and an area? | Recovery Starts

67b242795813.t: They are the steps between an A.A. group and the yearly General Service Conference in the U.S. and Canada. A group elects a general service representative…

8102677863c0.t: What is a GSR, a district and an area?

8744e52c4f3a.t: They are the steps between an A.A. group and the yearly General Service Conference in the U.S. and Canada. A group elects a <0>general service representative (GSR)</0>. The GSRs of nearby groups form a <1>district</1> and elect a district committee member (DCM). Districts make up an <2>area</2> (93 of them in the U.S. and Canada), whose assembly elects a <3>delegate</3> to the Conference every two years.

3958e24e407d.t: None of this is in the Big Book's 1939 text. It was built from 1951, when the first Conference met, and the Conference Charter (1955) set it out. Most details below come from the current <0>A.A. Service Manual</0> (2024–2026 edition) and are labelled that way.

09ab3f974606.t: Bill W.'s Concept IX (1962) calls GSRs, committee members and delegates "the direct agents of the A.A. groups" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). None of them governs a group.

4ababdc4a5f0.t: Intergroups and central offices, which the Long Form of Nine (1946) mentions, are a separate thing: local service offices, not part of this general service structure.

8e62bb43c963.t: The earliest text: Long Form Nine (1946)

73cae91dda27.t: The 1946 Long Form describes the service A.A. had then: "The small group may elect its secretary, the large group its rotating committee, and the groups of a large metropolitan area their central or intergroup committee, which often employs a full-time secretary" (p. 565). Above them were the trustees, A.A.'s General Service Committee in New York (p. 565). There were no GSRs, districts or delegates yet; the Conference that needed them came in 1951.

f61797e9b6a3.t: The original Conference Charter (1955) set up "State and Provincial Assemblies" of group representatives, which met every two years to elect committeemen and, from among them, a delegate "by a two-thirds written ballot or by lot" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955). Of delegates it says: "Delegates should be free to vote as their conscience dictates" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955). In 1971 the Conference allowed states and provinces to be joined into one assembly area, and in 1978 it renamed them area assemblies, made up of GSRs, district committee members and area officers (footnotes to the Charter, Appendix K).

c79853e9f4a4.t: In Concept IX (1962) Bill puts the base of the whole service structure on "several thousand General Service Representatives (GSRs), several hundred area Committee Members, and nearly a hundred Delegates" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). He asks groups to choose GSRs with care: "Hit-or-miss methods should be avoided" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). Only the GSRs, meeting in assembly, name the committee members and finally the delegates.

ac86428617d0.t: Concept III adds what the delegate is for. Delegates are "primarily the world servants of A.A. as a whole, that only in a secondary sense do they represent their respective areas" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III), so on final votes they should vote their own judgment and conscience.

356519044b39.t: How it works now (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026)

28e323c1f37f.t: <0>GSR.</0> Elected by a group, usually for two years, with an alternate. The manual calls the GSR "the link between the group and" A.A. as a whole and says "The GSR is that voice" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Chapter 1). A GSR attends district meetings and area assemblies with a vote, reports back to the group, and passes on the group's views. The manual suggests at least two years' sobriety. P-16, <1>The A.A. Group</1> (© 2018), calls the GSR "the group’s link with the General Service Conference" (P-16).

6c7216172da8.t: <0>District.</0> A cluster of groups near one another (the manual also describes language districts and, since the pandemic, virtual districts for online groups). The GSRs elect a <1>DCM</1>, who sits on the area committee. On how a DCM should lead, the manual says the GSRs will want "to be inspired and encouraged, but not told what to do" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Chapter 2).

385cce96f8c2.t: <0>Area.</0> "The U.S. and Canada are divided into 93 geographic areas" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Glossary), usually one per state or province, more where A.A. is large. The area assembly is made up of GSRs, DCMs, area officers and committee chairs. Every two years an election assembly chooses the delegate, usually by the Third Legacy Procedure: a two-thirds vote, or names drawn from a hat. The area also runs services too big for one group, such as public information, corrections and treatment facility work.

baba535454bf.t: <0>Delegate and Conference.</0> The delegate serves two years and goes to the Conference each spring in New York. It has about 135 voting members; area delegates "make up at least two-thirds of the Conference body" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Introduction), with the trustees, the directors of A.A. World Services and the Grapevine, and staff. Matters approved by two-thirds become Advisory Actions, and the delegate reports back to the area and its GSRs.

714073df5190.t: <0>Not bosses.</0> The current manual quotes Bill in "the first edition of this manual" (our copy gives no date; the manual grew out of his Third Legacy Manual, first drafted in 1951): "The Conference represents us, but cannot rule us" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Chapter 6). Concept XII (1962) bars the Conference from "any acts of government" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).

4c2391748742.t: <0>Not the intergroup.</0> Intergroups and central offices keep local meeting lists and phones. The manual says they are an important part of A.A. but "they are not part of the general service structure or a satellite of GSO" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Introduction).

432a5bcbdd7f.t: What does "half measures availed us nothing" mean in context? | Recovery Starts

03b1f7933713.t: The line is on page 59 of Chapter 5, "How It Works," a few sentences before the Twelve Steps are listed: "Half measures availed us nothing." (p. 59)

982076768f1c.t: What does "half measures availed us nothing" mean in context?

491dee066a7f.t: The line is on page 59 of Chapter 5, "How It Works," a few sentences before the Twelve Steps are listed: "Half measures availed us nothing." (p. 59)

3075f7520bae.t: It's in the past tense and about the writers themselves. The next sentences say what the whole measure was: "We stood at the turning point." (p. 59) "We asked His protection and care with complete abandon." (p. 59)

76a7b2363fbe.t: The paragraphs just before it name what had held them back: looking for "an easier, softer way" and holding on to "old ideas" (p. 58). "The result was nil until we let go absolutely." (p. 58)

d3a918813f84.t: Context confirms the usual reading: the book asks for thoroughness. But it doesn't ask for perfection. The next page says no one has managed "anything like perfect adherence to these principles" (p. 60).

572db217716d.t: The line comes in the run of short paragraphs between the opening of Chapter 5 and the list of Steps. In order (pp. 58–59):

6b3f5b191e86.t: The opening paragraph on who recovers and who doesn't, which turns on honesty (p. 58). See <0>What does "Rarely have we seen a person fail" really say, and who does it say may not recover?</0>

3f43501d8af1.t: If you want what the members have and are willing to go to any length to get it, "then you are ready to take certain steps" (p. 58).

4a9a64a9068f.t: "At some of these we balked." (p. 58) "We thought we could find an easier, softer way." (p. 58) "But we could not." (p. 58) The book begs the reader "to be fearless and thorough from the very start" (p. 58). Some had tried to hold on to their old ideas, "and the result was nil until we let go absolutely" (p. 58).

563ab101ebec.t: Alcohol is "cunning, baf-" (p. 58) / "fling, powerful!" (p. 59). "Without help it is too much for us." (p. 59) "But there is One who has all power—that One is God." (p. 59) "May you find Him now!" (p. 59)

b2d3ba808688.t: <0>"Half measures availed us nothing."</0> (p. 59) "We stood at the turning point." (p. 59) "We asked His protection and care with complete abandon." (p. 59)

786196999792.t: "Here are the steps we took, which are suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59).

ca0831eaab0e.t: The book doesn't list them. What it gives is the sentences around the line. Before it: balking at some of the steps, hunting for an easier, softer way, and holding on to old ideas, which got the same result, "nil" (p. 58). Just before it: alcohol is too much for us without help, but there is One who has all power (p. 59). After it, the whole measure: at the turning point, asking God's protection and care "with complete abandon" (p. 59).

21e7d3e1617c.t: So in its own place, the line sets holding back against letting go completely. "The result was nil" (p. 58) and "availed us nothing" (p. 59) are the same thought, said twice within a few lines.

2faae9dc5fe1.t: The sentence says "us": it reports what happened to the people who wrote the book. The paragraph around it is urgent. "With all the earnestness at our command, we beg of you to be fearless and thorough from the very start." (p. 58) But it is offered as experience, and the Steps that follow are introduced as "suggested" (p. 59). See <0>Are the Steps rules or suggestions?</0>

5ec3d4821cc9.t: The book separates thoroughness from perfection a page later. After the Steps, the book says many members exclaimed "What an order!" (p. 60), and it answers: "Do not be discouraged." (p. 60) "No one among us has been able to maintain anything like perfect adherence to these principles." (p. 60) "We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection." (p. 60) In its place, the line is about holding back at the turning point. It isn't about falling short of perfection afterwards.

4c08ce733439.t: Not much. It confirms it, and makes it clearer. The book does ask for complete commitment from the start, and says so more than once on these two pages. What context adds is what was being held back (old ideas, the search for an easier way, and trying without help), and that the line is about the turning point, not a demand to be perfect afterwards.

e8cee6270578.t: Related: <0>Where is "cunning, baffling, powerful," and what comes right after it?</0> · <1>What does "willing to go to any length" refer to?</1> · <2>Where are the Twelve Steps in the Big Book?</2>

e614b2ef2b6e.t: Is HALT (hungry, angry, lonely, tired) in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

cb58cf9d30b2.t: No. Neither the acronym HALT nor the list "hungry, angry, lonely, tired" is in the Big Book, or anywhere else in our sources.

33b64251410d.t: Is HALT (hungry, angry, lonely, tired) in the Big Book?

ae704ae7754f.t: No. Neither the acronym HALT nor the list "hungry, angry, lonely, tired" is in the Big Book, or anywhere else in our sources.

60e0c6a60de2.t: Each of the four words does turn up in the program text on its own, most strongly anger: resentment "destroys more alcoholics than anything else" (p. 64). The book never puts the four together as warning signs.

6ccab39b7dd3.t: The book's main point about relapse cuts against any checklist of moods: Fred drank on a day when "Physically, I felt fine" and he had no worries (p. 41). The program text says that at certain times the alcoholic has no mental defense against the first drink at all, and that his defense "must come from a Higher Power" (p. 43).

07f5ca1ba8e9.t: All our sources were searched for "HALT," "hungry, angry" and each of the four words, and for any two of them within a sentence of each other. Nothing turned up. Where "halt" appears it is the ordinary word, as in a therapy that "came to almost a complete halt" (p. 283) or a motion that brings debate to a halt (A.A. Service Manual); one hit in <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> is a scanning error for "Half." No story in any edition in our sources uses the acronym.

0c08b1ff5947.t: Where the four words do appear in the program text

e76ea4fb23fa.t: <0>Hungry.</0> In Chapter 3, Jim's relapse begins when "On the way I felt hungry so I stopped at a roadside place where they have a bar." (p. 36). The book doesn't treat the hunger as the cause. It calls what followed, the idea that whiskey in milk on a full stomach couldn't hurt him, "plain insanity" (p. 37). Elsewhere, Chapter 9 passes on a doctor's suggestion, "of course depending upon a doctor's advice" (p. 133), to keep chocolate on hand "for its quick energy value at times of fatigue" (p. 134), since a vague craving at night could be satisfied by candy (p. 134).

70a570aef23d.t: <0>Angry.</0> This is the one with the most weight. Resentment is the "number one" offender, and "It destroys more alcoholics than anything else." (p. 64). "If we were to live, we had to be free of anger." (p. 66). A wife's nagging about her husband's smoking and coffee threw him "into a fit of anger. He got drunk." (p. 135), and the book adds that he was "dead wrong" (p. 135). Chapter 10 names "The greatest enemies of us alcoholics" as "resentment, jealousy, envy, frustration, and fear" (p. 145). Chapter 3 also says that when they drank deliberately, feeling justified "by nervousness, anger, worry, depression, jealousy or the like," the justification was "insanely insufficient in the light of what always happened" (p. 37).

21540dd28fd8.t: <0>Lonely.</0> Bill's own story has loneliness leading to a drink, years before A.A.: sailing for the war, "I was very lonely and again turned to alcohol." (p. 1). After that, loneliness belongs to the drinking: Bill in "that bitter morass of self-pity" (p. 8), and "the chilling vapor that is loneliness" of the last days of drinking (p. 151). In the Akron hotel lobby, Bill thought that without a few drinks he might "have a lonely week-end" (p. 154); what he did was phone a clergyman to find another alcoholic (p. 154). Chapter 7 promises the helper the chance "to watch loneliness vanish" (p. 89).

734201fd6bc0.t: <0>Tired.</0> Step Eleven's practice of pausing through the day ends: "We do not tire so easily, for we are not burning up energy foolishly" (p. 88). Chapter 10 warns employers that a newly sober man "may overdo" and may need his sixteen-hour days curbed (p. 146). And there is the chocolate "at times of fatigue" (p. 134).

bb084a4c7ae9.t: What the book puts at the centre

44c339cb06b7.t: Chapter 3 is the book's study of "the mental states that precede a relapse into drinking" (p. 35). Its examples don't fit a list of moods:

35560aabc036.t: Jim was a little irritated and hungry (p. 36), but the book's point is that "parallel with our sound reasoning there inevitably ran some insanely trivial excuse for taking the first drink" (p. 37).

5e5ffcd27bbd.t: Fred had no trigger at all. "Physically, I felt fine. Neither did I have any pressing problems or worries." (p. 41). It was "the end of a perfect day, not a cloud on the horizon" (p. 41), and he ordered a cocktail without thinking of the consequences (p. 41).

2c6010c628bd.t: The chapter's conclusion: "The alcoholic at certain times has no effective mental defense against the first drink." (p. 43), and "His defense must come from a Higher Power." (p. 43). Chapter 2 says the same: "We are without defense against the first drink." (p. 24).

8d43a42d1093.t: So the book does want the alcoholic watching for resentment, fear, selfishness and dishonesty, every day (pp. 84, 86), and it takes anger very seriously. But it doesn't rest safety on noticing moods or meeting physical needs. A list like HALT can be sensible advice; the Big Book's own answer to the first drink is a spiritual one, kept up daily (pp. 84–85). See: <0>Is the definition of insanity in the Big Book?</0>

cde90b416833.t: All our sources (searched): Big Book, pamphlets, history, stories, service

4103a2962b03.t: "The Missing Link," Part II (ordinary use of "halt")

87f3d66cc00c.t: Does the Big Book say we're meant to be "happy, joyous, and free"? | Recovery Starts

9f7aff6f5fb2.t: Yes. "We are sure God wants us to be happy, joyous, and free." (p. 133) It's in Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward," in a passage about cheerfulness, play…

3a3146f35b7d.t: Does the Big Book say we're meant to be "happy, joyous, and free"?

50cadd46da96.t: Yes. "We are sure God wants us to be happy, joyous, and free." (p. 133) It's in Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward," in a passage about cheerfulness, play and health (pp. 132–133).

eb99358d3f84.t: The paragraphs around it tie happiness to the newcomer and to being useful: "If newcomers could see no joy or fun in our existence, they wouldn't want it." (p. 132) "So we think cheerfulness and laughter make for usefulness." (p. 132)

92125295e70b.t: It doesn't promise a life without trouble. The next lines say "we made our own misery. God didn't do it," and that if trouble comes, we should "cheerfully capitalize it as an opportunity to demonstrate His omnipotence" (p. 133). Right after, the book tells readers to take health problems to doctors and "never belittle a good doctor or psychiatrist" (p. 133).

11ca79e565e6.t: So context confirms the line and fills it in: joy is part of being useful and attractive to the next alcoholic, and trouble is expected and met, not ruled out.

d5b5b1db6121.t: Chapter 9 is written to recovering alcoholics and their families. After many pages on the strains of the first months at home, the chapter turns (p. 132): - "We have been speaking to you of serious, sometimes tragic things." (p. 132) "But we aren't a glum lot." (p. 132) - "We absolutely insist on enjoying life." (p. 132) The writers try not to be cynical about the state of the nations or carry the world's troubles on their shoulders (p. 132). - When they see a man sinking into alcoholism, they give him first aid and put what they have at his disposal, and for his sake they recount and almost relive the horrors of their past (p. 132). But those who tried to carry all of other people's burdens found they were soon overcome (p. 132). - "So we think cheerfulness and laughter make for usefulness." (p. 132) Outsiders are sometimes shocked when members laugh at a tragic past, "But why shouldn't we laugh? We have recovered, and have been given the power to help others." (p. 132) - Those in bad health and those who seldom play don't laugh much, so families should play, together or separately (pp. 132–133).

06b27c86b1bf.t: Then the line, and right after it: "We cannot subscribe to the belief that this life is a vale of tears, though it once was just that for many of us." (p. 133) The misery was our own making. Avoid manufacturing more of it, and treat trouble, when it comes, as a chance to show God's power (p. 133).

7374c993ac02.t: The next paragraph keeps its feet on the ground. "A body badly burned by alcohol does not often recover overnight nor do twisted thinking and depression vanish in a twinkling." (p. 133) The writers believe a spiritual way of living is a powerful health restorer, "But this does not mean that we disregard human health measures." (p. 133) God has supplied "fine doctors, psychologists, and practitioners of various kinds" (p. 133); take health problems to them.

0ac8524d577f.t: Bill W., in his own story: "There is, however, a vast amount of fun about it all." (p. 16) And: "The joy of living we really have, even under pressure and difficulty." (p. 15)

1ac693037213.t: Chapter 11, about the early meetings: a newcomer gave way to "that gay crowd inside, who laughed at their own misfortunes and understood his" (p. 160).

c2efacf14fd7.t: It confirms it. The book says it plainly and means it. What the context adds is what the joy is for and what it isn't: it's tied to usefulness and to drawing in the newcomer, it's held alongside an honest expectation of trouble, and it comes with advice to see a doctor when health needs one.

d8bb8aba20f5.t: Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward" (pp. 122–135), free from A.A.: <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt9.pdf</0>

e244c7bf382e.t: Related: <0>What does the Big Book say about helping the drinker's family?</0> · <1>Where are "the Promises," and what do they promise?</1>

4bd5512cc6e8.t: What does the Big Book say about helping the drinker's family? | Recovery Starts

ac2ebcfdd4b5.t: Help them, even if the drinker won't respond. "Though an alcoholic does not respond, there is no reason why you should neglect his family" (p. 97). Offer…

ac561066f7b9.t: What does the Big Book say about helping the drinker's family?

b600dd5ce915.t: Help them, even if the drinker won't respond. "Though an alcoholic does not respond, there is no reason why you should neglect his family" (p. 97). Offer them your way of life (p. 97).

f1fbd1bcdd49.t: When you work with a man and his family, stay out of their quarrels, help them see he has been very sick, and teach them by telling how your own home recovered, not by criticizing (p. 100).

d467b0108076.t: Two whole chapters are for families: Chapter 8, "To Wives," written in the voice of the wives of early members, addressed to the wives of men who drink (p. 104), and Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward."

b251256509dc.t: The first members did this from the start. When a man didn't recover, they tried to bring his family into a spiritual way of living (p. 159).

9b96cce28132.t: The family is part of the work from the first step: - <0>Before you meet him.</0> If he seems to want to stop, have a good talk with the person most interested in him, usually his wife, to learn about him (p. 90). The family should be patient, "realizing they are dealing with a sick person" (p. 90), shouldn't plead with him, and shouldn't try to tell your story (pp. 90–91). Meeting him through a doctor or hospital is better than through the family (p. 91), and leave the family out of the first talk (p. 91). - <1>If he won't respond.</1> "You should continue to be friendly to them. The family should be offered your way of life" (p. 97). If they practice spiritual principles there's a better chance he'll recover, "And even though he continues to drink, the family will find life more bearable" (p. 97). - <2>The cost.</2> Helping others may mean "counseling frantic wives and relatives" (p. 97). - <3>When he's recovering.</3> He should make what reparation he can and live his new principles at home, without fault-finding, even where the family is partly at fault (p. 98). There should be no hurry to reunite after a separation, and "Let no alcoholic say he cannot recover unless he has his family back" (p. 99). - <4>Your conduct with them.</4> "You should take care not to participate in their quarrels" (p. 100). Urge them to treat him as a very sick person, warn against resentment and jealousy, and point out his defects won't vanish overnight (p. 100). "The story of how you and your wife settled your difficulties is worth any amount of criticism" (p. 100).

7c510a7d9b8f.t: Written in 1939 in the voice of "the wives of Alcoholics Anonymous" (p. 104), for anyone "bound by ties of blood or affection to an alcoholic" (p. 104). (A note added later says it assumed the drinker was the husband because there were few women in A.A. then, p. 104.) Some of what it says: - Treat him as sick: "Treat him, when you can, as though he had pneumonia" (p. 108). It makes an exception for men who are "thoroughly bad-intentioned," and says a wife may feel she had better leave (p. 108). - "Never tell him what he must do about his drinking" (p. 111), and don't let his drinking spoil your relations with your children or friends (p. 111). - Meanwhile, "you might try to help the wife of another serious drinker" (p. 112). - Wives found they needed the program too, and urge others to try it (pp. 116–117). - When he recovers and spends long hours with other alcoholics, join him: "direct some of your thought to the wives of his new alcoholic friends" (p. 119).

0ae140c655a4.t: The whole family is affected. A doctor told the members that years with an alcoholic make the family, "to some extent, ill" (p. 122).

c72aea694b7b.t: The family's painful past becomes something to give: "each family which has been relieved owes something to those who have not" (p. 124).

e4e713e5357f.t: Let him go as far as he likes in helping other alcoholics in those first days (p. 129), but in time this should be balanced with his family and community (p. 131).

c196a1ac4d10.t: How it was done at first

1adb5caa8a11.t: Chapter 11 says that in early Akron, when a man failed, the members "made an effort to bring the man's family into a spiritual way of living, thus relieving much worry and suffering" (p. 159). A couple opened their home, and "Many a distracted wife" found there women who understood her problem, and advice on how her husband might be hospitalized and approached (p. 160).

ae9ec71157b9.t: A footnote added to Chapter 8 says Al-Anon Family Groups formed about thirteen years after the chapter was written, separate from A.A. but using its principles (p. 121). The 1939 text itself expects A.A. members and their wives to help families directly.

b8b69eca6865.t: 1939 (footnotes on pp. 104 and 121 added in later editions)

e60080afc957.t: Who was Henrietta Seiberling? | Recovery Starts

73bdf71a0570.t: Henrietta Seiberling was a nonalcoholic member of the Oxford Group in Akron, the daughter-in-law of the founder of the Goodyear rubber company. She lived…

c33a2a1fa4db.t: Henrietta Seiberling was a nonalcoholic member of the Oxford Group in Akron, the daughter-in-law of the founder of the Goodyear rubber company. She lived in the gatehouse of the Seiberling estate.

4527bf91c6bb.t: On the Saturday before Mother's Day, May 1935, Bill W., stranded in Akron and afraid he would drink, reached her by telephone after a minister's list of names ran out. She knew of a doctor in her Oxford Group who couldn't stop drinking, and the next afternoon she brought Dr. Bob and Bill together in her home.

7f088260da42.t: Bill wrote that she was the only one on that list "who had understood enough and cared enough" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and that A.A.'s debt to her was beyond reckoning. Dr. Bob called her "our good friend Henrietta."

df08f2581cca.t: The 1939 Big Book doesn't name her; Dr. Bob's story calls her only "a lady" (p. 179). A 1980 history, from her own and other members' recollections, shows she later disagreed with the alcoholics on money, on how much to speak of God, on the book, and on leaving the Oxford Group.

e13edd0c458a.t: In "Doctor Bob's Nightmare," written in 1939: "About this time a lady called up my wife one Saturday afternoon saying she wanted me to come over that evening to meet a friend of hers who might help me." (p. 179). He was in no shape that day; the next day she called again, and they went (p. 179). Chapter 11 tells the same meeting from Bill's side and doesn't mention her at all; the clergyman's call simply "led him presently to a certain resident of the town" (p. 155). See <0>How did Bill W. and Dr. Bob meet?</0>

932e975020a2.t: In his last major talk, printed in P-53, Dr. Bob named her. At the end of Bill's list, "his eyes happened to light on the name of Mrs. Seiberling — our good friend Henrietta" (P-53). She told him, "Come right out and have lunch with me." (P-53), and after hearing his story, "I have just the man for you." (P-53). When Anne put her off, "But Henry is very persistent, a very determined individual." (P-53), and the visit was set for the next day, Sunday and Mother's Day (P-53).

8c7888beb2c4.t: He also recalled asking her, while still drinking, whether she thought he really wanted to stop. She said: "No, Bob, I think you want to. You just haven't found a way to work it yet." (P-53).

f853cd5222c9.t: Bill says hers was the last name on a list of about ten from the Rev. Walter Tunks (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He remembered an elderly Mr. Seiberling, Goodyear's founder, and hesitated to call his wife; when he did, a young Southern voice answered, a Seiberling daughter-in-law (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). She said: "I'm no alcoholic, but I've had my difficulties." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and invited him out: "I live in the gatehouse of the Seiberling place." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). She had found her answers in the Oxford Groups (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The next afternoon Dr. Bob and Anne came to her door, and she put the two men in her library (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

c7edbf471d51.t: Bill set his thanks on record: of the ten people on the list, "Henrietta was the only one who had understood enough and cared enough." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). That first summer she counseled alcoholics' families as Anne did (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "What Alcoholics Anonymous owes to her will always be beyond anybody's reckoning." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill adds that she and the Williamses had tried hard to help Dr. Bob before he came, sharing their own defects with him (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

1117b65fc2c0.t: Her own account, and what came later (1980, 1984)

5b45fb9f61a3.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) quotes Henrietta's own memories, recorded in 1978, the year before her death (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). It says she was a Vassar graduate with three teenage children, all in the Oxford Group (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). In March or April 1935, before Bill came, a friend asked her what could be done about Bob Smith; she arranged an Oxford Group meeting at the Williamses' at which members shared costly things, and Dr. Bob told them: "I am a secret drinker" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Praying for him the next morning, she received what she called guidance: "Bob must not touch one drop of alcohol." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

71baf5b227c5.t: She remembered Bill's call on May 11, 1935 this way: "I'm from the Oxford Group, and I'm a rum hound from New York." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), and her thought: "This is really manna from heaven." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). She arranged for Bill to stay at a nearby country club so he could remain in Akron (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

83db576060df.t: The same book shows her differences with the alcoholics later on. She thought A.A. should not raise money and that it wasn't putting enough emphasis on God; she told Bill, "We are out to please God." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). An Akron member, Bob E., recalled that she "didn't like the book" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). When Dr. Bob led the alcoholics out of T. Henry Williams's house in late 1939, another member, Elgie, remembered that she "told Dr. Bob that it was the worst mistake he had ever made" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). The book adds that she later went with the A.A.s, but was not active in Akron for long; she moved to New York, where she died in 1979 (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

43cfcc3aaa1e.t: <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) adds that she was separated from her husband, who lived in the main house, Stan Hywet Hall (Pass It On, 1984).

e69d6dda6b0f.t: <0>How Bill found her.</0> Bill (1957) and Dr. Bob (1948) say her name was on the minister's list (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; P-53). In Henrietta's own telling (1978), a man on the list, Norman Sheppard, told Bill to call her (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

31c7b7628b1f.t: <0>What Bill said on the phone.</0> Bill (1957) says he explained he was an alcoholic from the New York Oxford Groups who needed to help another drunk (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); she remembered the "rum hound" line (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

0904b41f3cd9.t: <0>The first visit.</0> Dr. Bob (1948) says she asked Bill to lunch (P-53); Henrietta (1978) says he stayed for dinner and she told him to come to church with her the next morning (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

188c09d49bdd.t: Related: <0>How did Bill W. and Dr. Bob meet?</0> · <1>Who was Dr. Bob?</1> · <2>What did early A.A. take from the Oxford Group, and why did it separate?</2>

eee23d457c4b.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (Henrietta's recollections, 1978)

1f6c24fb5f94.t: Can your Higher Power be anything, a doorknob, the group? | Recovery Starts

bfadadc5ade2.t: The Big Book leaves the idea of God to the reader: "we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47), and a newcomer "can choose any conception he likes,…

609582c6e2fb.t: Can your Higher Power be anything, a doorknob, the group?

53c40e29ed0f.t: The Big Book leaves the idea of God to the reader: "we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47), and a newcomer "can choose any conception he likes, provided it makes sense to him" (p. 93).

c58248a12578.t: The program text (pp. 1–164) never offers a doorknob, an object or the group as an example. No book in our sources uses "doorknob" for a Higher Power. The group as a Higher Power comes up only in personal stories. In the earliest, about 1938, the writer calls it "at least a beginning" (p. 229).

7e4c5411113a.t: The book does set conditions: be willing to believe in "a Power greater than himself" and live by spiritual principles (p. 93), and don't close your mind to all spiritual ideas (p. 568). Its own writers call that Power God (p. 46) and expect a person's idea of it to grow (p. 47).

cfdec5937bbc.t: So the text gives no list of what's allowed or ruled out. "Anything at all" is not its wording, and it doesn't settle the doorknob.

baa162f72b2d.t: All our sources were searched for "Higher Power," doorknob and door knob, "light bulb," "power of the group," and the names the book gives the Power.

11d16c150836.t: <0>"Higher Power" in the program text</0> turns up twice: "His defense must come from a Higher Power" (p. 43) and "Follow the dictates of a Higher Power" (p. 100). Appendix III, doctors' comments on A.A. added with the second edition in 1955 (p. xi), has "a higher power" once more (p. 570). The program text's usual words are "a Power greater than ourselves" and "God as we understood Him" (p. 59).

2603a2a4b7dd.t: <0>"Doorknob"</0> appears only once, in a story in <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1>, where it means an actual door handle.

d945ffc5b75a.t: <0>"Light bulbs and Third Avenue buses."</0> <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) says the concept of a Higher Power held by some early A.A.s differed from the Oxford Groupers', who "were not prepared to accept light bulbs and Third Avenue buses" as examples of "God as I understand Him" (<2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2>, 1980). It names no one and says no more. The same passage, on the next page, adds that A.A.s were coming to let newer members find a concept of a Higher Power "in their own time and manner" (<3>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</3>, 1980).

2bba29b6e0c6.t: <0>The group.</0> In "The Vicious Cycle" (Part I), a man who found the Fellowship in January 1938, drank again that June, and came back sober on June 16, 1938 (pp. 228–229), writes that for a long time "the only Higher Power I could concede was the power of the group," and that it was "at least a beginning" (p. 229). In "Student of Life" (Part II), a later member, speaking at a meeting, saw understanding and love in the faces in the room: "Today I believe I saw my Higher Power for the first time in those faces." (p. 326). In "Tightrope" (Part II), another later member came to trust the A.A. group and the Fellowship's ideals "as a manifestation of a Power greater than myself" (p. 367). These are members' own experiences. The program text itself never names the group.

ab8b75446ff3.t: Chapter 4, "We Agnostics" (pp. 44–57), is written for this reader. Read in order: - About half the first members had thought they were atheists or agnostics (p. 44). - As soon as they were willing to believe in a Power greater than themselves, they "commenced to get results," even though none of them could fully define or understand "that Power, which is God" (p. 46). - They found they "did not need to consider another's conception of God" (p. 46). Their own, "however inadequate," was enough to begin (p. 46). The examples they give are a "Creative Intelligence, a Spirit of the Universe underlying the totality of things" (p. 46). - "When, therefore, we speak to you of God, we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47). The writers add that they later came to accept "many things which then seemed entirely out of reach" (p. 47). The starting idea is a beginning, not a fixed point. - The one question to ask yourself is whether you believe, or are even willing to believe, "that there is a Power greater than myself" (p. 47). - The personal stories show "a wide variation" in how each writer conceives of that Power, and the book says these are questions "for each individual to settle for himself" (p. 50).

3703b810fd26.t: The same chapter goes on to press the case for God. Crushed by a crisis they couldn't put off or evade, they had to face "the proposition that either God is everything or else He is nothing" (p. 53). They also write that "deep down in every man, woman, and child, is the fundamental idea of God" (p. 55). The chapter starts a reader wherever he is, and it plainly expects him to move toward God.

4ffded7bdc4c.t: Bill's own story shows the same thing (pp. 10–12). He could accept "Creative Intelligence, Universal Mind or Spirit of Nature" but not a personal God, until his friend asked, "Why don't you choose your own conception of God?" (p. 12). After that, being willing to believe in a Power greater than himself was all he needed to make his beginning (p. 12).

f6a83046ca35.t: In Chapter 7 the instruction for the helper is plain. If the man is agnostic or an atheist, make it clear he doesn't have to agree with your idea of God: "He can choose any conception he likes, provided it makes sense to him" (p. 93). Two conditions follow in the same paragraph: "The main thing is that he be willing to believe in a Power greater than himself and that he live by spiritual principles" (p. 93).

16aa54b7c333.t: Appendix II, added in 1955, says most members find an inner resource "which they presently identify with their own conception of a Power greater than themselves" (pp. 567–568). Any alcoholic capable of honestly facing his problems can recover, "provided he does not close his mind to all spiritual concepts" (p. 568).

3e8fa2b2ee66.t: Where "God as we understood Him" came from

a6716e6f71f8.t: <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) tells how the wording got into the Steps just before the manuscript was finished. After long arguments with members of little or no faith, the writers described God in Step Two as "a Power greater than ourselves" and added "God as we understood Him" to Steps Three and Eleven. Bill's summary: "God was certainly there in our Steps, but He was now expressed in terms that anybody—anybody at all—could accept and try" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957).

8f98cb88b0c9.t: The writer of "The Vicious Cycle," the man whose Higher Power was the group, says his one contribution to the book was insisting that the word God be qualified with "as we understand Him," "for that was the only way I could accept spirituality" (p. 229).

99aa573e6c94.t: The book never lists acceptable or unacceptable ideas of God. It never mentions an object, and the program text never mentions the group. What it does say: - The idea is yours, and it has to make sense to you (pp. 47, 93). - It is an idea of "a Power greater than" yourself (pp. 47, 93). Every example the writers give is of that kind: a Creative Intelligence, a Spirit of the Universe (p. 46). - It's a starting point that grows (p. 47), and the writers' own word for the Power is God (p. 46).

f283800eff82.t: Whether a doorknob or the group fits those words, the book leaves to the reader. A page that says the Big Book allows "anything" goes further than the text, and so does a page that says it forbids any particular idea.

c2dc1d70e6f9.t: See also: <0>Does Step 12 require believing in God a certain way?</0> and <1>Do I have to be religious to work the Steps?</1>

319a5f5afe05.t: Does the Big Book say you have to "hit bottom"? | Recovery Starts

3107c48b64df.t: The phrases "hit bottom" and "rock bottom" are not in the Big Book's 1939 program text, pages 1 to 164. "Hit bottom" appears in personal stories and in…

88ca37f81a77.t: Does the Big Book say you have to "hit bottom"?

279391d77069.t: The phrases "hit bottom" and "rock bottom" are not in the Big Book's 1939 program text, pages 1 to 164. "Hit bottom" appears in personal stories and in today's introduction to Part II, which says its writers "didn't wait to hit bottom" (p. 279).

e5d221fb4c99.t: The 1939 text never says you must lose everything. What it does insist on is the admission behind the phrase: that you "fully concede to our innermost selves" you're an alcoholic (p. 30). It says most alcoholics "have to be pretty badly mangled" before they start to solve their problems (p. 43), and its own example, Fred, had felt "only the first nip of the wringer" (p. 43).

acb25e563268.t: Bill W. wrote in 1957 that newcomers did have to "hit bottom emotionally," but not every possible bottom. In the early 1940s A.A. began "raising the bottom" for milder cases (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957).

20afbb31950c.t: All our sources were searched for "hit bottom," "hitting bottom," "rock bottom," "raise the bottom," "high bottom," "low bottom" and "bottom" alone.

5b17f3f7e6eb.t: In the program text (pp. 1–164), "bottom" turns up only in other senses: Langley's flying machine at "the bottom of the Potomac River" (p. 51), and thanking God "from the bottom of our heart" (p. 75).

80767a9f3c90.t: In the personal stories (fourth edition): - "Alcoholic Anonymous Number Three" (Part I), set in 1935: "I was willing to admit to myself that I had hit bottom" (p. 187). - The introduction to Part II, "They Stopped in Time," describes members who had seldom lost health, business, family or friends (p. 279). Its summary in their words: "We didn't wait to hit bottom because, thank God, we could see the bottom" (p. 279). - Other stories use it in their own ways: "Ninety days sober cleared my thinking enough to make me realize I'd hit bottom" (p. 314); a member told another, "You hit bottom when you stop digging" (p. 325); "That point is different for everyone" (p. 425).

64671dfee3aa.t: <0>The admission is required.</0> "We learned that we had to fully concede to our innermost selves that we were alcoholics. This is the first step in recovery" (p. 30). The delusion that we're like other people "has to be smashed" (p. 30).

9b53bdd70c23.t: <0>How you get there isn't fixed.</0> The book doesn't diagnose anyone: "We do not like to pronounce any individual as alcoholic, but you can quickly diagnose yourself" (p. 31). It suggests trying some controlled drinking (pp. 31–32), or trying to stay off liquor for a year (p. 34).

c177cc01d30e.t: <0>Many have to suffer first, but the book's own example didn't lose much.</0> Fred, the accountant in Chapter 3, had a fine home, a good income and a happy family. He was in hospital for the first time with a bad case of the jitters (p. 39). After one more spree he conceded he was licked, and recovered (pp. 40–43). The book's comment: "He had felt only the first nip of the wringer. Most alcoholics have to be pretty badly mangled before they really commence to solve their problems" (p. 43).

345bda87296b.t: <0>The helper works with hopelessness, and sometimes has to wait.</0> Chapter 7 tells a member to find drinkers who want to stop (pp. 89–90) and to talk about the hopelessness of alcoholism from his own experience (p. 92). "The more hopeless he feels, the better" (p. 94). If a man isn't interested, you may have to drop him "until he changes his mind. This he may do after he gets hurt some more" (p. 95). Left alone, he "may soon become convinced that he cannot recover by himself" (p. 96).

e1612610e656.t: <0>Young people are warned, not written off.</0> Several of the early members were thirty or younger and "found themselves as helpless as those who had been drinking twenty years" (p. 33). The book says it sees potential alcoholics among the young, "But try and get them to see it!" (p. 34).

911c6be163af.t: So the 1939 text expects an alcoholic to reach a point of real defeat about his drinking. It doesn't call that a "bottom," it doesn't set a level of loss, and it shows a man who got there early.

cbcc2e711205.t: <0>Bill W., 1957.</0> Writing about the years 1941–1945, Bill says A.A. began to succeed "with milder alcoholics and even some potential alcoholics" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). His account: - "Of course it was necessary for these types of newcomers to hit bottom emotionally" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957). - "But we found they did not have to hit every possible bottom there was in order to admit that they were licked" (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957). - A.A. developed "a conscious technique of 'raising the bottom' and hitting them with it" (<4>A.A. Comes of Age</4>, 1957). When a mild case became convinced he already had the main symptoms of alcoholism, that was usually enough.

e9815398ed1c.t: <0>Dr. Harry Tiebout, 1955.</0> The psychiatrist told A.A.'s St. Louis convention that he first heard from Bill and the early members "of the need to hit bottom" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957), and came to see hitting bottom as the point where an alcoholic stops fighting and surrenders. He called the change in emphasis, from hitting bottom to surrender and ego reduction, something he came to over his first five or six years with A.A. (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957).

a442768afc72.t: <0>Pass It On (1984)</0> says that in the early New York days, around 1939–40, Bill and Hank believed a drunk had to be at "absolute rock bottom physically, spiritually, and financially" (<1>Pass It On</1>, 1984), and turned away prospects who still had jobs and families. The same passage says the newcomer still had to want to stop drinking, and that they soon learned to stop predicting who would recover.

0fe853bb8884.t: The Big Book itself took in the change in 1955: the second edition divided the stories into the three parts used now (Preface, p. xii), and Part II, "They Stopped in Time," is for members who came before serious harm was done (p. 279).
