747d13eb813a.t: What is a home group, and how do the Traditions guide it? | Recovery Starts

00d4bd304640.t: "Home group" isn't a phrase the Big Book's program, the 1946 Long Form or Bill W.'s 1946–47 essays use. It shows up in later writing: P-16 (2018)…

ef221a365926.t: What is a home group, and how do the Traditions guide it?

cc649449e967.t: "Home group" isn't a phrase the Big Book's program, the 1946 Long Form or Bill W.'s 1946–47 essays use. It shows up in later writing: P-16 (2018) describes the home group as the one group a member belongs to, does service in and votes in.

947470105cbc.t: What the Long Form does define is the A.A. group itself: any two or three alcoholics gathered for sobriety, with no other affiliation (p. 563), "a spiritual entity" with one primary purpose, carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers (p. 563).

89e036e24298.t: Every Tradition guides a group: its own conscience decides its affairs (p. 563), it pays its own way (p. 564), it keeps the least possible organization with rotating leaders (p. 565), and it puts its purpose ahead of anyone's personality.

cdecd91de62f.t: Where the phrase is, and isn't

e2a9a8abdba5.t: Searching every text in our sources, the phrase doesn't appear in the Big Book's first 164 pages, its forewords or appendices, in the Long Form, in P-17's essays (1946–47 and 1955), in P-43 (1971) or in <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957). It appears in a few of the Big Book's later personal stories (Parts II and III), in P-16, <1>The A.A. Group</1> (© 2018), and in the current <2>A.A. Service Manual</2>. So the home group as a defined idea comes later than the Traditions. The <3>group</3>, though, is what the Traditions are about.

64a40868daf0.t: What the Long Form says a group is (1946)

98ae0f3205a3.t: <0>Who can form one.</0> "Any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation" (p. 563). Membership can't depend "upon money or conformity," and a group "may refuse none who wish to recover" (p. 563).

866bd27e4227.t: <0>What it's for.</0> Each group "ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose — that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers" (p. 563).

56f381ec7f6b.t: <0>Who it answers to.</0> In its own affairs, only "its own conscience" (p. 563), with the ultimate authority for its group purpose being a loving God as He may express Himself in the group conscience (p. 563). It consults neighbouring groups when its plans affect them (p. 563).

595922e5aff2.t: <0>How it's paid for.</0> By its own members' voluntary contributions (p. 564), and it shouldn't build up money beyond prudent reserves for no A.A. purpose (p. 564).

43c6fd0ebd04.t: <0>How it's run.</0> With "the least possible organization," and rotating leadership is best (p. 565); a small group may elect a secretary, a larger one a rotating committee (p. 565). Its leaders "do not govern" (p. 565).

48072cecf3c5.t: <0>What it must not do.</0> Go into business, or let cooperation turn into affiliation or endorsement (p. 564), or express views on outside controversial issues (p. 565).

66cff83cde60.t: Bill W. described the same group from experience in 1947: most groups preferred rotating committees, and each committee "carries out what it believes to be the wishes of its group" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38).

8a2f6e8742e9.t: What P-16 says a home group is (2018, dated)

880cbcc4c70c.t: Most members have found it important to belong to one group, "that they call their 'home group'" (P-16, 2018, p. 15), where they take on service and try to keep up friendships.

81bd8769508f.t: Membership brings "the right to vote on issues that might affect the group and might also affect A.A. as a whole" (P-16, 2018, p. 15). Each member has one vote, ideally voiced through the home group (P-16, pp. 15–16).

d357f738012c.t: In the home group members learn, through the group's workings, how to place principles before personalities "in the interest of carrying the A.A. message" (P-16, 2018, p. 16).

3f3abda651ad.t: Joining needs no application: "Just as we are members of A.A. if we say we are, so are we members of a group if we say we are" (P-16, 2018, p. 13).

f8d84d4d4c45.t: P-16 also separates a <0>group</0> from a <1>meeting</1>. A group continues to exist outside meeting hours, "ready to provide Twelfth Step help when needed" (P-16, 2018, p. 13).

0f1c3f1c38f2.t: That last point connects the home group back to the Long Form's purpose. A group is defined by what it does for the alcoholic who still suffers, not by the hour it meets.

44ad0b39cdc6.t: Related: <0>What is a group business meeting for?</0> · <1>Tradition Five: what is a group's one purpose?</1> · <2>What is the only requirement for membership?</2>

dac7646be492.t: How did A.A. grow from two people? | Recovery Starts

ed9733272c36.t: By going out and finding more alcoholics. After Bill W. and Dr. Bob met in Akron in 1935, the two of them phoned a hospital and asked for a prospect (p.…

b063d0666d88.t: How did A.A. grow from two people?

9f6d2121ca4c.t: By going out and finding more alcoholics. After Bill W. and Dr. Bob met in Akron in 1935, the two of them phoned a hospital and asked for a prospect (p. 156). That man became the third member, and the three went looking for a fourth (p. 158).

d8f37104e469.t: Each person who recovered did the same for the next. The Big Book, written in 1939, describes about a hundred people reached this way (p. xiii).

7a6ca76656f1.t: Dr. Bob, speaking in 1948, gave the same account: "We immediately started to look around for prospects."

bc48c35c84dc.t: There was no advertising and no program to join. The fellowship was what grew up around people rescuing drunks.

0033a6a1467b.t: Chapter 11, "A Vision for You," tells the story without names; footnotes added in later editions identify the people.

323838d8bd45.t: <0>One man, alone and shaky.</0> In 1935 a man sober "but a few months" (p. 154) was stranded in a strange city after a business failure. Tempted by a hotel bar, he thought of "those other alcoholics" (p. 154) and phoned a clergyman to find one (pp. 154–155). That led him to Dr. Bob (p. 155 footnote).

0dd1a2e6b7f2.t: <0>The second.</0> Dr. Bob had one more binge, then set out to face the people he feared and has not had a drink since (pp. 155–156).

a90f522c73b6.t: <0>The third, found on purpose.</0> "Both saw that they must keep spiritually active" (p. 156). They called a hospital's head nurse and asked for "a first class alcoholic prospect" (p. 156): a lawyer who had been in eight times in six months and was strapped to his bed. By the third day he had given his life to God's care; he walked out a free man in June 1935 and never drank again (p. 158).

0e657d4a7afb.t: <0>The fourth.</0> "So, you see, there were three alcoholics in that town, who now felt they had to give to others what they had found, or be sunk" (p. 158). "After several failures to find others, a fourth turned up" (p. 158).

1f02dbe796c5.t: <0>Then more.</0> "A year and six months later these three had succeeded with seven more" (p. 159). They began to meet one night a week, so new people had a time and place to bring their problems (pp. 159–160). By 1939 the Akron meeting drew "sixty or eighty as a rule" (p. 161), with something similar happening in an eastern city and in "Little clusters of twos and threes and fives" elsewhere (p. 162).

6f2d4ea34681.t: The book expected this to go on the same way: readers "will approach still other sick ones" (p. 153), and one member alone in a new city, working with a doctor and a hospital, would soon have "friends galore" (p. 163). The 1939 Foreword counts "more than one hundred men and women who have recovered" (p. xiii).

62a7d027e290.t: Dr. Bob's account (a talk given in 1948)

95ef237adac8.t: Dr. Bob's last major talk, given in Detroit in December 1948, was printed in the Grapevine in 1973 and is now in the pamphlet <0>The Co-Founders of Alcoholics Anonymous</0> (P-53, pp. 9–20).

27d7b4fc568d.t: He says that before Akron, Bill "had not created a single convert, not one" (P-53). He himself had done everything the Oxford Group asked and still got drunk every night. What they hadn't told him was the thing Bill did that Sunday, "attempt to be helpful to somebody else" (P-53). After his last drink on June 10, 1935: "We immediately started to look around for prospects" (P-53). The first was Bill D., then "three prospects dumped in our laps almost simultaneously" (P-53). Dr. Bob talked with men in hospital beds for hours at a time. Later, "As we grew, we began to get offshoots, one in Cleveland" (P-53).

f8efa5d85942.t: <0>Foreword to the Second Edition (1955).</0> After meeting Dr. Bob, the two men "set to work almost frantically upon alcoholics arriving in the ward of the Akron City Hospital" (p. xvii). When Bill went back to New York in the fall of 1935, a second group "promptly took shape" there, and a third started in Cleveland in 1937 (p. xvii); membership was about 100 when the book came out in the spring of 1939 (p. xvii). Then magazine articles brought floods of letters, and by the end of 1941 there were about 8,000 members (p. xviii).

3d6650268f9d.t: <0><1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957).</0> Bill recalls the New York side: meetings in his Brooklyn parlor and trips to the Calvary Mission and Towns Hospital "in the feverish search for more prospects" (<2>Comes of Age</2>, 1957). In November 1937 he and Dr. Bob counted results in Dr. Bob's living room and figured "upwards of forty alcoholics were staying bone dry" (<3>Comes of Age</3>, 1957). What struck them was a chain: "one alcoholic carrying the good news to the next" (<4>Comes of Age</4>, 1957).

c7a3c8e7a399.t: In the earliest sources the fellowship isn't the starting point. The rescue is. Two men had to find a third, or there would never have been more than two, and every member after that was found the same way: a drunk in a hospital or a home, reached by someone who had recovered. The meetings came afterwards, as a place for the people being found. That is the work Chapter 7 describes (pp. 89–103).

59779e0784bb.t: How did Bill W. and Dr. Bob meet? | Recovery Starts

f97bed7326d9.t: In 1935 Bill W., a New York stockbroker sober about six months, was stuck in Akron, Ohio, after a business deal collapsed. Afraid he would drink, he went…

5c8336263373.t: How did Bill W. and Dr. Bob meet?

125739b03bd8.t: In 1935 Bill W., a New York stockbroker sober about six months, was stuck in Akron, Ohio, after a business deal collapsed. Afraid he would drink, he went looking for another alcoholic to help.

0bd760af920a.t: A call to a clergyman led, through a chain of people, to Dr. Bob, an Akron surgeon who was still drinking. They met on a Sunday afternoon and talked for about six hours.

13c04b98e841.t: Dr. Bob said what reached him was a man who knew alcoholism from his own experience. Bill said he needed Dr. Bob as much as Dr. Bob needed him.

eade65bf66a3.t: The Big Book's 1939 text tells the story without names. The names (the Mayflower Hotel, Rev. Walter Tunks, Henrietta Seiberling) come from later accounts, in 1948 and 1957.

9874ea6fe505.t: The 1939 account: Chapter 11, "A Vision for You"

211f93e1746e.t: The Big Book's own first telling is in Chapter 11, written in 1939 (p. 161 note). It names nobody. One of the members, it says, made a business trip in 1935 to "a certain western city" that ended in a lawsuit and left him discouraged, nearly broke and alone (pp. 153–154). Physically weak and only a few months sober, "He wanted so much to talk with someone, but whom?" (p. 154).

a2afc47dcb82.t: In a hotel lobby he stood between a bar at one end and a church directory at the other (p. 154). He was tempted to sit in the bar with a ginger ale, and then saw the danger: "Again it was the old, insidious insanity—that first drink." (p. 154). What turned him around was thinking of his family and of "the men who would die because they would not know how to get well" (p. 154). "Selecting a church at random from the directory, he stepped into a booth and lifted the receiver." (p. 155).

07e5080a8348.t: The call to the clergyman led him to a local man, once able and respected, now near the bottom (p. 155). A footnote in today's edition says this was Bill's first visit with Dr. Bob (p. 155). The man agreed he could not stop on will power and that he needed a spiritual experience, but at first he would not pay the price of admitting his drinking to the people he depended on for a living (p. 155). He invited Bill to his home, went on one more bender, and then went round to the people he had hurt and told them the truth (pp. 155–156).

89286b1d6749.t: Dr. Bob's own account (his story, written 1939)

6cc0797156ff.t: "Doctor Bob's Nightmare," the first personal story in the book, was written while he was about four years sober (p. 180). A lady telephoned his wife on a Saturday, the day before Mother's Day, asking them to come and meet a friend of hers who might help him; he had come home drunk that day (p. 179). They went the next day, and he made his wife promise they would stay fifteen minutes (p. 179). "We entered her house at exactly five o'clock and it was eleven fifteen when we left." (p. 179).

30c2540bb312.t: He stopped drinking for about three weeks, then drank heavily at a medical meeting in Atlantic City; his new friend brought him home, and his last drink was on June 10, 1935 (pp. 179–180).

c612145b1cd1.t: Why did it work this time, when reading and talking to experts hadn't? Because he "was the first living human with whom I had ever talked, who knew what he was talking about in regard to alcoholism from actual experience" (p. 180). "In other words, he talked my language." (p. 180).

eb368b3148f5.t: The 1955 account: Foreword to the Second Edition

b49ce740609e.t: The 1955 foreword gives the outline, still without names. The broker had been relieved of his drink obsession about six months before, after meeting an alcoholic friend connected to the Oxford Groups (pp. xv–xvi). He had worked with many alcoholics but sobered none (p. xvi). Stranded in Akron after a failed business venture and afraid of drinking, "He suddenly realized that in order to save himself he must carry his message to another alcoholic." (p. xvi). The foreword dates the meeting "in June 1935, during a talk between a New York stockbroker and an Akron physician" (p. xv).

e1191c74ce95.t: <0>Dr. Bob, 1948.</0> His last major talk, recorded in Detroit in December 1948 and first printed in the Grapevine in 1973, is reprinted in P-53 (P-53). There he names the Mayflower Hotel, says Bill saw the name of Rev. Walter Tunks on a board in the lobby and called him, and that Tunks gave him a list of nine or ten Oxford Group people (P-53). Near the end of the list Bill came to Henrietta Seiberling, who had him to lunch and then called Dr. Bob's wife, Anne; because Dr. Bob was too drunk that day, they came the next day, Sunday and Mother's Day (P-53). He also names what was new to him: the Oxford Group had told him to read, pray and attend meetings, "But the one thing that they hadn't told me was the one thing that Bill did that Sunday — attempt to be helpful to somebody else." (P-53).

62f248d1f9c6.t: <0>Bill W., 1957.</0> In <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> Bill says he had gone to Akron in May 1935 in a proxy fight over a small machine-tool company, lost, and was left at the Mayflower with about ten dollars (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Pacing the lobby on Mother's Day eve, he realized for the first time that helping others had kept him sober: "You need another alcoholic just as much as he needs you!" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He picked a minister from the church directory, got a list of about ten names, and reached Henrietta Seiberling at the gatehouse of the Seiberling estate (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Dr. Bob and Anne came the next afternoon at five, and the two men talked alone until eleven (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill says he followed Dr. Silkworth's advice to stop preaching and talk about the medical facts and his own case, and that the talk was mutual: "I knew that I needed this alcoholic as much as he needed me." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

9d42951c157b.t: <0>The month.</0> The 1955 foreword says June 1935 (p. xv). Dr. Bob's 1939 story puts the meeting on Mother's Day, at least three weeks before his last drink on June 10 (pp. 179–180), and P-53's biographies (pamphlet © 2017) and <1>Comes of Age</1> (1957) say May 1935. Our sources don't explain the difference.

4bf7962e3b09.t: <0>The hour they left.</0> Dr. Bob, in 1939 and in 1948, says 11:15 (p. 179; P-53); Bill in 1957 says they talked until eleven (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

84f67d41c554.t: <0>Who arranged it.</0> The 1939 texts say only "a clergyman" (p. 155) and "a lady" (p. 179). The names are from 1948 and 1957.

7c669599ac1d.t: "Doctor Bob's Nightmare" (pp. 171–181), in Personal Stories Part I: <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_personalstories_partI.pdf</0>

346e0a010a09.t: P-53, <0>The Co-Founders of Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, free from A.A.: <1>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/literature/P-53_0725.pdf</1>

d9ba9121c371.t: Big Book page numbers are from the fourth edition (2001). The footnote on p. 155 identifying Dr. Bob was added in a later edition; our copy doesn't say when.

e90c3c970bdf.t: How long did the first members take to work the Steps? | Recovery Starts

d427f062b3f8.t: The Big Book never gives a timetable. But its instructions keep saying to take each Step straight after the last, and the earliest accounts describe days…

2c23a56ea196.t: How long did the first members take to work the Steps?

f775bda7a394.t: The Big Book never gives a timetable. But its instructions keep saying to take each Step straight after the last, and the earliest accounts describe days and weeks, not months or years.

5a386e7e2ec1.t: The very first members couldn't have "worked the Twelve Steps." The Steps weren't written until late 1938. Before that, newcomers got a spoken program of about six steps (<0>Comes of Age</0>, p. 160).

f50da515f047.t: In the Big Book's own accounts, A.A. number three made his decision on his third day in hospital and walked out that afternoon (p. 158). A Chicago man in 1937 spent two or three weeks in Akron and then went through the whole program with Dr. Bob in one afternoon of three or four hours (pp. 262–263).

6419c62afb15.t: Some parts were never done quickly: amends were worked out slowly (p. 263), rebuilding a family took a long time (p. 83), and Steps Ten and Eleven are for life (p. 84).

43df876ce02b.t: What the instructions say about pace

0d9d82559494.t: Read in order, Chapters 5 and 6 keep moving straight from one Step to the next: - The Third Step decision "could have little permanent effect unless at once followed by a strenuous effort to face, and to be rid of, the things in ourselves which had been blocking us" (p. 64). That effort is the inventory. - For the Fifth Step: "When we decide who is to hear our story, we waste no time" (p. 75). Waiting is allowed only when no suitable person is available, and even then "we must not use this as a mere excuse to postpone" (p. 75). - After the Fifth Step, back at home, you take an hour to review your work and then go on to Steps Six and Seven (pp. 75–76). - Then, "Now we need more action" (p. 76): the amends of Steps Eight and Nine. Some can't be made right away, "But we don't delay if it can be avoided" (p. 83).

07bbf1284992.t: Chapter 7 assumes the same speed. By the helper's second visit, the newcomer may have read the book and be "prepared to go through with the Twelve Steps" (p. 96). Chapter 8, written to wives, says that a book or another alcoholic "has accomplished in a few weeks that for which we struggled for years" (p. 118).

bcad4f943f64.t: What the first members actually did

cfd9148179ea.t: <0>Bill W.</0> did it in the hospital. There he offered himself to God and faced his wrongs, and when his friend visited they made a list of the people he had hurt (p. 13). A.A. Comes of Age (1957) dates the hospital stay to December 1934 (<1>Comes of Age</1>, p. 13).

b3257167613f.t: <0>Dr. Bob</0> had his last drink on June 10, 1935 (p. 180). Chapter 11 tells how he set out "one morning" to tell the people he feared and make the rounds of those he had hurt, coming home at midnight (p. 156). The Big Book doesn't say how soon after his last drink that was. <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) says he started making restitution on the same day (ch. VIII).

fef064c2d8d0.t: <0>A.A. number three, Bill D.,</0> met Bill W. and Dr. Bob in Akron City Hospital in June 1935. Chapter 11's account: "On the third day the lawyer gave his life to the care and direction of his Creator," and that afternoon he walked out of the hospital (p. 158). In his own story he puts his decision "in the next two or three days" (p. 189), and says they talked over his failings and "made a sort of an inventory" (p. 190).

e9505d05d0f8.t: <0>The writer of "He Sold Himself Short,"</0> a Chicago man, first heard of the Akron group from his father in January 1937, turned it down, and came to Akron "Several months later" (p. 260); he dates that visit almost a year before the summer of 1938 (p. 265). Eight or nine members visited him before he was allowed to a meeting (p. 262). He stayed two or three weeks, and on the day before he went home Dr. Bob spent "three or four hours formally going through the Six-Step program as it was at that time" (pp. 262–263). That afternoon covered deflation, dependence on a Higher Power, inventory, confession, and a list for restitution. The restitution itself he would work out "slowly" (p. 263).

df628b7a9486.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) describes Akron in those years. Newcomers spent five to eight days in hospital, made a "surrender" on their knees before they could attend a meeting, and "many of the steps—involving inventory, admission of character defects, and making restitution—were taken within a matter of days" (<1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1>, ch. VIII). It was written forty-five years later from interviews, so it's dated and used with care. Its account of Akron fits the Big Book's stories above, but its claim about Dr. Bob's restitution has no support in the Big Book itself.

569ffee54905.t: There were no Twelve Steps yet

0145039fb5d3.t: Bill W. tells in <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> how the Twelve Steps were written for the Big Book. Until then members passed on "the word-of-mouth program" of about six steps (<1>Comes of Age</1>, p. 160): admit you're licked, take a moral inventory, confess, make restitution, help other alcoholics, and pray for the power to do these things. "This was the substance of what, by the fall of 1938, we were telling newcomers" (<2>Comes of Age</2>, p. 160). The twelve were drafted after that, in about half an hour by Bill's account (<3>Comes of Age</3>, pp. 160–161). So for the 1935–38 pioneers the question is how long they took over that shorter program, and the answer is days to weeks.

a408df2e4368.t: The book is just as clear that some things take a lifetime: - Rebuilding a family: "there is a long period of reconstruction ahead" (p. 83). - Step Ten: "This is not an overnight matter. It should continue for our lifetime" (p. 84). - The spiritual change itself is usually gradual, the "educational variety," and "What often takes place in a few months could seldom have been accomplished by years of self-discipline" (p. 567). (Appendix II was added after the first printing; see the sources.)

1051a99bc232.t: The Big Book never records how long anyone took from the first Step to the twelfth, and it never sets a pace. The accounts here are a handful of stories about a few early members, written later. What they show is a pattern of taking the actions at once, within days or weeks, while the effects and the amends went on for years. Anyone who says the first members took a year, or took one weekend, is going beyond what these pages say.

7b421b4c0b33.t: How were the Twelve Steps written? | Recovery Starts

c8cd1472d951.t: Bill W. wrote the Twelve Steps in 1938, while drafting the Big Book's fifth chapter. Both co-founders date them to 1938; Dr. Bob said he had nothing to do…

cb1bd8c59b59.t: How were the Twelve Steps written?

ade81d7d8756.t: Bill W. wrote the Twelve Steps in 1938, while drafting the Big Book's fifth chapter. Both co-founders date them to 1938; Dr. Bob said he had nothing to do with the writing, though he thought their long talks in 1935 must have influenced them.

3094bbd38999.t: In Bill's 1957 account he wrote the first draft one night in bed at 182 Clinton Street, Brooklyn, in about half an hour, breaking the six-step word-of-mouth program into smaller pieces. They came to twelve.

97da30561d22.t: The draft was argued over for months. The words "a Power greater than ourselves," "God as we understood Him," and the line calling the Steps "suggested as a program of recovery" were compromises made with the atheist and agnostic members; "on our knees" was taken out of Step Seven. Bill says he doesn't know who first proposed the compromise words.

fa59d44e469f.t: The first draft itself is lost. The Big Book (1939) prints the finished Steps on pp. 59–60.

bd47f00a4816.t: The Steps appear in Chapter 5, "How It Works," introduced as "the steps we took, which are suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59). Right after them the book says no member has kept to them perfectly: "We are not saints." (p. 60). "The principles we have set down are guides to progress." (p. 60). The book doesn't tell how the Steps were written; that comes from later accounts. See <0>Where are the Twelve Steps in the Big Book?</0> and <1>Are the Steps rules or suggestions?</1>

bdae077c156e.t: <0>Dr. Bob, 1948</0> (his last major talk, printed in P-53): "It wasn't until 1938 that the teachings and efforts and studies that had been going on were crystallized in the form of the Twelve Steps." (P-53). "I didn't write the Twelve Steps. I had nothing to do with the writing of them." (P-53). But he and Bill had sat up night after night at his kitchen table in the summer of 1935, and he found it hard to believe nothing said there influenced the Steps (P-53).

eaeb0217387b.t: <0>Bill W., 1969</0> (his last major talk, in P-53): the Steps "were written in 1938" (P-53).

c51c3691c9ee.t: Bill's account of the night (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)

531179e61a93.t: By the time Bill reached the fifth chapter he had drafted his own story and three more chapters, and the arguments over them had worn him out (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He lay in bed at 182 Clinton Street with pencil and scratch pad (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The program they had been passing on by word of mouth came to six steps (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; see <0>What were the "six steps" used before the Twelve Steps?</0>), and he wanted something more explicit for distant readers, with no loophole "through which the rationalizing alcoholic could wiggle out" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

ef0ea83f9a80.t: "I set out to draft more than six steps; how many more I did not know." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He asked for guidance, and "It took perhaps half an hour." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). When he numbered them, "They added up to twelve." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), a number he connected with the twelve apostles (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

63dff10d7954.t: That night two callers came, his friend Howard A. and a newcomer. (<0>Pass It On</0>, 1984, names the friend Horace C. and says Bill used "Howard A." in 1957 so as not to offend him; Pass It On, 1984.) They objected: "You've got too much God in these steps; you will scare people away." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and they balked at getting drunks "on their knees" to ask for their shortcomings to be removed (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

2820728eaf45.t: In Akron, Bill says, members liked the new steps (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In New York there were three camps (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957): - <0>Conservatives</0>, led by Fitz M., wanted a Christian book in Biblical language. - <1>Liberals</1>, the largest group, had no objection to "God" but would have nothing to do with any other theological doctrine. - <2>Radicals</2>, the atheists and agnostics led by Henry P. and Jim B., at first wanted "God" taken out entirely.

faaed87d8851.t: Bill asked to be the final judge of what the book said, and most agreed (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He refused to change a word of the Steps until, just before the manuscript was finished, a meeting in Henry's office in Newark arrived at a compromise; "Who first suggested the actual compromise words I do not know" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The changes (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957): - Step Two: God described as "a Power greater than ourselves." - Steps Three and Eleven: the words "God as we understood Him" inserted. - Step Seven: "on our knees" deleted. - A lead-in sentence calling the Steps suggestions: "A.A.'s Twelve Steps were to be suggestions only." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)

4aed964ccc9c.t: Bill called this "the great contribution of our atheists and agnostics" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Earlier in the same book he gives a shorter version: the expression "God as we understood Him" came out of the debate between Fitz on one side and Henry and Jimmy on the other (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

88933a47ad80.t: <0>Pass It On (1984)</0> says Bill began the book in March or April of 1938, and that Ruth Hock, who typed it, first saw an outline of the Steps in his notes (Pass It On, 1984). It says the first draft "has been lost" and prints only "an approximate reconstruction" (Pass It On, 1984), in which, for example, Step Two read that God could restore us to sanity and Step Seven had "on our knees" (Pass It On, 1984). It adds Ruth's memory of the debate: Fitz wanted "God" all the way, Bill was in the middle, Hank wanted very little, and the result was "God as we understood Him" (Pass It On, 1984). The original drafts were probably thrown out when the office moved in 1940 (Pass It On, 1984).

59a7981f0b59.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (1980)</0> quotes an Akron member, Bob E.: in the first draft "people were to be on their knees when they surrendered. But the other drunks made Bill take it out." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). The same book doubts Bill's claim that Akron supported the Steps better than New York, saying "Bill might have been assuming that his part of the stove was warmer" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

673e27b5802e.t: <0>When in 1938.</0> Both co-founders say 1938 (P-53). Bill's 1957 account ties the night to the fifth chapter and says the six steps were what they told newcomers "by the fall of 1938" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); the "Landmarks" timeline in our later printing of that book lists "Twelve Steps written" under December 1938 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Our sources don't give an exact date.

d97b3fd175bc.t: <0>Who shaped "God as we understood Him."</0> Bill (1957) credits the debate and says he doesn't know who first suggested the words (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); Ruth Hock (in 1984) credits the same debate, with herself among those who wanted "very little" God (Pass It On, 1984).

97fce980044f.t: <0>The first draft's wording.</0> No copy survives in our sources; <1>Pass It On</1>'s version is labelled a reconstruction (Pass It On, 1984).

38da1a9217f1.t: Related: <0>What were the "six steps" used before the Twelve Steps?</0> · <1>Where are the Twelve Steps in the Big Book?</1> · <2>Are the Steps rules or suggestions?</2> · <3>Were the Traditions written with the Steps?</3>

9e478373a17a.t: How does the Big Book say to do Step 4? | Recovery Starts

fa10fb1b969c.t: Step 4 is "Made a searching and fearless moral inventory of ourselves." (p. 59) The Big Book explains how on pages 63 to 71, in Chapter 5.

8ae992db429d.t: How does the Big Book say to do Step 4?

dbfdd19cdd53.t: Step 4 is "Made a searching and fearless moral inventory of ourselves." (p. 59) The Big Book explains how on pages 63 to 71, in Chapter 5.

dc5158494afe.t: It's written down. The book looks at resentments first, then fears, then sex conduct, and in each it turns from what others did to where we were at fault.

aa0c80dcc9ce.t: The book's sample resentment list has three columns (p. 65). The fourth part, looking for our own mistakes, is described in the text that follows (p. 67), not drawn as a column.

597c0e5744f2.t: It's meant to be done promptly, right after the Third Step decision, and the list of people harmed that it produces becomes the Step Eight list (p. 76).

d790a79ee6f7.t: The book compares it to a business stocktaking: a fact-finding and fact-facing process to find "damaged or unsalable goods" and get rid of them "promptly and without regret" (p. 64). The point is to find the causes behind the drinking: "Our liquor was but a symptom" (p. 64). Being convinced that self was what had defeated them, they looked at its common forms (p. 64).

abb98853a127.t: "Resentment is the 'number one' offender" (p. 64). The method, in the book's order: - <0>Put it on paper.</0> List the people, institutions or principles you're angry with (p. 64). - <1>Ask why.</1> Usually it was found that self-esteem, pocketbook, ambitions or personal relationships, including sex, were "hurt or threatened" (pp. 64–65). - <2>Set the injury opposite each name.</2> The book's example (p. 65) has three columns: "I'm resentful at," "The Cause," and "Affects my." The word "fear" is written in beside several of the entries. - <3>Go back through your whole life.</3> "Nothing counted but thoroughness and honesty" (p. 65). - <4>Then look at it differently.</4> The book says concluding that others were wrong was as far as most people got, and it kept them sore (p. 66). Resentment, for the alcoholic, is fatal: it shuts us off "from the sunlight of the Spirit" (p. 66). So they came to see the people who wronged them as perhaps spiritually sick, and asked God to help them show those people the patience they'd give a sick friend (pp. 66–67). - <5>Find your own part.</5> Putting aside the other person's wrongs, they looked for their own mistakes: "Where had we been selfish, dishonest, self-seeking and frightened?" (p. 67) Even where it wasn't entirely their fault, they tried to disregard the other person. "The inventory was ours, not the other man's" (p. 67). They listed their faults in black and white (p. 67).

5bb612b3e84a.t: They noticed the word "fear" beside so many entries (p. 67), and so "We reviewed our fears thoroughly. We put them on paper" (p. 68), even where no resentment went with them. They asked why they had each one, and found that self-reliance had failed them (p. 68). They asked God to remove the fear and turn their attention to what He would have them be (p. 68).

3787524aac2a.t: The book says it wants to stay out of the controversy over sex and won't be "the arbiter of anyone's sex conduct" (p. 69). The inventory here is about one's own behaviour: Where had we been selfish, dishonest or inconsiderate? Whom had we hurt? What should we have done instead? (p. 69) "We got this all down on paper and looked at it" (p. 69). From it they shaped an ideal for the future, tested each relationship by whether it was selfish, and were willing to make amends where they'd done harm, provided they didn't cause more harm doing it (p. 69).

6578f7124992.t: The book's summary on page 70: if you've been thorough, you've written a lot. You've listed and analysed your resentments, begun to learn tolerance even toward enemies, and "listed the people we have hurt by our conduct" (p. 70). That list of people harmed is the one Step Eight uses: "We made it when we took inventory" (p. 76). The book doesn't describe a separate "harms inventory" with its own format.

e5cf3f05978d.t: Right away. The decision in Step Three "could have little permanent effect unless at once followed by" a strenuous effort to face what's been blocking us (p. 64). The next chapter then moves straight to Step Five (p. 72). The book says nothing about taking months over the inventory; it doesn't give a time either, beyond "at once."

669600b1773d.t: Chapter 5, "How It Works" (pp. 58–71), with the inventory on pages 63–71, free from A.A.: <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt5.pdf</0>

56e126e7725e.t: Chapter 6, "Into Action" (pp. 72–88), for what comes next: <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt6.pdf</0>

4049552a80e5.t: How does the Big Book say to make amends? | Recovery Starts

5f657dcad958.t: Steps 8 and 9 are explained in Chapter 6, "Into Action," pages 76 to 83. The list comes from the Fourth Step inventory; then "we go out to our fellows and…

cea15b981c06.t: How does the Big Book say to make amends?

a4ffe1d31239.t: Steps 8 and 9 are explained in Chapter 6, "Into Action," pages 76 to 83. The list comes from the Fourth Step inventory; then "we go out to our fellows and repair the damage done in the past" (p. 76).

298f4ae5c2f2.t: Go in person where you can, talk about your own faults and not theirs, and don't argue: "We are there to sweep off our side of the street" (p. 77).

adac5791d8d6.t: Be willing to pay the full cost yourself, but don't harm other people to clear your conscience. Get the consent of anyone your amends would involve (p. 80).

d27bb8adf6f0.t: At home, saying sorry isn't enough. The book asks for a long, patient change in how you live (pp. 82–83).

ff345034ec2a.t: Step 8: "Made a list of all persons we had harmed, and became willing to make amends to them all." Step 9: "Made direct amends to such people wherever possible, except when to do so would injure them or others." (p. 59)

9798a54c17e0.t: "We made it when we took inventory" (p. 76). The Fourth Step already listed the people we'd hurt (p. 70). Now the job is to "sweep away the debris" left by living on self-will (p. 76). If we haven't the will to do it, "we ask until it comes" (p. 76). The book reminds the reader of the agreement made at the start, to go to any lengths for victory over alcohol (p. 76).

78b74fdd1cde.t: <0>Lead with good will, not religion.</0> With some people we "need not, and probably should not" emphasize the spiritual side on the first approach (p. 76). Announcing that we've "gone religious" to someone still smarting from our injustice is "leading with the chin" (p. 77). He'll be more impressed by "a sincere desire to set right the wrong" (p. 77). This isn't an excuse to dodge the subject of God when it would help (p. 77).

d5fc587119a7.t: <0>The real purpose</0> isn't just tidying our lives; it is to fit ourselves "to be of maximum service to God and the people about us" (p. 77).

86056a012039.t: <0>Go to enemies too.</0> It's harder than going to a friend but more beneficial (p. 77). Go "in a helpful and forgiving spirit" (p. 77), admit the old ill feeling, express regret.

caf937a68d13.t: <0>Don't criticize or argue.</0> "His faults are not discussed. We stick to our own." (p. 78) Most of the time it goes well; if someone throws us out of his office, "We have made our demonstration, done our part" (p. 78).

7d0ea97375f5.t: Don't dodge creditors. Tell them what you're trying to do, don't hide the drinking, arrange the best deal you can and let them know you're sorry (p. 78). "We must lose our fear of creditors no matter how far we have to go" (p. 78), because fear of facing them can lead to drinking.

8ef9dbd1f7a4.t: When amends could cost you, or others

db03e855d941.t: The book is direct that amends can be costly. Facing a possible criminal offence or a debt that could cost a job, members asked for strength to do the right thing "no matter what the personal consequences may be" (p. 79): "We may lose our position or reputation or face jail, but we are willing" (p. 79).

98a20a41bf67.t: But other people are usually involved, so "we are not to be the hasty and foolish martyr" (p. 79) who sacrifices others to save himself. Its example: a man owed alimony and faced arrest. Walking into court would have been heroic, but in jail he could support neither family. So he wrote to his first wife, admitted his faults, sent a little money, and said he'd go to jail if she insisted (p. 79). The rule the book draws: "Before taking drastic action which might implicate other people we secure their consent" (p. 80). Then, if the drastic step is still called for, "we must not shrink" (p. 80). Another member, after consulting his wife and partner, cleared a rival he'd ruined by standing up in church and explaining (p. 80).

da75b01b5faa.t: <0>Infidelity.</0> If a wife doesn't know, should she be told? "Not always, we think" (p. 81). If she knows in a general way, admit the fault, but don't name the other person: "we have no right to involve another person" (p. 81). The writers add that they wish to "lay down no rule of any sort" (p. 81) and that some cases need more frankness; each couple decides (pp. 81–82).

23e0cbd42064.t: <0>Sobriety isn't enough.</0> A man who says sobriety is all he owes his family is like the farmer who comes out of his cyclone cellar, sees his house wrecked, and says the wind has stopped (p. 82). "A remorseful mumbling that we are sorry won't fill the bill at all" (p. 83). Sit down with the family, look at the past honestly, and don't criticize them (p. 83).

b36e63dd1b6a.t: <0>Don't preach at them.</0> Unless they want to, don't urge spiritual principles on your family: "Our behavior will convince them more than our words" (p. 83).

7967c92b277e.t: What can't be fully set right

ae3670f84b11.t: "There may be some wrongs we can never fully right" (p. 83). We don't worry about those if we can honestly say we'd right them if we could. People who can't be seen get "an honest letter" (p. 83). Some amends may have a valid reason to wait, but "we don't delay if it can be avoided" (p. 83). And the manner: sensible, tactful, considerate and humble "without being servile or scraping" (p. 83). "As God's people we stand on our feet; we don't crawl before anyone" (p. 83).

6db764029838.t: The promises that follow on pages 83–84 are tied to this part of the work: "If we are painstaking about this phase of our development" (p. 83). See <0>Where are "the Promises," and what do they promise?</0>

7430a11261c8.t: Do I have to say "I'm an alcoholic"? Is "Hi, I'm ___, and I'm an alcoholic" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

1b86a38d27e1.t: No, and no. The 1939 text asks for an admission made "to our innermost selves" (p. 30), not out loud at a meeting, and it describes no way of introducing…

e6178938942c.t: Do I have to say "I'm an alcoholic"? Is "Hi, I'm ___, and I'm an alcoholic" in the Big Book?

15c435d3802b.t: No, and no. The 1939 text asks for an admission made "to our innermost selves" (p. 30), not out loud at a meeting, and it describes no way of introducing yourself.

e873cfdea838.t: Bill W. wrote in 1946 that in most groups a newcomer "doesn't even have to admit he is an alcoholic" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). He can join on the suspicion that he may be one.

f0f074c07db8.t: The introduction "My name is ___, and I'm an alcoholic" turns up in the Big Book only in a few personal stories in Parts II and III of the fourth edition (2001), not in the 1939 text. <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) says Bill probably picked the custom up from the Oxford Group, and P-43 says groups differ in how it's done.

a940ef45a982.t: The book is firm about one thing: nobody should label another person an alcoholic. "Let him draw his own conclusion." (p. 92).

bec2de4a01c2.t: <0>An inner admission.</0> "We learned that we had to fully concede to our innermost selves that we were alcoholics." (p. 30). The book calls this the first step in recovery, and the concession is to oneself.

b8b9d4c426db.t: <0>Self-diagnosis.</0> "We do not like to pronounce any individual as alcoholic, but you can quickly diagnose yourself." (p. 31). See <1>How do I know if I'm an alcoholic?</1>

19410316f084.t: <0>No labeling by others.</0> When talking with a prospect, the member describes himself as an alcoholic (p. 91) but is told to "be careful not to brand him as an alcoholic" (p. 92). If the man insists he can still control his drinking, "tell him that possibly he can—if he is not too alcoholic" (p. 92).

d5d5b45c956b.t: <0>Step One</0> says "We admitted we were powerless over alcohol—that our lives had become unmanageable." (p. 59). The Step doesn't say to whom; Chapter 3's description of "the first step in recovery" (p. 30) is a concession to oneself.

93ed86af71be.t: Nowhere in pages 1–164 does the book describe members introducing themselves at a meeting, or require anyone to say anything there.

e367719e458c.t: The Long Form of Tradition Three says A.A.'s membership "ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism" (p. 563); the later short form (by 1950) asks only for a desire to stop drinking (p. 562). Neither asks for an admission. Bill's 1946 essay goes further: "Nowadays, in most groups, he doesn't even have to admit he is an alcoholic." (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). He can join "on the mere suspicion that he may be one" (same essay).

be5d68ee0106.t: <0>Personal stories in the fourth edition.</0> A search of the whole fourth-edition text finds the meeting introduction only in a few stories in Parts II and III, the sections that hold later members' stories: a newcomer who, because everyone around the table was saying they were alcoholics, said his name and "Hi, I'm an alcoholic" (p. 401); a "big clown" at a meeting shouting "My name is Frank, and I'm an alcoholic" (p. 414); a woman who, at her first meeting on her own, said "I am an alcoholic" after years of saying "I'm with him" at her father's meetings (p. 515). These are members' own experience, not the program text.

1462afaf0c8e.t: <0><1>Pass It On</1> (1984)</0> lists it among early customs: members introduced themselves with "My name is Bill W. I'm an alcoholic." (<2>Pass It On</2>, 1984). Bill probably got it from the Oxford Group meetings of the mid-1930s, where members in a circle said "My name is so-and-so" to identify themselves.

b69f8a24cf34.t: <0>P-43</0> (<1>The Twelve Traditions Illustrated</1>, © 1971, this printing updated 2023), on Tradition Four: in one part of the U.S. a speaker who begins "My name is Ann, and I am an alcoholic" gets respectful silence; in another everybody shouts "Hi, Ann!"; elsewhere she may use her full name. "In each neighborhood in every part of the world reached by A.A., the local group is free to work out its own customs." (P-43).

a06d75bc132e.t: Saying "I'm an alcoholic" at a meeting is a custom, with roots in the Oxford Group, that varies from place to place. The Big Book asks for something different and more private: an honest admission to yourself, reached by your own conclusion. A.A.'s membership statement asks only for a desire to stop drinking, and Bill's 1946 essay says that in most groups even the admission isn't required to join.

09643e222711.t: Is helping others selfish if it keeps me sober? | Recovery Starts

be09b566b3ce.t: The Big Book says openly that helping other alcoholics protects the helper's own sobriety (pp. 89, 94, 97). It doesn't hide that, and it never calls it…

57bb0eb57d31.t: Is helping others selfish if it keeps me sober?

f01787929e41.t: The Big Book says openly that helping other alcoholics protects the helper's own sobriety (pp. 89, 94, 97). It doesn't hide that, and it never calls it selfish.

6727f3d16f3c.t: It also expects that motive to be outgrown. Of the first members it says that they knew they had to help others to stay sober, but "that motive became secondary" (p. 159).

d00109736cea.t: Chapter 7 keeps turning the helper toward the other man: leave him free and owing nothing (p. 94), think of what you can bring rather than what you'll get (p. 102), and tell him to put "the welfare of other people ahead of his own" (p. 94).

4fce4c8edd66.t: Dr. Bob, speaking in 1948, admitted his own early helping was partly to keep himself from getting hurt, and said that if you called it selfish "you'd be quite correct."

ca0bed4bcc6d.t: This overlaps with <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0>, which covers the same pages more briefly.

51f8fc034d64.t: What the book says about the helper's own sobriety

291f93ce74f5.t: It says it more than once, without apology: - Chapter 7 opens: "nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (p. 89). - Tell the newcomer that "your attempt to pass this on to him plays a vital part in your own recovery" (p. 94). "Actually, he may be helping you more than you are helping him" (p. 94). - "Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery" (p. 97). - To wives: "he should work with other people to maintain his own sobriety" (p. 119), and to families, let him help other alcoholics, because in early days "this will do more to insure his sobriety than anything else" (pp. 129–130).

fdde5b6c2369.t: What it says about the motive

a4383f45401c.t: The same chapter that names the benefit pulls the helper's attention off himself: - The newcomer is told how important it is "that he place the welfare of other people ahead of his own" (p. 94). - The helper may lose sleep, money, his privacy and his peace at home (p. 97). - "Do not think of what you will get out of the occasion. Think of what you can bring to it" (p. 102). - Faith, to be vital, must come with "self sacrifice and unselfish, constructive action" (p. 93).

a9589f2fc309.t: Chapter 11 describes the change in the first Akron members. "Though they knew they must help other alcoholics if they would remain sober, that motive became secondary" (p. 159). "It was transcended by the happiness they found in giving themselves for others" (p. 159).

31f122d0b592.t: The book's diagnosis of the alcoholic makes this matter. "Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles" (p. 62). Work done only to protect yourself would leave that root alone, which is why the book doesn't stop at "it keeps you sober."

212107a6174b.t: In his last major talk, Dr. Bob was candid. He found it hard to love other people, and at first went through "the motions of trying to be helpful to the other fellow" partly so he wouldn't get drunk himself (P-53). "Well, you could say that was just a manifestation of selfishness, and you'd be quite correct" (P-53). He went on to say the service that counts "is giving of yourself" (P-53), in effort and time, not a coin to be rid of someone.

6e1925e9e68d.t: The text doesn't use that word for helping, and it doesn't pretend the helper gets nothing. What it does is treat the self-protective reason as a starting point that real work with drunks wears away. The book's own test is in Chapter 7: the newcomer owes you nothing (p. 94), and if he wants to call it off you shouldn't be offended (p. 94). Help that comes with a bill attached isn't what the chapter describes.

b08d50274b0a.t: What was the Jack Alexander article (1941), and what did it do? | Recovery Starts

7d83892214fe.t: It was a feature article about A.A. by Jack Alexander, a feature writer for the Saturday Evening Post, published in the issue of March 1, 1941.

44edf1cc13e9.t: What was the Jack Alexander article (1941), and what did it do?

bbb61c68108d.t: It was a feature article about A.A. by Jack Alexander, a feature writer for the <0>Saturday Evening Post</0>, published in the issue of March 1, 1941.

27f83e1b5e0a.t: Alexander, who was not an alcoholic, came to it a skeptic and spent about a month with A.A. members in several cities before he wrote it.

87372bc4835a.t: The Big Book's 1955 foreword says it brought a deluge of alcoholics asking for help: membership went from 2,000 in March 1941 to 8,000 by the end of the year, and "A.A. had become a national institution" (p. xviii).

1a9fbc073936.t: The flood of letters led the New York office to ask the groups for money for the first time, and the rush of new groups brought the quarrels out of which, Bill W. says, the Traditions came.

de2dea2a95d4.t: The Foreword to the Second Edition, written in 1955, gives the outline. After the book appeared in 1939, a magazine article and Mr. Rockefeller's dinner had brought membership to 2,000 by March 1941 (p. xviii). "Then Jack Alexander wrote a feature article in the Saturday Evening Post and placed such a compelling picture of A.A. before the general public that alcoholics in need of help really deluged us." (p. xviii). By the close of 1941 there were 8,000 members (p. xviii).

f96ae47adcc1.t: The foreword then says what came next: A.A. entered "a fearsome and exciting adolescent period" (p. xviii), with quarrels over membership, leadership and money, and out of that experience grew the principles later called the Twelve Traditions (p. xix).

9e7c7b702041.t: <0>P-44 (around 1955).</0> The <1>Post</1> assigned "one of its star writers, Jack Alexander" (P-44). He had just written about the New Jersey rackets and came to A.A. expecting little, but "he soon became an A.A. 'convert,' even though he wasn't an alcoholic" (P-44). He spent a whole month with them; Dr. Bob, Bill and the elders of the groups at Akron, New York, Cleveland, Philadelphia and Chicago spent hours with him (P-44). The piece "was the lead story in the Saturday Evening Post of March 1, 1941." (P-44).

0bd1f79cd66f.t: Then six thousand appeals for help hit the New York office (P-44). Form letters wouldn't do; every one had to have a personal reply, and Bill says, "An enormous Twelfth Step job had to be done and done quickly." (P-44). For the first time the office asked the groups for money, with $1.00 per member per year as the measure, kept in a fund for office work only (P-44). The year began with two thousand members and ended with eight thousand (P-44). Public relations on that scale were new, and the lessons learned, among them anonymity at the public level and "public relations by the principle of attraction rather than promotion," can be seen in the Traditions (P-44).

28e1822b8fb3.t: <0><1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957).</0> Bill adds how it started. Dr. A. Wiese Hammer, a Philadelphia physician, brought A.A. to the attention of Curtis Bok, one of the owners of the <2>Post</2> (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The members gave Alexander "the most exhaustive briefing on Alcoholics Anonymous any writer has ever had" and took him across the country (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Then the <3>Post</3> insisted on photographs. Over the protests of many members, A.A. agreed. Bill calls it "a crucial decision" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), which he says proved right, at least for the time being.

1742c93054ed.t: When the article appeared, appeals for help and orders for the book came in by the thousands (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Volunteers answered them at the Twenty-Fourth Street clubhouse, paid workers were added, and the groups were asked to contribute: "The A.A. Tradition of self-support began to be a reality." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Elsewhere in the same book Bill writes that the article "made A.A. a national institution" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), that 6,000 inquiries reached the New York post office, and that Alexander became one of A.A.'s trustees (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He also names the cost: as the new crop of members tried to form hundreds of groups, "the specters of disunity and collapse grew to frightening proportions" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

b743e2530c14.t: <0>P-53 (1969).</0> In his last major talk, Bill recalled that Alexander came "thinking at first he was investigating just another racket" (P-53), and that when the piece ran, "pandemonium broke loose" (P-53). Every letter got a personal reply, and the lists of prospects were passed to the existing groups (P-53).

dc06cb17ce40.t: <0><1>Pass It On</1> (1984)</0> says the <2>Post</2>'s owner and publisher, Judge Curtis Bok, heard of A.A. from two Philadelphia doctors, Hammer and C. Dudley Saul, and called in Alexander during the winter of 1940–41 because of his reputation for being hard-nosed (Pass It On, 1984). The four members who first visited him seemed to him like actors, and he suspected "my leg was being pulled" (Pass It On, 1984). The article was the lead story, titled "Alcoholics Anonymous," and was on the newsstands on February 24 (Pass It On, 1984). It ran to about 7,500 words with four photographs of members, none identified (Pass It On, 1984). It called Bill "Griffith" and Dr. Bob "Armstrong," and it printed the mailing address of the Alcoholic Foundation (Pass It On, 1984). Alexander served as a trustee from 1951 to 1956 (Pass It On, 1984).

ade153a4f3d6.t: <0><1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980)</0> quotes the article on Dr. Bob, called "Dr. Armstrong" to keep him anonymous: he was in debt "because of his contributions to the movement and the time he devotes gratis to alcoholics" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). A Cleveland member, Oscar W., remembers working with about 17 newcomers after the article came out (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). The book also mentions a second Jack Alexander article in the <2>Post</2> (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980); our sources don't give its date.

c542ef8bf03c.t: Our sources don't hold the article itself, only the short passages these books quote.

2dba6d2096cd.t: <0>"6,000."</0> Bill (around 1955 and 1957) uses it for the appeals and inquiries that came in (P-44; A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) quotes Lois W. estimating that 6,000 A.A.'s owe the start of their sobriety to the article (Pass It On, 1984). Those are different claims.

24e75b14c21f.t: <0>Who reached the <1>Post</1>.</0> Bill (1957) credits Dr. Hammer's friendship with Curtis Bok (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957;), though on the same page he names Dr. C. Dudley Saul among the three Philadelphia physicians who took an interest in A.A. (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <2>Pass It On</2> (1984) says Bok heard of A.A. through both Hammer and Saul (Pass It On, 1984).

743c80920274.t: <0>Membership before the article.</0> The 1955 foreword says 2,000 by March 1941 (p. xviii); P-44 says the year began with two thousand (P-44); Bill (1957) says 2,000 in the spring of 1941, "a gain of 1,200 in a single year" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill in 1969 put it a year earlier: "By 1940, membership had jumped to about 2,000" (P-53). The foreword, P-44 and Bill's 1957 book all give 8,000 by the end of 1941.

b5a845cfa72b.t: Is "keep coming back" in the Big Book?

2183f75df53e.t: No. The words "keep coming back" are not in the 1939 program text, the forewords or the appendices, and not in any of the stories printed in the first edition.

2b7844088812.t: The exact words appear in two personal stories in today's (fourth) edition (three more say "kept coming back" or "keeps me coming back"), and in <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980), where Anne Smith, Dr. Bob's wife, is remembered greeting newcomers at Akron meetings with "We hope you'll keep coming back."

91c907a44a7e.t: The program text's welcome runs the other way: it sends the sober member out to the newcomer, and tells him to leave the newcomer free to come back or not (pp. 94–96).

632402f92a2c.t: The whole fourth-edition text was searched for "keep coming back," "come back" and "coming back," with page breaks joined, and so were the stories dropped from earlier editions (<0>Experience, Strength and Hope</0>, 2003).

fd8ff5a603b3.t: <0>Program text (pp. 1–164), forewords, appendices:</0> not there. "Come back" in the program text is about a wife who may "never come back" to a recovering man (p. 99).

6d4985ef3fff.t: <0>Personal stories (fourth edition, 2001):</0> two. In "Because I'm an Alcoholic," a woman remembers her first meeting: "They said keep coming back. And I did." (p. 344). "Flooded With Feeling" ends, "I keep coming back because it works." (p. 374). Three more stories use the same idea in other tenses: "it is the peace and serenity I feel inside that keeps me coming back" (p. 381), "Fellowship and activity kept me coming back long enough to work the Twelve Steps" (p. 510), and "And I kept coming back." (p. 519).

674c623db028.t: <0>Stories printed in 1939 and later dropped:</0> not there.

3a2528c02749.t: <0>Later books:</0> <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) has Dan K., an Akron member, remember Anne Smith going from table to table after meetings to welcome new people, saying "We hope you'll keep coming back." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). That is a recollection printed thirty years after Dr. Bob's death.

1344e9090f7e.t: What the program text says about a newcomer coming back

59289d160f07.t: The 1939 text does talk about people returning, but the person doing the going is the sober member, and the newcomer is left free:

8c2608f900fe.t: On the first visit, the member is to make it clear that the newcomer "needn't see you again if he doesn't want to" (p. 94), and not to be offended if he calls it off (p. 94).

09f831c68c5a.t: "If he is sincerely interested and wants to see you again," ask him to read the book in the meantime, and then "he must decide for himself whether he wants to go on" (p. 95).

3087ad3284c8.t: If he isn't interested, or only wants money, "you may have to drop him until he changes his mind" (p. 95).

9a78fdabfbd2.t: "Do not be discouraged if your prospect does not respond at once. Search out another alcoholic and try again." (p. 96).

7bff22c332e5.t: When he does come, the welcome is real. Chapter 11 says of the early gatherings: "No one is too discredited or has sunk too low to be welcomed cordially—if he means business." (p. 161). The same chapter adds that A.A. life "is more than attending gatherings and visiting hospitals" (p. 161). See: <0>What if the person I'm helping doesn't want it?</0>

846c4ae3f340.t: The 1955 Foreword to the Second Edition gives the figure. Of those who came to a few meetings and decided at first they didn't want the program, "about two out of three—began to return as time passed" (p. xx).

a897e2a5d190.t: Two stories printed in the 1939 first edition, and since dropped, are about men who drank again after a year or two sober and then came back. In "The Back-Slider," the fellowship "treated me as though nothing had happened" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). In "The Seven Month Slip," he went back to friends "who never lectured me on my seven month failure" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). Bill W.'s 1946 Grapevine essay on membership says of those who slip and others who trouble a group: "Some of these have become our most respected and best loved." (P-17). See: <0>Does the Big Book say "relapse is part of recovery"? What does it say about a slip?</0>

df217084fc83.t: The saying is a welcome, and the welcome is in the early literature. The program text welcomes anyone who "means business" (p. 161) and tells a wife whose husband has drunk again that she "need not remind him of his spiritual deficiency" (p. 120); the 1939 stories and Bill's 1946 essay describe people being taken back without lectures. The phrase itself is not in the Big Book's program. And the program text puts the weight on the member who goes out to find the drinker (Chapter 7, pp. 89–103), more than on the newcomer who returns to a meeting.

eca5895e97e4.t: Not in the program. "Keep it simple" isn't in the 1939 text, the forewords, the appendices, or any story printed in the first edition. One personal story…

26539446372a.t: Is "keep it simple" in the Big Book?

5e7b6c544091.t: Not in the program. "Keep it simple" isn't in the 1939 text, the forewords, the appendices, or any story printed in the first edition. One personal story in today's edition lists it among A.A. sayings (p. 345).

6d07d11f323f.t: The program text calls its way "this simple program" (p. 58), and Bill adds the condition: "Simple, but not easy; a price had to be paid." (p. 14).

cbeb21cc066f.t: The saying is credited to Dr. Bob, and <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980), warning that many sayings are credited to him loosely, singles it out as one that is certainly his. <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957) gives his parting words to Bill in 1950: "Remember, Bill, let's not louse this thing up. Let's keep it simple!" Later it was often used to argue against A.A.'s service structure, which Bill answered by separating "spiritual simplicity" from "functional simplicity" (P-43).

1759307e23a8.t: All our sources were searched for "keep it simple," "let's keep it simple," "simple" and "simplicity," with page breaks joined.

b50e18752f76.t: <0>Program text, forewords, appendices:</0> no "keep it simple."

03406e02eee9.t: <0>Personal stories (fourth edition, 2001):</0> "Because I'm an Alcoholic" lists "Keep It Simple" with other slogans that came to "impress me as truths I could live by" (p. 345).

cf01ea03abd5.t: <0>Stories printed in 1939 and later dropped</0> (<1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1>, 2003): not there. A later-edition story collected there says "I keep it simple: go to many meetings; carry the message to those who listen." (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003).

d93e15ba5400.t: <0>Later books:</0> <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957), <2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2> (1980), <3>Pass It On</3> (1984), P-43 (1971) and Bill W.'s <4>Twelve Concepts</4> (1962, in the Service Manual), described below.

c216da3e25af.t: What the program text calls simple

cc71d6d22c06.t: "Those who do not recover are people who cannot or will not completely give themselves to this simple program" (p. 58).

936542f70c11.t: Bill, after his friend's visit: they had "told of a simple religious idea and a practical program of action" (p. 9). His own requirements, belief in God and enough willingness, honesty and humility, were "Simple, but not easy; a price had to be paid. It meant destruction of self-centeredness." (p. 14).

7c4f48305786.t: "There was nothing left for us but to pick up the simple kit of spiritual tools laid at our feet." (p. 25).

ccf0fc5b612d.t: Of the decision to let God be the Director: "Most good ideas are simple, and this concept was the keystone of the new and triumphant arch through which we passed to freedom." (p. 62).

c1b042a98a91.t: After the directions for Step Eleven: "So we let God discipline us in the simple way we have just outlined." (p. 88).

e03f40227d0c.t: So the program text does insist the program is simple. It doesn't say simple means easy, and it doesn't use simplicity to mean doing less: the same page that calls it simple says it "demands rigorous honesty" (p. 58).

1b06b07f2e21.t: <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) tells of Bill's visit to Dr. Bob in Akron, a few weeks after the July 1950 Cleveland convention, to ask his consent to a General Service Conference that would hand A.A.'s affairs to its members. Dr. Bob said, "Bill, it has to be A.A.'s decision, not ours." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). At the door, he said: "Remember, Bill, let's not louse this thing up. Let's keep it simple!" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill never saw him again (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The same book calls the line Dr. Bob's "famous final admonition" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See: <1>When did Dr. Bob die, and what were his last words to A.A.?</1>

9e938c9a264f.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) warns that many sayings are credited to Dr. Bob without proof, but "Apart from 'Let's keep it simple,' however, it is difficult to tell which are which." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). It quotes his September 1948 Grapevine article on the Twelve Steps: "simple in language, plain in meaning" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), workable by anyone with a sincere desire to get and keep sobriety. <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) says that in the 1940s, while Bill was formulating the principles that grew out of A.A.'s early troubles over affiliation and anonymity, he often went to Akron to consult Dr. Bob, and "Dr. Bob's ability to keep it simple always served as a guide to Bill" (Pass It On, 1984). At Cleveland in July 1950 he told the convention not to "louse it all up with Freudian complexes" (P-53). See: <2>What happened at the 1950 Cleveland convention?</2>

fea13ec728df.t: How the saying was used afterwards

390032f00bf4.t: The saying soon became an argument against organising A.A.'s services: - <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) describes old-timers setting up central offices to deal with hospitals and phone calls, "Ignoring the cries of 'Let us keep it simple,'" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). - Bill's <1>Twelve Concepts</1> (1962) recalls the resistance to the General Service Conference: "And the clincher was always, 'Let's keep it simple.'" (A.A. Service Manual combined with Twelve Concepts for World Service). - P-43 (1971) repeats that these were the last words Bill heard from Dr. Bob, and quotes Bill: "We need to distinguish sharply between spiritual simplicity and functional simplicity." (P-43). The "it," P-43 says, means the recovery program (P-43).

4395f47b909f.t: The first-hand account is worth holding next to that later use: Dr. Bob said "keep it simple" in the same conversation in which he agreed the Conference was A.A.'s decision to make (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

0fc6c07b4f50.t: The line is on page 45 of the Big Book, near the start of Chapter 4, "We Agnostics." The dilemma is set out in the sentences just before it: moral codes,…

6ab64df726ca.t: "Lack of power, that was our dilemma": what dilemma?

ecd8552f7780.t: The line is on page 45 of the Big Book, near the start of Chapter 4, "We Agnostics." The dilemma is set out in the sentences just before it: moral codes, better philosophies of life and willpower didn't save the writers from alcoholism, because "the needed power wasn't there" (p. 45).

3d331e990708.t: The next sentence names what they needed: "We had to find a power by which we could live, and it had to be a Power greater than ourselves." (p. 45)

cd7abfff1916.t: Then the book says what it's for. Its "main object is to enable you to find a Power greater than yourself which will solve your problem" (p. 45).

d92c3fad4e1f.t: So context confirms the usual reading and sharpens it. The lack was of power to live by what they already knew and wanted, and the line is the point where the book states its own purpose.

286eecee7604.t: Chapter 4 opens by saying that a reader who can't quit, or can't control the amount once he starts, is probably alcoholic and "may be suffering from an illness which only a spiritual experience will conquer" (p. 44). About half the original fellowship thought they were atheists or agnostics, and they faced the same choice: "To be doomed to an alcoholic death or to live on a spiritual basis are not always easy alternatives to face." (p. 44)

fbf1c43ef728.t: Then the dilemma, in order (pp. 44–45): 1. <0>Codes weren't enough.</0> "If a mere code of morals or a better philosophy of life were sufficient to overcome alcoholism, many of us would have recovered long ago." (p. 44) 2. <1>Wanting wasn't enough.</1> They could wish to be moral, wish to be comforted by philosophy, even will these things with all their might, "but the needed power wasn't there" (p. 45). 3. <2>Will wasn't enough.</2> "Our human resources, as marshalled by the will, were not sufficient; they failed utterly." (p. 45) 4. <3>The line.</3> "Lack of power, that was our dilemma." (p. 45) 5. <4>The answer and the question.</4> They had to find a Power greater than themselves. "Obviously. But where and how were we to find this Power?" (p. 45) 6. <5>The book's purpose.</5> "Well, that's exactly what this book is about." (p. 45) It means the book is spiritual as well as moral, and "that we are going to talk about God" (p. 45).

abc9b6e0595b.t: The rest of the page is about what happens next with an agnostic newcomer: his hope rises while the alcoholic problem is explained, and his face falls when God is mentioned (p. 45). The chapter is written for him.

9a312216d208.t: Chapter 2 uses the same word for the businessman a famous psychiatrist called hopeless. His knowledge of his own mind didn't keep him sober, and his religious convictions, the doctor said, weren't the "vital spiritual experience" he needed (pp. 26–27). "Here was the terrible dilemma in which our friend found himself" (p. 28). It's the same shape: what he had wasn't enough, and the way out was a spiritual experience.

96702ff0f176.t: How it relates to Step One

5fcd2469f1f9.t: Step One speaks of being "powerless over alcohol" (p. 59). Page 45 isn't the Step, and the book doesn't tie the two passages together itself. What page 45 describes is the failure of morals, philosophy and will to overcome alcoholism, looking forward to finding "a power by which we could live" (p. 45). On this page the answer to the lack is to find a greater Power, and the rest of the book is its account of how. For the Step itself, see <0>What does Step 1 say? Powerless over what?</0>

a850b06a039d.t: It confirms it. The line is a hinge: everything before it says what failed, and everything after it is the book's answer. Quoted alone it can sound like a diagnosis and nothing more. In place it is followed at once by the search for a Power greater than ourselves and the statement that this is "exactly what this book is about" (p. 45).
