bfc732b67498.t: What do the last lines of the Big Book say ("suggestive only," "we know only a little," "the Road of Happy Destiny")? | Recovery Starts

2f183eff6633.t: The last lines are on page 164, the end of Chapter 11, "A Vision for You," and of the 1939 main text. They're written to a reader who may be on his own,…

c3662a5698b5.t: What do the last lines of the Big Book say ("suggestive only," "we know only a little," "the Road of Happy Destiny")?

9e11cde0ec4b.t: The last lines are on page 164, the end of Chapter 11, "A Vision for You," and of the 1939 main text. They're written to a reader who may be on his own, with no A.A. group nearby and only the book in his hand (pp. 162–164).

6ab783b59baf.t: "Our book is meant to be suggestive only. We realize we know only a little." (p. 164) The next sentence: "God will constantly disclose more to you and to us." (p. 164) Just before, the reader is told that "your real reliance is always upon Him" (p. 164).

6ad2a522c191.t: The same paragraph goes straight to action: ask God each morning "what you can do each day for the man who is still sick" (p. 164), and get your own house in order, because "obviously you cannot transmit something you haven't got" (p. 164). The final paragraph is four plain instructions and a farewell on "the Road of Happy Destiny" (p. 164).

12090839ef22.t: So the context confirms that the book claims no final authority, and complicates using "suggestive only" to mean its directions matter little: in place, the phrase is humility about how much the writers know, set right beside the book's last and most direct instructions.

038fb02403d8.t: Who the ending is written to

b6f1768f235a.t: The last pages of Chapter 11 picture a reader alone: - "Some day we hope that every alcoholic who journeys will find a Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous at his destination." (p. 162) - "Thus we grow. And so can you" (p. 162), even if you are only one man with the book in your hand (pp. 162–163). "We believe and hope it contains all you will need to begin." (p. 163) - The reader thinks he's jittery and alone and couldn't do it. But he has "tapped a source of power much greater than yourself" (p. 163), and to repeat what the writers did "is only a matter of willingness, patience and labor" (p. 163). - A 1939 example follows: one member in a new city, a psychiatrist willing to test the approach, and the prospect that there "will be no stopping until everyone in that town has had his opportunity to recover—if he can and will" (p. 164). - The reader worries he won't have contact with the writers. "We cannot be sure. God will determine that" (p. 164). "He will show you how to create the fellowship you crave." (p. 164)

725903159c19.t: <0>The first</0> (p. 164) sets the book's limits and then gives the reader a daily task: - The book is "suggestive only," and the writers "know only a little" (p. 164). - God will show more, to the reader and to the writers. - Ask in morning meditation what you can do each day for the man who is still sick. "The answers will come, if your own house is in order." (p. 164) - You can't pass on what you don't have. "See to it that your relationship with Him is right, and great events will come to pass for you and countless others." (p. 164) "This is the Great Fact for us." (p. 164)

0d7c525d5583.t: <0>The last</0> (p. 164) is four short instructions and a farewell: 1. "Abandon yourself to God as you understand God." (p. 164) 2. "Admit your faults to Him and to your fellows." (p. 164) 3. "Clear away the wreckage of your past." (p. 164) 4. "Give freely of what you find and join us." (p. 164)

e3a5e31c1f45.t: "We shall be with you in the Fellowship of the Spirit, and you will surely meet some of us as you trudge the Road of Happy Destiny." (p. 164) "May God bless you and keep you—until then." (p. 164)

b69631de34c5.t: The book doesn't label them, but the four instructions follow the order of the Steps: turning to God, admitting faults, setting right the past, and giving to others.

e0b497d6588a.t: The words mean what they say: the book doesn't present itself as law. That fits the way it introduces the Steps, as "suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59). What the setting adds is what stands next to it. The very next sentences say the writers know only a little and that more will be shown, so the phrase sits with an admission about the limits of their knowledge. And it's followed within a few lines by the book's most direct sentences, written as instructions. Both are on the page, and the page needs both. For how the book handles "suggested" and "must" together, see <0>Are the Steps rules or suggestions?</0>

0a62fcac6908.t: It complicates it. "Suggestive only" and "we know only a little" are true to the book: it claims no final authority and expects more to be learned. Quoted alone, though, they can be made to mean the book's directions are loose. In place, they're the writers' humility, set in a closing that sends the reader to help "the man who is still sick" (p. 164) and to join the fellowship on the Road of Happy Destiny.

bdac3f6042bc.t: Related: <0>Are the Steps rules or suggestions?</0> · <1>How did A.A. grow from two people?</1> · <2>Why was the Big Book written, and when?</2>

51939accfd66.t: Page numbers are from the fourth edition (2001). The Preface says the program chapters have been "left largely untouched" since 1939 (p. xi). The footnotes on pp. 161 and 162 that begin "Written in 1939" were added later.

8a312cf1ebc1.t: Is "let go and let God" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

839004453288.t: Not as a phrase in the program. "Let go and let God" isn't in the 1939 text (pp. 1–164), the forewords or the appendices. It appears in one personal story…

bd16eb605196.t: Is "let go and let God" in the Big Book?

2c41389e30bc.t: Not as a phrase in the program. "Let go and let God" isn't in the 1939 text (pp. 1–164), the forewords or the appendices. It appears in one personal story in today's edition, in a list of slogans (p. 345), and in later history books.

741b3e0b10c4.t: Both halves are in the program text separately. "Let go": the result of holding on to old ideas "was nil until we let go absolutely" (p. 58). "Let God": "So we let God discipline us in the simple way we have just outlined." (p. 88), and Step Six asks whether we are "ready to let God remove" our defects (p. 76).

fc5b1cdae177.t: In the program text, letting go and letting God come together with action. Straight after the Third Step decision, "we launched out on a course of vigorous action" (p. 63).

7fd6699b96d0.t: All our sources were searched for "let go and let God," "let go" and "let God," with page breaks joined.

4dcc31ca8a94.t: <0>Program text, forewords, appendices:</0> no "let go and let God." "Let go" appears twice (pp. 58, 76). "Let God" or "let Him" appears at pp. 68, 70, 76 and 88.

5c816bd95bb8.t: <0>Personal stories (fourth edition, 2001):</0> "Because I'm an Alcoholic" lists "Let Go and Let God" with "One Day at a Time," "Easy Does It," "Keep It Simple" and "Live and Let Live" as sayings that at first made the writer shudder and later "began to impress me as truths I could live by" (p. 345).

2cd3f5bab64f.t: <0>"Alcoholic Anonymous Number Three"</0> (Part I) has the man on the hospital bed in 1935 decide "I was willing to let God take over instead of me" (p. 187). That story was written about nineteen years after the visit (p. 188), so it is a later telling, not 1939 program text, and it has "let God" without "let go."

6a38b2772b6f.t: <0>Stories printed in 1939 and later dropped</0> (<1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1>, 2003): not there. One 1939 story speaks of a "final agreement" to "let God be first in my life" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003).

facab6d9e25a.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980): the wife of an early Akron member, who says she "couldn't let go" of her drinking husband (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), remembers another wife telling her to surrender him to God: "Let go and let God" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). She prayed that night, "You can take over," and slept (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

f8cc9631800e.t: <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957): Bill W., describing the 1955 St. Louis convention where the founders handed A.A. over to its members, writes: "Clearly my job henceforth was to let go and let God." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) quotes the same line.

6541dceeb19b.t: So in the earliest-written book in our sources that uses it, <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957), "let go and let God" is about a founder letting go of control of A.A. itself. In the Akron recollection it is about a wife letting go of her husband's drinking.

8ae946a305bc.t: "Let go" and "let God" in the program text

9584c13ed6aa.t: <0>Letting go of old ideas.</0> Chapter 5's opening, read whole: "Some of us have tried to hold on to our old ideas and the result was nil until we let go absolutely." (p. 58). A few lines later come "Half measures availed us nothing." (p. 59) and "We asked His protection and care with complete abandon." (p. 59).

d7c2d2ddfec5.t: <0>Letting God remove defects.</0> Step Six: "Are we now ready to let God remove from us all the things which we have admitted are objectionable?" (p. 76). "If we still cling to something we will not let go, we ask God to help us be willing." (p. 76).

1047afa7aa16.t: <0>Letting God judge and lead.</0> On sex conduct, "we let God be the final judge" (p. 70). On fear: "We never apologize for God. Instead we let Him demonstrate, through us, what He can do." (p. 68). After Step Eleven's directions: "So we let God discipline us in the simple way we have just outlined." (p. 88).

6c05eabdfa25.t: <0>Step Three.</0> The decision "to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him" (p. 59), and the prayer: "God, I offer myself to Thee—to build with me and to do with me as Thou wilt." (p. 63). See: <1>What is the Third Step prayer, and where is it?</1>

54fdea44eded.t: The program text doesn't treat letting God as stopping there. Of the Third Step: "This was only a beginning" (p. 63). "Next we launched out on a course of vigorous action, the first step of which is a personal housecleaning" (p. 63). The decision "could have little permanent effect unless at once followed by a strenuous effort" to be rid of what blocked us (p. 64). And right after "we let God discipline us": "But this is not all. There is action and more action." (p. 88).

fb335d32363a.t: The phrase is a later slogan. Its two parts are faithful to words in the 1939 program text, which asks the reader to let go of old ideas absolutely and to let God remove defects, judge and discipline. In that text, surrender is the start of inventory, amends and work with others, not a substitute for them.

064063bb020d.t: Does the Big Book say alcohol is "but a symptom"? Is drinking the real problem? | Recovery Starts

f71f52ea811f.t: Yes, on page 64 of Chapter 5: "Our liquor was but a symptom." (p. 64) The next sentence: "So we had to get down to causes and conditions." (p. 64) In…

7810bc81831e.t: Does the Big Book say alcohol is "but a symptom"? Is drinking the real problem?

251054fdf7c1.t: Yes, on page 64 of Chapter 5: "Our liquor was but a symptom." (p. 64) The next sentence: "So we had to get down to causes and conditions." (p. 64) In place, it explains why the Third Step decision has to be followed at once by the Fourth Step inventory.

2eb2f94f6a83.t: So in Chapter 5 the book does treat drinking as the visible sign of something underneath, which it names as self (pp. 62, 64).

a452348a8680.t: But the same book insists that alcoholism has a physical side too. It says "the body of the alcoholic is quite as abnormal as his mind" (p. xxvi), and "any picture of the alcoholic which leaves out this physical factor is incomplete" (p. xxvi). The doctor's remedy is "entire abstinence" (p. xxx).

8f956188a90c.t: Context complicates the line. Quoted alone as "drinking isn't the real problem," it drops what the rest of the book says: the alcoholic can never drink safely, and even after recovery "We are not cured of alcoholism." (p. 85)

6f5a3e7e1920.t: The reader has just made the Third Step decision. The book says that decision, however vital, "could have little permanent effect" unless it was followed at once by a hard effort to face and be rid of "the things in ourselves which had been blocking us" (p. 64). Then: "Our liquor was but a symptom." (p. 64) "So we had to get down to causes and conditions." (p. 64) "Therefore, we started upon a personal inventory." (p. 64)

69abc939c665.t: The causes, in the next paragraph, are "the flaws in our make-up which caused our failure" (p. 64), and the book has already named the root: "Being convinced that self, manifested in various ways, was what had defeated us" (p. 64). Resentment is the first of those manifestations (p. 64).

8454c09269a4.t: So "but a symptom" is the book's reason for the inventory: stopping drinking isn't the whole job.

41ec4c436e83.t: The same word, used at another level

f7007325e2e4.t: The book uses "symptom" in more than one place, and not always for the same thing. - In the Doctor's Opinion, Dr. Silkworth says that all the types of alcoholic he describes "have one symptom in common: they cannot start drinking without developing the phenomenon of craving" (p. xxx). There the symptom is the craving that alcohol sets off in the body. - A few pages after p. 64, the book uses the word for the people we resent. They were perhaps spiritually sick, and "we did not like their symptoms" (p. 67).

7190f75972c2.t: The physical side the book won't drop

ce5d47215e68.t: The Big Book opens with a doctor, and with the members agreeing with him: - "In our belief, any picture of the alcoholic which leaves out this physical factor is incomplete." (p. xxvi) - Dr. Silkworth's theory is an allergy: "the phenomenon of craving is limited to this class and never occurs in the average temperate drinker" (p. xxviii). "These allergic types can never safely use alcohol in any form at all" (p. xxviii). - "The only relief we have to suggest is entire abstinence." (p. xxx) - Chapter 2: once the alcoholic takes any alcohol, "something happens, both in the bodily and mental sense" (p. 22), that makes it virtually impossible to stop. - Chapter 3: "We know that no real alcoholic ever recovers control." (p. 30) The illness is progressive, and "Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic" (p. 33).

db9df5658ab6.t: And the mind, and beneath it

934fdfe87bb5.t: The book also says where the main trouble lies. Since the cycle can't start without the first drink, "the main problem of the alcoholic centers in his mind, rather than in his body" (p. 23). Even the doctor writes that unless the alcoholic can experience "an entire psychic change there is very little hope of his recovery" (p. xxix). Chapter 5 goes a level further down, to self (p. 62).

dc1c8e6f1da1.t: Read together, these pages describe three layers (the grouping is ours, not the book's): a body that can't take alcohol, a mind with no defense against the first drink, and beneath both, the self that the Steps work on. "But a symptom" speaks about the last of these. It doesn't erase the other two.

2ba9506582b9.t: The book's answer is both. Drinking is what kills the alcoholic: "with us, to drink is to die" (p. 66). He can never safely do it, and he's never cured (p. 85). Drinking is also the sign of something deeper, which the inventory and the Steps go after. And by Step Ten, the book says, the drink problem goes too: "Instead, the problem has been removed." (p. 85) Even then, that holds only "so long as we keep in fit spiritual condition" (p. 85).

c4c88ef21b00.t: Why do some meetings close with the Lord's Prayer? | Recovery Starts

96b80584dae5.t: The Big Book's program text (pp. 1–164) never mentions the Lord's Prayer, and nothing in our sources say A.A. adopted it as a rule or explains where the…

67a9f495b98e.t: Why do some meetings close with the Lord's Prayer?

7ed8be7978d1.t: The Big Book's program text (pp. 1–164) never mentions the Lord's Prayer, and nothing in our sources say A.A. adopted it as a rule or explains where the custom began.

8b40f13b2098.t: What our sources do show is that it was already the custom before the Big Book. A member's story and members' recollections describe Akron meetings in the late 1930s, including those in an Oxford Group home, closing with the Lord's Prayer, and early Cleveland meetings did the same.

2894d8ffd2d2.t: Writing in 1957 about the early 1940s, Bill W. called it one of A.A.'s "favorites," alongside the Prayer of St. Francis, when the Serenity Prayer joined them (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

ceeb13bc55b0.t: The fourth-edition stories show members experiencing it differently: one found deep meaning in it, and a Jewish member was told by his sponsor he could say something else.

e301de568b78.t: What the Big Book's main text says

8252d38a19a2.t: The first 164 pages don't name the Lord's Prayer. They suggest prayer in the member's own words, with sample prayers and the line "Thy will be done" (pp. 67, 88), and they say members who aren't in a religious body sometimes "select and memorize a few set prayers" (p. 87). The book doesn't say which prayer, if any, should open or close a meeting.

4b0912f36448.t: The earliest pictures of the custom

e2c86776a56d.t: These come from members' memories and stories written down later, so they show the practice but not its origin. - <0>Akron, 1937.</0> "He Sold Himself Short," a story in Part I, describes the writer's first meeting in Akron in 1937, before the book: eight or nine alcoholics and their wives, no literature but religious pamphlets, and "The meeting lasted an hour and closed with the Lord's Prayer." (p. 262). - <1>Akron, at T. Henry Williams's house.</1> Until late 1939 the Akron members met in the home of T. Henry and Clarace Williams, who were Oxford Group members (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Wally G., an early member, remembered: "After the meeting closed with the Lord's Prayer, all the men beat it to the kitchen for coffee" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Bob E. remembered that Dr. Bob and T. Henry "teamed" the meeting, and that T. Henry, the Oxford Group host, "took care of the prayers with which the meeting was opened and closed" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - <2>Cleveland, from 1939.</2> Clarence S., one of the founders of the Cleveland group, described its meetings: "We opened with an audible prayer," then a 45-minute speaker, "and we closed with the Lord's Prayer." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - <3>Youngstown.</3> A member remembered an early meeting there of four people, two men and two women, who talked a little about the Oxford Group and about Dr. Bob and Bill: "They were using the Lord's Prayer." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - <4>Akron parties.</4> At the New Year's Eve dance, members gathered around Dr. Bob at midnight; he would say a few words, "and they'd have the Lord's Prayer" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

be2f9f50103f.t: So the books place the custom in the Oxford Group years in Akron and carry it into the first meetings that broke away. At T. Henry's house the closing prayer was led by the Oxford Group host, but none of the books says who started the Lord's Prayer custom or why. It would be easy to guess that it came from the Oxford Group or from the members' churches, but our sources don't say so, and this page doesn't either.

8046d5bca5e6.t: In <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, Bill mentions it twice. He remembers a bilingual meeting in Montreal "where I first heard the Lord's Prayer in French" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). And writing about the Serenity Prayer's spread in the early 1940s, he says it "took its place alongside our two other favorites, the Lord's Prayer and the Prayer of St. Francis" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). That shows how common it was by then; it doesn't explain the origin. (The same book prints a talk by Father Ed Dowling that mentions the Lord's Prayer, but as part of his reflection on Christianity, not about meetings: A.A. Comes of Age, 1957.)

850ae98058a1.t: An early Ohio member, Oscar W., speaking of the 1940s, said: "Most of us in Akron didn't like all this praying," (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980) because they'd had enough of it in the Oxford Group. He named the Serenity Prayer in particular, which New York brought in. See <0>Where did the Serenity Prayer come from in A.A.?</0>

9e500bc45ef3.t: The fourth edition's stories show the range: - In "It Might Have Been Worse," a member lists what spiritual experience meant to him, including "hearing the Lord's Prayer, which in an A.A. meeting has such great meaning" (p. 356). - In "A Drunk, Like You," a Jewish member found closing with it "the last big hurdle" (p. 406). His sponsor told him to "say something else that you like" (p. 406), and he came to separate religion from A.A.'s spiritual program (p. 406).

6537d5d2d83c.t: These are members' experiences, not program text. See <0>Are the personal stories part of the A.A. program?</0>

55aedfaaf98d.t: Nothing in our sources prescribes a closing prayer for meetings. On how much a group decides for itself, see <0>Tradition Four: can GSO tell a group what to do?</0>; on religion, <1>Is A.A. a religious organization?</1> The 1955 Foreword says plainly: "Alcoholics Anonymous is not a religious organization." (p. xx).

7578a4b07f98.t: Where is "love and tolerance of others is our code"? | Recovery Starts

b4e46353aed9.t: The line is on page 84 of the Big Book, in Chapter 6, "Into Action." It ends the book's paragraph on Step Ten: "Love and tolerance of others is our code."…

fd2559a2ab4a.t: Where is "love and tolerance of others is our code"?

ec194e45e258.t: The line is on page 84 of the Big Book, in Chapter 6, "Into Action." It ends the book's paragraph on Step Ten: "Love and tolerance of others is our code." (p. 84)

0b47a206faa1.t: Just before it, that paragraph gives Step Ten's daily practice: watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment and fear, ask God to remove them, talk them over with someone, make amends quickly, and "Then we resolutely turn our thoughts to someone we can help." (p. 84)

8e43f20f245d.t: Read in place, the line means what it is usually taken to mean, a code for how we treat other people. The context adds where it sits: it's the way of living that the Step Ten work leads into, not a slogan standing on its own.

977ebb3c5e7b.t: The book's other uses of "tolerance" show what it has in mind: treating people who wrong us as sick (pp. 67, 70), keeping talk about each other kind (p. 125), and showing no hatred of drinking as an institution (p. 103).

47ada7b8b933.t: Page 84 opens with the end of the Promises, then turns to Step Ten, which suggests we keep taking personal inventory and set right new mistakes as we go (p. 84). The paragraph says the reader has begun a new way of living by cleaning up the past: "We have entered the world of the Spirit." (p. 84) Growth from here "should continue for our lifetime" (p. 84).

ed70eb462844.t: Then come the instructions, in order (p. 84): 1. Watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment and fear. 2. When they show up, ask God at once to remove them. 3. Talk them over with someone immediately. 4. Make amends quickly if we have harmed anyone. 5. Turn our thoughts to someone we can help.

2e8fa4765729.t: The paragraph closes on the code. The next paragraph begins "And we have ceased fighting anything or anyone—even alcohol." (p. 84), and goes on to the problem of drink being removed, which holds "so long as we keep in fit spiritual condition" (p. 85).

3ae7eae58e24.t: So the code sits between the daily inventory and the book's description of a sober life without the fight. It's the last of a run of actions, all pointing away from self: catch the defect, hand it to God, tell someone, repair the harm, help another person, and treat others with love and tolerance.

5264871f2047.t: What "tolerance" means in the Big Book

de3689994624.t: The word comes up often, and nearly always about people: - <0>People who have wronged us.</0> In the resentment inventory, the writers saw that the people who hurt them were sick too, and asked God to help them show those people "the same tolerance, pity, and patience that we would cheerfully grant a sick friend" (p. 67). Finishing the inventory, "We have begun to learn tolerance, patience and good will toward all men, even our enemies" (p. 70). - <1>The family.</1> In the amends at home, the recovering man asks each morning that "our Creator show us the way of patience, tolerance, kindliness and love" (p. 83). Chapter 9 says the whole family should meet "upon the common ground of tolerance, understanding and love" (p. 122). - <2>Each other.</2> The book's only other "love and tolerance" is in Chapter 9. In A.A. everyone knows everyone else's troubles, which elsewhere might bring gossip, but "we almost invariably temper such talk by a spirit of love and tolerance" (p. 125). The next lines add a rule of thumb: don't tell another person's intimate experiences unless you're sure he'd approve (p. 125). - <3>Drinking and drinkers.</3> "We are careful never to show intolerance or hatred of drinking as an institution." (p. 103) A spirit of intolerance, the same page says, might drive away alcoholics whose lives could have been saved (p. 103). - <4>Other people's opinions.</4> "Real tolerance of other people's shortcomings and viewpoints" makes members more useful to others (p. 19), and newcomers at the early meetings Chapter 11 describes were won over partly by "the absence of intolerance of any kind" (p. 160).

98f37ac73331.t: Tolerance here isn't servility. On the page before the code, in the amends work, the book says: "As God's people we stand on our feet; we don't crawl before anyone." (p. 83)

1f562f1fa03e.t: Chapter 4 says a code alone didn't work for these men: "If a mere code of morals or a better philosophy of life were sufficient to overcome alcoholism, many of us would have recovered long ago." (p. 44) The code on page 84 comes after the inventory, the admission and the amends, inside a paragraph that asks God to remove the defects. The book doesn't link the two passages itself. But read in order, love and tolerance aren't offered as a way to get sober by effort alone. They're how the writers describe living once the work of Steps Four to Nine is under way.

9e0934b706b4.t: It confirms it. The line means what it says, and the chapter around it shows it as part of a daily practice that ends by turning to someone we can help.

2eccea351bab.t: Chapter 5, "How It Works," for the inventory (pp. 64–71): <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt5.pdf</0>

59badce840c5.t: Is "meeting makers make it" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

837b1ee388fb.t: Is "meeting makers make it" in the Big Book?

c945584b0930.t: The 1939 program text talks about A.A. meetings in only a few places. Bill says "We meet frequently so that newcomers may find the fellowship" (pp. 15–16), and Chapter 11 describes the Akron weekly meeting, whose "prime object" was a place where new people could bring their problems (pp. 159–160), and where many a newcomer "capitulated entirely" on hearing a story like his own (p. 160).

0110cbee9e72.t: What the program text says protects sobriety most is something else: "nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (p. 89).

694a28ae933b.t: All our sources were searched for "meeting maker(s)," "make it" and "meeting," with page breaks joined. The saying isn't there. In the program text (pp. 1–164), the word "meeting" for an A.A. gathering appears only in Chapter 11 (pp. 159, 162). The other use in the program, "avoid meeting a man through his family" (p. 91), is about something else. Bill's "We meet frequently" (p. 15) uses the verb.

26dd95eb99c9.t: What the program text says about meetings

ddd35d9ea799.t: <0>Why they meet.</0> Bill W., writing of the fellowship in "one western city and its environs" (p. 15): "We meet frequently so that newcomers may find the fellowship they seek." (pp. 15–16).

31f02ea25630.t: <0>How the first meeting started.</0> In Akron, besides casual evenings in members' homes, "it became customary to set apart one night a week for a meeting" (p. 159). "Aside from fellowship and sociability, the prime object was to provide a time and place where new people might bring their problems." (p. 160).

9da6663f5eca.t: <0>What happened there.</0> Many a man still dazed from the hospital "has stepped over the threshold of that home into freedom" (p. 160). Already impressed by the members who had visited him in the hospital, he "capitulated entirely" when, in an upper room of the house, he heard a man tell a story that closely matched his own (p. 160). By 1939 the house was drawing sixty or eighty visitors a week (p. 161). The chapter gives the meeting real weight in a newcomer's turning point, alongside the hospital visits that came before it.

de50d15162d1.t: <0>More than meetings.</0> The same chapter: "But life among Alcoholics Anonymous is more than attending gatherings and visiting hospitals." (p. 161). It goes on to cleaning up old scrapes, settling family differences, lending money and finding jobs for each other (p. 161).

e468f28b94c5.t: <0>Travellers.</0> "Those of us who travel drop in as often as we can." (p. 162). The book gives two reasons: it lets them lend a hand, and it helps them avoid "certain alluring distractions of the road" (p. 162). That is the one place the program text links going to A.A. gatherings with a member's own protection, and it puts lending a hand first.

ec6fc81b9a20.t: Chapter 7, "Working With Others," which tells a member how to help a newcomer, doesn't mention meetings at all. It tells the member to tell the newcomer about the Fellowship and lend him the book on the first visit (p. 94). See: <0>Does the Big Book say "90 meetings in 90 days"?</0>

4f507304535f.t: What the program text says keeps a member sober

b7d886f1de14.t: The program text is direct about this, and it isn't attendance:

ad25a19d83bf.t: Chapter 7 opens by saying practical experience shows that "nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (p. 89).

dde2b2860d24.t: Bill: when all other measures failed, "work with another alcoholic would save the day" (p. 15).

de5592c2950d.t: And beneath that, a spiritual condition kept up daily: "What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition." (p. 85).

a3b667167b93.t: An early warning about missing meetings

fedcc556222f.t: "The Back-Slider," a story printed in the 1939 first edition and dropped later, describes a man two years sober who decided it wouldn't hurt if he "carried on and missed a meeting or two" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). Then "I began to neglect my daily communication with God" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003), and from there it was a short step to drinking. <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) has an early Akron member, J. D., remember Dr. Bob saying one night that they should go and see a man who "had missed a meeting or two, and was just about ripe for a slip" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

e87beba8ff31.t: So the early sources do treat skipping meetings as one sign of drifting away. In the 1939 story it comes alongside dropping daily prayer and deciding he could stand on his own, and the story's answer is getting back to God and the fellowship. Neither source says that going to meetings is what keeps a person sober.

c10135c3e89b.t: Meetings are in the early program as a place for newcomers to find fellowship and bring their problems, and Chapter 11 shows newcomers finding their answer there (p. 160). The saying makes attendance the thing that gets a person through. The 1939 text gives that place to working with other alcoholics and to a daily spiritual life, and it says A.A. life is "more than attending gatherings" (p. 161).

de0d2dcb68c5.t: Is what I say at a meeting kept private? | Recovery Starts

a4bb404c9d40.t: A.A.'s literature asks members to keep each other's confidences, but it describes a principle and a custom, not an enforceable rule. Today's group…

030bdf08af8b.t: Is what I say at a meeting kept private?

27dfa4343dda.t: A.A.'s literature asks members to keep each other's confidences, but it describes a principle and a custom, not an enforceable rule. Today's group pamphlet: "We repeat no one's personal sharing made in A.A. meetings." (P-16, 2018). It calls the word "anonymous" in A.A.'s name "a promise of privacy" (P-16, 2018).

771b0fbd5ac6.t: The 1939 text's version is about the family of A.A.: "we do not relate intimate experiences of another person unless we are sure he would approve" (p. 125).

07a851702238.t: In 1946 Bill W. wrote that a newcomer's wish for privacy should be respected, even to the point of not discussing his case with other A.A. members (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946).

537991dc277d.t: The Traditions speak of anonymity at the public level (press, radio, films) and as a spiritual principle (pp. 562, 565–566); they don't address what is said inside a meeting. No A.A. text in our sources claims any legal protection for what is said at a meeting, and A.A. has no way to compel anyone.

cab08ed36ee1.t: The Big Book has no chapter on meeting confidentiality; it describes no meeting format at all. What it says about other people's stories is in Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward": - "We families of Alcoholics Anonymous keep few skeletons in the closet." (p. 125). Everyone knew about each other's alcoholic troubles. The book admits this would cause gossip in ordinary life; among them, it says, such things are rare, and talk is tempered "by a spirit of love and tolerance" (p. 125). - "Another principle we observe carefully is that we do not relate intimate experiences of another person unless we are sure he would approve." (p. 125). "We find it better, when possible, to stick to our own stories." (p. 125).

7537fda92535.t: Two other passages bear on keeping confidences: - The Fifth Step should be taken with someone "close-mouthed" (p. 74), and "It is important that he be able to keep a confidence" (p. 74). - An employer helping an alcoholic employee is asked to treat it as "a strictly personal matter" that will "never be discussed without his consent" (p. 143).

47e91fe4dc49.t: The 1939 Foreword's reasons for anonymity were practical: too few members to handle a flood of appeals, and business people who couldn't carry on their jobs if known (p. xiii).

c60e40195018.t: The Long Form's anonymity Traditions deal with the public: "Our names and pictures as A.A. members ought not be broadcast, filmed, or publicly printed." (p. 565). Tradition Twelve calls anonymity a spiritual principle that reminds members "to place principles before personalities" (p. 566). Neither speaks of what is said inside a meeting.

e4056b9175d2.t: Bill's 1946 essay "Anonymity" goes further on the personal level: - "It should be the privilege of each A.A. to cloak himself with as much personal anonymity as he desires." (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946). His fellow members should respect that. - Anonymity encourages alcoholics and their families to come for help, because they regard it "as an assurance their problems will be kept confidential" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946). - "We ought, of course, to preserve a new member's anonymity so long as he wishes it preserved" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946). "If he wishes us to refrain from discussing his case with anyone, even other A.A. members, we ought to respect that wish too." (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946).

670ee5c1cc84.t: He was also clear that anonymity isn't secrecy about oneself. Few members are anonymous in their daily contacts, he wrote in 1946, and in 1955: "Of course no A.A. need be anonymous to family, friends, or neighbors." (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955). See <0>Tradition Twelve: does anonymity mean keeping A.A. secret?</0>

d72964547158.t: <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16): - At the personal level, anonymity "assures privacy for all members" (P-16, 2018), which matters especially to newcomers who fear their alcoholism may be exposed. - "We repeat no one's personal sharing made in A.A. meetings." (P-16, 2018). Members respect others' right to keep their anonymity "however they wish, and as closely as they wish" (P-16, 2018). - A chair may remind those present to "leave any confidences you hear in these rooms behind when you go" (P-16, 2018). A group inventory question asks whether members "leave what they share at meetings behind" (P-16, 2018).

06bc4955107f.t: Where the books set no rule

fe1fbb995fe2.t: <0>No enforcement.</0> A.A. has no authority over its members. In 1947 Bill wrote that there is "no one set in personal authority over anyone else" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). The request to keep confidences rests on members honoring it.

d07ef5ece00c.t: <0>Open meetings.</0> Open meetings may include nonalcoholics as observers (P-16, 2018), who are not members.

f777972cc806.t: <0>Legal matters.</0> No text in our sources say anything about the legal status of what is said at a meeting. This page doesn't either.

4b4c8f11faee.t: So the honest answer from the literature is that members are asked, from 1939 on, not to repeat what others share; the literature offers that as a principle and a promise, not a guarantee.

459b76a6d64c.t: P-17, <0>A.A. Tradition — How It Developed</0> ("Anonymity," 1946; "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous," 1955): <1>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/literature/assets/p-17_AATraditions.pdf</1>

2a011c13bd69.t: P-16, <0>The A.A. Group</0> ("The Importance of Anonymity," pp. 8–9): <1>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/literature/p-16_0723.pdf</1>

214ce561cb5d.t: How many members did A.A. have in 1939? | Recovery Starts

87a948916a3c.t: When the Big Book came out in April 1939, A.A. had about a hundred members. The book's own foreword says "more than one hundred men and women" (p. xiii).

1024dac488c0.t: How many members did A.A. have in 1939?

2b8e404a7589.t: When the Big Book came out in April 1939, A.A. had about a hundred members. The book's own foreword says "more than one hundred men and women" (p. xiii).

bb60c170c536.t: They were mostly in two places: Akron, Ohio (with Cleveland nearby) and New York, plus a few scattered "twos and threes and fives" elsewhere (p. 162).

10f1d2f8ef9f.t: By the end of 1939, after a magazine article brought hundreds of inquiries, the 1955 foreword says about 800 alcoholics were estimated to be on their way to recovery (p. xviii).

d046b6e6b602.t: <0>Foreword to the First Edition.</0> Its first sentence says the members of Alcoholics Anonymous "are more than one hundred men and women who have recovered from a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body" (p. xiii). It gives that small number as the reason for anonymity: they were "too few, at present" to handle all the appeals the book might bring (p. xiii).

59c7b80ef442.t: <0>Chapter 11, "A Vision for You."</0> Footnotes in today's edition mark these passages "Written in 1939" (pp. 161, 162). The chapter describes the groups as they were: - In the first city (Akron), the three original men had "succeeded with seven more" a year and a half later (p. 159). By 1939 the weekly meeting at a member's home drew "sixty or eighty as a rule," counting families who drove in from nearby towns (p. 161). - A community thirty miles away "has fifteen fellows of Alcoholics Anonymous" (p. 161). - In an eastern city (New York) there were informal meetings "where you may now see scores of members" (p. 162). - Elsewhere, "Little clusters of twos and threes and fives of us have sprung up in other communities" (p. 162).

fe61aa54c11a.t: <0>Personal stories.</0> The first edition's story section held 28 stories, eighteen from Akron (two of them by Clevelanders) and ten from New York (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); P-44 also gives 28 (P-44).

63399bc290e3.t: <0>Dr. Silkworth, July 1939.</0> In the first medical paper about A.A., reprinted in <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, he wrote that "These ex-alcoholic men and women number about one hundred at present." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957, reprinting Silkworth, July 1939). He describes one group along the Atlantic seaboard centred on New York and a somewhat larger one in the Middle West (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

11433379c54f.t: <0>Dr. Harry Emerson Fosdick's 1939 review</0>, also reprinted there, calls the book "the pooled experience of one hundred men and women" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

94c1c340b6a6.t: <0>Foreword to the Second Edition (1955).</0> "The membership had then reached about 100 men and women." (p. xvii). It adds that in late 1937 enough members had lasting sobriety to convince them their way worked (p. xvii).

56306446a53a.t: <0><1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957).</0> When the book was printed, "The A.A. fellowship then had just about a hundred members." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In November 1937 Bill and Dr. Bob had counted upwards of forty alcoholics staying sober (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

f8d8ccc41490.t: <0>Bill W., 1969</0> (talk printed in P-53): "By 1939, membership in A.A. had reached about 100" (P-53).

da2aa7f8cdbf.t: All of these agree: about a hundred.

07ec341186f3.t: The 1955 foreword says that after <0>Liberty</0> magazine ran "Alcoholics and God" in the fall of 1939, about 800 inquiries came into the New York office (p. xviii). New groups started, and "By the end of 1939 it was estimated that 800 alcoholics were on their way to recovery." (p. xviii). That is an estimate of people on their way, not a count of members.

9d7d7bea8d33.t: In "Bill's Story" (Chapter 1), today's text says that in one western city and its surroundings "there are one thousand of us and our families" (p. 15), and that informal gatherings may draw "from 50 to 200 persons" (Chapter 1, p. 16). That count includes families, so it isn't a member count. The Preface says the program portion of the book "has been left largely untouched" since 1939 (p. xi), but our sources have only the fourth edition's text of Chapter 1, so it can't confirm that this sentence reads exactly as it did in the first printing. Every other 1939 source in our sources say about a hundred members.

4bb421259051.t: Should I give a newcomer money or a place to stay? | Recovery Starts

d3aae83ed887.t: The Big Book says you may: if he's broke and homeless, help him find a job, give him "a little financial assistance," or take him into your home "for a…

ce3840b4aeae.t: Should I give a newcomer money or a place to stay?

e05322cd7504.t: The Big Book says you may: if he's broke and homeless, help him find a job, give him "a little financial assistance," or take him into your home "for a few days" (p. 96).

38f29398a62f.t: It sets limits. Don't take money your family or creditors should have, make sure your family will welcome him, and make sure he isn't using you for money or shelter, because then "you only harm him" (p. 96). Members seldom let an alcoholic live with them for long (p. 97).

0f43383ad619.t: Money and shelter aren't the cure. Men who demand them "before conquering alcohol, are on the wrong track" (p. 98). The question is "when and how to give" (p. 98).

594d3de6ac5c.t: There's no yes-or-no rule in the text. It leaves this to judgment, and tells you to make sure you're doing the right thing before you take it on (p. 97).

1ab5dd537e26.t: <0>If all he wants is money or nursing.</0> If he expects you to act only as "a banker for his financial difficulties or a nurse for his sprees," you may have to drop him until he changes his mind (p. 95).

80842d82fea5.t: <0>If he's sincere and in need.</0> "He may be broke and homeless. If he is, you might try to help him about getting a job, or give him a little financial assistance" (p. 96). Not at your family's or creditors' expense (p. 96).

a206b14d3d8e.t: <0>Taking him in.</0> "Perhaps you will want to take the man into your home for a few days. But be sure you use discretion" (p. 96). Be certain your family welcomes him and that he isn't trying to impose on you "for money, connections, or shelter" (p. 96). If you allow that, you make it possible for him to be insincere, and "You may be aiding in his destruction rather than his recovery" (p. 97).

c8dc75cbafdb.t: <0>Don't dodge it, either.</0> "Never avoid these responsibilities, but be sure you are doing the right thing if you assume them" (p. 97). The work "may mean sharing your money and your home" (p. 97).

76abdb75c69c.t: <0>Not for long.</0> "We seldom allow an alcoholic to live in our homes for long at a time" (p. 97). It isn't good for him, and it can cause serious trouble in a family (p. 97).

0b6814e8a49a.t: <0>Why it isn't the main thing.</0> For the alcoholic who is able and willing to get well, "little charity, in the ordinary sense of the word, is needed or wanted" (pp. 97–98). Members still go to great lengths to provide each other these things "when such action is warranted" (p. 98). The minute the work becomes a service of handouts, the alcoholic starts relying on the helpers instead of on God (p. 98). "Burn the idea into the consciousness of every man that he can get well regardless of anyone" (p. 98).

08aecd0d814e.t: Chapter 11 says the early Akron members "shared their homes, their slender resources," and were willing day or night to put a new man in hospital and visit him (p. 159). In 1939, "lending money and securing jobs for each other, when justified" was an everyday thing (p. 161).

a155d4edc85f.t: Bill W. wrote in 1946 that in A.A.'s first years there were no group funds: "If an individual A.A. wished to grubstake a fellow alcoholic, he did so. It was purely his own affair" (P-17).

0f6b4ebfe699.t: Later, in <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957), Bill described how it went when he and his wife Lois filled their Brooklyn house with alcoholics, starting in the fall of 1935. Sometimes as many as five lived there at once, and all might be drunk at the same time. Of the people they housed, Bill says, "we did not sober up a single one" (<1>Comes of Age</1>, 1957). In Akron, he says, the same kind of care in the houses of Dr. Bob and another member "fared better" (<2>Comes of Age</2>, 1957). The Big Book's cautions on pages 96–98 read like the lessons of both.

817911c08a6d.t: Do I have to get a sponsor? | Recovery Starts

22dfc0f62dee.t: The Big Book doesn't say you have to. The word "sponsor" isn't in its program (pages 1–164), and nothing in the book makes having one a condition of…

6cd73d2fef84.t: Do I have to get a sponsor?

bd668cad65c6.t: The Big Book doesn't say you have to. The word "sponsor" isn't in its program (pages 1–164), and nothing in the book makes having one a condition of membership or of recovery.

b97ff3d176f2.t: The 1939 Foreword names one requirement for membership: "an honest desire to stop drinking" (p. xiv).

f893b4fca767.t: What the book does say is that you can't do this entirely alone. You tell your whole story to another person (Step Five), and you go out and help other alcoholics (Step Twelve). It leaves the choice of who that person is to you.

b571175bd822.t: The standing relationship many rooms now call sponsorship, a senior member guiding you through the Steps over months, isn't described anywhere in the program.

4dbbdde3373f.t: What the book asks of a newcomer

927f66b0b74e.t: The first edition's Foreword describes the fellowship in 1939: "There are no fees or dues whatsoever" and "The only requirement for membership is an honest desire to stop drinking" (p. xiv).

0969dbdbe06f.t: The Steps themselves are introduced as "suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59), and the last chapter says "Our book is meant to be suggestive only" (Ch. 11, p. 164).

2df7308bd0bc.t: The book even pictures a reader who has no A.A. member near him at all. After describing how the fellowship spread, it tells him he can do the same, though he be "one man with this book in your hand" (Ch. 11, p. 163). It hopes the book "contains all you will need to begin" (Ch. 11, p. 163), and tells that reader his real reliance is on God, who "will show you how to create the fellowship you crave" (Ch. 11, p. 164).

367c4a381cfd.t: Where you might expect a sponsor, and what's there instead

56ee9e36e0c8.t: <0>Step Five.</0> The book says plainly that a solitary self-appraisal usually isn't enough and that you must tell someone else your life story (pp. 72–73). Then it lists who that someone might be: a clergyman, "a close-mouthed, understanding friend" (p. 74), a doctor or psychologist, even a family member as long as it won't hurt them (p. 74). A sponsor isn't on the list. If no suitable person is available, the Step can be put off until one is, as long as it isn't an excuse (pp. 74–75).

05c5e925a500.t: <0>Step Twelve.</0> Chapter 7 describes an experienced member helping a newcomer, and it does picture guidance: "Having had the experience yourself, you can give him much practical advice" (p. 96). But the newcomer chooses. Let him know you're available to hear his story, "but do not insist upon it if he prefers to consult someone else" (p. 96). He's "under no obligation to you" (p. 94) and "needn't see you again if he doesn't want to" (p. 94). See: <1>Is "Working With Others" about sponsorship?</1>

083c1f95b2d2.t: What the text doesn't let us say

9c7f5e55a7d1.t: The book doesn't say "go it alone" either. "We must be entirely honest with somebody" (p. 73). Its last instructions are to admit your faults "to Him and to your fellows" (Ch. 11, p. 164), and to "Give freely of what you find and join us" (Ch. 11, p. 164). Fellowship with other alcoholics, and helping them, runs through the whole program. What the book doesn't do is assign you one person to answer to.

83f8db5c9f65.t: Where the word does turn up

7f4a780cb826.t: Only in the personal stories at the back. In "The Vicious Cycle," one of the earliest, a "sponsor" is the person who brought you the message while you were still drinking (pp. 220, 226); in an Akron story set in 1937, it is Dr. Bob taking a newcomer through the early program in one afternoon (p. 263). See: <0>Is the word "sponsor" in the Big Book?</0>

eac3f4fe5139.t: No. The first 164 pages, where the program is set out, never say "90 meetings in 90 days," and they never set any number of meetings.

bc41e8122f92.t: Does the Big Book say "90 meetings in 90 days"?

389c409afed6.t: No. The first 164 pages, where the program is set out, never say "90 meetings in 90 days," and they never set any number of meetings.

21fc2232c355.t: The phrase appears only in two personal stories added to later editions. Each describes what that writer chose to do.

ad4706e9abe9.t: What the program text asks for every day is different: inventory and prayer (pp. 84–88), and working with other alcoholics (p. 97).

96005be69970.t: The whole fourth-edition text was searched for "ninety," "90," and "meeting." In the main text, the forewords and the appendices, "90" appears only as a page number and in the Third Edition foreword's count of countries. "Ninety" doesn't appear at all.

981e461c9a1a.t: The phrase is in two personal stories: - <0>"Student of Life"</0> (Part II, "They Stopped in Time"): "I did ninety meetings in ninety days, got a sponsor, and joined a home group" (p. 326). - <1>"Grounded"</1> (Part III, "They Lost Nearly All"): a pilot who came to A.A. out of treatment set out to do ninety meetings in ninety days, and with a trial coming "completed my ninety meetings in sixty-seven days" (p. 525).

9481a0738f45.t: These are personal histories. The Big Book introduces its stories as each writer describing things "in his own language and from his own point of view" (p. 29). Neither story presents ninety in ninety as something the book requires.

d26b9482c711.t: Meetings are in the 1939 text, but as something that grew up among members, not as an assignment: - Bill W.: "We meet frequently so that newcomers may find the fellowship" they're looking for (p. 15). - Chapter 11 describes the first group's casual evenings at members' homes, and how "it became customary to set apart one night a week for a meeting" open to anyone interested, mainly so that new people had a time and place to bring their problems (pp. 159–160).

f09cec71e211.t: Chapter 7, the Big Book's chapter on helping a newcomer, never mentions meetings. (Its one use of the word is "avoid meeting a man through his family," p. 91.) The newcomer is told about the Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous on the first visit and lent the book (p. 94). He's asked to read it and decide for himself whether to go on (p. 95), and on a second visit he may be ready to go through with the Twelve Steps (p. 96).

fc6c792c52e1.t: It's sometimes said that "Working With Others" discusses meeting attendance. It doesn't: the chapter doesn't discuss meetings at all.

212f5212cd7b.t: What the program does ask daily

b950f7165d90.t: The daily disciplines in the text are Steps Ten and Eleven (pp. 84–88) and helping others: "You have to act the Good Samaritan every day, if need be" (p. 97).

1bbd76d492a0.t: The Preface says the personal stories have been revised in every edition (pp. xi–xii). Our sources have only the fourth edition, so this page doesn't say which edition first printed these two stories.

fe33f7f4736f.t: Is it true there are "no musts" in A.A.? | Recovery Starts

823f3f6ebb0f.t: "There are no musts in A.A." isn't in the Big Book. In our sources it appears once, in Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (1980), as a one-line gloss on…

f7cde4d7ff54.t: Is it true there are "no musts" in A.A.?

7048f1c6ff18.t: "There are no musts in A.A." isn't in the Big Book. In our sources it appears once, in <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980), as a one-line gloss on something Dr. Bob wrote in 1948.

0aaf0cbcbd9d.t: The 1939 program text uses "must" more than sixty times in Chapters 1 to 11, most often as "we must." Examples: "We must, or it kills us!" (p. 62), and "We must be entirely honest with somebody" (p. 73).

7d476cc4d3b4.t: The book is just as clear that no one should order anyone to follow it. The Steps are "suggested" (p. 59), the writers lay down "no rule of any sort" (p. 81), and "it is best that no one tell him he must abide by its suggestions" (p. 144).

a6835094c45d.t: So both halves are true. No one in A.A. can make you do anything. The book still says, from its writers' experience, that some things must be done if you want to recover.

2d2b6c36f55c.t: All our sources were searched for "no musts," "musts," "you must" and "Thou shalt not."

690483383f42.t: The only "no musts" is in <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980). It quotes Dr. Bob's article in the Grapevine of September 1948 about the Twelve Steps: - The Steps are "simple in language, plain in meaning" and workable by anyone with a sincere desire for sobriety (<1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1>, 1980). - "Yet, withal, there are no shibboleths in A.A." (<2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2>, 1980). Members aren't bound by theological doctrine, and "an A.A. decalogue in the language of 'Thou shalt not' would gall us indeed" (<3>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</3>, 1980).

b12ea86e4f51.t: The 1980 book then adds, in quotation marks: "That is, 'There are no musts in A.A.'" (<0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0>, 1980). The book doesn't say who first said it. The words quoted from 1948 are Dr. Bob's. The short form is the 1980 book's gloss.

28acbf68fdf8.t: The same article, quoted just before, also says that harmonious living comes in proportion to "our earnest attempt to follow them literally under divine guidance" (<0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0>, 1980). So Dr. Bob rejected an enforced code of "Thou shalt not." He didn't say the Steps were optional extras.

3d7e2312324b.t: (The question list said the "no musts" line sits next to a Bill W. passage. The passage is Dr. Bob's, from his 1948 Grapevine article.)

8e5c2d59c30e.t: The same 1980 book also uses "musts" the other way, about early Akron. Besides hospitalization and surrender, it says, "there were undoubtedly other musts, even though Dr. Bob and Bill weren't quite sure what they were" (<0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0>, 1980). Reading a 1938 report on the Akron group, it notes that members then thought meetings "desirable" but not necessary, while "Morning devotion and 'quiet time,' however, were musts" (<1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1>, 1980). So the book that prints the "no musts" gloss also records that the first members held some things to be musts for themselves. What Dr. Bob turned down in 1948 was a decalogue of "Thou shalt not" laid on members.

239e8a7366f6.t: <0>The writers took "you must" out on purpose.</0> Bill tells in <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957) that a psychiatrist who read the draft sent out before publication, Dr. Howard, said the text "was too full of the words 'you' and 'must'" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957). He suggested changing them where possible to "we ought" or "we should," to remove all coercion. Bill gave in: "it was perfectly apparent that the doctor was dead right" (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957).

6947beb4ea9b.t: <0>The commonest form left is "we must."</0> A count of the fourth-edition text of Chapters 1–11 finds "must" or "mustn't" about sixty-eight times. The most common form by far is "we must" (twenty-three times, six of them in a list of rules the book rejects, below), against seven "you must." Many of the musts that remain report what the writers found they had to do: - On selfishness: above everything, alcoholics must be rid of it. "We must, or it kills us!" (p. 62). - On the Fifth Step: "We must be entirely honest with somebody if we expect to live long or happily in this world" (pp. 73–74). - On amends: "We must not shrink at anything" (p. 79). "We must lose our fear of creditors" (p. 78). - On daily life: "Every day is a day when we must carry the vision of God's will into all of our activities" (p. 85). - On spiritual life: "we must find a spiritual basis of life—or else" (p. 44).

ab11e4e459e1.t: <0>Where the book refuses a "must."</0> Chapter 7 lists the musts other people had laid on alcoholics: "we must not go where liquor is served"; "we must shun friends who drink"; "we must not go into bars" (pp. 100–101). "Our experience shows that this is not necessarily so" (p. 101).

df74bba75ff4.t: <0>It never lets one person order another.</0> A man given the book should not be told "he must abide by its suggestions" (p. 144). "The man must decide for himself" (p. 144). The newcomer, after reading, "must decide for himself whether he wants to go on" (p. 95). A wife should "never tell him what he must do about his drinking" (p. 111). The Traditions say the same about membership: it should never depend "upon money or conformity" (p. 563).

f922316331da.t: <0>The Steps are suggested.</0> "Here are the steps we took, which are suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59). Bill says the suggestion wording was added in the same last-minute compromise as "God as we understood Him": the Steps "were to be suggestions only" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). On a hard question about amends at home, the writers say they wish "to lay down no rule of any sort" (p. 81).

f25583a5af2f.t: <0>But "suggested" isn't "unimportant."</0> The same pages report what happened when people skipped things. "Half measures availed us nothing" (p. 59). "If we skip this vital step, we may not overcome drinking" (p. 72).

0585e11bccea.t: "There are no musts in A.A." is fair about authority. No one in A.A. can order a member to do anything, and the book was deliberately rewritten to avoid "you must." It isn't fair about the content. The book's writers say, many times and in their own voice, that certain things <0>must</0> be done: honesty, getting rid of selfishness, amends, daily reliance on God, helping others. It presents them as what they found necessary to stay alive, offered to anyone who wants what they have (p. 58).

79e4aafc7144.t: It's sometimes said there are no "musts" or requirements for A.A. membership or for sobriety. The membership half is right (Long Form Three, p. 563). The sobriety half goes beyond the book, which does name what its writers found they must do.

2a0d7429d679.t: What does "no outside affiliation" mean in practice? | Recovery Starts

2603ea6454a7.t: It means an A.A. group may cooperate with anyone, but never so far as "affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied." "An A.A. group can bind itself to…

70972bd78990.t: What does "no outside affiliation" mean in practice?

03be5ccd6a2c.t: It means an A.A. group may cooperate with anyone, but never so far as "affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied." "An A.A. group can bind itself to no one" (p. 564).

d3b55015beff.t: A group is an A.A. group only if, as a group, it has "no other affiliation" (p. 563). It doesn't go into business, lend A.A.'s name to any facility or cause, take money with strings, or take sides on outside controversies.

d8057a63afc4.t: It limits A.A. groups and A.A. as a whole. In 1947 Bill W. wrote that individual members are free to work in hospitals, research or education, as individuals, so long as they keep A.A.'s name out of it.

272728159549.t: In practice it was learned from failures: groups that ran drying-out places and "A.A. hospitals," and members who tied A.A.'s name to causes.

8f383c2d25ae.t: <0>Tradition Three: what a group is.</0> Any two or three alcoholics gathered for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation" (p. 563).

e33269356306.t: <0>Tradition Six: how far cooperation goes.</0> Problems of money, property and authority "may easily divert us from our primary spiritual aim" (p. 563). So: - Any considerable property useful to A.A. should be separately incorporated, dividing the material from the spiritual (pp. 563–564). - "An A.A. group, as such, should never go into business" (p. 564). - Clubs and hospitals should be set apart so the groups can drop them if necessary, and shouldn't use the A.A. name (p. 564). - Hospitals and places of recuperation "ought to be well outside A.A. — and medically supervised" (p. 564). - "While an A.A. group may cooperate with anyone, such cooperation ought never go so far as affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564).

7fd90c06ebe3.t: <0>Tradition Seven: no strings.</0> No contributions "carrying any obligation whatever" (p. 564), and no public fund-raising in A.A.'s name, whether by groups, clubs, hospitals or outside agencies (p. 564).

bc1c87e985bb.t: <0>Tradition Ten: no sides.</0> "The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one" (p. 565).

d1bafb5b778f.t: What it looked like in practice (Bill W., 1946–47)

b9a538c227c0.t: <0>Groups running hospitals failed.</0> Where groups set up their own drying-out places with hired managers and nurses, it almost always backfired: "It has put the group into business" (P-17, "Hospitals and A.A.", 1947, p. 15). Groups that raised money publicly for "A.A. hospitals" got nowhere, because solicitation carrying A.A.'s endorsement is dangerous to everyone (P-17, pp. 15–16). What worked were rest farms run by individual members under medical supervision: "Not being a group project and not bearing the A.A. name," they could be taken or left alone (P-17, "Hospitals and A.A.", 1947, p. 16).

d3229f95c90b.t: <0>Cooperation is normal.</0> "Everywhere we cooperate with hospitals" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 33). Hospitals gave A.A. working arrangements, consulted it and employed A.A. nurses, and these relationships worked well, but none of these places were known as A.A. hospitals (P-17, p. 33).

f16cc102b667.t: <0>The line for groups.</0> "Neither A.A. as a whole nor any A.A. group ought to enter any activity other than straight A.A." (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947, p. 24). Groups can't endorse, finance or ally with any other cause, however good, or link A.A.'s name to other alcohol work so that the public thinks A.A. has given up its own aim (P-17, p. 24). Members and friends in those fields should be discouraged from stressing A.A.'s name in publicity or fund-raising (P-17, pp. 24–25).

1186a1f365cf.t: <0>The freedom for members.</0> Bill calls the "do nothing" view unthinkable (P-17, p. 25). Members can bring their experience to other noncontroversial alcohol work if they act as individuals: no A.A. label in public and no use of A.A. status to raise money (P-17, p. 25). His summary: "A.A. does not sponsor projects in other fields" (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947, p. 25), but members may work in constructive ones as individuals, careful of A.A.'s name (P-17, pp. 25–26).

b64559aa8a3e.t: Bill's 1955 foreword asks A.A. to "steadfastly decline all political, sectarian, or other alliances" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 4). The 1955 essay on anonymity puts it plainly: A.A. will cooperate with almost everybody, "yet we decline to marry our Society to anyone" (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955, p. 50). P-17 also prints a General Service Conference statement, undated, that A.A. follows a policy of cooperation but not affiliation with other organizations concerned with alcoholism (P-17, p. 36).

f82273ba39e5.t: It doesn't mean groups can't meet in churches, hospitals or treatment centres (a later pamphlet describes such groups as renting space there; P-16, 2018, pp. 17–18), or that A.A. can't work alongside hospitals and doctors; all of that is cooperation. It doesn't stop individual members working in other fields as individuals, provided they keep A.A.'s name out of it, and it doesn't bind outside organizations. What it rules out is a group, or A.A., belonging to, endorsing, financing, or lending its name to anything outside A.A.

0820e0835e04.t: P-17, <0>A.A. Tradition: How It Developed</0> ("Hospitals and A.A.," pp. 15–16; "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects," pp. 23–26; "Money," pp. 27–35): <1>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/literature/assets/p-17_AATraditions.pdf</1>

c8dff64b26c2.t: Which A.A. books are oldest, and why does the date matter?

451a3af6c969.t: The oldest A.A. text is the Big Book, <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, first published in April 1939. Its first 164 pages and the Foreword to the First Edition are the 1939 text.

327d2ad8fa66.t: Next come Bill W.'s Grapevine essays on the Traditions (1946–47) and the Traditions' Long Form (1946). Almost everything else in our sources were written or compiled after Dr. Bob died in 1950 (the exceptions are pieces reprinted inside later books, such as Dr. Bob's 1948 talk in P-53): the 1955 forewords and appendix, <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957), the pamphlets, <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) and <2>Pass It On</2> (1984).

d22ce2376997.t: The date matters because later accounts sometimes add details, change them, or disagree with the earlier text. When two sources differ, the earlier one is closer to the events, and the reader deserves to see both.

038f678832f1.t: A later book isn't wrong because it is later. It just has to be read with its date in view.

b4a9db477a13.t: Each date is read from the source's own pages where it prints one.

b2d62cde58c3.t: Why the date matters: examples from these pages

bdb9fb0e74f4.t: Reading the sources side by side shows details shifting as the story was retold: - <0>Bill D., A.A. number three.</0> His own story says he was hospitalized eight times in six months and came to on June 26, 1935 (p. 184). Bill W.'s 1957 account has him say six times in four months and puts the visit within days of June 10 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <1>Who was the third member, and how was he found?</1> - <2>Where Dr. Bob trained.</2> P-53 and the 1980 biography put his internship at City Hospital, Akron; Bill's 1957 account says Chicago (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <3>Who was Dr. Bob?</3> - <4>The first meeting.</4> The 1955 foreword says June 1935 (p. xv); Dr. Bob's own 1939 story puts it on Mother's Day, weeks before June 10 (p. 179). See <5>How did Bill W. and Dr. Bob meet?</5> - <6>Names appear later.</6> The 1939 text names no one in the founding story; the hotel, the minister and Henrietta Seiberling are named in 1948 and 1957 accounts. That isn't a contradiction: the 1939 book asked its members to stay anonymous in print (p. xiii), and the names came out later.

5988616b7b39.t: The later books are honest about this risk themselves. <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> quotes an oldtimer saying people are "always repeating things Dr. Bob said that I know he didn't" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

2071f99d4a4e.t: The earliest source leads. Where the 1939 or 1955 Big Book covers a point, it is quoted first, and later books add detail with their dates attached.

d4dc860b6d1a.t: Does the Big Book say "once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic"? | Recovery Starts

7c247c86adef.t: Yes. It's in the 1939 program text, in Chapter 3, in quotation marks: "We have seen the truth demonstrated again and again: 'Once an alcoholic, always an…

e524349696b0.t: Does the Big Book say "once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic"?

df5b9473ef52.t: Yes. It's in the 1939 program text, in Chapter 3, in quotation marks: "We have seen the truth demonstrated again and again: 'Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic'" (p. 33).

0b8efef8f9fb.t: In context it is about one thing: a real alcoholic never gets his control back, however long he stays sober. The proof given is a man who stayed bone dry for twenty-five years, started drinking again at fifty-five, and was dead within four years (pp. 32–33).

40af04435e09.t: The same book says its members "have recovered" (p. 17). In the book, staying an alcoholic means you can never safely drink again, "We are not cured of alcoholism" (p. 85); it doesn't mean you can't recover.

a9c4c32869d9.t: All our sources were searched for "once an alcoholic" and "always an alcoholic." The phrase is in the program text once (p. 33), and in two stories dropped from earlier editions, now in <0>Experience, Strength and Hope</0> (2003). It isn't in the fourth edition's personal stories.

266044db3a86.t: Chapter 3, "More About Alcoholism" (pp. 30–43), opens with the alcoholic's great illusion: "The idea that somehow, someday he will control and enjoy his drinking is the great obsession of every abnormal drinker" (p. 30). Then, in order: - "We know that no real alcoholic ever recovers control" (p. 30). Alcoholics of their type are "in the grip of a progressive illness" (p. 30). - "We are like men who have lost their legs; they never grow new ones" (p. 30). No treatment makes alcoholics of their kind like other men (pp. 30–31). - A man of thirty, a heavy spree drinker, decided not to touch a drop until he had made his fortune and retired. He stayed "bone dry for twenty-five years" (p. 32), then retired at fifty-five, sure that his long sobriety had qualified him to drink like other men. Within two months he was in hospital. He couldn't control his drinking or stop it, and he was dead within four years (pp. 32–33). - The lesson: "Most of us have believed that if we remained sober for a long stretch, we could thereafter drink normally" (p. 33). But this man "found he was just where he had left off at thirty" (p. 33). - Then the saying: "We have seen the truth demonstrated again and again: 'Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic'" (p. 33). - And what it means for the reader: "Commencing to drink after a period of sobriety, we are in a short time as bad as ever" (p. 33). So if we're planning to stop, "there must be no reservation of any kind, nor any lurking notion that someday we will be immune to alcohol" (p. 33).

146189242b51.t: The quotation marks show the book is quoting a saying it agrees with. The "truth" it says it has seen proven is about drinking after a long dry spell. The passage isn't about how a member should describe himself or how he should feel about the word.

f6a34da278fc.t: The same 1939 text says plainly that its members have recovered. Chapter 2 opens: "Nearly all have recovered. They have solved the drink problem" (p. 17). The 1939 Foreword introduces the writers as men and women "who have recovered from a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body" (p. xiii), and today's title page reads "Have Recovered from Alcoholism" (p. iii). Fred, in Chapter 3, says his alcoholic condition was relieved and life became "infinitely more satisfying" (pp. 42–43).

c575830b4e9e.t: The book holds both at once. The drink problem can be solved, and the obsession removed: "We will seldom be interested in liquor" (p. 84). But that freedom doesn't make a man a normal drinker. "We are not cured of alcoholism. What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition" (p. 85). Read that way, "once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic" and "recovered" are not in conflict: one is about whether you can ever drink safely again, the other about whether the drink problem has been solved.

3f75ff51bdc6.t: Two stories now in <0>Experience, Strength and Hope</0> (2003) use the saying the same way. "Annie the Cop Fighter," from the second edition (1955–1976), after five years sober: "There's another thing I must remember, that once an alcoholic always an alcoholic" (<1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1>, 2003, story from the 1955 edition). "Lifesaving Words," an Indian Army officer's story dropped in 2001, contrasts going on the wagon with knowing that if he stayed away from the first drink, he needn't worry about the hundredth, and ends: "Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic" (<2>Experience, Strength and Hope</2>, 2003, story from an earlier edition).
