11c044eebf1c.t: Is "one day at a time" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

194c658d3f36.t: Not in the program. The phrase "one day at a time" is nowhere in the 1939 program text, pages 1 to 164, nor in the forewords or the appendices.

c838843d2d9d.t: Is "one day at a time" in the Big Book?

382450b15b4f.t: Not in the program. The phrase "one day at a time" is nowhere in the 1939 program text, pages 1 to 164, nor in the forewords or the appendices.

0b5c465c86b6.t: It appears in ten personal stories in today's (fourth) edition, and in later history books.

679f71699c06.t: The program text has its own daily language: a "daily reprieve" that depends on keeping up a spiritual condition (p. 85), a morning look at "the twenty-four hours ahead" (p. 86), and a program walked "day by day" (pp. 99–100). In the program text the day is a unit of spiritual work and of helping others, not only a day without a drink.

eb336854e806.t: The whole fourth-edition text was searched for "one day at a time," "a day at a time," "day by day," "twenty-four hours," "24 hours" and "just for today," with page breaks and the chapters' drop-capital first words joined so a split phrase would still match.

f30e034030d4.t: <0>Program text, forewords, appendices:</0> no "one day at a time" and no "a day at a time."

a75c5993094b.t: <0>Personal stories (fourth edition, 2001):</0> the phrase is in stories in all three parts, for example "The Man Who Mastered Fear" (p. 255), "The Missing Link" (pp. 286–288), "Fear of Fear" (p. 293), "The Housewife Who Drank at Home" (p. 300), "Crossing the River of Denial" (pp. 333, 336), "Because I'm an Alcoholic" (pp. 345–346), "A Drunk, Like You" (p. 401), "Grounded" (p. 528) and "A.A. Taught Him to Handle Sobriety" (p. 559). The stories change with every edition (Preface, pp. xi–xii), so these are members' own words, not program text.

5c6efa22cdf1.t: <0>Stories printed in 1939 and later dropped</0> (collected in <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1>, 2003): the phrase isn't there either. The nearest is "The Back-Slider," whose writer, after a relapse, gets results by "asking Him to keep me a sober man for 24 hours" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003), and "The Salesman," whose surrender to a Higher Power "became a daily duty" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). Later stories collected in the same book, ones taken out of the third edition in 2001, do use the saying: "Calculating the Costs" ends with staying away from the first drink "one day at a time" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003).

271c763893b4.t: The stories use the phrase in more than one way. Some mean not drinking today: newcomers told one writer "They suggested I could just stay sober one day at a time" (p. 286). Others mean living in the present: "as we begin to live in the present, one day at a time" (p. 559). One writer lists it among the sayings that "began to impress me as truths I could live by" (p. 345).

48a144c0ac55.t: Where the idea shows up early

bb25b84f4e91.t: "Alcoholic Anonymous Number Three" describes the June 1935 hospital visit from Bill W. and Dr. Bob. Asked whether he could quit for twenty-four hours, the man said anybody could, and they answered: "Just twenty-four hours at a time" (p. 188). That story was written about nineteen years after the visit (p. 188), so it is a later telling of 1935, not 1939 program text.

c811c9c7f5c5.t: <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) has a man who met Bill in a New York brokerage office in 1935 remember Bill saying, "It's just one day at a time" (Pass It On, 1984). That is a recollection printed almost fifty years later.

e3f2e81a77a4.t: What the program text says about each day

2e6a76fd063a.t: The 1939 text is concerned with days, but in its own terms:

d36f601db7b8.t: <0>A reprieve, not a cure.</0> "What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition" (p. 85). The next sentence says what each day asks: "Every day is a day when we must carry the vision of God's will into all of our activities" (p. 85).

552194987025.t: <0>Morning and night.</0> Step Eleven's directions begin each day with "On awakening let us think about the twenty-four hours ahead" (p. 86) and end it with a review of the day (p. 86). See: <1>What do Steps 10 and 11 ask, day to day?</1>

bdecd221ba97.t: <0>Faith all day.</0> Bill W.: "Faith has to work twenty-four hours a day in and through us, or we perish" (p. 16).

75717f1b0008.t: <0>Walking it with a newcomer.</0> "Let the alcoholic continue his program day by day" (p. 99), and "Both you and the new man must walk day by day in the path of spiritual progress" (p. 100).

f4f07721cc58.t: <0>Each day for someone else.</0> The last page of the program: "Ask Him in your morning meditation what you can do each day for the man who is still sick" (p. 164). Chapter 7 says the same in other words: "You have to act the Good Samaritan every day, if need be" (p. 97).

73575d6adff2.t: So the program text does break life into days. What fills the day in that text is prayer, inventory, carrying God's will into activities and helping another alcoholic. As some stories use it, the saying can mean only not drinking today; the program text's days hold more than that.

ba2ba1329f9c.t: What Bill W. said about the saying later (1962)

98c2c6ed60b0.t: In his 1962 <0>Twelve Concepts for World Service</0> (Concept IX), writing about leadership and planning, Bill says members are always telling themselves "One day at a time," but that the principle means "not foolishly to repine over the past nor wishfully to day-dream about the future" (A.A. Service Manual combined with Twelve Concepts for World Service). He warns against using it as a reason not to plan ahead. That is 1962, after Dr. Bob's death, and about A.A.'s services rather than one person's recovery.

1ba097a81eed.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) has an Akron member recall Dr. Bob telling him in the 1940s that "Easy Does It" means "you take it a day at a time" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), and that it does not mean staying home from meetings. That is a recollection printed thirty years after Dr. Bob died. See: <1>Are "Easy Does It," "First Things First" and "Live and Let Live" in the Big Book?</1>

834336cec70d.t: What is the only requirement for A.A. membership? | Recovery Starts

25489b61e9e0.t: A desire to stop drinking. The short form of Tradition Three says: "The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking" (p. 562).

20722bc84cc4.t: What is the only requirement for A.A. membership?

ef2233c028f1.t: A desire to stop drinking. The short form of Tradition Three says: "The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking" (p. 562).

16bd7626c59d.t: The original Long Form doesn't use the word "requirement" at all. It says A.A. should include everyone who suffers from alcoholism, refuse no one who wants to recover, and never make membership depend on "money or conformity" (p. 563).

727cd66c1352.t: The person decides. In 1946 Bill W. wrote that a newcomer joins "on his own say-so" and needn't even admit he's an alcoholic. There are no dues, no pledge, and no requirement to believe anything or do the Steps.

268d05565216.t: The idea is older than the Traditions. The Foreword to the First Edition (1939) says: "The only requirement for membership is an honest desire to stop drinking" (p. xiv). In the same breath it says there are "no fees or dues whatsoever" (p. xiv) and that A.A. isn't allied with any faith, sect or denomination.

52a9982192c4.t: When Bill W. wrote the essay Tradition Three grew out of, in 1946, he began by quoting that 1939 statement as how the members had felt the year the book came out (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). The rest of the essay is about what happened next: groups piled up membership rules, the rules failed, and A.A. came back to the open door (see <0>Can anyone be thrown out of A.A.?</0>).

f12143faeea0.t: The Long Form of 1946 states Tradition Three this way: "Our membership ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism. Hence we may refuse none who wish to recover." (p. 563). It adds that membership should never depend "upon money or conformity" (p. 563), and that any two or three alcoholics gathered for sobriety may call themselves a group, if the group has no other affiliation (p. 563).

5e998dff0a17.t: The short form, condensed from the Long Form by 1950, is the one-line version: a desire to stop drinking (p. 562). The 1939 "honest desire" had become plain "desire." (In 1957 Bill quoted it as "a sincere desire to stop drinking" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957), an in-between wording.)

66cf5bc84cc4.t: The A.A. Preamble says the same: "The only requirement for membership is a desire to stop drinking" (P-16, 2018, the Preamble). The Preamble was first published in the Grapevine in June 1947, based on the 1939 foreword (A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026 edition). We quote it as printed today; we haven't seen the 1947 wording.

be6f4e3801b7.t: Bill's 1946 essay shows how low the bar is meant to be. "If alcohol is an uncontrollable problem to him and he wishes to do something about it, that is enough for us." (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). It doesn't matter whether his case is severe or light, whether his morals are good or bad, or whether he has other complications. A newcomer who starts to do anything about his problem is a member. "He joins us on his own say-so." (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). In most groups, Bill says, he doesn't even have to admit he's an alcoholic. He can join "on the mere suspicion that he may be one" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946).

328795326777.t: Read together, these texts rule out the usual add-ons: - <0>Money.</0> No fees or dues (p. xiv); membership never depends on money (p. 563). Contributions are "in no wise a condition of our A.A. membership" (P-17, "Money", 1946). - <1>Conformity.</1> Membership never depends on conformity (p. 563). Among the people early groups feared and tried to shut out, Bill lists those who refused to accept all the Twelve Steps and those who called "the God business" bunk (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). His conclusion was that such people "seldom harm an A.A. group for long" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). - <2>A sponsor, or someone to vouch for you.</2> Among the old rules Bill says would have kept the pioneers out was a sponsor refusing "to vouch for us as a candidate" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). - <3>Signing anything.</3> "He signs nothing, agrees to nothing, promises nothing." (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946).

319d1b788bc8.t: The Tradition doesn't say a person has to have stopped drinking to be a member, only that they want to. Nor does it say who judges the desire. The 1946 essay answers that: no one but the person. "He is a member as long as he says he is." (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946).

58585df957c8.t: What's the difference between open and closed meetings? Can family or friends come? | Recovery Starts

45c5c8af9f0f.t: Today's definitions come from The A.A. Group (P-16, 2018). Closed meetings are "for A.A. members only, or for those who have a drinking problem and 'have…

bf646a0b9802.t: What's the difference between open and closed meetings? Can family or friends come?

47d70aa276ba.t: Today's definitions come from <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16, 2018). Closed meetings are "for A.A. members only, or for those who have a drinking problem and 'have a desire to stop drinking.'" Open meetings are available to anyone interested in A.A.'s program, and "Nonalcoholics may attend open meetings as observers." (P-16, 2018).

2a30c79ca73a.t: So family and friends can come to open meetings. Closed meetings are for alcoholics.

c451fa421f61.t: The 1939 text has no such distinction. The first weekly meeting it describes was for "anyone or everyone interested in a spiritual way of life" (p. 160), and wives came too (p. 160).

14bf2de6d3cf.t: The distinction grew up later and unevenly. In 1946 Bill W. described some groups that kept out even wives and others that held public meetings (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946). Akron's meetings were open; closed meetings came later (<0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0>, 1980).

08f0f8c5dcd8.t: Chapter 11 describes the fellowship in "a certain western city" (p. 153), Akron (p. 156, later footnote), as it was when the book was written. Members met informally in each other's homes most evenings, and it became customary to "set apart one night a week for a meeting" (p. 159), open to anyone or everyone interested in a spiritual way of life. Its prime object was "to provide a time and place where new people might bring their problems" (p. 160).

a421abb75a12.t: The home where that meeting was held was open to families. "Many a distracted wife has visited this house to find loving and understanding companionship among women who knew her problem" (p. 160). A new man and his wife would leave "elated by the thought of what they could now do for some stricken acquaintance and his family" (p. 161), and families drove long distances to be there (p. 161).

7f1de6d63b3d.t: The 1939 text doesn't use the words "open meeting" or "closed meeting."

0b5298e8c0d6.t: In his 1946 essay on anonymity, Bill W. describes the range. Some groups, especially newer ones, acted like secret societies and did not want "preachers, doctors, or even their wives at any of their meetings" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946). Others held public or semipublic meetings with members speaking on the platform.

2bf366333161.t: Bill thought too much caution was a mistake. Groups that held no meetings except those for alcoholics only, year after year, would grow slowly: "Such groups are apt to grow slowly." (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946). In the usual course, "Little by little some meetings are opened to families and close friends." (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946), and clergymen and doctors are invited now and then.

c715c159fd0c.t: How closed meetings came about (a later account)

3db838c7d303.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) gives Akron's history as the old-timers remembered it. Dr. Bob didn't want separate meetings at first, because husbands and wives had been separated long enough; one old-timer recalled, "Doc didn't believe in closed meetings." (<1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1>, 1980). As single men and women alcoholics began coming in, there was friction with the wives, and that led to closed meetings for alcoholics only and open meetings at which the nonalcoholic wives were not allowed to speak. Later came "open discussion meetings" where wives and other nonmembers could take part.

e2378987d144.t: By 1957 Bill could write that doctors and clergy "are often seen at A.A.'s open meetings" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957).

3fd2cc9dbdf2.t: <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16): - The purpose of all group meetings, quoting the Preamble, is for members to share their experience, strength and hope with each other. - <1>Closed:</1> for A.A. members only, or for those with a drinking problem who have a desire to stop drinking. - <2>Open:</2> available to anyone interested in A.A.'s program of recovery from alcoholism; nonalcoholics may attend as observers. - At both kinds, the chair may ask that discussion keep to recovery from alcoholism. Meetings are "conducted by A.A. members who determine the format of their meetings" (P-16, 2018).

98eef03ed8b7.t: The pamphlet doesn't say which meetings must be open or closed; each group decides, under its own autonomy.

0cd3f4ad7b04.t: For families who want help of their own, the Big Book's later-edition note points to Al-Anon Family Groups, "entirely separate from Alcoholics Anonymous" (p. 121). See <0>Is Al-Anon part of A.A.?</0>

38876e3f6174.t: P-16, <0>The A.A. Group</0> ("The Difference Between Open and Closed A.A. Meetings," p. 13): <1>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/literature/p-16_0723.pdf</1>

e4a69809ed84.t: What did early A.A. take from the Oxford Group, and why did it separate? | Recovery Starts

14417475b755.t: Both co-founders got their start in the Oxford Group, a Christian movement of the 1930s. Bill W. came to it through his friend Ebby in late 1934; Dr. Bob…

8a294314bf50.t: What did early A.A. take from the Oxford Group, and why did it separate?

07157bfa771d.t: Both co-founders got their start in the Oxford Group, a Christian movement of the 1930s. Bill W. came to it through his friend Ebby in late 1934; Dr. Bob had been going to its meetings in Akron for about two and a half years.

51d8ad03ba2d.t: From it early A.A. took the practices of self-examination, admitting defects to another person, making restitution, and giving of oneself to others, along with prayer and dependence on God. Bill said these came "straight from the Oxford Groups" and from its American leader, the Rev. Sam Shoemaker.

66a510757503.t: The alcoholics left because some Oxford Group ways did not work with drunks: pressure and aggressive evangelism, "team guidance," the "absolutes" as a dose too strong at first, and an emphasis on prominent names that clashed with the alcoholics' wish to stay anonymous. The Oxford Group also aimed to change the whole world, while the alcoholics kept to alcoholics.

c2deb9508cd6.t: New York separated in 1937. Cleveland's members broke away in May 1939, and Akron's late in 1939. The 1939 Big Book never names the Oxford Group.

de70a1bb3dd0.t: <0>The 1939 Big Book</0> describes the program but doesn't name the Oxford Group anywhere in its text. Bill's friend simply has "a simple religious idea and a practical program of action" (p. 9).

730c24baa491.t: <0>The 1955 Foreword to the Second Edition</0> gives the connection in one sentence: the broker had met "an alcoholic friend who had been in contact with the Oxford Groups of that day" (pp. xv–xvi). "Though he could not accept all the tenets of the Oxford Groups" (p. xvi), he was convinced of the need for moral inventory, confession of defects, restitution, helpfulness to others, and dependence on God (p. xvi).

1b7848bf989c.t: <0>Dr. Bob, 1948</0> (his last major talk, printed in P-53). Both men had been associated with the Oxford Group, "Bill in New York, for five months, and I in Akron, for two and a half years" (P-53). The group had told Dr. Bob to attend meetings, join a church and pray, and he did, but kept getting drunk (P-53). "Bill had acquired their idea of service. I had not" (P-53). The one thing they hadn't told him was what Bill did that first Sunday: "attempt to be helpful to somebody else." (P-53). He also said the Oxford Group's Four Absolutes were "the only yardsticks we had in the early days, before the Steps" (P-53). See <1>What were the "Four Absolutes"? Are they in the Big Book?</1>

42dde74eb188.t: What A.A. took (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)

16cf0ef7a60e.t: At the 1955 convention Bill said the early A.A. got "its ideas of self-examination, acknowledgment of character defects, restitution for harm done, and working with others straight from the Oxford Groups and directly from Sam Shoemaker" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), "and from nowhere else." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He adds that some Oxford Group attitudes had proved unsuited to A.A.'s purpose, and that Shoemaker's own views on those had later changed (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In the same book, Bill names three sources of the word-of-mouth program: the Oxford Groups, William James and Dr. Silkworth (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

5c4933f4af57.t: Why they separated (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)

628331557457.t: Bill says the New York alcoholics worked alongside the Oxford Groups until the middle of 1937 and parted in the latter part of that year (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). His reasons (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957): - The Oxford Groups did not think much of an aim limited to alcoholics; the alcoholics, for their part, felt sure they could not help save the whole world, but could sober up many drunks. - Drinkers would not take pressure of any kind: "They always had to be led, not pushed." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). They would not stand for aggressive evangelism, nor accept "team guidance" for their personal lives. - The absolutes (honesty, purity, unselfishness, love) were often too much at first: "These ideas had to be fed with teaspoons rather than by buckets." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The terms were also the Oxford Group's own and would tie A.A. to it in the public mind. - Most alcoholics wanted to be anonymous, while the Oxford Groups "depended very much upon the use of prominent names" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

d9dcd9879c7a.t: "Our debt to them, nevertheless, was and is immense, and so the final breakaway was very painful." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In Akron, he says, the members withdrew "later, and well after the A.A. book was published" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

edd4c79e9c9a.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (1980)</0> describes the Oxford Group as a movement founded by Frank Buchman, a Lutheran minister, which sought to recapture first-century Christianity through surrender to God, self-examination, confession, restitution and giving without reward (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). It says many Oxford Groupers were disappointed in the Big Book because it didn't mention the group and the Twelve Steps had replaced the absolutes (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). It gives the reasons offered for leaving the group unnamed: A.A. had to avoid looking affiliated with any religious group, Catholics were coming in, and, a reason it says "never came out publicly," Buchman was regarded by some as sympathetic to Hitler after a widely publicized interview in 1936 (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). After the Cleveland members left in May 1939 (see <1>How did the Cleveland group become the first to call itself Alcoholics Anonymous?</1>), the Akron alcoholics moved their meeting to Dr. Bob's house late that year, and on January 2, 1940, he wrote to Bill: "Have definitely shaken off the shackles of the Oxford Group" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

d813309a553c.t: <0>Pass It On (1984)</0> says the Oxford Group leaders in New York resented Bill's separate meetings for alcoholics, and that Bill left in 1937 (Pass It On, 1984). It quotes his 1940 letter: "some of the Oxford Group presentation and emphasis upon the Christian message saved my life" (Pass It On, 1984), yet "other attitudes of the O.G. nearly got me drunk again" (Pass It On, 1984). He listed aggressive evangelism, personal publicity, the word "absolute," coercion and "checking," and too little emphasis on tolerance (Pass It On, 1984). He did not credit the group publicly, he wrote, for fear of tying A.A. to it in the public mind (Pass It On, 1984). The book dates the Akron break to November and December 1939 (Pass It On, 1984).

e3d8cf19b93f.t: <0>When Akron left.</0> Bill (1957) says "well after the A.A. book was published" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and the timeline in our later printing of his book says the Midwest withdrew in the summer of 1939 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The 1980 and 1984 books put Cleveland's break in May 1939 and Akron's in November–December 1939 (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980; Pass It On, 1984). Dr. Bob in 1948 remembered holding the Akron meetings at "a friend's house" (P-53), unnamed in his talk (the other accounts place them at T. Henry Williams's), "Until 1940, or maybe early in 1941" (P-53).

75180f9dbe81.t: <0>The new name, Moral Re-Armament.</0> <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> says Buchman renamed the movement in 1939 (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980); <2>Pass It On</2> says 1938 (Pass It On, 1984).

b0f9ee5439ca.t: Is "people, places and things" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

7020a3ace25e.t: No. The phrase isn't in the Big Book or anywhere else in our sources.

cdb5f817cf3f.t: Is "people, places and things" in the Big Book?

b4c6b8dfb69a.t: No. The phrase isn't in the Big Book or anywhere else in our sources.

e5da3c665e82.t: The nearest list in the program text is a different idea: in the resentment inventory "We listed people, institutions or principles with whom we were angry" (p. 64).

2c3c133e91ad.t: On the advice the phrase usually carries, to stay away from drinking people and places, the program text mostly says the opposite. Any plan "which proposes to shield the sick man from temptation is doomed to failure" (p. 101), and the rule is "not to avoid a place where there is drinking, if we have a legitimate reason for being there" (p. 101). It adds a real condition: be spiritually fit, have a good reason, and if you're shaky, go and work with another alcoholic instead (pp. 100–102).

8f5bcf3cb97f.t: All our sources were searched for "people, places," "places and things," "people and places," "persons, places," "old haunts" and "drinking pals," with page breaks joined. The phrase doesn't appear anywhere: not in the program text, the stories of any edition, the pamphlets or the history books. (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> has a picture section headed "People and places," which is a caption, not the saying.)

9a16b2d6054a.t: The list the book does have

8699d159ae62.t: Step Four's resentment inventory: "We listed people, institutions or principles with whom we were angry." (p. 64). The point there is to find our own part in each resentment, not to avoid anyone: "The inventory was ours, not the other man's." (p. 67). See: <0>How does the Big Book say to do Step 4?</0>

dcd3d51e6e34.t: What the book says about drinking places and drinking friends

4e1501bee9f5.t: Chapter 7 takes the question head on (pp. 100–103). It starts with a condition: "Assuming we are spiritually fit, we can do all sorts of things alcoholics are not supposed to do." (p. 100). Then it lists what "People have said" (p. 100): don't go where liquor is served, don't have it at home, shun friends who drink, avoid films with drinking scenes, stay out of bars (pp. 100–101). Its answer: "Our experience shows that this is not necessarily so." (p. 101). An alcoholic who can't face these things "still has an alcoholic mind" (p. 101).

3ba6d1f92e8d.t: "In our belief any scheme of combating alcoholism which proposes to shield the sick man from temptation is doomed to failure." (p. 101). "So our rule is not to avoid a place where there is drinking, if we have a legitimate reason for being there." (p. 101).

a899f31ae9b2.t: The same pages set limits, and they matter: - Ask each time, "Have I any good social, business, or personal reason for going to this place?" (p. 101), or am I hoping to steal some pleasure from the atmosphere (pp. 101–102). - "But be sure you are on solid spiritual ground before you start and that your motive in going is thoroughly good." (p. 102). - "But if you are shaky, you had better work with another alcoholic instead!" (p. 102). - "Don't start to withdraw again just because your friends drink liquor." (p. 102).

053a53e7373e.t: The same idea comes back elsewhere. To the wife: "We never, never try to arrange a man's life so as to shield him from temptation." (p. 120). To the employer: if the man is following the program, "he can go anywhere your business may call him" (p. 147). And in Step Ten, the result described is "We are not fighting it, neither are we avoiding temptation." (p. 85).

12af21e6d048.t: A fourth-edition story, "Safe Haven" (Part III), lists among the things the writer did that "were suggested for me not to do" in his first year: "hanging around old haunts with my old drinking pals" (p. 455), along with not using his sponsor and avoiding the Steps (p. 455). That is one member's experience in a later edition. It is close to the saying's advice, and it isn't program text.

5f8ea7ffb722.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) leans the same way for Dr. Bob himself. Its writers say that, remembering his own disastrous trip to Atlantic City, "Dr. Bob advocated that members stay in dry places whenever possible" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). An Akron member, Alex M., remembers him saying of a bar on Main Street, "Stay away from that place." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). These are recollections printed thirty years after Dr. Bob's death, not program text, but they show that one co-founder's personal advice leaned toward keeping out of drinking places, more than Chapter 7's rule does.

0c08a6a6ca7d.t: The phrase isn't the Big Book's. Its usual advice, keep away from drinking people and places, has a partial footing in Chapter 7's caution that a shaky person should not go and should work with another alcoholic instead (p. 102), and in Dr. Bob's remembered advice to stay in dry places whenever possible (1980). But the program text's rule runs the other way: a spiritually fit member with a good reason goes where his life takes him, and protection comes from his spiritual condition, not from avoiding places (pp. 100–102). See: <0>Does the Big Book say to avoid bars and drinkers?</0>

554f38706d48.t: Are the personal stories part of the A.A. program? | Recovery Starts

cace6dee7808.t: The Big Book itself separates the two. The program is set out in the first part of the book, the "clear-cut directions" (p. 29), with the Steps offered…

cd7ad65902f7.t: Are the personal stories part of the A.A. program?

a28d59748578.t: The Big Book itself separates the two. The program is set out in the first part of the book, the "clear-cut directions" (p. 29), with the Steps offered "as a program of recovery" (p. 59). The personal stories that follow are members' accounts of their own recovery.

60d7cbb98a29.t: The book says what the stories are for: each writer tells "in his own language and from his own point of view" (p. 29) how he found his relationship with God, so a reader can recognize himself and say, "Yes, I am one of them too" (p. 29).

fa835d5af35a.t: The stories change with every edition; the program text has been "left largely untouched" since 1939 (p. xi). Most of today's stories were written long after 1939.

aa7a4e66eb05.t: So a line from a story is one member's experience, not program text, however well it's loved. The program text has a few stories of its own, above all Bill's in Chapter 1, and those are 1939 text; Bill's story and Dr. Bob's, which opens the story section, were kept intact when the stories were revised in 1955 (p. xi).

af4506bd36f5.t: How the Big Book describes its own parts

555c3c02e786.t: <0>Chapter 2, "There Is a Solution" (1939).</0> The book lays out its plan: chapters explaining alcoholism and addressing the agnostic, then "Further on, clear-cut directions are given showing how we recovered. These are followed by forty-two personal experiences." (p. 29). The stories, it says, "give a fair cross section of our membership" (p. 29) and show what has actually happened in the writers' lives. Their purpose is identification: the authors believe that only by disclosing themselves will readers be "persuaded to say, 'Yes, I am one of them too; I must have this thing.'" (p. 29).

3a1dfa85480b.t: <0>Chapter 4, "We Agnostics" (1939).</0> The stories are where the book shows how differently members understand God: "In our personal stories you will find a wide variation in the way each teller approaches and conceives of the Power which is greater than himself." (p. 50). Whether a reader agrees with any one of them "seems to make little difference" (p. 50); such questions are "for each individual to settle for himself" (p. 50).

27e39e19e8ab.t: <0>Chapter 5, "How It Works" (1939).</0> The chapter moves from the stories to the program: "Our stories disclose in a general way what we used to be like, what happened, and what we are like now." (p. 58). Then, for a reader who wants what they have: "Here are the steps we took, which are suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59).

d54ed5205d99.t: <0>The story section itself.</0> Its title page says the stories show "How Forty-Two Alcoholics Recovered From Their Malady" (p. 165), and each part has its own aim: Part I shows "that sobriety in A.A. can be lasting," Part II may help a reader decide whether he is alcoholic and whether A.A. is for him, and Part III offers hope to those who think their drinking hopeless (p. 167).

f43dea10bb77.t: The stories change; the program doesn't

f55d85d86547.t: The Preface (fourth edition, 2001) explains that, because the book has become A.A.'s basic text, "the first portion of this volume, describing the A.A. recovery program, has been left largely untouched" in the 1955, 1976 and 2001 revisions (p. xi). "But the chief change was in the section of personal stories" (p. xi): stories were added, edited and removed in every edition (pp. xi–xii). The reason given is "to represent the current membership of Alcoholics Anonymous more accurately, and thereby to reach more alcoholics" (p. xii). The Preface's hope is that a reader will pause in a story and think, most important of all, "Yes, I believe this program can work for me too." (p. xii). The story leads to the program; it isn't the program.

07129ff6df21.t: Even the count in Chapter 2 follows the story section: the fourth edition's p. 29 says "forty-two," the number of stories in the fourth edition (p. xii). See <0>What changed between the four editions of the Big Book?</0>

1d15a8b7cef9.t: What the early writers said the stories were for

09bb75205a27.t: <0>Bill W. (1957)</0> says the story section was added because "We would have to produce evidence in the form of living proof" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and because the stories could "identify us with the distant reader in a way that the text itself might not" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

4b7758826b9f.t: <0>Bill W. (1954 letter, printed in <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1>, 2003)</0>, while gathering stories for the second edition: the story section "is our principal means of identifying with the reader outside of A.A." (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003) and "our show window of results" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). "The main purpose of the revision is to bring the story section up to date" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003).

6ded9776263f.t: Both describe the stories as evidence that the program works and as a bridge to the reader. Neither treats them as instructions.

b96d361c0fc1.t: Personal stories aren't only at the back. Chapter 1 is "Bill's Story," and the Preface says it, "Doctor Bob's Nightmare" and one other first-edition story were "retained intact" in 1955 (p. xi). Chapter 10, "To Employers," is told largely by one member (p. 136), and Chapter 11 tells the story of the Akron beginnings (pp. 153–158). These belong to the 1939 text, and the book uses them to show the program at work. The stories that change from edition to edition are the ones from p. 165 on.

31d86da5d2b1.t: Lines from the stories are often quoted at meetings as if they were Big Book program text. Some well-known examples: "acceptance is the answer" is from a story that wasn't in the 1939 book (see <0>Is "Acceptance is the answer" part of the main text?</0>), and the word "sponsor" appears only in the stories, never in the program text (see <1>Is the word "sponsor" in the Big Book?</1>). A story is a member's honest experience, and the book offers it as such: "in his own language and from his own point of view" (p. 29). That's why Recovery Starts pages say "a member's story, not the program text" when they quote one.

e5b28fdd5ca3.t: The book is modest even about its program text: "Our book is meant to be suggestive only." (p. 164).

cb005b986ca0.t: What is "the phenomenon of craving," and what is the "allergy"? | Recovery Starts

8ad490e9037f.t: Both phrases come from Dr. William D. Silkworth's statement in "The Doctor's Opinion" at the front of the Big Book, kept as he wrote it in 1939 (p. xi).…

ce13eda8edaa.t: What is "the phenomenon of craving," and what is the "allergy"?

2559220d0075.t: Both phrases come from Dr. William D. Silkworth's statement in "The Doctor's Opinion" at the front of the Big Book, kept as he wrote it in 1939 (p. xi). He suggests that alcohol's action on chronic alcoholics is "a manifestation of an allergy" and that "the phenomenon of craving is limited to this class and never occurs in the average temperate drinker" (p. xxviii).

cc99ef79b0a1.t: In his account the craving is set off by drinking. These alcoholics "cannot start drinking without developing the phenomenon of craving" (p. xxx). The only relief he knows is "entire abstinence" (p. xxx).

d5b7d14ae13c.t: Quoted alone, "allergy" can sound like settled medicine. In its setting it's a theory: Silkworth says the craving "may be the manifestation of an allergy" (p. xxx), and the A.A. members who introduce him call it "The doctor's theory," saying that as laymen their opinion of it "may, of course, mean little" (p. xxvi). They add that it "makes good sense" to them (p. xxvi).

16e886deb60d.t: The familiar pairing of an allergy of the body with an obsession of the mind isn't in the Doctor's Opinion. In the Big Book it's in two members' stories (pp. 261, 355). Bill W. credits it to Silkworth in <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957, after 1950).

471fec4032d1.t: The craving, in the doctor's words

bae017ddc1f0.t: Silkworth's longer statement (pp. xxvii–xxxii) comes back to the craving again and again: - <0>It's physical, and it's treated first.</0> An alcoholic ought first to be freed from his physical craving for liquor, which often takes a hospital procedure, before psychological measures can be of most benefit (pp. xxvii–xxviii). - <1>It's the mark of a type.</1> The craving belongs to chronic alcoholics and never occurs in the temperate drinker. "These allergic types can never safely use alcohol in any form at all" (p. xxviii). - <2>It takes over once drinking starts.</2> He describes men who worked for months on a deal, took a drink a day or two before it closed, and "the phenomenon of craving at once became paramount to all other interests" (p. xxix), so they missed the appointment. "These men were not drinking to escape; they were drinking to overcome a craving beyond their mental control." (p. xxx) - <3>It's what all types share.</3> He lists several kinds of alcoholic, then says they have "one symptom in common" (p. xxx): they can't start drinking without the craving developing. It "has never been, by any treatment with which we are familiar, permanently eradicated" (p. xxx).

4a884b9e910d.t: How sure the book is about the allergy

7790f8eb740e.t: The text is careful: - Silkworth: "We believe, and so suggested a few years ago" (p. xxviii) that it is a manifestation of an allergy; and later, the craving "may be" one (p. xxx). - The A.A. members: "The doctor's theory that we have an allergy to alcohol interests us." (p. xxvi) As laymen they can't judge its soundness, but as ex-problem drinkers "his explanation makes good sense" (p. xxvi).

cbd2a73c0053.t: What they're sure of is the physical side itself. They write that "the body of the alcoholic is quite as abnormal as his mind" (p. xxvi), and "any picture of the alcoholic which leaves out this physical factor is incomplete" (p. xxvi).

1a483ab8c23c.t: The allergy isn't the doctor's whole picture. Between drinks, he says, the alcoholic is "restless, irritable and discontented" (p. xxviii) until he can feel again the ease a few drinks bring. After the spree comes remorse and a firm resolution, repeated over and over (p. xxix). He doesn't think alcoholism is "entirely a problem of mental control" (p. xxix), but he also says there is very little hope "unless this person can experience an entire psychic change" (p. xxix).

57adaf3d3b8d.t: Chapter 2 says the same from the members' side. Once the alcoholic takes any alcohol, "something happens, both in the bodily and mental sense" (p. 22). But because the cycle can't start without the first drink, "the main problem of the alcoholic centers in his mind, rather than in his body" (p. 23).

0d9f27c57163.t: Where the allergy-and-obsession pairing comes from

f3db782c43c1.t: The two-part phrase, often quoted as if it were the Big Book's own definition, doesn't appear in the Doctor's Opinion or the 1939 chapters. In the Big Book it turns up in members' stories. In "He Sold Himself Short" (Part I), the writer recalls being told that drinking was "a fatal illness made up of an allergy plus an obsession" (p. 261). In "It Might Have Been Worse" (Part II), the writer says the explanation of alcoholism as "an allergy of the body and an obsession of the mind" (p. 355) cleared up a lot for him. The 1939 chapters do speak of obsession in their own words: the idea that he will somehow control and enjoy his drinking "is the great obsession of every abnormal drinker" (p. 30).

78d5b03280a5.t: Bill W., writing in 1957, credits the pairing to Silkworth: "the obsession of the mind that compels us to drink and the allergy of the body that condemns us to go mad or die" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) reports that Bill later said Silkworth used "allergy" knowing it wasn't exact: "He knew this was a misnomer" (<2>Pass It On</2>, 1984). Both books are after 1950, and both give Bill's later recollection; they're useful for where the phrase came from, not as part of the 1939 text.

dd0ac528daa9.t: It complicates it. The phrases are quoted accurately and Silkworth means them. But the book offers the allergy as a theory, hedged by both the doctor and the members, while holding firmly that the alcoholic's body is abnormal. The craving it describes starts with drinking, and the book pairs it with a mind that is "without defense against the first drink" (p. 24) and with Silkworth's own view that recovery takes a psychic change. For the section as a whole, see <0>What is "The Doctor's Opinion," and who wrote it?</0>

37d4cb6f4dbf.t: What is the "pink cloud"? Is it in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

6e3950d922e4.t: The phrase "pink cloud" isn't in the Big Book's 1939 program text, pages 1 to 164. It appears in two personal stories in the fourth edition (pp. 304,…

20d026f2e113.t: What is the "pink cloud"? Is it in the Big Book?

dd024b99c225.t: The phrase "pink cloud" isn't in the Big Book's 1939 program text, pages 1 to 164. It appears in two personal stories in the fourth edition (pp. 304, 346), both describing a high that came early in sobriety and didn't last.

2d16e1d08cf0.t: Bill W. uses it in <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) for his own excitement in 1937: "riding high on pink cloud number 17," when he thought the Rockefellers would fund A.A. They didn't, not on the scale he hoped.

7e00f0ebc47f.t: The fullest description is by a psychiatrist, Dr. Harry Tiebout, at A.A.'s 1955 convention, printed in the same book. He calls it "a logical aftermath of surrender" and says everyone knows the person on it is "doomed for a fall."

1db75d12c75d.t: The program text describes something similar in its own words. It warns against resting on your laurels (p. 85), and it tells families that a man's "spiritual intoxication" early on is a phase (pp. 128–129).

ee972d185bd9.t: All our sources were searched for "pink cloud," "cloud" and other wordings such as "honeymoon."

e92f40d0a9bc.t: <0>Personal stories (fourth edition):</0> - "Physician, Heal Thyself!" (Part II): three months sober and reading everything spiritual he could find, the writer "floated higher and higher" until he was "way up on a pink cloud, which is known as Pink Seven, and I felt miserable again" (p. 304). A friend told him he'd "been floating way up on a cloud somewhere" and sent him to page 58 of the Big Book, where the word "thoroughly" struck him (p. 305). - "Because I'm an Alcoholic" (Part II): "For a time I floated on that pink cloud. Then I cried for a year, raged for another year" (p. 346).

225aecefb282.t: <0>Bill W., about 1937.</0> After a promising lunch with Willard Richardson, who ran Mr. Rockefeller's private charities, and the promise of a meeting in Mr. Rockefeller's board room, Bill rushed home and phoned Dr. Bob: "We were riding high on pink cloud number 17" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). At the December 1937 meeting the businessmen were moved, but asked, "Won't money spoil this thing?" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957). Mr. Rockefeller later gave $5,000 and asked not to be asked for more. Bill looks back on it as "very great news" for A.A. that seemed bad at the time, "a shattering blow to our hopes" (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957).

7cb25743913f.t: <0>Dr. Harry Tiebout, 1955.</0> At the St. Louis convention, Dr. Tiebout, a psychiatrist who said he had "joined A.A. by proxy in 1939" when a patient of his became a member (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957), spoke about the ego. He said perhaps the commonest sign of the ego coming back is "the individual who falls from his pink cloud, a state of mind familiar to you all" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957). His explanation, in short: - "The blissful pink cloud state is a logical aftermath of surrender" (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957). The ego stops striving, the person feels peace and release, and "thinks he has found heaven on earth" (<4>A.A. Comes of Age</4>, 1957). - What brings him down is "the ego slowly making its comeback" (<5>A.A. Comes of Age</5>, 1957). The descent puts him back into ordinary life, where, with A.A.'s help, he can learn to be "a sober person and not an angel" (<6>A.A. Comes of Age</6>, 1957). - Tiebout said he had ridden the pink cloud himself in his first years with A.A., went through a period of disillusionment, and came out with a stronger faith than anything a pink cloud can supply (<7>A.A. Comes of Age</7>, 1957).

cd09dceeb4d1.t: Tiebout's talk is one doctor's view, given in 1955 and printed in 1957. It is not program text.

40005680d3ca.t: What the program text says on the same subject

83498af6a73a.t: The 1939 text doesn't use the phrase, but it describes the early high and the danger of trusting it: - <0>Spiritual intoxication.</0> Chapter 9 tells families that a father may come out of a "stirring spiritual experience" as a religious enthusiast who can talk of nothing else (p. 128). The writers say they've been there: "We have indulged in spiritual intoxication" (p. 128). Like a prospector who has struck gold, he may try to hoard it, not seeing that it pays only if he keeps working it and gives it away (pp. 128–129). The book calls this "a phase of his development" that will pass in an understanding family (p. 129). - <1>Resting on laurels.</1> "It is easy to let up on the spiritual program of action and rest on our laurels. We are headed for trouble if we do" (p. 85). The relief from drinking lasts "so long as we keep in fit spiritual condition" (p. 85). - <2>Not every awakening is sudden.</2> Appendix II (added in 1955) says the first printing left many readers thinking spiritual change had to come as "sudden and spectacular upheavals," and that this is wrong (p. 567). Most change is the slow "educational variety" (p. 567). Bill's own release was sudden, but he writes that "God comes to most men gradually" (p. 14). - <3>The promises come at their own pace.</3> The promises of Chapter 6 come true "sometimes quickly, sometimes slowly" (p. 84).

94b2e5fcef59.t: Is the A.A. Preamble in the Big Book? Where did it come from?

6f86bc3a99bc.t: No. The Preamble that many meetings open with ("Alcoholics Anonymous is a fellowship of people who share their experience, strength and hope…") is not in the fourth-edition Big Book. It is printed in A.A. pamphlets such as P-16 and P-17 and in <0>The A.A. Service Manual</0>.

e339b6f7f0a5.t: It was first published in the Grapevine in June 1947, written by a Grapevine editor and "based on the foreword to the first edition of the Big Book" (<0>A.A. Service Manual</0>, 2024–2026 edition). It is copyrighted by AA Grapevine, Inc.

56454380546a.t: Set side by side, most of it does come from the 1939 Foreword (pp. xiii–xiv): the one requirement, no fees or dues, not allied with any sect or denomination, opposing no one. The opening sentence and the closing statement of purpose are not in the Foreword.

cfe643f299f9.t: Our sources have the Preamble only as it is printed today. It doesn't have the 1947 wording, so changes since then can't be traced here.

c4444c661402.t: The whole fourth-edition text of <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0> was searched for the Preamble's wording. It isn't there. The nearest phrase is in the Forewords to the Third Edition (1976) and Fourth Edition (2001), which say that recovery begins when one alcoholic talks with another, "sharing experience, strength, and hope" (p. xxii), and that in any meeting "A.A.'s share experience, strength, and hope with each other" (p. xxiv).

2ec884203995.t: Three texts in our sources speak to its origin: - <0>The A.A. Service Manual</0> (2024–2026 edition): "First published in the June 1947 issue, the A.A. Preamble (based on the foreword to the first edition of the Big Book) was written by a Grapevine editor" (<1>A.A. Service Manual</1>, 2024–2026 edition). - <2>Pass It On</2> (1984), after quoting the 1939 Foreword: "With a few changes and additions, that statement of purpose would be repeated as a preamble to thousands of A.A. meetings every day in the years to come." (<3>Pass It On</3>, 1984). - The copyright line under the Preamble in P-16, P-17 and the Service Manual: © AA Grapevine, Inc.

80c3db19a09c.t: The 1939 Foreword (pp. xiii–xiv) against the Preamble as printed today (P-16, 2018; P-17, 2019 printing; Service Manual, 2024):

9dfcafb1a991.t: "We are not an organization in the conventional sense of the word." (pp. xiii–xiv)

c09811a9b322.t: A fellowship of people who share their experience, strength and hope with each other, to solve their common problem and help others recover from alcoholism

8823e3c975c5.t: "There are no fees or dues whatsoever." (p. xiv)

fd821054f509.t: No dues or fees for A.A. membership; self-supporting through members' own contributions

edaa7bbd31b0.t: "The only requirement for membership is an honest desire to stop drinking." (p. xiv)

454089331f99.t: "The only requirement for membership is a desire to stop drinking." (P-16, 2018)

989a3ac82f89.t: Not allied with "any particular faith, sect or denomination, nor do we oppose anyone" (p. xiv)

ef9bb17eaebb.t: Not allied with any sect, denomination, politics, organization or institution; does not wish to engage in any controversy; neither endorses nor opposes any causes

74da0a2b0a86.t: "We simply wish to be helpful to those who are afflicted." (p. xiv)

f698f8b5f57d.t: "Our primary purpose is to stay sober and help other alcoholics to achieve sobriety." (P-16, 2018)

e6c38bbd838c.t: What changed, reading the two: - "Honest desire" became "desire," the same change Tradition Three's short form made (p. 562). See <0>What is the only requirement for A.A. membership?</0> - "Faith, sect or denomination" widened to include politics, organizations and institutions, and "nor do we oppose anyone" became "neither endorses nor opposes any causes," wording close to the Traditions on endorsement and outside issues (pp. 562, 564–565). - Self-support was added, in the spirit of Tradition Seven (p. 562). - The Foreword's statement of purpose, being helpful to those afflicted, became a two-part purpose: staying sober, and helping other alcoholics to sobriety. - The opening description, a fellowship sharing "experience, strength and hope," has no counterpart in the 1939 Foreword.

db64584bddd0.t: One small puzzle our sources can't settle: the fourth edition prints the Foreword "as it appeared in the first printing of the first edition in 1939" (p. xiii) and reads "no fees or dues," while <0>Pass It On</0> (1984), quoting the same first printing, has "no fees nor dues." The meaning is the same.

Preamble and a few remarks" (P-16, 2018), and quotes the Preamble as the purpose of all group meetings. It is a custom described in a later pamphlet; the 1939 text describes no meeting format (see <1>What happens at an A.A. meeting?</1>).

b2428157f40c.t: Yes, in substance, and in the program text itself. The exact three words aren't there, but Chapter 5 says: "We claim spiritual progress rather than…

7b2d9f1354d7.t: Is "progress, not perfection" in the Big Book?

d2c1280f2a21.t: Yes, in substance, and in the program text itself. The exact three words aren't there, but Chapter 5 says: "We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection." (p. 60), in the same paragraph as "We are not saints." (p. 60).

a3efeaf81161.t: The paragraph is written to a reader who has just read the Twelve Steps and thinks he can't do them. Its point is stated outright: "The point is, that we are willing to grow along spiritual lines." (p. 60).

65b8fe2a444d.t: The same pages also ask the reader to be "fearless and thorough from the very start" (p. 58) and say "Half measures availed us nothing" (p. 59). So "progress rather than perfection" is about not expecting to be perfect, not about doing less.

90581f4398e7.t: All our sources were searched for "progress, not perfection," "progress rather than," "perfection," "perfect" and "saints," with page breaks joined.

f0d8075b2a98.t: <0>Program text:</0> "spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection" (p. 60), the only place the program text uses the word "perfection."

91cbba58cae7.t: <0>The exact wording "progress, not perfection":</0> not in any book in our sources.

cddfd58c8795.t: <0>Stories and later books:</0> "perfection" turns up in some personal stories and in <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957) in other connections; none uses the saying.

8259e161fbe2.t: Chapter 5 opens by asking a great deal. Those who don't recover are those who cannot or will not "completely give themselves to this simple program" (p. 58), a way of living that "demands rigorous honesty" (p. 58). "With all the earnestness at our command, we beg of you to be fearless and thorough from the very start." (p. 58). "Half measures availed us nothing." (p. 59). Then come the Twelve Steps (pp. 59–60).

75a25da51b14.t: The next paragraph answers the reader's reaction: - Many of us exclaimed, "What an order! I can't go through with it." (p. 60). - "Do not be discouraged. No one among us has been able to maintain anything like perfect adherence to these principles." (p. 60). - "We are not saints." (p. 60). - "The point is, that we are willing to grow along spiritual lines." (p. 60). - "The principles we have set down are guides to progress." (p. 60). - "We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection." (p. 60).

0d4a1d4ca51c.t: Read together, the pages ask for complete willingness and thoroughness, and promise no one that he will carry the principles out perfectly. Neither half cancels the other. See: <0>What does "half measures availed us nothing" mean in context?</0>

ff50129d85df.t: The same idea elsewhere in the program text

f949217a73e4.t: <0>Growth over a lifetime.</0> Step Ten: "Our next function is to grow in understanding and effectiveness. This is not an overnight matter. It should continue for our lifetime." (p. 84). The Promises come true "sometimes quickly, sometimes slowly" (p. 84).

f5f330c3f1d1.t: <0>Falling short.</0> "Of course, we all fall much below this standard many times. But we must try to repair the damage immediately lest we pay the penalty by a spree." (p. 99).

f8e260493715.t: <0>An ideal to grow toward.</0> On sex conduct: "Whatever our ideal turns out to be, we must be willing to grow toward it." (p. 69).

934918e202c9.t: <0>Walking a path.</0> "Both you and the new man must walk day by day in the path of spiritual progress." (p. 100). Families are told to "praise his progress" (p. 127) and to see his defects won't vanish overnight (p. 100).

d12242481a68.t: In <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957), Bill W., describing early A.A.'s dreams of reforming the world, wrote that most alcoholics were idealists: "We were perfectionists who, failing to attain perfection, had gone to the other extreme and settled for the bottle and the blackout." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). That is 1957, after Dr. Bob's death, and it isn't program text.

1493a0a69ac8.t: How can I tell when a quote has been taken out of context? | Recovery Starts

cb24e5f9de45.t: Look the quote up and read the whole passage it comes from: the whole chapter, the whole story or the whole talk. The Big Book is free on aa.org, so this…

dbb3fe4ed06a.t: How can I tell when a quote has been taken out of context?

1f54ad750209.t: Look the quote up and read the whole passage it comes from: the whole chapter, the whole story or the whole talk. The Big Book is free on aa.org, so this takes minutes.

8675a9256553.t: Ask whether the rest of the passage points the same way as the quote. If the pages around it turn its meaning around, it has been taken out of context.

7cfa578d561b.t: Check who is speaking and when: the 1939 program text, a personal story, or a book written decades later.

59edd4f4b64a.t: The clearest example is the first line of Chapter 7, "Working With Others," which is often quoted to mean "help others to keep yourself sober." The chapter's other fourteen pages say the aim is the other alcoholic's life.

4ea739f27de3.t: The worked example: the first line of Chapter 7

4e0a28b1bd1c.t: <0>The line, read alone.</0> Chapter 7 opens: "nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (p. 89). "It works when other activities fail." (p. 89). Lifted out by itself, that sounds like a reason to help others: it keeps <1>you</1> sober. Taught that way, Step Twelve becomes something you do for yourself.

8506d7dcd1da.t: <0>The same page.</0> Read to the bottom of p. 89 and the chapter has already named its subject, "Carry this message to other alcoholics!" (p. 89), and told you how to find drinkers who want to stop, through doctors, ministers and hospitals (p. 89). The page ends, after advising the reader to cooperate with doctors and ministers rather than criticize them: "To be helpful is our only aim." (p. 89).

b5ecc4a06e3b.t: <0>The whole chapter.</0> Read all fifteen pages (pp. 89–103) and the direction is plain: - The man you help is "under no obligation to you" (p. 94), and he's asked to "place the welfare of other people ahead of his own" (p. 94). - Don't stay too long with a man who isn't ready, because that "is to deny some other alcoholic an opportunity to live and be happy" (p. 96). - Expect the work to cost you nights' sleep, interruptions to your business, sharing your money and your home, and trips to courts, hospitals and jails (p. 97). - "Do not think of what you will get out of the occasion." (p. 102). "Think of what you can bring to it." (p. 102).

473170d16423.t: So the first line is true, and the book means it: the work does protect the helper. But it's a result, not the aim. Read whole, Chapter 7 is about rescuing the alcoholic who is still drinking. This page is laid out in full in <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0>

2e61666bf397.t: <0>The same thing, said again in 1939.</0> Chapter 11 says the same about the first Akron members: "Though they knew they must help other alcoholics if they would remain sober, that motive became secondary." (Chapter 11, p. 159). "It was transcended by the happiness they found in giving themselves for others." (Chapter 11, p. 159). When a second passage in the same book confirms the reading of the whole, you can be more confident the lifted line was misleading.

0e589af9a0b6.t: In "Bill's Story," the phrase "Faith without works was dead, he said." (p. 14) is often quoted as a general saying. The sentence just before it tells you what "works" meant to the friend who said it: "Particularly was it imperative to work with others as he had worked with me." (p. 14). The next lines say that an alcoholic who didn't work for others would drink again (pp. 14–15). In context, the "works" are work with other alcoholics.

3c97850742e3.t: Dr. Bob's 1950 Cleveland talk is usually remembered for one line about simplicity. <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980), which prints the whole talk, says so and adds: "But Dr. Bob said a good deal more than that" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). The rest of the talk is about love, service, guarding the tongue, and never becoming too complacent to help the next alcoholic. See <1>When did Dr. Bob die, and what were his last words to A.A.?</1>

80ff5ffa314a.t: <0>Find the exact words and page.</0> If you can't find the quote in the book at all, it may be a misquote or a saying credited to A.A. that isn't in its literature.

f11365fd8078.t: <0>Read the whole unit:</0> the chapter, the story, the essay, or the talk. Start at its beginning.

5c9c66f9e056.t: <0>Read what's right before and after.</0> The sentence before often says what a word means, as with "works" on p. 14.

56bc02a2a3ae.t: <0>Ask whether the rest agrees.</0> If later pages qualify or reverse the line, the line alone is misleading.

fdb98d932e74.t: <0>Check who is speaking.</0> Program text (pp. 1–164), a member's personal story, and an editor's footnote are different kinds of evidence. So are a later book or pamphlet quoting an earlier one, or quoting a different book entirely.

1e28905a6133.t: <0>Check the date.</0> A 1939 passage and a 1980 retelling may not agree. See <1>Which A.A. books are oldest, and why does the date matter?</1>

f9a15ee25152.t: A long book gives anyone plenty of lines to choose from. A line taken from its pages without the pages around it can be made to support almost anything, including the opposite of what the book says. The defence is simple: read it whole, from A.A.'s own free copy.

94b2fbda936b.t: Chapter 7, <0>Working With Others</0> (pp. 89–103), free from A.A.: <1>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt7.pdf</1>

95af1c491e6a.t: Related: <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0> · <1>Is "Working With Others" about sponsorship?</1> · <2>Where can I read the Big Book free, from A.A. itself?</2>

2587b613d979.t: Big Book page numbers are from the fourth edition (2001). The Preface says the program text, Chapters 1–11, "has been left largely untouched" since 1939 (p. xi).

83301b769577.t: What does "Rarely have we seen a person fail" really say, and who does it say may not recover? | Recovery Starts

bfec6bd13b9f.t: It's the first sentence of Chapter 5, "How It Works." The book says that rarely "have we seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path" (p. 58).…

eb775820373b.t: What does "Rarely have we seen a person fail" really say, and who does it say may not recover?

7a9f82a67e06.t: It's the first sentence of Chapter 5, "How It Works." The book says that rarely "have we seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path" (p. 58). It's a strong claim, but it has a condition: it's about people who follow the path thoroughly.

e96513c98fb3.t: The same paragraph names who may not recover: people who "cannot or will not completely give themselves to this simple program" (p. 58). These are usually people "constitutionally incapable of being honest with themselves" (p. 58), and some with "grave emotional and mental disorders" (p. 58).

ac8c850f8510.t: It doesn't blame them. Of the first group it says "They are not at fault; they seem to have been born that way." (p. 58) Their chances are "less than average" (p. 58), which is not the same as none. Of the second group, "many of them do recover if they have the capacity to be honest" (p. 58).

e0bf03498f7c.t: Read in place, the paragraph turns on honesty. Right after the Steps, the book says no one has managed "anything like perfect adherence to these principles" (p. 60), so "thoroughly" doesn't mean perfectly.

aed804349492.t: Quoted by itself, the first sentence can be heard two ways. One is as a guarantee: follow the path and you won't fail. The other turns it around into a verdict on anyone who doesn't recover: he must not have followed it thoroughly. Neither reading can be checked against the sentence alone. It needs the rest of its paragraph.

866a8883d29c.t: The opening paragraph of Chapter 5 is short. In order, it says:

d5ef1e5b3af1.t: <0>The claim.</0> Rarely "have we seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path" (p. 58). The word is "rarely," not "never."

0b7284ba1f5a.t: <0>Who doesn't recover.</0> Those who "cannot or will not" give themselves completely to the program (p. 58). The paragraph names both: "will not" is a refusal, "cannot" is an inability.

e63b9c66e938.t: <0>The usual reason.</0> Most are "constitutionally incapable of being honest with themselves" (p. 58). The book goes on: "There are such unfortunates." (p. 58) "They are not at fault; they seem to have been born that way." (p. 58) They can't grasp and develop a way of living "which demands rigorous honesty" (p. 58). And: "Their chances are less than average." (p. 58)

c3ac9433cd08.t: <0>A second group.</0> "There are those, too, who suffer from grave emotional and mental disorders" (p. 58), and "many of them do recover if they have the capacity to be honest" (p. 58).

75901aac3ca0.t: So the paragraph names two conditions for recovery: giving oneself completely to "this simple program," and the capacity to be honest. Where people fall short of the second, it calls them unfortunate, not guilty.

d844bad8ad1e.t: The "path" isn't left vague. The paragraph itself calls it "this simple program" (p. 58), and the next page introduces the Twelve Steps as "suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59). In between, the book says what it asks of the reader. If you want what the members have and are willing to go to any length for it, "then you are ready to take certain steps" (p. 58). "At some of these we balked." (p. 58) And it begs the reader "to be fearless and thorough from the very start" (p. 58).

a1851cde3c2e.t: Then, right after the Steps, the book heads off the idea that "thoroughly" means flawlessly. "No one among us has been able to maintain anything like perfect adherence to these principles." (p. 60) "We are not saints." (p. 60) "We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection." (p. 60)

a8990b35c484.t: <0>As a guarantee:</0> the book does mean the claim, and repeats its call for thoroughness. But it says "rarely," and the condition is following the path thoroughly. The same chapter says nobody follows it perfectly.

fc31ad7ab055.t: <0>As a verdict on those who don't recover:</0> the paragraph won't carry it. Its own explanation includes people who "cannot," who are "not at fault," and whose chances are lower but not gone. It describes people who are incapable of being honest with themselves, and it calls them unfortunates. It doesn't talk about relapse at all.

c27d73f75333.t: <0>The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955)</0> gives A.A.'s own figures as they stood then. Of alcoholics "who came to A.A. and really tried" (p. xx), half got sober at once and stayed that way, a quarter sobered up "after some relapses," and of the rest, those who stayed on showed improvement (p. xx). So by 1955 the book itself counted people who really tried and still relapsed before they recovered.

406e64a73100.t: <0><1>Pass It On</1> (1984)</0>, a biography of Bill W., says he wrote this paragraph when he wrote the Steps, and that an earlier manuscript said "directions" where the book now says "path." It also tells a story that Bill later wanted to change "rarely" to "never." The book calls that story apocryphal: "Bill himself said he never considered that change." (Pass It On, 1984)

9e3887418ca8.t: Mostly the Bible. Dr. Bob said in 1948 that the older members found three parts "absolutely essential": the Sermon on the Mount, the thirteenth chapter of…

7b1b58a27814.t: What did the first members read before the Big Book existed?

50323fbe04e0.t: Mostly the Bible. Dr. Bob said in 1948 that the older members found three parts "absolutely essential": the Sermon on the Mount, the thirteenth chapter of First Corinthians, and the Book of James (P-53).

7803734aee47.t: In Akron, members' recollections gathered in 1980 add three small books that were passed around by 1938–39, while the Big Book was being written: <0>The Upper Room</0> (a Methodist booklet of daily readings), Emmet Fox's <1>The Sermon on the Mount</1>, and Henry Drummond's <2>The Greatest Thing in the World</2>.

2fa8156ffe0c.t: That reading came with the Oxford Group's morning "quiet time." The program itself was passed on by word of mouth. A member's story describing Akron in 1937 says there was "no literature except various religious pamphlets" (p. 262).

9d75d1544b35.t: The 1939 Big Book doesn't list any of these books. It says only that "There are many helpful books also" (p. 87) and sends the reader to a priest, minister or rabbi for suggestions.

47ca6c9b2f10.t: In his last major talk, recorded in Detroit in December 1948, Dr. Bob described the early days at Akron. Before he met Bill W., he had spent two and a half years with the Oxford Group, had "done an immense amount of reading they had recommended" (P-53), and had refreshed his memory of the Bible. None of it kept him sober; what Bill brought him was the idea of helping someone else (P-53).

130a53c494ec.t: Of the time when he and Bill began working with Bill D., A.A. number three, in June 1935, he said: "we had no Twelve Steps, either; we had no Traditions" (P-53). "But we were convinced that the answer to our problems was in the Good Book." (P-53). Then the passage most often repeated: "To some of us older ones, the parts that we found absolutely essential were the Sermon on the Mount, the thirteenth chapter of First Corinthians, and the Book of James." (P-53). He is talking about parts of the Bible here, not about a separate book.

cd8ab0f08077.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) and <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) both quote the same words (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980; Pass It On, 1984). The 1980 book adds: "They had the Bible, and they had the precepts of the Oxford Group." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

7a6d0e473756.t: When Bill lived with Dr. Bob and Anne Smith in the summer of 1935, the day began with the Oxford Group practice of a morning quiet time. Bill (1957) remembers Anne sitting by the fireplace to "read from the Bible, and then we would huddle together in stillness, awaiting inspiration and guidance" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The 1980 book quotes him: "James was our favorite" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), and Anne would end with the verse "Faith without works is dead" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). The Book of James was liked so well that some wanted to call the fellowship "The James Club" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). See <0>Is "faith without works is dead" in the Big Book?</0>

e2ba2684c304.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> gathers the recollections of early Akron members. They are memories recorded decades later, and the book itself notes how often they differ; as one member put it, they had all seen the same events "from different angles" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - <1>The Bible first.</1> "The Bible was stressed as reading material, of course." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Patients in the hospital in the early days were allowed only a Bible to read (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - <2><3>The Upper Room.</3></2> Dr. Bob's daughter, Sue, remembered that the morning Bible reading was later joined by <4>The Upper Room</4>, "a Methodist publication that provided a daily inspirational message" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Another early member, Dorothy S. M., called it "that little nickel book" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980) and said members were told to read it every morning (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). At the weekly meeting in T. Henry Williams's house, the leader usually took something from it, or from other literature, as a subject (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - <5>Emmet Fox's <6>The Sermon on the Mount</6>.</5> Dorothy remembered it as "required reading for everybody" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), handed to men in the hospital as soon as they could focus their eyes. - <7>Henry Drummond's <8>The Greatest Thing in the World</8>.</7> Bob E. of Akron recalled it as another popular book of the time, which, like <9>The Upper Room</9>, was given out to members by a woman remembered as Mother G. (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

fcc811a345b4.t: Dorothy summed up: "Those were the three main books at the time" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), meaning Drummond, <0>The Upper Room</0> and Fox. Dr. Bob himself read widely: his son remembered that he read the Bible through three times and owned books from William James's <1>Varieties</1> to <2>For Sinners Only</2>, a book about the Oxford Group (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), but Dorothy said "he didn't push books at people" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

23d7a61b1992.t: A caution on dates: the 1980 book sets this reading in "1938-39" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), when the Big Book was being written, and it doesn't say when each of the three books first came into use. So our sources show they were read around the time the Big Book appeared, not that all three were in use from 1935.

730d340001a0.t: Frank Amos, soon to be one of A.A.'s first nonalcoholic trustees, looked into the Akron group for Mr. Rockefeller, and his report of February 1938 lists the practice: daily devotions, "a 'quiet time' of prayer and some reading from the Bible and other religious literature" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

5e9014f43110.t: The same book is plain about what was missing: "there was definitely a need for literature directed specifically to the alcoholic" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). That was the book, begun in 1938.

c9ee90e43fa9.t: What the Big Book and its stories say

47ca7c9fc60b.t: The 1939 main text names no devotional book. In its section on morning meditation it says members who belong to a religious body follow its practice, others may memorize a few prayers, and "There are many helpful books also." (p. 87). Suggestions are to come from "one's priest, minister, or rabbi" (p. 87).

7aa38ea9b3eb.t: "He Sold Himself Short," a story in Part I describing Akron in 1937, says that at his first meeting "The big A.A. book had not been written, and there was no literature except various religious pamphlets." (p. 262). "The program was carried on entirely by word of mouth." (p. 262).

416624bba5dc.t: <0>A note on "upper room."</0> Chapter 11 describes a newcomer who heard a member's story "in an upper room of this house" (p. 160). That is a room upstairs in the home the chapter describes, not the booklet.

eb446dc0ca20.t: Our sources say much less about New York. Bill's own reading was William James's <0>The Varieties of Religious Experience</0>, which he says a friend, Ebby he thinks, brought him at Towns Hospital in 1934 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). By 1938 the word-of-mouth program's basic ideas, as he put it, "had come from the Oxford Groups, William James, and Dr. Silk-worth" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <1>Why does the Big Book mention William James?</1>

31c19010be28.t: Chapter 6, "Into Action" (pp. 72–88), on morning meditation and "helpful books": <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt6.pdf</0>
