1f6dbae4a15d.t: "Recovered" or "recovering": which word does the Big Book use? | Recovery Starts

7f7d927fd342.t: The Big Book's members call themselves "recovered." The 1939 Foreword opens with "more than one hundred men and women who have recovered from a seemingly…

e94887fb8dbd.t: "Recovered" or "recovering": which word does the Big Book use?

b24eaafd8420.t: The Big Book's members call themselves "recovered." The 1939 Foreword opens with "more than one hundred men and women who have recovered from a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body" (p. xiii), and Chapter 2 says of the thousands they know, "Nearly all have recovered." (p. 17).

d5319ac825fa.t: The phrase "recovering alcoholic" is not in the fourth-edition Big Book. In our sources it appears in later books: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980), <1>Pass It On</1> (1984), P-16 (2018) and the current Service Manual.

a70cebafef5a.t: But "recovered" in the book doesn't mean cured or able to drink again. The same text says "We are not cured of alcoholism" and calls what members have "a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition" (p. 85).

39fee1ec1402.t: The book also uses "recovering" for someone in the process: the husband "who is recovering" (p. 122). The word isn't foreign to it; the self-description is "recovered."

8781e9901f71.t: The word runs through the book: - The Foreword to the First Edition: the members "have recovered from a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body" (p. xiii), and "To show other alcoholics precisely how we have recovered is the main purpose of this book." (p. xiii). - Dr. Silkworth's letter: "This man and over one hundred others appear to have recovered." (p. xxv). - Chapter 2: "Nearly all have recovered." (p. 17). "They have solved the drink problem." (p. 17). Readers are told the book will explain how "we have recovered from a hopeless condition of mind and body" (p. 20), followed by "clear-cut directions … showing how we recovered" (p. 29). - Chapter 7: the prospect's attention is drawn to the member "as a person who has recovered" (p. 90). - Chapter 9: "We have recovered, and have been given the power to help others." (p. 132). "We, who have recovered from serious drinking, are miracles of mental health." (p. 133). - Chapter 10: "An alcoholic who has recovered" can talk to another employee (p. 146).

a63d96f6a8fd.t: The fourth-edition title page reads "The Story of How Many Thousands of Men and Women Have Recovered from Alcoholism" (p. iii). Later A.A. writing keeps the word: in 1955 the Foreword to the Second Edition counted membership as "far above 150,000 recovered alcoholics" (p. xv), and <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) says that clergymen and physicians are the experts and "we, the recovered alcoholics, are their assistants" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957).

c16314dd92b3.t: What "recovered" does and doesn't mean in the book

5421daafacd6.t: The book is careful about what has been recovered from: - Not from alcoholism as a condition. "We know that no real alcoholic ever recovers control." (p. 30). "Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic." (p. 33). - Not once and for all. "We are not cured of alcoholism." (p. 85). The reprieve is daily and depends on the member's spiritual condition (p. 85). Step Ten's work "should continue for our lifetime" (p. 84). - What members say they have recovered from is "a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body" (p. xiii): the drink problem is solved (p. 17), so long as they keep in fit spiritual condition (p. 85).

904ab59fb5d0.t: The verb appears for someone in the middle of the process: - Chapter 9 opens by saying the members' "women folk have suggested certain attitudes a wife may take with the husband who is recovering" (p. 122). The chapter adds that "dad, though marvelously improved, is still convalescing" (p. 127). - Chapter 10: an employee who drinks "and is still trying to recover" will be honest about it (p. 146). - A later-edition footnote to Chapter 8 speaks of a woman alcoholic "whether she is still drinking or is recovering in A.A." (p. 104).

010a9a8a8881.t: What doesn't appear anywhere in the fourth-edition text, stories included, is the label "recovering alcoholic." "Recovered alcoholic(s)" appears in a few personal stories (pp. 273–274, 442).

27666e2ff955.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980): Dr. Bob's adult years "as an active and then as a recovering alcoholic" (<1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1>, 1980).

40c7b7885230.t: <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) uses "recovering alcoholics" in its narrative of the 1930s and early 1940s .

293aa292b198.t: <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16, 2018): members may tell nonalcoholics "that we are recovering alcoholics" (P-16, 2018); GSO staff members "are themselves recovering alcoholics" (P-16, 2018).

d4e9ffd1160a.t: <0>The A.A. Service Manual</0> (2024–2026 edition): members in a home group "sustain connections with other recovering alcoholics."

7163a91aab5f.t: The 1939 text describes its members as recovered: rescued from a hopeless state, with the drink problem solved on a spiritual basis as a daily reprieve, and never able to drink safely again. "Recovering" as an identity is later usage. Neither the Big Book nor the later books in our sources say one word is right and the other wrong; this page only reports which word each source uses.

4b37b838f37c.t: Does the Big Book say "relapse is part of recovery"? What does it say about a slip? | Recovery Starts

ff978e23c0f1.t: No. "Relapse is part of recovery" is not in the Big Book or anywhere else in our sources.

314581274bf3.t: Does the Big Book say "relapse is part of recovery"? What does it say about a slip?

101aca6b6669.t: No. "Relapse is part of recovery" is not in the Big Book or anywhere else in our sources.

8c5978586f8d.t: The program text's fullest word on it is to a wife whose husband comes home drunk: "Though it is infinitely better that he have no relapse at all, as has been true with many of our men, it is by no means a bad thing in some cases." (p. 120). In those cases he sees that he must "redouble his spiritual activities if he expects to survive" (p. 120).

67e8d30922b2.t: So the text neither treats relapse as an expected stage nor writes off the person who drinks again. It treats drinking as deadly ("to drink is to die," p. 66), and it treats the man who slips and keeps trying with patience (pp. 120, 147).

f0206529e737.t: All our sources were searched for "part of recovery," "relapse," "slip" and their forms, with page breaks joined. "Part of recovery" turns up once, in a story where "Commitment and service were part of recovery" (p. 345). Nothing in any book says relapse is part of recovery.

8061ea455cb2.t: In the program text, "relapse" appears at pp. 26, 31, 35, 120 and 125. "Slip" meaning a drink appears at p. 100 ("We have seen others slip when the family came back too soon") and p. 139 (an executive who "did slip and was fired"). At p. 84 ("Self-seeking will slip away") and p. 110 (friends who "slipped away") it means something else.

7470d86a8cc6.t: <0>The danger.</0> Of the remedies they tried before A.A., the book says that in some instances there was "brief recovery, followed always by a still worse relapse" (p. 31). "Commencing to drink after a period of sobriety, we are in a short time as bad as ever." (p. 33). Chapter 3 is written to describe "the mental states that precede a relapse into drinking, for obviously this is the crux of the problem" (p. 35). Bill: if an alcoholic didn't work with others "he would surely drink again, and if he drank, he would surely die" (p. 15). "And with us, to drink is to die." (p. 66).

a9ada318c624.t: <0>Its causes.</0> Newcomers who kept certain facts to themselves: "Almost invariably they got drunk." (p. 73). Resentment brings it back (p. 66). Family quarrels and old affairs dug up again: "In most cases, the alcoholic survived this ordeal without relapse, but not always." (p. 125).

c9386b5acd74.t: <0>When it happens.</0> The passage that speaks most fully to a relapse in a man who has started the program is in "To Wives" (p. 120). Read in full, it says: - If you are satisfied he really wants to get over drinking, "you need not be alarmed" (p. 120). - "Though it is infinitely better that he have no relapse at all, as has been true with many of our men, it is by no means a bad thing in some cases." (p. 120). - He will see at once that he must "redouble his spiritual activities if he expects to survive" (p. 120). Don't remind him of his spiritual deficiency; "Cheer him up and ask him how you can be still more helpful." (p. 120). - "If he gets drunk, don't blame yourself." (p. 120). "God has either removed your husband's liquor problem or He has not. If not, it had better be found out right away." (p. 120).

8385a3127ece.t: <0>Falling short in daily life.</0> In Chapter 7: "Of course, we all fall much below this standard many times. But we must try to repair the damage immediately lest we pay the penalty by a spree." (p. 99).

996749edea9a.t: <0>At work.</0> "In case he does stumble, even once, you will have to decide whether to let him go." (p. 147). If you are sure he doesn't mean business, discharge him; if you are sure he is doing his utmost, "you may wish to give him another chance" (p. 147). A man still trying to recover who does get drunk "will tell you about it even if it means the loss of his job" (p. 146).

10e81c2700ea.t: So "by no means a bad thing in some cases" is as far as the program text goes. It says that, and it says no relapse is "infinitely better." It never says relapse is needed, normal, or a stage everyone goes through.

14a110fde2aa.t: The Foreword to the Second Edition: of alcoholics who came to A.A. and really tried, "50% got sober at once and remained that way; 25% sobered up after some relapses" (p. xx), and among the rest, those who stayed showed improvement (p. xx). That is 1955, after Dr. Bob's death.

4a41613e913a.t: The early stories and Bill's essays

c0ca0463d034.t: Slips were written about openly from the start: - Two stories printed in the 1939 first edition, "The Back-Slider" and "The Seven Month Slip" (since dropped, now in <0>Experience, Strength and Hope</0>, 2003), are about men who drank again after one or two years sober. Both put it down to drifting from the program and relying on themselves, and both came back to friends who welcomed them. One says the fellowship "treated me as though nothing had happened" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). - Dr. Bob's own story (1939) says he carries the message partly because each time "I take out a little more insurance for myself against a possible slip" (p. 181). - "He Sold Himself Short" (Part I, set in 1937–38) tells of a deliberate drunk a few months after the writer's start: "That was my only slip. It taught me a valuable lesson." (p. 265), namely that inventory has to be taken every day (pp. 264–265). - Bill W.'s 1946 Grapevine essay on membership says most early members "would have been thrown out because they slipped too much" (P-17) if the groups' early rules had been enforced, and of those who slip: "Some of these have become our most respected and best loved." (P-17).

6ceac62cc846.t: Later books, all after 1950: - <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957): at first slips were "always a genuine catastrophe" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); by 1955, "Slips are a very serious difficulty, but as a group we take them in stride." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). - <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) quotes an undated letter of Bill's about members two or three years sober who slipped: he knew of none who hadn't, in a sense, benefited, and "The slip invariably kicks them upstairs instead of down." (Pass It On, 1984). The same letter calls these slips a lot of worry for the families (Pass It On, 1984). That is the nearest thing in our sources to the saying, and it is about what a slip can teach, not a claim that relapse is a necessary part of recovery. - <2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2> (1980) says that of the Akron members counted in February 1937, half "had or would have some sort of slip" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), and "For most, however, the slip was the convincer." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

fd380234e9b1.t: The Big Book doesn't say relapse is part of recovery. It says drinking again is deadly, that no relapse is infinitely better, and that in some cases a relapse is "by no means a bad thing" (p. 120), the next sentence saying the man sees he must redouble his spiritual activities. Its tone toward the person who slips and is still trying is patient: a wife told not to lecture him, a possible second chance from the employer, and, in the early stories, a welcome back. See: <0>Is "keep coming back" in the Big Book?</0>

2426c9292b17.t: Do I have to be religious to work the Steps? | Recovery Starts

78811d7d7c12.t: No. You don't have to belong to a religion or accept anyone else's idea of God. The Big Book says "we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47), and about…

cfc4af6fd634.t: Do I have to be religious to work the Steps?

2e3947cc5f62.t: No. You don't have to belong to a religion or accept anyone else's idea of God. The Big Book says "we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47), and about half the first members thought they were atheists or agnostics (p. 44).

22cbcf4c1a4b.t: What the book does ask for is a willingness to believe in a Power greater than yourself. It calls this the starting point, and says that is enough to begin (p. 47).

b70fb8452918.t: The book is open that it is a spiritual book and that it talks about God (p. 45). Five of the Twelve Steps name God or Him. It doesn't pretend otherwise; it leaves the meaning of the word to you.

5581d611000d.t: What the book asks for at the start

51f4ae3f7047.t: Chapter 4 (pp. 44–57), "We Agnostics," was written for the reader this question is about. Its main points, in order: - Something like half the original fellowship "thought we were atheists or agnostics" (p. 44). - The book is "spiritual as well as moral," and so "we are going to talk about God" (p. 45). Here the writers expect the agnostic's face to fall, and say they've shared his doubt; some of them had been "violently anti-religious" (p. 45). - They found they "did not need to consider another's conception of God" (p. 46). Their own conception, however inadequate, was enough to begin. - "When, therefore, we speak to you of God, we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47). - The one question needed at the start: "Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe, that there is a Power greater than myself?" (p. 47) Someone who can say yes to that is "on his way" (p. 47). - How each member conceives of that Power varies widely in the stories, and these "are questions for each individual to settle for himself" (p. 50).

06476020d9a6.t: Where the book is not neutral

a391a7bc4030.t: To be fair to the text, Chapter 4 isn't indifferent about God. It argues, at length, that faith is more reasonable than unbelief (pp. 48–55). It puts the choice starkly: "either God is everything or else He is nothing" (p. 53). It asks agnostics to "lay aside prejudice, even against organized religion" (p. 49), and it ends with the story of a man who thought he was an atheist and came to "conscious companionship with his Creator" (p. 56).

24a5e3764b3d.t: So the book hopes the reader will come to a faith of his own. What it doesn't do is require any religion, church, creed or particular conception of God to start, or to work the Steps.

47f37e4b965f.t: Appendix II, written after the first printing (p. 567), says the "spiritual experience" or "spiritual awakening" the book talks about is a personality change, and that most of these develop slowly (p. 567). Interestingly, it uses "religious experiences" as another name for the same personality changes (p. 567). It then says any alcoholic can recover "provided he does not close his mind to all spiritual concepts" (p. 568), and that "no one need have difficulty with the spirituality of the program" (p. 568). Willingness, honesty and open-mindedness are what's essential (p. 568).

ed9c08998ed6.t: How a member is told to talk about it

db538b73853d.t: Chapter 7 tells the person carrying the message how to handle this with a newcomer: - With an agnostic or atheist, make it plain he doesn't have to agree with your conception of God. "He can choose any conception he likes, provided it makes sense to him" (p. 93). - Use everyday language, and don't raise theological issues "no matter what your own convictions are" (p. 93). - You're not there to instruct anyone in religion (p. 93), and A.A. represents no "particular faith or denomination" (p. 94). - "We have no monopoly on God" (p. 95). If he prefers some other spiritual approach, encourage him to follow his own conscience (p. 95).

687e616338b6.t: The book also has room for people who are religious. Members who belong to a church are told to keep its practices (pp. 74, 87), and everyone is told to "Be quick to see where religious people are right" (p. 87).

a46783a716e5.t: written after the first printing (p. 567); the Preface says the appendices came into the book with the second edition, 1955 (p. xi)

27abd4bd0c64.t: Where is "resentment is the number one offender," and what does it mean? | Recovery Starts

88fa79d13519.t: It's on page 64 of Chapter 5, at the start of the Fourth Step inventory: "Resentment is the 'number one' offender." (p. 64) (The quotation marks around…

73f7888ae869.t: Where is "resentment is the number one offender," and what does it mean?

47942f7acdca.t: It's on page 64 of Chapter 5, at the start of the Fourth Step inventory: "Resentment is the 'number one' offender." (p. 64) (The quotation marks around "number one" are the book's own.) The next sentence says why: "It destroys more alcoholics than anything else." (p. 64)

4c8f5d759db3.t: It's the first of the "common manifestations" of self, which the book had just named as what "had defeated us" (p. 64). Fear and sex conduct follow in the same inventory (pp. 67–70).

2521183030d9.t: Context confirms the line. The book calls resentment fatal for an alcoholic: harbouring it, "we shut ourselves off from the sunlight of the Spirit" (p. 66), and "The insanity of alcohol returns and we drink again." (p. 66)

20f3d7ace7e7.t: It also shows where the inventory goes next: from what others did to us, to "our own mistakes" (p. 67).

197a763e3a65.t: Chapter 5 has just explained Step Three and the decision to turn our will and life over to God. That decision, the book says, would have little lasting effect without a hard look at what had been blocking us, and so comes the inventory (p. 64). The paragraph that leads to the line sets its frame: "Being convinced that self, manifested in various ways, was what had defeated us, we considered its common manifestations." (p. 64)

fcecf1105752.t: Resentment is the first of them. "Resentment is the 'number one' offender." (p. 64) "It destroys more alcoholics than anything else." (p. 64) The book adds that "From it stem all forms of spiritual disease" (p. 64). See <0>What is the "spiritual malady"?</0>

19c5b2f533d1.t: What the inventory does with it (pp. 64–67)

05282399bdbe.t: <0>Write it down.</0> "We listed people, institutions or principles with whom we were angry." (p. 64) We asked why, and found that most often our self-esteem, our pocketbooks, our ambitions or our personal relationships, including sex, "were hurt or threatened" (pp. 64–65). The book prints a sample grudge list (p. 65).

4304f5173312.t: <0>Look at the result.</0> At first the list seems to prove that the world and its people were often quite wrong. "To conclude that others were wrong was as far as most of us ever got." (p. 66) The more we fought, the worse it got (p. 66).

69fe4c759582.t: <0>See why it's grave.</0> For an alcoholic, "this business of resentment is infinitely grave" (p. 66). "We found that it is fatal." (p. 66) Holding it, we cut ourselves off from the sunlight of the Spirit, and the insanity of alcohol returns (p. 66). "If we were to live, we had to be free of anger." (p. 66)

b32acd7649ae.t: <0>Deal with it.</0> "We could not wish them away any more than alcohol." (p. 66) The book's course is to see the people who wronged us as perhaps spiritually sick, and to ask God to help us show them the tolerance, pity and patience we'd give a sick friend (pp. 66–67). See <1>Does the Big Book really say to pray for people you resent ("This is a sick man")?</1>

6cee45769e1b.t: <0>Then look at our own part.</0> "Putting out of our minds the wrongs others had done, we resolutely looked for our own mistakes." (p. 67) "The inventory was ours, not the other man's." (p. 67)

3717738f69a2.t: "Number one" is the book's ranking for the inventory, and it puts resentment in company elsewhere: - Right after resentment comes fear, "an evil and corroding thread" (p. 67). The book says "we think fear ought to be classed with stealing" (p. 68) and that "It seems to cause more trouble." (p. 68) - Step Ten, the daily version of the inventory, watches for four things: "selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear" (p. 84). - Chapter 10, "To Employers": "The greatest enemies of us alcoholics are resentment, jealousy, envy, frustration, and fear." (p. 145)

57a14f16e012.t: No, it confirms it. The book does name resentment as what destroys more alcoholics than anything else, and it explains why: resentment shuts out the Spirit and leads back to drinking. Context adds two things the bare line leaves out. Resentment is one form of self, which the book treats as the root (p. 62). And the inventory doesn't stop at listing resentments: it moves to our own mistakes, and on to fear and sex conduct.

78f7e6f3f370.t: Chapter 5, "How It Works" (pp. 58–71), with the inventory on pp. 63–71, free from A.A.: <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt5.pdf</0>

bc5675f67784.t: Who said "restless, irritable and discontented," and about what? | Recovery Starts

5771e93d257a.t: The words are Dr. William D. Silkworth's, not Bill W.'s. They're in his statement in "The Doctor's Opinion" at the front of the Big Book (p. xxviii), kept…

5709baa4fcbd.t: Who said "restless, irritable and discontented," and about what?

6a1a09b082bf.t: The words are Dr. William D. Silkworth's, not Bill W.'s. They're in his statement in "The Doctor's Opinion" at the front of the Big Book (p. xxviii), kept as he wrote it in 1939 (p. xi).

d6351b93de2e.t: He uses them about the drinker between drinks: "They are restless, irritable and discontented, unless they can again experience" (p. xxviii) "the sense of ease and comfort which comes at once by taking a few drinks" (p. xxix). The sentence before gives the reason men drink: "Men and women drink essentially because they like the effect produced by alcohol." (p. xxviii)

71ec16ece7b2.t: What follows is a cycle: they give in again, the craving develops, a spree, remorse, a firm resolution, and "This is repeated over and over" (p. xxix), with very little hope "unless this person can experience an entire psychic change" (p. xxix).

f54a0f3f6085.t: The printed word is "discontented," not "discontent." The context confirms the usual sense of the phrase, the alcoholic's state without a drink. It complicates one common use: Silkworth is describing drinkers caught in the cycle, not members in recovery. A member's story later in the book uses the phrase about her own sobriety (p. 317), an example of how members have come to apply it to sober life.

48c0fa5d6ca5.t: "The Doctor's Opinion" has three voices: A.A. members introducing the doctor, Silkworth's short letter, and his longer statement (pp. xxv–xxxii). This sentence is in the longer statement, which he signs at the end (p. xxxii). See <0>What is "The Doctor's Opinion," and who wrote it?</0> for the whole section.

136cd8dd74a1.t: The paragraph explains why the alcoholic keeps going back: 1. <0>The reason.</0> "Men and women drink essentially because they like the effect produced by alcohol." (p. xxviii) 2. <1>The confusion.</1> "The sensation is so elusive that, while they admit it is injurious, they cannot after a time differentiate the true from the false." (p. xxviii) "To them, their alcoholic life seems the only normal one." (p. xxviii) 3. <2>The state without a drink.</2> Restless, irritable and discontented, until they can feel again the ease and comfort a few drinks bring, drinks they see others take "with impunity" (p. xxix). 4. <3>The cycle.</3> They give in again, as so many do; the phenomenon of craving develops; they go through the stages of a spree and come out remorseful, "with a firm resolution not to drink again" (p. xxix). Then it repeats. 5. <4>The only way out he sees.</4> An entire psychic change (p. xxix). Once that happens, the same person who seemed doomed finds he can control his desire for alcohol, "the only effort necessary being that required to follow a few simple rules" (p. xxix).

faaa055a077b.t: So the restlessness is the doorway back to the drink. It sits between the sprees, in a person for whom drinking seems normal, and in the doctor's account it leads back to the drink after each firm resolution.

83d6d92f39c9.t: How the phrase is used in the stories

0ceea83eec12.t: In "My Chance to Live," a member's story in Part II of the fourth edition, the writer uses it about her own sober life: "When I am unwilling to do the right thing, I become restless, irritable, and discontent." (p. 317) That is her experience, told in her words. It's an example of the phrase used for sober life, where the doctor used it for the active drinker.

3062e63d35d8.t: The Doctor's Opinion itself doesn't say whether a sober member can feel this way. It ties the feeling to the pull back toward a drink, and its answer is the psychic change.

8799b750a246.t: It confirms the core of it and complicates the rest. The phrase does describe the alcoholic without a drink. But it's the doctor speaking, not Bill W.; the word is "discontented"; and in its place it describes the drinker in the cycle of craving, remorse and resolution, for whom the doctor sees little hope without a psychic change.

f334fc9d3d4d.t: What is the Right of Appeal, and why does the minority matter? | Recovery Starts

acca228a6813.t: The Right of Appeal is Bill W.'s Fifth Concept (1962): throughout A.A.'s world service structure, "minority opinion will be heard and personal grievances…

0ec064f36fea.t: What is the Right of Appeal, and why does the minority matter?

ccbccaca4ba2.t: The Right of Appeal is Bill W.'s Fifth Concept (1962): throughout A.A.'s world service structure, "minority opinion will be heard and personal grievances receive careful consideration" (p. 574).

b5459f0fb19e.t: It has two parts. A minority that thinks the majority is badly wrong is encouraged to file a minority report, and on a grave issue has a duty to take it to the General Service Conference. And anyone working in the structure, paid or unpaid, may petition the General Service Board over a personal grievance "without prejudice or fear of reprisal" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).

9921af8a4655.t: Why: minorities are often right, and even when they're wrong they force a real debate. "The well-heard minority, therefore, is our chief protection against an uninformed, misinformed, hasty or angry majority" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).

3a451ac99a5e.t: A related idea is older than the Concepts. In 1946, writing about who should pay for clubs, Bill said that "the majority ought not to try to coerce the minority" (P-17, Money, 1946).

89a9dc477c76.t: The Long Form of the Traditions protects the individual first: A.A. "may refuse none who wish to recover," and membership should never depend "upon money or conformity" (p. 563).

c0ecb6382310.t: Bill's 1946 essay on money applies it to a disagreement. Most members liked clubs, but not all, so club support should come from those who wanted them: "But the majority ought not to try to coerce the minority into supporting clubs they do not want or need" (P-17, Money, 1946).

bdb928cf0aa3.t: His 1947 essay on government lists among A.A.'s freedoms "no one set in personal authority over anyone else" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947).

2065005e0c34.t: The 1955 Conference Charter built minority protection into elections: delegates are chosen "by a two-thirds written ballot or by lot" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955).

6b4bbef97bf1.t: <0>Appeal.</0> All minorities, "whether in our staffs, committees, corporate boards or among the Trustees," should be encouraged to file minority reports when they think the majority is in considerable error (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). Where a wrong decision could seriously affect A.A. as a whole, the minority should treat presenting a report to the Conference as an actual duty.

de423c61d9b1.t: <0>Why minorities matter.</0> "In granting this traditional ‘Right of Appeal,’ we recognize that minorities frequently can be right" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). Even when partly or wholly wrong, they compel a thorough debate.

8ff760f94a6a.t: <0>Petition.</0> Any person in the structure may carry a personal grievance directly to the General Service Board. Bill expected it to be used seldom, but "its very existence will always tend to restrain those in authority from unjust uses of their power" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).

7fab1d4d3617.t: <0>Where it comes from.</0> Bill ties it to A.A.'s membership freedoms: "any alcoholic is a member of A.A. the moment he says so; we cannot take away his right to belong" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). "Neither can we force our members to believe anything or pay anything" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).

e80a12d65c23.t: <0>How it already worked in 1962.</0> - <1>Electing delegates.</1> Unless a candidate gets two-thirds of the assembly, his name goes in a hat with the minority's choices, and the delegate is drawn by lot. Bill admits this sometimes sets aside the simple-majority rule, and says it has strengthened the spirit of democracy: no discontented minority trails behind the winner. - <2>The Conference's own habit.</2> "Unless it has been absolutely unavoidable, the Conference has usually refused to take important decisions on anything less than a two-thirds vote" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). - <3>The trustees' check.</3> Under the Charter, a Conference vote binds the trustees only at two-thirds of a quorum, so a narrow majority can't force them; they can insist on more debate.

b64a7e7426a7.t: Bill closes with Alexis de Tocqueville's warning against the "tyranny" of apathetic, self-seeking, uninformed or angry majorities, and adds the opposite danger: "the even worse tyranny of very small minorities invested with absolute power" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).

d8857d17f7f5.t: The limit: a minority can't block everything

c5c37d5077bf.t: Concept XII's Fourth Warranty asks for decisions by "substantial unanimity" whenever possible, but sets a limit. In a real emergency, or when "a small minority obstinately tries to use the principle of substantial unanimity to block a clearly needed action," Bill writes, "it would be the plain duty of the majority to override such a misuse of the principle of substantial unanimity" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). The Right of Appeal guarantees a hearing, not a veto.

218cd5804863.t: How it's done now (later sources, dated)

1e74e710a322.t: P-8 (first printed 1986; © 2017) describes the current Conference: after a vote reaches substantial unanimity, "those opposed are polled individually to see if they wish to speak further to their minority view" (P-8), and the Conference has sometimes reversed itself.

e2d828e43118.t: The 2024–2026 Service Manual: "After each vote on a matter of policy, the side that did not prevail will always be given an opportunity to speak to their position" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Chapter 6).

9048015e766a.t: In 1962 Bill hoped A.A. would "one day inscribe these traditional Rights" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V) in the Conference Charter. The current Charter now says the Conference recognizes "the Rights of Petition and Appeal reflected in Concepts IV and V" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Current Conference Charter) and may hear Concept V appeals from members below the Conference level. Our copy doesn't say when this was added.

c570d68c3122.t: Concept V was written for the world service structure: staffs, committees, boards, trustees, the Conference. It doesn't set out a procedure for a member who disagrees with a home group's decision. Bill's introduction says these principles "can of course be used to good effect throughout our entire structure" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction), and P-8 says the same principle should apply to area committees and boards, but neither lays down rules for a group.

2a5dc2ad0b54.t: The Concepts, short form (Appendix VII, p. 574), free from A.A.: <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_appendicevii_.pdf</0>

b63ef571a11f.t: The full Concept V essay is in <0>The A.A. Service Manual combined with Twelve Concepts for World Service</0>: <1>https://www.aa.org/aa-service-manual</1> (sold at <2>https://onlineliterature.aa.org</2>)

fd9a3a5de5d7.t: Why did early A.A. turn down Rockefeller money? | Recovery Starts

181370fc6feb.t: The popular telling has it backwards in one respect. In 1937–38 the founders asked John D. Rockefeller, Jr. for large sums, for hospitals, paid workers…

3b6e4499f201.t: Why did early A.A. turn down Rockefeller money?

8db3b79014b6.t: The popular telling has it backwards in one respect. In 1937–38 the founders asked John D. Rockefeller, Jr. for large sums, for hospitals, paid workers and a book. It was Rockefeller who turned the request down, saying, in Bill W.'s account, "I think money will spoil this."

84a75089092c.t: A.A. did take some Rockefeller help: $5,000 in 1938 to tide Bill and Dr. Bob over, then $1,000 and small gifts from his guests after a 1940 dinner, and a loan to buy back the Big Book's shares, which was repaid.

8ab3dd291ce6.t: What A.A. turned down came later. In the mid-1940s it wrote Rockefeller and the dinner guests that it needed no more money, and its trustees refused a $10,000 bequest (Bill's account doesn't date that refusal). By then the founders had come to agree with him: large outside money would bring a paid professional class, property and quarrels, and divert them from carrying the message.

95fd80cdf8ae.t: Bill credited Rockefeller, along with St. Francis's idea of corporate poverty, for A.A.'s tradition on money.

15b9e869cdf9.t: The 1939 Big Book doesn't mention Rockefeller. The Traditions' Long Form, first published in 1946 and printed in today's book, states the principle without names: the groups should be supported by their own members' contributions, and "acceptance of large gifts from any source, or of contributions carrying any obligation whatever, is unwise" (pp. 564–565). See <0>Tradition Seven: does A.A. take outside money?</0>

a3b7f3ce7fba.t: Bill's 1946 Grapevine essay on money, in P-17, looks back without naming anyone: "There was a time some years ago when we desperately needed a little outside aid. This we received." (P-17, 1946). Those gifts, he says, made possible the Alcoholic Foundation, the book and the office, but times had changed (P-17, 1946).

547c230711a2.t: The 1955 Foreword to the Second Edition mentions only the dinner: "In the spring of 1940, John D. Rockefeller, Jr. gave a dinner for many of his friends to which he invited A.A. members to tell their stories." (p. xviii). The publicity brought inquiries and book sales (p. xviii).

6dfa9d151f6a.t: 1937–38: Rockefeller says no (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)

141e9ea49da1.t: After the November 1937 count of about forty sober members, Bill went looking for big money (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Through his brother-in-law he met Willard Richardson, who managed Rockefeller's charities, and in December 1937 Bill, Dr. Bob, Dr. Silkworth and others told their stories in Rockefeller's board room (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The chairman, Albert Scott, asked: "Won't money spoil this thing?" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Frank Amos investigated Akron and recommended $50,000 to start (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

69af2595a1b6.t: Rockefeller flatly declined. Bill says his reasons were the same as those of the Akron minority who had opposed paid missionaries and hospitals (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He placed $5,000 in the treasury of Riverside Church for Bill and Dr. Bob, said the fellowship should soon support itself, and added, "But please don't ever ask me for any more." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In another chapter Bill gives Rockefeller's words as: "I think money will spoil this." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "St. Francis had given us the idea, but John D. wisely forced us to live up to it." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

d90eb7dd8578.t: On February 8, 1940, Rockefeller gave a dinner for A.A.; he fell ill, and his son Nelson presided (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill and Dr. Bob expected wealth to follow. Instead Nelson said, for his father, that "Alcoholics Anonymous should be self-supporting so far as money is concerned. It needs only our good will." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Rockefeller bought 400 books at a dollar each to send the guests, gave $1,000, and allowed the trustees to ask the guests for gifts, which brought about $2,000 more (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). That money paid Bill and Dr. Bob $30 a week (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill concludes: "They had put A.A. on the map." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

56d3d2ee7f14.t: Rockefeller, two of his sons and some dinner guests also lent the Foundation $8,000 to buy back the Big Book's shares from its subscribers, to be repaid from book profits (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <0>How was the Big Book paid for and published (Works Publishing)?</0>

ebc9fac54707.t: Bill writes that once book royalties could support him and Dr. Bob and the groups were paying for the office, they wrote Rockefeller and the guests that no more funds were needed, and "At that point the A.A. Tradition of 'no outside contributions' went into full force and effect." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Then the trustees faced a $10,000 bequest at a time when they badly needed it; they declined it, and "They declared for the principle that A.A. must always stay poor." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

37e1a045d8d8.t: P-44 (Bill, describing events through 1955) tells it the same way: Rockefeller declined a large sum "for fear of professionalizing A.A." (P-44), and in doing so "saved us from the perils of property management and professionalism" (P-44).

7335b0437daa.t: <0>Who said money would spoil it.</0> Bill's 1957 book has Albert Scott ask the question at the 1937 meeting (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and Rockefeller say it afterward (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) notes that Richardson had already written in November 1937 that professionalizing the work would be undesirable, so "it is unclear whose idea this had originally been" (Pass It On, 1984).

b679dc8706cb.t: <0>The mortgage.</0> P-44 says "About half of the $5,000" paid Dr. Bob's mortgage (P-44); <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) says "$3,000 went to pay off Bob's mortgage" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

c769abf28f5e.t: <0>The dinner.</0> Bill's 1957 book and <1>Pass It On</1> say the Union Club, February 8, 1940 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; Pass It On, 1984). P-44 says it "came off early in February at New York's Union League Club" (P-44). The 1955 foreword says "the spring of 1940" (p. xviii).

0aefaf5a4788.t: <0>When the help stopped.</0> In one chapter Bill says they wrote "Four years later" than 1940 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); in another, "In 1945 we wrote Mr. John D. Rockefeller, Jr., and the 1940 dinner guests that we would no longer need their financial help." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

ad2292398db6.t: "Rule 62" is "Don't take yourself too damned seriously." It isn't in the Big Book. In our sources it appears only in A.A. Comes of Age (1957), in a story…

55933fb4a5f6.t: "Rule 62" is "Don't take yourself too damned seriously." It isn't in the Big Book. In our sources it appears only in <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957), in a story Bill W. tells to explain Tradition Four.

f8fb9be7ab92.t: In the story, a promoter in one town got sober, drew up a grand A.A. center with a club, a clinic and a loan office, and wrote sixty-one rules and by-laws to run it. It collapsed. Afterward he mailed every group in the United States a card reading "Rule No. 62," and inside: "Don't take yourself too damned seriously" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957).

4e503e7d947d.t: Bill tells it as an example of a group's right to be wrong, and of the humility to learn from it and laugh.

4c7dc86557c2.t: All our sources were searched for "Rule 62," "Rule No. 62," "sixty-one rules" and "too damned seriously." The only place is <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957). It isn't in the Big Book, P-17 or the other pamphlets in our sources.

d7cf324ca2ad.t: Bill tells it while explaining Tradition Four, "Each group should be autonomous, except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957). He first explains that the groups told New York, in effect, "Services, yes. But government, no," and claimed "the right to be wrong" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). Then the example: - "Years ago in a certain town a super-promoter got sobered up in A.A." (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957). He planned a big building: a club on one floor, a meeting room on the next, then a clinic and rehabilitation center, and upstairs a loan agency for broke alcoholics. - It needed three corporations, and "Altogether, he wrote sixty-one rules, regulations, and by-laws" (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957). He sold the town and most of his fellow members on the idea, and was to be the general manager himself. - He asked New York for a "super-charter." Some dissenters in the group wrote to New York too. Headquarters told them that each group could run its own affairs as long as it didn't harm other groups, but warned "as strongly as we dared" that smaller schemes like it had failed everywhere (<4>A.A. Comes of Age</4>, 1957). The group ignored the warning, as it had a right to. - It crashed: "The thump of colliding egos could be heard and felt for miles" (<5>A.A. Comes of Age</5>, 1957). - Later the promoter wrote that New York had been right and he had been wrong. With the letter came the card he had already sent to every group in the country: on the outside "Rule No. 62," and inside, "Don't take yourself too damned seriously" (<6>A.A. Comes of Age</6>, 1957).

8078fb698eaa.t: Bill's comment: the group had used its right to be wrong, and had done A.A. a service because it had been "humbly willing to apply the lessons" it learned (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957). The promoter, standing in the ruins of his own plan, "could laugh at himself—and that is the acme of humility" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957).

199e0ccf5a88.t: The number follows from the story: he had written sixty-one rules, and this was the sixty-second.

1139715ad916.t: The story touches two of the Traditions, both in the Long Form of 1946 (now in the Big Book's Appendix I): - <0>Autonomy.</0> Each group "should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience," but when its plans affect neighboring groups or A.A. as a whole, others should be consulted (p. 563). The group was free to try. See <1>Tradition Four: can GSO tell a group what to do?</1> - <2>Keeping property apart.</2> "An A.A. group, as such, should never go into business" (p. 564). Clubs and hospitals should be separately incorporated, kept outside A.A., and set apart so that "they can be freely discarded by the groups" if necessary (p. 564). The promoter did plan three corporations, but it was the group's project: his fellow members backed it and he asked New York for a "super-charter" (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957). His letter afterward admits New York had told him such enterprises "could not be mixed with A.A." (<4>A.A. Comes of Age</4>, 1957). See <5>What did Bill W. say about clubs and A.A.?</5>

0900343a9cb6.t: The same spirit in the 1939 text

555861fe00ad.t: The Big Book has no Rule 62, but it says something close in its own words: - "But we aren't a glum lot" (p. 132). If newcomers saw no joy or fun in A.A., they wouldn't want it. "We absolutely insist on enjoying life" (p. 132). - "So we think cheerfulness and laughter make for usefulness" (p. 132). Why shouldn't we laugh, the book asks: "We have recovered, and have been given the power to help others" (p. 132). - Bill's story: "There is, however, a vast amount of fun about it all" (p. 16), with "deadly earnestness" just underneath (p. 16). - And the book's picture of self-will is a man who "wants to run the whole show" (p. 60), which fits a promoter who planned to be general manager of it all.

e3eb6d17975a.t: What do "selfishness—self-centeredness!" and "self-will run riot" mean in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

c385c7811de2.t: Both are on page 62 of Chapter 5, in the book's explanation of Step Three. "Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles."…

b22259e5cbad.t: What do "selfishness—self-centeredness!" and "self-will run riot" mean in the Big Book?

6264304cc9ae.t: Both are on page 62 of Chapter 5, in the book's explanation of Step Three. "Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles." (p. 62) The alcoholic is "an extreme example of self-will run riot, though he usually doesn't think so" (p. 62).

399eae4fb82b.t: The book's picture of self-will is an actor who wants to run the whole show (pp. 60–61). He may be "kind, considerate, patient, generous" (p. 61). In this sense, selfishness isn't only greed. It is trying to arrange life to suit ourselves, "even though our motives are good" (p. 60).

9d34758207c8.t: It isn't offered as name-calling or as a flaw only alcoholics have. "Most people try to live by self-propulsion." (p. 60) The alcoholic is an extreme case (p. 62).

e7e55b5b6061.t: The diagnosis leads straight to a remedy. "Above everything, we alcoholics must be rid of this selfishness." (p. 62) "We must, or it kills us!" (p. 62) "God makes that possible." (p. 62)

cd0c5e7673df.t: The lines come in the book's explanation of Step Three. Right after the a, b, c, the book asks what turning our will and our life over to God means, and starts with self-will: "The first requirement is that we be convinced that any life run on self-will can hardly be a success." (p. 60) Living that way, "we are almost always in collision with something or somebody, even though our motives are good" (p. 60).

dbaa74b75ae7.t: The book draws a picture. Each person is "like an actor who wants to run the whole show" (p. 60), arranging the lights, the scenery and the other players his own way. If only people would do as he wished, the show would be great (p. 61). He may be quite virtuous while he does it, or he may be mean and dishonest, or most likely a mix (p. 61). The show goes badly, he tries harder, he gets angry and self-pitying, and he blames others (p. 61).

215871ed2135.t: Then the questions. "Is he not really a self-seeker even when trying to be kind?" (p. 61) "Is he not, even in his best moments, a producer of confusion rather than harmony?" (p. 61) The book lines up the retired businessman, the minister, politicians and reformers, the safe-cracker and the alcoholic who is locked up, and asks: "are not most of us concerned with ourselves, our resentments, or our self-pity?" (p. 62)

45b160a344dc.t: "Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles." (p. 62) The book says what drives it: fear, self-delusion, self-seeking and self-pity. Driven by them, we step on other people's toes, and they hit back (p. 62). Even when we're hurt seemingly without provocation, we find that some earlier decision "based on self" put us in a position to be hurt (p. 62).

087e606ad70f.t: "So our troubles, we think, are basically of our own making." (p. 62) The alcoholic is "an extreme example of self-will run riot, though he usually doesn't think so" (p. 62).

0e06ebddf590.t: Twice the book says "we think." It offers this as its conclusion from experience.

65bff4b88f5f.t: The lines are a diagnosis, and the book moves straight to the treatment.

1e31e6f3d04e.t: <0>It can't be done alone.</0> Many members had moral convictions they couldn't live up to. "Neither could we reduce our self-centeredness much by wishing or trying on our own power." (p. 62) "We had to have God's help." (p. 62)

704dee4b3d7c.t: <0>Quit playing God.</0> "First of all, we had to quit playing God." (p. 62) God is to be the Director, and we his agents (p. 62).

7895dd68f1b5.t: <0>The result.</0> "Established on such a footing we became less and less interested in ourselves, our little plans and designs." (p. 63) "More and more we became interested in seeing what we could contribute to life." (p. 63)

b4254df58aeb.t: <0>The Third Step prayer</0> asks: "Relieve me of the bondage of self, that I may better do Thy will." (p. 63)

8f585426eed7.t: Self-will is not the same as will

e04969e8e7bd.t: The book doesn't condemn willpower as such. In Chapter 6, after the daily prayer "Thy will (not mine) be done," it says: "We can exercise our will power along this line all we wish." (p. 85) "It is the proper use of the will." (p. 85) Self-will, in the book's sense, is a life run on self: "our effort to live on self-will and run the show ourselves" (p. 76). In the morning prayer of Step Eleven, "We ask especially for freedom from self-will" (p. 87).

4623af263152.t: Bill's own story says the same thing earlier. The new way of life was "Simple, but not easy" (p. 14), and "It meant destruction of self-centeredness." (p. 14)

81626a2c2427.t: It complicates it. Quoted alone, "selfishness" can sound like plain greed, and "self-will run riot" like a label for bad people. In the book, self-centredness includes our kind and generous moments when they are aimed at arranging life our way. Most people live like that, and the alcoholic is an extreme case. The passage is a diagnosis, given so the reader can see why he needs God's help, and it ends in a prayer to be relieved of self "that I may better do Thy will." The book does mean it when it calls self the root of our troubles. That part stands.

3d9ad62f50f5.t: Related: <0>What are the a, b, c of p. 60 ("probably no human power… God could and would if He were sought")?</0> · <1>What is the Third Step prayer, and where is it?</1> · <2>Is helping others selfish if it keeps me sober?</2> · <3>Where is "resentment is the number one offender," and what does it mean?</3>

78adec0a07fd.t: Is "A.A. is a selfish program" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

98c37ae6f2f7.t: No. "A selfish program" isn't anywhere in our sources: not in the Big Book, the pamphlets, the history books or the story collection.

e7d2612ef3f9.t: Is "A.A. is a selfish program" in the Big Book?

4492f266b987.t: No. "A selfish program" isn't anywhere in our sources: not in the Big Book, the pamphlets, the history books or the story collection.

e592c771a96c.t: Every time the program text (pp. 1–164) uses "selfish" or "selfishness," it means a defect. "Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles" (p. 62). "Above everything, we alcoholics must be rid of this selfishness" (p. 62).

48a67ed9623c.t: What the book does say is that helping others protects the helper's own sobriety (pp. 89, 94, 97), and that a man must keep sober (p. 82). It never calls either of these selfish. It says the self-protective motive "became secondary" for the first members (p. 159).

c4b9f4120791.t: Dr. Bob, in a 1948 talk, admitted that part of his own early helping was to keep himself from getting drunk, and said that if you called it selfishness "you'd be quite correct."

634fed4e3c80.t: All our sources were searched for "selfish program," "program is selfish," "be selfish," "selfish about my sobriety," "healthy selfishness" and "sobriety first." None of them turns up in this sense. The only "be selfish" in our sources are in a dropped story in <0>Experience, Strength and Hope</0>, where a man reasons that one who loves his neighbour "could not be selfish" (<1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1>, 2003, story from an earlier edition).

1d33fed44f59.t: Read in place, each "selfish" is something to get rid of, and each "unselfish" something to aim for (with one neutral exception, noted): - Bill, in hospital: a doctor told him that though he was "certainly selfish and foolish," he had been seriously ill (p. 7). - The real alcoholic is sensible about everything except liquor, "but in that respect he is incredibly dishonest and selfish" (p. 21). - The actor who wants to run the show may be "mean, egotistical, selfish and dishonest" (p. 61). Even when he's kind, he's "really a self-seeker" (p. 61). - "Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles" (p. 62). "Above everything, we alcoholics must be rid of this selfishness" (p. 62). "We must, or it kills us!" (p. 62). - In the resentment inventory: "Where had we been selfish, dishonest, self-seeking and frightened?" (p. 67). On sex conduct, each relationship is tested: "was it selfish or not?" (p. 69). - At home: "Selfish and inconsiderate habits have kept the home in turmoil" (p. 82). - Chapter 8, written in the voice of alcoholics' wives, says they "were not above selfishness or dishonesty" (p. 116). Earlier it lists, among all the wives tried with their drinking husbands, "We have been unselfish and self-sacrificing" (p. 105); there it is simply one of many things that didn't work. - The promises: "We will lose interest in selfish things and gain interest in our fellows" (p. 84). - Step Ten: "Continue to watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear" (p. 84). - Step Eleven: each night ask, "Were we resentful, selfish, dishonest or afraid?" (p. 86). In prayer, "We are careful never to pray for our own selfish ends" (p. 87). - To make faith vital, it "must be accompanied by self sacrifice and unselfish, constructive action" (p. 93). - The man getting over alcoholism won't get far "if he fails to show unselfishness and love under his own roof" (p. 127). - Dr. Silkworth praised "the unselfishness of these men" (p. xxvii).

be467d482a59.t: What the saying may be reaching for

aec809958efc.t: The book does treat the alcoholic's sobriety as essential, and says so without apology: - "Certainly he must keep sober, for there will be no home if he doesn't" (p. 82). It adds at once that sobriety alone isn't enough to make good at home (p. 82). - Helping other alcoholics protects the helper. "Nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (p. 89). Tell the newcomer that your helping him "plays a vital part in your own recovery" (p. 94). "Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery" (p. 97). - A family is told to let a newly sober father go as far as he likes in helping other alcoholics, even with some neglect of the family, because "this will do more to insure his sobriety than anything else" (p. 129).

3832f298ef9d.t: None of this is called selfish. It is all aimed outward: at other alcoholics, at the family, at being "of maximum service to God and the people about us" (p. 77). Of the first Akron members the book says: "Though they knew they must help other alcoholics if they would remain sober, that motive became secondary" (p. 159).

e61583240745.t: The Traditions put it the same way for the group. The Long Form's first point: "Hence our common welfare comes first. But individual welfare follows close afterward" (p. 563). See <0>Tradition One: does it mean "my sobriety comes first"?</0>

2c963f7cdaac.t: In his last major talk, given in December 1948 and printed in P-53, Dr. Bob said he found it hard to love his fellow man. At first he went through "the motions of trying to be helpful to the other fellow" partly so he wouldn't get drunk himself (P-53). "Well, you could say that was just a manifestation of selfishness, and you'd be quite correct" (P-53). That is the closest anything in our sources comes to the saying. It's one man's honest account of his own early motive. He doesn't call the program selfish, and in the same passage the service he means by "absolute unselfishness" is "actually giving of yourself" (P-53). See <0>Is helping others selfish if it keeps me sober?</0>

169f2b6fa848.t: "A.A. is a selfish program" isn't the Big Book's language, and it runs against the book's own diagnosis. The book calls selfishness "the root of our troubles" (p. 62) and asks a member to watch for it every day (p. 84). What the book does say is narrower: a member must stay sober, and he protects his sobriety by working with others. It expects even that motive to give way to giving himself for others (p. 159).

32063fa26e53.t: Where did the Serenity Prayer come from in A.A.? | Recovery Starts

604747adcee2.t: The Serenity Prayer is not in the Big Book's program text (pp. 1–164), its forewords or its appendices. It appears only in some of the members' stories at…

ad178493d2ce.t: Where did the Serenity Prayer come from in A.A.?

3c0c6241e10a.t: The Serenity Prayer is not in the Big Book's program text (pp. 1–164), its forewords or its appendices. It appears only in some of the members' stories at the back of the fourth edition.

c99249a3ed22.t: It came into A.A. in New York in the early 1940s. A member saw it in a newspaper obituary notice and brought it to the office, and A.A. began printing it on cards and putting one in every letter it sent out.

0d7dbd7157ba.t: Bill W. wrote in 1957: "No one can tell for sure who first wrote the Serenity Prayer" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He listed several claims, including the one that it was by Reinhold Niebuhr.

70be0dd716c4.t: The sources disagree on the date (1941 or early 1942), on the exact wording of the clipping, and on the name of the man who paid for the first cards.

c0988b0df15b.t: A search of the whole fourth edition finds the prayer only in the personal stories, for example pp. 345, 357, 401, 419 and 559. The word "serenity" does appear in the main text, in other senses: Bill's peace and serenity after his experience at Towns Hospital (p. 14), the hope "to match calamity with serenity" (p. 68), and the promise "We will comprehend the word serenity and we will know peace" (p. 84). None of these is the prayer.

d8a22f0f06b4.t: How it came into A.A.: Bill's account (1957)

77cd4a4bd856.t: In <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, Bill says that just before Ruth Hock, the office secretary, left in early 1942, "newsman Jack," a New York member, showed them a clipping (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). It was an obituary notice, and under it were the words: "God grant us the serenity to accept the things we cannot change, courage to change the things we can, and wisdom to know the difference." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

986a2aa96779.t: "Never had we seen so much A.A. in so few words." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). A friend, Howard, came into the office and offered to pay for printing it on cards to go into every piece of mail (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). They did that for several years, and the prayer quickly came into general use, alongside "our two other favorites, the Lord's Prayer and the Prayer of St. Francis" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

272cabe6796d.t: On who wrote it, Bill says some credited the early Greeks, some an anonymous English poet, some an American naval officer, and that Jack Alexander, who had looked into it, "attributes it to the Rev. Reinhold Niebuhr of the Union Theological Seminary" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill's conclusion: "Anyhow, we have the prayer and it is said thousands of times daily." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

452226aba42d.t: The later biography gives more detail. It says the prayer was found in the "In Memoriam" column of an early June 1941 edition of the New York Herald-Tribune (Pass It On, 1984). It gives the notice's wording, addressed to "Mother" and beginning "Mother — God grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change" (Pass It On, 1984), going on with "I can" in the second line and ending "Goodbye."

733c2ee52855.t: It quotes Ruth Hock: "Jack C. appeared at the office one morning, and he showed me the obituary notice" (Pass It On, 1984), and she copied it to use in letters to groups and loners. In her account, "Horace C. had the idea of printing it on cards and paid for the first printing" (Pass It On, 1984). Elsewhere <0>Pass It On</0> notes that in his 1957 book Bill called Horace C. "Howard A." (Pass It On, 1984), so the two accounts may name the same man.

544b95e6341b.t: A note in <0>Pass It On</0> says the prayer's origins are obscure: it may go back to the philosopher Boethius, about 500 A.D.; it is usually credited to Reinhold Niebuhr, a 20th-century theologian, who in turn credited an 18th-century theologian (Pass It On, 1984). Our copy of that note is damaged by the scan, so the second theologian's name can't be read with confidence.

c6ef7348b0fe.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> quotes an early Ohio member, Oscar W., describing the friction between the Midwest and New York in the 1940s: "I don't like the Serenity Prayer. New York brought it in, and we resented it." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). To him it felt like the Oxford Group's praying coming back.

1d610b0679ea.t: Later A.A. literature describes the prayer as a common part of meetings. P-16, <0>The A.A. Group</0> (© 2018), describing how a chairperson usually opens a meeting with the Preamble, adds: "Some call for a moment of silence and/or recite the Serenity Prayer" (P-16). In one fourth-edition story, a member describes the slogans on a meeting-room wall, ending with "The Serenity Prayer" (p. 345). Another says he had misread "the courage to change" as being about changing his marriage, when it meant changing himself (p. 419).

2430c68e69ba.t: <0>When.</0> Bill (1957) puts it just before Ruth Hock left in early 1942 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) says an early June 1941 newspaper (Pass It On, 1984).

08bf1ca240ab.t: <0>The wording.</0> Bill's version reads "grant us… we cannot change… we can" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); <1>Pass It On</1> gives the clipping as "grant me… I cannot change… I can" (Pass It On, 1984). The fourth-edition stories that quote it use the "us… we" form (pp. 357, 559).

7387e03ceca8.t: <0>Who paid for the cards.</0> "Friend Howard" in 1957 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); Horace C. in Ruth Hock's memory, 1984 (Pass It On, 1984).

bdb4caa2ae06.t: <0>Who wrote it.</0> Bill (1957) says no one can be sure (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) calls the origins obscure (Pass It On, 1984). Both mention Niebuhr as the usual attribution; neither settles it, and neither does our sources.
