5a350a27f8e1.t: What is the Seventh Step prayer, and where is it? | Recovery Starts

e7808194b2c4.t: It's on page 76 of the Big Book, in Chapter 6, "Into Action." It begins "My Creator, I am now willing that you should have all of me, good and bad." (p. 76)

5e353acd3ba7.t: What is the Seventh Step prayer, and where is it?

802d4a9ed473.t: It's on page 76 of the Big Book, in Chapter 6, "Into Action." It begins "My Creator, I am now willing that you should have all of me, good and bad." (p. 76)

98a0cc0a7071.t: The book introduces it with "When ready, we say something like this" (p. 76). So it's an example, not a set form, and the book doesn't call it "the Seventh Step prayer."

2239597effde.t: It asks for defects to be removed for a reason outside yourself: because they stand in the way of "my usefulness to you and my fellows" (p. 76).

8137df30c280.t: Steps Six and Seven read: "Were entirely ready to have God remove all these defects of character." and "Humbly asked Him to remove our shortcomings." (p. 59)

e003c3befe52.t: In Chapter 6 they come right after the Fifth Step. Having told someone their whole story, members go home, find a quiet hour, and reread the first five Steps to check nothing has been left out (p. 75). Then the book turns to Step Six, and the whole of Steps Six and Seven takes one paragraph each (p. 76).

6b91bf774390.t: Step Six, in the book's words

2c6fa4b73daf.t: Step Six is about willingness, which the book has "emphasized" as "indispensable" (p. 76). The question is whether we're ready to let God remove all the things we've admitted are objectionable: "Can He now take them all—every one?" (p. 76) If we still cling to something, "we ask God to help us be willing" (p. 76).

a610502be460.t: "When ready" (p. 76), the book gives the prayer. After its opening line, it asks God to remove "every single defect of character" that stands in the way of usefulness to God and to other people, and asks for strength to do God's bidding "as I go out from here" (p. 76). Then: "We have then completed Step Seven." (p. 76)

630be8a894c9.t: Two things stand out when it's read in place: - <0>It's about usefulness.</0> The defects are to go because they get in the way of being useful to God and "my fellows" (p. 76), the same outward aim the Third Step prayer has (p. 63). - <1>It leads straight to action.</1> The very next sentence says more action is needed, "without which we find that 'Faith without works is dead'" (p. 76), and moves to Steps Eight and Nine.

c69fe339e5f3.t: Chapter 6, "Into Action" (pp. 72–88), with the prayer on page 76, free from A.A.: <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt6.pdf</0>

ccad39e6b3d2.t: Related: <0>What is the Third Step prayer, and where is it?</0> · <1>How does the Big Book say to make amends?</1>

ef214c5000fb.t: Is "we're only as sick as our secrets" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

c4a3483a7b7d.t: Is "we're only as sick as our secrets" in the Big Book?

52ed8062945c.t: Its idea is close to the Fifth Step in Chapter 6: of newcomers who tried to keep certain facts about their lives to themselves, the book says "Almost invariably they got drunk." (pp. 72–73), and "We must be entirely honest with somebody if we expect to live long or happily in this world." (pp. 73–74).

a6980047a9d1.t: The text also sets limits the saying leaves out: choose the person carefully, tell family nothing that would hurt them (those parts go to someone unaffected), keep other people's confidences, and don't dig up the past unless it serves a good purpose (pp. 74, 81, 125).

c8e0797f8f4d.t: All our sources were searched for "sick as," "secret(s)," "skeletons" and "double life," with page breaks joined. The saying doesn't appear. In the program text "secret" appears once, for a husband's "secret and exciting affair" (p. 81).

94b5435a555b.t: What the program text says about keeping things hidden

2516de5ff9bf.t: <0>The Fifth Step's reason.</0> Chapter 6 gives "The best reason first: If we skip this vital step, we may not overcome drinking." (p. 72). "Time after time newcomers have tried to keep to themselves certain facts about their lives." (p. 72). "Almost invariably they got drunk." (p. 73). They had taken inventory, the book says, "but hung on to some of the worst items in stock" (p. 73).

698b0685eb98.t: <0>The double life.</0> "More than most people, the alcoholic leads a double life." (p. 73). He pushes the memories of his sprees deep inside and "hopes they will never see the light of day" (p. 73). "He is under constant fear and tension—that makes for more drinking." (p. 73). That passage is the closest the book comes to the saying: what is hidden keeps him afraid and drinking.

6d2bb7f48368.t: <0>The result of telling.</0> "Once we have taken this step, withholding nothing, we are delighted." (p. 75). "Our fears fall from us." (p. 75).

d74c9be2dd05.t: <0>Every day after.</0> Step Ten: when selfishness, dishonesty, resentment or fear crop up, "We discuss them with someone immediately" (p. 84). The nightly review asks: "Have we kept something to ourselves which should be discussed with another person at once?" (p. 86).

160cf1de2e93.t: <0>Dr. Bob.</0> Chapter 11 says he "lived in constant worry about those who might find out about his alcoholism" (p. 155). After his last spree he went round and told the people he feared, "and learned that many knew of his drinking" (p. 156). See: <1>Who do I tell my Fifth Step to?</1>

cebcc668404b.t: The program text doesn't say "tell everyone everything." It says tell someone everything, with care:

8461df7940f8.t: <0>Choose the person.</0> "Rightly and naturally, we think well before we choose the person or persons with whom to take this intimate and confidential step." (p. 74). It is important "that he be able to keep a confidence" (p. 74).

406660729a5e.t: <0>Don't hurt others to relieve yourself.</0> "We have no right to save our own skin at another person's expense." (p. 74). We cannot disclose anything to wives or parents "which will hurt them and make them unhappy" (p. 74); such parts go to someone who will understand "yet be unaffected" (p. 74). On an affair the wife doesn't know about, should he tell her? "Not always, we think." (p. 81).

68bfc3fc52f4.t: <0>Others' secrets stay theirs.</0> "We do not relate intimate experiences of another person unless we are sure he would approve." (p. 125).

1125e32f99d4.t: <0>The past, with purpose.</0> The family's dark past can be its greatest asset when it helps others (p. 124), and A.A. families "keep few skeletons in the closet" (p. 125). But "unless some good and useful purpose is to be served, past occurrences should not be discussed" (p. 125).

50fbbd8b3729.t: The saying matches one of the book's strongest warnings: facts held back from the Fifth Step lead back to drinking, and the double life feeds fear and more drinking. The book's own answer is to be entirely honest with somebody, a carefully chosen somebody, while protecting other people from harm. A reader who takes the saying to mean that every secret must be told to everyone has gone past the text.

a090fed31ded.t: Is "keep your side of the street clean" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

602f878a3eca.t: Nearly. The 1939 program text says "sweep off our side of the street" (p. 77). "Keep your side of the street clean" isn't in our sources in those words.

73279577966f.t: Is "keep your side of the street clean" in the Big Book?

76cc3ce15381.t: Nearly. The 1939 program text says "sweep off our side of the street" (p. 77). "Keep your side of the street clean" isn't in our sources in those words.

fdffc0a82f56.t: The line is in Chapter 6's directions for amends (Step Nine), about one hard case: going to a man you hated, who may have done you more harm than you did him (p. 77).

3fac75982e49.t: In context, sweeping your side of the street is something you do, face to face where you can: admit your own wrongs and your old ill feeling, without criticizing him or arguing, and "never trying to tell him what he should do" (pp. 77–78).

62baf44467ed.t: Heard as "mind your own part," the saying fits the text: "His faults are not discussed. We stick to our own" (p. 78). But the phrase itself, in the book, names an action in making amends, not a general rule for staying out of other people's business.

90311bb8d25a.t: All our sources were searched for "side of the street," "clean my side," "sweep off" and "own side." The only match in this sense is in Chapter 6, "Into Action," on p. 77. (One story in <0>Experience, Strength and Hope</0> uses "one side of the street" for a couple ringing doorbells for work, which isn't the saying.)

b0955254d9fa.t: Chapter 6 takes up Steps Eight and Nine on p. 76. The list of people harmed was made during the inventory, and "Now we go out to our fellows and repair the damage done in the past" (p. 76). The aim is to "sweep away the debris which has accumulated out of our effort to live on self-will and run the show ourselves" (p. 76).

1fa7c4cec992.t: Then the book turns to the hardest case, "how to approach the man we hated" (p. 77): - He may have done us more harm than we did him, and we may still not be keen to admit our faults. "Nevertheless, with a person we dislike, we take the bit in our teeth" (p. 77). - "It is harder to go to an enemy than to a friend, but we find it much more beneficial to us" (p. 77). We go "in a helpful and forgiving spirit, confessing our former ill feeling and expressing our regret" (p. 77). - "Under no condition do we criticize such a person or argue" (p. 77). We tell him only that we'll never get over drinking until we have done our utmost to straighten out the past. - "We are there to sweep off our side of the street, realizing that nothing worth while can be accomplished until we do so, never trying to tell him what he should do" (pp. 77–78). - "His faults are not discussed. We stick to our own" (p. 78). - The result: "In nine cases out of ten the unexpected happens" (p. 78). Sometimes the other man admits his own fault. But if he throws us out of his office, it shouldn't matter: "We have made our demonstration, done our part" (p. 78).

631ecb6ef218.t: The line isn't alone. Looking at our own part, not the other person's, runs through the inventory and amends: - In the resentment inventory: "Putting out of our minds the wrongs others had done, we resolutely looked for our own mistakes" (p. 67). "The inventory was ours, not the other man's" (p. 67). - At home: "We ought to sit down with the family and frankly analyze the past as we now see it, being very careful not to criticize them" (p. 83). "Their defects may be glaring, but the chances are that our own actions are partly responsible" (p. 83). - With his own family, a newcomer should concentrate "on his own spiritual demonstration," and "Argument and fault-finding are to be avoided like the plague" (p. 98).

94b1e18976e7.t: The saying keeps the core: your job is your own part, not the other person's. What the short form can lose is how active the book's version is. In the text you don't just keep your side clean by staying out of trouble. You go to the man you resent, in person where you can (others get "an honest letter," p. 83), admit your wrongs and your ill feeling, and sweep your own side, whatever he does about his. The book also sets limits on it: amends are not made at the cost of harming other people (pp. 79–80), and some people "need not, and probably should not" hear about our spiritual life on the first approach (p. 76).

13f5f67196bb.t: See also: <0>How does the Big Book say to make amends?</0>

0e165648f4d7.t: The full book, <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, is sold by A.A. World Services: <1>https://onlineliterature.aa.org</1>

2bb04d830e02.t: Where does "singleness of purpose" come from? Is it in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

ba760604385f.t: The phrase "singleness of purpose" is not in the Big Book. It isn't in the 1946 Long Form of the Traditions or in Bill W.'s 1946–47 essays either.

0988d9e844ec.t: Where does "singleness of purpose" come from? Is it in the Big Book?

036898414c15.t: The phrase "singleness of purpose" is not in the Big Book. It isn't in the 1946 Long Form of the Traditions or in Bill W.'s 1946–47 essays either.

8f59432fcbe3.t: In our sources it first appears in Bill W.'s own history of how the Traditions were written, from around 1955 (<0>A.A.'s Legacy of Service</0>, P-44) and in <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957). There it names one of the subjects a code of traditions would cover: "membership, group autonomy, singleness of purpose, nonendorsement of other enterprises…" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957).

f624a4427260.t: The idea is older than the phrase. The Long Form gives each group "but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers" (p. 564), and the 1939 text says of working with alcoholics, "To be helpful is our only aim." (p. 89).

16c70c50ef30.t: In our sources the phrase is about what A.A. and its groups do: carry the message to alcoholics, and not take on other causes, however good.

e7cab7999cb2.t: The whole fourth-edition text of <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, front matter, stories and appendices, was searched for "singleness," "single purpose," "sole purpose" and "one purpose." None of them appears in the program text or the Traditions. "Sole purpose" turns up twice in fourth-edition personal stories, in other senses.

f002d3337884.t: The nearest early wording is in Bill's 1947 essay on government: most groups, he wrote, avoid controversy over outside issues and "stick to their single purpose of helping alcoholics to recover" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947).

bb643cc2a14e.t: The Foreword to the First Edition: "We simply wish to be helpful to those who are afflicted." (p. xiv).

42f094c57b46.t: Chapter 7, on carrying the message: "To be helpful is our only aim." (p. 89).

6e31b93378ee.t: The Long Form of Tradition Five: "Each Alcoholics Anonymous group ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." (p. 564). The short form keeps the core: "Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." (p. 562).

b4acff4514fd.t: Tradition Six warns that money, property and authority "may easily divert us from our primary spiritual aim" (p. 563).

ffe4aa477ca4.t: Where the phrase appears, and what it means there

3edca0054cd6.t: <0>Around 1955 and 1957.</0> In Bill's account of where the Traditions came from, a friend suggested in late 1945 that the mass of experience in headquarters' correspondence be codified. If A.A. had become sure enough where it stood on certain matters, Bill wrote, such a set of principles could be written, and he lists the matters: membership, group autonomy, singleness of purpose, nonendorsement of other enterprises, professionalism, public controversy and anonymity (P-44; <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). The same passage is reprinted in today's <2>A.A. Service Manual</2> (2024–2026 edition).

1a11222dd1aa.t: <0>What he meant by it.</0> In <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> Bill explains Tradition Five this way: A.A. should "do one thing well" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957) instead of many things it isn't called to. His illustration: "If we had discovered a widely applicable cancer cure, we would be begged to attend to that and that only." (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957). The fields A.A. stays out of, he says, are education, research, neurosis and the like, which members may help with as individuals. "A.A. has but one single purpose" (<4>A.A. Comes of Age</4>, 1957): carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. In 1955 he put it as "We have but one purpose: to carry the A.A. message to the sick alcoholic who wants it." (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955).

4d172301b159.t: <0>A warning against grandeur.</0> Near its beginning, today's group pamphlet prints a 1955 passage of Bill's under the heading "A.A.'s Single Purpose": friends who predicted A.A. might spearhead a spiritual awakening for the world were sincere, but A.A. "will prudently cleave to its single purpose: the carrying of the message to the alcoholic who still suffers" (P-16, 2018, quoting Bill W., 1955).

d5c3470b7f4c.t: <0>Applied to meeting listings (2018).</0> The same pamphlet reports a General Service Conference recommendation that "family," "double trouble" and "alcohol and pill" meetings not be listed in A.A. directories. The next paragraph restates that the primary purpose of any A.A. group is to carry the A.A. message to alcoholics, and that experience with alcohol is what all members have in common (P-16, 2018). See <1>Is A.A. for people addicted to drugs or other things?</1>

0ce3832b1c86.t: What the phrase is not used for in our sources

dcb67edee74a.t: In every passage found, "singleness of purpose" or "single purpose" is about what A.A. as a society, or an A.A. group, sets out to do. Who may belong is a separate subject in Bill's own list ("membership" comes first), and the Traditions answer it in Tradition Three (see <0>What is the only requirement for A.A. membership?</0>).

5d5dc229da14.t: P-16, <0>The A.A. Group</0> ("A.A.'s Single Purpose," p. 7): <1>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/literature/p-16_0723.pdf</1>

b9f29544b63c.t: Who was Sister Ignatia, and what part did St. Thomas Hospital play? | Recovery Starts

2ab1ee19e3ed.t: Sister Ignatia was a nun of the Sisters of Charity of St. Augustine who worked in the admitting office of St. Thomas Hospital in Akron, Ohio. Starting…

86b10a366a0b.t: Who was Sister Ignatia, and what part did St. Thomas Hospital play?

220777fdab5c.t: Sister Ignatia was a nun of the Sisters of Charity of St. Augustine who worked in the admitting office of St. Thomas Hospital in Akron, Ohio. Starting around 1939–40, she and Dr. Bob admitted alcoholics there for treatment, the first religious hospital to take A.A. prospects on a regular basis.

c1e81dc3aad3.t: In the St. Thomas ward a newcomer was treated medically and visited by A.A. members, and Dr. Bob saw the patients without charge. By the time he died in 1950, the sources say about 5,000 alcoholics had passed through.

b775716776bb.t: Today's Big Book calls her "one of the greatest friends our Fellowship will ever know" (p. 171). That line is in the introduction to Dr. Bob's story, written after 1950; the 1939 text doesn't mention her.

49fa22fb4274.t: She later ran an alcoholic ward at St. Vincent Charity Hospital in Cleveland. Our later printing of <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> says she died in 1966.

8183421662ed.t: The 1939 Big Book doesn't mention Sister Ignatia or St. Thomas Hospital. The introduction to "Doctor Bob's Nightmare" in today's edition, written after his death in 1950, says that he carried the message to more than 5,000 alcoholics and gave his medical services "without thought of charge" (p. 171), and that "In this prodigy of service, he was well assisted by Sister Ignatia at St. Thomas Hospital in Akron, Ohio" (p. 171), "one of the greatest friends our Fellowship will ever know" (p. 171).

2479cfa1897c.t: <0>Dr. Bob, 1948</0> (his last major talk, in P-53): "The ward theoretically accommodates seven alcoholics, but the good Sister Ignatia sees that it's stretched a little bit." (P-53). Whenever he caught himself thinking he could take a drink, he said, he knew he had been neglecting "the boys in the ward" (P-53).

53c9db2f2dfd.t: <0>Bill W., 1969</0> (his last major talk, in P-53): "Between 1940 and 1950, in the company of that marvelous nun, Sister Ignatia, he had treated 5,000 drunks at St. Thomas Hospital in Akron." (P-53).

168cd4dba8aa.t: <0>P-53's sketch of Dr. Bob</0> (pamphlet © 2017) says he first met Sister Ignatia at St. Thomas in 1928, became associated with the hospital in 1934 and joined its active staff in 1943 (P-53).

6c4973cb3d79.t: Bill's account (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; P-44)

72b5c855ee6d.t: Bill calls St. Thomas "the first religious hospital to receive prospective members of A.A. for treatment on a regular basis" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He tells how, when Dr. Bob asked for a private room for his first patient, Sister Ignatia said: "Doctor, we do not have any beds, much less private rooms, but I will do what I can." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and put the man in the hospital's flower room (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "From 1939 to the time Dr. Bob took his leave of us in 1950, over 5,000 had thus been treated." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

98ada2775325.t: In April 1950, Ohio members placed a plaque in the alcoholic ward, written by Bill, honoring the Sisters and staff; it calls Akron the birthplace of A.A. and St. Thomas the first religious institution to open its door to the society (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "Characteristically, Sister Ignatia would not let her name appear on the inscription." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). By 1957, Bill writes, she was working at St. Vincent Charity Hospital in Cleveland, in a ward called Rosary Hall (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

141bad8b82e1.t: P-44 (Bill, describing events through 1955) says the St. Thomas ward "had ministered to five thousand alcoholics by the time Doctor Bob passed away in 1950" (P-44), and that this hospital and Knickerbocker Hospital in New York were where "the best techniques of combined medicine and A.A. were worked out" (P-44).

1ede861327a5.t: The ward (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980)

3cd7422d92b8.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> says Dr. Bob met Sister Ignatia in 1928, when she worked in the admitting office (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). When another hospital told him to take his alcoholic patients elsewhere, he came to her; she was wary, having once been scolded for admitting a man in the D.T.'s: "I was fearful to admit an alcoholic" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). She agreed, used the flower room, and "This was in August 1939." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). The book says that "between that day and the time he died 4,800 alcoholics were admitted into St. Thomas under his care" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

164398dc2fad.t: It describes how the ward worked: a priest she sent to look into A.A. reported well of it; the ward grew to eight beds; patients saw only A.A. visitors, often fifteen a day; a man could be admitted only once; and Dr. Bob visited daily without pay until his health failed (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). "In 1952, Sister Ignatia was transferred from St. Thomas to administer the alcoholic ward at St. Vincent's Charity Hospital in Cleveland" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). A footnote in our later printing of <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> says: "Sister Ignatia died in 1966" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

1d5b0d21733a.t: <0>When it started.</0> <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) says August 1939 . Bill (1957) says "From 1939" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), but in the same passage calls 1950 "ten years after the start of Dr. Bob's and Sister Ignatia's pioneering" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In 1969 he said "Between 1940 and 1950" (P-53).

a4dd86f769aa.t: <0>How many.</0> About 5,000 (p. 171; P-53; P-44); "over 5,000" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); "several thousand alcoholics by the time of Dr. Bob's death in 1950" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); 4,800 admitted under his care (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). The 1939 Big Book gives no figure, since the ward hadn't begun.

27dee3d67eb2.t: <0>Treated, or recovered.</0> Most sources say treated or admitted; P-53's sketch says he "guided some 5,000 fellow alcoholics to recovery" (P-53). Our sources don't say how many of those treated stayed sober.

33068976efb1.t: What were the "six steps" used before the Twelve Steps? | Recovery Starts

4987b1466fad.t: Before the Twelve Steps were written in 1938, the first members passed the program on by word of mouth. Bill W. later summed it up as six steps: admit you…

80d39dcda09c.t: What were the "six steps" used before the Twelve Steps?

11f9f521674c.t: Before the Twelve Steps were written in 1938, the first members passed the program on by word of mouth. Bill W. later summed it up as six steps: admit you are licked, take a moral inventory, confess your defects to another person, make restitution, help other alcoholics without reward, and pray to whatever God you think there is for the power to do these things.

89a4598bb4c5.t: That list is Bill's own summary, written in 1957. He said it was "approximately" what they were telling newcomers by the fall of 1938. The 1939 Big Book doesn't print any "six steps."

e1903884c3cc.t: An Akron member's story, written after the Big Book came out, gives a different six-step list that Dr. Bob took him through in 1937. The two lists don't match word for word or in order.

8bab50f5c8cd.t: Our sources don't confirm that the six steps came from the Oxford Group as a set. <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) says there is no evidence the Oxford Group had such a program.

d4648eb89ab3.t: What the 1939 Big Book shows instead

194dd86f6cd1.t: The 1939 text never uses the phrase "six steps." What it does give is the program as Bill received it in late 1934. In "Bill's Story," his old school friend tells him to choose his own conception of God (p. 12). In the hospital Bill offered himself to God, faced his sins, and became willing to have them taken away (p. 13). His friend came back; they made a list of people Bill had hurt, and Bill became willing to go to them and admit his wrongs (p. 13). He was to sit quietly when in doubt, asking only for direction (p. 13), and to work with others as his friend had worked with him: "Faith without works was dead, he said." (p. 14).

4f7f560de387.t: The 1955 Foreword to the Second Edition puts the same ideas in a list, still not called steps: the broker "was convinced of the need for moral inventory, confession of personality defects, restitution to those harmed, helpfulness to others, and the necessity of belief in and dependence upon God." (p. xvi).

44661e2dc01b.t: Bill's six steps (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)

5ef08ecef58b.t: In <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, Bill describes the night he wrote the Twelve Steps. Since Ebby's visit in the fall of 1934, he says, they had evolved a word-of-mouth program, with most of its basic ideas taken from the Oxford Groups, William James and Dr. Silkworth (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Though it varied a good deal, it boiled down to a procedure that "comprised six steps" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "These were approximately as follows:" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)

e00c8e582a48.t: "We admitted that we were licked, that we were powerless over alcohol." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)

46e6db9ede03.t: We made a moral inventory of our defects or sins.

2d72937fc7b5.t: We confessed or shared our shortcomings with another person in confidence.

feccae5c5efa.t: We made restitution to all those we had harmed by our drinking.

2aefca292708.t: We tried to help other alcoholics, with no thought of reward in money or prestige.

051f9ee93e7a.t: "We prayed to whatever God we thought there was for power to practice these precepts." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)

9d9fc531fa36.t: "This was the substance of what, by the fall of 1938, we were telling newcomers." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill wanted something more explicit for readers he would never meet, so he set out to break these "six chunks of truth" into smaller pieces, and the result was twelve (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <0>How were the Twelve Steps written?</0>

730dda005d5d.t: The same book has Ebby giving Bill nearly the same points in 1934: admit you are licked, get honest with yourself, talk it out with somebody else, make restitution, give of yourself without stint, and pray to whatever God you think there is, even as an experiment (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

ba034a52fe9d.t: The Akron version (a Big Book story, written after 1939)

82f386ec6813.t: "He Sold Himself Short," a story in Part I of today's Big Book, was written after the book was printed (it mentions the spring of 1939, p. 265) and describes Akron in 1937 (p. 260). The day before the writer went home to Chicago, Dr. Bob spent three or four hours "formally going through the Six-Step program as it was at that time" (p. 263):

b78ad6be03de.t: Dependence and guidance from a Higher Power.

17ff41ac9c9d.t: At the inventory, Dr. Bob named the man's defects, asked if he wanted them removed, and the two knelt and prayed (p. 263). The writer says Dr. Bob "always emphasized the religious angle very strongly" (p. 263).

0a49e7ce0cde.t: <0>Frank Amos, February 1938.</0> A report written for John D. Rockefeller, Jr., quoted in <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980), describes the Akron "Program" in seven points: realize you are an incurable alcoholic and never drink again; surrender absolutely to God; remove other sins from your life; daily morning devotions; be willing to help other alcoholics; meeting with other members is important "but not vital"; and attending a religious service weekly, also not vital (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

353912e13284.t: <0>Dr. Bob, 1948.</0> In his last major talk, printed in P-53, Dr. Bob said: "When we started in on Bill D., we had no Twelve Steps, either; we had no Traditions." (P-53). He called the Oxford Group's Four Absolutes "the only yardsticks we had in the early days, before the Steps" (P-53). See <1>What were the "Four Absolutes"? Are they in the Big Book?</1>

7c12cd9b3c11.t: <0>Pass It On (1984)</0> repeats Bill's six steps and adds: "There is no evidence that the Oxford Group had such a specific program" (Pass It On, 1984). A footnote says some members later called them the six tenets of the Oxford Group, and quotes a longtime Oxford Group staff member who had never heard of any such tenets (Pass It On, 1984).

486d394203c3.t: <0>The lists.</0> Bill's 1957 list ends with prayer and has no separate step about a Higher Power at the start; the Akron story's list puts "Dependence and guidance from a Higher Power" second and ends with work with other alcoholics (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; p. 263). Amos's 1938 report has seven points, not six (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

ac768ca93f8a.t: <0>What the yardstick was.</0> Bill speaks of six steps; Dr. Bob, in 1948, said the Four Absolutes were the only yardsticks before the Steps (P-53). Our sources don't explain whether these were two ways of describing the same practice.

f4abdb71c1bf.t: <0>Where they came from.</0> Bill credits the Oxford Groups, William James and Dr. Silkworth for most of the basic ideas (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The saying that the six steps were an Oxford Group program isn't confirmed by our sources, and <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) says there is no evidence for it.

09184b59bba1.t: What is the "spiritual awakening" in Step 12? | Recovery Starts

a5447e8f3d40.t: Step Twelve says the awakening comes "as the result of these steps" (p. 60). It follows the work of the first eleven Steps; it isn't a precondition for…

8da4c99f6dd4.t: What is the "spiritual awakening" in Step 12?

9a751a3f6953.t: Step Twelve says the awakening comes "as the result of these steps" (p. 60). It follows the work of the first eleven Steps; it isn't a precondition for starting them.

0dd26fa6d918.t: The Big Book's Appendix II, "Spiritual Experience," says the book uses "spiritual experience" and "spiritual awakening" for the same thing: "the personality change sufficient to bring about recovery from alcoholism" (p. 567).

3e205fca5c28.t: Most such changes are slow, what William James called the "educational variety" (p. 567). Friends often notice before the person does (p. 567).

38dff0090ac8.t: Members usually find an inner resource they hadn't suspected, which they come to identify with their own idea of a Power greater than themselves (pp. 567–568).

38a8e440cfc0.t: The appendix was added after the first printing of 1939, because that printing had given readers the wrong idea (p. 567). Its main points, in order:

460e26db3394.t: The terms "spiritual experience" and "spiritual awakening" are used throughout the book, and a careful reading shows the personality change behind recovery "has manifested itself among us in many different forms" (p. 567).

9b7423b13011.t: The first printing left many readers thinking these changes had to be "sudden and spectacular upheavals" (p. 567). "Happily for everyone, this conclusion is erroneous" (p. 567).

37162c5b99b1.t: Sudden transformations, "though frequent, are by no means the rule" (p. 567). Most are of the "educational variety because they develop slowly over a period of time" (p. 567).

038a01171d49.t: The person finally realizes he has "undergone a profound alteration in his reaction to life" that he couldn't have brought about alone (p. 567).

53fb2f22a52a.t: Members find they have "tapped an unsuspected … inner resource which they presently identify with their own conception of a Power greater than themselves" (pp. 567–568). "Our more religious members call it God-consciousness" (p. 568).

86d40129e0d8.t: Anyone who honestly faces his problems in the light of A.A. experience can recover, "provided he does not close his mind to all spiritual concepts" (p. 568). "Willingness, honesty and open mindedness are the essentials of recovery" (p. 568).

fe74f754e463.t: How the rest of the book shows it

2a5da4a98437.t: <0>Both kinds are in the book.</0> Chapter 4 tells of an atheist minister's son whose change came in one night, then adds: "To this man, the revelation was sudden. Some of us grow into it more slowly" (Ch. 4, p. 57).

f7c68af1cb76.t: <0>It comes with the work.</0> After Step Five: "We may have had certain spiritual beliefs, but now we begin to have a spiritual experience" (p. 75). The lawyer in Chapter 11, after deciding to do whatever was needed, "had begun to have a spiritual experience" (p. 158).

4c0adecce9c7.t: <0>It's a change in a person, not only a feeling.</0> The doctor quoted in Chapter 2 describes such experiences as "huge emotional displacements and rearrangements" in which old ideas and motives are replaced by new ones (p. 27).

0aa2a61c72a0.t: It isn't a requirement to have a dramatic moment, and the book's own appendix was written to correct that idea (p. 567). Nor does Step Twelve make the awakening the point of the Step. It names the awakening as what the Steps produced, and then asks for action: carry the message and practice these principles (p. 60). See: <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0>

d04e1a22fa80.t: Chapter 5, "How It Works," with the Steps (pp. 58–71): <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt5.pdf</0>

ec2d814a8339.t: What does "the spiritual life is not a theory. We have to live it" refer to? | Recovery Starts

2e6ea109d538.t: The lines are on page 83 of the Big Book, in Chapter 6, "Into Action," in the part about making amends at home to the wife and family (pp. 82–83).

90e2406ecd1e.t: What does "the spiritual life is not a theory. We have to live it" refer to?

eb84ce468820.t: The lines are on page 83 of the Big Book, in Chapter 6, "Into Action," in the part about making amends at home to the wife and family (pp. 82–83).

528032808042.t: Just before them, the book tells the recovering man to sit down with his family, look honestly at the past without criticizing them, and ask each morning to be shown "the way of patience, tolerance, kindliness and love" (p. 83).

53994ddfa9cf.t: Just after, it says not to push spiritual principles on the family or talk to them constantly about spiritual matters: "Our behavior will convince them more than our words." (p. 83)

abbeb719529e.t: So the context confirms the usual reading, that the spiritual life is something you do and not only something you believe, and makes it specific. In its place, "live it" means at home, through how you treat your family, instead of preaching to them.

4cea1b4473d5.t: The amends section of Chapter 6 deals with creditors, enemies, legal trouble and infidelity, and then turns to the home: "If we have no such complication, there is plenty we should do at home." (p. 82)

6e81edba769b.t: The book answers the man who thinks staying sober is enough. He must stay sober, "for there will be no home if he doesn't" (p. 82), but he's still a long way from making good to the people he treated so badly. "The alcoholic is like a tornado roaring his way through the lives of others." (p. 82) A man who says sobriety is enough is like the farmer who comes up from his storm cellar, finds his home in ruins, and remarks to his wife that it's grand the wind has stopped (p. 82).

c748c1d22d3d.t: Then page 83, in order: 1. <0>Reconstruction.</0> "Yes, there is a long period of reconstruction ahead." (p. 83) "We must take the lead." (p. 83) A remorseful mumble that we're sorry "won't fill the bill at all" (p. 83). 2. <1>The family talk.</1> Sit down with the family and frankly look at the past as we now see it, "being very careful not to criticize them" (p. 83). Their defects may be glaring, but our actions are likely partly responsible (p. 83). 3. <2>The morning prayer.</2> "So we clean house with the family," asking each morning in meditation for patience, tolerance, kindliness and love (p. 83). 4. <3>The line.</3> "The spiritual life is not a theory. We have to live it." (p. 83) 5. <4>Don't preach.</4> Unless the family wants to live on spiritual principles, "we think we ought not to urge them" (p. 83). Don't talk incessantly to them about spiritual matters. "They will change in time." (p. 83) Behaviour convinces more than words, and "ten or twenty years of drunkenness would make a skeptic out of anyone" (p. 83).

9e476f05bc4a.t: The paragraph after that covers wrongs that can never be fully righted (p. 83), and then come the Promises (pp. 83–84).

b00ae10c8443.t: Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward," gives the other side of it. A father who has a sudden spiritual experience may become a religious enthusiast who talks about spiritual matters "morning, noon and night" (p. 128) and tells his family to find God in a hurry. The book's answer is that "a spiritual life which does not include his family obligations may not be so perfect after all" (p. 129). The writers say they believe God would like them to keep their heads in the clouds with Him, "but that our feet ought to be firmly planted on earth" (p. 130). "We have found nothing incompatible between a powerful spiritual experience and a life of sane and happy usefulness." (p. 130)

f884d5e4f1c7.t: Chapter 9 is gentle with this father, though, and its advice here is mostly to the family. If they cooperate he will soon see that his spiritual growth is lopsided (p. 129). Meanwhile they "should let him have his head" (p. 129), and the book judges him on a firmer foundation than the man who puts business or professional success "ahead of spiritual development" (p. 130).

9117d8e0e7c0.t: It confirms it and narrows it. Quoted alone, the line works as a general saying about practice over belief, and the book would agree with that. In its place it has a particular target: the man who thinks sobriety is enough at home, or who talks about his new spiritual life instead of changing how he treats his family. Living it, there, means patience and kindness at home, and leaving the family free.

97442e31ede9.t: What is the "spiritual malady"? | Recovery Starts

e797583ed078.t: The phrase is used once in the 1939 program text (pp. 1–164), on page 64, at the start of the Fourth Step inventory: "When the spiritual malady is…

cb7b939af871.t: The phrase is used once in the 1939 program text (pp. 1–164), on page 64, at the start of the Fourth Step inventory: "When the spiritual malady is overcome, we straighten out mentally and physically." (p. 64)

0f5041213d81.t: In place, it's tied to resentment. The sentence before says of resentment, "From it stem all forms of spiritual disease" (p. 64).

e91fa4e078ca.t: The passage adds the spiritual to the mental and physical; it doesn't replace them: "we have been not only mentally and physically ill, we have been spiritually sick" (p. 64).

cf02bd8f694d.t: The book doesn't define the phrase further. The pages around it describe the sickness as self-centredness showing up as resentment and fear (pp. 62–68), and the remedy as the inventory and the Steps that follow.

e15c0cbaaf33.t: The book has just said that self was what defeated us, and turns to its "common manifestations" (p. 64). Then, in four sentences:

9e70f479edbc.t: "It destroys more alcoholics than anything else." (p. 64)

8f9426388e2b.t: "From it stem all forms of spiritual disease, for we have been not only mentally and physically ill, we have been spiritually sick." (p. 64)

37253e799ff1.t: "When the spiritual malady is overcome, we straighten out mentally and physically." (p. 64)

9012d1affaf9.t: So "the spiritual malady" in sentence 4 points back to the "spiritual disease" and being "spiritually sick" of sentence 3, which the book says stems from resentment.

c14a599e48e2.t: What the sickness looks like in the pages around it

117a49af1ed4.t: <0>Its root is self.</0> Two pages earlier: "Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles." (p. 62)

10069b6dcae8.t: <0>It cuts a person off.</0> Harbouring resentment, "we shut ourselves off from the sunlight of the Spirit" (p. 66), and "The insanity of alcohol returns and we drink again." (p. 66)

91d6953dec34.t: <0>Fear runs through it.</0> "This short word somehow touches about every aspect of our lives." (p. 67)

5b36287b96a6.t: <0>It isn't only alcoholics who have it.</0> The book asks the reader to see that the people who wronged us "were perhaps spiritually sick" (p. 66), and "they, like ourselves, were sick too" (p. 67).

d27dc2fcb4af.t: Everywhere else in the main text, "malady" means alcoholism itself. Chapter 2 says that once "this malady has a real hold," drinkers are baffled (p. 23). Chapter 7 tells the helper to speak of alcoholism "as an illness, a fatal malady" (p. 92). Chapter 10 talks about explaining "alcoholism, the malady" to an employer (p. 138). The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) says Dr. Bob began "to pursue the spiritual remedy for his malady" (p. xvi). Page 64 is the one place in the program text where the word is qualified as "spiritual." (One fourth-edition personal story, "A Vision of Recovery," uses the phrase too: the member writes that "the spiritual malady should be my main concern" (p. 499). That's a member's account from the stories, which change by edition, not the 1939 text.)

c61c4baaf5ed.t: The book doesn't use those words. What it says about alcoholism as a whole, to a reader who finds he can't quit or can't control the amount, is that "you may be suffering from an illness which only a spiritual experience will conquer" (p. 44), and that it is an illness of body and mind (p. xxvi). On p. 64 it says that underneath the mental and physical illness there was a spiritual one, and that dealing with that one straightens out the others.

ef741b080968.t: The book is careful not to make that a cure. It makes room for medical help: although the members work out their solution "on the spiritual as well as an altruistic plane" (p. xxvi), they "favor hospitalization for the alcoholic who is very jittery or befogged" (p. xxvi). And after the Steps, "We are not cured of alcoholism." (p. 85)

f058190d9b88.t: The book doesn't give a separate method for the spiritual malady. The sentence sits at the start of the inventory, and what follows is the inventory itself: listing resentments, seeing the people involved as sick, praying, finding our own part, and looking at fear and sex conduct (pp. 64–70). After that come the Fifth through Ninth Steps in Chapter 6. See <0>How does the Big Book say to do Step 4?</0>

097a785e5352.t: It confirms that the book puts a spiritual sickness beneath the drinking. It complicates the shorthand "alcoholism is a spiritual malady." In the program text, the phrase is used once. It's tied to resentment and self, and it's named <0>alongside</0> being mentally and physically ill, not instead of them.

6d482df6ec7e.t: Is the word "sponsor" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

acd249cdd316.t: The word "sponsor" does not appear anywhere in the Big Book's program: not in the forewords, not in "The Doctor's Opinion," not in Chapters 1 to 11 (pages…

bfc1c0da6c06.t: Is the word "sponsor" in the Big Book?

3196e29ab67a.t: The word "sponsor" does not appear anywhere in the Big Book's program: not in the forewords, not in "The Doctor's Opinion," not in Chapters 1 to 11 (pages 1–164), and not in the appendices.

4948f69ef3eb.t: It appears only in the personal stories at the back of the book.

aeb1799ca64e.t: In "The Vicious Cycle," one of the earliest of those stories (set in 1938), a "sponsor" is simply the person who brought you the message while you were still drinking. In an Akron story set in 1937, the word describes Dr. Bob taking a newcomer through the early program in one afternoon.

1d62674fcf6a.t: Where the word is, and isn't

fd1a6bb09261.t: Searching the whole fourth edition, every use of "sponsor" or "sponsorship" is in the personal stories (from page 165 on). There are none in the 164 pages that set out the program, none in the forewords, and none in the seven appendices.

7443289625e3.t: The program's own instructions for helping another alcoholic are in Chapter 7, "Working With Others" (pp. 89–103). That chapter never uses the word. It describes reaching a man who is still drinking, who owes you nothing (p. 94), and who is free to go to someone else when he's ready to tell his story (p. 96). See: <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0>

d916be8dbcc4.t: "The Vicious Cycle" (Part I, "Pioneers of A.A.") is the story of a man who got sober on January 8, 1938, more than a year before the fellowship had the name Alcoholics Anonymous (p. 220).

d3c0d1f97263.t: His sponsor was Jackie, the man who came to him while he was still drinking. Jackie "brought in many of our original members, yet he himself could not make it and died of alcoholism" (p. 220). Jackie had been sober only a month or so when he carried the message (p. 226). Two weeks later Jackie got drunk, and the writer says he had "become the sponsor of my sponsor" (p. 226).

6334dfedb29e.t: In that story a sponsor isn't an experienced member who manages a newcomer's program. He's whoever went out and brought the message to a drunk, even someone barely sober himself. That is Chapter 7's work.

331a4d441feb.t: "He Sold Himself Short" (also in Part I) describes Akron in 1937, before the Big Book was written (p. 260). Before the writer was allowed to his first meeting, eight or nine members came to see him, one after another (p. 262). Then Dr. Bob spent an afternoon taking him through the program as it was then, six steps, the last being "Continued work with other alcoholics" (p. 263). The writer calls that afternoon "this type of sponsorship" (p. 263), and adds that Dr. Bob "always emphasized the religious angle very strongly" (p. 263). Here the sponsor is the most experienced member there was, leading a newcomer through every step, but it is one afternoon, after which the man went home to Chicago to start a group (pp. 263–264).

260851774116.t: Sponsorship as many rooms describe it today, a standing relationship with a senior member who guides you through the Steps over months, isn't described in the Big Book's program at all. Where the word appears in the earliest stories, it describes someone going out to a drinker and carrying the message, which is what Chapter 7 tells every member to do, and, in Akron, an older member taking a newcomer through the program in a single sitting. Neither is the months-long arrangement.

af4fb32aba70.t: The personal stories, also free from A.A.: Part I, "Pioneers of A.A.": <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_personalstories_partI.pdf</0>

7d817b880a3a.t: <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, pp. 1–164 and appendices (searched in full)

a47a6cc1e440.t: story describes Akron in 1937 (p. 260; p. 265 dates the visit almost a year before summer 1938)

c1e6e02726e5.t: Page numbers are from the fourth edition. The Preface explains the difference that matters here: the first portion, "describing the A.A. recovery program, has been left largely untouched" since 1939, while the personal stories have been added, edited and removed with each edition (pp. xi–xii). These two stories are in today's Part I, "Pioneers of A.A."

4749f2d9d6d5.t: My husband (or wife) drinks. What does the Big Book say to do? | Recovery Starts

b749cda8ee4f.t: Chapter 8, "To Wives" (pp. 104–121), is the Big Book's answer. It was written in 1939 in the voice of members' wives, addressed to the wives of men who…

eb6b8a308797.t: My husband (or wife) drinks. What does the Big Book say to do?

2c86c2bb2568.t: Chapter 8, "To Wives" (pp. 104–121), is the Big Book's answer. It was written in 1939 in the voice of members' wives, addressed to the wives of men who drink (the later history books say Bill W. wrote it), and its suggestions "may be adapted" for anyone living with an alcoholic, man or woman (p. 104, later-edition note).

8b6f8f9a1b05.t: Its core advice: don't be angry, don't nag or tell him what he must do about his drinking, don't let his drinking ruin your life with your children and friends, and treat him as a sick person, "as though he had pneumonia" (p. 108).

c7caf4abd820.t: It also makes an exception for a husband who is "thoroughly bad-intentioned" (p. 108), on whom no amount of patience will make any difference: "If you are positive he is one of this type you may feel you had better leave." (p. 108).

3c39cb58e07c.t: It ends by urging the wife to try the program herself: the wives found that putting spiritual principles to work "solves our problems too" (p. 116). Al-Anon, which uses the general principles of the A.A. program as a guide, was formed about thirteen years after the chapter was written and is entirely separate from A.A. (p. 121, later-edition note).

e9fa7e64c332.t: Who wrote it, and for whom

a6812bdd5e7c.t: The chapter is in the voice of "wives of Alcoholics Anonymous" (p. 104), some of whose problems had been solved and some not. The book itself doesn't say who held the pen. Both later history books say Bill W. wrote it: "Bill himself wrote the chapter that came to be called 'To Wives'" (<0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0>, 1980), and Lois W. recalled, "Bill wrote it, and I was mad" (<1>Pass It On</1>, 1984); she had offered to write it, and he wanted it in the same style as the rest of the book (<2>Pass It On</2>). What they say, they write, "will apply to nearly everyone bound by ties of blood or affection to an alcoholic" (p. 104). A later-edition footnote says it was written when there were few women in A.A. and so assumes the drinker is the husband, but "many of the suggestions given here may be adapted to help the person who lives with a woman alcoholic" (p. 104).

aa64bc9fd2e3.t: The opening pages are a frank list of what the wives lived with and how they reacted: lies to protect pride and reputation, begging, patience, striking out, running away, retaliatory affairs, loneliness, money that "melted like snow in June" (p. 106), violence toward the children and the home, and at the end "commitment to health resorts, sanitariums, hospitals, and jails" (p. 107). Many of their mistakes, they say, "rose out of ignorance of alcoholism" (p. 107).

1d4084c3299f.t: <0>He is sick.</0> "Try not to condemn your alcoholic husband no matter what he says or does." (p. 108). "He is just another very sick, unreasonable person." (p. 108). "Treat him, when you can, as though he had pneumonia." (p. 108).

7d5210a183ff.t: <0>Except when he means harm.</0> "We realize some men are thoroughly bad-intentioned, that no amount of patience will make any difference." (p. 108). Such a man may use the chapter "as a club over your head" (p. 108), and the wife shouldn't let him. "Is it right to let him ruin your life and the lives of your children?" (p. 108).

ad46297de526.t: <0>Know what you're dealing with.</0> The chapter describes four kinds of drinking husband: the heavy drinker who may moderate or stop; the one showing loss of control, with "the earmarks of a real alcoholic" (p. 109); the one much further gone, of whom "You can be quite hopeful" (p. 110); and the one whose family has despaired, who may still recover (p. 110).

d350f30fdd36.t: <0>Never angry.</0> "The first principle of success is that you should never be angry." (p. 111). Even if she has to leave temporarily, she should go without rancor (p. 111).

11637eae09e3.t: <0>Don't tell him what to do.</0> "Our next thought is that you should never tell him what he must do about his drinking." (p. 111). If he sees her as a nag, her chances of helping "may be zero" (p. 111).

99e304489add.t: <0>Your own life.</0> "Be determined that your husband's drinking is not going to spoil your relations with your children or your friends." (p. 111). "It is possible to have a full and useful life, though your husband continues to drink." (p. 111). "Do not set your heart on reforming your husband." (p. 111).

27a4f65121d0.t: <0>When he's ready to talk.</0> Let him bring it up. Suggest he read the book, or just the chapter on alcoholism (pp. 111–112). For the second kind of husband, after a binge, ask whether he would really like to stop for good, not for her sake (p. 112). If he isn't interested, leave him alone; "the more you hurry him the longer his recovery may be delayed" (p. 113).

48b8d41e5e11.t: <0>Don't lie for him.</0> Avoid covering for him with his employer and friends; "Whenever possible, let your husband explain." (p. 115). Quietly letting friends know the nature of his illness ends much of the embarrassment (p. 115).

2658e736fe22.t: <0>Children.</0> Unless they need protection from their father, don't take sides in his arguments with them while he's drinking (p. 115).

91f0b3c63a65.t: <0>If he loses his job,</0> it may prove a blessing, opening the way to his wanting to stop (p. 116).

076dcc986599.t: <0>Committed or dangerous.</0> If he can't or won't stop and becomes too dangerous, "we think the kind thing is to lock them up, but of course a good doctor should always be consulted" (p. 114). "But sometimes you must start life anew." (p. 114).

36ae95073266.t: The wives found they too had pride, self-pity, vanity and selfishness, and that "it was a silly idea that we were too good to need God" (p. 116). When they put spiritual principles to work, they say, "we find it solves our problems too" (p. 116). "We urge you to try our program" (p. 117).

1016f840bd67.t: Not every problem goes away. The chapter warns against resentment that "the contents of a book or the work of another alcoholic" did in weeks what her love couldn't do in years (p. 118), against jealousy of the time he spends helping other alcoholics (p. 119), and against trying to shield him from temptation (p. 120). If he slips after a fair start and really wants to stop, "it is by no means a bad thing in some cases" (p. 120). "If he gets drunk, don't blame yourself." (p. 120).

8e1ceedb6f24.t: What does Step 1 say? Powerless over what? | Recovery Starts

44b004c2000a.t: Step 1 as printed reads: "We admitted we were powerless over alcohol—that our lives had become unmanageable." (p. 59) The two halves are joined by a dash,…

2f5b92448217.t: What does Step 1 say? Powerless over what?

374791c81fd8.t: Step 1 as printed reads: "We admitted we were powerless over alcohol—that our lives had become unmanageable." (p. 59) The two halves are joined by a dash, not "and."

f18eadb449bb.t: The powerlessness the Step names is over alcohol. The word "powerless" appears exactly once in the forewords, the Doctor's Opinion, Chapters 1 to 11 and the appendices: in this Step.

a03f0d242bb3.t: The book does say that our own power fell short in other ways too, but its answer there is a Power greater than ourselves and a lot of action. It never tells the reader to accept being powerless over everything.

10be89f7a0b5.t: Step 1 is the first of the twelve listed on page 59: "We admitted we were powerless over alcohol—that our lives had become unmanageable." (p. 59) Note the punctuation: it's a dash, so the two halves read as one statement. Read that way, lives became unmanageable because of the powerlessness over alcohol; the book doesn't spell the link out further.

256ae5d8daac.t: A search of our text of the Big Book's opening sections, all eleven chapters and the appendices finds "powerless" only here. The book doesn't use the word anywhere else to describe the alcoholic's condition.

ced03acad630.t: What Chapter 3 says the powerlessness is

6d691bf364a7.t: Chapter 3 (pp. 30–43), "More About Alcoholism," is the book's own explanation of Step 1's ground. Read in full, it's about one thing: drinking. - It opens by saying the first step in recovery is to concede fully, to our innermost selves, that we are alcoholics, and that alcoholics are people who have lost the ability to control their drinking (p. 30). - It lists the ways members tried to control it, from drinking beer only to going to sanitariums (p. 31). - Whether a person can quit on a nonspiritual basis "depends upon the extent to which he has already lost the power to choose whether he will drink or not" (p. 34). - The stories of Jim and Fred show the "insanely trivial excuse for taking the first drink" (p. 37) that wins out over sound reasoning and self-knowledge (pp. 35–43). - The chapter ends: the alcoholic "at certain times has no effective mental defense against the first drink" (p. 43), and "His defense must come from a Higher Power" (p. 43).

2ad7fe6f479f.t: Page 60 sums up what the earlier chapters establish: "That we were alcoholic and could not manage our own lives" (p. 60).

1631e438b219.t: The text doesn't teach that, but it's worth being exact about what it does say, because it's easy to overcorrect.

009df56b5355.t: The book does say our own resources failed beyond the bottle. "Lack of power, that was our dilemma" (p. 45), about the failure of moral codes and philosophies to keep alcoholics sober. Self-centredness couldn't be reduced "by wishing or trying on our own power" (p. 62). Fear wasn't solved by self-reliance (p. 68).

1dd7c6036223.t: What it never does is call the alcoholic powerless over those things and leave it there. In each case the answer is help from a Power greater than ourselves plus action. And the rest of the program is a list of things to do, with responsibility squarely on the person: write the inventory (pp. 64–71), face creditors "no matter how far we have to go" (p. 78), make amends even at the risk of losing a job or going to jail (p. 79). The book even names a right use of will power: keeping God's will in view through the day "is the proper use of the will" (p. 85).

d2ec9e13c3a3.t: So the Step names alcohol. The book's broader point is that self-will alone didn't work, not that a sober alcoholic has no power over his life.

021021243c78.t: Does Step 12 require believing in God a certain way? | Recovery Starts

17c035887c8b.t: No particular way. Step Twelve itself doesn't mention God (p. 60). The Steps that do say "God as we understood Him" (Steps 3 and 11, p. 59).

947f65430a22.t: Does Step 12 require believing in God a certain way?

3933d1a63497.t: No particular way. Step Twelve itself doesn't mention God (p. 60). The Steps that do say "God as we understood Him" (Steps 3 and 11, p. 59).

fb0f026bb4d9.t: The book says that when it speaks of God, "we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47). In Chapter 7 the newcomer "can choose any conception he likes, provided it makes sense to him" (p. 93).

3d5fe7e47869.t: The book does not say belief doesn't matter. It asks at least for willingness to believe in a Power greater than yourself (pp. 47, 93), and its own writers call that Power God.

27f0b29990d5.t: When you carry the message, you're told not to push your own idea of God on anyone (pp. 93, 95).

b9bb8dacc53a.t: "Having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps, we tried to carry this message to alcoholics, and to practice these principles in all our affairs" (p. 60). There's no statement of belief in it. The awakening it mentions is described in Appendix II as a change of personality that most people go through slowly (p. 567). See: <0>What is the "spiritual awakening" in Step 12?</0>

76c0d3e5c82c.t: Chapter 4, "We Agnostics," was written for people who can't accept God as others describe Him. It says about half the original fellowship thought they were atheists or agnostics (p. 44). Its main points: - "Much to our relief, we discovered we did not need to consider another's conception of God" (p. 46). Your own conception, however inadequate, was enough to start with (p. 46). - "When, therefore, we speak to you of God, we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47), and the same goes for the book's other spiritual terms (p. 47). - The one question to ask yourself: "Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe, that there is a Power greater than myself?" (p. 47). - Differences in how members conceive of that Power "are questions for each individual to settle for himself" (p. 50).

8630fba5239b.t: Chapter 2 says the same: "We have no desire to convince anyone that there is only one way by which faith can be acquired" (p. 28), and which religious body a member belongs to, if any, is "an entirely personal affair" (p. 28).

10a1934f283e.t: Every instruction in the Step Twelve chapter about how to present God to the newcomer is about holding back: - If the man is agnostic or atheist, make it emphatic "that he does not have to agree with your conception of God" (p. 93). - Use everyday language, and don't raise theological issues, "no matter what your own convictions are" (p. 93). - The chapter says the members represent no particular faith or denomination (pp. 93–94). - "If he is to find God, the desire must come from within" (p. 95). - If he prefers some other spiritual approach, encourage him to follow his own conscience. "We have no monopoly on God; we merely have an approach that worked with us" (p. 95).

6c236ff712a2.t: Where the text cuts the other way

2667b5cf4905.t: It would be wrong to say the Big Book treats God as optional or unimportant. It doesn't. - The "main thing," Chapter 7 says, is that the newcomer "be willing to believe in a Power greater than himself and that he live by spiritual principles" (p. 93). - The same chapter tells the helper to "Burn the idea into the consciousness of every man that he can get well regardless of anyone" (p. 98), because "The only condition is that he trust in God and clean house" (p. 98), and to remind him that his recovery "is dependent upon his relationship with God" (p. 100). - "We Agnostics" argues at length that faith is reasonable, and says that, faced with alcoholism, "either God is everything or else He is nothing" (p. 53). - Chapter 5 says, before listing the Steps, "there is One who has all power—that One is God" (p. 59). - Appendix II's minimum is that a person not "close his mind to all spiritual concepts" (p. 568).

2cafb328efd4.t: So the text settles the question asked here: no specific conception of God is required, and no one may impose theirs. It doesn't settle a different question some people mean, whether a person with no belief and no willingness to believe in any Power greater than himself fits the program. The book's answer to that person is an invitation and an argument (Chapter 4), not a rule.

82e4f634a77e.t: Step Twelve: what the Big Book actually says | Recovery Starts

f40ccb1973d4.t: Step Twelve asks a sober alcoholic to carry the message to alcoholics who are still drinking.

4283b8fb9f1b.t: Step Twelve: what the Big Book actually says

c478e92eca03.t: The Big Book explains how in Chapter 7, "Working With Others," pages 89 to 103.

5e0ada787e9b.t: The chapter is a practical guide to finding a drinking stranger and helping him recover. It is not about sponsorship, and it is not about a private spiritual experience.

69365735de60.t: The person being helped owes the helper nothing, and the chapter repeatedly puts his welfare ahead of the helper's.

43de43fd0459.t: "Having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps, we tried to carry this message to alcoholics, and to practice these principles in all our affairs." (p. 60)

5c9eba22fd09.t: The Big Book doesn't leave the Step there. It gives a whole chapter to how it's done.

e165a796e49e.t: Chapter 7 begins by naming its subject: "This is our twelfth suggestion: Carry this message to other alcoholics!" (p. 89).

be40b104a2a6.t: Almost everything after that is instructions. They make sense once you remember where A.A. began. In 1935 there were two sober alcoholics (Ch. 11, pp. 153–156). The only way there would ever be a third was for them to go out and find one, someone still drinking who had never heard of them. Chapter 7 is what they learned doing that.

e7665b0633e2.t: What the chapter tells you to do

9f4fec1af6ab.t: Read straight through, the fifteen pages work as a field guide:

e8cfaebdb53b.t: <0>Find drinkers who want to stop.</0> Ask doctors, ministers and hospitals (p. 89). Don't try to persuade someone who doesn't want to quit (p. 90).

605c8123dcd8.t: <0>Learn about the man first, and choose your moment.</0> Talk with the person closest to him, wait for the end of a binge, and never force yourself on him (p. 90). An approach through a doctor or an institution is better than through his family (p. 91).

9d9664b0475e.t: <0>Talk about your own drinking, not his.</0> See him alone. Tell him enough of your story that he'll start telling his, and for now say nothing about how you got sober (p. 91).

b04578d37e53.t: <0>Let him decide whether he's an alcoholic.</0> Describe the illness from your own experience, and don't label him (p. 92).

fb9159ca9754.t: <0>Tell him how you recovered only when he asks</0> (p. 93). Outline the program of action and say why you're helping (p. 94).

e7d46eb4bb2e.t: <0>Leave him free.</0> Make it plain he's under no obligation and needn't see you again (p. 94). Don't wear out your welcome or rush him (p. 95).

1b1e8a7da334.t: <0>If he isn't interested, find someone who is.</0> The book is blunt about it: spending too long on one person "is to deny some other alcoholic an opportunity to live and be happy" (p. 96).

aa70fb7144c7.t: <0>Be ready for what it costs.</0> Lost sleep, your money and your home, trips to courts, hospitals and jails (p. 97). Help his family even if he keeps drinking (p. 97).

0133a3e4f5bc.t: <0>Go wherever you can be useful.</0> Even "the most sordid spot on earth," if you're there to help (p. 102).

a0d6275d821c.t: <0>It isn't sponsorship.</0> The word doesn't appear in the chapter. The relationship it describes is with a man who may not be in A.A. at all yet, who owes you nothing (p. 94), and who is free to go to someone else when he's ready to make his decision and tell his story (p. 96). Nothing in these pages describes an ongoing arrangement with a member already in the rooms.

80cc3f11dd5d.t: <0>It isn't a private spiritual experience.</0> The Step opens with a spiritual awakening, and the Big Book's own appendix on that phrase, written after the first printing (p. 567), says most such changes are of the "educational variety" and develop slowly over time, not as sudden upheavals (p. 567). The action the Step asks for is carrying the message.

79be20c9a1d9.t: <0>It isn't self-serving.</0> The chapter's first line says that working with other alcoholics protects the helper's own sobriety (p. 89), and it says so again: your effort "plays a vital part in your own recovery" (p. 94), and "Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery" (p. 97). Taken alone, those lines can sound like "help others to keep yourself sober." But the chapter doesn't stop there. It asks the newcomer to "place the welfare of other people ahead of his own" (p. 94), it lists what the helper gives up (p. 97), and it says "Do not think of what you will get out of the occasion. Think of what you can bring to it" (p. 102). The helper's sobriety is real and named, but the chapter's stated aim is the other man: "To be helpful is our only aim" (p. 89).

25c25fd8b32c.t: God is mentioned, and the helper is told to "stress the spiritual feature freely" when describing his own recovery (p. 93). The chapter is also plain that recovery rests on God: the helper is to "Burn the idea into the consciousness of every man that he can get well regardless of anyone," and "The only condition is that he trust in God and clean house" (p. 98); his recovery "is dependent upon his relationship with God" (p. 100). But every instruction about how to present God to the newcomer is an instruction to hold back. The newcomer can choose any conception of God that makes sense to him (p. 93). Use everyday language, and don't raise theological issues "no matter what your own convictions are" (p. 93). You're not there to instruct him in religion (p. 93). "We have no monopoly on God" (p. 95). "Never talk down to an alcoholic from any moral or spiritual hilltop" (p. 95). The chapter forbids preaching. What it asks for is rescue.

d1ef77bb8b59.t: A.A. publishes these chapters free on its own website: - Chapter 7, "Working With Others" (pp. 89–103): <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt7.pdf</0> - Chapter 5, "How It Works," where the Twelve Steps are listed (pp. 58–71): <1>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt5.pdf</1> - Appendix II, "Spiritual Experience" (pp. 567–568): <2>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_appendiceii.pdf</2>

cb31f3d9c896.t: What do Steps 10 and 11 ask, day to day? | Recovery Starts

21a46a2d9c6f.t: Step Ten asks you to keep taking personal inventory and to admit it promptly when you're wrong. The Big Book's directions take one paragraph: watch for…

c5ac43b95da0.t: What do Steps 10 and 11 ask, day to day?

3ff1def0ac5f.t: Step Ten asks you to keep taking personal inventory and to admit it promptly when you're wrong. The Big Book's directions take one paragraph: watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment and fear, ask God to remove them, talk them over with someone straight away, make amends quickly, and then turn your mind to someone you can help (p. 84).

06f70668f028.t: Step Eleven asks for prayer and meditation. The book sets out a plain daily routine for it: review the day at night, plan the day each morning, and stop to ask for the right thought or action whenever you're agitated or unsure during the day (pp. 86–88).

0ab2e5b7ac0b.t: Both Steps point outward. The night review asks whether you were thinking of others. The morning prayer is never to be for yourself alone. The chapter ends by sending the reader on to Step Twelve (p. 88).

7994d7916cdb.t: The Big Book lists them with the other ten on page 59. Step Ten: continued to take personal inventory and promptly admitted it when we were wrong. Step Eleven: sought through prayer and meditation to improve our conscious contact with God as we understood Him, praying only for knowledge of His will and the power to carry it out (p. 59).

fd535ee3b101.t: The book explains both in the last five pages of Chapter 6, "Into Action" (pp. 84–88). They come right after amends, so they're presented as how to keep living once the past has been cleared up.

532207a4245e.t: The book calls this continuing to "set right any new mistakes as we go along" (p. 84). "This is not an overnight matter. It should continue for our lifetime" (p. 84). The whole method is in one passage (p. 84):

49e831daea54.t: <0>Watch</0> for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment and fear.

cecf3ff2622d.t: <0>When they show up, ask God at once to remove them.</0>

c9c07c7003eb.t: <0>Talk them over with someone immediately</0>, and make amends quickly if you've harmed anyone.

0b80481d555f.t: <0>Then turn outward:</0> "Then we resolutely turn our thoughts to someone we can help" (p. 84).

186d0ca11fbe.t: "Love and tolerance of others is our code" (p. 84). The book says the result is that we stop fighting "anything or anyone—even alcohol" (p. 84), and that it lasts only as long as the spiritual work does: "What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition" (p. 85).

a6d1ed598605.t: Step Eleven: a day with three parts

3b4263e205f4.t: "Step Eleven suggests prayer and meditation" (p. 85). The book then makes "some definite and valuable suggestions" (p. 86):

430d995772de.t: <0>At night</0> (p. 86), review the day. The questions it gives: "Were we resentful, selfish, dishonest or afraid?" Do we owe an apology? Have we kept something to ourselves that should be discussed with someone? Were we kind and loving? "Were we thinking of ourselves most of the time? Or were we thinking of what we could do for others". It warns against sliding into worry or morbid reflection, "for that would diminish our usefulness to others" (p. 86). Then ask God's forgiveness and what should be put right.

5caf3198a0d3.t: <0>In the morning</0> (pp. 86–87), think about the twenty-four hours ahead. Ask God to direct your thinking, especially to keep it free of self-pity, dishonesty and self-seeking. The book adds that God "gave us brains to use" (p. 86). When you can't decide, ask for inspiration or an intuitive thought, relax, and don't struggle (p. 86). It warns that a newcomer shouldn't expect to be inspired all the time (p. 87). End with a prayer to be shown the next step through the day, and be "careful to make no request for ourselves only" (p. 87).

29ea959d3da4.t: <0>During the day</0> (pp. 87–88), "when agitated or doubtful," pause and ask for the right thought or action, and keep reminding yourself you're no longer running the show (pp. 87–88).

65d23925b672.t: The book doesn't prescribe a method of meditation beyond this. It says members who belong to a religion keep its morning devotions, others may learn a few set prayers, helpful books can be suggested by a priest, minister or rabbi, and "Be quick to see where religious people are right" (p. 87). It ends: "It works—it really does" (p. 88).

897ef717ebd8.t: The book doesn't let these Steps become a private routine. Step Ten's paragraph ends with someone you can help (p. 84). The night review asks what you did for others (p. 86). The chapter's last lines are "There is action and more action" and a pointer to the next chapter, which "is entirely devoted to Step Twelve" (p. 88): going out to find and help another alcoholic (Chapter 7, pp. 89–103).

fbe747534ee9.t: It doesn't say the night review must be written down, how long meditation should last, or which prayers to use. Those details aren't in the text, so this page doesn't supply them.
