5a94fe1f3438.t: Are the Steps rules or suggestions? | Recovery Starts

ba207e7ec6a8.t: The Big Book calls the Steps suggestions. It introduces them as "the steps we took, which are suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59), and says on its…

8c37788db847.t: Are the Steps rules or suggestions?

678f6a59d1f4.t: The Big Book calls the Steps suggestions. It introduces them as "the steps we took, which are suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59), and says on its last page that the whole book is meant only to suggest (p. 164).

3faf51c75bd9.t: Nobody can make anyone take them. The book tells employers that no one should tell a man "he must abide by its suggestions" (p. 144).

1efb846ae4d6.t: But "suggested" doesn't mean "optional and harmless to skip." The same pages report, from the writers' experience, that half measures got them nowhere and that newcomers who skipped the Fifth Step nearly always got drunk. The Steps are offered as what worked, not as rules anyone enforces.

2fc183720962.t: The wording around the Steps is consistently the language of suggestion and experience: - The list is introduced as the steps "we took," suggested "as a program of recovery" (p. 59). - Right after the list, the book answers the reader who thinks it's too much: no one has kept "anything like perfect adherence to these principles" (p. 60). They are "guides to progress," and the aim is "spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection" (p. 60). - Step Twelve is introduced as "our twelfth suggestion" (p. 89). Steps Ten and Eleven are each said to "suggest" (pp. 84–85). - On a hard question about amends at home, the writers say they "wish to lay down no rule of any sort" (p. 81). - The book's closing page says the whole book is meant only as a suggestion, and that the writers know only a little; more will be disclosed to the reader and to them (p. 164). - To employers: when the man is given the book, no one should tell him he must follow it. "The man must decide for himself" (p. 144).

992d07e2e14d.t: What the book says about skipping them

0f12da4da367.t: The same text is just as plain that leaving Steps out has a cost. It reports what happened to its members; it doesn't threaten anyone. - The chapter opens by saying the writers have rarely "seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path" (p. 58). The writers ask the reader to be "fearless and thorough from the very start" (p. 58), and say "Half measures availed us nothing" (p. 59). - Some members looked for "an easier, softer way. But we could not" (p. 58). - On the Fifth Step: "If we skip this vital step, we may not overcome drinking" (p. 72). Newcomers who tried to keep certain facts about their lives to themselves nearly always got drunk (pp. 72–73). - On self-centredness: "We must, or it kills us!" (p. 62). - Appendix II, written after the first printing (p. 567), says willingness, honesty and open-mindedness "are the essentials of recovery. But these are indispensable" (p. 568).

a4d5fdc11777.t: The text doesn't make the Steps into rules. No one in A.A. is given the power to enforce them, and the book insists the reader decides for himself (p. 144). It also doesn't treat them as optional extras. It offers them as a record of what a group of alcoholics did and what happened to those who did and didn't, and leaves the choice with the reader. Where the book uses "must," it's describing the alcoholic's situation as the writers found it, not giving an order from an authority.

4b6d56825940.t: Chapter 11 (pp. 151–164), "A Vision for You," for the closing page: <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt11.pdf</0>

2679c4561d89.t: Does the Big Book say to "stick with the winners"? | Recovery Starts

bba771efbb0e.t: No. The saying isn't in the Big Book or anywhere else in our sources, and the word "winners" never appears in the program text.

a93094a4386b.t: Does the Big Book say to "stick with the winners"?

13efe94e3781.t: No. The saying isn't in the Big Book or anywhere else in our sources, and the word "winners" never appears in the program text.

355471b5e141.t: The program text points the sober member the other way: toward the man who is still drinking, "very ill" (p. 89), even to "the most sordid spot on earth" if he can help there (p. 102).

99c82a776cf3.t: It does describe newcomers being helped by people who have recovered, and it does say not to waste time chasing someone who won't work with you (p. 96). But it describes a fellowship where "No one is too discredited or has sunk too low to be welcomed cordially—if he means business" (p. 161), not one sorted into winners and losers.

4762e824972e.t: All our sources were searched for "winner(s)," "stick with," "stick around," "old-timers" and "successful," with page breaks joined. The saying isn't there. "Winner" appears only in a story title, "Winner Takes All" (Part II, p. 375), and in history books in unrelated senses.

0b4e1a444913.t: Where the program text sends the member

5f26b6abc49d.t: Chapter 7, the chapter on carrying the message, is about going toward the sick: - Find drinkers who want to recover through doctors, ministers and hospitals (p. 89). "Remember they are very ill." (p. 89). - "Call on him while he is still jittery." (p. 91). - "You have to act the Good Samaritan every day, if need be." (p. 97), with trips to "police courts, sanitariums, hospitals, jails and asylums" (p. 97). - "Your job now is to be at the place where you may be of maximum helpfulness to others, so never hesitate to go anywhere if you can be helpful." (p. 102).

0e23ac28fbd7.t: The chapter also says the company of sober members matters: "Frequent contact with newcomers and with each other is the bright spot of our lives." (p. 89), and it promises "a host of friends" (p. 89).

1332b155ca48.t: Where the text is close to the saying

18c8d67daf7f.t: Some of the saying's sense is in the text: - <0>Learning from people who have recovered.</0> The newcomer's attention is drawn to the member "as a person who has recovered" (p. 90), and the approach works because the helper has had the same difficulty and "obviously knows what he is talking about" (p. 18). In Chapter 11 the newcomer "capitulated entirely" when he heard the story of a man "whose experience closely tallied with his own" (p. 160). - <1>Not staying with those who won't try.</1> "We find it a waste of time to keep chasing a man who cannot or will not work with you." (p. 96). But the same paragraph's instruction is to find another drinker: "Search out another alcoholic and try again." (p. 96). It is about where the helper spends his effort, not about whose company protects him.

3e58dd5c4d9d.t: What the text says about who belongs

ab414ebad05d.t: Chapter 11 describes the early gatherings: "No one is too discredited or has sunk too low to be welcomed cordially—if he means business." (p. 161). "Social distinctions, petty rivalries and jealousies—these are laughed out of countenance." (p. 161). The newcomer was won by "the absence of intolerance of any kind" (p. 160).

afc6f6668ac4.t: Bill W.'s 1946 Grapevine essay on membership goes further. Of those who slip, panhandle, rebel or scandalize: "We have begun to regard these not as menaces, but rather as our teachers." (P-17). Some of them, he says, "have become our most respected and best loved" (P-17).

4da8b431ba46.t: If the saying means "learn from people who have what you want," the text is near it: Chapter 5's first page addresses the reader who has "decided you want what we have" (p. 58), and the newcomer is helped by the recovered man's story. If it means "keep company with the successful and avoid those who are struggling," the 1939 text and Bill's 1946 essay both point the other way: the sober member's job is to go to the one still sick. See: <0>What is a "Twelfth Step call"?</0>

4404f8dffcca.t: Can I go to A.A. if I'm still drinking? | Recovery Starts

4f3fc4cdf786.t: Yes, as A.A.'s own literature describes it. Tradition Three, in its short form (by 1950), asks for a desire to stop drinking, not for having stopped (p.…

4e8bf5a4cbb1.t: Can I go to A.A. if I'm still drinking?

6f250cba8b86.t: Yes, as A.A.'s own literature describes it. Tradition Three, in its short form (by 1950), asks for a desire to stop drinking, not for having stopped (p. 562). The 1946 Long Form says A.A. "may refuse none who wish to recover" (p. 563).

4dc0d3709a61.t: Bill W. wrote in 1946 that under the groups' old membership rules most of the early members would have been thrown out, for reasons that included that they "slipped too much." A member who keeps coming to meetings drunk "may be led outside," but in most groups he can come back the next day if sober, and "He is a member as long as he says he is." (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946).

e2ac74bd9154.t: The 1939 text was written to reach people who were still drinking. Chapter 7 is a guide to approaching them (pp. 89–96).

d49d7cbb9514.t: The texts set no rule about how long you must be sober to attend. Today's group pamphlet leaves sobriety minimums for speakers and officers to each group (P-16, 2018).

d7d2aed781f0.t: The short form: "The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking." (p. 562). The 1939 Foreword said "an honest desire to stop drinking" (p. xiv). Neither says a person must already have stopped.

a59f4848c8a8.t: The Long Form puts it more widely: "Our membership ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism." (p. 563). Hence A.A. "may refuse none who wish to recover" (p. 563). See <0>What is the only requirement for A.A. membership?</0>

0f23766d9d7b.t: Bill's essay on membership describes what happened when groups made membership rules. If all the groups' membership rules had been enforced at once, about nine-tenths of the oldest and best members "could never have got by!" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). Most of the early members would have been thrown out, among other reasons "because they slipped too much" (same essay).

878aa7f9dc19.t: His description of A.A.'s practice by 1946: - A newcomer who "commences to do anything at all about his problem" is considered a member (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). In most groups he needn't even admit he is an alcoholic. - Some groups still had membership rules. "If a member persists in coming to meetings drunk he may be led outside; we may ask someone to take him away." (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). But in most groups he can come back next day, if sober. - "Though he may be thrown out of a club, nobody thinks of throwing him out of A.A." (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946).

0b1c84d244b7.t: So the 1946 picture, which Bill says was "not yet unanimous" (same essay) but was the main current, is that a group may deal with someone who is drunk at a meeting, but his membership doesn't end. See <0>Can anyone be thrown out of A.A.?</0>

b127fb80bfeb.t: What the 1939 text says about drinkers

6359e4c5b4fd.t: The Big Book's way of carrying the message starts with people who are still drinking: - Find drinkers who want to recover (p. 89). If a man doesn't want to stop, don't waste time persuading him (p. 90). - "Don't deal with him when he is very drunk, unless he is ugly and the family needs your help." (p. 90). Wait for the end of the spree, or a lucid interval (p. 90). Call on him "while he is still jittery" (p. 91). - Chapter 11's first weekly meeting, in the western city a later footnote identifies as Akron (p. 156), was set apart as "a time and place where new people might bring their problems" (p. 160).

66fe25123ca9.t: The book is also plain that some people drink again after starting. Chapter 3 says the many remedies members tried brought, at best, "brief recovery, followed always by a still worse relapse" (p. 31). Chapter 8 tells a wife whose husband comes home drunk after a fair start that it is "infinitely better that he have no relapse at all," but that a relapse "is by no means a bad thing in some cases" if he really wants to stop (p. 120). The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) reports that of those who came to A.A. and really tried, 25% "sobered up after some relapses" (p. xx).

6940c6247fd9.t: <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16) says closed meetings are for A.A. members or for those who have a drinking problem and "have a desire to stop drinking" (P-16, 2018); open meetings are open to anyone interested. It lists "What should the group do about members who return to drinking?" (P-16, 2018) among common group problems and gives no rule, only the group conscience and the Traditions. Each group decides any minimum sobriety for its speakers and its officers (P-16, 2018).

f5dc5872507a.t: None of these texts says a person has to arrive sober, or has to have stopped drinking for any length of time, to attend an A.A. meeting or to be a member. They don't promise that a group will put up with any behavior either: the 1946 essay expects a drunk who disrupts meetings to be led outside, for the day.

ace5a0143e76.t: Where are "the Promises," and what do they promise? | Recovery Starts

1c5a3cc2c174.t: The passage known as "the Promises" is on pages 83 and 84 of the Big Book, in Chapter 6, "Into Action." It begins "If we are painstaking about this phase…

400e82caaa83.t: Where are "the Promises," and what do they promise?

eae8e103266b.t: The passage known as "the Promises" is on pages 83 and 84 of the Big Book, in Chapter 6, "Into Action." It begins "If we are painstaking about this phase of our development, we will be amazed before we are half way through." (p. 83)

401d220b2748.t: It closes the book's account of the amends work of Steps Eight and Nine, and "this phase" refers to that work. It ends with "We will suddenly realize that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves." (p. 84)

ddbe34beea52.t: The book doesn't number them or give them a title. It calls them promises once, just after: "Are these extravagant promises? We think not." (p. 84) And it attaches a condition: "They will always materialize if we work for them." (p. 84)

bf9d6122fb91.t: Chapter 6 takes the reader through Steps Eight and Nine on pages 76 to 83: creditors, old enemies, legal trouble, the family. The last paragraph before the promises is about wrongs that can never be fully righted, honest letters to people who can't be seen, and standing on our feet as God's people, without crawling before anyone (p. 83).

1a6f2db29a1d.t: Then comes the promise, conditional on that work: if we are painstaking "about this phase of our development" (p. 83). Read in place, "this phase" is the amends. The passage isn't a general description of sobriety, and it isn't placed at the end of the Steps. Right after it, the book moves on to Step Ten (p. 84).

b4404dd4a987.t: In our own words, in the order the book gives them (pp. 83–84): 1. A new freedom and a new happiness. 2. Not regretting the past, nor wanting to shut the door on it. 3. Understanding the word serenity, and knowing peace. 4. Seeing how our own experience, however far down we went, can benefit others. 5. The feeling of uselessness and self-pity disappearing. 6. Losing interest in selfish things and gaining interest in other people. 7. Self-seeking slipping away. 8. A change in our whole attitude and outlook on life. 9. Fear of people and of economic insecurity leaving us. 10. Knowing intuitively how to handle situations that used to baffle us. 11. Suddenly realizing that God is doing for us what we couldn't do for ourselves.

75fe18e6a733.t: The book doesn't number them, so counts vary; how many there are is a matter of how you split the sentences.

da73640536f9.t: What the book says about them

717751c9012e.t: "Are these extravagant promises? We think not." (p. 84) They are "being fulfilled among us—sometimes quickly, sometimes slowly" (p. 84). And the condition: they will always come true "if we work for them" (p. 84).

a15d2b776eb3.t: Several of them point outward: our experience benefiting others, gaining interest in our fellows, self-seeking slipping away (p. 84). They describe a person turned toward other people, which is where the book goes next: Step Ten's daily practice ends with turning our thoughts "to someone we can help" (p. 84), and Chapter 7 is about carrying the message.

dffdac7ab97d.t: The text continues past page 84 with another passage often read alongside them: after Step Ten, "sanity will have returned," and the problem of drink "has been removed" (pp. 84–85). The book ties that one to a condition too: it holds "so long as we keep in fit spiritual condition" (p. 85), and it's only "a daily reprieve" (p. 85).

b178cb17223d.t: Chapter 6, "Into Action" (pp. 72–88), with the promises on pages 83–84, free from A.A.: <0>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/2021-11/en_bigbook_chapt6.pdf</0>

d9112196085a.t: Is "it's not a drinking problem, it's a thinking problem" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

c05eb612c122.t: The saying isn't in the Big Book or anywhere else in our sources.

46887fb9a02a.t: Is "it's not a drinking problem, it's a thinking problem" in the Big Book?

2b7d7f89aa65.t: The saying isn't in the Big Book or anywhere else in our sources.

462d63404d6c.t: Half of it is close to the text. The program says plainly: "Therefore, the main problem of the alcoholic centers in his mind, rather than in his body." (p. 23), and "Our liquor was but a symptom." (p. 64).

45fe106ff78f.t: The other half isn't. The book never says it isn't a drinking problem. It keeps a physical side in the picture ("the body of the alcoholic is quite as abnormal as his mind," p. xxvi), and it puts the root of the trouble deeper than thinking: in selfishness, and in a spiritual sickness whose overcoming, it says, straightens out mind and body (pp. 62, 64).

8d42e5af2c74.t: All our sources were searched for "thinking problem," "drinking problem," "stinking thinking" and "problem of the mind," with page breaks joined. "Thinking problem" appears nowhere. "Drinking problem" appears in the program text only in ordinary use, such as a book meant for "anyone concerned with a drinking problem" (p. 19). One fourth-edition story, "Flooded With Feeling," has a near-cousin: the writer once joked of not having a drinking problem but "a stopping problem" (p. 372), and later saw "I had a starting problem too" (p. 372).

88c1afd2447f.t: Chapter 2 asks why the alcoholic takes the first drink when he knows what follows (p. 22). It answers that the body's reaction would be beside the point if he never took that drink: "Therefore, the main problem of the alcoholic centers in his mind, rather than in his body." (p. 23). Ask him why he started his last bender and he'll give one of a hundred alibis, or admit he doesn't know (p. 23).

d83098e58c79.t: Other passages point the same way: - "Our liquor was but a symptom. So we had to get down to causes and conditions." (p. 64). - "Bottles were only a symbol." (p. 103). - Chapter 3 is a study of "the mental states that precede a relapse into drinking" (p. 35), the "curious mental phenomenon" of an insanely trivial excuse beating sound reasoning (p. 37).

ead57b566525.t: So a reader who says "the Big Book says the main problem is in the mind" is quoting it fairly, as long as he reads p. 23 with the page before it: what's "in his mind" there is the first drink.

07ba3e4e40ef.t: Where the text parts company with the saying

0f00f4599bf7.t: <0>The body is in the picture too.</0> The same paragraph that puts the main problem in the mind starts from the body: "once he takes any alcohol whatever into his system, something happens, both in the bodily and mental sense, which makes it virtually impossible for him to stop" (pp. 22–23). The writers introduce Dr. Silkworth's longer statement as confirming "that the body of the alcoholic is quite as abnormal as his mind" (p. xxvi), and say "any picture of the alcoholic which leaves out this physical factor is incomplete" (p. xxvi). Silkworth himself: "I do not hold with those who believe that alcoholism is entirely a problem of mental control." (p. xxix). Some of his patients "were drinking to overcome a craving beyond their mental control" (p. xxx). See: <1>What is "The Doctor's Opinion," and who wrote it?</1>

98ecf9a91f44.t: <0>It is a drinking problem.</0> The book's opening claim about its members is "They have solved the drink problem." (p. 17). Step One is about being powerless over alcohol (p. 59). The only relief Silkworth knew was "entire abstinence" (p. xxx).

aeee76d05545.t: <0>The root is not "thinking" but self, and the cure is spiritual.</0> "Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles." (p. 62). And in the inventory: "we have been not only mentally and physically ill, we have been spiritually sick" (p. 64). "When the spiritual malady is overcome, we straighten out mentally and physically." (p. 64). Chapter 4's opening says the alcoholic may be suffering from an illness "which only a spiritual experience will conquer" (p. 44).

b02f876bb4ec.t: The book's picture has three parts: a body that reacts abnormally once alcohol is in it, a mind that can't hold out against the first drink, and a spiritual sickness rooted in self that the program sets out to cure. The saying keeps the middle part and drops the other two. Where it says "not a drinking problem," the text disagrees: drinking is the problem the book was written to solve, and where liquor is called a symptom, the causes the book goes on to name are self, resentment and fear (pp. 62–68), not thinking as such. See: <0>What does the Big Book mean by alcoholism as an illness?</0>

2c3bfd3b6fa9.t: What is the Third Step prayer, and where is it? | Recovery Starts

b4b15dd314aa.t: It's on page 63 of the Big Book, in Chapter 5, "How It Works" (pp. 58–71). It begins "God, I offer myself to Thee—to build with me and to do with me as…

57d3aa59055c.t: What is the Third Step prayer, and where is it?

8166d1c5808a.t: It's on page 63 of the Big Book, in Chapter 5, "How It Works" (pp. 58–71). It begins "God, I offer myself to Thee—to build with me and to do with me as Thou wilt." (p. 63)

f813a098d5a7.t: The book doesn't call it "the Third Step prayer." It introduces it as something "Many of us said to our Maker, as we understood Him" (p. 63) when they took Step Three.

fe1514d60308.t: The book says the exact words don't matter: "The wording was, of course, quite optional so long as we expressed the idea" (p. 63).

2186fd463811.t: Step Three reads: "Made a decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him." (p. 59)

f2e0dbe74353.t: The book explains the Step on pages 60 to 63 before giving any prayer. Read in order: - The first requirement is to be convinced that a life run on self-will "can hardly be a success" (p. 60). - It describes the alcoholic as an actor trying to run the whole show (pp. 60–61), and names "Selfishness—self-centeredness!" as the root of our troubles (p. 62). - Members found they couldn't get rid of self-centredness on their own and needed God's help (p. 62). "First of all, we had to quit playing God" (p. 62). - When they took that position, they became less interested in themselves and "More and more we became interested in seeing what we could contribute to life" (p. 63).

73613907d7bf.t: Then: "We were now at Step Three" (p. 63), and the prayer follows.

21db2e3e867e.t: After its opening line, the prayer asks to be relieved of "the bondage of self" so as to better do God's will (p. 63). It asks God to take away the person's difficulties, and gives a reason that points outward: so that victory over them may bear witness, to the people the person would help, of God's power, love and way of life (p. 63). It ends by asking to do God's will always (p. 63).

11fc54f1d669.t: So even this prayer, said at the moment of decision, is aimed past the person praying, at "those I would help" (p. 63).

8132fae31e34.t: What the book says around it

a018029dd530.t: <0>Be ready first.</0> "We thought well before taking this step making sure we were ready" (p. 63).

96d46dc32636.t: <0>Alone or with someone.</0> It was "very desirable" to take the step with an understanding person, "such as our wife, best friend, or spiritual adviser" (p. 63). But "it is better to meet God alone than with one who might misunderstand" (p. 63). The book doesn't say to say it with a sponsor, or with anyone in particular.

79b81af86271.t: <0>Your own words are fine.</0> The wording was "quite optional" (p. 63).

50677d9909bb.t: <0>It's only a start.</0> The decision "could have little permanent effect unless at once followed by" a strenuous effort at the inventory (p. 64). Step Four follows straight away.

212bebdb6768.t: What is the "Thirteenth Step"? | Recovery Starts

aca77cafd87d.t: There is no Thirteenth Step in the Big Book. The phrase isn't anywhere in the fourth edition: not in the program text, the appendices, or the personal…

c8c9768bb4c6.t: There is no Thirteenth Step in the Big Book. The phrase isn't anywhere in the fourth edition: not in the program text, the appendices, or the personal stories.

05d2b2a3185c.t: In the rest of our sources it turns up three times, with three different meanings. In 1946 Bill W. joked about the book becoming the "Thirteenth Way Out." In 1947 he cautioned against treating clubs as a "Thirteenth Step." In 1980, <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> used "thirteenth step," with a wink, about an early man and woman in Akron in 1935.

a76c49982f21.t: The 1980 use is the only one about two people pairing off. No book in our sources defines the phrase. A later A.A. pamphlet (P-16) lists a member's "attempts to attract the romantic interest of newcomers" as a group problem, without using the phrase.

d2993a845cda.t: All our sources were searched for "thirteenth step," "13th step," "step thirteen" and "thirteenth" alone. The fourth-edition Big Book has none of them. Here is each use found, oldest first.

dd0ee4229a16.t: <0>1. The "Thirteenth Way Out" (1946).</0> In his Grapevine article "Anonymity" (1946), Bill tells how the book got its title. A narrow vote had favored "The Way Out," but the Library of Congress already had twelve books by that name: "we shivered at the possibility of being the 'Thirteenth Way Out'" (P-17, "Anonymity," 1946). So the book, and the fellowship, became "Alcoholics Anonymous." Bill tells the same story in <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957). This isn't a step at all. It's a joke about a book title.

3e10fb9bacda.t: <0>2. Clubs as a "Thirteenth Step" (1947).</0> In "Clubs in A.A." (1947), Bill writes that so many members value clubs that "we might conceive them as a central A.A. institution — a sort of 'Thirteenth Step' of our recovery program without which the other Twelve Steps wouldn't work" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.," 1947). He raises it as the far end of the pro-club view: some enthusiasts act as if club life alone could handle the drinking problem, and they "are apt to depend upon clubs rather than upon the A.A. program" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.," 1947). He then gives the opposite view and settles on a middle ground. Members who want clubs should have them, but clubs should be separately incorporated and kept apart from the groups' A.A. affairs, "to separate the material from the spiritual" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.," 1947). (See <1>What did Bill W. say about clubs and A.A.?</1>)

b7615c7ae3af.t: <0>3. "Victor" and "Lil" (written 1980, about 1935).</0> <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> tells of a former Akron mayor and "the first woman to seek help," two of the alcoholics around Akron in the summer and fall of 1935 "who didn't jell" (<2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2>, 1980). "Together, Victor and the lady known as Lil started out to write the 'thirteenth step,' long before the first twelve were ever thought of" (<3>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</3>, 1980). The book adds that "they say it began in Dr. Bob's office—on his examination table" (<4>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</4>, 1980). The night ended with Lil, drunk, grabbing pills and lunging for a window. Bill later recalled that they were all "scandalized by the episode" (<5>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</5>, 1980), and "they say" Dr. Bob was wary of alcoholic women for a long time afterward, though he still tried to help any who came along. The book passes the story on as A.A. "folklore" and as hearsay ("they say"). It doesn't define the phrase. It uses it knowingly, for a man and a woman pairing off, and expects the reader to get the joke.

2dc2228d94f2.t: What the books say about it, without the phrase

e3c10ef746f0.t: The 1939 program text doesn't take this up as a group matter. On a member's own sex conduct, Chapter 5 asks of every relationship "was it selfish or not?" (p. 69), and asks where we had "unjustifiably" aroused jealousy, suspicion or bitterness (p. 69). Chapter 7's instructions for a helper put the newcomer's welfare first throughout, and say to keep your work with him free of any claim on him: he "is under no obligation to you" (p. 94).

701d15a26710.t: The modern pamphlet <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16, 2018) lists, among common group problems for an informed group conscience to work out, "another's attempts to attract the romantic interest of newcomers" (P-16, 2018). It doesn't call this the Thirteenth Step, and it gives no rule beyond the group conscience.

0397a794016c.t: None of the books in our sources defines "Thirteenth Step." Many people use it today for a member pursuing a newcomer romantically, but no book here says so, and our sources can't confirm how the phrase is used now. The nearest is the 1980 story, which uses it for two drinkers pairing off in 1935. This page reports what the books say and leaves current usage to the reader.

fcecf76b214f.t: Does the Big Book really say to pray for people you resent ("This is a sick man")? | Recovery Starts

9b5cf6c8d727.t: The words are on page 67 of Chapter 5, in the Fourth Step inventory. When someone offended, "we said to ourselves, 'This is a sick man.'" (p. 67) It goes…

e8111a705556.t: Does the Big Book really say to pray for people you resent ("This is a sick man")?

3080074bfd22.t: The words are on page 67 of Chapter 5, in the Fourth Step inventory. When someone offended, "we said to ourselves, 'This is a sick man.'" (p. 67) It goes on: "How can I be helpful to him?" (p. 67) "God save me from being angry." (p. 67) "Thy will be done." (p. 67)

16f930468962.t: The main text's prayer is about the person, and it asks for a change in the one praying. We "asked God to help us show them the same tolerance, pity, and patience that we would cheerfully grant a sick friend" (p. 67), and to save us from anger. In place of retaliation it asks how to be helpful to him. It doesn't ask God for things on his behalf.

9448e91dc26d.t: Praying for a resented person's health, prosperity and happiness is in a personal story, "Freedom From Bondage" (p. 552), where the member credits the idea to a magazine article by a clergyman. That's a member's experience in the fourth edition's stories, not the 1939 program text.

af55b3c2d609.t: Calling the other person sick doesn't put us above him: "they, like ourselves, were sick too" (p. 67). And it isn't the end of the inventory. Next we put "out of our minds the wrongs others had done" and look for our own (p. 67).

39499218df4f.t: The reader has listed his resentments and seen that they're fatal for an alcoholic (p. 66). "We saw that these resentments must be mastered, but how?" (p. 66) "We could not wish them away any more than alcohol." (p. 66) Then the book gives its course:

e58de54e37ea.t: "We realized that the people who wronged us were perhaps spiritually sick." (p. 66)

4d154695e5c3.t: We didn't like their symptoms, but "they, like ourselves, were sick too" (p. 67).

155607cdf805.t: We asked God to help us show them the tolerance, pity and patience we would cheerfully grant a sick friend (p. 67).

8c1457b638d6.t: When a person offended, we said to ourselves: "This is a sick man." (p. 67) "How can I be helpful to him?" (p. 67) "God save me from being angry." (p. 67) "Thy will be done." (p. 67)

6464c71000af.t: "We avoid retaliation or argument." (p. 67) "We wouldn't treat sick people that way." (p. 67) "If we do, we destroy our chance of being helpful." (p. 67)

5ff11a6c676f.t: "We cannot be helpful to all people, but at least God will show us how to take a kindly and tolerant view of each and every one." (p. 67)

f6a18d0d4862.t: Then back to the list: "Putting out of our minds the wrongs others had done, we resolutely looked for our own mistakes." (p. 67)

6450512c27c9.t: The summary on p. 70 puts the result this way: we have begun to learn "tolerance, patience and good will toward all men, even our enemies, for we look on them as sick people" (p. 70).

a5f0b748b8e4.t: The same words the book uses for the alcoholic

601793a1eb31.t: "Sick man" appears in three other places in the main text. Every time, it means the alcoholic: - Chapter 7: any scheme that tries "to shield the sick man from temptation is doomed to failure" (p. 101). A page earlier, the helper is told to urge the family that the man "has been a very sick person and should be treated accordingly" (p. 100). - Chapter 8, "To Wives": looking back, the wives "sensed dimly that we were dealing with sick men" (p. 107): their drinking husbands, in the plural. - Chapter 10: a manager can tell a drinking employee, "If you are an alcoholic, you are a mighty sick man." (p. 147) - Chapter 11: "said the sick man" is the man in the hospital bed (p. 157), whom the book's footnote identifies as A.A. Number Three (p. 156).

ac0e9918461e.t: On p. 67, the book asks the alcoholic to see the people he resents the way it asks families and employers to see him.

f804419be6f3.t: Praying <0>for</0> the person: the personal story

fd78ce6da174.t: The practice of praying for the resented person is in "Freedom From Bondage," a personal story in Part III of the fourth edition (pp. 544–553). The member read a clergyman's article. In her paraphrase, he said: "Ask for their health, their prosperity, their happiness, and you will be free." (p. 552) She was to do it every day for two weeks, even without meaning it, until she came to mean it (p. 552). "It worked for me then, and it has worked for me many times since" (p. 552).

6246c2f90db5.t: That's a member's experience, printed among the stories, which change from edition to edition. The fourth edition is 2001, and our text doesn't say when the story was first printed. It doesn't contradict p. 67, but it isn't what p. 67 says.

e637bc7979e5.t: It sharpens it. The main text does tell the reader to pray when resentment comes, and its prayer is about the other person. But what it asks for is tolerance, patience and freedom from anger in the one praying, plus a way to be helpful. Calling the other person "sick" isn't a put-down, because the book says it of ourselves in the same breath, and it's the word the book uses for the alcoholic. Praying for the other person's welfare, in so many words, comes from a member's story. And on p. 67 the prayer clears the way for the next part of the inventory: looking at our own mistakes.

cdfefed22614.t: What are A.A.'s Three Legacies? | Recovery Starts

db1aa321830f.t: A.A.'s Three Legacies are Recovery, Unity and Service: the Twelve Steps, the Twelve Traditions, and the services that carry the message.

c881e892f217.t: A.A.'s Three Legacies are Recovery, Unity and Service: the Twelve Steps, the Twelve Traditions, and the services that carry the message.

43c1137b69d8.t: Bill W. handed them over to the whole fellowship, speaking for himself, the late Dr. Bob and the oldtimers, at A.A.'s 20th anniversary convention in St. Louis on July 3, 1955.

a84a12f8a60a.t: In Bill's words, by the first we recover, by the second we stay together, and by the third A.A. carries its message to all who need it.

c3a13f274233.t: Bill called carrying the message, the Twelfth Step, "the basic service" (P-44); every other service, from a phone call to the General Service Office, exists to help reach the alcoholic.

2c176b7e3243.t: The term isn't in the Big Book's 1939 text. It comes from 1955, after Dr. Bob's death, when A.A. was twenty years old. The Big Book's own pages show the first two Legacies (the Steps, p. 59–60; the Traditions, Appendix I, pp. 561–566) but not the name.

45d2f41a4793.t: <0><1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957)</0> opens with it. During the first three days of July 1955, A.A. held a convention in St. Louis for its twentieth anniversary, and "there it received from its founders and old-timers permanent keeping of its three great legacies of Recovery, Unity, and Service" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). About 5,000 people were in the Kiel Auditorium on the final afternoon (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The General Service Conference took over custody of the Traditions and the guardianship of A.A.'s world services, and was named the permanent successor to the founders (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

34c0ea85dafe.t: The resolution the convention adopted declared the fellowship ready "to assume full and permanent possession of the Three Legacies of our A.A. inheritance" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and made the Conference, as of July 3, 1955, the guardian of the Traditions (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

46936adeb281.t: <0>P-44, <1>A.A.'s Legacy of Service</1></0> (Bill W., text through 1955; pamphlet © 2018) says the same in its introduction: the Legacies were announced at St. Louis in 1955, Dr. Bob was already gone, and Bill spoke for him and the other pioneers in turning over to all members "the responsibility for A.A.'s continuation and growth" (P-44).

2b0c7dee8bea.t: <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> states it in one sentence: by the first Legacy "we recover from alcoholism," by the second "we stay together in unity," and by the third the society "functions and serves its primary purpose of carrying the A.A. message to all who need it and want it" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The book is built on Bill's three talks at St. Louis, one for each Legacy (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

a6efa3d236fb.t: <0>Recovery</0> is the Twelve Steps and the story of how the program came together (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill called it the base of the triangle, "on which everything rests and depends" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

2a216e7134df.t: <0>Unity</0> is the Twelve Traditions, which "represent the distilled experience of our past" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

3a6e75d06e15.t: <0>Service</0> is everything that helps carry the message. P-44 begins: "Our Twelfth Step — carrying the message — is the basic service that the A.A. Fellowship gives; this is our principal aim and the main reason for our existence." (P-44). "Hence, an A.A. service is anything whatever that helps us to reach a fellow sufferer" (P-44), from the Twelfth Step call itself to a ten-cent phone call, a cup of coffee, and the General Service Office (P-44). "The sum total of all these services is our Third Legacy of Service." (P-44).

0dcdd3b4a6d1.t: The St. Louis banner showed a circle around a triangle: the circle for the whole world of A.A., the triangle's three sides for the three Legacies (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

e6b702e875fb.t: Why Service sits next to Recovery

40fba084ea59.t: In Bill's telling, Service is not paperwork added on top of the program. It is the Twelfth Step made practical: "We must carry the message, else we ourselves can wither and those who haven't been given the truth may die." (P-44). The question he says to ask of any service is only whether it is really needed to reach those who seek A.A. (P-44). That is the same work as Chapter 7 of the Big Book, going out to the alcoholic who is still drinking (see <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0>).

0c828717fc06.t: Can anyone be thrown out of A.A.? | Recovery Starts

7c507407693d.t: No one can be expelled from A.A. itself. The Long Form of Tradition Three says "we may refuse none who wish to recover" (p. 563), and that membership…

d8cc26aaf7a9.t: Can anyone be thrown out of A.A.?

3ea61b581b3f.t: No one can be expelled from A.A. itself. The Long Form of Tradition Three says "we may refuse none who wish to recover" (p. 563), and that membership should never depend on money or conformity.

d7e67205552e.t: Bill W., writing in 1946: a member "is a member as long as he says he is" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946).

b75965ab84f8.t: That isn't the same as putting up with anything at a meeting. In 1946 a member who kept turning up drunk could be "led outside" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946), then welcomed back the next day if sober. A club, which is separate from A.A., could bar him. Neither takes away his membership in A.A.

a700a56da090.t: Bill was honest that in 1946 this view was "not yet unanimous" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946) and membership rules still existed in places. The Tradition is the lesson A.A. drew from those rules.

d3c9be50a172.t: Tradition Three in its original form says A.A.'s membership "ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism" (p. 563). From that it follows, in the Tradition's own word "Hence," that "we may refuse none who wish to recover" (p. 563). And membership should never "depend upon money or conformity" (p. 563): not on dues, and not on agreeing with anyone or behaving a certain way.

3ee413331139.t: The short form puts it as one requirement, "a desire to stop drinking" (p. 562). The Long Form puts it the other way round: there's no one A.A. may turn away.

dc28b45dd57e.t: Bill's Grapevine piece "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?" (1946) is the essay Tradition Three grew out of, and it's mostly about throwing people out.

c933a0cbc8a3.t: A few years earlier, the New York office had asked groups to send in their membership rules. Put together, the rules filled "a great many sheets of paper" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). If all of them had been in force at once, almost no alcoholic could have joined, and about nine-tenths of the oldest and best members "could never have got by!" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). Early members would have been put out for slipping too often, for bad morals, for mental troubles, or for not coming from the "better classes."

a0b46481177c.t: Bill describes groups going on "rule-making benders" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946): committees given power to filter out undesirables, elders casting out the troublemakers. It didn't work. The fights over enforcement turned out to be worse for the group "than the very worst that the worst ever did" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). Some of the people once judged hopeless became the group's most respected and best-loved members, and Bill calls those who condemned them "the Pharisees" whose false righteousness did the group "the deeper spiritual damage" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946).

266497b68740.t: His conclusion: "Our A.A. door stands wide open" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). A newcomer "signs nothing, agrees to nothing, promises nothing" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). He joins on his own say-so.

50ad295a17d2.t: A meeting, a club, and A.A.

67266884e932.t: The same essay draws the line that answers most real cases. A member who "persists in coming to meetings drunk" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946) may be led outside, but in most groups he can come back the next day if he's sober. "Though he may be thrown out of a club, nobody thinks of throwing him out of A.A." (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946).

fc27c5afb590.t: So three different things: - <0>A.A. membership</0> belongs to the person. No group, committee or office can take it away. - <1>A meeting</1> can ask someone who is disrupting it to leave for now. Bill's 1946 essay on money mentions a steward who can "eject a troublesome drunk" (P-17, "Money", 1946). How a group runs its own meetings is its own affair under Tradition Four (p. 563). - <2>A club</2> is a separate thing that the Long Form says should be "set apart" from A.A. (p. 564). It can have its own rules for its own premises.

b651800ffe34.t: Bill didn't pretend everyone agreed. The open door wasn't yet the universal practice, he wrote: "Membership rules still exist." (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). He called the broad view "the main current of A.A. thought today" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946), while adding it was not yet unanimous.

4e1ae1f70ed4.t: The 1946–47 texts deal with drunkenness, slips, panhandling, gossip and "mental twists." They don't take up a member who puts other people in danger. They say a group can lead someone out of a meeting and that a group runs its own affairs, but they don't spell out more than that, and we won't add to them.

7567851d126a.t: In 1957 Bill summed up Tradition Three as: "You are an A.A. member if you say so" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957). The A.A. group pamphlet (P-16, 2018) quotes the 1962 Twelve Concepts: "no member to be expelled from A.A. — membership always to be the choice of the individual" (P-16, 2018).

d2afc14665de.t: What does the Big Book say to employers? | Recovery Starts

8c26f1537f87.t: Chapter 10, "To Employers" (pp. 136–150), is written by a member who had hired and fired hundreds of men before becoming an alcoholic himself. Its…

30009c3e390f.t: What does the Big Book say to employers?

f6ce42f4f5a1.t: Chapter 10, "To Employers" (pp. 136–150), is written by a member who had hired and fired hundreds of men before becoming an alcoholic himself. Its summary: "No man should be fired just because he is alcoholic." (p. 148). If he wants to stop, he should be given a real chance. If he can't or won't stop, "he should be discharged" (p. 148).

7c81159b9e76.t: It asks the employer to see alcoholism as an illness, not weakness or stubbornness, and to give a sick employee who wants to recover the same consideration as other ailing employees (pp. 139–141).

d7a683abfa32.t: Its suggested approach: be firm that the drinking must stop, don't lecture, make sure he really wants to quit, arrange medical treatment through a doctor, keep it confidential, and give him the book, without telling him he must follow it (pp. 141–145).

27c3450809b7.t: It warns against the opposite mistake too: covering for a man who doesn't want to stop. "You are not doing him a favor by keeping him on." (p. 141).

494f10a2dc3b.t: The chapter is one member's account; the book doesn't name him. <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) says only that "there is some reason to believe" Hank may have written it (<1>Pass It On</1>, 1984). As an assistant manager in a large corporation, he lost three exceptional men to alcoholism, each of whom took his own life after being let go, "because I did not understand alcoholism as I do now" (p. 137). Then he became an alcoholic himself. He tells of trying to help a banker friend understand a fellow executive's drinking: the bank was sure the man was done, because he had taken a cure and been told it was his last chance. The man drank again and was fired; afterward the members reached him (pp. 138–139).

c0d5f05a51e5.t: <0>Set your own drinking aside.</0> A moderate drinker can be more annoyed with an alcoholic than a teetotaler, because he controls his own drinking and "cannot see why it should be to anyone else, save the spineless and stupid" (p. 139).

59c4bf51be97.t: <0>Is he worth salvaging?</0> The alcoholic employee is often brilliant and quick, "imaginative and likeable" (p. 139). If he would be worth keeping without the drinking, should he have "the same consideration as other ailing employees?" (p. 140). If the reader isn't sure the man is sick and not just weak, the chapter suggests re-reading Chapters 2 and 3 (p. 140).

40dce601071a.t: <0>His past scrapes.</0> These can generally be charged "to the abnormal action of alcohol on his mind" (p. 140). Not all alcoholics are honest when sober, and some will take advantage of kindness. "If you are sure your man does not want to stop, he may as well be discharged, the sooner the better." (p. 141). The writer says being fired first, then shown the solution, might have brought him back "a well man" six months later (p. 141).

79d3a4647bf0.t: <0>Be firm.</0> Tell him you know about his drinking "and that it must stop" (p. 141); you'd like to keep him, but can't if he keeps drinking. "A firm attitude at this point has helped many of us." (p. 142).

90e2eeeff9d6.t: <0>Don't lecture.</0> Assure him you won't moralize or condemn, and explain alcoholism as an illness (p. 142).

bb965f02224e.t: <0>Probe whether he really wants to stop.</0> "Will he take every necessary step, submit to anything to get well, to stop drinking forever?" (p. 142). If he still thinks he can drink again, even beer, he may as well be discharged after his next bender (p. 142).

ab0abdb90c39.t: <0>Medical treatment, through a doctor.</0> For a man drinking or just off a spree, "a certain amount of physical treatment is desirable, even imperative" (p. 143), referred to the employer's own doctor. The employer may advance the cost, to be deducted later from his pay, so he feels responsible (p. 143). But "physical treatment is but a small part of the picture" (p. 143); he must undergo "a change of heart" (p. 143).

38c5e7a90a9e.t: <0>Keep it confidential.</0> Treat it as "a strictly personal matter" (p. 143), never discussed without his consent.

81c13e30c62f.t: <0>The book, not a command.</0> Give the book to his doctor and to him; "it is best that no one tell him he must abide by its suggestions" (p. 144). "The man must decide for himself." (p. 144). The writer doesn't offer the approach "as the last word on this subject" (p. 144): "After all, are you not looking for results rather than methods?" (p. 144).

f5ed2a20a612.t: <0>When he comes back.</0> Be ready to hear shocking things, such as a padded expense account; his new honesty demands it (p. 145).

e91c993b647f.t: Protect him from office gossip and malicious jokes about his drinking (pp. 145–146).

adfbb1780c3b.t: He may overwork; encourage him to play, and allow reasonable time for helping other alcoholics, which is "necessary to maintain his sobriety" (p. 146).

f9ee11fad9a2.t: "Your man may be trusted." (p. 146). If he does drink and is really trying, he'll tell you, even at the cost of his job.

7184fc04dcf6.t: If he stumbles, you decide whether to keep him; "you should feel under no obligation to keep him on, for your obligation has been well discharged already" (p. 147).

19939af7b88f.t: Give junior executives the book, so they stop covering for drinking employees and can be fair and square with them (pp. 147–148).

c5e8b103e185.t: Many firms think they have no alcoholic problem; it might pay "to take another look down the line" (p. 149). The chapter is about alcoholics, "sick people," not the habitual or whoopee drinker, for whom a strict policy is "undoubtedly sound" (p. 149).

c5bec41944b8.t: The writer ends with his own small company, where two alcoholic employees "produce as much as five normal salesmen" (p. 150).

8c0a3c607526.t: The chapter speaks to employers as employers. It doesn't ask them to join or support A.A. It hopes employees may be "put in personal contact with some of us" (p. 144), and says a great deal can be done with the book alone. Appendix VI gives A.A.'s address for anyone who wants help (p. 150, note).

07e06ae82f4b.t: What happened to Bill W. at Towns Hospital? | Recovery Starts

e3e29c32c3d8.t: Towns Hospital in New York, where Dr. William D. Silkworth was the physician, treated Bill W. several times. On his last stay, in December 1934, a few…

6cc519874f0a.t: What happened to Bill W. at Towns Hospital?

ed938069c469.t: Towns Hospital in New York, where Dr. William D. Silkworth was the physician, treated Bill W. several times. On his last stay, in December 1934, a few weeks after his friend Ebby's visit, Bill had the sudden spiritual experience that ended his drinking.

4c471c591acb.t: The 1939 Big Book tells it quietly: in the hospital he offered himself to God, became willing to have his sins taken away, and felt a peace and a "great clean wind of a mountain top" blow through him. He asked the doctor if he was still sane; the doctor said something had happened he didn't understand, but Bill had better hang on to it.

48e05d00cdec.t: Bill's later accounts add a cry of despair ("If there is a God, let Him show Himself!"), a room lit with white light, and a sense of Presence. They also give the doctor's reassurance in different words.

8967faddf4b0.t: Silkworth's own letter in the Big Book says the idea that led to A.A. came to this patient "in the course of his third treatment."

93be108d338a.t: <0>"Bill's Story."</0> On an earlier stay at "a nationally-known hospital for the mental and physical rehabilitation of alcoholics" (p. 7), "Under the so-called belladonna treatment my brain cleared." (p. 7), and a kind doctor explained that he had been seriously ill, bodily and mentally (p. 7). He drank again, went back, and his wife was told he would die or go mad within a year (p. 7).

8d1326b690e7.t: After Ebby's visit, he went back once more. "At the hospital I was separated from alcohol for the last time." (p. 13). "There I humbly offered myself to God, as I then understood Him, to do with me as He would." (p. 13). His friend visited, and they made a list of the people Bill had hurt (p. 13). When Bill fully accepted these proposals, "the effect was electric. There was a sense of victory, followed by such a peace and serenity as I had never known." (p. 14). "I felt lifted up, as though the great clean wind of a mountain top blew through and through." (p. 14). "God comes to most men gradually, but His impact on me was sudden and profound." (p. 14).

641739287a4b.t: Alarmed, he asked the doctor if he was still sane. The doctor said: "Something has happened to you I don't understand. But you had better hang on to it." (p. 14). Still in the hospital, Bill thought of the thousands of hopeless alcoholics he might help (p. 14). The 1939 text names neither the hospital nor the doctor; the names come from later accounts.

ca44a1eb9dd0.t: <0>"The Doctor's Opinion."</0> Dr. Silkworth's letter, also from 1939, doesn't name Bill: "In late 1934 I attended a patient who, though he had been a competent businessman of good earning capacity, was an alcoholic of a type I had come to regard as hopeless." (p. xxv). "In the course of his third treatment he acquired certain ideas concerning a possible means of recovery." (p. xxv). See <1>What is "The Doctor's Opinion," and who wrote it?</1>

80c5d435a3e3.t: Bill's later accounts (1957, and as told in 1984)

5a26223e433f.t: <0>A.A. Comes of Age (1957).</0> In the summer of 1934 Bill lay in Towns, and Dr. Silkworth told Lois he was hopeless (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In December, after Ebby's visit and a night at the Calvary Mission, he walked into Towns carrying a bottle of beer (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "In three or four days I was free of what little sedative they gave me" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), but very depressed and still choking on the idea of God. Ebby came and repeated his formula (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Then, at the bottom of the pit, he cried out: "If there is a God, let Him show Himself! I am ready to do anything, anything!" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The room lit up with a great white light; he felt he was on a mountain in a wind of spirit, and that he was a free man (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "So this is the God of the preachers!" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

d8caf7a8c2db.t: Frightened that he was hallucinating, he called the doctor, who said: "No, Bill, you are not crazy." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Elsewhere in the same book Bill quotes him: "you are not hallucinating" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The next day, Bill thinks Ebby brought him William James's <0>Varieties of Religious Experience</0>, which helped him understand what had happened (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <1>Why does the Big Book mention William James?</1>

b47da3f787b6.t: <0>P-53</0> (Bill's biographical sketch, pamphlet © 2017): in Towns Hospital a month after Ebby's message, "in total despair, he cried out for help" (P-53), and the experience brought a conviction of release and the insight that helping other alcoholics could keep him sober (P-53).

903a599a337f.t: <0>Pass It On (1984)</0> dates his admission to December 11, 1934, and says the treatment then was barbiturates for sedation and belladonna (Pass It On, 1984). It gives the cry as "If there be a God, let Him show Himself!" (Pass It On, 1984), and Silkworth's answer as: "Yes, my boy, you are sane, perfectly sane in my judgment." (Pass It On, 1984). He left the hospital on December 18 (Pass It On, 1984). The book calls 1934 "a year that had seen Bill hospitalized four times" (Pass It On, 1984).

18a58be8c21a.t: Bill went back to Towns to work with patients, with Dr. Silkworth's permission (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "Many times I have gone to my old hospital in despair. On talking to a man there, I would be amazingly lifted up and set on my feet." (p. 15). Chapter 11 mentions an unnamed, well-known hospital in an eastern city where a doctor sends members patients and "Many of us have felt, for the first time, the Presence and Power of God within its walls." (p. 162). Later, the owner, Charles B. Towns, offered Bill a paid position as a lay therapist, which Bill turned down after his group objected (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; Pass It On, 1984), and lent money toward the Big Book (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

b7717cb8d123.t: <0>The experience itself.</0> The 1939 text has no cry, no light and no "Presence"; it describes humble surrender, then a sense of victory, peace and a mountain wind (pp. 13–14). The cry and the white light are in Bill's 1957 account and later (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; Pass It On, 1984). The wording of the cry differs slightly between them.

9fbb8dbc5ea9.t: <0>What the doctor said.</0> 1939: something had happened he didn't understand; hang on to it (p. 14). 1957: "you are not crazy," and that he had read of such events and they sometimes release people from alcoholism (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), or, in another passage, "you are not hallucinating" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). 1984: "you are sane, perfectly sane" (Pass It On, 1984).

798b18751ebd.t: <0>Which stay.</0> Silkworth's 1939 letter says the ideas came in the patient's "third treatment" (p. xxv); <1>Pass It On</1> says Bill was hospitalized four times in 1934 (Pass It On, 1984). Our sources don't reconcile the counts.

7b90528cebc7.t: <0>The medicine.</0> <1>Pass It On</1> lists barbiturates and belladonna as the treatment of that time (Pass It On, 1984); Bill (1957) says he was free of the sedative after three or four days, before the experience (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Our sources draws no connection between the treatment and the experience.

22c97df1257b.t: Tradition One: does it mean "my sobriety comes first"? | Recovery Starts

93adc4c3f0cd.t: No. Tradition One says the opposite order: "our common welfare comes first. But individual welfare follows close afterward" (p. 563).

623693c8a504.t: Tradition One: does it mean "my sobriety comes first"?

b83a0708d184.t: No. Tradition One says the opposite order: "our common welfare comes first. But individual welfare follows close afterward" (p. 563).

2ef498a96b13.t: The reason it gives is that the individual's life depends on A.A.'s: "A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die" (p. 563). Putting A.A.'s unity first is how members protect their own recovery, and the recovery of alcoholics who haven't arrived yet.

861953ca9d94.t: The individual isn't dismissed. The Long Form keeps him in the same sentence: second, and "close afterward."

5bcaf062715a.t: The whole of Tradition One in its original form is four short sentences (p. 563): - Each member is "but a small part of a great whole" (p. 563). - A.A. must go on living, or most members will die. - "Hence our common welfare comes first" (p. 563). - "But individual welfare follows close afterward" (p. 563).

11f9f704db10.t: The short form keeps the first half of the idea and the reason behind it: "Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity" (p. 562). The line about individual welfare following close behind is only in the Long Form.

fa642aee3412.t: The opening of Appendix I gives the same reasoning. Because A.A. makes the difference between life and death for its members, and could for many more, it needs "permanent unity" (p. 561). Alcoholics must "work together and hang together" or most will "die alone" (p. 561).

586d251c6871.t: Where "my sobriety comes first" goes wrong

b77597163e75.t: The phrase isn't in the Tradition. It reverses the order the text gives. The Tradition doesn't say a member's welfare doesn't matter; it says the member's welfare depends on something bigger than him, so that comes first.

3ae47fe845e5.t: Bill W.'s later writing keeps pointing the same way. In the foreword to P-17 he asked every member to be as aware of what endangers A.A. as a whole as of the personal defects "which threaten his own sobriety" (P-17, Foreword, 1955), and added: "For whole movements have, before now, gone on benders, too!" (P-17, Foreword, 1955). A.A. unity doesn't keep itself, he wrote; like personal recovery, members will always "have to work to maintain it" (P-17, Foreword, 1955).

8372faa29ad4.t: In 1955 he described the Traditions as sacrifices. Each member "had to make willing sacrifices for the group itself, sacrifices for the common welfare" (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955), and the group in turn gave up rights "for the protection and welfare of each member" (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955). The giving goes both ways, but it starts with the member giving.

51f396695c72.t: In <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957), Bill tells a story he places under Tradition Two, the group conscience, which ends with Tradition One's principle. In 1937, broke and with Lois supporting the household, he was offered a paid job as a lay therapist at Towns Hospital. It would have helped him, and it was ethical. His New York group told him no: A.A. couldn't be tied to one hospital or have paid therapists. He listened. Three principles, he wrote, had fallen that night on "the anvil of group experience" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957), and the first he lists is "The common welfare must come first" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957). Bill's own welfare that night came second, and he says the group was right.

ea75e4d0cc02.t: He also compares the early members to a crew adrift on a raft after a plane crash: "Nobody dared rock that raft, lest they all perish" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957). In the same passage he insists that "Probably no society sets a higher value on the personal welfare of the individual member than does A.A." (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). The common welfare comes first because without it there would be little personal welfare at all.

b596bc87546d.t: A later pamphlet on the same point

43bd1f2c5257.t: <0>The Twelve Traditions Illustrated</0> (P-43, 1971) takes up the "selfish program" idea under Tradition One directly. It asks, "Oh well, it's a selfish program, isn't it?" (P-43, 1971), and answers that self-indulgence threatens both the member's own sobriety and the unity of the group.

ff85acc952b6.t: Tradition Ten: does A.A. take sides on outside issues? | Recovery Starts

41b9f0e5c9c9.t: No. The Long Form of Tradition Ten says no A.A. group or member should ever express an opinion on outside controversial issues "in such a way as to…

931feda4fd82.t: Tradition Ten: does A.A. take sides on outside issues?

e8b8b80a33f1.t: No. The Long Form of Tradition Ten says no A.A. group or member should ever express an opinion on outside controversial issues "in such a way as to implicate A.A." It names politics, alcohol reform and sectarian religion in particular (p. 565).

f0e3bf156e88.t: "The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one" (p. 565). On such matters the groups express no views at all.

27c3dfb45565.t: The Tradition doesn't ask members to have no opinions. It asks them never to put A.A.'s name behind one.

e5f32d45591a.t: The whole Tenth Tradition is three sentences:

0a565815feb4.t: No A.A. group or member should ever, "in such a way as to implicate A.A.," express any opinion on outside controversial issues, "particularly those of politics, alcohol reform, or sectarian religion" (p. 565).

591faf199882.t: "The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one" (p. 565).

76f0da21e9d3.t: "Concerning such matters they can express no views whatever" (p. 565).

9e869e07c804.t: Notice who it covers and how. The groups have no views on these issues at all. A member is covered too, but the limit is on speaking in a way that drags A.A. in. The text doesn't say a member can't vote, hold beliefs or take part in public life.

07fdf7644b71.t: The idea is older than the Traditions. The Big Book's 1939 foreword already said A.A. was not allied with any faith, sect or denomination, "nor do we oppose anyone" (p. xiv).

cdae42b44d1b.t: <0>The Washingtonians.</0> In 1947 Bill pointed to the Washingtonian movement, a society of alcoholics a hundred years earlier that fell apart partly because its members publicly took up abolition, prohibition and other causes (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947, p. 23).

5475fec7f014.t: <0>What a group can't do.</0> "Neither A.A. as a whole nor any A.A. group ought to enter any activity other than straight A.A." (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947, p. 24). Groups can't endorse, finance or ally with any other cause, "however good" (P-17, p. 24), and to do otherwise would put A.A.'s unity at risk (P-17, pp. 24–25).

fc4e9ea9adcf.t: <0>What a member can do.</0> Bill rejects the "do nothing" view. Members can work in noncontroversial alcohol fields such as hospitals, research and education, as individuals only, without describing themselves as A.A.s in public (P-17, p. 25). That way "A.A. as a whole could remain uncommitted yet friendly" toward good causes (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947, p. 25).

931c9ea9db12.t: <0>Money from either side.</0> In 1946 Bill wrote that money offered from "wet" or "dry" sources was obviously dangerous, because "we must stay out of that ill-starred controversy" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 34).

08a17b677d62.t: <0>What went wrong when members did take sides (1955, dated).</0> Looking back in 1955, Bill listed cases from A.A.'s files: a member who published a Prohibition magazine and used A.A.'s name to attack drinking (P-17, p. 52); a proposed job doing "education" for a liquor-trade group under a member's full A.A. name (P-17, p. 53); members lobbying state legislatures as A.A.s (P-17, p. 54); a candidate who advertised his A.A. membership (P-17, p. 55); and A.A.'s name pulled into a member's libel suit (P-17, p. 55). Each, he wrote, showed that one member breaking anonymity could tie A.A. to almost any cause or controversy (P-17, p. 53). His 1955 summary: A.A. abstains from public controversy and "will not quarrel among ourselves" about religion, politics and reform (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955, p. 50).

2deeee5439eb.t: The Long Form gives three examples of outside issues, politics, alcohol reform and sectarian religion, introduced with "particularly." It doesn't list everything else that counts, and it doesn't name treatment methods or any modern topic. Deciding whether a new question is an "outside controversial issue" is left to experience.

07b3af948e3d.t: P-17, <0>A.A. Tradition: How It Developed</0> ("Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects," pp. 23–26; "Money," pp. 27–35; "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous," pp. 48–58): <1>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/literature/assets/p-17_AATraditions.pdf</1>

d78dac2c215b.t: Tradition Eleven: does A.A. advertise? | Recovery Starts

14c7a184c86a.t: The Long Form of Tradition Eleven says A.A. "ought to avoid sensational advertising," that members' names and pictures as A.A. members should not be…

8a1898d6fb38.t: The Long Form of Tradition Eleven says A.A. "ought to avoid sensational advertising," that members' names and pictures as A.A. members should not be broadcast, filmed or printed, and that public relations should rest on "attraction rather than promotion" (p. 565).

6e91359dcbb8.t: It doesn't say A.A. must stay hidden. In 1946 Bill W. criticized groups that shunned all publicity, because they forgot the alcoholics in town who hadn't heard A.A. existed.

87a1c424fca1.t: What A.A. avoids is selling itself and praising itself: "There is never need to praise ourselves. We feel it better to let our friends recommend us" (p. 565).

8e2adf5322e6.t: The Eleventh Tradition's Long Form has five sentences:

d08407390540.t: Relations with the general public "should be characterized by personal anonymity" (p. 565).

c45019bee5c5.t: "We think A.A. ought to avoid sensational advertising" (p. 565).

6eaee958cc8f.t: Members' names and pictures as A.A. members "ought not be broadcast, filmed, or publicly printed" (p. 565).

eca67ceaa9ae.t: Public relations "should be guided by the principle of attraction rather than promotion" (p. 565).

aa19dd64464a.t: "There is never need to praise ourselves. We feel it better to let our friends recommend us" (p. 565).

f9b4a732cbbc.t: The word in the Long Form is <0>sensational</0> advertising. The short form drops that and keeps "attraction rather than promotion" together with personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films (p. 562). The Long Form doesn't forbid letting the public know A.A. exists. It also gives the trustees the job of handling A.A.'s overall public relations, on the groups' authority (p. 565), which assumes A.A. has public relations.

95604d101445.t: <0>Two kinds of mistake.</0> Bill describes groups at both extremes (P-17, p. 43). Some, especially new ones, behaved "like secret societies," keeping even their friends and families out (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 43). Others advertised their activities at every chance and put members' names on public platforms (P-17, p. 43).

6cee7e0812f3.t: <0>Hiding has a cost.</0> Groups that shun all publicity year after year grow slowly and "become stale" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 46). In their anxiety to keep secrets, "they forget their obligation to other alcoholics in their communities" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 46) who haven't heard A.A. has come to town. Usually the caution breaks down: meetings open to families and friends, doctors and clergy are invited, and "Finally the group enlists the aid of the local newspaper" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 47).

4493c2b5904c.t: <0>Why quiet works better than promotion.</0> Reporters who cover A.A. complain at first about writing without names, then become friends of A.A. when they see a group of people who want no personal publicity (P-17, p. 45). The public, tired of pressure selling and spectacular promotion, is drawn by A.A.'s quietness, modesty and anonymity (P-17, p. 45). Bill's summary: "Our public relations policy should mainly rest upon the principle of attraction and seldom, if ever, upon promotion" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 47).

6e9f8afc709a.t: <0>The line.</0> A new member shouldn't rush to a newspaper or a microphone, and nobody should publicize A.A. "without being sure of the approval of his own group" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 46). Members and groups may decide for themselves how far to drop anonymity, with one exception: nobody, writing or speaking for publication as an A.A. member, discloses their full name (P-17, p. 47).

3bd03f06eab2.t: In 1955 Bill told of members who tried to use A.A.'s name commercially, including one who planned a sponsored series of radio "lectures" on A.A. for a life insurance company (P-17, p. 53). A.A.'s headquarters objected and the project was dropped (P-17, pp. 53–54). Bill feared every advertising man in A.A. finding a commercial sponsor and using A.A.'s name to sell anything (P-17, p. 54). Editors, he wrote, trusted A.A. because it refused to advertise its leaders or members, a "strange and refreshing novelty" to them (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955, p. 57).

fa006fed0c14.t: <0>The Twelve Traditions Illustrated</0> (P-43, 1971) makes the same point from the other direction: a sick alcoholic who never meets a member will struggle to find A.A. "if the local group thinks it should be anonymous, too" (P-43, 1971, "The Eleventh Tradition").

16de2125111a.t: A.A. doesn't promote itself, praise itself, use sensational advertising or put members' faces and names before the public. It does make itself known, and the 1946 text treats a group that hides from the alcoholics around it as failing them. Where exactly "making known" becomes "promotion" isn't spelled out; the Long Form gives the principle, not a list.

ab1939a58be3.t: P-17, <0>A.A. Tradition: How It Developed</0> ("Anonymity," pp. 41–47; "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous," pp. 48–58): <1>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/literature/assets/p-17_AATraditions.pdf</1>

e004a63857bc.t: Tradition Twelve: does anonymity mean keeping A.A. secret? | Recovery Starts

a3ab1fda8f24.t: No. The Long Form of Tradition Twelve is about humility, not secrecy: anonymity "reminds us that we are to place principles before personalities; that we…

1e38325197e9.t: Tradition Twelve: does anonymity mean keeping A.A. secret?

78de23956f19.t: No. The Long Form of Tradition Twelve is about humility, not secrecy: anonymity "reminds us that we are to place principles before personalities; that we are actually to practice a genuine humility" (p. 566).

cbab8486113c.t: In 1946 Bill W. wrote that few members were anonymous in daily life, and that they had dropped anonymity with friends and associates on purpose, because those people "ought to know about Alcoholics Anonymous."

8d1e3efbb6d7.t: The one firm line is at the level of the public media: no full names or pictures as A.A. members in the press, radio or film. Everything closer to home is left to each member and group.

3019610e0a43.t: Each member may keep as much personal anonymity as he wants, and others must respect it.

81aa6b038503.t: The Twelfth Tradition is the last of the twelve. A.A. believes that the principle of anonymity has "an immense spiritual" significance (pp. 565–566). It reminds members to put principles before personalities and to practice "a genuine humility" (p. 566). The purpose: "that our great blessings may never spoil us; that we shall forever live in thankful contemplation of Him who presides over us all" (p. 566).

c1c8597fd289.t: There's nothing in it about hiding A.A., hiding meetings, or hiding that you belong. The practical rule about names is in Tradition Eleven, and it's about the public media: members' names and pictures "as A.A. members ought not be broadcast, filmed, or publicly printed" (p. 565).

7eca47299640.t: <0>What anonymity means.</0> The word "anonymous" reminds members to put principles before personalities, and shows that the movement has given up personal glorification in public (P-17, p. 41).

172e81d12715.t: <0>Members weren't hiding.</0> Bill says plainly that few members were anonymous in their daily contacts (P-17, pp. 43–44). "We have dropped anonymity at this level because we think our friends and associates ought to know about Alcoholics Anonymous" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 44), and because members wanted to lose the fear of admitting they were alcoholics. Members often spoke under their own names at semipublic gatherings, asking only that reporters not print them (P-17, p. 44).

99b5d6935439.t: <0>Where the line is.</0> If every member felt free to publish his own name, picture and story, A.A. would be launched on endless personal publicity, so the line has to be drawn there (P-17, p. 44). Bill proposed three points (P-17, p. 44): 1. It is "the privilege of each A.A. to cloak himself" in as much anonymity as he wants, and others should respect that (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 44). 2. A member should respect his own group's feeling about anonymity in their town. 3. No member should publish his name or picture in public media in connection with A.A. activity, though he can use his name in other public activities so long as he doesn't disclose his A.A. membership.

8f62f094dcfd.t: <0>Protecting newcomers.</0> A newcomer's anonymity should be kept as long as he wants it, even under an assumed name, because A.A. promised it when he came (P-17, p. 46).

93e47e7388c6.t: <0>Secrecy is a mistake too.</0> Groups that shut themselves away year after year grow stale and forget "their obligation to other alcoholics in their communities" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 46). See <1>Tradition Eleven: does A.A. advertise?</1>

c139109f0588.t: <0>His summary.</0> With one important exception, how far each member or group drops anonymity is "left strictly to the individual or group concerned" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 47). The exception is publication: writing or speaking for publication as A.A. members, nobody discloses their full name (P-17, p. 47).

eaf31dd00019.t: Nine years later he was just as clear: "no A.A. need be anonymous to" family, friends or neighbors, and telling them is usually right and good (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955, p. 56). Speaking at group or semipublic A.A. meetings carries no special danger, "provided, press reports reveal first names only" (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955, p. 56). Before the general public, though, "the revelation of full names and pictures is the point of peril" (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955, p. 56).

35da27629c1e.t: Anonymity in the Traditions isn't a vow of secrecy. It's humility (no personal glory from A.A.) plus one public rule (no names and faces as A.A. members in the media), plus respect for anyone who wants to stay private. Telling your friends and associates that you're in A.A. is something the 1946 text describes members doing as a matter of course, and the 1955 piece adds family and neighbours.
