1d79133976bd.t: The Twelve Traditions, Long Form, Traditions Eleven and Twelve (Big Book Appendix I)

0bd0318b51ce.t: Tradition Two: does anyone have authority in A.A.? | Recovery Starts

2215b425cf6e.t: No person does. The Long Form of Tradition Two says that "for our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself…

b3fc5e1fa170.t: Tradition Two: does anyone have authority in A.A.?

7c7ae4453998.t: No person does. The Long Form of Tradition Two says that "for our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience" (p. 563).

063f53399ffb.t: Leaders, committees, trustees and the New York office serve; they don't rule. The Long Form says A.A.'s leaders "derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern" (p. 565).

54cabb4b1170.t: Bill W. tried to run A.A. himself in its early years and found he couldn't. In 1947 he wrote that the only real authority in A.A. "is that of spiritual principle. It is never personal authority." (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947).

c607c9b4d96d.t: That includes old-timers and sponsors. The texts set no member in authority over another.

7a0ffaa740f0.t: Tradition Two is the one Tradition whose original wording survived whole into the short form (P-17, introduction). It is a single sentence: "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." (p. 563).

7c4984e4031d.t: Two things in that sentence are worth noticing. The authority it names is not a person, a committee or an office. And it is authority "for our group purpose": the Tradition is about how a group decides its affairs, not about anyone's control over a member's life.

5051ebf42c1a.t: The familiar second half, "Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not govern" (p. 562), comes from the Long Form of Tradition Nine. There, after describing secretaries, rotating committees, intergroups and the trustees, it says "true leaders in A.A. are but trusted and experienced servants of the whole" (p. 565). They have no real authority from their titles; "Universal respect is the key to their usefulness" (p. 565).

60d59db596b5.t: His Grapevine essay "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?" (1947) answers the question in its first line: "almost surely 'no'" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947).

bdd209b7aea5.t: His reasons: - <0>Alcoholics can't be governed, but they can be led.</0> Families, doctors and judges had all failed to discipline alcoholics by force. So "the only real authority to be found in A.A. is that of spiritual principle. It is never personal authority." (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). - <1>No one is over anyone.</1> A.A. has no fees, no dues, no rules, and "no one set in personal authority over anyone else" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). - <2>Leaders persuade.</2> An elected leader "can always guide by example or persuasion he can never boss" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947), or he'll be passed over at the next election. Committees "have only the authorization to serve, never to command" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947), and carry out what they believe the group wants. - <3>Bill included.</3> He tried to run A.A. for a few years. "Personal power always failed." (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). In A.A., he concluded, "one can be a servant only" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). - <4>The office and trustees too.</4> The General Office supplies information, literature and advice "if asked." The trustees are custodians: "caretakers only" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). None of them has authority to govern A.A.

6036d43bb30f.t: The early texts don't give experience any authority. Bill's 1946 essay on membership tells how "Group Elders, now clothed with authority" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946) began throwing people out, and how badly it went.

a4e47325837c.t: In 1957 he wrote that many old-timers still thought their experience gave them "a sort of vested right" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957) to run things and pick their successors. The groups wouldn't have it. Bill called it a hard fact that the group conscience, "when properly informed of the facts and issues and principles involved" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957), was often wiser than any leader. Old-timers still had something to give: when groups got into trouble, they'd turn to them for guidance. But guidance asked for is not authority.

43524e275f7e.t: Bill says his own "first dose" of this doctrine came in 1937, the night his New York group told him not to become a paid therapist at Towns Hospital (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957). "The group was right and I was wrong" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957).

1f521424af22.t: The Long Form doesn't explain how a "loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience" works in practice, or how a group should reach its conscience. It names the authority and leaves the rest to experience. (For whether group conscience means a majority vote, see <0>Is group conscience a majority vote?</0>)

bce42f6bf61d.t: It also doesn't say the trustees and offices have no function. The Long Form of Tradition Nine says the groups authorize the trustees to handle A.A.'s overall public relations (p. 565), and Tradition Four asks groups to confer with the trustees before acting in ways that could greatly affect A.A. as a whole (p. 563). Those are services the groups delegate, not a power over them.

3dcf76ad5c6d.t: P-17, <0>A.A. Tradition — How It Developed</0> ("Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?" is near the end): <1>https://www.aa.org/aa-tradition-how-it-developed</1>

a8b8fdff47c9.t: Tradition Four: can GSO tell a group what to do? | Recovery Starts

da88f321d40f.t: Not about the group's own affairs. The Long Form says that in its own affairs each group "should be responsible to no other authority than its own…

5774368681e8.t: Tradition Four: can GSO tell a group what to do?

85c3cc20f526.t: Not about the group's own affairs. The Long Form says that in its own affairs each group "should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience" (p. 563).

a1f9e1304291.t: The Long Form does set limits on the group, though. If its plans affect neighbouring groups, it should consult them. And no group, committee or individual should take an action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole "without conferring with the trustees of the General Service Board" (p. 563).

c70f629626ee.t: Conferring isn't obeying. Bill W. wrote in 1947 that there is no human authority in A.A. that "can compel an A.A. group to do anything" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). The New York office gives information and advice; a group is free to take it or leave it, and free to be wrong.

86dce6b5b76b.t: Tradition Four in its original form has three parts (p. 563): 1. <0>Its own affairs.</0> "With respect to its own affairs, each A.A. group should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience." (p. 563). 2. <1>Its neighbours.</1> When a group's plans concern the welfare of neighbouring groups, "those groups ought to be consulted" (p. 563). 3. <2>A.A. as a whole.</2> No group, regional committee or individual should take any action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole without conferring with the trustees. "On such issues our common welfare is paramount." (p. 563).

908161e0ed90.t: The short form shrinks this to "Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole" (p. 562). The Long Form makes clear what "except" asks for: consulting and conferring.

4bf69bb752ab.t: A note on names. In 1946 the text said "the trustees of The Alcoholic Foundation" (P-17, Foreword, 1955). The Foundation was renamed the General Service Board in 1954, and "the Foundation office is now the General Service Office" (P-17, Foreword, 1955). So "GSO" is the office the trustees oversee. The Big Book's printing of the Long Form uses the new name (p. 563).

5a076620f7b9.t: What the office can and can't do (1946–47)

d7c614aaf642.t: Bill W.'s essays describe the office as a service, not a government.

07c5de8fc3bd.t: In "Money" (1946) he wrote of the clubs, local offices and the General Office: "These are places of service" (P-17, "Money", 1946). They can't control A.A., and if one became inefficient or overbearing, members would stop sending money until things changed. Because no one is compelled to support them, "they can never dictate" (P-17, "Money", 1946).

c8f8da5fe5a7.t: In "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?" (1947) he listed what the General Office does: supply information and literature, report how most members feel about current problems, look after A.A.'s overall public relations, sometimes mediate, and help new groups start, "giving advice if asked" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). The trustees are custodians, "caretakers only" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). And there is no human authority in A.A. that "can compel an A.A. group to do anything" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947).

e3dbaa948b0e.t: In <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> Bill tells how he first thought he could manage A.A. from New York, and how the groups told him otherwise: "Services, yes. But government, no." (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). He says the groups' autonomy "included the right to be wrong" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957).

3081dd041702.t: His example: a promoter in one town sold his group on a building with a club, a clinic and a loan office, three corporations and sixty-one rules. Dissenters wrote to New York. The office replied that each group could manage its affairs as it liked if it didn't harm other groups, and warned as strongly as it dared that such schemes had failed elsewhere. The group ignored the warning, as it had a right to. The scheme collapsed. Afterwards the promoter mailed every group a card, "Rule No. 62": "Don't take yourself too damned seriously." (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957).

a3d793456581.t: That story shows Tradition Four working both ways. New York gave its experience; the group decided; the group lived with the result.

4cc9e88135ae.t: It doesn't say a group may do anything at all. Its own conscience is the authority over its own affairs, but the Long Form asks it to think of other groups and of A.A. as a whole, and the other Traditions still apply to it: no outside affiliation (p. 563), no business, no endorsements (p. 564).

9581b2531e4b.t: It also doesn't make the trustees or GSO a court that rules on what a group does. The Long Form asks groups to confer with the trustees on A.A.-wide matters; it gives the trustees no power to command, and the 1946–47 essays say plainly they have none.

03bb0fc251c9.t: <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, Appendix I, Tradition Four (short and Long Form); Long Form Three and Six

87a08fe6e999.t: P-17, Foreword (original Point Four and its 1954 footnote)

05517c72c88b.t: Tradition Five: what is a group's one purpose? | Recovery Starts

15a603c50a9e.t: Carrying the A.A. message to alcoholics who are still suffering. The Long Form says each group "ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary…

3b96cd95d6ee.t: Tradition Five: what is a group's one purpose?

178860d213a9.t: Carrying the A.A. message to alcoholics who are still suffering. The Long Form says each group "ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers" (p. 563).

24fafcf2502b.t: The purpose points outward, to the alcoholic who still suffers. The Tradition doesn't describe the group's purpose as looking after the members it already has.

42683ad7596f.t: Everything else a group might do, from running a club or a hospital to backing a cause, is what the Traditions after Five keep at arm's length, so it doesn't pull the group off that one purpose.

778bb46b35f0.t: The whole of Tradition Five: "Each Alcoholics Anonymous group ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." (p. 563).

15b6ef5f821a.t: <0>"A spiritual entity."</0> The next Tradition explains what that rules out. "Problems of money, property, and authority may easily divert us from our primary spiritual aim" (p. 563), so property should be separately incorporated, "thus dividing the material from the spiritual" (p. 564), and "An A.A. group, as such, should never go into business" (p. 564). Bill W. said the same in 1946: "an A.A. group is a spiritual entity, not a business concern" (P-17, "Money", 1946). In 1947, after groups had tried running their own drying-out places, he wrote that a group "is primarily a spiritual entity" and "as a group the less business it has to transact, the better" (P-17, "Hospitals and A.A.", 1947).

b8686e6eb1bc.t: <0>"The alcoholic who still suffers."</0> The message is carried to someone who is still in trouble with alcohol. The Big Book's own instructions for doing that are in Chapter 7, "Working With Others," whose opening paragraph says: "Carry this message to other alcoholics!" (p. 89). The Long Form doesn't refer to Chapter 7 by name, but it describes the same work, done by a group.

180733e9d290.t: Bill's essays come back to it again and again: - Groups "stick to their single purpose of helping alcoholics to recover" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). - "Neither A.A. as a whole nor any A.A. group ought to enter any activity other than straight A.A." (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947). A.A. mustn't let the public think it has abandoned "our sole aim" (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947). - In 1955: "We have but one purpose: to carry the A.A. message to the sick alcoholic who wants it." (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955).

c45c1dff5710.t: In 1957 he put it as a proverb, "Shoemaker, stick to thy last" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957), and said the message to the alcoholic who still suffers is "our basic objective, our real reason for existence" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). His reasoning: if A.A. had found a cure for cancer, no one would want it to branch out into every other disease. Its members can reach suffering alcoholics as no one else can, so that's where its strength should go (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957).

09ec25e3ea8b.t: "Primary purpose" in the Preamble is a different sentence

5ed169177206.t: The A.A. Preamble says: "Our primary purpose is to stay sober and help other alcoholics to achieve sobriety" (P-16, 2018, the Preamble). That sentence is about members ("our"), and it puts staying sober first. Tradition Five is about the group, and it names one purpose: carrying the message to the alcoholic who still suffers (p. 563). The two aren't in conflict, since a member has to be sober to carry the message, but they aren't the same statement, and only one of them is the Tradition. The Preamble was written by a Grapevine editor and first published in June 1947 (<0>A.A. Service Manual</0>, 2024–2026 edition); Tradition Five's Long Form is Bill's 1946 text.

fc2776954044.t: It says "primary," and it doesn't list secondary purposes. A group still has to find a room, pay rent and hold meetings. The Long Form treats those as means, and keeps anything that needs much property or management set apart from the group (p. 564).

714ea4299eea.t: It also doesn't say a group's purpose is to keep its own members sober, or to be a support group for its members. That may well happen, but the one purpose the Tradition names is the person who hasn't been reached yet.

266400890cdb.t: Related: <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0> · <1>Tradition Six: can an A.A. group partner with a treatment centre?</1>

304b51325832.t: <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, Appendix I, Long Form Five and Six

cf94bdbe1241.t: P-17, "Hospitals and A.A." (from "Adequate Hospitalization"); "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?"; "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects"

f0d667992fd8.t: Tradition Six: can an A.A. group partner with a treatment centre? | Recovery Starts

99e86250fb10.t: No. The Long Form says an A.A. group "may cooperate with anyone," but "such cooperation ought never go so far as affiliation or endorsement, actual or…

dc95aa297cea.t: Tradition Six: can an A.A. group partner with a treatment centre?

bcccb9b1c40a.t: No. The Long Form says an A.A. group "may cooperate with anyone," but "such cooperation ought never go so far as affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564). "An A.A. group can bind itself to no one" (p. 564).

2d4d661200ed.t: The 1946 text doesn't use the words "treatment centre." Its words are "hospitals, as well as other places of recuperation," and it says they "ought to be well outside A.A.—and medically supervised" (p. 564).

c3308cb40b03.t: Cooperation is fine. In 1946 Bill W. wrote, "Everywhere we cooperate with hospitals" (P-17, "Money", 1946), and today's group pamphlet describes groups renting rooms in facilities and members taking A.A. to patients (P-16, 2018). A partnership, a shared name, money in either direction, or anything that makes the group look like part of the facility is not.

6642fc24f9f1.t: The Tradition binds A.A. groups. It doesn't govern treatment centres, which are free to run as their owners decide.

89f4edcda67c.t: Tradition Six is the longest of the twelve (pp. 563–564). In order: - Money, property and authority "may easily divert us from our primary spiritual aim" (p. 563). - Property of real use to A.A. should be separately incorporated, "thus dividing the material from the spiritual" (p. 564). - "An A.A. group, as such, should never go into business." (p. 564). - Clubs and hospitals that need much property or administration should be incorporated "and so set apart that, if necessary, they can be freely discarded by the groups" (p. 564). "Hence such facilities ought not to use the A.A. name." (p. 564). Running them is "the sole responsibility of those people who financially support them" (p. 564). - "But hospitals, as well as other places of recuperation, ought to be well outside A.A.—and medically supervised." (p. 564). - Cooperation with anyone, but never "affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564). "An A.A. group can bind itself to no one." (p. 564).

5c28b35c37a6.t: Tradition Three's Long Form makes the same point from the other side: two or three alcoholics may call themselves an A.A. group "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation" (p. 563).

e771ab636a26.t: The short form keeps the core: "An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise" (p. 562). A treatment centre is a related facility.

c9f14640d7c5.t: Why: what A.A. tried in the 1940s

b1f302571222.t: Bill W.'s essays show the Tradition came from experience with exactly this kind of arrangement.

835c1a52791c.t: <0>Group-run drying-out places.</0> Some groups, short of affordable hospital beds, set up their own, hiring managers and nurses. Run by a group, it "has almost always backfired" (P-17, "Hospitals and A.A.", 1947), because it put the group into a business few A.A.s knew anything about. Groups that raised public money for "A.A. hospitals" fared no better. Places run by individual A.A.s under medical supervision did better, and the reason Bill gives is the Tradition in a sentence: "Not being a group project and not bearing the A.A. name, these ventures can be taken or left alone." (P-17, "Hospitals and A.A.", 1947).

ec8a10446598.t: <0>A.A. hospitals.</0> "Years ago we used to think A.A. should have its own hospitals, rest homes and farms." By 1946: "Nowadays we are equally convinced we should have nothing of the sort." (P-17, "Money", 1946). "Hospitalization is most definitely the job of the doctor" (P-17, "Money", 1946).

c04a9c01f468.t: <0>What cooperation looked like.</0> In the same essay: "Everywhere we cooperate with hospitals." (P-17, "Money", 1946). Hospitals gave A.A. special privileges and working arrangements; some consulted A.A.; some hired A.A. nurses and attendants. "But none of these institutions are known as 'A.A. hospitals.'" (P-17, "Money", 1946).

480caf1681c8.t: <0>Other causes, however good.</0> "As groups, we cannot endorse, finance or form an alliance with any other cause, however good" (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947). A.A. members may work in the alcohol field, including treatment, "if they act as individuals only, and are careful of the A.A. name" (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947). Bill's summary: "A.A. does not sponsor projects in other fields." (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947).

3593bae6a83c.t: In 1957 he was specific about treatment. Nor should an A.A. group ally itself, he wrote, "with any particular brand of medical or psychiatric treatment" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957). In the next breath: "We can cooperate with anyone." (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957).

1904158de0d1.t: Putting the Long Form and the essays together: - <0>Fine:</0> a group renting a room in a treatment facility; members carrying meetings into a facility; members working at a facility as individuals; giving staff information about A.A. - <1>Not fine for a group:</1> being run, funded or paid by a facility, or funding one; a facility using the group's A.A. name, or the group taking the facility's name; any joint program or "partnership" that would make the group look like part of the facility, even by implication ("actual or implied," p. 564).

902548bef341.t: A later pamphlet applies the same reasoning to group names: a group that meets in a treatment facility should call itself something quite different from the facility, so it's clear the group "simply rents space there for meetings" (P-16, 2018). It sums up the policy as "cooperation but not affiliation" (P-16, 2018).

4091945f319d.t: It doesn't judge treatment. The Long Form says hospitals and places of recuperation belong outside A.A. and under medical supervision; it doesn't say they're bad. Bill thought hospitalization was the doctor's job (P-17, "Money", 1946), and praised the A.A. members who managed such places well (P-17, "Hospitals and A.A.", 1947).

b975668bf971.t: And it doesn't bind the treatment centre. The Traditions govern A.A. groups and A.A. as a whole. A facility is responsible to the people who pay for it (p. 564), not to A.A.'s Traditions. The question the Tradition answers is what an A.A. group may tie itself to, and the answer is no one.

98e94caa4e98.t: P-17, <0>A.A. Tradition — How It Developed</0> ("Hospitals and A.A.," "Money," "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects"): <1>https://www.aa.org/aa-tradition-how-it-developed</1>

5d938d0db151.t: P-16, <0>The A.A. Group</0> ("Naming an A.A. Group"): <1>https://www.aa.org/sites/default/files/literature/p-16_0723.pdf</1>

f598cd43b478.t: Tradition Seven: does A.A. take outside money? | Recovery Starts

9a4d0b657fbf.t: The Long Form of Tradition Seven says A.A. groups ought to be fully supported by the voluntary contributions of their own members.

195dabc13e1b.t: Tradition Seven: does A.A. take outside money?

0274f933c229.t: It names what is dangerous or unwise: public fund-raising in A.A.'s name, large gifts from any source, any contribution that carries an obligation, and group treasuries that pile up money for no A.A. purpose.

1b6cd0b7d380.t: Bill W.'s 1946 essay "Money" shows A.A. did take outside help in its first years and was grateful for it. By 1946, he wrote, a strong feeling had spread among members that A.A. could and should pay its own way, and the trustees had resolved to decline gifts carrying any obligation.

1ca4202cc795.t: The Tradition is about A.A. groups and A.A. as a whole. It isn't a rule about members' own jobs or about the charities they support.

7c4c5f6e5932.t: The Seventh Tradition's Long Form says five things, in this order:

bb1ef3378e62.t: <0>Members pay.</0> The groups "ought to be fully supported by the voluntary contributions of their own members" (p. 564). In 1946 this was still a goal; the text says each group "should soon achieve this ideal" (p. 564).

a477784522ee.t: <0>No public appeals in A.A.'s name.</0> Public solicitation of funds using the A.A. name is "highly dangerous," whoever does it: groups, clubs, hospitals or outside agencies (p. 564).

3e028fbb4734.t: <0>No big gifts, and no strings.</0> Accepting "large gifts from any source," or contributions "carrying any obligation whatever," is unwise (p. 564). "Any source" includes members.

4d7f6cbc2046.t: <0>No hoarding.</0> It views "with much concern" group treasuries that keep accumulating money, beyond prudent reserves, for no stated A.A. purpose (p. 564).

c028a029cda5.t: <0>Why.</0> "Experience has often warned us that nothing can so surely destroy our spiritual heritage as futile disputes over property, money, and authority" (p. 564).

15e728c0abf9.t: The short form, "Every A.A. group ought to be fully self-supporting, declining outside contributions" (p. 562), condenses all of this into one line.

ab337a3ebbac.t: How it came about: Bill W.'s "Money" (1946)

7a2cf50a302d.t: <0>At first there was no money to argue about.</0> Members met in homes, and if one wanted to help another alcoholic financially, that was his own affair (P-17, p. 27). Bill accepts that this couldn't last: meeting places, clubs and offices cost money, so the real question was how to limit money so that it never topples the spiritual foundation (P-17, pp. 27–28).

8a631d0df6c0.t: <0>Members' contributions keep the services honest.</0> Contributions are never a condition of membership (P-17, p. 28). Because nobody is compelled to pay, A.A.'s offices "can never dictate" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 29): if they serve badly, members stop paying. That is why members' own voluntary contributions should be "eventually our sole support" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 32).

c2fa15809939.t: <0>A.A. did take outside help once, and says so.</0> There was a time "when we desperately needed a little outside aid" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 33). Friends' gifts made possible the Alcoholic Foundation, the book <1>Alcoholics Anonymous</1> and the General Office, and Bill writes that A.A. would never stop being grateful (P-17, p. 33).

ed0a1c4ee894.t: <0>Why that changed.</0> By 1946 A.A. had thousands of members earning a living, and a strong feeling spread that A.A. should support itself (P-17, p. 33). Let the public's money go to research, hospitals and education, which need it; "We can, and we should, pay our own way" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 34).

cda0b6d524f6.t: <0>What counts and what doesn't.</0> A nonalcoholic friend dropping a dollar in the hat is hardly an exception to self-support (P-17, p. 34). The concern is "the large contributions, especially those that may carry future obligations" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 34), and money left to A.A. in wills, public solicitation in A.A.'s name, and money from "wet" or "dry" sources, which would drag A.A. into the alcohol controversy (P-17, p. 34). Bill even questions a large gift from a wealthy member: might the group feel in his debt, and might he think he had bought his sobriety (P-17, p. 34)? His conclusion is that "acceptance of large donations from any source whatever is very questionable" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 34).

017cc2f198b3.t: <0>The trustees' decision.</0> Bill reports that the trustees of the Alcoholic Foundation had just resolved to turn down any gift carrying the slightest obligation and any earnings offered from a commercial source, including money from film companies interested in an A.A. film, because "A.A. has nothing to sell" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 35).

6d76cdc77aa1.t: What the text does not say

c4fe9de6cf15.t: The Long Form governs the A.A. groups and A.A.'s own services. It doesn't tell members not to earn a living, give to other causes, or work for organizations that do take outside money. Bill's concern throughout is A.A.'s name and A.A.'s treasuries.

c775aa071ff3.t: The Long Form says large gifts and gifts with obligations are "unwise" and public appeals are "highly dangerous" (p. 564). The flat wording "declining outside contributions" belongs to the short form (p. 562).

10a63e8ea4e0.t: <0>The Twelve Traditions Illustrated</0> (P-43, 1971, updated 2023) adds that A.A. limits how much a member may give each year or leave in a will, "so that none of us can buy influence in A.A." (P-43, 1971, "The Seventh Tradition"). That limit is later practice, not part of the 1946 text.

91ad2d9190ef.t: Tradition Eight: can anyone be paid for Twelfth Step work?

6b34c0400a05.t: No. The Long Form of Tradition Eight says A.A.'s usual Twelfth Step work, one alcoholic carrying the message to another, is never to be paid for (pp. 564–565). In the 1946 wording: "our usual A.A. Twelfth Step work is never to be paid for" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 9).

52ace99483ad.t: A.A. can pay people for other jobs: running an office, cooking, keeping a club, editing a magazine. The Long Form says such special services "may be well recompensed" (p. 564).

bcf64ac464b0.t: The Long Form defines professionalism as counseling alcoholics for fees. Bill W. wrote that members who go into that work as a career aren't excluded, but they must never present themselves as "A.A. therapists": "there is not, and can never be," such a thing (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 32).

6f90349822f0.t: It defines what that means: "We define professionalism as the occupation of counseling alcoholics for fees or hire" (p. 564).

1238609f38d9.t: A.A. may employ alcoholics to do work it would otherwise have to hire nonalcoholics for, and "Such special services may be well recompensed" (p. 564).

ae28374d1bf0.t: Its last sentence: our usual A.A. "12 Step" work is never to be paid for (pp. 564–565).

3be5dfd31867.t: The 1946 original, reprinted in P-17, reads "Twelfth Step work" where the Big Book has "'12 Step' work" (P-17, pp. 8–9); the meaning is the same.

d7bf8fc6fa7f.t: How Bill W. worked it out in "Money" (1946)

4934a5dd74cc.t: <0>Why members worried.</0> Clubs and offices were hiring paid workers, and members feared a paid class would grow inside A.A. Bill says the fear was understandable: in A.A. every member is a volunteer missionary in his own right, so there is no need for anyone to be paid for simple Twelfth Step work, "a purely spiritual undertaking" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 30).

1dead803d821.t: <0>The line he drew.</0> "A janitor can sweep the floor, a cook can boil the beef," a steward can remove a troublesome drunk, a secretary can run an office, an editor can put out a paper, and none of that professionalizes A.A. (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 30). If members didn't do these jobs, A.A. would have to hire nonalcoholics, and nobody expects a nonalcoholic to work full time for nothing (P-17, p. 30). If such a worker also does some Twelfth Step work along the way, that changes nothing. The principle: "we may pay well for special services — but never for straight Twelfth Step work" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 31).

628047068331.t: <0>What professionalizing would look like.</0> Bill gives his own example: a sign on an office door reading "Bill W. — Alcoholics Anonymous Therapist," with an hourly fee (P-17, p. 31). That would be treating alcoholics for money while trading on A.A.'s name, which he calls legal but "hardly ethical" (P-17, p. 31).

bd9cb7a7dc36.t: <0>Members who work in the field.</0> Bill doesn't condemn therapists, and doesn't bar members from the work. Trained social workers, psychologists and psychiatrists who are A.A. members shouldn't "feel excluded" (P-17, p. 31). What they must not do is advertise themselves as A.A. therapists or use their A.A. connection publicly; like a tennis player turning pro, they drop their amateur standing (P-17, p. 31). He goes on: members offered jobs as nurses, doctors, social workers, educators or personnel officers can take them, as long as they avoid "A.A. therapy" and anything that would hurt A.A. as a whole (P-17, pp. 32–33).

d3feaa136bce.t: His summary, point (f): A.A. must avoid professionalization at all costs; "simple Twelfth Step work is never to be paid for" (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 32); members in alcohol therapy must never trade on their A.A. connection; and there can never be an "A.A. therapist." Point (g): members may be employed by A.A. full time if they have real duties beyond Twelfth Step work (P-17, p. 32).

18297b4ebc95.t: In "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects," Bill applies the same idea to members who work in hospitals, research or alcohol education. They may, as long as they remember "first and last they are A.A.s" and that in that work "they are individuals only" (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947, p. 25): no A.A. name in the press, and no leaning on A.A. in appeals for money or publicity (P-17, p. 25).

75423bdd6b81.t: It settles the main question: nobody is paid for carrying the message to another alcoholic. It also settles that A.A. may pay for office and service work, and that a member's outside career in the alcohol field isn't forbidden, so long as A.A.'s name stays out of it.

d5f86505e0c8.t: The 1946–47 texts don't take up pay for sponsorship, chairing meetings or speaking at them (the 1946 membership essay mentions a sponsor only once, as someone early groups wanted to vouch for a newcomer). They speak of "Twelfth Step work," which in the Big Book means carrying the message to alcoholics (pp. 89–103). See <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0>

5857bf70dbca.t: Nobody runs A.A. in the sense of governing it. The Long Form of Tradition Nine says each group needs "the least possible organization" and that A.A.'s…

9e9746e60834.t: Tradition Nine: is A.A. organized? Who runs it?

e5d9e76a8ad1.t: Nobody runs A.A. in the sense of governing it. The Long Form of Tradition Nine says each group needs "the least possible organization" and that A.A.'s leaders "derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern" (p. 565).

fea535e52f9c.t: A.A. does have some organization: a group secretary or rotating committee, an intergroup committee in a city, and the trustees and General Service Office in New York. The Long Form describes them all as servants of the groups.

fb291dab5ccf.t: Bill W. wrote in 1947 that no human authority in A.A. can make a group do anything, and that when he tried to run A.A. himself, it didn't work.

a2081b185585.t: The Ninth Tradition's Long Form walks through A.A.'s structure from the bottom up:

6222966647f0.t: <0>The group.</0> Each group "needs the least possible organization," and rotating leadership is best (p. 565). A small group may elect a secretary; a large one, a rotating committee (p. 565).

32ac1a9f5c6b.t: <0>The city.</0> The groups of a large metropolitan area may elect a central or intergroup committee, which often employs a full-time secretary (p. 565).

52739545861b.t: <0>New York.</0> The trustees "are, in effect, our A.A. General Service Committee" (p. 565). They look after the A.A. Tradition, receive the voluntary contributions that pay for the General Service Office, handle overall public relations because the groups have authorized them to, and guarantee the integrity of the Grapevine (p. 565).

1da151711899.t: <0>What all of them are.</0> Every such representative is to be guided by the spirit of service, "for true leaders in A.A. are but trusted and experienced servants of the whole" (p. 565). They have no real authority from their titles, "they do not govern," and "Universal respect is the key to their usefulness" (p. 565).

d0797bf90ca2.t: Two notes on wording. The Big Book prints "the trustees of the General Service Board"; the 1946 original said "The Alcoholic Foundation," which was renamed in 1954 (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 7). And the Long Form doesn't say A.A. "ought never be organized." That phrase is the short form's (p. 562). The Long Form says <0>the least possible</0> organization, and then names the organization A.A. has.

136edeec8f66.t: Bill W., "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?" (1947)

4a3588281d2b.t: <0>His answer.</0> "The answer to this question is almost surely" no, and he says experience has settled it (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 37).

509517ff35e0.t: <0>Why.</0> Alcoholics could rarely govern themselves, and families, doctors, clergy and judges had failed to govern them by force (P-17, p. 37). But alcoholics can be led and inspired, so the only real authority in A.A. is spiritual principle: "It is never personal authority" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 37). He lists what A.A. lacks: no fees, no dues, no rules, no demand that anyone conform, "no one set in personal authority over anyone else" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 37).

181089843f2f.t: <0>Why groups follow the Traditions anyway.</0> Members follow the Steps by choice, because they prefer recovery to death: "We conform because we want to" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38). Groups follow the Twelve Points of Tradition for the same reason: they see they would fall apart if they didn't (P-17, p. 38).

0f1d8574117d.t: <0>No one can compel a group.</0> There is no constituted "human authority that can compel an A.A. group to do anything" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38). An elected leader can guide by example or persuasion but can never boss, or he is passed over at the next election (P-17, p. 38). Rotating committees "have only the authorization to serve, never to command" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38); each carries out what it thinks its group wants. Committees that tried to discipline members or police their morals achieved nothing lasting, except perhaps getting a new committee elected (P-17, p. 38).

a7c49dbc4f2c.t: <0>Bill's own attempt.</0> He tried to govern A.A. himself, and each time "I have been shouted down" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 39). Personal power always failed, and he concluded that in A.A. "one can be a servant only" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 39).

200b1dca171c.t: <0>The center is a center of service.</0> The General Office supplies information and literature, helps new groups when asked, looks after public relations and sometimes mediates (P-17, p. 39). The Grapevine's editors see themselves as a mirror of A.A., unable to rule or propagandize, and the trustees are "caretakers only" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 39). Even at the center there are only custodians, editors and secretaries, none with authority to govern A.A. (P-17, p. 39). So long as A.A. avoids piling up wealth or personal government at these centers, he writes, it can't go astray (P-17, pp. 39–40).

0d0cd80f9e25.t: It settles that no person, committee, office or board in A.A. has authority over a group or a member. It doesn't say A.A. has no structure: the Long Form names the structure and explains whom it answers to. For how a group's own decisions are reached, see <0>Is group conscience a majority vote?</0> and <1>Tradition Two: does anyone have authority in A.A.?</1>

c1b49c21d97c.t: Were the Traditions written with the Steps? | Recovery Starts

181f98ffbe11.t: No. The Twelve Steps were published in the Big Book in 1939. The Twelve Traditions were first printed seven years later, in 1946, in the A.A. Grapevine.

f58d5d45ad40.t: Were the Traditions written with the Steps?

74e7408e0710.t: The short form most people know today was cut down from that 1946 "long form" around 1947–1950, and A.A.'s first International Convention, at Cleveland in July 1950, confirmed it.

6a35ba2f2474.t: The Traditions answer different questions from the Steps. The Steps are how one alcoholic recovered; the Traditions are how A.A. groups and A.A. as a whole learned to survive.

35dbf6b3934d.t: The dates, from the books themselves

00d4e2612482.t: <0>1939: the Steps.</0> The Twelve Steps are in Chapter 5, "How It Works" (pp. 59–60), part of the first edition, whose first printing was in 1939 (p. xiii). The 1939 book has no Traditions. The nearest thing is a few lines in the Foreword to the First Edition: no fees or dues, "The only requirement for membership is an honest desire to stop drinking," no alliance with any sect, and a request that members stay anonymous in the press (pp. xiii–xiv).

c7e85cb26d67.t: <0>1946: the Long Form.</0> The Big Book's own appendix calls the short form "a condensed version of the original 'long form' A.A. Traditions as first printed in 1946" (p. 561). Bill W. dates it to "the Grapevine of May, 1946" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957), with more Grapevine pieces explaining each point over the following months. Those essays, from 1946 and 1947, are reprinted in the pamphlet P-17.

2bddc13d6515.t: <0>About 1947–1950: the short form.</0> Bill credits Earl T., founder of the Chicago group, with the idea of cutting the Long Form down to statements as short as the Steps. Earl came to him with it "One day in 1947, or thereabouts" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). After months of refining, the Grapevine printed the new wording in every issue.

e5770aad7d3a.t: <0>1950: confirmed at Cleveland.</0> The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) says the principles "had become so widely accepted by 1950 that they were confirmed by our first International Conference held at Cleveland" (p. xix). Bill puts it in July 1950 and records the Convention's "unanimous voice of consent" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957).

b80ce8908ce0.t: So the Steps came first by seven years, and the Traditions in their familiar form came about eleven years after the Steps.

1db840a306fc.t: The Traditions grew out of problems that didn't exist in 1939. When the Big Book came out, A.A. was "more than one hundred men and women" (p. xiii). By the close of 1941 it was about 8,000 (p. xviii). Then came what the Second Edition foreword calls a "fearsome and exciting adolescent period" (p. xviii), with quarrels over membership, leadership and money (pp. xviii–xix). The Traditions were the lessons drawn from those years (see <0>Why were the Twelve Traditions written?</0>).

1959cab54724.t: Bill described the order in which things happened: "Nobody invented Alcoholics Anonymous. It grew." (P-17, Foreword, 1955). Lessons were adopted "first as policy and then as tradition" (P-17, Foreword, 1955).

384bc00345ac.t: Bill himself compared them. In the foreword to P-17 he wrote that many members already felt "we ought to apply them as seriously to our group life as we do the Twelve Recovery Steps" (P-17, Foreword, 1955) to each member's own life. He added: "Of this, it will take time to tell." In 1947 he wrote that groups follow the Traditions "for the very same reason that the individual A.A. follows the Twelve Steps to recovery" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). By 1957 he could write that, a few years after 1946, the Traditions were seen to be as necessary to the society as the Steps were to each member, and "the key to the unity, the functioning, and even the survival" of A.A. (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957). At first, though, many members found them a bore.

2209aea089f6.t: A later pamphlet (P-43, 1971) makes the same point about how both were made: "Like the Steps, the Traditions were not figured out in advance" (P-43, 1971).

45dde51cde1b.t: <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, Chapter 5 (the Steps) and Foreword to the First Edition

2710cda256b8.t: text 1946; in the Big Book from 1955

0754fa21f2a4.t: Are the Traditions just formalities? | Recovery Starts

7ae97059b5b8.t: No. The Big Book introduces the Traditions as A.A.'s best answers to two life-or-death questions: how A.A. can best function, and how it can stay whole…

720c5027a6b0.t: No. The Big Book introduces the Traditions as A.A.'s best answers to two life-or-death questions: how A.A. can best function, and how it can stay whole and survive (p. 561). Without unity, it says, "most of us will finally die alone" (p. 561).

c25e5b54f865.t: The Traditions record things that had already gone wrong: membership rules that would have kept out nine-tenths of the early members, groups that went into the hospital business, fights over money and clubs, members who used A.A.'s name for their own causes.

ef19db76990a.t: They aren't rules either. In 1955 the Big Book said none of them had "the force of rules or laws" (p. xix), and Bill W. warned that if A.A. hardened them, "the letter might crush that spirit." Groups follow them by choice, for the same reason members follow the Steps.

65d7380e2f17.t: What the Big Book says they are for (Appendix I)

af166bc7f372.t: Appendix I opens by saying what's at stake. A.A. has made "the difference between misery and sobriety, and often the difference between life and death" for its members, and could mean as much to alcoholics not yet reached (p. 561). So no society ever had a more urgent need for lasting unity: "We alcoholics see that we must work together and hang together, else most of us will finally die alone" (p. 561). The Traditions are "the best answers that our experience has yet given" to how A.A. can best function and stay whole (p. 561).

b4c1e5b5f425.t: The Long Form starts from the same place. Each member is a small part of a great whole, and "A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die" (p. 563). Its Seventh Tradition gives the reason behind several of the others: "Experience has often warned us that nothing can so surely destroy our spiritual heritage as futile disputes over property, money, and authority" (p. 564).

d55b2fb17edd.t: Where they came from: experience, not theory

c7d6ae05cdb0.t: Bill W.'s essays from 1946–47 show the Traditions growing out of trouble:

1b48d93077b9.t: <0>Membership.</0> When the office collected the groups' membership rules, Bill found that if all of them had been enforced, "it would have been practically impossible for any alcoholic" to join; about nine-tenths of the oldest members would never have got in (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946, p. 11).

c4d634e57be1.t: <0>Hospitals and business.</0> Groups that ran their own drying-out places found it put them into business, and it almost always backfired (P-17, p. 15).

4dcd288f408e.t: <0>Clubs.</0> New York's first club tangled the groups, the club and the area's money for years (P-17, pp. 19–20).

47b8a4bedc67.t: <0>Money.</0> Bill saw "the great ordeal of its own prosperity and success" as A.A.'s supreme test (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 35).

e9f3a9a7e1c7.t: <0>Authority.</0> Every time Bill tried to govern A.A. himself, he was "shouted down" (P-17, p. 39).

ed20c5add5ff.t: The Big Book's 1955 foreword sums it up: as A.A. grew, it faced the very problems feared, over money, power and splits, "in every group" (p. xix). Out of that came the conviction that A.A. had to unify or die (p. xix).

58b712c885de.t: How seriously Bill meant them (P-17 foreword, 1955)

93832f3d945d.t: Unity doesn't look after itself. Like personal recovery, A.A. would always have to work at it, with honesty, humility and "above all — vigilance" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5). Bill asks every member to be as aware of what endangers A.A. as of his own defects, "For whole movements have, before now, gone on benders, too!" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5).

be29fe994b7a.t: He calls the Twelve Points "our first attempt to state sound principles of group conduct and public relations" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5), and reports that many members felt "we ought to apply them as seriously to our group life as we do the Twelve Recovery Steps" to themselves (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5).

db472bb01e34.t: In the same foreword Bill warns against the opposite mistake. "Nobody invented Alcoholics Anonymous. It grew" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5). Experience became policy, then tradition, and he hoped that process would never stop. "Should we ever harden too much, the letter might crush that spirit" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5). A.A. could victimize itself "by petty rules and prohibitions" or ask alcoholics to accept rigid ideas or stay away (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5). "Yet the lessons of our experience count for a great deal" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 5).

637cf80e4373.t: In 1947 he explained why groups keep them without anyone enforcing them. Members follow the Steps from choice because they prefer recovery to death; groups follow the Traditions "for the very same reason," because they see "they would disintegrate if they didn't" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38).

23e533da2d22.t: The Big Book's 1955 foreword adds that though none of the principles had the force of rules or laws, they were so widely accepted by 1950 that A.A.'s first International Conference, held at Cleveland, confirmed them (p. xix).

b97b3fffb9ed.t: The Traditions aren't decoration and aren't red tape. They're A.A.'s record of how groups nearly destroyed themselves, written down so newer groups don't have to learn it the same way. They also aren't laws: nobody can enforce them, and Bill feared what would happen if anyone tried. A group that reads only the one-line short forms misses most of that history. The Long Form and Bill's essays keep the reasons attached. See <0>What is the Long Form, and why read it instead of the short form?</0>

ead76e3f5296.t: Where are the Traditions in the Big Book?

14a3ef4b1686.t: The Twelve Traditions are in Appendix I at the back of the Big Book, "The A.A. Tradition," pages 561–566 in the fourth edition.

a977b2e6cb1f.t: Page 561 introduces them, page 562 gives the short form, and pages 563–566 give the original "long form."

6b7216521812.t: They aren't in the first 164 pages, because they didn't exist yet when the book came out in 1939. They were first printed in 1946.

85fd600ac8ee.t: <0>Page 561: the introduction.</0> Appendix I begins by saying why the Traditions matter and what they are: the best answers experience has given to "How can A.A. best function?" and "How can A.A. best stay whole and so survive?" (p. 561). It then explains that the next page has the short form, "the form in general use today" (p. 561), and that the original long form is reproduced too, because it "is more explicit and of possible historic value" (p. 561).

5bab17af9640.t: <0>Page 562: the short form.</0> All twelve Traditions in their short wording (p. 562), the version the appendix calls "the form in general use today" (p. 561).

dce945612170.t: <0>Pages 563–566: the Long Form.</0> The original wording, headed "Our A.A. experience has taught us that:" (p. 563). Where each one is:

17104d67e387.t: The first five are short enough to fit together on page 563. Six is the longest and runs onto page 564.

a756e350a92e.t: The main text of the Big Book, Chapters 1 to 11, comes from the first edition of 1939, when A.A. was "more than one hundred men and women" (p. xiii). The Traditions grew out of the problems of the 1940s and were first printed in 1946 (p. 561). They were added to the book later. The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) summarizes them and points the reader to where they're "stated in full" in the back of the book (p. xix).

050fe4513c0f.t: What the 1939 text does have is the seed of a few of them, in the Foreword to the First Edition: no fees or dues, "an honest desire to stop drinking" as the only requirement for membership, no alliance with any sect, and anonymity in the press (pp. xiii–xiv).

c5b45987db1a.t: The Long Form also appears, in its original 1946 wording, at the front of the pamphlet P-17, <0>A.A. Tradition — How It Developed</0>, as Bill W.'s "Twelve Points to Assure Our Future" (P-17, Foreword, 1955), with the short form printed under each one. The two copies differ in small ways; see <1>What is the Long Form?</1>

7b82a02119dc.t: The Long Form is the original wording of the Twelve Traditions, first printed in the A.A. Grapevine in 1946. The short form, which the Big Book calls "the…

e072e25311b7.t: What is the Long Form of the Traditions, and why read it instead of the short form?

ef6fc7452de7.t: The Long Form is the original wording of the Twelve Traditions, first printed in the A.A. Grapevine in 1946. The short form, which the Big Book calls "the form in general use today" (p. 561), is a condensed version made from it a few years later.

ad9f6bc39199.t: The Big Book prints both, in Appendix I: the short form on page 562 and the Long Form on pages 563–566. It says the Long Form is "more explicit" (p. 561).

16b6251326fc.t: The short form drops a great deal: who a group may refuse (no one), what counts as a group, how clubs and hospitals must be set apart from the groups (hospitals "well outside A.A."), what professionalism means, and more. Reading only the short form, you miss much of what the Traditions actually say.

5ff028bf1188.t: Appendix I calls the short form "a condensed version of the original 'long form' A.A. Traditions as first printed in 1946" (p. 561). Bill W. published those original twelve points as "Twelve Points to Assure Our Future" (P-17, Foreword, 1955), and explained them in a series of Grapevine essays in 1946 and 1947, now reprinted in the pamphlet P-17.

ff28ae36c9d9.t: The short form came later. Bill says the idea of cutting the Long Form down to the length of the Steps came from Earl T. of Chicago "in 1947, or thereabouts" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957). The Traditions were confirmed at Cleveland in 1950 (p. xix), and Bill says they had already been cut down to the short form by then (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957).

15351357bda3.t: P-17's introduction says plainly what happened to the wording. "In all but the Second Tradition" (P-17, introduction), it says, the original language was changed or shortened.

e76bb97749fe.t: What the short form leaves out

d80b38d79862.t: Laid side by side, the Long Form says much more. Some of the biggest differences:

165f56c09020.t: <0>One.</0> The short form says the common welfare comes first. The Long Form says why (each member is "but a small part of a great whole," and A.A. must live or most of us will die) and adds a line the short form drops: "But individual welfare follows close afterward" (p. 563).

c64114af7fa6.t: <0>Three.</0> The short form gives the one requirement for membership. The Long Form says A.A. should include all who suffer from alcoholism, "Hence we may refuse none who wish to recover" (p. 563), that membership should never depend on "money or conformity" (p. 563), and that any two or three alcoholics gathered for sobriety may call themselves a group, "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation" (p. 563). The definition of an A.A. group, and its ban on outside affiliation, are only in the Long Form.

a4149bb8b053.t: <0>Four.</0> The short form says groups are autonomous except where others are affected. The Long Form spells out the exceptions: consult neighbouring groups when your plans affect them, and confer with the trustees before any action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole (p. 563).

9e1e75d404aa.t: <0>Six.</0> The short form is one sentence about endorsing, financing or lending the A.A. name. The Long Form is a full paragraph: property should be separately incorporated, "thus dividing the material from the spiritual" (p. 564); a group "should never go into business" (p. 564); clubs and hospitals should be set apart so the groups can drop them; hospitals belong "well outside A.A.—and medically supervised" (p. 564); and a group "can bind itself to no one" (p. 564).

c20a9ccd2db2.t: <0>Seven.</0> The Long Form warns against public fundraising in A.A.'s name, large gifts, gifts with strings, and treasuries that pile up money "for no stated A.A. purpose" (p. 564).

7e8964defd53.t: <0>Eight.</0> Only the Long Form defines professionalism: "the occupation of counseling alcoholics for fees or hire" (p. 564).

4c086cd2c2ee.t: <0>Nine.</0> The Long Form describes rotating leadership and says leaders "derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern" (p. 565). The short form moved "they do not govern" into Tradition Two.

b8e4bfba955d.t: <0>Ten.</0> The Long Form names the outside issues: "politics, alcohol reform, or sectarian religion" (p. 565), and says the groups "oppose no one" (p. 565).

fcdfb053be05.t: <0>Eleven.</0> Only the Long Form says: "There is never need to praise ourselves" (p. 565).

d8e9a5d22a78.t: <0>Twelve.</0> The Long Form says anonymity means practising "a genuine humility" (p. 566).

b096d48a1507.t: Two, the one Tradition P-17 says kept its original language, is the same sentence in both forms; the short form adds the "trusted servants" line from Nine (pp. 562–563).

c49d3f8a7b0d.t: Two printings of the Long Form

e11ed5a7c7a3.t: The Long Form in the Big Book and the one in P-17 are almost word for word the same, with small updates. In P-17, Tradition Four tells groups to confer with "the trustees of The Alcoholic Foundation" (P-17, Foreword, 1955), with a footnote that the Foundation was renamed the General Service Board in 1954. The Big Book's printing says "the trustees of the General Service Board" (p. 563). P-17's Tradition Three reads "all who suffer alcoholism," where the Big Book has "all who suffer from alcoholism" (p. 563). Neither change alters the meaning, but it's worth knowing that the Big Book copy has been brought up to date.

fa47c5f198ee.t: A short summary is easy to quote and easy to bend. "Each group should be autonomous" can be made to sound as if a group can do anything, until you read the Long Form's limits. "An A.A. group ought never endorse..." can sound like a narrow rule about logos, until you read a paragraph that keeps hospitals outside A.A. altogether. The Long Form is the fuller statement, and the Big Book reprints it for that reason.

ca6e614e3d44.t: Are the Traditions rules? Who do they apply to: groups or members? | Recovery Starts

306620541081.t: They aren't rules in the sense of laws someone can enforce. The Big Book says "none of these principles had the force of rules or laws" (p. xix), and no…

8b6a86b46308.t: Are the Traditions rules? Who do they apply to: groups or members?

c7931a6b541c.t: They aren't rules in the sense of laws someone can enforce. The Big Book says "none of these principles had the force of rules or laws" (p. xix), and no one in A.A. has the power to make a group obey them.

031d3d25b113.t: They aren't mild either. The Long Form says "never" in plain words: a group should "never go into business" (p. 564), and ordinary A.A. Twelfth Step work is never to be paid for (pp. 564–565). Groups keep them because experience showed what happens when they don't.

25a86b042eab.t: Most of the Traditions speak to A.A. groups and to A.A. as a whole. But several also speak to members when they act as A.A. members or could implicate A.A.: in public, in the press, and when money is involved.

a751f059c723.t: They govern A.A. They don't govern anyone outside it.

b918bb758803.t: Not rules: what the books say

34527dd983a5.t: The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) says it directly: "Though none of these principles had the force of rules or laws, they had become so widely accepted by 1950 that they were confirmed" at Cleveland (p. xix).

2cc10561b0d4.t: Introducing the original Twelve Points, Bill W. called them "these suggestions" (P-17, Foreword, 1955) for a tradition of relations, and asked whether they could grow into traditions held "by his own deep conviction and by the common consent of his fellows" (P-17, Foreword, 1955). Looking back in 1957, he wrote that a code of traditions "could not, of course, ever become rule or law" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957), but could guide the trustees, the New York office, and "especially" groups with growing pains.

e560e5ffbb9a.t: Bill's 1947 essay on authority explains why there's no one to enforce them. Nowhere in A.A., he wrote, is there any human authority that "can compel an A.A. group to do anything" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). Groups follow the Traditions for the same reason members follow the Steps: "Groups see they would disintegrate if they didn't" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947).

f8b23e7b3786.t: He also warned against turning them into a rulebook: "We could victimize ourselves by petty rules and prohibitions" (P-17, Foreword, 1955).

f238b80c0cdc.t: The Long Form opens "Our A.A. experience has taught us that:" (p. 563). Its language is "ought" and "should," and in places "never": - "An A.A. group, as such, should never go into business" (p. 564). - Cooperation with outsiders "ought never go so far as affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564). - "Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional" (p. 564).

f9f58d6e8a4c.t: Bill's essays explain each "never" with what went wrong when groups tried otherwise (see <0>Why were the Twelve Traditions written?</0>). So the honest answer is: unenforced, but firm.

84ad9e4b3266.t: <0>Groups and A.A. as a whole, mainly.</0> Appendix I says they answer "How can A.A. best function?" and "How can A.A. best stay whole and so survive?" (p. 561). The Long Form keeps addressing "each A.A. group" (pp. 563–565). Tradition Two is "For our group purpose" (p. 563). Tradition Four is about each group's own affairs (p. 563). Five, Six and Seven are about what a group is for, what it may get involved in, and how it pays its way (pp. 563–564). Nine is about how groups and their service boards are organized (p. 565).

18116ec450cf.t: <0>Members too, where A.A. is involved.</0> The Long Form doesn't leave the individual out: - One starts with the member: "Each member of Alcoholics Anonymous is but a small part of a great whole" (p. 563). - Eight says counseling alcoholics for fees is professionalism, and that ordinary Twelfth Step work is never to be paid for (pp. 564–565). That's work members do. - Ten: "No A.A. group or member should ever, in such a way as to implicate A.A., express any opinion on outside controversial issues" (p. 565). - Eleven: "Our names and pictures as A.A. members ought not be broadcast, filmed, or publicly printed" (p. 565).

0ab864ccf538.t: The line the texts draw is where A.A. is involved. Bill's 1947 essay on outside projects says members are free to work in other fields "if they act as individuals only, and are careful of the A.A. name" (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947). In 1957 he wrote that the Traditions "ask for personal as well as group sacrifice" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957), including never to use the A.A. name for personal power, distinction or money.

9ed31337c198.t: So "the Steps are for members, the Traditions are for groups" is only half right. The Traditions are about A.A.'s unity, and a member acting as an A.A., or speaking publicly as one, is inside that.

e94f2e17cd19.t: Nothing in the Long Form governs people or organizations outside A.A. It tells A.A. groups to keep outside enterprises at a distance, and says the management of clubs and hospitals "should be the sole responsibility of those people who financially support them" (p. 564). The Long Form does say public fundraising in A.A.'s name is "highly dangerous" even when done by "other outside agencies" (p. 564), but that is A.A. stating its concern, not a rule anyone outside can be held to. A hospital, a treatment centre or an independent website isn't bound by A.A.'s Traditions; an A.A. group's relationship with it is.

e4067c6c181e.t: A later pamphlet says the same thing about rules and members: "the Traditions are not rules — and they are not just for officers" (P-43, 1971). The A.A. group pamphlet (P-16, 2018) quotes the 1962 Twelve Concepts: "no penalties to be inflicted for nonconformity to A.A. principles" (P-16, 2018).

a66cafe3df53.t: Why were the Twelve Traditions written? | Recovery Starts

7f562cd6ef12.t: The Traditions were written to keep A.A. alive and in one piece. The Big Book says they answer two questions: "How can A.A. best function?" and "How can…

ff1947d8675e.t: The Traditions were written to keep A.A. alive and in one piece. The Big Book says they answer two questions: "How can A.A. best function?" and "How can A.A. best stay whole and so survive?" (p. 561).

b796c75274ba.t: They came out of real trouble in the 1940s, as A.A. grew from about a hundred members to many thousands: fights over membership, leadership, money, property and publicity.

95a93f2bd080.t: Bill W. put the lessons into words and published them in the A.A. Grapevine in 1946. He said he hadn't invented them; the groups had learned them the hard way.

beba78bf1612.t: The reason given is survival, for the members as much as for A.A.: "A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die" (p. 563).

43320aa29801.t: Appendix I, "The A.A. Tradition," opens by saying A.A. has made the difference between misery and sobriety, often between life and death, for those in it, and could do the same for alcoholics not yet reached (p. 561). So no society ever had "a more urgent need for continuous effectiveness and permanent unity" (p. 561). Alcoholics have to "work together and hang together" or most will "die alone" (p. 561).

8cd82af321be.t: The Long Form itself opens with the words "Our A.A. experience has taught us that:" (p. 563). Each Tradition is stated as something experience taught, not as a plan worked out in advance.

41ec0de53c88.t: The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) tells the same story in brief. After the publicity of 1939–1941, A.A. entered an "adolescent period" (p. xviii). Could thousands of alcoholics meet and work together? Would there be quarrels over membership, leadership and money, or splits that broke A.A. apart (pp. xviii–xix)? The answer that grew out of it was that "A.A.'s had to hang together or die separately" (p. xix). Just as the Steps were principles an alcoholic could live by, the groups and A.A. as a whole needed principles to "survive and function effectively" (p. xix).

f5aa23f6b222.t: What Bill W. said when he wrote them (1946–1947)

77db99f2779f.t: Bill's introduction to the original "Twelve Points to Assure Our Future" is printed in the pamphlet P-17. "Almost any A.A. can tell you what our group problems are," he wrote (P-17, Foreword, 1955). They were about the member's relation to his group, the group's relation to A.A. as a whole, and A.A.'s place in the world outside, and above all about leadership, money and authority. He asked whether A.A. had enough experience yet to state principles "which could grow into vital traditions" (P-17, Foreword, 1955), and offered the Twelve Points as his attempt. (The pamphlet dates its whole foreword 1955, though this part introduces the 1946 Points, so we date it 1955.)

c453b0385487.t: His 1946–47 Grapevine essays fill in the troubles behind each point: - <0>Membership.</0> Groups had written so many membership rules that, if all had been enforced at once, almost no alcoholic could have joined (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). - <1>Money and property.</1> Groups that set up their own drying-out places, or raised money from the public in A.A.'s name, ran into trouble, and disputes over money threatened what A.A. was for (P-17, "Money", 1946; "Hospitals and A.A.", 1947). - <2>Outside causes.</2> Members wanted A.A. to put its name behind education, research and reform (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947). - <3>Authority.</3> Committees and old-timers, Bill included, tried to run things and failed (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947).

a66ba66e5edf.t: He also said why groups would keep them without anyone enforcing them: "Groups see they would disintegrate if they didn't" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947).

c727d0299a52.t: How they were put on paper (1957 account)

847ddafb0299.t: In <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957), Bill gives the history. Letters about group problems poured into the New York office, and "The basic ideas for the Twelve Traditions of Alcoholics Anonymous came directly out of this vast correspondence" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957). In late 1945 a friend suggested turning that experience into a set of principles. Bill adds that such a code "could not, of course, ever become rule or law" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957), but might guide the trustees, the office, and groups with growing pains. The Long Form appeared in "the Grapevine of May, 1946" (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957).

0b6872f8b814.t: He is clear that he only wrote down what the groups had already learned. The first lessons came as early as 1937, when the New York group talked him out of becoming a paid therapist at Towns Hospital. He says three "embryo principles" rang in his mind from it, the first being "The common welfare must come first" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957); the others were that A.A. can't have a class of professional therapists and that God, speaking in the group conscience, is the final authority.

c907865e7641.t: None of these sources says the Traditions were written to govern an individual member's private life or recovery. That job belongs to the Steps. The Traditions are about how A.A. groups, and members acting as A.A., relate to each other and to the world (see <0>Are the Traditions rules? Who do they apply to?</0>).

ceeb0a379b70.t: Does the Big Book endorse treatment centres? | Recovery Starts

a81e694108df.t: No. The words "treatment center" and "rehab" never appear in the Big Book's program text. They turn up only in some fourth-edition personal stories, as…

acd7fcd44f99.t: Does the Big Book endorse treatment centres?

23c114cac451.t: No. The words "treatment center" and "rehab" never appear in the Big Book's program text. They turn up only in some fourth-edition personal stories, as part of what those writers went through. One writer who was told to go didn't.

660039e8fb4d.t: The 1939 text does favor medical help in its place. It favors hospitalization for a drinker who is "very jittery or befogged" (p. xxvi). It calls physical treatment "desirable, even imperative" for someone just off a spree, but only "a small part of the picture" (p. 143). It speaks warmly of a hospital and a doctor who cooperated with A.A. (p. 162).

12b94d222264.t: What the book says actually recovers the alcoholic is not the medical care itself but a spiritual change and working with other alcoholics (pp. xxix, 89, 143), though for many early members that began inside a hospital's walls (p. 162).

4b92e6163231.t: The Traditions keep A.A. and hospitals apart. Hospitals and "other places of recuperation" are to be "well outside A.A.," and cooperation must never go so far as "affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564).

37fc903d4415.t: In the first 164 pages, the forewords and the appendices, "treatment" means a doctor's or hospital's care of a drinker. It never means a program that replaces A.A. "Treatment center" and "rehab" don't appear there at all. They appear only in personal stories in Parts II and III, which reflect the membership at the time of the fourth edition (2001). Some examples: - One writer was sent to a treatment center, and it "introduced me to the Big Book" (p. 498). - Another writes: "I didn't have anything against treatment centers then, nor do I now" (p. 315). - Another, asked to enter a treatment center, writes: "I did not go to a rehab" (p. 425). - Another remarks that when their father drank "they didn't have treatment centers" (p. 513).

5c7df84ab317.t: These are personal experiences, told "in his own language and from his own point of view" (p. 29). They don't make the program text say anything about treatment centres.

b3be64419925.t: What the 1939 text says about medical help

4ca11bf6a0a0.t: The Big Book isn't against doctors or hospitals. It was introduced by one, Dr. Silkworth, who ran a hospital for alcoholics (pp. xxv–xxvii). Bill W. got sober in a hospital, where "Treatment seemed wise, for I showed signs of delirium tremens" (p. 13). The text: - <0>Favors hospitalization</0> for the drinker who is very jittery or befogged, so his mind is clear before he is approached (p. xxvi). - <1>Uses doctors and hospitals to find drinkers.</1> A member can find drinkers who want to recover by asking "doctors, ministers, priests or hospitals" (p. 89). "Approach through a doctor or an institution is a better bet" than through his family (p. 91). "If your man needs hospitalization, he should have it" (p. 91). - <2>Treats physical treatment as a first step.</2> In "To Employers," for a man still drinking or just off a spree, "a certain amount of physical treatment is desirable, even imperative" (p. 143). "In competent hands, this seldom takes long nor is it very expensive" (p. 143). - <3>Thanks a hospital.</3> Chapter 11 describes "a well-known hospital for the treatment of alcoholic and drug addiction" in the East, whose doctor suggests A.A. to patients able to recover on a spiritual basis. "Many of us, former patients, go there to help" (p. 162).

7ef5a15f4691.t: What it says treatment can't do

56a0ce1d4225.t: The same pages are blunt about the limits: - "Physical treatment is but a small part of the picture." The man "must undergo a change of heart" (p. 143). - Dr. Silkworth: the craving "has never been, by any treatment with which we are familiar, permanently eradicated" (p. xxx), and doctors "have made little impression upon the problem as a whole" (p. xxix). Recovery takes "an entire psychic change" (p. xxix). - The book's own early members had tried "health farms and sanitariums" and voluntary commitment to asylums without success (p. 31). One man "floundered from one sanitarium to another" (p. 26). - The way out it offers is the Steps and Chapter 7's work. Practical experience shows, it says, that "nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (p. 89).

8550bf2ca25f.t: The Long Form of the Traditions (written 1946, printed in the Big Book from 1955) answers the question for A.A. itself: - Tradition Six: clubs and hospitals are "secondary aids" that should be incorporated separately and not use the A.A. name, and "hospitals, as well as other places of recuperation, ought to be well outside A.A.—and medically supervised" (p. 564). "While an A.A. group may cooperate with anyone, such cooperation ought never go so far as affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564). - The short form: an A.A. group "ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise" (p. 562). - Tradition Eight: "We define professionalism as the occupation of counseling alcoholics for fees or hire" (p. 564), and A.A.'s Twelfth Step work is never to be paid for (pp. 564–565).

ad23dd081c1d.t: The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) sums up the stance: A.A. doesn't "take any particular medical point of view, though we cooperate widely with the men of medicine" (p. xx), and "Upon therapy for the alcoholic himself, we surely have no monopoly" (p. xxi).

d449d557f44a.t: The Big Book doesn't endorse treatment centres. The 1939 text speaks warmly of one hospital that treated alcoholics and cooperated with A.A. (p. 162), but as a place where members went to help and found God, not as a substitute for the program; and the Traditions written after it tell A.A. groups never to endorse or affiliate with any such facility (pp. 562, 564). What the book does endorse is short, practical medical care to clear the drinker's head, followed by the spiritual program and one alcoholic working with another. It never treats a hospital stay as the recovery itself.
