9fbe0d35bd42.t: Is "turn it over" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

798ff1ceb8b3.t: Not as a saying in the program. The words "turn it over" don't appear in the 1939 program text, pages 1 to 164. What the program text has is Step Three:…

50c326a188eb.t: Is "turn it over" in the Big Book?

8d6c0bd6291d.t: Not as a saying in the program. The words "turn it over" don't appear in the 1939 program text, pages 1 to 164. What the program text has is Step Three: "Made a decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him." (p. 59).

a1ea9d9b18cd.t: The phrase itself is in a personal story, a man's prayer in 1938, his first in thirty years: "Please let me turn it over to you." (p. 251), and in <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980).

4a8b36d27b3b.t: In the program text, what is turned over is the whole will and life, and the book explains it at length (pp. 60–63): quit playing God, take Him as Director, then act. It also speaks of placing a particular outcome or problem "in God's hands" (pp. 80, 120); in the clearest case, the man hands the outcome to God and still makes his amend (p. 80).

27d49fed9961.t: All our sources were searched for "turn it over," "turned it over," "turn everything over," "turn(ed) ... over" and "God's hands," with page breaks joined.

1020e77a8a91.t: <0>Program text, forewords, appendices:</0> no "turn it over." "Turn ... over" appears only in Step Three and its explanation (pp. 59, 60). "In God's hands" appears at pp. 80, 100, 120 and 124.

8b32d77f5a0f.t: <0>Personal stories (fourth edition, 2001):</0> "The Man Who Mastered Fear" (Part I) has the writer, just out of the hospital and shut in his room at Dr. Bob's house "in a strange city" in September 1938, gripped by fear, pray, "God, for eighteen years I have been unable to handle this problem. Please let me turn it over to you." (p. 251). "Physician, Heal Thyself!" (Part II) describes the alcoholic's rage at being told he must "turn the whole business over to someone else" (p. 306).

8033d9260c5c.t: <0>Stories printed in 1939 and later dropped</0> (<1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1>, 2003): not as a phrase. "The Back-Slider" gets results by placing his life "in God's hands every day" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003).

e2aabe3b265f.t: <0><1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980):</0> writing about the 1939 split between the Akron and Cleveland members, the book guesses, "Perhaps Dr. Bob just turned it over." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), and quotes words attributed to him then: "There's no use worrying about these things." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). That is the 1980 book's suggestion, not Dr. Bob's own phrase.

b7f997278919.t: What Step Three turns over, and how the book explains it (pp. 59–64)

4d6fb1336107.t: Step Three is the decision "to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him" (p. 59). The book doesn't leave it there: "Just what do we mean by that, and just what do we do?" (p. 60).

6fb608562c08.t: <0>Why.</0> "The first requirement is that we be convinced that any life run on self-will can hardly be a success." (p. 60). The self-willed man is like an actor trying to run the whole show (pp. 60–61), and selfishness is "the root of our troubles" (p. 62).

57a7524914e9.t: <0>What changes.</0> "First of all, we had to quit playing God." (p. 62). "Next, we decided that hereafter in this drama of life, God was going to be our Director." (p. 62). With that, "We had a new Employer." (p. 63).

84adfe84103c.t: <0>The words.</0> The Third Step prayer: "God, I offer myself to Thee—to build with me and to do with me as Thou wilt." (p. 63). See: <1>What is the Third Step prayer, and where is it?</1>

4df3e2b32a52.t: <0>What comes next.</0> "This was only a beginning" (p. 63). "Next we launched out on a course of vigorous action" (p. 63), the inventory, because the decision "could have little permanent effect unless at once followed by a strenuous effort" to face and be rid of what blocked us (p. 64).

24612aeedb61.t: Bill describes doing the same in the hospital: "I placed myself unreservedly under His care and direction." (p. 13), and "I must turn in all things to the Father of Light who presides over us all." (p. 14).

b41cad624ef2.t: Placing a problem in God's hands

be52e35a5bec.t: The program text does also speak of handing over particular troubles, which is how "turn it over" is often used: - A man facing an amend that could ruin him "saw that he had to place the outcome in God's hands or he would soon start drinking again" (p. 80). He then made the amend, publicly (p. 80). - To a wife whose husband has drunk again: "If a repetition is to be prevented, place the problem, along with everything else, in God's hands." (p. 120). - "When we look back, we realize that the things which came to us when we put ourselves in God's hands were better than anything we could have planned." (p. 100). - Through the day, Step Eleven has us pause "when agitated or doubtful" and ask for the right thought or action, saying "Thy will be done" (pp. 87–88).

b6c629c76e51.t: Handing the outcome to God doesn't replace action in these pages: the man at p. 80 still makes his amend, and after Step Three's surrender the inventory still gets written (pp. 63–64). The wife at p. 120 is in the same passage told to cheer her husband up and not to try to shield him from temptation (p. 120).

eefcefc69ca2.t: It's the name members came to use for going to see an alcoholic who needs help, to carry the message to him. It's the work Chapter 7, "Working With…

6553a88cfd64.t: It's the name members came to use for going to see an alcoholic who needs help, to carry the message to him. It's the work Chapter 7, "Working With Others," describes (pp. 89–103).

79410da9e5ac.t: The phrase itself isn't in the Big Book's program (pages 1–164). Chapter 7 just calls it a visit: "your first visit" (p. 94), "your second visit" (p. 96).

73065d4a40e7.t: "Twelfth Step call" appears only in the personal stories. The earliest dated use in our sources are Bill W.'s 1946 Grapevine essay on money, which calls it "simple Twelfth Step work" and says it is never paid for.

97ae3cf8290b.t: Searching the whole fourth edition: the program chapters never say "Twelfth Step call." Chapter 7 names the work only as "our twelfth suggestion: Carry this message to other alcoholics!" (p. 89).

cab93f0236f1.t: The phrase turns up in the personal stories, written or revised later. In <0>The Vicious Cycle</0> the writer, sober since 1938, mentions a call he made in June 1945 (p. 230). <1>Jim's Story</1> says other groups taught his group "a great deal about Twelfth Step work" (p. 245). It appears again in stories in Parts II and III (pp. 303, 345, 429, 469, 521).

bd2ccbab8e4d.t: Two early non-story sources use the idea: - Tradition Eight in its 1946 Long Form says A.A. should stay nonprofessional and that ordinary "12 Step" work is never to be paid for (pp. 564–565). - Bill W.'s Grapevine essay "Money" (1946) calls it "simple Twelfth Step work — a purely spiritual undertaking" (P-17), and says we may pay for special services, "but never for straight Twelfth Step work" (P-17).

c6186d7dbc7c.t: What the visit is, in the Big Book

6b1a7ea4d9d3.t: Chapter 7 gives the whole procedure (see <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0> for a walk through it). In short: - Find a drinker who wants to stop, through a doctor, minister or hospital (p. 89), and learn about him from his family first (p. 90). - See him when the binge is over, or at least in a lucid interval, and see him alone (pp. 90–91). - Tell him about your own drinking until he starts talking about his. Describe the illness. Tell him how you recovered when he asks (pp. 91–93). - "On your first visit tell him about the Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous" (p. 94). Leave him free, under no obligation (p. 94). - If he's interested, a second visit follows (p. 96).

71ee8724b01d.t: Chapter 11 shows one in action: two men visiting a stranger in a hospital bed for an hour, telling him about their own drinking until he says, "That's me. That's me. I drink like that" (p. 157).

a826f6c5c34e.t: The Big Book never defines the phrase, because it never uses it in the program. Any rules or customs now attached to the phrase come from later practice, not from the book. Chapter 7 itself says the person you visit may still be drinking and may never have heard of A.A. (pp. 89–90).

5969c92c26f1.t: Where are the Twelve Steps in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

6e2cdc9902b8.t: The Twelve Steps are printed in Chapter 5, "How It Works," on pages 59 and 60 of the Big Book. Steps 1 to 11 are on page 59; Step 12 runs onto page 60.

e3bb2873d5df.t: Where are the Twelve Steps in the Big Book?

1b0516bda940.t: The Twelve Steps are printed in Chapter 5, "How It Works," on pages 59 and 60 of the Big Book. Steps 1 to 11 are on page 59; Step 12 runs onto page 60.

55896d0f4861.t: Chapter 5 opens on page 58 by saying the writers have rarely "seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path" (p. 58). The often-heard line "Rarely is a man constituted…" isn't in the book.

a46af400e1ff.t: The list is only the summary. The book explains how the Steps are taken across Chapters 5, 6 and 7 (pp. 58–103), and Chapters 1 to 4 lay the ground for the first two.

38bc08fed034.t: The page the Steps are on

346ee6006192.t: Chapter 5 starts on page 58. A few paragraphs in, after "Half measures availed us nothing" (p. 59), the book introduces the list with the words "Here are the steps we took, which are suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59). Steps 1 to 11 follow on page 59, and Step 12 finishes on page 60.

2f83197be1dd.t: The book itself refers back to this page as the place to find them. After the Fifth Step, the reader is told to take the book down and turn "to the page which contains the twelve steps" (p. 75).

1a7ce29f0411.t: The list on pages 59–60 is followed by the chapters that say how each Step was done:

d2880ac51c65.t: The chapters before: "There Is a Solution," "More About Alcoholism," "We Agnostics." Page 60 says those chapters and the stories make clear "That we were alcoholic and could not manage our own lives" (p. 60), and that God could help.

036c658c0c18.t: Chapter 5, the decision and the prayer that goes with it

fb39eb6d6731.t: Chapter 7, "Working With Others." Chapter 6 ends by saying the next chapter "is entirely devoted to Step Twelve" (p. 88).

6e9e1b21ba22.t: Chapter 5's first sentence is the one quoted above, about people who have "thoroughly followed our path" (p. 58). A search of the whole text in our sources finds no "Rarely is a man constituted." The page goes on to say that those who don't recover are usually people "constitutionally incapable of being honest with themselves" (p. 58), which is probably where the misquote's "constituted" comes from.

35f0454c05a0.t: The twelve were not the first form of the program. One of the early stories in the back of the book, "He Sold Himself Short," describes Akron before the Big Book was written, when Dr. Bob took a newcomer through "the Six-Step program as it was at that time" (p. 263). That is a later retelling of the early days, so it's a pointer, not a history; see <0>How long did the first members take to work the Steps?</0>

6087a4445145.t: What does "carry this message" mean — which message? | Recovery Starts

b30ae32a116a.t: Step Twelve doesn't spell the message out (p. 60). The book shows what it is by what it tells you to say.

0a9906aa4766.t: What does "carry this message" mean — which message?

5da91e3105fd.t: Step Twelve doesn't spell the message out (p. 60). The book shows what it is by what it tells you to say.

288813338c18.t: Chapter 2 calls it a solution: alcoholics have found "a common solution" (p. 17) to a problem nothing else had solved, through spiritual experiences that changed their lives (p. 25).

2bff43f71673.t: Chapter 7 gives the content: your own drinking story, alcoholism as a fatal illness and how hopeless it is alone, and then, when he asks, exactly how you recovered, stressing the spiritual side, and the program of action (pp. 91–94). "You may talk to him about the hopelessness of alcoholism because you offer a solution" (p. 92).

27e17d5e88d7.t: The 1939 Foreword says the book's main purpose is "To show other alcoholics precisely how we have recovered" (p. xiii).

af9165e168c2.t: "Having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps, we tried to carry this message to alcoholics" (p. 60). The word "this" points back to what comes before it in the sentence: a spiritual awakening that came from doing the Steps. That is a reading of the sentence, not something the book says outright. The book never gives a one-line definition of "the message." It does show it, in two places.

9cd6e2b1a7fd.t: Chapter 2, "There Is a Solution" (pp. 17–29), opens with people "who were once just as hopeless" and have recovered (p. 17). They have "discovered a common solution" (p. 17). "This is the great news this book carries to those who suffer from alcoholism" (p. 17).

db2108cb6baa.t: The chapter then lays out both halves of the message: - <0>The problem.</0> The real alcoholic has "lost the power of choice in drink" (p. 24) and is without defense against the first drink (p. 24). - <1>The solution.</1> "There is a solution" (p. 25). The members have had "deep and effective spiritual experiences" which changed their whole attitude toward life (p. 25), described more fully in Appendix II.

c3355a41f405.t: It also says who carries it best: an ex-problem drinker who knows the facts about himself, with no "Holier Than Thou" attitude, no fees, "no axes to grind," nothing but a wish to help (p. 18). And it asks the question the rest of the book answers: "How then shall we present that which has been so freely given us?" (p. 19).

7c83ddcc93af.t: Chapter 7 turns that into a conversation, in an order (pp. 91–94): 1. Your drinking: enough of your own story that he starts telling his (p. 91). 2. The illness: how baffled you were, the mental twist before the first drink, alcoholism as "an illness, a fatal malady" (p. 92). Let him decide for himself whether he's alcoholic (p. 92). 3. The hope: you can talk about how hopeless it is "because you offer a solution" (p. 92). 4. How you got well, only when he asks: "Tell him exactly what happened to you. Stress the spiritual feature freely" (p. 93). He doesn't have to agree with your idea of God (p. 93). 5. What you did: "Outline the program of action" (p. 94), how you took stock of yourself, straightened out your past, and why you're now trying to help him (p. 94). 6. The fellowship: on the first visit tell him about A.A. (p. 94).

0ab439bf76fb.t: What the message is not: a lecture (p. 91), pressure (p. 94), or religious instruction. "Let him see that you are not there to instruct him in religion" (p. 93).

e88b3d0de489.t: Chapter 11 adds a condition on the messenger: "obviously you cannot transmit something you haven't got" (Ch. 11, p. 164). The message is your own experience of recovery, not a set of ideas about it.

8472d6e84ef4.t: Who has the final say in A.A.? | Recovery Starts

240ce92dd201.t: No person. The earliest answer is Tradition Two (1946): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself…

11b3662a1a1f.t: Who has the final say in A.A.?

e74fab49070b.t: No person. The earliest answer is Tradition Two (1946): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience" (p. 563). In its own affairs, the Long Form says, each group answers to "no other authority than its own conscience" (p. 563).

6df823039353.t: For A.A.'s world services (the General Service Office, literature, the Grapevine, public information), Bill W.'s Concept I (1962) puts final responsibility and ultimate authority in "the collective conscience of our whole Fellowship" (p. 574): the groups. They took it over from the founders at St. Louis in 1955.

2c3be47baea4.t: In practice the groups delegate. The General Service Conference has the final decision on large matters of policy and finance, the trustees hold the legal power, and Bill says the Conference's practical power will nearly always win.

767860c57b2c.t: A few things are kept back for the groups themselves: no Tradition, and none of the Conference's Warranties, can be changed without the written consent of three-quarters of the groups that respond.

fef9d90ce282.t: The earliest text: Tradition Two and Four (1946)

2eceb87d7fcb.t: The Long Form of Tradition Two is one sentence: the one ultimate authority for a group's purpose is "a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience" (p. 563). The short form adds a line moved from Nine: "Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not govern" (p. 562). The Long Form of Nine says the same of every A.A. representative: "They derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern" (p. 565).

a3865a40510b.t: Long Form Four sets the limits. "With respect to its own affairs, each A.A. group should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience" (p. 563). When its plans affect neighbouring groups, they should be consulted, and no group, committee or individual should take action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole "without conferring with the trustees of the General Service Board" (p. 563); in 1946 they were the trustees of the Alcoholic Foundation, renamed in 1954. Conferring is not obeying: the text asks for consultation, and gives no one the power to overrule a group.

d9e9e8a5779d.t: Bill's 1947 essay on government sums up the early view: "the only real authority to be found in A.A. is that of spiritual principle" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947). He adds that he had tried to govern A.A. himself and been shouted down each time.

6c5585d8aa4f.t: The Concepts deal with a narrower question: who has the last word over A.A.'s shared services. Concept I's answer is the groups. Bill writes that "The A.A. groups today hold ultimate responsibility and final authority for our world services" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I), and that "The groups assumed that responsibility at the St. Louis International Convention of 1955" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I).

5a6d9cdd72fe.t: Before that, the trustees (then the Alcoholic Foundation, from 1938) held the money, but policy questions went to Bill and Dr. Bob. When Dr. Bob's fatal illness became known in 1948, the risk was plain: "For the first time it was seen that only a representative conference could take the place of Dr. Bob and me" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). The Conference met experimentally from 1951; in 1955 the groups confirmed it permanently.

1cf53616b6a2.t: Bill grounds this in Tradition Two. He says its main principles are "crystal clear: the A.A. groups are to be the final authority; their leaders are to be entrusted with delegated responsibilities only" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I).

f1b8e149faee.t: Who actually decides, day to day

9626a9b96da7.t: Bill is clear that ultimate authority alone gets nothing done. The groups delegate:

34f4d85417f3.t: <0>To the Conference.</0> Concept II: since 1955 the Conference has been "the active voice and the effective conscience of our whole Society in its world affairs" (p. 574), except for any change in the Traditions or in Article 12 of its Charter. "The final say — the ultimate sanction in matters of large importance — has not been given to the Trustees alone" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept II). Concept VI: the Conference "traditionally has the final decision respecting large matters of general policy and finance" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VI).

0198f306f2a4.t: <0>To the trustees.</0> The trustees take the active lead (Concept VI) and are the only body with legal power (Concept VII). Even so, Bill writes, "Theoretically, the Conference is an advisory body only, but practically speaking it has all of the ultimate rights and powers that it may ever need" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept VII), because the delegates represent the groups and could withhold the groups' money. The trustees keep a legal veto, which Bill expected to be used seldom.

bf0300ddd7a2.t: <0>To delegates' own judgment.</0> The groups have the right to instruct their delegates; Bill writes that "If they insist, they can give directives to their Delegates on any and all A.A. matters" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III). He thinks it unwise to carry it far, because a delegate who can't vote his conscience "is not a ‘trusted servant’ at all; he is just a messenger" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III).

4ba99810da69.t: The Conference Charter (1955) gives the working rule: a two-thirds vote of the Conference, with a quorum, is "considered binding upon the General Service Board" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955).

170248628eff.t: What only the groups can change

33c95b900f95.t: The 1955 St. Louis resolution, which made the Conference the successor to the founders, keeps two things back: neither the Twelve Traditions nor the Warranties of Article 12 can be changed by the Conference without the written consent of "at least three-quarters of all those registered groups who respond to such proposal" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix L). The Steps were added to that list later.

b9f6ea5d0b92.t: Tradition Two names God, as expressed in group conscience, as the one ultimate authority. Concept I's short form speaks only of "collective conscience" (p. 574). Bill's essay quotes Tradition Two in full and treats the two as one idea; it doesn't discuss what happens if they were thought to differ.

d6d8fba01f7b.t: Bill admits the term is hard to pin down: "Perhaps many of us are still vague about the ‘group conscience’ of Alcoholics Anonymous, about what it really is" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). His essay describes it in terms of members' responsibility and love of the principles, not as a procedure.

4d0eacdfa407.t: Concept I is about world services. It doesn't give the Conference or anyone else a say over how a group runs its own meetings; for that, the Long Form of Four (1946) is the text.

3d8f033333b5.t: Who do I tell my Fifth Step to? | Recovery Starts

8d78e4494111.t: The Big Book leaves the choice to you, and gives a list: a clergyman, a close-mouthed and understanding friend, your doctor or psychologist, or a family…

6ba41b2a8a65.t: Who do I tell my Fifth Step to?

eff1af3523d2.t: The Big Book leaves the choice to you, and gives a list: a clergyman, a close-mouthed and understanding friend, your doctor or psychologist, or a family member, with care not to hurt them (p. 74).

72964cf7031f.t: It doesn't say it has to be a sponsor, or an A.A. member at all. The word "sponsor" doesn't appear in the chapter.

0b2d0d9127c2.t: Chapter 7 tells the member carrying the message to offer to hear a newcomer's story, but "do not insist upon it if he prefers to consult someone else" (p. 96).

657d8ca898cd.t: What matters is that the person can keep a confidence, understands what you're doing, and won't try to change your plan (pp. 74–75).

f2669b4b2477.t: Step 5 reads: "Admitted to God, to ourselves, and to another human being the exact nature of our wrongs." (p. 59) Chapter 6, "Into Action," explains it on pages 72 to 75.

30e70c982981.t: The book says admitting things only to ourselves isn't enough: "we usually find a solitary self-appraisal insufficient" (p. 72). Its first reason is blunt: "If we skip this vital step, we may not overcome drinking" (p. 72). Newcomers who kept certain facts to themselves nearly always got drunk, because they never finished their housecleaning (pp. 72–73). "We must be entirely honest with somebody" (p. 73), the book says, if we expect to live long or happily (pp. 73–74).

c6260bf344ed.t: The book says to think well before choosing "the person or persons" (p. 74). Its suggestions, in its own order: 1. <0>Clergy.</0> Those whose religion requires confession will go to the proper authority. Those with no religious connection may still do well to talk with someone ordained, who is often quick to understand (p. 74). 2. <1>A friend.</1> If not clergy, "we search our acquaintance for a close-mouthed, understanding friend" (p. 74). 3. <2>A doctor or psychologist</2> (p. 74). 4. <3>Family, with a limit.</3> It may be a family member, but we can't tell our wives or parents anything that will hurt them. "We have no right to save our own skin at another person's expense" (p. 74). Those parts go to someone who will understand "yet be unaffected" (p. 74).

eb8e94fddd87.t: What the person needs to be: able to keep a confidence, fully understanding and approving what we're doing, and not trying to change our plan (pp. 74–75). We explain what we're about to do and why; most people asked this way "will be honored by our confidence" (p. 75).

961e512bf549.t: If no suitable person is available, the Step may be put off, but only if we're ready to do it at the first chance, and never as "a mere excuse to postpone" (pp. 74–75).

adfbe521cb58.t: Chapter 7 shows a member offering. When a man has read the book and wants to go through with the Steps, the member who visited him lets him know he's available "if he wishes to make a decision and tell his story" (p. 96), the Third and Fifth Steps. But it's an offer, and the man is free to go to someone else (p. 96).

58abf18091bf.t: An early story in the back of the book, "He Sold Himself Short," describes Akron in 1937, before the Big Book was written, when Dr. Bob took a newcomer through a six-step program that included "Confession" (p. 263). So in that story an A.A. member heard it. But the program as written in Chapter 6 doesn't require that, and its list doesn't mention A.A. members at all.

8840809c6d4f.t: Who was Dr. Bob? | Recovery Starts

5d5f0b5a04ac.t: Dr. Bob was Robert Holbrook Smith (1879–1950), an Akron, Ohio surgeon and one of A.A.'s two co-founders.

94de66ccf2cb.t: Dr. Bob was Robert Holbrook Smith (1879–1950), an Akron, Ohio surgeon and one of A.A.'s two co-founders.

549ec5763f8b.t: He drank heavily for most of his adult life. After meeting Bill W. in 1935 he took his last drink on June 10, 1935, the date A.A. counts as its beginning.

c52bef8c3307.t: From then until his death in 1950 he worked with alcoholics in Akron, more than 5,000 of them by A.A.'s count, many in the alcoholic ward at St. Thomas Hospital with Sister Ignatia, and he never charged them for his medical care.

e721db296867.t: His own words about why he did it are plain and practical, and they're in the Big Book as the first personal story, "Doctor Bob's Nightmare."

991cfc13266b.t: "Doctor Bob's Nightmare" opens the personal stories in the Big Book. He wrote it when he was "nearly four years" sober (p. 180). It names no places, but tells the whole arc:

c53853d22d2a.t: <0>Childhood.</0> An only child in a small New England village, made to go to church so often that he resolved never to go again once he was free, and kept that resolution for forty years (pp. 171–172). He thought being an only child "perhaps engendered the selfishness" that helped bring on his alcoholism (p. 172).

3fc4e4f5fbaf.t: <0>College and medical school.</0> Heavy drinking from college on (p. 172). In medical school he left once, came back, and later handed in blank exam books because his hand shook too much to hold a pencil; he had to stay dry for two more quarters to graduate (pp. 173–174).

9a17ac73e0cd.t: <0>Practice.</0> After an internship he opened an office, and drank to ease his stomach trouble; he checked himself into sanitariums at least a dozen times (p. 174). Through Prohibition and after, he spent about seventeen years in a cycle of drinking at night and sedatives in the morning so he could work (pp. 175–177). "It was really a horrible nightmare" (p. 177).

16f4a9856673.t: <0>The spiritual search that didn't work.</0> For two and a half years before meeting Bill he studied the spiritual ideas of a group he had met, read everything, and still got drunk every night (p. 178).

a4fcbf1d2d0d.t: <0>The meeting.</0> A man who knew alcoholism from his own experience "talked my language" (p. 180). His last drink was June 10, 1935 (p. 180).

ac78d32cdeaf.t: He gives four reasons he spends so much time passing it on: a sense of duty, pleasure, paying his debt to the man who passed it to him, and "a little more insurance for myself against a possible slip" (p. 181). He also admits his craving for liquor stayed with him for the first two and a half years (p. 181).

dfae26e2d362.t: The book's introduction to the story calls him a co-founder and says the Society's birth "dates from his first day of permanent sobriety, June 10, 1935" (p. 171). It says that to 1950, the year he died, he carried the message to more than 5,000 alcoholics and gave all of them his medical services "without thought of charge" (p. 171).

6033a3853ef6.t: A.A.'s pamphlet <0>The Co-Founders of Alcoholics Anonymous</0> (P-53, © 2017) gives the biographical outline (P-53): - Born August 8, 1879, in St. Johnsbury, Vermont, the only son of Judge and Mrs. W. P. Smith. - St. Johnsbury Academy (1898), Dartmouth College (graduated 1902), then the University of Michigan and further training at Rush in Chicago; medical degree 1910. - Internship at City Hospital, Akron; opened his own office in Akron in 1912 and practised there until he retired in 1948. - Married Anne Ripley in 1915. - In the early 1930s he went to Oxford Group meetings looking for an answer, and kept drinking. - Met Bill W. in May 1935; worked with Sister Ignatia at St. Thomas Hospital, Akron. - Died of cancer at City Hospital, Akron, on November 16, 1950.

68431bbfcaef.t: P-53 names three things he held in high regard: simplicity, tolerance of other people's ideas, and the belief that one's job in A.A. was to "get sober and stay sober" and "never to be so complacent that we're not willing to extend that help to our less fortunate brothers" (P-53). It adds that he believed "love and service" are the cornerstones of A.A. (P-53). In his last major talk (Detroit, 1948, printed in P-53) he says Bill had learned the value of service in New York, and the kind of service that counts is "giving of yourself" (P-53). He also says the Twelve Steps weren't written until 1938, that he didn't write them, and that in the early days the members leaned on the Bible, the Four Absolutes and daily meetings (P-53).

bb1eeb9675ca.t: <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) has Bill's description of the man he met: fifty-five, a Vermonter, a gifted surgeon whose drinking had cost him most of his practice and nearly his home (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill calls him the friend he was "never to have a hard word" with (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

bf9a4e582581.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) is a full biography, written after the 1977 General Service Conference approved the project (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). It is a later book that leans heavily on the memories of people who knew him, and it is careful about that: one oldtimer says people often repeat things Dr. Bob said "that I know he didn't" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

344aa24b1a19.t: <0>Dartmouth.</0> P-53 (© 2017) and <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) say he graduated from Dartmouth in 1902 (P-53). Bill's 1957 account says he "busted out of Dartmouth College" because of his drinking (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Dr. Bob's own 1939 story says he graduated, "but not in the eyes of the Dean" (p. 172).

66184418a629.t: <0>The internship.</0> P-53 and the 1980 biography put it at City Hospital, Akron (P-53). Bill's 1957 account says his medical school and internship were "in Chicago" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Dr. Bob's 1939 story says only "a western city" (p. 174).

a4770382d8b1.t: Who wrote the Big Book's chapters, including "To Wives"? | Recovery Starts

6e85f6dd1840.t: The Big Book names no author. It presents itself as the work of "more than one hundred men and women" (p. xiii), and "The Doctor's Opinion" is by Dr.…

4536155c84de.t: Who wrote the Big Book's chapters, including "To Wives"?

6c3607a23b85.t: The Big Book names no author. It presents itself as the work of "more than one hundred men and women" (p. xiii), and "The Doctor's Opinion" is by Dr. William D. Silkworth (p. xi).

1622830618b4.t: The later histories agree that Bill W. drafted the main chapters in 1938, reading them to the New York group, which argued over them hard, and sending them to Dr. Bob in Akron for comment. Bill himself said he was "much more of an umpire than I ever was an author" (P-44).

57098f33e2e8.t: "To Wives" is written in the voice of the wives of A.A. members (p. 104), but the 1980 and 1984 histories both say Bill wrote it. Lois W. said she offered and was told no.

4b09788b8798.t: <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) says Bill wrote at least ten of the opening chapters and that "To Employers" may have been written by Hank P. No other source in our sources say so, and none names a different author for any other main chapter.

ae2a7fe97a98.t: What the Big Book itself says

cec04beaa69c.t: The book signs itself only as Alcoholics Anonymous (p. xiv). The Foreword to the First Edition speaks for "more than one hundred men and women who have recovered" (p. xiii), and the last chapter addresses a reader who may never meet "you who write this book" (p. 164).

46d555250c62.t: Two chapters say who is speaking: - <0>"To Wives."</0> The chapter says the members want "the wives of Alcoholics Anonymous to address the wives of men who drink too much" (p. 104), and it goes on in the wives' voice: "As wives of Alcoholics Anonymous, we would like you to feel that we understand" (p. 104). A footnote added later says it was "Written in 1939, when there were few women in A.A." (p. 104). - <1>"To Employers."</1> The chapter opens by introducing one member who had spent much of his life in big business and had hired and fired hundreds of men, then hands over to him: "But let him tell you:" (p. 136). The rest is in his first person.

c8328213893c.t: <0>"The Doctor's Opinion"</0> is Dr. Silkworth's, kept intact "just as it was originally written in 1939" (p. xi). See <1>What is "The Doctor's Opinion," and who wrote it?</1>

4d23c8838920.t: The book doesn't say who drafted the other chapters. For that our sources have only accounts written later.

6be84ca3a43d.t: Bill's own accounts (P-44, around 1955; <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957)

8ec5e1a14282.t: <0>P-44.</0> Bill says he dictated the chapters to Ruth Hock, the nonalcoholic secretary, while the New York and Akron groups argued over the drafts "for months on end" (P-44). "I became much more of an umpire than I ever was an author." (P-44). Members in Akron, New York and "a couple in Cleveland" wrote their stories, 28 in all (P-44).

0916363e39d3.t: <0>A.A. Comes of Age (1957).</0> Bill says he began the book in March or April 1938, and by the time the 1938 money-raising campaign got under way had finished his own story and roughed out the second chapter (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He dictated rough drafts in Henry P.'s office in Newark, working from "a hastily drawn-up list of possible chapter headings" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), read each chapter to the New York group, and sent copies to Dr. Bob in Akron "for checking and criticism" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Before Chapter 5 he had written his own story and "There Is a Solution," "More About Alcoholism" and "We Agnostics" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). When the New York arguments over God and religion threatened to stall the work, "I finally asked that I might be the final judge of what the book said" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

afb26d426bbe.t: Others shaped the text. A psychiatrist, Dr. Howard, read the prepublication copy and said it was too full of "you" and "must"; Bill argued weakly, then gave in and changed it throughout to a "we ought" basis (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The compromise wording in the Steps, "God as we understood Him," came out of the New York arguments, and Bill says, "Who first suggested the actual compromise words I do not know" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

441f66d1b96c.t: <0>The stories.</0> In Akron a former newspaperman, Jim S., interviewed the members with long sobriety and wrote most of their stories; "Dr. Bob wrote his own" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The New Yorkers wrote their own, and Bill and Henry edited them over the writers' protests (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Looking back, Bill wrote that the book "was everybody's book and that I had been mostly the umpire of the discussions that had created it" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

27cf2b63a28a.t: Neither of Bill's own accounts in our sources say who wrote "To Wives." The two later histories do: - <0><1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980)</0> quotes a June 1938 letter in which Bill suggested that Dr. Bob's wife, Anne, write the chapter: "Anne should do the one portraying the wife" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). She didn't; the book guesses her modesty was the reason. Lois, Bill's wife, wasn't asked, and when she suggested it Bill said it "should be in the same style as the book" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). "Bill himself wrote the chapter that came to be called 'To Wives,'" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Lois is quoted: "I've always been hurt by it" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). - <2><3>Pass It On</3> (1984)</2> says "there is no doubt about the authorship of 'To Wives.'" (Pass It On, 1984) and quotes Lois: "Bill wrote it, and I was mad." (Pass It On, 1984). She asked whether he wanted her to write it, and he said it should be in the same style as the rest of the book (Pass It On, 1984).

078f6e8b5a5a.t: So the chapter is written as the wives speaking, and both later histories say Bill wrote it. Our sources have nothing from 1939 that says either way.

ae669c26da88.t: <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) is the only source in our sources that takes up the question chapter by chapter: "Bill wrote at least ten of the opening chapters of the book; there is some reason to believe that 'To Employers' may have been written by Hank." (Pass It On, 1984). Hank P. was Bill's partner in Works Publishing, the company that published the book (P-44); Bill's 1957 book calls him Henry P. <1>Pass It On</1> doesn't say what the reason is, and none of the other sources mentions it.

79ac01237e38.t: The same book says that although Bill was "the nominal author of the fifth chapter, he was in fact serving as spokesman for all the others" (Pass It On, 1984), and that final editing was done by Tom Uzzell of New York University, who cut the manuscript by at least a third (Pass It On, 1984). Ruth Hock is quoted saying the two were about equally responsible: without Bill the book wouldn't have been written, and "it wouldn't have been published without Hank" (Pass It On, 1984). See <0>How was the Big Book paid for and published (Works Publishing)?</0>

73ad838caa66.t: <0>When Bill started.</0> Bill (1957) says March or April 1938 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); the 1980 book says the book "was begun in May 1938" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

993b10bc7a2b.t: <0>How many stories, from where.</0> Bill (around 1955) says 28 in all (P-44). Bill (1957) says the Akronites produced eighteen, two of them from Clevelanders, and New York ten (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) says 16 from Akron and 12 from New York, besides Bill's and Dr. Bob's (Pass It On, 1984).

9ccf8aa1eb6e.t: <0>Marie B.</0> The one story by a wife: Bill (1957) calls her "the wife of an Akron alcoholic" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); the 1980 book calls her the wife of "a member from Cleveland" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

4c125c805b11.t: <0>"To Employers."</0> Only the 1984 book raises Hank P., and only as "some reason to believe" (Pass It On, 1984). Our sources don't settle it.

7debedb21b86.t: <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, <2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2> and <3>Pass It On</3> are sold by A.A. World Services: <4>https://onlineliterature.aa.org</4>

bf77c9812916.t: Why is A.A. anonymous? | Recovery Starts

72d9a46838e7.t: In 1939 the reason was practical. The first hundred members said they were too few to handle the flood of personal appeals the book might bring, and most…

200cfb148588.t: In 1939 the reason was practical. The first hundred members said they were too few to handle the flood of personal appeals the book might bring, and most of them had jobs to keep (p. xiii).

9ce1e2a9288f.t: By 1946 Bill W. gave four reasons: anonymity makes it safe for alcoholics and their families to ask for help; it keeps any "founder" or leader from becoming a public face who could get drunk and disgrace A.A.; it wins the trust of reporters; and the public respects a society that seeks no credit.

ebdaf26dda1b.t: Underneath those, the Long Form names a spiritual reason: anonymity keeps principles ahead of personalities and teaches humility (p. 566). In 1955 Bill called it A.A.'s protection against its own members' hunger for fame, power and money, starting with his own.

93fe5b2618a5.t: Before the book was published in 1939, the fellowship had no name (P-17, p. 41). The members debated about two hundred titles and narrowed them to "The Way Out" or "Alcoholics Anonymous" (P-17, pp. 41–42). "The Way Out" won a close vote, until a member checked the Library of Congress and found "exactly twelve books already titled" that (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 42). Nobody wanted to be the thirteenth, so the book, and then the fellowship, became Alcoholics Anonymous (P-17, p. 42).

c0bb48136129.t: 1939: the first reasons (Foreword to the First Edition)

85f663b0245e.t: The foreword gives the reason directly: "It is important that we remain anonymous because we are too few, at present to handle the overwhelming number of personal appeals which may result from this publication" (p. xiii). Most members were business or professional people who couldn't keep up their occupations if that happened, and "our alcoholic work is an avocation" (p. xiii). So the foreword asks members writing or speaking publicly about alcoholism to call themselves "a member of Alcoholics Anonymous" instead of using their names, and asks the press to respect this (p. xiii).

583ee6e08399.t: When Bill quoted this foreword in 1946, he gave its wording as some members being unable to carry on their occupations "if known" (P-17, p. 42). The printed foreword ties the point to the flood of appeals. Both are about protecting members while A.A. was small.

2f466b6fe211.t: By 1946 every group was asking how anonymous members should be and what good it did (P-17, p. 42). Bill set out what most older members agreed on (P-17, pp. 44–45):

b212baf646b3.t: <0>It makes it safe to ask for help.</0> Alcoholics and their families, still afraid of the stigma, see anonymity as a promise that their problem will be kept confidential (P-17, p. 45).

8263b7364318.t: <0>It protects A.A. from its own leaders.</0> "The policy of anonymity is a protection to our cause" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 45). It stops founders or leaders from becoming household names who "might at any time get drunk and give A.A. a black eye" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 45).

f17fba90d934.t: <0>It makes friends of reporters.</0> A reporter who sees "a group of people who care nothing for personal gain" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 45) writes a friendly story.

3307bdddcb23.t: <0>The public trusts it.</0> People tired of promotion and loud public figures are drawn by A.A.'s quietness and modesty (P-17, p. 45).

d472995652dc.t: Then the spiritual point: "anonymity amounts to the renunciation of personal prestige as an instrument of general policy" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 46).

4365a0d44191.t: Tradition Eleven asks for personal anonymity in public relations, with no names or pictures as A.A. members in broadcast, film or print (p. 565). Tradition Twelve gives the reason under all the others: anonymity reminds members to place principles before personalities and "to practice a genuine humility," so that A.A.'s blessings never spoil it (p. 566).

b8c9c044b347.t: 1955: Bill's own story ("Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous," dated)

db93b471db14.t: Nine years later Bill explained anonymity by confessing. After a famous ballplayer's recovery made headlines, Bill went on the road giving interviews and pictures, and for two or three years he was "A.A.'s number one anonymity-breaker" (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955, p. 51). Members grumbled that Bill was "hogging the big time" and might get drunk on them (P-17, p. 51). Others followed his example, and broken anonymity began tying A.A. to Prohibition, the liquor trade, advertising, politics and a lawsuit (P-17, pp. 52–55). His conclusion: anonymity before the general public is A.A.'s main protection against its members' old drive for power, prestige and money, and "the greatest symbol of self-sacrifice that we know" (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955, p. 56).

bf3b8ed8662d.t: He ends with Dr. Bob, who declined a monument shortly before he died: "why don't you and I get buried like other folks?" (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955, p. 58). The Smiths' gravestone in Akron doesn't mention Alcoholics Anonymous (P-17, p. 58).

f6a341c2a9db.t: The 1955 piece quotes <0>Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions</0> (1953) twice (P-17, pp. 48–49). This page doesn't use those lines.

d1672e14b8ef.t: None of these reasons asks members to hide A.A. from the people around them. In 1946 Bill wrote that members had dropped anonymity with friends and associates on purpose, and in 1955 that disclosure to family, friends and neighbors is usually right (P-17, pp. 44, 56). See <0>Tradition Twelve: does anonymity mean keeping A.A. secret?</0>

d871464f4e09.t: Why was the Big Book written, and when? | Recovery Starts

e9e106e08dc8.t: The Big Book, Alcoholics Anonymous, was written in 1938 and early 1939 and published in April 1939, when the fellowship had about a hundred members.

fdfae69d3c56.t: Why was the Big Book written, and when?

24a62a5a6d1c.t: The Big Book, <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, was written in 1938 and early 1939 and published in April 1939, when the fellowship had about a hundred members.

c9e87896c945.t: Its own foreword gives the reason: to show other alcoholics exactly how the first members recovered.

10d0b68dcada.t: By late 1937 Bill W. and Dr. Bob could see that their method worked, but word of mouth was too slow to reach the millions who needed it, and the message would get garbled as it spread. A book could go where they couldn't.

753ca4159568.t: The fellowship took its name from the book.

e1021c30da24.t: What the book says about itself

c076885206ae.t: <0>Foreword to the First Edition (1939).</0> The first paragraph states the aim: "To show other alcoholics precisely how we have recovered is the main purpose of this book." (p. xiii). It also hopes to help everyone understand that the alcoholic is a very sick person (p. xiii), and it asks to hear from readers who get results, "particularly from those who have commenced work with other alcoholics" (p. xiv).

4f9debe7019c.t: <0>Chapter 11, "A Vision for You" (1939).</0> The last chapter pictures what the authors hoped the book would do: that "when this chip of a book is launched on the world tide of alcoholism" (p. 153), defeated drinkers would follow it, approach other sick drinkers, and start fellowships in every city (p. 153). It speaks directly to a reader who may never meet them: "We believe and hope it contains all you will need to begin." (p. 163). And it stays modest: "Our book is meant to be suggestive only." (Chapter 11, p. 164).

7cc07f854751.t: <0>Foreword to the Second Edition (1955).</0> Looking back, it says that by late 1937 enough members had lasting sobriety to convince them "a new light had entered the dark world of the alcoholic" (p. xvii). "It was now time, the struggling groups thought, to place their message and unique experience before the world." (p. xvii). The result was this volume, published in the spring of 1939, when membership "had then reached about 100 men and women" (p. xvii). "The fledgling society, which had been nameless, now began to be called Alcoholics Anonymous, from the title of its own book." (p. xvii).

e00300a71411.t: How the decision was made (later accounts)

51dc296f8d9e.t: <0>P-44, <1>A.A.'s Legacy of Service</1></0> (Bill W., describing events up to 1955; pamphlet © 2018). In 1937, at Dr. Bob's home in Akron, the two men added up two years' work and saw for the first time that recovery on a large scale was possible (P-44). The question was how a few recovered alcoholics could reach millions (P-44). They met with eighteen members of the Akron group; the majority wanted hospitals, paid workers and, above all, "a book for other alcoholics that could explain to them our methods and results" (P-44). The big money never came: John D. Rockefeller, Jr. gave $5,000 but declined to give more "for fear of professionalizing A.A." (P-44). Bill drafted the first two chapters in the late spring of 1938 for a fund-raising prospectus that failed, turned down a publisher's advance, and with a friend set up the fellowship's own book company, because: "It was evident that our Society ought to own and publish its own literature." (P-44). Akron, New York and Cleveland members wrote 28 stories, and the drafts were argued over for months; Bill says, "I became much more of an umpire than I ever was an author." (P-44). "The book finally appeared in April, 1939." (P-44).

9a1bca45c7c6.t: <0>A.A. Comes of Age (1957).</0> Bill tells the same November 1937 meeting in more detail. Word of mouth was slow, and it was also dangerous, because the message might be "garbled and twisted beyond recognition" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "A book of experience could carry our message to distant places we could never visit ourselves." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). It could also "prevent the otherwise inevitable garble and distortion that would start as soon as publicity came" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The Akron meeting approved the plan only by the barest majority, and a strong minority rejected paid missionaries and hospitals; Bill later said that minority was right about those (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The story section was finished in late January 1939 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

04e9786a62e2.t: The dates, as the sources give them

c1de4c8b5636.t: Bill and Dr. Bob count about forty sober and decide to spread the message

b8385cdb5e61.t: Bill drafts the first two chapters

90e593cd9843.t: P-53, Bill W.'s 1969 talk; Dr. Bob's 1948 talk ("It wasn't until 1938")

8d17dfe0a4d3.t: April 1939 ("spring of 1939" in the 1955 foreword, p. xvii)

071fd12991e3.t: The sources agree on these dates. The Big Book itself, in 1939, doesn't date its own writing; the details come from Bill's later accounts.

711548f19286.t: The reason the book gives for itself is practical: there were only about a hundred members, and they wanted to show other alcoholics precisely how they had recovered (p. xiii). Bill's later accounts add that they couldn't reach every drinker in person and wanted a text that would carry the message without being twisted (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). It was written so that "one man with this book in your hand" (p. 163) could begin the same work alone.

48c35cf4faa4.t: Why does the Big Book mention William James? | Recovery Starts

a9fefe93e2a9.t: William James was an American psychologist and philosopher whose book The Varieties of Religious Experience Bill W. read in Towns Hospital right after his…

b3224c452f88.t: Why does the Big Book mention William James?

784396347354.t: William James was an American psychologist and philosopher whose book <0>The Varieties of Religious Experience</0> Bill W. read in Towns Hospital right after his own spiritual experience in December 1934. It helped him understand what had happened to him.

c32765ab2c12.t: The 1939 Big Book cites James once, in Chapter 2, to make a point about tolerance: James shows "a multitude of ways in which men have discovered God," and the authors have no wish to convince anyone there is only one way (p. 28).

14855a9c3555.t: Appendix II, added after the first printing, cites James again: most members' spiritual experiences are what James called "the educational variety," which develop slowly (p. 567).

102b2baf5f77.t: In Bill's later accounts, James supplied the idea that a transforming experience usually comes out of calamity and "deflation at depth." Bill named James, with the Oxford Group and Dr. Silkworth, as a main source of the early program.

38b1d2a78ad5.t: <0>Chapter 2, "There Is a Solution" (1939).</0> Right after the story of the man treated by Dr. Jung, the chapter says: "The distinguished American psychologist, William James, in his book 'Varieties of Religious Experience,' indicates a multitude of ways in which men have discovered God." (p. 28). It draws the conclusion: "We have no desire to convince anyone that there is only one way by which faith can be acquired." (p. 28). It adds that people of any religion will find nothing disturbing to their beliefs, and that what religious body a member joins "should be an entirely personal affair" (p. 28).

77dedc591deb.t: <0>Appendix II, "Spiritual Experience" (added after the first printing).</0> The appendix says the first printing left many readers thinking a spiritual experience had to be sudden and spectacular (p. 567). Not so: "Most of our experiences are what the psychologist William James calls the 'educational variety' because they develop slowly over a period of time." (p. 567). See <1>What is the "spiritual awakening" in Step 12?</1>

100009b6e7ff.t: Those are the only two places the Big Book names him.

8fe57c33de64.t: <0>A.A. Comes of Age (1957).</0> The day after his experience at Towns, "It was Ebby, I think, who brought me a copy" of James's book (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill read it cover to cover. James held that such experiences could be real and transforming, some sudden and some gradual, but nearly all came out of pain and calamity: "Complete hopelessness and deflation at depth were almost always required to make the recipient ready." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "Deflation at depth—yes, that was it." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

34c960afbcb1.t: James's idea then shaped how A.A. carried its message. After six months of failure with drunks, Dr. Silkworth reminded Bill of James's observation that "truly transforming spiritual experiences are nearly always founded on calamity and collapse" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and told him to give prospects the hard medical facts first to deflate them (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). That is what Bill did with Dr. Bob; and of what reached Dr. Bob, Bill writes: "It was Dr. Silkworth's idea, confirmed by William James, that struck him at great depth." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill also names James, with the Oxford Groups and Dr. Silkworth, as the source of most of the basic ideas in the early word-of-mouth program (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). At the 1955 convention the Rev. Sam Shoemaker listed "William James' great wisdom" among A.A.'s strands (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

a435bf7231fc.t: <0>Pass It On (1984)</0> says Ebby brought the book when he came "on the third day" (Pass It On, 1984), though "Ebby had not read the book" (Pass It On, 1984); it had been recommended by Oxford Group members (Pass It On, 1984). It names three common denominators Bill drew from James's cases: calamity, admission of defeat, and an appeal to a Higher Power (Pass It On, 1984), and says the first three Steps were drawn from James, Shoemaker and the Oxford Group (Pass It On, 1984). It reports that Bill would later say James, "though long in his grave," "had been a founder of Alcoholics Anonymous" (Pass It On, 1984).

ecd0684fbe17.t: <0>Who brought the book.</0> Bill in 1957 wasn't sure ("It was Ebby, I think") (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) says it was Ebby (Pass It On, 1984).

c5ff66ed14d3.t: <0>When.</0> Bill (1957) says the book came "the next day" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957) after his experience, which itself came after three or four days in the hospital; <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) has Ebby bringing it when he came "on the third day" (Pass It On, 1984). Our sources don't settle the day.

7141318d4d98.t: <0>What James is cited for.</0> The 1939 chapter uses James for the variety of ways to God (p. 28); the later appendix uses him for the slow, "educational" kind of experience (p. 567); Bill's later accounts use him for deflation at depth (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). These are different parts of James, not contradictions.

51e16cedc5c3.t: <0>"Founder."</0> The saying that James was a founder of A.A. is reported by <1>Pass It On</1> without a date or source for Bill's words (Pass It On, 1984). Our sources don't give Bill's own wording.

8d57b32fc9b1.t: Was the Big Book written only for men? Is A.A. for women? | Recovery Starts

ad5b700cb47d.t: The 1939 text mostly speaks of men, and it says so itself: "our book thus far has spoken of men" (p. 104), with few exceptions. In the next breath it says…

4bf4e7ed0b91.t: Was the Big Book written only for men? Is A.A. for women?

dc40f571d321.t: The 1939 text mostly speaks of men, and it says so itself: "our book thus far has spoken of men" (p. 104), with few exceptions. In the next breath it says that what it has said "applies quite as much to women" (p. 104).

734643c48136.t: From its first page the book describes the fellowship as men and women. The 1939 Foreword opens by describing the members as "more than one hundred men and women who have recovered" (p. xiii).

7f17d0908d81.t: A.A.'s membership statement covers everyone: the Long Form says membership "ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism" (p. 563).

e60e238518f7.t: The early years were harder for women than the texts' wording suggests. A later history (1980) records that Dr. Bob and other early members were at first wary of women alcoholics, and that the first woman one old-timer remembered was turned away by the wives.

07cfce0adcfb.t: <0>Men and women from the start.</0> The Foreword's "more than one hundred men and women" (p. xiii). Chapter 2 opens with the "thousands of men and women who were once just as hopeless as Bill" (p. 17) that the members know.

34330bc7ecca.t: <0>Written mostly about men.</0> The program chapters use "he" and "man" throughout. Chapter 8 begins by naming that: with few exceptions, "our book thus far has spoken of men" (p. 104). It goes on: "Our activities in behalf of women who drink are on the increase." and "There is every evidence that women regain their health as readily as men if they try our suggestions." (p. 104).

0a75da62984b.t: <0>Women and the speed of the illness.</0> Chapter 3 says one doesn't have to drink long to be gravely affected, and "This is particularly true of women." (p. 33). "Potential female alcoholics often turn into the real thing and are gone beyond recall in a few years." (p. 33).

3e8e5e85f08e.t: <0>"To Wives."</0> Chapter 8 is written in the voice of members' wives, to the wives of drinking men (p. 104). Later histories say Bill W. wrote it himself; Lois said, "Bill wrote it, and I was mad." (<1>Pass It On</1>, 1984; also <2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2>, 1980). A later-edition footnote explains: "Written in 1939, when there were few women in A.A., this chapter assumes that the alcoholic in the home is likely to be the husband." (p. 104). It adds that the suggestions can be adapted for someone living with a woman alcoholic.

4b87a1ec1bb0.t: <0>The Foreword to the Fourth Edition (2001)</0> says that when the phrase "We are people who normally would not mix" (p. 17) was written in 1939, it described a fellowship "composed largely of men (and a few women)" with similar backgrounds (p. xxiii).

b3da7857d1b5.t: Tradition Three: "Our membership ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism." (p. 563). A.A. "may refuse none who wish to recover" (p. 563). Nothing in it limits membership by sex.

8f5dc89ebf6e.t: The numbers, as the later forewords report them

f95413532183.t: 1955: "More than 15% of us are women." (p. xx).

00bfcbeb0095.t: 1976: "Women now make up more than one-fourth of the membership; among newer members, the proportion is nearly one-third." (p. xxii).

90bc05678166.t: 2001: the stories added to the fourth edition represent a membership that has widened in "age, gender, race, and culture" (p. xxiii).

e0e20503c8aa.t: <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957): in 1939 "a woman alcoholic known to so many of us as Marty" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957) read the manuscript of the book at Blythewood Sanitarium, came to a meeting in Bill and Lois's living room at 182 Clinton Street, and carried the message back to a fellow patient. Her story, "Women Suffer Too," is in Part I of the fourth edition: "An early member, she spread the word among women in our pioneering period." (p. 200). She writes that she had been active in A.A. "since 1939" (p. 207).

dc12ea9ff78b.t: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) is frank about the early years in Ohio. Women alcoholics were "the most unwelcome minority in A.A.'s olden days" (<1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1>, 1980). Dr. Bob was unsure how to help them and usually passed them to Anne Smith and other wives; the first woman one old-timer remembered was not allowed in the wives' homes; women "had to overcome a double standard" about drinking. The same book records that Anne and other wives kept working with them, and that attitudes changed.

4b7007c69761.t: <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16) says some A.A.s form specialized groups "for men, women, young people, doctors, LGBTQ+ and others," and that they may call themselves A.A. groups if their members are all alcoholics and "they open the door to all alcoholics who seek help" (P-16, 2018).

8cc89196d94a.t: The Big Book was written mostly in the language of men by a fellowship that was mostly men, and it says so. It was never written as a book for men only: its first page and its own correction on page 104 say it applies to women as well, and Tradition Three's membership statement includes all alcoholics.

7c036d03c8af.t: Is "Working With Others" about sponsorship? | Recovery Starts

5516d86c794e.t: No. Chapter 7 of the Big Book, "Working With Others," is about finding an alcoholic who is still drinking and helping him recover.

175a6905fcef.t: No. Chapter 7 of the Big Book, "Working With Others," is about finding an alcoholic who is still drinking and helping him recover.

ed518d494cba.t: The word "sponsor" doesn't appear in it, or anywhere in the Big Book's program.

3cb9cecf0328.t: The person you help may not be in A.A. at all, owes you nothing, and can turn to someone else whenever he likes.

2d8bfba44ca5.t: The chapter's subject is "other alcoholics" who need the message, and it begins with how to find them: through doctors, ministers, priests and hospitals (p. 89). It calls the man you're helping a "prospect," a "candidate," "your man" (pp. 90–94). He's someone who is still drinking, or has just stopped, and the chapter assumes he doesn't know you: he is to be told about you "as a person who has recovered" (p. 90). The chapter tells you to wait for the end of a binge before you see him (p. 90).

3f4777b275f0.t: That isn't a member of a group asking an old-timer to guide him. It's a stranger, reached from the outside.

43313f43c7f5.t: Everything the chapter says about the relationship keeps it loose and free: - "Make it plain he is under no obligation to you" (p. 94). - He "needn't see you again if he doesn't want to" (p. 94). - When he's ready to make his decision and tell his story, he can do it with you, "but do not insist upon it if he prefers to consult someone else" (p. 96). - If he isn't interested, move on and find another alcoholic (p. 96).

5c95db9b3272.t: There's nothing here about taking someone through the Steps on a schedule, calling you every day, or answering to you. The chapter's instructions run the other way: don't rush him, don't push him, let him steer (p. 95).

9d144f8f251c.t: The helper's job is to carry the message: tell his own drinking story, describe the illness, explain how he recovered when he's asked, and offer friendship (pp. 91–95). After that, the man is free.

9046d7779e17.t: The chapter is honest that this work protects the helper's own sobriety (p. 89). But it puts the other man first. It asks the newcomer to "place the welfare of other people ahead of his own" (p. 94), lists what the work costs the helper (p. 97), and says "Think of what you can bring to it" (p. 102).

1f5f6278e69d.t: When "Working With Others" is taught as a chapter about sponsorship, it shrinks. A chapter about going out to rescue drinking alcoholics, the work that turned two sober men into a fellowship, becomes a chapter about relationships inside the rooms. The people it was written for, the ones still drinking, drop out of it.

9fe4ba034bae.t: Related: <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0> · <1>Is the word "sponsor" in the Big Book?</1>

ea02905a72e9.t: Is "it works if you work it" in the Big Book? | Recovery Starts

eee02a3e1706.t: The saying itself is not in the 1939 program text or anywhere else in our sources in that form. The nearest wording anywhere in the Big Book is in a…

96a540ecf264.t: Is "it works if you work it" in the Big Book?

c66c47f2075f.t: The saying itself is not in the 1939 program text or anywhere else in our sources in that form. The nearest wording anywhere in the Big Book is in a fourth-edition personal story, about praying for a person you resent: "it will work for me every time I am willing to work it" (p. 552).

24726c534fd2.t: The program text's nearest wording is about prayer: "It works, if we have the proper attitude and work at it" (p. 86). Two pages later, at the end of the same daily practice: "It works—it really does" (p. 88).

c8b2c0032a81.t: Elsewhere the text makes promises in the same spirit, each about something specific: the promises of Chapter 6 "will always materialize if we work for them" (p. 84), and work with other alcoholics "works when other activities fail" (p. 89).

9293e2bc2d80.t: The many other "How It Works" lines in Chapter 5 are just the chapter's title printed at the top of its pages.

5140fcafe694.t: All our sources were searched for "works if you work," "if you work it," "work it," "it works," "work at it" and "really works."

ea0ae602a41b.t: The exact saying doesn't turn up. In Chapter 5 "HOW IT WORKS" is the running head printed at the top of every other page, not a sentence.

5097f580043a.t: The places in the program text where something is said to work: - Bill, about working with other alcoholics when he was low: "It is a design for living that works in rough going" (p. 15). - Chapter 2: a new life has been given us or, if you prefer, "a design for living" that "really works" (p. 28). - Chapter 6, the promises: "They will always materialize if we work for them" (p. 84). - Chapter 6, Step Eleven: prayer "works, if we have the proper attitude and work at it" (p. 86). - Chapter 6, the end of Step Eleven: "It works—it really does" (p. 88). - Chapter 7, the opening: intensive work with other alcoholics "works when other activities fail" (p. 89).

fb1deccaf9f0.t: In the personal stories, one fourth-edition writer ends: "I keep coming back because it works" (p. 374). Another, in "Freedom From Bondage" (Part III), comes closest to the saying. She describes being freed of a resentment by praying every day for the person she resented, as a clergyman's article advised, and says: "It worked for me then, and it has worked for me many times since, and it will work for me every time I am willing to work it." (p. 552). Like the program text's own nearest line (p. 86), it is about a particular practice of prayer, and it is one member's words in a later edition, not program text. <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) says some members thought Works Publishing, the company formed to publish the book, was named after a favorite slogan of the membership, "It works!" (<1>Pass It On</1>, 1984). Others said it came from "Faith without works is dead."

3304bcc4f548.t: The nearest line, read in context

43eb1e5f75de.t: The line on p. 86 comes at the start of the book's directions for Step Eleven. "We shouldn't be shy on this matter of prayer. Better men than we are using it constantly. It works, if we have the proper attitude and work at it" (pp. 85–86). The "it" is prayer. The book follows with exactly what the work is (pp. 86–88): - At night, review the day: were we resentful, selfish, dishonest or afraid? Do we owe an apology? Were we thinking of ourselves most of the time, "Or were we thinking of what we could do for others" (p. 86)? Then ask God's forgiveness and what should be put right. - On waking, think about the day ahead and ask God to direct our thinking, especially that it be free of self-pity and dishonest or self-seeking motives (p. 86). - When unsure what to do, ask for inspiration, relax, and "don't struggle" (p. 86). - End the morning's meditation asking to be shown the next step through the day, and be careful "never to pray for our own selfish ends" (p. 87). - During the day, when agitated or doubtful, pause and ask for the right thought or action, saying many times each day "Thy will be done" (pp. 87–88).

c11fbb3bb8f8.t: Then: "It works—it really does" (p. 88). The next lines say this isn't all: "There is action and more action" (p. 88), and the next chapter is about carrying the message.

5de4aa3dd627.t: So the closest the book comes to the saying is a promise about one daily practice, prayer and self-review, with the conditions spelled out: "the proper attitude" and working at it.

ac44aac4c097.t: The idea that results depend on doing the work runs all through the text. The promises "will always materialize if we work for them" (p. 84). The chapter on the Steps opens by saying the writers have rarely "seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path" (p. 58), and "Half measures availed us nothing" (p. 59).

9a4860985d68.t: What the short slogan leaves out is what the text names as the source of the result. Chapter 6 says the new attitude toward liquor "has been given us without any thought or effort on our part" (p. 85), and that it lasts "so long as we keep in fit spiritual condition" (p. 85). Chapter 5 says faith "did for us what we could not do for ourselves" (pp. 70–71). In the book, the member does the work, and the work is what keeps him in the condition where the change is given.

3042c808a188.t: See also: <0>What do Steps 10 and 11 ask, day to day?</0> and <1>Where are "the Promises," and what do they promise?</1>

714e410c790a.t: How was the Big Book paid for and published (Works Publishing)? | Recovery Starts

6c137abe9a86.t: In 1938 the publisher Harper offered Bill W. an advance for the book. He and his partner Hank P. decided the fellowship should own its own book, and…

3417efd60a23.t: How was the Big Book paid for and published (Works Publishing)?

b922fc912849.t: In 1938 the publisher Harper offered Bill W. an advance for the book. He and his partner Hank P. decided the fellowship should own its own book, and instead formed their own company, Works Publishing, selling $25 shares to members and friends.

b9ba80d96af7.t: They sold 200 shares for $5,000, mostly in monthly installments, after a Reader's Digest editor seemed to promise an article. A loan from Charles B. Towns, owner of the hospital where Bill got sober, helped too. Cornwall Press printed 5,000 copies for a $500 down payment, and the book came out in April 1939 at $3.50.

b340eb874e16.t: The Digest article never came, and for months the book didn't sell. Publicity in 1939 and 1940 finally moved it.

58f5dcd63834.t: In 1940 the Alcoholic Foundation bought out the cash shareholders with money lent by Rockefeller and his friends, and Bill and Hank gave up their shares, so the Big Book came to belong to A.A. as a whole.

2b2c91303880.t: The 1939 text doesn't tell how it was financed. The copyright page of today's edition lists the first edition as running from 1939 to 1955, and the copyright is now held by A.A. World Services, Inc. (p. iv). The 1955 foreword says only that the members' determination "bore fruit in the spring of 1939 by the publication of this volume" (p. xvii). See <0>Why was the Big Book written, and when?</0>

fa2ed05fe98c.t: The decision to self-publish (1957, and P-44)

d60f85133141.t: In the fall of 1938, through trustee Frank Amos, Bill showed two chapters to Eugene Exman, religious editor at Harper, who offered a $1,500 advance on royalties (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill had second thoughts: if the book became the fellowship's main text, "Our principal written asset would then be owned by an outside publisher" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The trustees favored Harper, but Hank P. pressed for a stock company of their own (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Exman himself agreed that a society like theirs should publish its own literature (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). P-44 (Bill, describing events through 1955) puts the reason plainly: "No publisher, however good, ought to own our best asset." (P-44).

403efde29c4f.t: Hank's prospectus offered 600 shares at $25: a third for cash to New York members and friends, two-thirds to Hank and Bill for their work, with the author's royalty assigned to the Foundation to soothe the trustees (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He named the company "Since the forthcoming volume would be only the first of many such 'works,'" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and bought blank stock certificates at a stationery store (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

c08a63c6d858.t: At first nobody bought: "What made you think that we would buy stock in a book not yet written?" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Then the managing editor of the Reader's Digest said he was almost sure the magazine would run a story when the book was ready (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). With that, "Soon we had a subscription of 200 shares which amounted to $5,000" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), paid in installments of five dollars a month (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Charles B. Towns lent $2,500 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), a sum Bill elsewhere says later grew to over $4,000 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The money went for office costs and groceries for Bill, Lois, Hank and the secretary, Ruth Hock, until publication (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

29b7ae92d4a6.t: Edward Blackwell of Cornwall Press suggested a first printing of 5,000 and accepted $500 down (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). They set the price at $3.50 after heated argument, and to give buyers their money's worth used the thickest paper in the shop: "The original volume proved to be so bulky that it became known as the 'Big Book.'" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

aa05009e96bb.t: When Bill and Hank went back to the Reader's Digest, the editor had forgotten them; his staff had turned the idea down (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "The book enterprise had collapsed." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Twenty-eight copies were owed to the story writers and forty-nine to subscribers (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Blackwell stood by them (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). A radio appearance and 20,000 postcards to doctors brought two orders (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). An A.A. tailor, Bert T., borrowed $1,000 against his own business to keep the company going (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Sales began with a Liberty magazine article in September 1939 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and grew after Rockefeller's dinner in 1940 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <0>Why did early A.A. turn down Rockefeller money?</0>

8093e8100431.t: How A.A. came to own it

9969317b1a83.t: By 1940 some cash subscribers wanted their money back (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Trustee A. LeRoy Chipman borrowed $8,000 from Rockefeller, two of his sons and dinner guests to buy their shares at par, to be repaid from book profits (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill turned his 200 shares over to the Foundation; Hank, then drinking, agreed only when the Foundation paid him $200 for office furniture he owned (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "And that is how the society of Alcoholics Anonymous, through its Trustees, came to own the Big Book." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). P-44 adds that two years later the book had done so well that the loan was paid off (P-44).

2ee9a22d6c09.t: <0>Hank's shares.</0> P-44 says "Hank P. and I donated our shares in it to the Alcoholic Foundation" (P-44). Bill's 1957 book and <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) say Hank resisted and gave his up for a $200 payment for furniture (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; Pass It On, 1984).

ea82004b1e2b.t: <0>The company's name.</0> Bill (1957) says Hank chose "Works" because the book would be the first of many works (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1> calls it "a matter of some dispute": some said it came from Anne Smith's favorite verse, "Faith without works is dead"; "others said it was named for a favorite slogan of the membership" (Pass It On, 1984), "It works!"

10b7575d4ea0.t: <0>The Towns loan.</0> $2,500 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957; P-44), or "later increased to over $4,000" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).

7875bab723d2.t: <0>Who was responsible.</0> <1>Pass It On</1> reports Hank's son's view that Hank got the project rolling, and Ruth Hock's that the two were about equally responsible: without Bill it wouldn't have been written, and "it wouldn't have been published without Hank" (Pass It On, 1984).
